title: The Scripture of the Human Dao

chapters.title: The Third Bell
chapters.text:
The ore bell rang twice, and nobody stopped working.

Two strokes meant a delay at the upper platform. Three meant an accident. Su Fan knew the difference because Ren Bo deducted half a copper whenever somebody put down a tool for the wrong number.

He kept the hot pin on the anvil.

Master Duan had gone to argue about charcoal. That left Su Fan with an order for twenty hauling pins, a cracked hammer, and an apprentice who was supposed to turn the bellows.

Ah-Du had stopped turning.

“Two,” Su Fan said.

“I heard something else.”

“So did I. Turn.”

The boy bent over the handle. Air breathed through the coals. Su Fan turned the pin a quarter circle and struck the shoulder, watching the pale edge where the heat was going out of it. One more blow, then back into the fire. Duan could tell when a piece had been worked too cold. He could tell without looking up from whatever else he was doing, which Su Fan considered an unreasonable quality in an employer.

Above the smithy, beyond the sorting sheds, somebody shouted.

The sound ended too sharply.

Su Fan set the hammer down.

“That will be half a copper,” Ah-Du warned.

“Put it on my account.”

He took the iron hook from beside the furnace and went uphill.

Behind him Ah-Du started to follow.

“Bank it,” Su Fan said. “Then stay here.”

The boy hesitated between the doorway and the fire. Su Fan left before he saw which instruction won.

The quarry road ran behind the sheds. At the bend a loaded stone cradle hung above it on four chains. Usually it waited there while carts passed underneath; then the brake operator lowered it to the sorting floor. Today one chain was slack. The cradle tilted toward the road, and grit sifted through its boards in a continuous pale curtain.

Bao Shun was pinned against the brake wheel.

He had both arms through its spokes. Blood shone on the wood below his elbow. A dozen workers stood at the rope station, leaning backward together. Their shoes slid in the loose grit. One had lost a sandal and was trying to recover it without releasing the line.

Ren Bo had a knife out. He was cutting at the bell rope where it had tangled in the broken gear.

There had been a third stroke.

The bell had simply failed to make it.

“Clear the road,” Su Fan said.

Ren Bo did not turn. His knife slipped. He swore and caught the rope again.

“The road below us.”

This time the tallyman looked. Six carts waited by the sheds. Teamsters, animals, men eating lunch under their loads. A woman had laid two shirts on the warm stones beside the track. Nobody down there could see Bao Shun from where they sat.

“Clear it!” Ren Bo shouted.

A teamster raised his head.

“The cradle! Get off the road!”

The woman left the shirts. The men moved more slowly, looking up first, then looking for the owners of the animals. Su Fan saw a boy reach for the nose rope of a cart mule that had already begun to pull away.

“Let the cart go!”

He could not tell whether the boy heard him. Then one of the teamsters grabbed the boy by the back of his tunic and dragged him toward the shed wall.

Su Fan went to the wheel.

Bao Shun shook his head before Su Fan touched him.

“The moment I move.”

“I see it.”

He did. A broken locking pin lay beside Bao Shun’s boot. Without it the ratchet dog had tipped out of its seat, leaving the cradle’s weight on the brake. Bao Shun must have caught the wheel as it ran backward. The spokes now trapped his arms against the housing.

A strong man could have held it for a breath or two.

Bao Shun had already held it longer.

Su Fan pushed the hook through an empty spoke and braced its butt against the stone wall. It was a long hook, made for moving heavy iron without putting a hand into the furnace. He had used it that morning to drag a bent axle out of the coals.

The iron bent.

He had expected that. He had not expected it to bend so quickly.

“Leave it,” Bao Shun gasped. “You can’t.”

Su Fan shifted his hands away from the crushing point. The hook bowed another finger’s width. He tried to set its lower end deeper against the wall, but the floor there was dust over smooth stone. No purchase. No room for a timber brace without first taking pressure off the wheel.

“Don’t move your arm yet.”

Bao Shun made a sound through his teeth.

Su Fan wished he had said something else.

A stone slipped from the cradle and struck the road. It bounced past Ren Bo’s leg, hit the edge of a shed and went through. The rope crew flinched together. Their line jumped in their hands.

“Keep it even!” one of them shouted.

Su Fan looked along the line. It ran around a grounded capstan before reaching the brake shaft: old timber, six iron hoops, a groove worn smooth by years of passing rope. The crew could not raise the cradle from where they stood. Their job was to check the speed when the brake was released.

Released properly, with a man choosing how much weight to let through.

“Ren Bo. Second line. Around the capstan twice.”

“That line won’t hold the cradle.”

“It won’t have to. Just this wheel.”

Ren Bo looked at the spare rope coiled beneath the shelter. Then at the cradle. Su Fan could almost see him trying to decide which loss he would be held responsible for.

“Cut it yourself afterward,” Su Fan said. “You won’t lose the rope.”

He did not know that. He needed Ren Bo to move.

The tallyman called two men over. One crawled beneath the tightening haul line to reach the spare coil. The other began pulling it free, shaking out loops that caught on the legs of the shelter.

Bao Shun’s breathing had become a thin, wet whistle. Su Fan kept pressure on the hook. There was no room to bind the arm without loosening his grip, and the iron was still bending.

“Look at me,” he told Bao Shun.

The operator’s eyes shifted toward him.

“We’re putting another line on.”

“I heard.”

“Good.”

“Stop saying things.”

Su Fan stopped.

Below them the last mule stumbled clear. The cart behind it overturned, leaving a wheel turning in the air. Somebody was shouting about the sacks beneath it. Su Fan could not spare a hand to wave them back.

Then a young man in a grey work sash came running from the weighing house.

Tan Wei stopped beside Su Fan, took in the wheel and the bent iron, and reached inside his shirt.

“No,” Su Fan said.

Tan Wei pulled out a yellow charm.

It had cost him eighteen copper. Su Fan knew because he had spent an evening telling him not to buy it. They had sat outside the smithy while Tan Wei turned the square of paper over in his fingers and tried to explain what it meant to own even one use of a cultivator’s power.

Su Fan had suggested boots.

“Move your hand,” Tan Wei said.

“You have one use.”

“I can count.”

He pressed the charm against a spoke. It did nothing.

For a sick instant Su Fan thought of the stall where Tan Wei had bought it, of the seller’s bright teeth, of eighteen copper paid for a scrap of coloured paper.

Tan Wei scraped his thumb across the inked corner, tearing it open.

Blue cords leaped from the paper.

They wound themselves through the spokes and snapped tight against the housing. The wheel shuddered. Su Fan felt the load leave the hook. Bao Shun screamed as the pressure lifted from his arm.

“Now!”

Tan Wei caught the operator under one shoulder. Su Fan pulled the trapped wrist toward the wide part of the spoke. It would not come. Bao Shun’s sleeve had wound around a splinter.

Su Fan tore the sleeve.

They dragged him free.

For one breath the brake held without human hands. Blue light lay across the wheel, bright enough to show every grain of dust floating between the spokes.

Then the paper browned at its edges.

“Rope!” Tan Wei shouted.

Ren Bo’s men threw the second line around the shaft. The loose end struck Su Fan across the face. He caught it, wrapped it against the turning direction and hauled. The first loop slipped. The second gripped.

“Down behind the wall.”

Tan Wei was already moving Bao Shun toward the stone buttress. The injured man’s boots dragged furrows through the grit. Su Fan held the rope long enough for them to clear the wheel, then dropped with them.

The charm burned through.

The wheel kicked backward and broke his hook in two.

The cradle dropped.

The rope around the capstan smoked, slowed the fall, then parted with a crack like a door slammed beside his head. Stone burst across the cleared road. One rock punched through the smithy roof. Another rolled down to the carts and stopped against an overturned trough.

The buttress shook beneath Su Fan’s back.

He put his sleeve over Bao Shun’s mouth and bent his head. Dust filled everything. It settled on his tongue, inside his collar, between his teeth. Something struck the other side of the wall hard enough to knock a chip onto his shoulder.

For a moment he could hear nothing except the ringing in his ears.

Then Tan Wei began coughing.

Then somebody below shouted that the road was clear.

Nobody shouted a name.

Su Fan lifted his head.

The cradle lay broken across the track, its chains hanging uselessly above it. The shirts the woman had left were buried. Through the dust he could see the smithy’s roof beam pointing up at an angle it had never possessed before.

Ah-Du stood outside the door, both hands on his head.

Alive. Standing. Far enough away.

Su Fan sat back against the stone.

Tan Wei crouched on Bao Shun’s other side, coughing and laughing at once.

“Eighteen copper,” he said.

A blackened patch of paper clung to his palm. Under it, a faint blue trace flickered and faded.

“Worth it,” Su Fan said.

“Say that again. More clearly.”

Bao Shun made a noise that might have been a laugh.

Then he fainted.

***

They carried him to Mudgate on a shed door.

Getting the door took longer than finding men willing to carry it. The first one opened inward against a fallen shelf. The second was so badly split that Su Fan refused it. Ah-Du brought a hammer and knocked the hinges off the third while two teamsters held it steady.

He had banked the furnace before coming out. He told Su Fan twice, very quickly, as though the hole in the roof might otherwise be considered his fault.

“Good,” Su Fan said. “Find something clean.”

“How clean?”

“Cleaner than us.”

The boy ran.

Ren Bo bound Bao Shun’s arm with a strip torn from the only unsoiled corner of a teamster’s undershirt. He tied the knot one-handed. His other hand had been cut by his own knife, and he kept hiding it against his trousers whenever anyone looked.

The foreman arrived before they left.

He listened to Ren Bo, inspected the broken wheel and walked down to look at the damage. There was a stone inside the smithy. There were spilled loads, a crushed trough, damaged chains, a snapped rope. He called for a clerk.

“Write them separately. Machinery and stores.”

Bao Shun opened his eyes and closed them again.

Su Fan crouched beside the brake housing. The broken pin lay where he had first seen it. Its head was intact. The centre of the fracture looked wrong: too dark, too loose, nothing like the close-grained iron Duan insisted on for a piece that held men’s lives above a road.

He wrapped it in a cloth and put it in his pocket. On the edge of the torn loss sheet, he copied the number stamped beneath the maker’s mark.

“Put the hook on the smithy’s losses,” the foreman told him.

“The pin,” Su Fan said.

“What about it?”

“It was the wrong iron.”

The foreman looked toward the broken gear.

“You’re an apprentice.”

“Yes.”

“Then let a smith decide.”

Su Fan looked at the clerk. The clerk’s brush hovered above the paper. He had written the hook down. He had not written anything about the pin.

There was an answer Su Fan wanted to give. He could hear its words clearly. Bao Shun’s blood began dripping from the lower edge of the door, and the answer ceased to matter for the moment.

“Lift,” he said.

Tan Wei took the front handles. Su Fan took the back. Two others came alongside to steady the door on the first steep turn.

They passed beneath the carved reed over the quarry gate. Above it hung the founder’s tablet that protected the works. Fresh incense smoked from its bronze cup. A disciple emerged from the guardhouse and asked where they were taking the injured man.

“To Mother Wei,” Tan Wei said.

“The work healer should record—”

“Then tell him to come there.”

The disciple looked at the blood on the door. He stepped aside.

Below the gate the road narrowed between the old spoil heaps. Su Fan walked backward down the worst part so the door would remain level. His fingers were already beginning to stiffen. Each time Tan Wei changed his grip, he announced it before moving.

“Left hand.”

“Ready.”

“Changing.”

They had carried enough awkward things together to know how to do this. Sacks, broken wheels, a drunken uncle on a festival night. Su Fan tried to remember the joke Tan Wei had told then, something about charging transport by weight. He could not retrieve it.

Bao Shun opened his eyes.

“My girl,” he whispered.

“We’ll send for her.”

“Don’t say the arm.”

Su Fan adjusted his grip.

“What do I say?”

“Say I’m late.”

Tan Wei looked back at him. Neither spoke.

At the first houses a woman saw them and ran ahead. Doors opened. A man moved a drying rack out of the lane. Someone asked whether the cradle had killed anyone. Somebody else answered before Su Fan could.

Mother Wei was waiting at the clinic door.

She had cleared the nearest pallet. A kettle stood beside it, and a stack of folded cloth lay on a stool.

“How long?” she asked.

Su Fan told her.

“Conscious all the way?”

“Most of it.”

She looked at Bao Shun, then at his arm.

“Put him here. You, wash. You, find his daughter. Nobody crowd the door.”

People obeyed. She did not raise her voice.

Su Fan tried to straighten his hands after they lowered the door. His fingers refused. Mother Wei saw him pressing them against his thigh and put a bowl of warm water on the stool beside him.

“Slowly.”

“I can help.”

“You will. When you can hold what I give you.”

Tan Wei returned with Bao Mei before Su Fan’s hands had stopped shaking. She was barefoot, with paint on her chin and a school scrap clenched in one fist. She went straight toward the pallet until Mother Wei intercepted her, knelt briefly and spoke where the others could not hear.

The girl nodded. She sat outside the curtain.

Tan Wei sat beside her.

Su Fan stood by the washing bowl, unable to remember whether he had eaten that morning. From behind the curtain came Mother Wei’s instructions, Bao Shun’s uneven replies, the little clink of an instrument touching a dish.

He reached into his pocket.

The cloth around the pin was damp. He spread it on the table beneath the window and rolled the broken metal into the light.

Inside the fracture, beneath the dark shell of good iron, was a core of dull, crumbling slag.

Stamped into its head was the Hollow Reed Sect’s inspection mark.

chapters.title: The Price of a Hand
chapters.text:
Mother Wei made Tan Wei hold the basin.

He held it for three breaths before looking away.

“Look where you put your feet, then,” she said. “Faint on my patient and I’ll sew you to him.”

“I wasn’t going to faint.”

“Excellent. Then this will be a long afternoon for both of us.”

Su Fan stood beside the lamp. His job was to move it when she asked and stay out of the way when she didn’t. The window gave good light until someone crossed the lane outside. Then a shadow swept over the pallet, and Mother Wei had to wait for the hand to become visible again.

After the third interruption she sent a neighbour to hang a cloth across the outer gate. People stopped coming to stare. The room grew quieter, though the noise from the square still reached them: cart wheels, the vegetable seller, a little bell somebody kept ringing at hopeful intervals.

Bao Shun tried to turn his head.

“Mei?”

“Outside,” Mother Wei said. “Tan, move that basin closer. No, towards me.”

“Can she—”

“Not while I work. You can talk to her through the curtain.”

The operator swallowed.

“Girl.”

“I’m here.”

“You left your things at school?”

“No.”

Su Fan could see her feet beneath the hanging cloth. Bare toes pressed together, pale except where dust had settled into the creases. One heel kept lifting and lowering against the floorboards.

“The brush?” Bao Shun asked.

“I put it away.”

“The lid on the paint?”

“I put it on.”

He nodded as though this settled something important. Mother Wei waited until his head lay still again before continuing.

Bao Mei was thirteen, with her father’s wide hands and a paint stain on her chin. She had arrived carrying a scrap from school. Now she held it flat on her knees and looked at it without reading. Every time her father made a sound, her bare toes curled against the boards.

“Lamp.”

Su Fan moved it.

“Other side.”

He moved it again. His wrist protested. He kept his face still, not because he thought this would fool Mother Wei, but because she had enough to do without him adding himself to the list.

The cloth on the tray was no longer white. He looked past it at the shelf where she kept the medicine jars. Several labels were in his handwriting. He recognized the cramped final character on one, made while the ink was drying on the brush. He had meant to replace that label. Months had passed.

“Su Fan.”

He looked down.

“Here with me.”

“Yes.”

The work took longer than he expected. He had imagined there would be a single moment when the danger passed, some decisive task after which everyone could breathe. Instead Mother Wei kept finding things that required another cloth, another position of the lamp, another answer from the injured man.

Could he feel her touch there? And there? Did the pain go into the fingers or stay above the wrist?

Bao Shun answered some questions at once. Others he had to think about. Once he said yes and then admitted he did not know.

“Don’t help me by guessing,” she told him.

He closed his eyes. “I want the good answer.”

“So do I.”

She changed what she was doing and asked him again.

At last she covered the injury. Tan Wei set the basin down with such care that Su Fan realized his arms were shaking.

Mother Wei saved Bao Shun’s hand.

She would not say whether he would ever close it properly again.

“What can he do with it?” Tan Wei asked.

“Today? Keep it where I put it.”

“And after?”

“Come back after.”

She checked the binding once more and pulled the blanket over Bao Shun’s legs. Only then did she lift the curtain.

Bao Mei stood immediately.

“You may sit beside him,” Mother Wei said. “On that side. Don’t lean on the frame.”

The girl climbed onto the pallet with the care of someone approaching a sleeping animal. She took her father’s uninjured hand between both of hers.

“Found your shoes yet?” he murmured.

Her face crumpled.

“No.”

“Well,” he said. “You’ll have to.”

She bent her head over their hands. Mother Wei let the curtain fall.

***

Tan Wei went to heat more water. Su Fan went to find food.

The square had carried on while the clinic room stood still. A man was repairing the handle of a handcart. Two children argued over a hoop. Near the well, under a striped awning, a Hollow Reed clerk had arranged papers in four neat stacks.

The little bell belonged to him.

Su Fan passed without stopping. At the bakery the afternoon trays were almost empty. He bought the last two plain buns and stood aside while a woman argued that yesterday’s cakes should not cost today’s prices.

He had been hungry on the way there. Now the hot cloth in his hands made his stomach feel uncertain.

A porter from the quarry caught him at the corner.

“How is he?”

“Alive.”

“The hand?”

“Still there.”

The porter nodded too quickly. “Good. That’s good.”

He had brought Bao Shun’s work jacket, folded around the little lunch pot they had found by the brake station. Its lid was dented. Something inside had leaked onto the lining.

“Tell him I put his tools in the shed.”

“Tell him yourself.”

The porter glanced toward the clinic.

“I have to get back.”

Su Fan nearly told him that they all had work to get back to. Then he saw the dust on the man’s lips, the cut across the knuckles of his left hand, and remembered him crawling under the haul line for the spare rope.

“I’ll tell him.”

“Thanks.”

The man left, walking fast until he reached the crowd.

At the clinic Bao Mei was still on the pallet. Her father had fallen asleep. She lifted her head when Su Fan entered, but did not let go of the hand.

He put the buns within reach.

“Eat while they’re warm.”

“One’s for Father?”

“Yes.”

She broke hers in half, then broke the larger half again. The smallest piece went into her mouth. She chewed without seeming to taste it.

Su Fan put the jacket on a stool. He wiped the lunch pot before setting it beside the food.

“What do they say at the quarry?” she asked.

“They put his tools away.”

“That’s not what I meant.”

He had no better answer. She looked back at her father, and he left them alone.

Mother Wei was washing her hands at the kitchen basin. The water had gone pink around the rim. She changed it, washed again and scrubbed beneath her nails with a little brush worn smooth at the handle.

“Did you eat?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

She dried her hands, took his wrist and pressed the swollen patch beside his thumb.

He flinched.

“Good,” she said. “Still capable of ordinary human behaviour.”

“It’s only strained.”

“Then you’ll be delighted by how little work it needs.”

She sat him at the table. He started to explain the angle of the hook and the point where the pressure had caught his hand. She listened while rubbing bitter-smelling ointment into the swollen area, then asked him to move each finger.

He could move them. The thumb hurt most.

“Duan will find something you can do without gripping hot iron.”

“He has an order waiting.”

“So have I.”

She pulled the cloth firmly around his wrist and held out its loose end. He caught it with his good hand while she tied the knot.

His thumb carried an older scar, a pale ridge from a hammer blow when he was fifteen. Mother Wei had stitched that one too. At eleven she had taken him in after the fever. At thirteen she had washed his best shirt for the sect assessment. At fourteen she had found him work with Duan.

Her care appeared in his memory as separate tasks. A bowl beside his bed. A torn cuff repaired. A page held straight while he sounded out the characters. When he had been younger, he had thought she remembered everything because she never seemed to need a list. Later he had found the scraps tucked beneath jars and pinned inside cupboards.

She forgot her own meals. She forgot that a patient had repaid her until she found the coin in the wrong pocket. She did not forget which medicine made his stomach hurt.

He never knew how to thank her without making her uncomfortable.

Instead he put the broken pin on the table.

She looked at it, then at him.

“Duan should see that.”

“I know.”

“And after Duan?”

“I haven’t decided.”

“You have your deciding face.”

“I only have one face.”

“It’s a crowded face.”

She turned the pin with her bandaged fingers. A cut ran across one knuckle. She had worked through it without mentioning it.

“The mark says it passed,” Su Fan said.

“I can read the mark.”

“It broke.”

“I have noticed.”

He fell silent.

Mother Wei set the pin down carefully. “Bao Shun needs a month’s food. His daughter needs somebody to go to the school and explain why she left. The clinic needs clean linen. Decide those things first.”

“I’m not forgetting him.”

“No. But an injured man has to eat while you find the person to blame.”

Through the wall came Tan Wei’s voice, asking which kettle was meant for clean water. Mother Wei answered without turning.

Su Fan looked at the cloth shelves. The stack beside the treatment room was nearly gone. A basket of washed strips waited by the door, none of them dry.

“I can take that into the sun.”

“With your good hand.”

“And go to the school.”

“After eating.”

She softened, but only a little.

“Bring me the dangerous decisions when you’ve fed yourself.”

***

Outside, Tan Wei leaned against the wall with the empty basin beside him.

He had washed the dust from his face. There was a pale streak where the water had missed the underside of his jaw. He kept rubbing his palm with his thumb, though Mother Wei had told him to leave it alone.

“Your charm,” Su Fan said. “I’ll pay half.”

“You didn’t want it bought.”

“I’ve revised my opinion.”

“An event for the histories.”

Tan Wei opened his hand. A faint blue pattern remained where the paper had burned away. It would fade by morning. Su Fan knew he was sorry it would.

“Did it hurt?”

“The paper?”

“The power.”

Tan Wei considered. “Not like the burn. More like somebody caught my wrist and showed me where to put it.”

“Somebody?”

“There wasn’t a person standing there, Fan.”

“I know.”

“Do you? You look as though I’ve swallowed one.”

Su Fan sat beside him. Across the square, the recruitment clerk rang his bell again. Young people stood in a line extending past the well. Some held family tablets. Others held only coins.

“Eighteen copper,” Su Fan said.

“You were there.”

“For something gone in a breath.”

Tan Wei nodded toward the clinic. “A fairly important breath.”

“Yes.”

The admission cost Su Fan less than he had expected. He could still feel the instant when the hook stopped bending, when Bao Shun’s arm became something they could free rather than something they would have to leave in the wheel.

“I meant it,” he said. “About half.”

“Pay when you can. Don’t buy me another one tomorrow and then go hungry for a week.”

“I wouldn’t.”

Tan Wei looked at him.

Su Fan changed the subject.

“How much?”

His friend followed his gaze toward the awning.

“Six silver for assessment and registration.”

“That isn’t a lease.”

“No. A lease costs more.”

“How much more?”

“Depends what answers.”

A girl emerged from the awning with a white token. Her father lifted her off the ground, then put her down when the clerk called him back to sign another paper. Behind them, an applicant folded his rejection sheet very carefully. He folded it twice more than necessary before putting it into his sleeve.

Su Fan knew that particular care. Six years earlier, his jade bowl had remained dark. He remembered the cold against his palm, the pressure of the elder’s fingers turning his wrist to try another angle. The elder had tested him twice and written *none* beside his name.

Tan Wei had been in the same hall. They had walked home together. Neither had asked the other what happened.

For a while afterward they had made jokes about the test. Tan Wei said the bowls preferred people with clean fingernails. Su Fan had suggested going back with somebody else’s hand. The jokes had become less frequent without either of them deciding to stop.

“The charm worked,” Tan Wei said now.

“Yes.”

“A thread of somebody else’s power. Barely a thread. It held what we couldn’t.”

“For one breath.”

“And you used the breath.”

Su Fan glanced at him.

There was no anger in Tan Wei’s face. That made answering harder.

“Borrowing something doesn’t stop it being useful,” Tan Wei said. “Duan doesn’t make his own ore.”

“A hammer doesn’t live in your blood.”

“Neither does a full belly. Yet you keep recommending one.”

The clerk beckoned to the next applicant. The boy had come alone. He laid three small bundles of coins on the table and watched the clerk count them.

Tan Wei leaned forward, elbows on knees.

“I know there’s a price,” he said. “You don’t have to keep explaining that part.”

“Then I’ll explain the part where the price changes.”

“You don’t know whether it will.”

“Neither do you.”

“No.” Tan Wei rubbed his palm once, then stopped himself. “That’s why I’m going to ask.”

He stood.

“You don’t have six silver.”

“Then I’ll ask what a man without six silver can do.”

He picked up the basin and put it inside the clinic door before crossing the square. Su Fan watched him join the end of the line. He expected his friend to turn back, perhaps to make another joke, perhaps to ask him to come along.

Tan Wei did neither.

Auntie Lu appeared at Su Fan’s elbow carrying a bowl.

“Eat.”

“Mother Wei sent you.”

“She threatened to make her own soup. I acted in the public interest.”

There were noodles beneath the broth and a strip of meat she would normally have charged extra for. He took the bowl in his good hand.

“Does that woman know I have paying customers?” Auntie Lu demanded.

“Yes.”

“Does she know you have legs?”

“Yes.”

“Then use them next time. I’m not running a delivery service.”

She stayed until he took the first mouthful. Then she went back to her stall, taking a discarded wrapper off the bench as she passed.

Across the square, Tan Wei reached the table. He pointed to one of the posted notices. The clerk answered. Tan Wei listened closely, his head bent so he could hear over the crowd.

He asked another question.

The clerk took a paper from a different stack.

Tan Wei nodded twice.

Then, for the first time that day, he smiled without making a joke.

chapters.title: Paper for the Fire
chapters.text:
Duan tested the pin with a file, a hammer and a curse.

The curse came last.

“Three years,” he said. “I’ve sent this mountain sound iron for three years, and they buy this because the seller has a sash.”

Su Fan stood on the unbroken side of the smithy. The roof hole let in an oblong of morning light. Ah-Du had placed a bucket beneath it although it was not raining.

“For later,” the boy explained.

Duan ignored him. He set the pin on a scrap of pale leather and scraped the fracture. Black grains fell onto it. He touched the outer edge with the file, turned the piece and tried again.

“What do you see?” he asked.

“Good metal outside. Waste in the middle.”

“What do you know?”

Su Fan considered the difference.

“That the centre isn’t like the shell.”

“Better.”

Duan tapped the pin with the small hammer. Then he took a sound offcut from beneath the bench and struck it with the same force. The notes were different, though Su Fan could not have described the difference to anyone who had never stood in a smithy.

“Cast shell,” Duan said. “Packed centre.”

He passed the file across another part of the fracture and held up the grey dust on its teeth.

“Not a sound forging broken by too much load. Don’t let anybody persuade you those are the same problem.”

“Can you prove it?”

“To a smith.”

“And to someone else?”

“Depends whether they want to know.”

Duan spoke without the satisfaction Su Fan expected. He took longer than necessary putting down the file. His eyes travelled to the shattered roof beam, then to the bench where yesterday’s unfinished pins lay in a row.

Ah-Du had brushed the dust from them and lined them up by size. Three were beyond saving. The largest piece of fallen stone rested in the corner, too heavy for either apprentice to move safely.

“Who stamped it?” Duan asked.

“The sect.”

“I can see the mark. Who inspected it?”

Su Fan unfolded the scrap bearing the number he had copied at the quarry. The foreman’s loss sheet had been poor paper; a corner tore as he opened it.

Duan read the figures. He read them again.

Then he went to the little cupboard above the tool chest and brought down a bundle of old quotations, tied with cord. He sorted through them while Ah-Du peered over his arm.

“That batch wasn’t for the quarry,” he said.

“What was it for?”

“The river gate.”

Su Fan looked at the pin.

Duan pulled one of the old papers free. He did not hand it over. He compared its heading with the number on Su Fan’s scrap, following the line with a blackened fingernail.

“I priced work under that order. Didn’t get it.”

“Because they bought this.”

“Because they bought elsewhere. Don’t write more than you know.”

There were nine gates above Mudgate. The town’s children learned their names before they could count the month’s taxes. In spring the gates fed the channels. In the rainy months they held the upland water off the valley floor. Every household had some opinion about when they should open, when they should close, and which field received too much of what another lacked.

Su Fan had thought of them as large things far away. White stone against the northern slope. Bronze leaves bright in the sun. Even the smallest piece he pictured had been beyond the scale of his workbench.

The broken pin fitted inside his palm.

“Is that holding one of them shut?” he asked.

“I don’t know where they fitted the rest.”

“But it was ordered for—”

“I heard what I said.” Duan set down the quotation. “A gate has more parts than the bit that holds the water. We ask which part before we announce the whole mountain’s coming down.”

He sat on the edge of the anvil.

“I’ll send word to the steward.”

“Will she read it?”

“She reads complaints against her suppliers. They cost her money.”

***

Writing the complaint took almost as long as testing the pin.

Duan dictated. Su Fan wrote with his good hand, using the inside of an old account wrapper because the clean paper was meant for invoices. Ah-Du stood over them offering advice until Duan sent him to find the roof nails.

The first version began with Bao Shun’s arm.

Duan had Su Fan move that part below the batch number, the date and the description of the piece.

“They need to know what it did.”

“They need to find it among their orders before they stop reading.”

Su Fan pressed hard enough to split the brush tip.

Duan watched him straighten it.

“You can be angry and still write a legible character.”

“I am writing legibly.”

“That one says ‘marsh’.”

“It says ‘metal’.”

“It says we found defective marsh in the pin. Start that line again.”

By the time they finished, the account wrapper contained the number twice, an account of where the pin had been fitted and a request to inspect the remaining batch. Duan added his own name at the bottom. His writing was larger than Su Fan’s and less neat, but he put it down without hesitation.

He wrapped the specimen in leather, locked it in his tool chest and threaded the key onto the cord under his shirt. The letter would go first. The pin would follow if Jiang asked for it.

Su Fan stood with the folded paper while Duan counted out the messenger’s fee.

“I can take it.”

“And who replaces your hours here?”

“I’ll work later.”

“You worked later yesterday. Then you forgot to eat.”

“Mother Wei told you.”

“Most of the valley told me. Apparently I employ a man who needs a written instruction to use his mouth.”

He handed the letter to a porter going uphill with charcoal accounts. Su Fan watched the man tuck it carefully into a sleeve, accept the coin and go.

He had expected anger to become a plan. Instead it became a letter in somebody else’s clothes.

Then Duan gave him the day’s work, and there was no room to dislike anything except the work.

They moved the undamaged stock away from the roof hole. Ah-Du gathered broken tiles, sorting those large enough to use again. Duan marked the surviving beam while Su Fan held the measuring cord. Every movement required them to step around the stone in the corner.

“We could sell that,” Ah-Du suggested.

“To whom?”

“The quarry.”

Duan looked at him for a moment.

“Get the ladder.”

The morning warmed. A woman came for a repaired cooking ring and stood beneath the hole while deciding whether she could pay tomorrow. A carter wanted an axle pin immediately. Duan told him to examine the roof and reconsider the word.

Su Fan kept a list of what still needed doing. When the list filled one side of the scrap, he turned it over and found the beginnings of an old letter he had never sent.

He wrote between its lines.

***

Scholar Min arrived while they were repairing the roof.

He wore a patched blue coat and carried a wicker basket lined with paper. Two books stuck out of it. A third was tied shut with a strip torn from a different coat.

“Good morning,” he called.

Duan looked down from the ladder.

“It was.”

“I see your ventilation has improved.”

“Did you come to pay your bill?”

“I came with employment.”

“Paying employment?”

“The distinction is always central to our conversations.”

Min set his basket on the only dry-looking place near the doorway. The place was clean because Ah-Du had just moved a pile of soot from it. He picked the basket up again when he saw the bottom.

Su Fan fetched a stool.

Min thanked him and did not sit. His eyes followed the brace Duan was fitting beneath the damaged beam.

“Will it hold?”

“When you leave us to do it.”

“Then I’ll speak quickly.”

He wanted two rusted clamps opened at the Sealed Stack. The archive’s old bindings had swollen. The clerks clearing it could not shift the lower shelves without damaging the wall, and nobody wished to pay for the wall.

Duan came down one rung.

“Who pays for the clamps?”

“The archive office. I have their approval.”

Min produced a folded slip. It bore a clerk’s mark and an amount.

Duan took it. “You’ve learned.”

“I have always been capable of learning. My creditors lack patience with the demonstration.”

“What are they clearing?” Su Fan asked.

Min glanced at him.

“Anything without a recognized founder, an active claimant or a paying patron.”

“That sounds thorough.”

“It is exceptionally thorough.”

His smile had gone.

The Sealed Stack occupied a cold corner of the sect’s oldest quarter. Su Fan had carried charcoal past it and swept the steps on labour rotation. On warm days the open shutters released the smell of old paper into the lane. He liked that smell. It belonged to work he had never been allowed to do.

“They’re burning the books?”

“Some. Selling the clean paper by weight. A merchant has already made an offer on the bindings.”

“Can’t you take what’s useful?”

Min shifted the basket against his knee.

“I have two hands and a room that leaks.”

“There are other rooms.”

“Whose?”

Su Fan had no answer that would put a roof over a book by that afternoon.

Min looked at the approval slip in Duan’s hand. “I’m trying to save a set of rainfall tables. Forty-three years of measurements. The third volume has no cover, which apparently makes it a different kind of object from the first two.”

“Tell them it’s a lidless pot,” Duan said. “People save those.”

“I’m considering every category available.”

Ah-Du leaned over the roof edge.

“Do they pay for carrying?”

“One copper a basket.”

“How big a basket?”

Min indicated his own.

Ah-Du looked disappointed.

“That’s a book basket. I have a basket basket.”

“Your distinction is also central.”

Duan climbed the rest of the way down. He inspected Min’s hands. There was a tremor in them that the older man tried to hide by moving the basket.

“You should be at Wei’s.”

“I visited yesterday.”

“What did she say?”

“Several things I was already aware of.”

Duan took the basket from him and placed it on the stool. This time Min sat.

For a few moments nobody spoke. A cart passed outside, bells rattling against the harness. Min watched its shadow slide across the threshold. His breath gradually lost the catch Su Fan had noticed beneath the jokes.

Duan gave Su Fan a pry bar and two wedges.

“Go. Take the small hammer. You’re not swinging it hard with that wrist. If the piece needs force, send for me.”

“The roof—”

“Will still have a hole when you return. Ah-Du and I will try not to fall through it.”

“I can do the clamps,” Ah-Du said from above.

“You can find the nails I asked for.”

The boy’s head disappeared.

Duan lowered his voice. “Get the money before Min starts explaining the historical value of the work.”

“I can hear you,” Min said.

“That was intentional.”

***

The climb to the old quarter took them past the assessment hall.

Su Fan carried the tools in a roll over one shoulder and Min’s basket in his uninjured hand. The basket was heavier than it looked. Beneath the two books lay packets of loose pages, tied in different colours of thread.

“Which are the rainfall tables?” he asked.

“None of those. Those are what I could remove yesterday.”

“All important?”

“To someone.”

Min stopped to let a pair of disciples pass. Their sleeves brushed neither man. One carried a covered tray from which a pale mist escaped through a crack. Su Fan caught a sweet smell before they turned uphill.

Min watched the tray go, then resumed walking.

Three children waited outside the assessment hall with their mothers. One had a blue sash tied around his wrist. He kept touching it to make sure it was there. Another stood very straight while his mother worked at a stain on his collar with a damp thumb.

Su Fan looked past them.

Min slowed to catch his breath.

“You read,” he said.

“A little.”

“Wei told me you copy her medicine labels.”

“Those are mostly the same words.”

“Most books are mostly the same words. People pay for the order.”

Su Fan smiled despite himself.

“What do they pay you?”

“Not enough, evidently.”

They rested beside a low wall until Min’s breathing eased. From there Su Fan could see the quarry road and the small dark interruption where the damaged smithy roof should have been. Beyond it lay Mudgate’s reeds, the slow river, a scattering of roofs that looked far less crowded from above.

Min did not give him a speech about the view. He bent to tighten the knot on one shoe, failed twice and let Su Fan do it.

At the Stack, two clerks stood over a table covered with tablets. Each tablet bore a founder’s name. A porter tied rejected books into bundles. Another man scraped old labels from boxes so they could be used again.

The youngest clerk looked at Su Fan’s tools.

“Six copper for both clamps. Damage comes out of the fee.”

“How much damage?”

“The cost of repair.”

“Then I inspect it first.”

The clerk looked toward Min. Min had already begun searching the table for a particular tablet and appeared not to have heard.

“Fine,” the clerk said. “Don’t disturb the sorted shelves.”

A porter tried to pull a bundle from beneath the table. Its cord caught a stool leg, and loose pages slid across the floor. He looked at the clerk before bending to collect them.

“Keep the bundles together,” the clerk said.

“They weren’t together when you gave them to me.”

“Then do your best.”

Su Fan set down the basket and helped retrieve a page from under his boot. It contained a drawing of something with six wheels. He handed it back without knowing which bundle it belonged to. The porter tucked it into the nearest one.

Min saw, took the page out again, and began looking for the rest.

The clamps held the bottom of a tall shelving frame against the wall. The metal had rusted into its own bedding. Someone had once painted over it. Someone else had chipped the paint away and abandoned the attempt.

Su Fan ran a finger along the join. The surrounding stone was older than the repair work. Its surface bore shallow tool marks unlike the neat cuts in the corridor outside.

Behind one clamp, barely visible beneath the rust, someone had carved a mark.

Three plain strokes around an open centre.

He touched it while testing where to set the wedge.

The stone was warm.

He moved his fingers an inch to the side. Cold. Back to the mark. Warm again, too distinctly to dismiss as the touch of his own hand.

There was no sun on that wall.

“Work’s on the metal,” the clerk said.

Su Fan took his hand away.

Min had seen him touch the mark.

The old man’s expression was difficult to read. Not surprise. Something tired, sharpened for a moment into attention.

He opened his mouth, closed it, and went back to sorting the books.

chapters.title: The Unclaimed Shelf
chapters.text:
The first clamp took half an hour.

Su Fan worked its edges loose with the smaller wedge, pausing whenever the shelf frame moved instead of the iron. Dust shook down from the boards above him. The porter held a lamp at an angle that illuminated his own fingers better than the join.

“Lower.”

The lamp went lower.

“Towards the wall.”

“If I put it much closer, I’ll light the shelf.”

“Then stay there.”

He changed position and worked by touch. Duan would have had the clamp out sooner. Duan also had two hands he could use properly. Su Fan braced the pry bar against his hip and eased the metal away one short movement at a time.

When it finally came free, the clerk inspected the stone.

“That chip was already there,” Su Fan said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were looking.”

“I’m permitted.”

The clerk marked the first job complete on his tablet. Su Fan drank from the cup beside the door and moved to the second clamp.

It had been driven through a shelf bracket into the stone behind it. Rust had swallowed the join. The board above sagged beneath a row of tightly packed volumes. He could force the clamp loose, but the shelf would come with it.

He went to the clerk.

“Empty that one first.”

“It’s condemned.”

“Then condemn it on the floor. It will fall on me.”

The clerk sighed and called a porter.

The porter had already tied most of the rejected books into bundles. He looked at the shelf, at the tools, then at the six-copper figure on the work slip.

“Do I get part of that?”

“Ask him,” the clerk said.

“I’m being paid to take the shelf apart,” Su Fan said. “You’re being paid to carry it away.”

“And neither of us is being paid enough.”

The porter fetched an empty tray.

While he worked, Su Fan carried the wedges into the back room. Dust lay deep enough to preserve the tracks of a small animal. A nest occupied the space where a lamp had once hung. The shutter would open only a hand’s breadth before striking the wall outside, so he propped it with a broken tile and waited for his eyes to adjust.

At first the books looked alike. Bad bindings. Darkened pages. Pale tunnels left by insects. Then he began reading titles.

*A Treatise on Rice Blight.*

*Comparative River Levels in the Years of Broken Rain.*

*Exercises for the Lower Limbs Following Injury.*

He knew most of the characters. The ones he did not know he worked around, using the pictures and the next line. Someone had drawn a diseased stalk of rice so carefully that he could distinguish the mottled leaf from its shadow.

“What founder does rice blight need?” he asked.

Min, who had followed him, set down his basket.

“The purchasing clerk needs a category.”

“And these have none?”

“They have several. None is worth storage to the people paying for storage.”

Min took up a loose board used as a catalogue marker. Names ran down one side. Most had been crossed through. He found the entry he wanted, traced it to the shelf and discovered an empty space.

He stood looking at it.

“Was it important?” Su Fan asked.

“The second part of an account I still have the first part of.”

“Could it be somewhere else?”

“Certainly.”

Min put down the marker and began examining the nearest pile. He did not say whether certainty helped.

Su Fan pulled the exercise book free. Someone had drawn a foot in the margin. Beside it, in smaller writing, was a note about swelling. Further on, a series of figures stood beside a chair, one hand on its back.

Mother Wei might use that.

The book smelled faintly of damp cloth. Its lower corner had hardened where water had dried the pages together. He tried to separate two leaves, stopped before tearing them and closed it.

“Can I buy this?”

“Ask the clerk.”

The clerk wanted two copper.

“It’s in the condemned room.”

“It still has a cover.”

“Some pages are stuck.”

“Then you get the stuck pages with it.”

Su Fan held the book for another moment. Two copper was not an impossible price. That made deciding worse. There was food to take to Bao Shun, the debt he had offered to share with Tan Wei, ordinary things he had already promised to pay for before the book entered his hands.

He put it back.

Min watched him without speaking.

Su Fan disliked being watched while deciding whether he could afford a book. He could carry stone all day without embarrassment. Two copper for knowledge made him feel as though he had reached for somebody else’s bowl.

He returned to the clamp.

***

The porter had cleared the board, but not the weight pressing against it from the frame above.

Su Fan set a short prop beneath the upright. The available wood was a discarded binding board, too thin on its own. He doubled it with another and drove a wedge beneath them. The frame lifted just enough to release the bracket.

“Hold there,” he told the porter.

“With what?”

“Your hands.”

The man showed him his empty palms. “I was enjoying having those.”

“Not beneath it. Against the side.”

That he would do.

Su Fan loosened the outer fastening. His wrist hurt if he pulled straight, so he used the pry bar as a lever and kept his elbow close. Once the bracket moved, he could see a narrow gap between the shelf backing and the wall.

Something lay inside it.

He thought at first it was a strip of wood used to level the frame. He eased the last part of the bracket free. The upright shifted against the porter’s hands, the gap widened, and a narrow wooden cover slipped out.

Su Fan caught it against his chest.

The porter swore.

“Tell me before you let go.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“The shelf doesn’t know what you mean.”

Su Fan set the object on a clear board, caught the frame and helped lower it. Together they laid the upright on the floor. No stone broke. No book fell. The porter flexed his hands and went to demand that the clerk count the extra load.

Su Fan picked up the cover.

It was no larger than his forearm. Inside lay thin bamboo slips, stained with age but intact. The cord holding them had been replaced at least twice. One old hole was worn nearly through. The last knot was clumsy, with an unnecessary turn that tightened against itself.

No founder’s name appeared on the cover.

He opened it.

The first line was ordinary enough.

*Stand where you can fall without striking your head.*

He read the next.

*The frightened body wastes strength holding itself against movements that have not happened.*

Below that a figure stood with its knees slightly bent. Arrows showed the position of the breath, but not in the familiar colours of the sect’s teaching boards. No blue for water. No white for frost. No red for flame.

One channel had been crossed out.

Beside it was another hand’s note: *This hurt. Do not follow the old drawing.*

Someone had answered beneath it: *Then draw your own correctly.*

Su Fan read that twice.

The answer was smaller than the complaint. Its writer had crowded the final characters into the remaining space rather than start on another slip. A third hand had added a mark that might have been agreement or annoyance. He could not tell.

The books he had seen displayed in the assessment hall did not look like this. Their headings were large and their founders’ names larger. Disciples pointed to the diagrams with polished rods. Nobody appeared to have written in the margins that the instruction hurt.

He turned one slip carefully. The binding tightened. He eased it back rather than risk breaking the cord.

“Found something?” the clerk called.

“More bamboo.”

“Put it with the rest.”

The rest lay beside the doorway in a pile for the furnace. Broken boxes. Damaged bindings. A stack of slips too short to fit the bundles the porter was making.

Su Fan looked toward Min.

The old man had his back to him. Deliberately, Su Fan thought. But he could not be certain. Min was holding two pages side by side, attempting to decide whether they belonged together.

Su Fan placed the slips in the burn pile.

His tool roll lay open beside his knee. There was room in it. He could see how easily the narrow cover would fit between the pry bar and the wedges, how ordinary the bundle would look when he tied it shut.

Then the porter came back for the shelf upright and stepped over the roll.

Su Fan closed it around the tools.

He had never been searched leaving a paid job. He did not know what happened to a smith whose assistant was caught taking something from a sect building, even something the building intended to burn. Duan would have to answer for him. The old man already had a broken roof and an injured customer to think about.

The clerk called across the room to ask whether the second clamp was finished.

“Nearly.”

“Then finish. I have to settle your fee before the afternoon count.”

Su Fan looked once more at the bamboo cover. He needed a way to carry it through the door openly. He did not yet have one.

He finished the repair.

There was still a bracket to straighten, a stone edge to brush clear and the work slip to get marked. The clerk insisted on testing the remaining shelf with both hands before agreeing that it stood safely. Su Fan waited while he wrote.

The bamboo cover was visible beside the door.

A kitchen boy arrived with a sack for kindling. He began filling it from the loose wood at the edge of the pile.

Su Fan looked back at the clerk’s brush.

The brush stopped. The clerk blew on a wet character, examined it and amended the last stroke.

“Six,” he said.

He counted the coins onto the table.

Su Fan closed his hand around them before the kitchen boy reached the centre of the pile.

***

“Paper,” he said. “How much for a basket?”

The clerk glanced at the rejected shelves.

“Clean paper?”

“Fire paper. For the smithy.”

“One copper. Bring your own basket.”

Su Fan looked at Min.

The old man followed his gaze to the wicker basket. For a moment he seemed about to object. Then he removed the books, setting them on the stool in a careful stack.

“Don’t take it home full of coal,” he said.

Su Fan handed the clerk one copper. Five remained in his palm. He put them away before they could become money he had already spent in his head.

The injury book went at the bottom of the basket. The clerk saw it and said nothing. Sold separately it had been an object with a price. In the basket it was part of a small load the office no longer had to pay someone to remove.

Su Fan added a water-damaged almanac and three stitched pamphlets. He did not know what two of them concerned. The third had a drawing of a pump, though several of its labels had washed away.

Then he lifted the bamboo slips from the kindling pile.

The kitchen boy looked at the wooden covers.

“Those burn well.”

“They’re coming with this.”

“Fine.” The boy held open his sack. “Pass that broken box, then.”

Su Fan did. He laid loose pages too spoiled to read over the contents of his basket and brought it to the table.

The clerk barely looked inside.

“That’s a small basket.”

“It will do.”

“Duan know you’re buying fuel by the handful?”

“He can complain when I bring it.”

The clerk made a mark beside the fee and returned to his tablets. Su Fan waited another breath, expecting someone to identify a rule he had broken without knowing it.

Nobody did.

He collected the pry bar and wedges. Min insisted on carrying his own books, though he had to bind them into two bundles to do it. The porter lifted the empty shelf frame with an expression suggesting that everyone else in the building had found a way to leave work behind.

Su Fan helped him carry it into the corridor before going.

Outside, the light made his eyes water. He had forgotten how warm the day was. They stopped beside the dry fountain, where a crack ran through the basin and someone had planted two onions in the accumulated soil.

Min put his bundles down.

“The knot,” he said.

Su Fan waited.

“On the bamboo binding. I tied it. Twenty-seven years ago.”

“Have you read it?”

“Yes.”

“Does it work?”

Min looked uphill, toward the bright roof of the assessment hall.

“I couldn’t tell you.”

“Couldn’t, or won’t?”

The old scholar rubbed the stained pad of his thumb. His fingers had begun to tremble again. Su Fan nearly offered to take the books, then held the basket where it was.

“I tried the first exercise once,” Min said. “I was frightened by what I thought I felt. I never tried it again.”

That was not the answer Su Fan had expected from a keeper of books.

“What did you feel?”

“Something I wanted to explain before I was willing to feel it twice.”

“And you couldn’t explain it?”

“No.”

Min said the word plainly. Su Fan found himself looking for the hidden answer behind it and discovering only an old man standing in the sun.

“Why leave it in the wall?”

“I didn’t. I put it on the unclaimed shelf. Someone shelved it more thoroughly than I did.”

For a moment the humour returned. Then Min coughed into his sleeve. When he lowered it, he folded the fabric inward.

Su Fan pretended not to see. Min pretended not to notice the courtesy.

“Take the injury book to Wei,” the scholar said. “She’ll get more use from it than we did.”

“And the other?”

Min looked at the basket.

“Read the corrections.”

“Will you look at it with me?”

“Another day. I have to find the end of those rainfall tables before it becomes a cooking fire.”

He picked up his bundles and went back toward the archive. At the door he paused, shifted the weight of the books and called for the porter. His voice regained some of its earlier briskness as soon as there was a task to explain.

Su Fan watched him disappear into the building.

Downhill, the first cartload of books had reached the burn pit. A kitchen worker broke a bundle over his knee to make it fit the opening. Smoke rose behind the kitchens. At this distance it looked no different from cooking smoke.

The basket handle pressed into Su Fan’s good hand. He could take the steep path and be back sooner, but it crossed the dusty yard where porters were still shifting stone from yesterday’s collapse.

He took the longer lane through the old terraces.

At the first turn he stopped and moved the bamboo cover beneath the almanac, where it would not catch against the tools. Then he continued downhill, holding the basket away from the sweat on his shirt.

chapters.title: An Error in the Margin
chapters.text:
Su Fan read the bamboo slips beside the smithy’s banked furnace.

He had brought a bowl of water, a length of string, and the smallest weight from Duan’s scale. The first three instructions asked for none of these things. He preferred to have something he could check.

The method was called the Scripture of the Human Dao.

That name occupied less space than the warnings.

*Do not hold the breath until your sight changes.*

*Do not seek numbness.*

*Do not mistake the loss of feeling for the end of resistance.*

The letters belonged to several hands. Some were square and patient. Others leaned hard to the right. A few corrections had been scraped into the bamboo after the ink faded. One slip had cracked near the binding hole and been repaired with a narrow piece of silk. Someone had spent more care on that repair than on making the title impressive.

It looked less like a sacred scripture than a workshop book that had passed through difficult owners.

That made him trust it a little.

Not enough to believe the page with three different drawings of the same shoulder. He set that one aside and started again at the beginning.

The smithy was quiet now. Duan had gone home after telling him twice not to leave the tools where the roof leaked. The repaired section would hold a light rain. Nobody had promised it would hold anything heavier. Su Fan moved the basket beneath the bench before spreading the slips on a board.

The injury manual had gone to Mother Wei. She had opened it at once and asked where he found it. He had told her the archive was clearing its shelves. That answer was true. It had also allowed him not to mention the bamboo bundle still in the basket.

He wanted to understand it before he showed anyone.

At least, that was how he described the decision to himself.

The sect’s public teaching began with the founder. An apprentice recalled a name, followed the named channel, and persuaded the dead pattern to answer. Element, lineage, vessel. Su Fan had copied enough medicine labels to recognize those terms on examination notices. He knew which parts of the notice were promises and which parts concerned the fee.

This book began with the reader’s feet.

He took off his shoes. The packed earth felt cool through his stockings, except near the furnace where it held the day’s heat. He moved farther away.

*Stand where you can fall without striking your head.*

He looked at the bench behind him, then at the anvil to his left.

It was an unpromising room in which to fall safely.

He shifted the charcoal sacks, leaned a loose length of iron against the wall and cleared a space near the door. Then he put the instruction board where the lamplight could reach it.

All this effort to stand still.

He nearly laughed. Instead he arranged his feet as the drawing showed.

At once he felt foolish.

He had climbed the ore road for six years. He had carried baskets, worked the bellows and stood beside an anvil through days when his back hurt before breakfast. He knew how to stand.

The instructions asked him to let his knees turn slightly outward. His left heel lifted. He corrected it. His shoulders rose.

*Begin again.*

He lowered his shoulders and lost the alignment in his knees.

He tried five times.

By the fifth he had decided the illustrator’s legs were shorter than a real person’s legs, and that the difference probably mattered. He put a strip of paper beside the drawing and tried to copy the angle in a size he could see clearly.

His copy looked worse.

On the sixth attempt, Ah-Du came through the door carrying a turnip.

“What are you doing?”

“Standing.”

“I’ve seen better.”

“Whose turnip?”

“The vegetable woman’s.”

“Then put it back.”

“She threw it at me. Ownership was transferred by force.”

Su Fan looked at him.

Ah-Du sighed, broke the turnip in half against the edge of a board and offered him the clean side.

“Paid for,” he admitted. “The story was better.”

***

They ate beside the furnace.

Ah-Du turned the scale weight over between finger and thumb. Su Fan took it from him before he could drop it into the turnip peelings.

“Is that part of it?”

“No.”

“Then why is it there?”

“I haven’t decided.”

The boy regarded this as evidence that the lesson was already going badly.

“Does it teach flying?”

“No.”

“Fire?”

“No.”

“Then why does it cost a copper?”

“It came with other books.”

Ah-Du considered that and accepted it. He leaned over the board, careful to keep his half of the turnip away from the bamboo. His reading was slow enough that Su Fan could follow which word he had reached by the movement of his lips.

“What’s that one?”

“Resistance.”

“What does it mean?”

“Something fighting a movement.”

“Like Duan when a customer asks for credit.”

“Not exactly.”

“Strong resistance, though.”

Su Fan moved the board before the boy’s elbow struck the water bowl.

Ah-Du tried the stance. He bent his knees too far and spread his arms to balance, looking pleased with himself until one foot slipped on a turnip peeling.

Su Fan caught his shoulder.

“That,” he said, pointing at the first warning.

“I didn’t hit my head.”

“Because I caught you.”

“Then it works better with two people.”

He righted himself and tried again, this time less theatrically. His shoulders stayed low without apparent effort. Su Fan watched, annoyed by how easily the boy did the part he had struggled with.

Then Ah-Du’s knees began to shake.

“How long?”

“I don’t know.”

“Does it say?”

“Not there.”

“That seems important.”

The boy straightened and went back to his turnip. He had lost interest in becoming an immortal for the evening. The roof work had tired him more than he wanted to admit. He found a roll of sacking beneath the repaired section, pushed it into a shape that suited him and lay down with one arm beneath his head.

“Wake me before you go,” he said.

Su Fan said he would.

A few minutes later Ah-Du was asleep. His mouth hung slightly open. Even in sleep he frowned when a cart rattled past the door.

Su Fan finished the turnip, washed his fingers and returned to the exercise.

This time he noticed that his jaw was clenched.

It seemed an irrelevant thing to be doing. Nothing in the drawing concerned teeth. He loosened it, and something changed beneath his ribs.

Not power. Space. A movement so small he nearly missed it.

He tried to hold it.

It vanished.

He stayed in the same position, waiting. His knee began to ache. He shifted his foot, lost the alignment and started over.

Nothing.

He looked at Ah-Du to see whether the boy had noticed. Ah-Du snored softly into the sacking.

Su Fan was glad. Then, unexpectedly, he wished there had been someone awake to tell.

***

For the next hour he pursued that movement.

At first he tried to copy everything he remembered about the instant before it happened. Where he had put his foot. How far he had turned his head. Whether he had been looking at the book or the furnace.

The reconstruction became so complicated that he could no longer tell which parts had actually occurred.

He returned to the drawing.

Perhaps the arrow beneath the breastbone meant he should press inward. He tightened his stomach. Perhaps the longer line meant the exhalation should continue past the point where he ordinarily drew breath again. He held it, waiting for the sensation to arrive.

His shoulders crept up. He lowered them sharply.

That felt disciplined. It also made his neck hurt.

The tiny mark beside the drawn mouth seemed to point towards the teeth. He pressed his tongue there. The page offered no explanation of why this should help, but there were many things he did at the forge because Duan had shown him before he understood the reason.

He tried harder.

A dull ache gathered behind his eyes.

He blinked at the lamp. Its edges had become disagreeably bright.

The warning about changed sight was underlined twice.

He stopped.

For several breaths he stood with his hands hanging at his sides, listening to the ordinary sounds of the room. The furnace ticked. A beetle worked its way along the doorpost. Ah-Du turned over and kicked the wall.

Su Fan sat on the low stool and drank some water. It tasted faintly of iron because he had used the bowl that usually held the scale weights. He emptied it, rinsed it and fetched more.

The small tasks steadied him.

When the ache eased, he brought the slip closer to the lamp and read from the top rather than looking only at the figure.

He had skipped a correction at the bottom.

*The tongue is relaxed. This mark is a stain.*

He read the sentence again, then examined the little mark beside the mouth. In the stronger light he could see that it followed the grain of the bamboo instead of the direction of the brush.

He laughed once, without humour.

For half an hour he had been obeying a stain.

The person who wrote the correction had probably made the same mistake. Su Fan found this comforting until he realized it meant the book’s previous readers had been capable of missing instructions directly in front of them.

Like him.

He set aside the slip and made a separate copy of the warnings. His handwriting grew smaller near the bottom. He started to squeeze the final line into the remaining space, caught himself doing it and turned the paper over.

If it mattered enough to copy, it mattered enough to read.

Outside, the mountain’s evening bell sounded. The town quieted by degrees. A cart rattled past. Someone called for a missing goat. Someone else called back that the goat was not missing, it was eating their washing.

Su Fan opened the door wider to let in the cool air.

He could have stopped there. He had work in the morning. His wrist was sore, and the first lesson had taught him chiefly that he could make himself uncomfortable by concentrating.

Instead he moved the scale weight to the cleared space.

He wanted something that did not care what he hoped to feel.

***

He tied the weight to the string and held it in front of his chest.

The little piece of iron hung crookedly. He retied the knot. It still hung crookedly, but now he could see that its hole had been drilled off-centre. The string was not at fault.

As his arm tired, the weight trembled.

He watched the movement. His breathing disturbed it. So did the strain in his shoulder. So did every attempt to stop it.

Holding his breath did not make his hand still. It replaced one small movement with several others. Lowering his shoulders too deliberately tugged the string. Trying to copy the drawing while staring at the weight made him turn his knee inwards again.

Eventually he lowered his arm.

He hung the string from a nail in the bench and waited for the weight to settle. It continued moving. He shut the door. That helped, but the string still turned slowly, unwinding the twist he had put into it while tying the knot.

Su Fan watched it for a long time.

He had been prepared to call a change in that movement evidence of something inside his chest. The string had difficulties of its own.

He untied it, smoothed it between his fingers and hung it again. This time the weight settled sooner. He touched the bench with one foot and saw the iron move. A cart going past outside did the same thing, more faintly.

The instrument was not useless. He simply needed to know what else could disturb it before deciding that he had.

He reopened the door. Cool air moved over his face. On the sacking, Ah-Du pulled one knee closer to his belly and continued sleeping.

Su Fan had been treating every movement as a mistake.

At the forge, an iron piece held rigidly against every change would tear the tongs from his hand. Duan let it move where movement was harmless and held it where the blow needed resistance. Su Fan knew how to do that with metal better than he knew how to explain it.

He picked up the empty tongs.

For a few moments he worked through the familiar motion, turning an imagined piece on the anvil. His hand knew where the grip needed to be firm. His elbow did not stay locked. When he tried to hold the whole arm motionless, the movement became awkward at once.

He put the tongs away.

The first exercise was not asking him to stop moving. It was asking him to notice how much effort he spent moving against himself.

That was something he could test.

He tried the stance again without searching for the unfamiliar feeling. His feet stayed on the floor. His knees ached. He let the ache remain an ache instead of taking it as a sign that he was approaching some important boundary.

His jaw stayed loose.

At the end of the exhalation, warmth passed through the centre of his chest and disappeared into his back.

He turned too quickly.

Nothing stood behind him. Only tools, charcoal sacks and the shadow of the ladder.

He sat down until his heart slowed.

The furnace was behind his right shoulder, several paces away. He had felt the warmth travel the other way. That did not prove anything. He knew almost nothing about what a tired body might invent after an evening of watching itself.

Still, he moved the stool farther from the furnace.

He waited. He tried again.

Nothing happened.

He tried once more and felt an itch between his shoulder blades. He scratched it. The itch stopped. There was no reason to give that a grander name either.

For a while he sat with the book open on his knees, too alert to be sleepy and too tired to judge whether that alertness meant anything. The lamp flame had grown low. He trimmed the wick and saw how much oil he had already used.

On a scrap of paper he wrote: *Warmth. No colour. Not from the furnace. Repeat before believing.*

He read the third sentence again. He had moved away from the furnace only after the feeling. That was weaker evidence than the sentence suggested.

Beneath it he added: *Test farther away.*

He considered adding his name.

The empty space seemed suddenly too conspicuous. A smith’s assistant’s name among all these unknown hands, attached to one uncertain feeling and a headache caused by a stain.

He tucked the paper into the bamboo binding without signing it.

For the first time since the assessment hall, he had a question that the dark bowl had not already answered.

He meant to put the slips away. Instead he turned back to the first figure and compared its feet with the position he had finally found comfortable.

Ah-Du stirred on the sacking.

“Are we going?” he mumbled.

“In a moment.”

The boy went back to sleep.

Su Fan stayed awake too long trying to ask the question again.

chapters.title: What the Body Knows
chapters.text:
On the third morning, Su Fan dropped a perfectly good hinge into the quenching barrel.

Duan watched it sink.

“Were we making a cold hinge?”

“No.”

“A drowned hinge?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps you should go home.”

Su Fan bent to retrieve it. The smithy tilted. He caught the barrel rim, waited for the floor to settle and found Duan beside him.

“How long since you slept?”

“I slept.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

The old smith took the tongs from his hand. He did it gently, which made Su Fan feel worse than being shouted at would have done.

“It’s only a moment,” Su Fan said. “I stood too quickly.”

“You bent down.”

He could think of no useful way to disagree with that.

Duan put the hinge on the bench after fishing it from the water. Its leaves were still straight. The work was not ruined. Su Fan was grateful for this until the smith pushed a stool behind his knees and made him sit.

“What have you been doing at night?”

“Reading.”

“Try doing it with your eyes shut next time.”

Ah-Du had stopped at the bellows. He looked from Duan to Su Fan and wisely offered no joke.

The smith poured water into a cup and waited until Su Fan drank. Then he sent Ah-Du to Mother Wei with a message. Su Fan objected. Duan ignored him and began explaining the next job to the boy as though the argument had ended when the tongs changed hands.

Within the hour, Su Fan was sitting in Mother Wei’s kitchen while she read the first bamboo slip.

He had not intended to show her yet. That intention lasted until she threatened to examine the place where he worked. She knew every hiding place in the smithy. She had used several of them to store the medicine Duan claimed he did not need.

Bringing the book himself was less embarrassing than having her find it behind the axle patterns.

She read in silence.

The kitchen smelled of beans and drying herbs. A patched cloth covered a bowl on the shelf. Through the half-open door he could hear Bao Shun asking his daughter to leave the binding alone. The girl replied that she was only looking.

Mother Wei turned the slip over.

“What did you eat last night?”

“Rice.”

“What with?”

“More rice.”

She looked at him.

“There were greens.”

“And the night before?”

He could remember the book more clearly than the meal. That was enough of an answer for her.

Then she asked him to demonstrate.

He stood, lowered his shoulders and let his breath pass naturally. He tried not to remember the warmth. Remembering it made him chase it, and chasing it had not helped.

“Again,” she said.

He did it again.

She pressed two fingers against the lower edge of his ribs.

“Here.”

It hurt.

“You’re forcing it.”

“The book says to remove resistance.”

“And you’ve been fighting the resistance.”

“I’m trying to feel where it is.”

“By making more of it?”

He looked at the floor.

Mother Wei asked him to breathe without arranging himself first. He did. She moved her fingers, waited and asked another question about the ache behind his eyes. He admitted that it had happened twice.

“Twice after the warning told you to stop?”

“I stopped both times.”

“And began again before you understood why.”

He said nothing.

She withdrew her hand and pushed a bowl towards him.

“Eat.”

There were beans, greens and a piece of fish. He had no idea where she had found the fish. He ate carefully at first, then faster when his body remembered what food was for.

Mother Wei resumed reading.

“Is this cultivation?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

She spoke without embarrassment. He wished he could learn that as easily as he learned characters.

“Something happens when I get it right.”

“Does something happen when you get it wrong?”

He touched his side.

“Then we know at least half of it.”

He told her about the warmth, the direction it moved, the lack of colour. He described the string experiment and admitted that the weight turned because he had twisted it. She asked whether anyone else had seen a change.

“Ah-Du saw me standing.”

“That appears to be within your ordinary abilities.”

“He didn’t see the warmth.”

“Could he have?”

“I don’t know.”

There. He had said it. The kitchen did not collapse around him.

Mother Wei reached the mark on the inner cover. Her thumb stopped.

Su Fan noticed because it had been moving steadily before that.

“You’ve seen it.”

“A similar mark.”

“Where?”

“On a medical case. Long ago.”

“What kind of case?”

“The kind a patient had rather I forgot.”

He waited.

She put the slip down.

“Were they practising this?” he asked.

“That is their story, Su Fan. Not a purse I open because you ask.”

He accepted the rebuke. He disliked it too.

There might be somebody who had already made sense of the book. Somebody who could tell him whether the warmth meant anything, whether the corrections were trustworthy, whether trying again would do more than hurt his ribs. Mother Wei knew something about such a person, and she was choosing not to give it to him.

He looked at the closed door to the treatment room.

Bao Shun was still talking. His voice came through indistinctly, private words about his hand and his daughter’s worries.

Su Fan turned back to his food.

Mother Wei took a clean page and copied four warnings. She did not copy the diagrams.

“When you’ve rested, two sessions a day. Brief ones. Stop while you still feel ordinary. If the pain returns, you come here.”

“How much rest?”

“Enough that you stop falling over the furniture.”

She tucked the copied warnings around the first slip, where he would have to move them to read.

“And you do not stop eating because you’re busy becoming an immortal.”

“I haven’t become anything.”

“Then you need the fish.”

***

The rest helped.

That annoyed him more than the pain had.

For three days he did nothing with the scripture except read it. He slept when the lamps went out, ate meals he could remember afterward and stopped trying to find a hidden movement every time he breathed.

His strength returned. So did his ability to distinguish a real sensation from the expectation of one.

Duan gave him work that used more eyes than force. Su Fan checked the marks on unfinished pieces, sorted good offcuts from metal that needed remelting and wrote down measurements while the smith worked.

At first he regarded this as being put aside.

Then he caught an error in his own previous list: two fittings with the same length but different shoulders, copied onto one line because he had been tired. Duan looked at the corrected figures and said nothing.

Being spared a remark was almost worse.

On the second afternoon Bao Mei came for a thin piece of discarded board. She wanted a flat one. Ah-Du offered her three bent ones and a strip with a nail through it, explaining that artists were supposed to overcome difficulties.

She left the nail strip on his stool.

Su Fan found her a better piece. He started to trim it for her, then remembered the wrist and asked Duan to make the cut.

The old smith did not charge. He did ask what the board was for.

“Practising boats,” she said.

“Boats need thicker wood.”

“Painted boats.”

“Then we can save on nails.”

After she left, the afternoon seemed less like waiting for his hand to recover.

At the forge Su Fan began noticing unnecessary movements. His right shoulder rose before every difficult blow. His left foot turned out when he was tired. He locked his knees while waiting for iron to heat.
