The habits had reasons. Raising the shoulder made him feel ready. Locking his knees let him lean without admitting he needed to sit. He did not remove them simply by noticing them.

Once, concentrating on his stance, he nearly missed Duan’s instruction to turn a piece.

“Watch the work,” the smith said.

Su Fan did.

Correcting the habits gave him no miraculous strength. It made the day slightly less painful. He could carry that small improvement to the next task without requiring it to prove anything larger.

At night he read the warnings and the corrections. Several disagreed. He began leaving blank space beside copied passages rather than choosing a meaning just because the page looked unfinished without one.

By the fourth evening he was well enough to want to do too much again.

Tan Wei arrived before he had the chance.

***

His friend carried a folded notice.

“Work bond,” he said. “They take the fee from future wages.”

Su Fan dried his hands before touching the paper.

Tan Wei watched him unfold it. He had flattened the creases so thoroughly that one corner had grown soft. Whatever the clerk said beneath the striped awning, Tan Wei had been thinking about it ever since.

The offer concerned a seasonal hauling crew at the river works. Successful candidates could qualify for a minor lease. The wages were poor. The promise was not.

“There’s no amount here for failure,” Su Fan said.

“Because I don’t intend to fail.”

“That isn’t an amount.”

Tan Wei sat on the anvil block.

“Read the rest.”

Su Fan did.

Accommodation. Meals. An instructor twice a week. A chance of admission to the branch. For someone who had spent six years being told to wait outside, the paper offered a door and a bed beyond it.

It also gave the contractor the right to extend service in an emergency.

“How long an extension?”

“I asked. They said emergencies don’t keep calendars.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is the answer they’re offering.”

Tan Wei held out his hand for the paper. Su Fan did not give it back immediately.

Duan was out. Ah-Du had gone to the market. The forge ticked as it cooled.

“What about work here?” Su Fan asked.

“What work here?”

“The weighing house. Carting.”

“They pay me when they need another pair of arms. Sometimes there’s work. Sometimes I walk up the hill to be told there isn’t.”

“The river crew can do that too.”

“The paper says they provide a bed even when the work stops.”

“For which they deduct—”

“I can read that line.”

Su Fan looked up.

Tan Wei’s face had closed slightly. Not into anger yet. Into the careful expression he wore when somebody explained a job he had already done for years.

“I’m not saying you can’t.”

“You’re saying all the reasons I shouldn’t.”

“There are reasons.”

“Yes. There are also reasons I went to the clerk.”

Su Fan handed the paper back.

Tan Wei smoothed it over his knee. “I asked about the instructor. His name is Han. He’s been at the gates longer than we’ve been alive. I asked whether somebody can start late. They said I’d hardly be the first.”

“They want workers.”

“I am a worker.”

Tan Wei rubbed the softened corner of the notice.

“Last week they needed someone to copy the delivery tables. I asked for it. They gave me the first page and watched while I tried to work out which figures belonged together.”

“You could have brought it here.”

“They needed somebody there, then. Not somebody who knew somebody who could do it.”

Su Fan looked down at the paper.

“I can read a notice,” Tan Wei continued. “I can count sacks. I can tell when the tally is short. But there are jobs where that isn't enough. The clerk says the trainees get lessons after work.”

“He said that, or it's written?”

“He said it. Yes, Fan, I know. Ask about that too.”

His friend drew a breath, then let it out more slowly.

“I'm not asking you to pretend the paper's wonderful. I'm asking you to understand that I found something on it I don't already have.”

Su Fan thought of the labels Mother Wei had held steady for him, the afternoons Duan spent teaching him measurements while pretending it was simply work that needed doing. He had not counted those lessons when comparing the two jobs.

The words were simple enough to leave him with nothing to improve in them.

For a moment he considered showing his friend the bamboo slips. There was another possibility, something he could not yet name or prove. He imagined Tan Wei looking at the stance drawing, then at the work-bond notice with its real address and real place to report.

The comparison would not favour the book.

“Let me ask Jiang’s office about the clause,” he said.

“The names go in tomorrow.”

“I know a porter who carries their letters.”

“Ask, then. But don’t miss tomorrow.”

Su Fan nodded.

Tan Wei stood, folded the notice and tucked it into his shirt. Before leaving he picked up one of the sound pins from the bench and admired the finish.

“You make this?”

“Most of it.”

“Good.”

He put it back exactly where he found it.

Then he went down the lane towards the square, walking with more purpose than he had brought into the smithy.

***

Su Fan borrowed the notice’s wording from memory and copied the emergency clause onto a scrap.

That was not good enough. He crossed it out. A mistaken word could produce an answer to a different question. He knew that much from Duan’s complaint.

Instead he described the offer and asked the clerk to identify its limits. What happened if a candidate failed to qualify? What obligation remained if he became ill? How long could service be extended, and who decided that an emergency had ended?

Those were reasonable questions.

He read them back and felt better.

Then he added the line asking for clarification before Tan Wei’s registration went forward.

His brush stopped above the page.

He could hear Tan Wei saying that the names went in tomorrow. He could also see Bao Shun’s arm on Mother Wei’s pallet, the foreman dictating the losses, the empty place on the record where the defective pin should have been mentioned.

A promise was harder to repair after somebody’s body depended on it.

He changed *before registration* to *before the registration is finalized*. The second wording seemed less obstructive. He left it.

Outside, the porter he knew was finishing a meal at the soup stall. Su Fan took the note to him before he could think of another question. The man said he could deliver it with the morning packets.

“Quick answer?” Su Fan asked.

“Depends who reads it.”

That should have made him hesitate. Instead he asked the porter to say it concerned the next intake.

On the way back he passed the turn leading to Tan Wei’s lodging.

There was still light enough to go there. He could explain the exact request. His friend might be annoyed, but he would know what Su Fan had asked on his behalf.

Su Fan stopped at the corner.

Then he went back to the smithy.

He told himself there was no answer to discuss yet. It would be better to bring useful information than another worry.

He did not write a second note to tell his friend exactly what he had asked.

chapters.title: The Uses of a Basket
chapters.text:
Auntie Lu had acquired a goose.

Nobody in Mudgate knew how. Old Pock claimed she had won it at dice. Auntie Lu claimed the goose had recognized superior management.

Whatever the arrangement, the bird now guarded the soup stall and bit anyone who tried to leave without paying.

It had bitten three paying customers as well.

“Still learning the trade,” Auntie Lu said.

Su Fan stopped beyond the reach of its neck. The goose tilted its head to inspect his shoes, then the bundle under his arm, then his shoes again. It seemed dissatisfied with all three.

“Bao Shun’s food,” he said.

“On the bench. Take the bowl back this time.”

“I took the last one back.”

“You brought back a bowl. Mine had no crack.”

“The crack was in the glaze.”

“That is where cracks begin.”

Old Pock sat at the end of the bench, holding his feet well clear of the ground. He was eating slowly enough that the goose had mistaken him for part of the furniture.

“Someone should teach it to recognize a paid account,” he said.

“Someone should settle one.”

“I was discussing the bird.”

“So was I.”

Auntie Lu wrapped two small jars of broth inside a cloth bundle heavy with rice. She tested both lids, tucked the loose cloth beneath them and placed the bundle where Su Fan could lift it without bending his bandaged wrist.

He counted out the five copper left after buying the books.

She took three and pushed the others back.

“That’s the price.”

“It was five yesterday.”

“Yesterday you wanted two people’s food. Today I am selling one person’s food in two containers. Keep up.”

Old Pock opened his mouth.

“Your price hasn’t changed,” she told him.

He closed it.

Su Fan put away the two coins. He knew better than to thank her in the particular voice people used when they thought they had caught her being kind. Instead he promised to return both jars.

“And the cloth.”

“And the cloth.”

“And nothing chipped.”

He moved around the goose. It followed him three steps, hissed at the bundle and abandoned the pursuit when a customer placed a coin on the counter.

Behind him Auntie Lu said, “No. That one has paid.”

The bird bit the customer anyway.

***

Bao Shun’s house stood far enough from the square that the laughter faded before Su Fan reached it.

The door was propped open. Bao Mei sat outside painting the edge of a discarded board. A row of tiny blue boats ran along it. She had set the paint cup inside a larger empty bowl so it would not spill when she dipped the brush.

“For the river festival?” Su Fan asked.

“For the shop.”

“What shop?”

“The one we’ll have if Father can’t pull ropes.”

She spoke without looking up. The brush travelled the last length of a boat, lifted and paused while she considered whether it needed a sail.

Inside, Bao Shun lay beneath a patched blanket. His arm rested in a wooden frame Mother Wei had made from broken shelving. The room smelled of broth from the previous day and the bitter ointment that seemed to follow everyone she treated.

He watched his daughter through the open door.

“She’s decided I’ll sell painted things,” he said.

“You might.”

“I can’t paint.”

“She can.”

“Then what will I do?”

Su Fan set down the food.

“Sell them.”

Bao Shun considered that with evident suspicion.

“I’m not much at talking people out of money.”

“Auntie Lu might teach you.”

“She’ll charge.”

“Probably.”

For a moment they both smiled.

Su Fan moved a chair beside the pallet and checked whether the jars would fit on it without touching the frame. Bao Shun tried to reach for one with the injured hand, stopped halfway through the movement and looked angrily at his own arm.

“Keep forgetting.”

“Here.”

Su Fan opened the lid before giving him the jar.

“I can do that,” Bao Shun said.

“I know.”

He put the second jar down unopened.

Bao Shun worked its lid free with his good hand and the edge of the blanket. It took longer. Neither man commented when he succeeded.

Outside, Bao Mei wiped her brush against the rim of the paint cup. She listened without appearing to listen.

“Anything from the quarry?” her father asked.

Su Fan had gone to the office that morning. He had expected an answer about compensation. The clerk had given him a list.

A certified incident account. Proof of employment. A witness to the condition of the brake. The work period in which the injury occurred. The date written in the same form on every sheet.

At the office, Su Fan had asked why the injury needed another witness when half the quarry had watched the cradle fall.

“Then you should have no difficulty finding one,” the clerk had said.

“I've found one. Ren Bo.”

“His signed account.”

“He'll sign.”

“When he has, bring it.”

The clerk had turned a sheet towards him. There were separate spaces for the worker's account and the supervisor's certification. The first space was nearly twice as large. Su Fan had mistaken that for a useful arrangement until the clerk explained that it was the second space that authorized payment.

“And if the supervisor won't?”

“Then the office requests his response.”

“How long?”

“That depends on when he responds.”

Su Fan had looked at the man's own hands. Ink stained two fingers. A little cut across the thumb had been wrapped in paper because there was no cloth within reach.

“Can I write the worker's account for him?”

“Yes. Read it to him afterward. He marks it.”

“His hand—”

“The other hand. A witness can confirm the mark.”

The clerk had pointed to a third space Su Fan had not noticed. That one could be completed without the foreman's permission.

It was not the money Bao Shun needed. It was still something that could be done.

Su Fan had copied the required headings carefully before leaving. On the way down he stopped at the weighing shed. Ren Bo agreed to describe what he had seen, but told him to bring the account when the afternoon carts had finished. There was a difference between willingness to help and having an hour in which to do it.

Now Su Fan took out the list.

Bao Shun looked at it without reaching for it.

“They have the employment record.”

“They want a copy.”

“They made the record.”

“I know.”

“Ren Bo saw the brake.”

“He’s agreed to sign.”

“The foreman?”

Su Fan folded the list along its existing crease.

“Not yet.”

Bao Shun nodded. He had worked enough years to understand what that meant.

“What does he say happened?”

“He hasn’t signed an account.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Su Fan could have repeated the suggestion that the pin might be the wrong problem to discuss, the way the clerk had written equipment losses before injury. He did not know whether any of it would help the man lying in front of him.

“I’m still collecting the papers,” he said.

Bao Shun turned the open jar slowly in his good hand.

“Don’t lose your own job over it.”

“I won’t.”

“You say that quickly.”

“I’ll be careful.”

“That’s slower. Better.”

He drank some broth. A drop ran down the outside of the jar. Before Su Fan could move, Bao Shun caught it with his thumb and wiped it on the cloth.

Through the doorway Bao Mei said, “I can go to the office.”

“You can go to school,” her father answered.

“I can do both.”

“The last time you argued with a clerk, you were buying paint.”

“He was selling the wrong blue.”

“An important dispute. We’ll save you for that.”

Her brush stopped. For a moment Su Fan thought she might cry. Then she dipped it into the colour and added another short line to the board.

Bao Shun saw too. He let his head rest against the wall and closed his eyes.

Su Fan left the food within reach, stacked the empty jars from the previous visit and went outside.

***

Bao Mei had added a ninth boat.

He found himself watching the brush. She did not grip it hard. When a line went wrong, she worked it into the next boat instead of scraping it away.

“Who taught you?”

“A woman on a ferry. She said my boats looked like shoes.”

“And now?”

“Better shoes.”

She held the board up.

The boats were not identical. One rode higher than the others. One had a sail so broad it looked likely to overturn. A small pair at the edge seemed to be following a fishing float rather than the current.

Su Fan liked the crowded, busy row. He could imagine it above the smithy bench, where nothing on the wall had been placed simply because somebody wanted to look at it.

“How much?”

Bao Mei glanced towards the door.

“For this?”

“Yes.”

“I haven’t finished the edge.”

“I can wait.”

She studied his face. He tried not to make an encouraging expression; she was already old enough to recognize that as a different kind of bargain.

“One copper.”

He had two left. He put one on the dry part of her work board.

She finished the edge before giving it to him. When he reached for it, she made him take the unpainted underside so he would not leave a thumbprint in the sky.

Bao Shun saw the transaction through the open doorway and closed his eyes.

Su Fan could not tell whether the purchase had helped.

He carried the board away flat, with the empty jars balanced in the crook of his other arm. Halfway down the lane he realized he had been holding his breath to keep from tilting it.

He stopped, rearranged the jars and breathed normally.

The painted boats survived.

***

That evening he used Min’s basket to carry six flat stones from the river.

He chose them from the shallow edge, where he would not have to pull them out of mud or brace himself against the current. Mother Wei had forbidden exertion while he recovered. She had not forbidden preparation. He repeated that distinction to himself while rejecting a stone that would plainly have broken the spirit of it.

A boy fishing from the bank watched him take the second load.

“Those aren’t skipping stones.”

“I’m not skipping them.”

“Why take them?”

“Practice.”

“For what?”

Su Fan set the basket down to adjust the cloth wrapped around its handle.

“I’ll tell you when I know.”

The boy regarded that as an unsatisfactory answer and returned to his float.

Su Fan made several trips rather than carry all six together. It took longer, which was probably part of Mother Wei’s intended lesson. By the time he finished, the light had turned soft on the river and the evening cooking fires were beginning.

At the smithy he set the stones in a row. Each was a different weight. He could not yet weigh the larger ones properly, so he marked their sizes in chalk and numbered them instead of pretending the numbers were measures.

He placed Bao Mei’s board on the bench where the paint could finish drying.

Duan came out with his supper.

“Are we selling stones?”

“No.”

“Good. Difficult market.”

He sat beside the largest one.

For a while Su Fan read and Duan ate. The town smelled of woodsmoke and damp reeds. Through an open door someone practised a flute badly and with considerable confidence. The same passage began three times, failing at a different note each time.

Duan looked towards the sound.

“Getting closer.”

“To what?”

“Finding a different instrument.”

He finished the last of his food and set the bowl between his feet.

“Min brought that to you?”

“I bought it.”

“Better. He gets peculiar when he thinks he’s giving a gift.”

“Do you know what it is?”

“A book you’ve stopped trying to hide. That’s progress.”

Su Fan hesitated, then showed him the first drawing.

Duan studied it with his head tilted. He turned the slip, brought it closer to his face and held it away again.

“My old master stood like that.”

“He cultivated?”

“He worked until he was eighty-three. At eighty-four he married a woman who kept ducks. I stopped visiting.”

“Why?”

“I disliked the ducks.”

“Did he ever say anything about the way he stood?”

“Usually that I was standing wrong.”

Duan rose to demonstrate. His knees were less willing than the drawing’s knees. He changed the angle of one foot and stopped before the movement became a performance.

“He’d put me beside the anvil and make me work with a light hammer until I stopped chasing the blow with my whole body. Miserable afternoons. I thought he was keeping me off the important work.”

“Was he?”

“Some days. I broke things.”

He returned the slip.

“A thing can be useful without being a secret of the heavens. Try not to overlook that.”

Su Fan looked at the six stones.

“I want to know which it is.”

“Then find out without making me hire someone to replace you.”

The smith picked up his bowl and went inside.

Su Fan placed Bao Mei’s painted board above the stones. Nine blue boats beneath the cracked eaves. The largest sail leaned slightly, and from this angle the boat beneath it looked cheerful rather than badly balanced.

He was still arranging the stones when Tan Wei came down the lane.

***

The notice in his friend’s hand had a red mark across the top.

“Delayed,” Tan Wei said. “The office has a question about my bond.”

Su Fan rose.

“What question?”

“They want clarification from the contractor before putting me through. The clerk showed me the mark. There’s a name for it, but I’ve forgotten.”

Su Fan had not forgotten the wording of his letter.

“When did they tell you?”

“This afternoon.”

“Did they give you an answer about the extension?”

“No. They gave me another date.”

Tan Wei looked at the notice, then smiled. The smile took a little effort, but he got it into place.

“Three weeks. They say there’s another intake. We can earn half the fee by then.”

“I didn’t say I was—”

“I know. But you’ll tell me where somebody needs a cart unloaded, and you’ll pretend that isn’t helping.”

He put the rejected notice in the cold furnace and sat beside the smallest stone.

Su Fan could have told him then. The words were short enough. *I asked them to clarify it before you were registered.* There would be anger. Perhaps not as much anger as he expected. Perhaps more.

Tan Wei stretched his legs and inspected the painted board.

“Mei?”

“Yes.”

“She’s getting good.”

“One copper.”

“I didn’t ask the price.”

Su Fan looked down.

“What are these?” Tan Wei asked, touching the nearest chalk mark.

“Practice.”

“For what?”

Su Fan looked at the unread scripture on his knee.

“I’m not sure yet.”

Tan Wei picked up the smallest stone, tested its weight and put it back in the same place.

“Well,” he said. “We’ve got three weeks.”

chapters.title: The Dark Bowl
chapters.text:
The annual assessment came to Mudgate in a wagon with polished wheels.

Two disciples unloaded the jade bowls. A third hung a banner explaining that the Hollow Reed Sect offered every worthy child a path to greatness.

Old Pock read it aloud.

“Every worthy child,” he repeated. “We’ve been misplacing ours.”

Auntie Lu told him to stop talking in front of the children.

Then she charged the disciples twice the usual price for breakfast.

Su Fan had come to carry water. Mother Wei wanted every child to drink before standing in the sun. The assessor allowed it because a fainting applicant made a poor impression on his report.

“Keep the wet cups away from the papers,” he said.

Su Fan placed the water table on the other side of the awning. A disciple moved it back because it interfered with the line. They settled the matter by turning the table sideways and having the children approach from the lane.

Such arrangements occupied the important people for several minutes. The children watched them with the intense attention of prisoners learning the habits of their guards.

One small boy asked whether drinking would wash the lineage out of his hand.

“No,” Su Fan said.

“Not even a little?”

“No.”

His older sister took the cup from him. “He asked me that six times.”

“Ask me again after you drink,” Su Fan told the boy.

The child drank cautiously, inspecting his palm between mouthfuls.

At the edge of the awning, Tan Wei waited in his cleanest shirt. He had repaired a loose fastening with thread that did not quite match.

“Again?” Su Fan asked.

“Again.”

“You’re too old for the children’s test.”

“They have a work-bond bowl.”

It stood on a smaller table beyond the main one. The jade was less polished. The attendant used it to check whether a candidate’s body could bear a minor lineage thread, rather than whether a preserved founder’s pattern would answer directly.

Su Fan looked away before his concern became an argument.

“The delay?”

“Registration. They said I can still get the eligibility paper.”

Tan Wei spoke matter-of-factly. He had learned another distinction while Su Fan was deciding what the distinction ought to be.

“Then that’s useful,” Su Fan said.

His friend gave him a brief, surprised look.

The assessor rang the bell.

***

The first child knelt.

Nothing happened.

The assessor turned her hand, waited, and had the attendant wipe the bowl before trying once more. Her mother leaned forward so far that the disciple beside the table had to ask her to step back.

Still nothing.

The girl stood without looking at anyone. At the water table she asked whether she could drink now. Su Fan gave her a full cup. She held it in both hands and stayed beside him until her mother was ready to leave.

The second child produced a faint green light.

At first it was only a glimmer around the fingers. The assessor adjusted something beneath the bowl, and the light steadied. Her grandmother began to cry. The child looked frightened by the crying until the old woman laughed through it.

The assessor spoke a founder’s name and gave them a paper directing them to the branch office.

They remained under the awning longer than the first family. There were questions about dates, a place to report, what to bring and which payment was due first. Success required more explanation than failure.

The family would have to sell their mule to pay for registration.

They were already discussing which relative might buy it when Su Fan brought another cup. The grandmother wanted the child’s uncle to take the animal. The mother said the uncle had not paid for the last thing he bought. The newly eligible child touched the wet patch her hand had left on the cup and said nothing.

“You’ve had that mule years,” Su Fan said before thinking.

Her mother looked up.

“And I’ve had her longer.”

He nodded, embarrassed. She took the cup and thanked him anyway.

The child tugged her sleeve.

“Do I go today?”

“No,” her mother said. Then she looked at the paper again. “I don't think so.”

The grandmother began describing a relative who lived nearer the branch. She knew someone who might take the girl for a night. The mother wanted to ask about bedding first. They had brought their best shirt and a packet of food; nobody had thought to bring the dimensions of a future bed.

Su Fan pointed to the line naming the reporting day.

“There. You have time to ask.”

The child studied it with him.

“Can I take my things?”

“Ask them,” her mother said.

“Can I come home?”

That question stopped both women. The grandmother opened her mouth, closed it and handed the paper back to the mother.

“We'll ask that too.”

They returned to the attendant, waiting at the side of the awning rather than stepping into the assessment line. The girl carried the cup with both hands. At the table she put it down well away from the documents, remembering the rule the adults had spent so long arguing about.

Su Fan watched the attendant find another notice. This time the mother read it before smiling. Her finger followed several lines, and she asked him to explain one twice.

When they left, the grandmother was still discussing the mule. The girl had begun telling her which of her clothes needed mending before she went. The light in the bowl had not settled their lives. It had given them a great deal to arrange.

The line moved.

Some children answered faintly. Most did not. A few were too restless to keep a hand still, and one boy began to cry before he reached the table. His father tried to lift him into place. The assessor told them to walk around the square and return when he could breathe without sobbing.

It was kinder than Su Fan expected. It did not make the dark bowls less dark.

By late morning he knew which parents wanted a word and which wanted only room to gather their children. He stopped saying that the test did not matter. To people who had spent money washing a good shirt and taking a day away from work, it plainly did.

Instead he kept the cups full.

A disciple complained that someone had set a muddy shoe against a box intended for the bowls. Old Pock moved the shoe, wiped the box with his sleeve and asked whether that restored the founder’s dignity.

Auntie Lu called him back before the disciple answered.

Su Fan fetched more water.

***

At midday Ko Lin arrived wearing a disciple’s sash.

He was Tan Wei’s cousin, eighteen and visibly pleased to be recognized. Mudgate had talked about his admission for months. He had gone up the mountain two years earlier with a lineage response bright enough to draw a patron’s notice.

The sash still changed the way people made space around him.

He paused to greet a woman who had known him before he wore it. She asked whether he was eating properly. He said yes. She told him he looked thin and offered him a bun. His careful dignity lasted until she wrapped two for him to take away.

Then he stopped beside Tan Wei and adjusted a cuff that needed no adjusting.

“You should have asked me.”

“I did,” Tan Wei said.

Ko Lin’s smile faltered.

“I’ve been busy.”

“So have we.”

Su Fan handed him water before the pause hardened.

Ko Lin accepted it, then noticed the bandaged wrist.

“Still at the forge?”

“Yes.”

“You ought to try for labour admission. Better than staying here.”

“What do they pay?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then I’ll keep looking.”

Ko Lin frowned. Su Fan had meant the answer more sharply than necessary and could hear it now that it was too late to take the sharpness back.

“I meant there are opportunities,” the disciple said.

“I know.”

“No, you make it sound as though I came down to insult you.”

Tan Wei took one of the wrapped buns from his cousin’s hand.

“He sounds like that before he eats. Give him the other one.”

Ko Lin looked from one friend to the other, then surrendered the bun with a reluctant laugh.

Su Fan accepted it. “Thank you.”

They ate standing beside the water table. For a few moments the conversation concerned ordinary things: a familiar roof repaired badly, somebody’s brother taking work upriver, the goose that now supervised Auntie Lu’s customers.

Ko Lin had not heard about the goose. He listened with evident delight until he realized two children were watching him laugh with his mouth full. Then he swallowed, straightened his sash and asked where the work-bond attendant was.

As he lifted his cup, his fingers trembled.

Su Fan had seen the same tremor in men who worked through exhaustion. He did not know what caused it in a disciple who smelled faintly of expensive medicine.

Ko Lin steadied the cup with his other hand. He saw Su Fan notice and lowered it at once.

“Cold water,” he said.

Su Fan did not agree or contradict him. He took the empty cup and rinsed it.

The attendant called Tan Wei’s name.

***

Tan Wei went under the awning.

He handed over the delayed notice first. The attendant examined the red mark, found his name on another list and drew a short line beside it. He did not ask why registration had been delayed.

Su Fan stood where he could see without crowding the table.

Tan Wei wiped his palm against his trousers, realized what he had done and looked around for a clean cloth. The attendant supplied one with the bored patience of someone who had watched the same gesture all morning.

“Flat. Don’t press.”

The little bowl glowed blue.

Only a thread of light. Nothing like the green blaze around the child from the morning. It ran along the base of Tan Wei’s fingers, dimmed, then held.

But it was light.

Tan Wei stared until the attendant told him to move his hand.

“Work-bond eligibility confirmed. Water branch, grade four.”

“Grade four?”

“The paper explains where to report.”

“I can see it again?”

The attendant looked at the waiting candidates. His expression softened by a fraction.

“You’ll have plenty of time to look at water in the branch.”

Tan Wei took the paper carefully between finger and thumb. Outside the awning he stopped in the sun as though he needed different light to make certain the characters remained the same.

Ko Lin slapped his shoulder.

“There. Our family isn’t finished yet.”

Tan Wei laughed. He looked for Su Fan in the crowd.

Su Fan raised his cup.

He was glad. The gladness did not quite cover the other thing he felt.

His friend had gone to the table and received an answer that could be carried in a sleeve, shown at a gate, used to obtain instruction. Su Fan had a book with disputed arrows and sensations he could not reliably repeat.

He disliked himself for making the comparison while Tan Wei was smiling.

So he crossed the space between them and asked to see the paper.

Tan Wei handed it over at once.

“Read the last part,” he said.

Su Fan read the reporting instructions and the note about training. They were practical, ordinary sentences. He read them aloud anyway.

Ko Lin was called away by one of the visiting disciples. He promised to ask after the registration and left before either friend could tell him whether that would help.

Tan Wei watched his cousin go.

“He means it when he says it.”

“Will he remember?”

“We’ll find out.”

He folded the eligibility paper and put it inside the notice with the red mark. For the moment the two documents could share a pocket without spoiling each other.

***

Near the end of the day the assessor asked Su Fan to help pack the bowls.

He had carried six buckets and earned one copper. A second copper for packing was difficult to refuse.

The disciples dismantled the awning while he wrapped the jade. Each bowl had its own fitted place in the travelling case. The attendant checked the padding, corrected the position of one hinge and told him not to leave the smaller bowl on the edge of the table.

Su Fan moved it inward.

Six years since the first test.

In the evenings since finding the bamboo slips, he had felt something pass from his chest into his back. Nothing stable enough to name. Nothing anyone else had verified. Yet the memory waited in his hand as he touched the bowl’s rim.

He knew what the bowl tested.

He also knew what he wanted from it.

The attendant had turned to help fold the banner. Su Fan placed his palm inside the smaller bowl.

The jade stayed cool.

He waited.

He did not arrange his breath into the new exercise. Doing so felt like asking a question in one language and demanding the answer in another. He simply stood with his hand in the bowl while the square emptied around him.

The jade remained dark.

“Nothing?” the attendant asked.

Su Fan took his hand away.

“Nothing.”

“Don’t fret. Most don’t answer.”

The man meant it kindly. Su Fan was too tired to decide whether that made it easier.

He wrapped the bowl in cloth. The case lid would not close because one corner of the wrapping had folded over the latch. He opened it, smoothed the cloth and tried again.

This time it shut properly.

The attendant paid him. The disciples loaded the cases. When the wagon moved, its polished wheels cut through the same wet patch left by Su Fan’s water buckets.

He found Tan Wei waiting by the well.

***

On the walk home, his friend talked about Master Han.

Han would teach the new work-bond candidates. He had been a gate operator for forty years, had put his own sons through training and lost one to a fever. The clerk said he was patient with late beginners.

Tan Wei repeated the last detail twice.

“He sounds decent,” Su Fan said.

His friend stopped walking.

“What?”

“He sounds decent.”

“No. Say the first part again. Without that face.”

Su Fan tried.

Tan Wei laughed and went ahead.

At the lane leading to the smithy they parted. Tan Wei wanted to show the eligibility paper to someone else before the light went. He did not say who. Su Fan did not ask for a list of everybody entitled to share his good news.

The six stones waited beneath Bao Mei’s painted board.

He set the two earned copper on the bench. Then he stood in the yard, looking at the smallest stone until the urge to prove something immediately began to subside.

The bowl had done what it was made to do. It had answered one question about him, the same question it answered six years before. His disappointment did not make it a dishonest instrument.

It also did not make it the only instrument in the world.

He bent, picked up the smallest stone and felt its familiar weight settle into his palm.

Tomorrow he would ask it a question he could count.

chapters.title: The First Circuit
chapters.text:
The stone did not rise by itself.

Su Fan had not seriously expected it to. He was still disappointed.

He held it at shoulder height, breathed as the scripture directed and watched his wrist tremble. Bao Mei’s painted boats hung above the other stones. The largest sail leaned towards the door, where Ah-Du had pinned a scrap bearing a crooked warning that nobody was to borrow the practice weights for throwing at dogs.

Su Fan had made him add *or people*.

On an ordinary day he could hold the smallest stone for one hundred slow counts. On a bad day, eighty. His injured wrist currently allowed sixty-three.

He wrote the number down.

The next evening: sixty-eight.

The evening after: sixty-five.

Duan watched him record the failure.

“You’re healing,” the smith said. “Don’t give the book credit for your hand.”

“I held it longer yesterday.”

“Perhaps yesterday you’d done less work.”

Su Fan looked at the list. Yesterday he had sorted finished fittings. Today he had spent the morning on the bellows before Duan reminded him to change hands.

“Then I need to do it at the same time.”

“That might help.”

“Before work.”

“After breakfast.”

Su Fan crossed out the heading he had written above the figures. Under the numbers he added: *No proof.*

It was irritating how often a useful correction resembled being told to eat.

He moved the paper to a board where he could record the hour, the work done beforehand and whether the wrist hurt. The page grew more complicated. The result did not become more impressive.

A week passed.

He did his work. He carried food to Bao Shun. He practised briefly before the day began and again after the furnace cooled. Some days the warmth came. On others he felt only the pulse beneath his skin and a strong desire for something less patient to happen.

The book described a complete circuit, beginning below the breastbone and returning without changing character. Its drawing had arrows, but several were disputed by later readers. One return line had been scratched so thoroughly that the bamboo beneath it was nearly transparent.

Su Fan tried copying the alternatives on separate scraps.

Laid side by side, they looked like instructions to different bodies.

He had only his own.

***

At first he tried to follow the clearest drawing because it was the clearest.

The feeling moved where it chose, which was mostly nowhere. If he anticipated the next part of the route, he tightened around it. If he tried to ignore the route completely, he became so busy ignoring it that his breath changed anyway.

Once he caught himself wondering what face he would make when he told Tan Wei.

The warmth disappeared while he rehearsed the conversation.

He put the book down and spent the rest of that session cleaning the lamp.

The next morning he followed the sensation he actually had.

It went down the right side of his torso, caught near the hip and vanished whenever he anticipated the catch. Nothing in the drawing explained why that particular place should resist. He shifted his stance, tried again and felt the same small interruption.

There was an old bruise there, though bruise was no longer the right word. The skin had long since returned to its ordinary colour. The spot remained tender if he knocked it against a bench corner, and he had developed a way of turning that kept the sore side away from heavy loads.

He had stopped noticing that he did it.

Mother Wei noticed when he went to ask.

“You fell from Duan’s loft at sixteen.”

“I remember.”

“You remember getting up. I remember putting you back down.”

He had been reaching for a bundle of old iron when the board shifted. He remembered the floor arriving before he had found anything to catch. He also remembered insisting that the fall had not been far, as though height were the only thing that could make landing hurt.

Mother Wei examined the place. Then she made him step sideways, turn and reach for an empty bowl on a shelf.

He performed the little movements easily until she asked him to do the same ones without turning his foot first.

“There,” she said.

He felt it. A tightening that arrived before the movement, as if his body expected the floor to strike him again.

“It kept the sore place safe,” she said. “Now you’re asking it to stop.”

“How?”

“Carefully.”

“That’s not much of an instruction.”

“It has kept you alive through several of your better ideas.”

She showed him the ordinary range he could move through without pain. When he tried to go farther to prove the difference, she stopped him.

“Not today.”

He wanted to argue that the book concerned resistance and that this appeared to be the particular resistance preventing the circuit. Before he could, she asked whether the book had examined his hip.

“No.”

“Then let me finish.”

He did.

She sent him away with a warning against proving her right.

***

For four days he worked on that small tightening.

Not continuously. That had gone badly before. He let the ordinary tasks tell him when he was doing it: turning away from the anvil, reaching for a tool, stepping aside in a narrow lane. At times he relaxed it. At other times he forgot, then remembered too late to do anything except notice.

One afternoon he carried a repaired stool to Bao Shun's house. The old one rocked whenever the injured man tried to stand, and Bao Mei had asked whether Duan could shorten a leg.

“It's the floor,” Bao Shun said when Su Fan set it down.

The repaired stool rocked too.

Su Fan looked at the shortened leg, then at the uneven boards beneath it. He had measured a piece of furniture on the smithy's level bench and fixed the wrong part of the problem.

Bao Shun waited while he turned the stool and found a position where all four legs touched.

“There,” Su Fan said.

“Good. Now I can't reach the table.”

They moved the table. That blocked the passage to the door. Bao Mei put down her brush, took a thin offcut from her painting pile and slid it beneath the short leg.

The stool stopped rocking in its original place.

Su Fan looked at her.

“Father told me that yesterday,” she said. “I forgot to tell you.”

Bao Shun began to laugh, carefully, so he would not jar his arm. Su Fan joined him. There was nothing else useful to do with the morning he had spent correcting a sound stool.

On the walk back, he noticed himself preparing to turn his sore hip away from a gap between two carts. He slowed, passed through at an ordinary angle and found the movement painless.

He did not decide the hip had been cured. He tried the same turn again in the empty yard, where there was no cart to blame if it hurt.

He did not announce each discovery to Ah-Du.

The boy nevertheless became suspicious when Su Fan stopped halfway through crossing the yard to stare at his own foot.

“Dropped something?”

“No.”

“You keep looking.”

“I’m checking a movement.”

“Does it need a witness?”

“Not yet.”

Ah-Du went back to grinding a rough edge off a small hinge. He disliked the work because a hinge had to be smooth in places nobody admired. Su Fan sat beside him and held the piece while the boy changed his grip.

“That way,” he said. “You’re pressing against yourself.”

Ah-Du tried the new angle. The file moved more easily.

“Did the book teach you that?”

“Duan.”

“Then why didn’t you tell me yesterday?”

Because yesterday he had been looking for something important inside his chest rather than watching the apprentice struggle with the file.

“I wasn’t paying attention.”

The boy accepted the answer and handed him the hinge to inspect.

That evening the smallest stone felt ordinary. His wrist trembled at a slightly higher count than before. He wrote it down without adding a triumphant heading.

The warmth reached the hip and stopped.

He went to bed.

Then, on a morning so ordinary that he later struggled to recall the weather, it passed.

***

He stood in the yard before the furnace reached working heat.

The air smelled of cold ash and somebody’s breakfast onions. Ah-Du was inside opening the shutters. Duan had gone to collect a delivery. There was no audience worth performing for, and Su Fan had not expected the morning to differ from the last one.

The warmth moved down the right side of his torso.

He felt the familiar point at the hip. His body prepared to tighten. He noticed the preparation before it became the movement and let the next breath occur without correcting it.

The warmth travelled down his leg.

He nearly lost it in surprise.

His first impulse was to shift his stance so it could continue. He stayed where he was instead. The sensation reached his foot, crossed into a return he could feel more clearly than he could explain and rose through his back.

Under the breastbone, it met its own beginning.

For a moment everything in him seemed to settle against something solid.

His knees bent.

A hairline crack opened in the yard’s hard-packed surface beneath his left heel.

Su Fan stopped breathing by accident.

The sensation broke.

He sat down hard enough to bruise himself.

Ah-Du leaned out of the smithy window.

“Did standing defeat you?”

“Go inside.”

“Should I get Wei?”

Su Fan considered his body carefully. The place where he had landed hurt. His pulse raced. His right hip felt unfamiliar but not painful. Nothing suggested that a bone or a muscle had suddenly become something it was not supposed to be.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“No. Stay there.”

The boy stayed.

For a while Su Fan did nothing. He listened to the small noises from the street and waited until he could distinguish a change in his body from the excitement of believing something had changed.

The warmth remained, faintly. It occupied a route rather than appearing at one isolated point. He could not hold it steadily, but he could find it without chasing the first feeling through his ribs.

He looked at the crack beneath his heel.

The yard had been dry for several days. Packed earth cracked for ordinary reasons. He knew this. He also knew what the ground had felt like under his foot a moment before he sat down.

He was not going to decide everything from one mark in the dirt.

He took the smallest stone.

This time it felt different.

Not lighter. He still knew its weight. His arm simply accepted the load without the scattered trembling he had used to carry it. There was effort, but it no longer seemed to arrive from several parts of him arguing over the same burden.

At one hundred counts he was still holding it.

He nearly set it down from habit.

At two hundred he lowered it carefully onto the others.

His muscles were tired. His wrist did not throb.

He stared at the chalk mark on the stone until Ah-Du came outside.

“Well?” the boy asked.

Su Fan held out his hand. Ah-Du put two fingers in it. Su Fan closed his grip gently, expecting to show a small difference.

The boy’s eyes widened.

“Don’t.”

Su Fan released him at once.

For a while neither spoke.

“Did I hurt you?”

“No.” Ah-Du flexed his fingers. “Just don’t do it again without saying.”

“I thought I was being gentle.”

“Try thinking slower.”

Su Fan nodded. That was fair.

Then Ah-Du whispered, “Does this mean you can hit Ko Lin?”

“No.”

“Eventually?”

“We are not practising for Ko Lin.”

The boy looked disappointed but not discouraged.

Su Fan sent him for Mother Wei.

***

Waiting for her was worse than waiting for the warmth had been.

He put the stones back in order. He checked the crack in the earth without touching it. He washed his hands, then realized washing them had accomplished nothing relevant and laughed at himself once.

When Mother Wei arrived, he had prepared three different ways to explain what happened.

She asked him to sit before he could use any of them.

She checked his pulse, listened to his breathing and made him walk the length of the yard. He told her about the circuit. She asked where the discomfort had been, whether he had lost feeling anywhere, whether the fall had struck the old hip injury.

“No. No. The other side.”

“Then stop looking offended by the questions.”

“I’m not offended.”

“You want a different set.”

He did. He wanted her to ask what it had felt like to cross the boundary he had been told all his life did not exist for him. He wanted her to name it before he dared name it himself.

Instead she examined his wrist and asked him to lift the stone again.

This time, under observation, the circuit faltered.

The warmth reached his side, wavered and disappeared. He tried to recover it. His shoulder rose. Pain flickered in the wrist.

Mother Wei took the stone from him.

“That will do.”

“You saw.”

“I saw.”

“What is it?”

She looked at the cracked earth beneath his foot, then at the notes on the board.

“I think you know.”

“Think.”

“Yes. Think. I don’t have a bowl in my kitchen that answers this question for me.”

He had wanted an announcement. A name spoken by somebody entitled to speak it. The kind of certainty given freely to a child with a bright bowl.

Mother Wei could offer an uncertain diagnosis and a hand on his shoulder.

It should have felt insufficient.

Instead he found that he could not speak.

She sat beside him until he could.

Ah-Du had gone back to the furnace. He made an unnecessary amount of noise opening and closing a tool chest, giving them privacy in the only way the small yard allowed.

Su Fan rubbed his palms against his knees. They looked exactly as they had looked yesterday: old burns, ingrained soot, the tender place at the base of the thumb.

“I did it once,” he said at last.

“Then learn whether you can do it again without hurting yourself.”

“And if I can?”

“We’ll have another question.”

He nodded.

The joy came slowly, too large to fit the little smile he tried first. It was not certainty. It was enough that he no longer had to borrow certainty from the people who had tested him at thirteen.

“Don’t tell the whole town yet,” he said.

“No.”

“Or Tan Wei.”

Her hand paused.

“Not yet,” he added.

He could have said he wanted a stable result before telling his friend. That was true. He could have said he did not want to distract Tan Wei from the work-bond opportunity. That was less true, and he knew it before the words formed.

Mother Wei took her hand away.

“That is your choice.”

He heard the difference between agreement and permission.

He chose not to answer it.

chapters.title: The Wrong Batch
chapters.text:
Steward Jiang returned Duan’s letter with the pin inside a sealed box.

The box arrived in the hands of a woman who introduced herself as Sun Lian and asked whether the smithy repaired boat knees.

Duan asked which boat had knees.

“The kind that keeps its sides attached.”

“I know what a knee is.”

“Then why ask?”

“To establish the tone.”

Sun Lian put the box on the bench and smiled.

She was about twenty-six, sun-browned and broad across the shoulders. Her braid had been looped through itself to keep it out of the way. A short knife hung from a belt crowded with measuring cords. She looked at the roof repair, the sorted stock and the forge before she looked at the sign above the door.

“I was coming downriver. The steward paid me to bring this.”

“Paid you what?” Duan asked.

“Enough not to tell you.”

He liked her immediately and tried not to show it.

Su Fan took the delivery slip. The number matched the receipt Duan had kept when Jiang’s office requested the sample. He checked the seal before handing the box to the smith.

Sun Lian watched.

“You expected someone to change it?”

“I expected to check.”

“Good. Sign there, then.”

She did not hand over her copy until his name was dry.

Inside the box the pin lay in fresh wrapping. Its broken centre remained visible. Jiang’s reply was brief: the batch had been manufactured for secondary gate fittings, not load-bearing quarry gear. The contractor would replace the affected pieces. Compensation required the original purchase order.

Duan read that part twice.

“The purchase order is in the foreman’s office,” Su Fan said.

“Then that’s where we’ll ask.”

“Does it say why it was used?”

“No.”

Su Fan read the letter himself. Jiang had named the material specification and the intended category of work. She had not claimed the pin sound, nor admitted that the office knew how it reached the brake. The distinction mattered. It also left Bao Shun waiting for a paper someone else held.

Sun Lian had picked up a sound pin from the bench.

“This is yours?”

“Yes,” Duan said.

“Make me six.”

“You haven’t asked the price.”

“I’ve asked the quality.”

She turned the piece, inspected the shoulder and tested the fit against a small wooden pattern from her belt. The pattern had been used often enough that the edges shone.

“Not exactly this length,” she said. “This shoulder. A little more here. I’ll leave the pattern.”

“Leave the dimensions too.”

“Can’t you measure?”

“I can. So can you. Best to discover whether we agree before the iron’s finished.”

Sun Lian found a clear scrap and drew the required shape. Duan corrected the way she had indicated one allowance. She explained where the pin would seat. Neither appeared offended by the other’s insistence on details.

She put down two silver as a deposit.

Duan stopped pretending not to like her.

“The first two by dusk,” he said.

“I’ll collect them here.”

“Bring the knee after.”

“I’ll bring the measurements. The knee is attached to the boat.”

“That would explain its reluctance to visit.”

She laughed, took her signed receipt and went out.

For a few breaths the smithy seemed more like a place where useful work brought money than a room full of unanswered complaints.

Then Duan put Jiang’s letter into his coat.

“Come on.”

***

The quarry road had been cleared.

Su Fan could still identify the scar where the cradle struck, but new dust lay over it. The crushed trough had gone. A replacement line hung at the rope station. Men worked above the same stretch of road, looking down more often than they used to.

At the gate Ren Bo was counting carts. He saw them, glanced at Duan’s coat where the letter protruded and returned to his tally.

The foreman received them standing behind a desk too large for the room.

Duan laid out Jiang’s reply.

“We need the original order for this batch.”

The foreman read without offering them seats. His eyes slowed over the compensation sentence, moved to the seal and went back to the beginning.

“The office handles that.”

“The steward’s office says the purchase order comes from here.”

“All orders come through records.”

“Then fetch the record.”

The foreman looked at Duan over the paper. The smith returned the look without changing his expression.

At last the foreman opened a drawer. He shifted two bundles, examined a folded sheet and put it back. He opened another drawer, moving more things than he appeared to read.

Then he sent a clerk to the records shed.

Su Fan watched the clerk pass through the yard. Outside the window four guards stood beneath the wall’s strip of shade. Two wore cultivation sashes. One was peeling an apple with a small bright knife, keeping the skin in a single curling strip.

The clerk returned without the order.

“Misfiled,” the foreman said.

Duan stood in the doorway with his arms folded.

“Find it.”

“You don’t give instructions here.”

“No. I sell you iron. Different arrangement.”

“We buy from more than one smith.”

“I’ve seen what that gets you.”

Su Fan felt the room tighten around the words.

The foreman put down Jiang’s letter. Carefully. He aligned its edge with a ledger already on the desk.

“You brought the pin down,” he said to Su Fan.

“Yes.”

“Before anyone could examine it here.”

“Bao Shun needed the clinic.”

“I asked about the pin.”

Su Fan looked at Duan. The old smith’s arms had come unfolded.

“The number was recorded at the quarry,” Su Fan said. “Before we left.”

“By you.”

“Yes.”

The foreman leaned back.

“Perhaps it was switched.”

Duan moved so quickly that Su Fan caught his sleeve before thinking.

The old smith stopped.

Outside, the guard with the apple looked through the open doorway. His knife had ceased moving. The peel hung from its blade.

Duan was a man with a hammer. Su Fan was newly able to hold a stone longer than before. Neither fact changed the number of guards in the yard or the authority they carried.

He released Duan’s sleeve as soon as he was certain the smith would stay where he was.

“We’ll ask the steward about the missing order,” he said.

“Ask whoever you like.”

“And the account of the accident?”

“Under review.”

“Ren Bo has—”

“Under review.”

The foreman slid the letter back across the desk.

They left with no paper.

***

Halfway down the road Duan shook off Su Fan’s hand, though Su Fan had not been holding him since the office.

“I wasn’t going to hit him.”

“I know.”

“You don’t know.”

“No.”

Duan breathed out through his nose.

“The boy has some sense. Infuriating.”

They walked in silence until they reached the weighing shed. The afternoon carts had begun arriving, each driver hoping to be counted before the line grew. Ren Bo called out a weight, waited for the man beside him to repeat it and cut the figure into his tally.

He stepped away as they approached.

“Dropped this,” he said.

Neither of them had.

Duan took the stick he offered. One face carried the number of the rejected batch. The other held smaller figures cut shallowly beneath the wax.

Night deliveries. Three carts. Not to the quarry, but through it.

Su Fan looked up.

“Who collected them?”

Ren Bo watched the guardhouse.

“River works. Men with blue cords around their wrists.”

“Lease workers?”

“I count carts.”

“Which gate?”

“That’s not what I count.”

The foreman appeared at the top of the steps.

Ren Bo lifted his voice.

“Don’t leave your tools lying about. Somebody has to clean up.”

He went inside.

Su Fan and Duan continued walking. They did not look back until the bend hid the office from view.

Duan turned the tally once in his palm, then wrapped it inside the letter.

“He’ll be asked about it,” Su Fan said.

“Then don’t give the foreman an easy answer.”

“He could lose his place.”

“He knew where he was standing when he handed it over.”

Su Fan remembered Ren Bo hesitating over the spare rope while Bao Shun bled against the wheel. It had been easy to judge that hesitation. Harder to know what the man stood to lose on a day when nobody was watching a cradle fall.

He could not make the tally safer by being grateful loudly.

At the smithy, Duan put the papers away and went to the fire. The new pins still had to be finished. Their customer would not accept anger in place of the two pieces promised by dusk.

Su Fan took the tongs.

***

The work steadied them.

Duan checked the metal’s heat. Su Fan turned the piece. Ah-Du watched the bellows and stayed unusually quiet until the first pin came off the anvil.

“Did they pay?” he asked.

“No.”

“Did they promise to pay?”

“No.”

“Then why did you go?”

Duan held the pin against the wooden pattern.

“To establish what kind of people we’re dealing with.”

Ah-Du looked at Su Fan. “Didn’t we know?”

“Turn,” Su Fan told him.

The boy turned the handle.

Su Fan felt the warmth of his first circuit while moving the iron. It came and went. He did not try to strengthen it with the hot piece in the tongs. The work required him to hold something dangerous at the right angle, not discover what happened when he lost concentration.

One of the pin shoulders was slightly too broad. Duan marked it for filing. The second came out closer to the pattern. Neither was perfect merely because Su Fan had begun to cultivate.

By dusk the first two were ready.

Sun Lian arrived carrying a roll of sailcloth and a parcel that smelled of fried onions. She put both beside the door, inspected the pins and passed them through the wooden pattern without comment.

Duan waited.

“Good,” she said.

“You make a man work for praise.”

“I paid a deposit. That was fairly enthusiastic.”

Su Fan brought out the delivery marks.

Sun Lian stopped turning the new iron in her hand.

“I’ve seen those carts.”

“Where?”

“At the eighth gate. They were unloading after dark.”

“Why after dark?”

She looked at him long enough to decide something.

“Because daytime is when the inspectors come.”

Duan shut the smithy door.

***

The three of them sat around the bench. Su Fan laid out the broken pin, a sound replacement and Ren Bo’s tally. Jiang’s letter stayed beside the pieces, its official seal visible in the lamplight.

Sun Lian read it twice.

“This says secondary fittings,” she said.

“Yes.”

“That doesn’t mean the water can reach the valley if one breaks.”

“It means this shouldn’t have been in the quarry brake,” Duan said.

She nodded. “That much it means.”

Su Fan was impatient for the pieces to form a larger answer. He could see how they might. He could not yet show where each piece joined the next.

Sun Lian tapped the gate number on the tally.

“They’re renewing the lower couplings before the high-water season. My boat’s on their supply contract. That’s why I’m here.”

“You carried these?”

“No. Those three carts went by road. I carried timber and other stores. I was still unloading when they arrived.”

“Did you see the pieces?”

“Crates. Men moving crates. The marks were clear enough. I had no reason then to ask what was inside.”

Duan turned the broken pin so the centre faced her.

“Will the gates hold?”

“With the right materials? Probably.”

“Will they hold with these?”

“No.”

She let the answer stand, then added, “We still need to know where they put them.”

Su Fan nodded. He disliked the qualification less coming from someone who had actually stood at the gate.

“What can you see from the landing?”

“Less than you want.”

“And with a delivery tally?”

“More.”

Outside, somebody was testing festival drums. The rhythm stumbled, recovered and began again. Through the shutter crack came the smell of evening meals and the ordinary traffic of a town that expected the river to stay where it belonged.

Sun Lian wrapped the new pins and tied them to her belt.

“I go upriver tomorrow,” she said. “A smith who wants to inspect his own goods can come with me.”

“Both of us?” Su Fan asked.

“One pays for a place. One works for it.”

“What work?”

“Loading. Mooring. Whatever needs another pair of hands. You're not being hired to tell me how to sail.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“You asked three questions about my landing before you asked whether you could come. I thought we should settle it.”

Duan covered his mouth with the back of his hand.

Sun Lian took a charcoal stub and drew the landing on a spare piece of wood. A narrow jetty, a storehouse, the path rising to the gate. She marked the unloading space with a cross.

“This is where my contract takes me. Beyond here, the gate supervisor decides. I can bring your goods and you with them. I can't promise he'll let you touch anything.”

“Then we ask to check the couplings we supplied,” Duan said.

“Those are yours?”

“Some. I have the order copies.”

“Bring them. Not a general complaint about bad iron. A number somebody can check.”

Su Fan reached for the broken pin.

Duan put a hand over it.

“That stays.”

“They should see what—”

“They have Jiang's report. We nearly lost this by taking it away once. I'm not carrying it into a place where a man can decide it's his property.”

Su Fan withdrew his hand. He could draw the fracture and copy the stamp. Neither would prove as much as the piece, but neither would leave the workshop without a second copy.

Sun Lian folded the scrap with her measurements. “And that stick?”

“Stays too,” Duan said.

“Good. Whoever gave it to you didn't give it to the gate supervisor.”

The forge had settled to a red glow. Ah-Du came to the door with the bucket from beneath the repaired roof. He had found a use for it carrying water and was displeased to discover the conversation blocking his way.

“Are we going somewhere?”

“No,” Duan said.

“Then why are you discussing what to bring?”

“Because some of us are going somewhere.”

“That was a badly made answer.”

“It was a well-made answer to the wrong question.”

The boy squeezed past them. Su Fan glanced at the waiting hinges. A farmer needed two before his storehouse could be closed. The remaining four pins were promised. Leaving did not make those people less in need of iron.

“I could finish the hinges tonight.”

“You could finish one,” Duan said. “The other needs fitting to a frame you haven't seen.”

“Then at first light.”

“And when will you eat?”

Sun Lian opened the onion parcel and broke its bread into three pieces. She handed the largest to Ah-Du, who had begun listening very closely.

“Boat leaves after the morning market bell,” she said. “Do what you can before then. What you can't do, tell the customer. I won't have someone asleep on the mooring line because he promised the same morning to four people.”

Su Fan accepted the bread. He had been arranging the hours as though every task would take the shortest possible time.

Duan pulled the order book toward him.

“We'll tell the farmer first. He can decide whether to wait. Then the pins.”

He loosened the wrapping at his wrist with his teeth and flexed his fingers beneath the table. Sun Lian noticed, but did not offer to decide for him whether he could travel.

“After the market bell,” she repeated.


Duan looked at the roof, the waiting orders and his wrapped left wrist.

Su Fan was already measuring how much work he could finish before the morning bell.

chapters.title: The River Above Them
chapters.text:
Sun Lian's boat was called *Honest Measure*.

Su Fan asked whether it was an old family name.

“No. It makes customers nervous about arguing.”

The hull was shallow, with a wide working deck and two small cabins. She carried timber, medicine chests, six sacks of lime and an elderly passenger who insisted she had paid for a seat on the sunny side.

Sun Lian explained that the sunny side changed when the boat turned.

The passenger said that sounded like poor planning.

Su Fan found a place beside the timber and began checking lashings.

He had expected to be useful. He had not expected how much work a boat required before it even left its moorings.

The six pins lay wrapped in oiled cloth beside the mast. Su Fan had carried them down from the smithy himself, holding the bundle clear of the quay mud. Duan had made him count them twice and name the work that remained on his bench before allowing him to leave.

He could still hear the second question. Not whether the river was interesting. Who would finish the hinges?

Ah-Du had volunteered, which had delayed their departure while Duan explained the difference between volunteering for hinges and volunteering to be left alone with a furnace.

Now Su Fan put a knee against a lime sack and pulled its rope tight.

“Not that one,” Sun Lian said.

“The knot's loose.”

“Because I'm moving the sack.”

He looked at the other five. They appeared to occupy the same place they had occupied when he came aboard.

She set a short plank across the rail and pointed to the water below it. The stern sat lower than the bow. The difference was small enough that he would have blamed the current.

“Three sacks forward. Timber stays. Medicine in the shade, clear of the lime.”

“It's wrapped.”

“And I would like it to remain medicine if the wrapping leaks.”

He untied his excellent knot.

The passenger watched him with approval. She had a round bundle on her lap and a smaller bundle tied to the first. Whenever a porter came near, she put one hand over both.

“Have you done this before?” she asked.

“Carried sacks?”

“Been on a boat.”

“Several times.”

“As a sack?”

Sun Lian laughed without looking up from the mooring line.

Su Fan moved the lime. A boy on the quay offered to help with the timber, named a fee, and promptly increased it when he saw how far aboard it lay. Sun Lian refused both prices. They settled on a third, lower than the first, after she reminded him of the pole he had borrowed and not returned.

While they argued, Su Fan tried to lift the forward end alone. The new warmth answered beneath his ribs. The timber rose more easily than he expected, and the boat rolled toward him. He set it down at once.

“Wait for the stern,” Sun Lian said. “You can lift it as high as you like after we fall in.”

He kept his hands on the wood until the boy was ready. Together they slid it across two rollers and lowered it onto the bearing blocks. No cultivated strength was needed. That annoyed him more than it deserved to.

The elderly passenger opened her top bundle. Inside was a cloth of sesame cakes. She took out one, examined the cracked edge, and handed the broken piece to the boy.

“For the pole,” she told him.

“It wasn't her pole,” the boy protested.

“It isn't my cake anymore either.”

The mooring men began their final preparations. Sun Lian collected the little quay tally, tucked it beneath her belt and inspected each lashing herself. She tested Su Fan's knots without praising or replacing them. When she reached the medicine chests, she crouched to check that their painted arrows faced upward.

He noticed a narrow split in the deck beside her boot. A fresh wooden wedge filled its upper end.

“Does that leak?”

“Not at this height.”

He looked over the rail at the water.

“Does the answer change?”

“Constantly. That's why I own an oar.”

Three men pushed them into the current. Sun Lian guided the stern with a long oar. At a narrow reach she touched the deck, and a soft brown light passed through the planks.

The boat steadied against a crosscurrent.

Su Fan watched her hand.

“Earth art?”

“Mostly joinery.”

“The light.”

“That too.”

“Which founder?”

She looked up.

“None you would know.”

He waited for the name. She gave him a coil of line instead.

“Fasten that to the forward cleat.”

***

The river made Su Fan useful in ways he had not anticipated.

He bailed first. Then he bailed from a different place because the water he had chased beneath one bench had appeared under another. He fetched a rag for the passenger, who said the spray was not rain and therefore should not be included in the fare. He held a pole against the bank while Sun Lian changed lines at a towing reach, and discovered that standing firmly could be the quickest way to be dragged off a boat.

“Move your feet,” she called.

He did, too late. The pole slipped from his hands.

Sun Lian caught its end with her oar and drew it alongside. She said nothing until he had recovered it.

“Your master's iron doesn't pull back.”

“It does sometimes.”

“Then pretend this is that iron.”

Upstream, the current narrowed between banks cut by old floods. Willow roots hung out over raw soil. A man in a reed hat walked the towpath beside a mule, singing with an earnestness that survived every note. The mule stopped when the song stopped and began again when its owner found another verse.

The passenger knew the song. She supplied a verse the mule's owner apparently did not, and Sun Lian nearly lost her stroke laughing.

Su Fan felt himself smile. He had gone upriver before, but always on another person's errand, watching the distance to the place where he would put down a load. From the working deck he could see orchards behind the bank, children dragging a branch out of an irrigation ditch, laundry stretched between two posts on a roof. None of them looked toward Greywing's white halls.

At the narrow reach the brown light returned beneath Sun Lian's fingers. He watched the wedge beside her boot draw tight into the split. The planks still flexed, but together now; the seam did not open as the crosscurrent pushed them.

“Does the boat follow your hand?” he asked.

“No. It follows the water. I persuade it to remain a boat.”

“How long?”

“As long as I can afford the effort.”

She took her hand away as they cleared the reach. A sheen of sweat showed above her collar.

He had thought of cultivation in strikes and sudden strength. Here it appeared to mean keeping a repaired joint from becoming three separate pieces while somebody's medicine travelled past a rock.

He wanted to tell her about the stone in the yard. The urge came unexpectedly, encouraged by the ease with which she discussed her own work. Then he remembered that she had declined to name her founder, and that a pleasant journey was not an invitation to offer every secret he had.

He picked up the coil instead.

Near the next landing, a boy stood knee-deep in the shallows balancing a basket on his head. His mother waited on the bank with her shoes in one hand. Sun Lian called out that the lower ferry would come soon. The woman waved her thanks. The boy wanted to know whether the boat carried soldiers.

“Worse,” the passenger told him. “Lime.”

He looked sufficiently disappointed that she threw him a cake. It broke against the basket. He saved half before the river took the rest.

Sun Lian turned upstream again, and the channel widened toward the first white tower.

They reached the ninth gate by noon.

From Mudgate, the river works were a line of white structures on the northern slope. Up close they were stone towers joined by channels wide enough to swallow a house. Water pressed against carved slabs. Bronze reeds rose from each tower, their narrow leaves trembling though there was little wind.

A row of workers sat beneath the lowest tower.

Blue cords circled their wrists.

They breathed together.

With every exhalation, the reeds above them brightened.

Su Fan had known the gates used cultivation. He had not thought about whose bodies supplied it.

“Seasonal crew,” Sun Lian said. “They keep the local formations responsive while the main reservoir is low.”

“Can't an elder do it?”

“An elder has one pair of lungs. These people have thirty.”

“He has more power.”

“And you can lift more than a child. Ask yourself how many jars you can hold at once.”

She tied up at the landing.

A guard inspected her cargo marks. He counted the medicine chests twice and made Su Fan open the top sack of lime.

He did not inspect the timber.

Su Fan noticed. Sun Lian noticed him noticing.

“Trees don't change hands as easily as pills,” she said when the guard moved on.

At the eighth gate, a repair crew had assembled beside an open housing. The coupling inside it turned slowly. Water dripped from a seam above the bearings.

Su Fan presented Duan's delivery tally.

The overseer read it and pointed him toward a stack of crates.

“Your master's pieces are there.”

Most were sound. Two had been unpacked. A third crate held fittings that were not Duan's.

He did not begin with the suspect crate. Duan had taught him what happened when a customer found a fault before confirming what had actually been delivered.

The tally listed lengths, head sizes and the receiving mark. He laid two of the sound pieces on the cloth and measured them against the little wooden gauge in his tool roll. They matched. He counted the untouched bundles, then the empty slots in the opened crate.

A labourer stopped beside him, carrying a tray of grease cups.

“You're the smith's boy?”

“Assistant.”

“Then you can tell him the long grips were useful.”

Su Fan looked up. He had helped forge those grips during a week of cold rain. Duan had complained about the waste of iron in the handles, then made them longer than the order specified because the men would wear gloves.

“He'll be pleased.”

“He won't. Tell him anyway.”

The labourer went back to the housing. He moved around it with the confidence of someone who knew which surfaces were hot without testing them. At the far side he waited until a seated operator raised two fingers, then adjusted a screw by less than a quarter turn.

The bronze reed above the operator quivered. Its light steadied.

Su Fan watched the man's wrist. The blue cord was not tied to the machinery. It lay against his skin, its ends tucked into the knot. Yet the little movement of his fingers appeared to matter as much as the labourer's screw.

He waited for the next cycle. Water clicked in the housing. A brace shifted; the operator's shoulders followed. On the third cycle the same thing happened, though the labourer had moved away and no screw was being turned.

Then the overseer called him back to the crates.

“Find your mark and leave the rest.”

“I've found ours. There are other pieces in the box.”

“Boxes get reused.”

“They're listed together.”

“Take it to the office.”

The overseer was holding three different tallies. A man at the landing called for him; another waited with a cracked grease cup. He appeared neither pleased nor surprised by any of it. Su Fan could imagine spending a day here and learning to dislike questions simply because a question was one more thing that needed an answer.

He could also see that the piece at the bottom of the crate had the same head profile as the broken pin.

He took it out. It felt too light.

The overseer looked over at the movement.

“That's inventory.”

“So are these.” Su Fan placed a sound pin beside it. “Same length. Same diameter.”

“Different supplier.”

“That doesn't change the weight of iron.”

He regretted the tone as soon as he heard it. The overseer's eyes moved from the pieces to Su Fan's work-stained clothes.

Sun Lian had been helping unload medicine at the next berth. She looked across, saw the two men standing still, and left her porter with the chest.

“Need a witness for the delivery?” she asked.

The overseer drew breath to answer. Su Fan turned the suspect fitting over in his hand, finding an old nick where a tool had struck it.

Su Fan scraped one with his knife.

The same dark shell. The same softer centre.

“Don't damage stores,” the overseer said.

“This is the wrong grade.”

“It passed inspection.”

“For which load?”

The overseer's face changed.

“Who sent you?”

“My master.”

“Then tell your master the steward's office handles specifications.”

Su Fan could have kept arguing. He saw three ways to phrase the objection. None would make the overseer more willing to let him inspect the coupling.

Instead he asked for a receipt for the two replacement pins.

While the overseer fetched it, Su Fan studied the open housing.

The mismatched pieces were not in the heaviest part of the machine. They were in the little braces that held the bronze reeds in alignment.

A simple fault, at first glance.

But every time the seated workers exhaled, the alignment shifted.

***

They slept aboard the boat below the gate.

The elderly passenger had gone ashore to stay with her son. Before leaving, she told Sun Lian the afternoon side had been satisfactory.

Su Fan sat on deck with a bowl of rice. The bronze reeds glowed faintly above the water.

Before supper, Sun Lian made him help unload the remaining timber.

The landing crew had gone, and she refused to leave the cargo high on the deck overnight. They used rollers and a short tackle secured to the quay ring. Su Fan was tired enough to think of the circuit again. He could save them several pulls. He could also drop a beam through the thin deck if he misjudged what came after the lift.

He kept hauling in time with her.

A family from the workers' houses came to collect the elderly passenger. Her son hugged her, then tried to take the larger bundle. She retained it until she had introduced Sun Lian as the woman who had finally arranged an acceptable sun.

There were no complaints about the price. Su Fan thought that might be her highest compliment.

When the deck was clear, Sun Lian checked the wedge he had noticed that morning. She tapped it with the heel of her knife and asked him for a sliver from the kindling box.

“Wouldn't more of the brown light hold it?”

“For tonight.”

“And tomorrow?”

“For tomorrow as well, until I wanted to sleep.”

She pared the sliver, tested it, and gave it to him to fit. He drove it in gently. A bead of dark water rose along the grain and stopped.

“Now tomorrow has less work for me,” she said.
