They cooked on a little clay stove whose three feet had been sunk into a wooden tray. Sun Lian let the rice catch at the bottom and scraped the crisp pieces into her own bowl. When he offered her the unburned part, she looked offended.

“I cooked it that way.”

“Then why stir?”

“So it doesn't all become the best part.”

They ate facing the tower. A night crew replaced the seated workers one position at a time. Su Fan watched an incoming man put his feet on the same two worn marks as the man he relieved. For a while both men breathed in the same rhythm. Then the older one stood, slowly, pressing a hand against his back.

He did not seem injured. He seemed like a porter at the end of a long day. Su Fan recognized that much without needing to understand blue cords.

A boy brought a covered pot down from the houses. He waited while the man finished putting on his sandals, then spoke so fast that none of the words reached the boat. The man listened with his head bent. They went uphill together, the boy carrying the pot despite an unsuccessful attempt to surrender it.

Sun Lian followed his gaze.

“Don't make every face down here a mystery,” she said. “Sometimes a man is hungry.”

“Do you know them?”

“Some. Enough to know I'm not asking one to stay another hour because unloading was late.”

He looked at the receipt for Duan's pins. The overseer had finally signed it after Sun Lian named each item aloud and Su Fan agreed not to cut any more stores. The paper proved delivery. It did not prove that the brace would hold, or that anybody had understood what worried him.

He rubbed a rice grain from the edge of the tally. Across the water, the shift settled into its shared breathing. A bronze leaf moved, then a shoulder. He waited for the next cycle before speaking.

“Those braces move,” he said.

“They're meant to move.”

“They move differently.”

Sun Lian stopped eating.

He described what he had seen.

She asked him to draw it with a wet finger on the deck. He did. She corrected the placement of one channel, then went silent.

“What?”

“If you're right, the workers are compensating for mechanical errors with their own circulation.”

“Can they?”

“For a while.”

She put down her bowl.

Across the water, a man in the seated row coughed out of time.

The reed above his head flared blue.

chapters.title: A Bed Beyond the Gate
chapters.text:
Tan Wei liked Master Han almost immediately.

This made him suspicious of his own judgment.

He had wanted the admission badly enough that a warm bed would have seemed a personal kindness. The bed was narrow. The blanket smelled of somebody else's soap. He liked those too.

He had put his bundle on the bed three times before choosing which end would be his head.

The room had six beds and one window. The bed nearest the window was already occupied by a woman with a broad face and a cord tied through her sleeve to keep it out of her work. She was testing the mattress by kneeling on its corners.

“Bad one?” Tan Wei asked.

“Uneven one. Different crime.”

She shifted the straw beneath the ticking, stood and offered her hand.

“Qiu Lan.”

He gave his name. She asked where he was from. When he said Mudgate she knew the lower ferry and asked whether Old Pock still charged more for a goat than a child.

“Goats argue less,” Tan Wei said.

“Then the price ought to be the other way round.”

One of the men laughed from the next bed. He had a new belt too stiff to tie comfortably and was pretending not to notice. Tan Wei offered to work the leather soft. The man offered, in exchange, to show him which laundry tubs had sound bottoms.

These were useful introductions. By the time they were called to the table, Tan Wei knew where to leave boots, which hook was his, and that the quiet recruit at the end of the room had brought twice as many socks as shirts. He envied the socks. He had packed as though passing the gate would make him a different person with different needs. Already he wanted a spare rag and a needle.

He had also brought the old shirt he had been wearing when the jade bowl stayed dark. He had considered leaving it behind as a declaration, then remembered it was the better of his two.

Someone knocked on the open door with a cane.

“Beds still yours tomorrow,” a voice said. “Come and learn how to pay for them.”

Tan Wei followed the others into a low room smelling of cabbage and linseed oil. A slate stood on a table. Beside it lay a stack of printed notices, a covered bowl and a cup whose handle had been repaired with wire.

He had expected a hall. There were plenty of halls above them, roofs shining beyond the yard wall, but this room could have belonged to any warehouse with enough money to keep the rain out.

The absence of ceremony unsettled him. He had spent so much time wanting admission that he had neglected to imagine what happened after somebody admitted him. He wanted a sign that he had reached the right place. A word spoken over him, perhaps. Something difficult to mistake for the beginning of another work shift.

The man with the cane pulled a stool away from the table with his foot. He did not make the new workers stand while he sat.

“Bring the lamp closer,” he said. “If you've come to learn a water art, we might begin by seeing the paper.”

Han wore no ceremonial sash. His grey hair had been cut badly, perhaps by himself. He limped on the right leg and carried a cane that he used for pointing, not striking.

“Put your papers on the table,” he told the six new workers. “Your family tablets can stay in your bags. None of them will carry timber for you.”

Tan Wei put down the provisional registration.

Han noticed the red delay mark.

“Questioned bond?”

“The office wanted clarification.”

“Did you ask for it?”

“No.”

Han read the attached note, folded it inward and moved to the next recruit.

“Good. Someone reads on your behalf. You should learn to do it yourself.”

Tan Wei could read simple notices. He said so.

“Then you'll help the other two who can't. We begin after supper.”

Before supper, Han took them through the stores.

The low rooms held coils of line, gloves stiff with old use, poles, oil for the bearings and stacks of folded work clothes. The recruits received one set each. Tan Wei's sleeves were too long. He rolled them and immediately felt better dressed than he had in years.

Han noticed him smoothing the front.

“Try lifting your arms.”

Tan Wei did. The seam under his right shoulder pulled tight.

“Change it.”

“It fits.”

“It fits standing still. We don't pay much for that.”

The replacement had a repaired cuff and more room across the back. He accepted it reluctantly, then felt the difference when they carried a timber brace across the yard. Qiu Lan took the other end. Her new sleeve cord kept catching a splinter; she stopped, tied it differently, and did not apologize for making him wait.

Han gave them no lesson in glorious service. He showed them how to put a load down without taking another person's fingers with it, where to stack damaged equipment and who was permitted to isolate a small gate. At a painted red line he made all six stop.

“Beyond this, wait for an operator.”

“Even if the wheel's stopped?” one man asked.

“Especially if you don't know why it stopped.”

Through an opening in the wall Tan Wei could see two older workers examining a bronze coupling. One held a tool against it. The other watched the seated operators beyond the housing. Neither looked like the disciples who had ridden past him on the mountain road. Their clothes were greasy at the knees.

A bell rang for a change of work. Tan Wei felt a familiar impulse to hurry before someone accused him of wasting time. Han stopped at a water jar, drank, and passed the dipper to Qiu Lan.

“First lesson in meals,” he said. “They stop serving eventually. Arguments about who's too important to eat won't persuade the cook.”

The food was ordinary: rice, cabbage, beans and a ladle of broth. Tan Wei tasted each item as though looking for the hidden fee. There would be a fee. The difference was that he could ask what it was instead of discovering it when the wage clerk counted out less than expected.

The recruit with the stiff belt tried to eat quickly. Qiu Lan told him no one intended to steal his bowl. He slowed, then began describing a place he had worked where that assumption would have cost a man his dinner.

Tan Wei listened and put his bundle of notices flat beside his elbow. He had expected strangers to know more than he did. It was oddly comforting to discover that each knew a different small collection of things.

When supper ended, Han brought the slate to their table rather than calling them to another room. The cook wiped around his elbow and told him not to get chalk in the pickles.

He moved the pickle bowl himself.

The lesson began with wages.

Han explained what was deducted for meals, what remained Tan Wei's property if he failed training, and what happened if he was injured. The emergency extension had a maximum term for ordinary labour. It had no fixed end for a bonded operator already attached to the gate.

Qiu Lan raised her hand.

“What keeps them from calling everything an emergency?”

“Paperwork, witnesses, and the fact that I dislike it.”

“That doesn't sound strong.”

“It isn't as strong as it should be.”

Han let the answer stand.

Tan Wei found that he liked him more for that.

They worked through a sample fortnight. Han drew columns for days, food and the work-clothing charge. He used a pretend sum rather than promising any one recruit an amount before their duties had been assigned.

Tan Wei added the figures correctly and failed to notice that one line was a returnable deposit.

Qiu Lan tapped it.

“Do we get that back?”

“If the coat does.”

“In what condition?”

“Recognizable as a coat.”

She examined her repaired cuff. Han amended the example so that everybody could see the deposit carried forward rather than vanished.

The two men who could not read watched Tan Wei's finger move beneath the printed lines. At first he read too quickly, embarrassed by the role of teacher when so many of the characters still troubled him. One man stopped him at *retained*.

“Does that mean paid?”

“It means kept.”

“By whom?”

Tan Wei looked again. The sentence did not say until the following line. He read both lines together, more slowly.

They stayed at the table after the bowls had been removed. Outside, the evening work moved on. A wheel turned somewhere beyond the wall with a regular wooden knock. Each time it sounded, Tan Wei imagined himself helping to move it, admitted to something that had previously operated over his head.

He tried to examine that feeling. Su Fan would have distrusted it. Sometimes Su Fan distrusted pleasure simply because somebody else might profit from it.

But Su Fan had been right about things before. The emergency clause lay on the table in front of them. Han had not hidden it; neither had he made it harmless by answering a question.

“Could I stay on ordinary labour?” Tan Wei asked.

“Yes.”

“And still learn?”

“The introductory forms. Not every duty and not every advancement.”

There it was. No shout, no threat. A gate inside the gate, standing in the way of the thing he actually wanted.

He folded the wage sheet along its existing crease. It fitted in his pocket. The office no longer possessed the only copy of the words that described his work.

When Han dismissed them, Qiu Lan remained long enough to ask where an independent witness could be found if the office declined a complaint. Han gave her a name and a room. She wrote both on the back of her paper.

Then the others went to argue over the wash tubs, leaving Tan Wei with the question he had carried uphill.

After the others left, he asked about the lease.

Han opened a small case.

Inside lay six beads, each no larger than a pea. A cloudy blue thread moved within each one.

“The Ferryman's Return,” Han said. “A minor water method. Balance, endurance, the recovery of a wasted movement. Useful on boats and at gates. Less useful if you intend to throw rivers at enemies.”

“I don't.”

“Most say that until they can move a cup.”

Tan Wei leaned closer.

“Whose method?”

“Master Liang Sui. Dead two hundred and fourteen years. These are approved impressions taken from a preserved branch. I learned through the same line.”

“Will it make me like him?”

“In the way a good lesson makes you like your teacher. And in a few less comfortable ways.”

Han closed the case.

“Dreams, sometimes. Habits that arrive before you know you've learned them. Most fade as you grow accustomed. If they don't, you tell me. You do not pretend to be well because you want the next stage.”

Tan Wei thought of Ko Lin's shaking hand.

“And I can stop?”

“Before the permanent bond, yes. Later, stopping is a longer business.”

Outside, someone dropped a bucket. Laughter ran down the dormitory passage.

Tan Wei looked at the case.

Su Fan would ask more questions. Useful questions. Tan Wei could hear several already.

He would bring them to Han tomorrow.

Tonight he asked his own.

“Can I send money home?”

Han pointed to the wage sheet.

“After the first fortnight.”

Tan Wei put his hand beside the case, palm up.

***

Han washed his hands before opening the case again.

The care of the gesture steadied Tan Wei more than a recital of the founder's achievements would have. The old man dried between each finger, inspected the small bead against the lamp and asked him whether he had eaten.

“Yes.”

“What?”

Tan Wei laughed. Han looked mildly surprised.

“A healer I know asks that.”

“A sensible healer. What?”

He listed the meal. Han nodded and moved the drinking cup to the centre of the table.

“Only the first contact tonight. If you feel pain, say where. If you feel nothing, say that too.”

Tan Wei put both feet flat. He had seen initiates kneel in painted teaching scrolls. Sitting on a kitchen stool felt insufficiently solemn, which made him ashamed of wanting solemnity at all.

Han turned his wrist outward and checked the skin.

“The hand is yours,” he said. “Don't give me credit for sensations I haven't caused.”

Tan Wei almost asked how to know the difference. Instead he described the warmth in his palm and the tightness in his shoulder before the bead had touched him. Han thanked him. The feelings did not vanish, but now he did not have to mistake them for a miracle.

The bead rested in a little shallow groove on a wooden holder. Han placed that holder against the inside of Tan Wei's wrist. It weighed almost nothing. The blue within it turned slowly, a movement too small to resemble a stream until the light caught its edge.

Outside the door, Qiu Lan called for someone to pass her a dry cloth. A man complained that it had been dry before she took it. The ordinary voices went on while Tan Wei looked at a dead man's surviving lesson.

He thought of the charm against the quarry wheel, the blue cords taking weight his own arms could not bear. He had not bought that breath to prove Su Fan wrong. He had bought it because he wanted, at least once, to possess something that might make him useful when strength failed.

Now there was no cradle falling. There was only a cup and the chance to try.

He nodded. Han let the bead's thread meet his skin.

The first touch felt cold.

Then it felt familiar.

That frightened him more than the cold.

A movement opened along his arm, guiding the breath toward a channel he had never felt. Han kept two fingers on his wrist. When Tan Wei tried to follow too eagerly, the old teacher tapped the table.

“Slowly. You're learning a road, not fleeing a fire.”

The movement returned.

A drop rose from the drinking cup.

It trembled above the rim, catching lamplight.

Tan Wei stared at it until his eyes watered.

Then he laughed, and the drop fell.

Han handed him a cloth.

“Most laugh,” he said. “A few cry. Both spill the water.”

They tried once more after he had stopped laughing.

This time Tan Wei wanted the drop too badly. He could feel his own wrist stiffen, the borrowed motion pressing against an effort that had nothing to do with water. Nothing rose. The disappointment arrived so quickly that he looked at Han to see whether he had broken something.

The teacher took the bead away.

“Enough.”

“But it worked before.”

“Yes.”

“What changed?”

“You started asking it to perform for an audience.”

“There isn't one.”

Han raised his eyebrows. Tan Wei looked down at the cup.

He wiped the table while Han cleaned the holder and returned the bead to its numbered recess. There was water beneath the cup, water on Tan Wei's cuff, and one small wet mark on the slate. None of it looked extraordinary now. He kept smiling whenever the old man turned away.

At the dormitory Qiu Lan asked what had happened.

“A drop.”

“How large?”

He showed her with two fingers. She studied the gap, reduced it by half and asked whether this version was more accurate.

He conceded that it was.

“Still,” she said, “you lifted it.”

She went back to mending her sleeve cord. He sat on his narrow bed and listened to the room settling around him. The man with the new belt had already begun to snore. It came in two notes, one low and one unexpectedly high. Tan Wei tried to count the interval and lost track because he wanted to laugh again.

He took out his paper before the lamp was lowered.

That night Tan Wei wrote a letter to Su Fan.

He described the bed, the food and Master Han's crooked haircut. He did not know how to describe the drop.

After three attempts he wrote: *It worked.*

He folded the letter twice.

For once he had something to tell his friend that Su Fan had not already understood before him.

chapters.title: A Yard Six Paces Wide
chapters.text:
Su Fan practised in a space between the smithy and the neighbour's wash line.

It was six paces wide when no washing hung there.

On laundry days he had four.

He had imagined cultivation would require silence, mountains and perhaps a waterfall. In practice it required explaining to Auntie Lu why her tablecloth had a heel mark on it.

“Training,” he said.

“For what? A career in ruining linen?”

He washed the cloth himself.

The washing took longer than the exercise had.

Auntie Lu inspected the cloth when he hung it back up, found the mark still faintly visible and sent him to do it again. He tried to explain that the yard was ordinarily empty at that hour. She said the cloth was ordinarily clean at that hour.

The second washing removed the mark and most of the warmth from his hands. He wrung the water into a basin, watching it run dark between his fingers. Had anyone told him a month earlier that cultivating would involve apologizing to a tablecloth, he might have found the prospect less intimidating.

Ah-Du stood in the back doorway eating the heel of a loaf.

“Can you make it dry?”

“No.”

“Can you throw it up high enough to reach the sun?”

“No.”

“Then what does it do?”

Su Fan put down the basin a little harder than necessary. The boy immediately disappeared.

That evening he moved the stones. The old arrangement put his turning heel beneath the wash line; the new one left enough room for a wet sleeve. One stone would not lie flat. He fetched a knife, cut away the root beneath it and found the corner of a neighbour's lost comb in the soil.

He returned the comb. The neighbour asked whether he intended to dig a drain next.

“No.”

“A pity. The water sits by my door.”

She showed him the patch. He had crossed it for years without considering where the water came from. Auntie Lu's basin, the smithy's washing, rain off both roofs. His newly valuable six paces were several other people's path to the latrine and back.

He moved the difficult stone again, this time leaving the shallow runnel clear. The neighbour gave him a broken tile to cover it.

After supper he finally stood where the scripture told him. Somebody opened the back door. He stepped aside to let a bucket pass. A moment later the door opened again because the bucket's owner had forgotten the cloth.

By the third interruption he was laughing, though not generously.

Duan glanced out from the furnace.

“Move it inside your head,” he said.

“The exercise?”

“The idea that everybody else has gone away.”

Su Fan waited until the doorway was clear and began again. Water dripped from the tablecloth close enough to touch his sleeve. He kept his foot out of it.

His first stage remained uneven. The circuit came readily when he stood still. Work disturbed it. Anger broke it. Trying to impress Ah-Du ended it at once.

He stopped allowing the boy to watch.

Ah-Du watched through a hole in the fence.

Duan discovered this, charged him one copper for admission, and gave the money to Su Fan without explanation.

For the first week, strength was the most tempting part.

Su Fan could lift a sack he had previously dragged. He could work longer before his shoulders burned. A hammer blow landed with a deep, satisfying solidity when the circuit completed at the right moment.

When the timing was wrong, the jolt travelled into his elbow.

On the third morning he finished a small batch of nails faster than Duan expected.

The smith weighed the finished pieces, chose one and bent it sideways against the bench. It snapped where the shaft met the head.

Su Fan felt his pleasure go sour.

“The iron was cool.”

“It was. Why didn't you heat it?”

“I thought—”

Duan waited. He had learned that waiting could be considerably worse than shouting.

Su Fan looked at the broken nail. The blow had made it take the shape he wanted, quickly and neatly. The metal had not become better iron merely because his arm had found a new way to hit it.

He put the remaining nails back in the scrap tray.

“Not all,” Duan said. “Test them. Waste honestly.”

Two were sound. Three needed reheating. One broke in the same place as the first. Su Fan labelled the little bundles so Ah-Du would not mix them into an order, then went out to carry charcoal with his elbow folded close against his body.

The sacks felt lighter. That was the maddening part. Something had genuinely improved. He could not make the improvement arrive only where it was useful.

He tried timing a lift to the warm circuit. If he waited for the sensation before moving, his shoulders tightened while he waited. If he hurried, the warmth broke apart and left him doing ordinary work with unnecessary effort added to it. Once he lifted smoothly and became so pleased that he nearly walked into the doorway.

Ah-Du watched from behind a stack of scrap.

“Would it be easier without a door?”

“Would you like to work?”

“I was working on the problem.”

Su Fan sent him to bring a smaller sack. Together they filled it from the larger ones and counted how many trips the charcoal required. That afternoon he carried ordinary amounts, refusing the urge to prove he could do more. It was irritatingly successful.

When the circuit stayed with him, the work took less out of his back. When it did not, he still delivered the charcoal. He wrote down which had happened without making the good entries larger than the bad ones.

Then a customer came to collect a hinge and asked whether Duan's new assistant was any stronger than the last one.

“He's the same assistant,” Duan said.

“Looks thinner.”

Su Fan turned to move the anvil block they had been using as a seat. It was not an especially sensible reply to either remark. He felt the warmth close, lifted, and set the block where the customer could see it.

The man nodded, impressed.

Pain ran up the outside of Su Fan's elbow. He put his hand behind his back before anybody noticed.

Duan noticed.

After the customer left, the smith made him name every joint in his arm that had helped move the block. Su Fan got as far as the shoulder before Duan asked why, with so many contributors, he had tried to give the elbow all the work.

He had no answer that sounded less foolish aloud.

By the end of the week his elbow hurt enough to make the lesson clear.

He returned to the scripture.

One of the later hands had written: *A stronger mistake remains a mistake.*

He disliked how often the margins anticipated him.

***

Sun Lian returned from the gates with a loose fitting wrapped in sailcloth.

She had acquired permission to remove it after the brace failed during a controlled shift. Nobody had been injured. The overseer had become far more interested in correct materials once he had to stand beside them.

Duan examined the fitting and called Su Fan over.

“Hold it.”

Su Fan braced it against the bench.

Duan struck it with a light hammer. A crack ran down the cast shell.

“Again.”

The second blow split it.

“Strong outside,” Duan said. “Garbage inside. It passes a glance. Doesn't pass a day of work.”

He looked at Su Fan's aching elbow.

Su Fan wished everyone would stop learning lessons about him from objects.

Sun Lian brought out a receipt bearing the steward's seal.

“Jiang's coming down herself.”

Duan grunted approval.

“When?”

“Tomorrow.”

Su Fan felt the circuit tighten beneath his ribs.

Sun Lian noticed the slight change in his posture.

“You owe her money?”

“No.”

“Then breathe. She mostly wants people to stop costing her some.”

Before leaving, Sun Lian spread the removal receipt beside the broken brace.

“The old one stays here until the steward's looked at it. Don't let Ah-Du melt it.”

“I know the difference between evidence and scrap,” the boy said from the doorway.

“Then you'll know why I'm saying it.”

Duan traced a stamped line with his thumb. The overseer had acknowledged that the brace had shifted under an ordinary operating load. He had not acknowledged what that meant for the seated workers.

“Did they give the man who coughed any rest?” Su Fan asked.

“Until the next change.”

“How long was that?”

“I didn't see him after.”

He wanted a fuller answer. She could not supply one merely because he wanted it. She had spent her morning getting a piece of metal released from stores and had other customers, other cargo, a boat still needing the care he had watched her give it.

“The clerk wrote the position down,” she added. “That gives Jiang someone to ask. I don't know his name.”

Su Fan wrote the position on the cloth around the fitting. He thought of the boy carrying a covered pot uphill beside the older worker. They might not even have been the same man. From a deck across the water he had begun making lives out of silhouettes.

Duan set the brace and its paperwork in the chest with the quarry pin. The lid would not close until he shifted a box of fine punches.

“More room for bad iron than good tools,” he grumbled.

Sun Lian paid for the small repair she had brought as an excuse to visit. She inspected Duan's joint, flexed it, and asked him to trim an edge that would catch a line. He did so without arguing. Su Fan took quiet pleasure in seeing his master receive a correction and simply make the work better.

At the door she paused beside him.

“If you tell Jiang something, tell her what you saw. Not what we said over supper.”

“Those things connect.”

“They may. Let her test the connection.”

He nodded. His elbow throbbed. Between Duan and the boatwoman, the afternoon had become crowded with people telling him the difference between something being promising and something being proved.

Sun Lian lifted her repaired fitting and went down the lane. Ah-Du followed her for six steps to ask whether she could take him on the next journey. She asked whether Duan had agreed. The boy returned looking disgusted by the consistency of adults.

After she left, Su Fan tried to make his breath completely ordinary.

That made it less ordinary.

He practised while carrying charcoal, sorting nails and fetching water. The circuit did not disappear, but its movement became less obvious to him when his attention was on a task.

He could not judge what another cultivator might notice.

He had never had anything worth concealing from one.

***

Tan Wei's letter arrived at supper.

Su Fan read it beside the furnace. The handwriting began carefully and grew larger toward the end.

*It worked.*

He read those two words again.

He wanted to write back immediately. To describe the stone, the circuit, the warmth. To say that something had worked for him too.

Then he imagined the letter passing through a dormitory office. A teacher reading over Tan Wei's shoulder. A friend saying one careless, happy sentence to someone who understood its significance.

He set the paper down.

He opened Tan Wei's letter a third time, looking for anything that might make the decision for him.

There was no warning in it. No hint that a clerk read their post. Han had apparently insisted that the first wage sheet be copied, and Tan Wei had complained cheerfully about learning to read food deductions before learning to move water. Su Fan could hear the complaint in his friend's voice, the little pause before the joke.

Below it was a description of the dormitory mattress. Tan Wei had found a wooden spoon in the straw. Nobody claimed it. Qiu Lan said it had belonged to a previous sleeper who had eaten the bed by mistake.

Su Fan laughed, then felt ashamed of having considered the letter first as a possible danger rather than a thing his friend had taken trouble to send.

He laid out a clean page. The furnace gave enough light, though the first strokes came out thick. He wrote *There is something here as well* and stopped.

The sentence looked absurdly competitive. Tan Wei had raised a drop of water; must Su Fan immediately inform him that a different and possibly more interesting event had occurred at home?

He crossed it out, relieved to have found an objection that sounded generous.

He tried *I found an old practice book*. That was true, modest and unlikely to excite anyone who had not seen what the book could do. But it invited the next question. Which book? Which practice? Could Tan Wei show it to Han?

He imagined his friend asking that last question with pleasure, wanting to bring two useful things together. He could not imagine answering without making it sound as though he distrusted the person who had welcomed him.

Across the forge, Ah-Du was sorting nails into boxes. Each one made a small sound. Outside, the neighbour drew in a sheet before the evening damp could settle on it.

Su Fan put the first page aside.

He could tell him in person. That would be safer, more respectful, easier to explain. The reasoning was good enough that he hardly noticed how much of its appeal lay in not having to tell him tonight.

On a second page he began with the goose. It had bitten the tax collector's horse, and the horse had knocked over a basket that did not belong to the collector, which had produced a legal debate Auntie Lu considered better than any festival entertainment.

The words came easily now. He was a better letter writer when he stopped trying to write the thing that mattered.

He left room at the bottom, just enough for one more paragraph. Several times he looked at that space while describing the town. By the time he reached it, his friend's question about work seemed almost an invitation to say as little as possible.

In his reply he asked about Han and the wages. He told Tan Wei that Bao Shun could move two fingers. He described Auntie Lu's goose attacking the tax collector's horse.

He wrote that work was much as usual.

The lie was small enough to fit comfortably between ordinary truths.

Before folding the page, he corrected one sentence about Bao Shun.

He had written that the hand was getting better. That was what everyone hoped, not quite what Mother Wei had said. He changed it to say which fingers moved and that the splint remained.

Ah-Du leaned over his shoulder.

“Tell him my bellows repair worked.”

“It squeaks.”

“It blows air.”

Su Fan added the repair and left out the squeak. The boy watched until he was satisfied that his work had received its proper place in the news, then went to wash the supper bowls.

There were people all through the letter now. Their small successes, their complaints, the things Tan Wei would recognize. Su Fan could imagine him reading it aloud and laughing.

He put his own crossed-out page beneath a stack of receipts. It was not waste paper yet. He told himself that meant he intended to use it.

After sealing it, he went outside.

The washing had been brought in. For a little while he had all six paces.

He moved through them, trying to learn how to carry his new strength without letting anyone see the effort.

chapters.title: The Steward's Shoes
chapters.text:
Steward Jiang arrived on foot.

Her attendants had horses. She had a walking stick, a plain dark coat and boots with fresh mud on them.

She went first to the broken brake.

Su Fan saw her first from the roof hole.

He was helping Ah-Du fit the last board over the patch. The boy had dropped a nail, and Su Fan was looking for its dark head against the pale road when a walking stick stopped beside it. The woman bent, picked up the nail and placed it on the wall rather than leave it where a mule would tread.

Only when her attendants caught up did he understand who she was.

One carried a document box. Another held the reins of a horse that appeared annoyed by the pace of its morning. They went past the smithy toward the upper platform without asking where the foreman's office stood.

Su Fan came down the ladder.

“Finish your edge,” Duan told him.

“She's here.”

“She'll still be here after a nail.”

He drove it crooked because he was watching the road. Duan made him take it out and start again.

At the brake station, Jiang did not begin by touching the great founder's tablet. She crouched beside the capstan, examined the scorch in its old groove and asked one of the rope workers where he had stood. The man pointed from a safe distance. She asked him to stand there again.

He obeyed with visible unease. His mates watched. None offered to be next.

Jiang looked from his position to the road below, then to the broken housing. She asked a question Su Fan could not hear. The man answered with his hands, showing how the line had slipped. She moved around him until she could see the angle for herself.

Ren Bo arrived at a run and stopped running before he reached her.

“Steward.”

“Your bell rope?”

He nodded.

“Show me where it caught.”

For a moment Su Fan expected him to lie. Ren Bo had fined people for late signals and early breaks for as long as Su Fan had worked there. Admitting that the alarm itself had failed would cost him something.

But he took Jiang to the wheel and demonstrated the snag with the cut end of the old rope. She asked whether the replacement followed the same route. He said no and showed her where he had moved it.

“Better?”

“It rings.”

“Those are not necessarily the same thing. Test it with the wheel under load before you call it done.”

Ren Bo nodded again. The instruction gave him work rather than a pardon. Su Fan found that less satisfying than he had expected, then thought of the next man who might need a third stroke to be heard.

Jiang rose and brushed pale quarry dust from her palm. She had listened to three accounts by then. Two agreed about the first chain. The third did not. Her clerk wrote the disagreement down instead of smoothing it into a single story.

Su Fan wished he could see the page.

By the time the quarry foreman hurried out with a tray of tea, she had already spoken to three workers and found the place where the replacement rope had been tied.

“Put that down,” she told him.

He did.

“Who signed for this batch?”

“The order seems to have been misfiled.”

“I heard.”

She turned to her clerk.

“Seal the stores until the files return.”

The foreman's face reddened.

“My lady, the interruption—”

“Will be expensive. Yes.”

The order to seal the stores had consequences beyond the foreman's expression.

A carter waiting for a replacement axle pin began arguing with the clerk. His loaded cart stood on three wheels, and he could not take it down the road merely because someone important wished to inspect papers. Jiang went with him, looked at the cart and permitted one numbered pin to be issued under witness.

The rest stayed shut.

The foreman tried to turn the exception into a discussion of normal operations. Jiang returned to her earlier question.

“Who signed?”

He named the storekeeper. The storekeeper, brought from behind the shed, named an assistant. The assistant was found within shouting distance, carrying a tray of cups intended for the tea that nobody had drunk.

Su Fan watched the circle close. He had imagined wrongdoing as a hand deliberately putting bad iron into a good machine. Here were several hands, each pointing toward another place on the yard.

The assistant said he had signed only for quantity.

“Then the document will say that,” Jiang replied.

There was a silence. The man went to fetch it.

While he was gone, Jiang asked for the dispatch marks from Duan's earlier sound pieces. Her clerk took a rubbing rather than remove the marks. The practical care mattered. Su Fan had seen evidence become useless after the person collecting it destroyed the little feature that distinguished one item from another.

He went to the smithy and fetched the gauge they had used on the pin. Duan accepted it from him without comment and set it on a clean cloth beside the chest.

“You were right to send the letter,” Su Fan said.

“I know.”

“You could pretend to be less pleased.”

“I could. It would waste the occasion.”

Outside, the storekeeper emerged with a folded paper protected between two boards. The foreman made a small movement toward him, then stopped. Jiang held out her hand.

Nobody mentioned the tea again.

Within a quarter of an hour, the purchase order was found.

Su Fan watched from the smithy's doorway. He enjoyed that more than he should have.

Jiang came to Duan afterward.

She appeared to be somewhere past fifty. Duan addressed her with the careful courtesy he used for people old enough to remember his own master.

He later told Su Fan she was one hundred and fourteen.

The fact made Su Fan study the mud on her boots. A person could live that long and still have to walk through it.

Jiang inspected the sound pins, the broken ones and the tools used to test them.

Then she asked Su Fan what he had seen at the gate.

He gave the details in order.

She interrupted only twice. Once to ask where he had stood. Once to ask whether the workers had changed their breathing before or after the brace moved.

“After,” he said.

“Certain?”

“I watched three cycles.”

“Then certain three times. Good.”

She made him draw the coupling.

His first drawing placed a channel too low. Sun Lian corrected it. Jiang crossed out the error without comment.

Su Fan appreciated that. She seemed more interested in a correct picture than in who deserved to be embarrassed by it.

The clerk asked Su Fan to repeat the time of the cough.

“After the evening shift changed. I don't know the exact bell.”

“Write that,” Jiang said.

Su Fan looked at the diagram. He wanted a clearer account, one that would carry more weight. He could describe the light and the movement with certainty. He could not supply the man's name, or prove that the cough came from the same operator he had watched beside the coupling.

He said so.

Jiang circled the part he had seen during the day and drew a separate mark beside the evening observation. Her clerk did not look disappointed. That made it easier to resist improving the story.

Duan opened the chest. The quarry pin lay in its leather wrap; the gate brace in Sun Lian's sailcloth. Jiang checked their marks against the two receipts before allowing either to be moved.

“Who cut this edge?”

“I did,” Duan said.

“And this?”

“Already broken when she brought it.”

Jiang tested the gate piece with his file. She did not perform a spectacular cultivation technique. The file chattered, bit through the harder skin and found the crumbling material beneath. She wiped the filings onto paper and folded them inside it.

“Will you need them?” Su Fan asked.

“Someone may say the pieces were spoiled here. Better to know what every piece contains before it leaves.”

“Will they say that?”

“Someone already did.”

Duan swore. Jiang let him finish, then asked for a sound offcut of the same stock he used in his own pins. He supplied one. She labelled it separately.

Sun Lian wanted to know whether replacement braces could be delivered immediately or would wait for the contractor's appeal. Jiang said temporary sound fittings could be issued before blame was settled. The charge would remain disputed.

“Whose work gets delayed?” Sun Lian asked.

“Mine, apparently.”

It was the first thing Jiang had said that might have been a joke. Her clerk did not smile, which persuaded Su Fan that it probably was not.

They went back through the drawing. With the channel in its corrected position, Su Fan found that the brace he had drawn could not move the way he remembered unless he altered its support. Jiang asked him whether he wanted the record changed.

“Yes.”

“Then change it. Your first drawing isn't an oath.”

He rubbed away the line. Beneath it the paper went rough, but the second line was more useful. He looked at the corrected mechanism until the sequence in his memory matched it.

Jiang waited without reaching for her tea.

When they finished, she sat back.

“Two contractors have supplied mixed fittings. That will stop.”

“And the workers?” Su Fan asked.

“They'll be examined.”

“Bao Shun?”

“His compensation has been approved.”

Duan let out a breath.

Jiang raised a finger.

“Approved does not mean paid. My clerk will return within eight days. If he doesn't, send me this.”

She gave Duan a small wooden token.

It was not a magical promise. It had a number cut into it.

Su Fan found that he trusted it more than he had expected to.

***

As Jiang rose, a young attendant carried in the medicine chest from her pack.

He stumbled over a loose floorboard.

Su Fan reached automatically.

The chest was heavier than it looked. He caught it, turned with the weight and set it down without spilling its contents.

For a fraction of a moment the circuit completed beneath his ribs.

Jiang's eyes shifted toward him.

“Duan trains you well,” she said.

“He complains that I still waste iron.”

“Then he trains you honestly.”

The attendant apologized to Jiang, then Duan, then the chest. Its latch had sprung but none of the glass inside had broken. Su Fan kept his hand on the lid until the young man had a proper grip.

He had caught loads before. There was nothing unusual in that. He repeated the thought with such determination that it ceased to comfort him.

Jiang asked the attendant to carry the chest with both hands. She did not ask Su Fan to repeat the movement.

At the doorway she turned back to confirm where the sound replacements would be delivered. Duan answered. Su Fan stood beside the bench, aware of every small change in his own shoulders. If she noticed him noticing, she gave no sign.

Sun Lian left with the clerk to settle her transport receipt. The document box went back onto the horse. Jiang took her walking stick rather than the reins.

For one foolish moment Su Fan imagined that a woman who had lived more than a century ought to move without leaving footprints. Her boot sank into the soft patch outside the door exactly as his did. She wiped it against a stone and continued downhill.

Su Fan did not breathe freely until she had gone down the lane.

Duan shut the door.

“Whatever you're hiding,” he said, “don't hold it like a hot coal.”

Su Fan stared at him.

“I'm a smith. I notice people trying not to burn their fingers.”

***

Jiang stopped at Mother Wei's clinic before returning uphill.

Su Fan did not hear their conversation. He learned only that it lasted a long time and that Mother Wei closed the outer door afterward.

That evening, he found her sitting at the kitchen table with an old seal in front of her.

The stone bore a name he did not recognize.

“Will the gate workers be all right?” he asked.

“Some will. Some need rest they won't take.”

“Did she ask you to examine them?”

“Yes.”

“Will you?”

Mother Wei turned the seal facedown.

“I haven't decided.”

He almost told her that people needed her.

Then he saw the way she held her wrist beneath the table, where nobody coming through the door would notice.

The old stone lay in a patch of clean table between the bowls. Mother Wei had moved her ordinary papers aside to make room for it. Su Fan could not read the face from the doorway. He could see the impression it had left in its wrapping: a pale square in fabric that had darkened everywhere else.

He had almost made his appeal before noticing her wrist. He knew what he would have said. The men at the gates could not wait. She was the best healer they had. Jiang had asked because the work mattered.

All of those things might be true. They did not explain why Mother Wei had taken out an object she ordinarily kept hidden, or why the hand beneath the table looked so tired.

He hung his work shirt on its peg and asked whether there was water in the jar.

“Enough.”

He checked anyway. There was enough for tea and not enough for the evening wash. He took the second jar to the well. On his way back he met Bao Mei carrying a board with wet paint on it. She warned him away from the blue edge and asked whether the steward had seen her father's pin.

“Yes.”

“What did she say?”

“That the compensation's approved. Not paid yet.”

The girl's mouth tightened. She had begun to understand that some encouraging words came with another word attached.

“When?”

“Within eight days, or we ask again.”

“We've asked already.”

“I know.”

He did not show her Jiang's numbered token. It belonged with Duan, and showing it would not put food in her cupboard. He offered to hold the board while she adjusted the cloth around its dry end. She let him.

Back in the kitchen, Mother Wei had turned the seal facedown but had not put it away. She looked at the refilled jar, then at him.

“You needn't hover.”

“I'm thirsty.”

“Then you've found an excellent excuse.”

He cut kindling smaller than the stove required and set the pieces together. The work gave his hands somewhere to go. From the bench behind him came the faint scrape of stone against cloth.

He could ask tomorrow. He could ask after she chose. The patients would still need care, and she would still be a person before she was the answer to their need.

He found the tea tin on the upper shelf. It was nearly empty. He used less than he usually did and left the lid loose where she could reach it without stretching.

When he turned, her hand was on the table again. She had uncurled her fingers.

He put the kettle on instead.

chapters.title: A Sword Has Two Ends
chapters.text:
Duan gave Su Fan a wooden sword and hit him with a broom handle.

The first blow landed across his fingers.

“Ow.”

“Correct response.”

“I wasn't ready.”

“Neither was the man the sword belonged to. That's why I still have it.”

Su Fan looked at the wooden blade.

“The real one,” Duan said.

They stood behind the smithy at dawn. Duan had put his work aside for half an hour, a generosity that made Su Fan more nervous than the broom handle.

The wooden blade had an old chip near the point and a smooth place on the grip where another thumb had rested. It was not a practice sword carved for a child. Its weight drew his wrist down if he forgot it.

Duan took the broom head off the handle and leaned it against the wall. Without its straw, the length of wood appeared considerably less domestic.

“Is this because of Jiang?” Su Fan asked.

“This is because you keep looking at the kitchen knife as though it will solve an argument.”

“I don't.”

“You're looking at it now.”

It lay on the windowsill beside half an onion. Su Fan looked away.

Duan set a sandglass on a stool. The glass was cloudy and one end had been repaired with resin. Su Fan had not known his master owned it.

“Half an hour. After that, the iron needs us.”

“Every morning?”

“Every morning I have half an hour and you have fingers left.”

Su Fan shifted the wooden sword to his unbruised hand. Duan made him put it back.

“You can hold it either side later. First learn what one side is doing.”

Auntie Lu's shutters opened above them. She looked at the two weapons, then the sandglass.

“No breaking the wash line.”

“We're improving his character,” Duan said.

“Then put something down. He'll leak.”

She shut the window. Su Fan found himself smiling despite the ache in his fingers. He had been prepared for instructions about courage, the spirit of a swordsman, the proper contempt for pain. So far everyone seemed mostly concerned about the furniture.

Duan stepped back until there was room between them. He did not lower the handle.

Su Fan realized he was supposed to begin.

“Show me your stance.”

Su Fan stood as the scripture directed.

Duan walked around him.

“Good for carrying a load. Bad for reaching a throat.”

He tapped Su Fan's knee.

“You need to move.”

Su Fan moved.

The handle hit his shoulder.

“Not there.”

For the second attempt, Su Fan watched the far end of the handle.

Duan moved it left. Su Fan followed. The other end came forward and touched his shoulder before he understood that there was another end to watch.

“Your eyes aren't a dog,” Duan said. “Stop sending them after every stick.”

“What do I watch?”

“The person holding it.”

He tried. That was worse. Duan's face remained exactly the expression he wore while waiting for a badly fitted hinge to confess what was wrong with it. Su Fan looked at his hands, then his feet, then the space between them. By the time he returned to the handle, it was resting against his sleeve.

The third lesson was distance. Duan laid one toe beside the first stone and told him to stay out of reach. Su Fan moved back. His heel caught the second stone. He recovered awkwardly, the circuit tightening as he tried to make a small mistake disappear through strength.

The handle stopped short of his chest.

“Why didn't you hit me?”

“Because you'd land on the bucket.”

Su Fan moved the bucket. Duan let him, then changed where he stood. The useful space had altered again.

A faint breeze lifted the drying cloth on the line. It brushed Su Fan's shoulder, and he nearly turned toward it. Duan smiled for the first time.

“You'd be dead of laundry.”

“That isn't an ordinary battlefield condition.”

“You intend to fight only in places swept for you?”

He said nothing. He could feel how badly he wanted a rule he could master and keep. Stand this way. Wait this long. Move when the other man raised an elbow. The yard offered him six paces and a teacher who declined to remain in the correct part of them.

Once, briefly, Su Fan got the timing right. He stepped aside and left the wooden point between himself and Duan's ribs. The smith stopped.

“Better.”

The word warmed him more than the circuit. He immediately tried to repeat the movement. Duan shifted his grip. Su Fan's point went past an empty space, and the handle found his wrist.

He pulled back too quickly. The wooden sword slid against his palm.

“Keep it,” Duan said. “Winning isn't worth giving him the blade.”

The sandglass had almost run out. Su Fan was breathing harder than he would have after carrying two sacks from the quay. He had hardly crossed the yard.

By the end of the lesson he had been struck seven times. None of the blows was hard enough to damage him. All were hard enough to remain memorable.

He had tried completing the circuit before stepping. Duan had hit him while he waited.

He had tried using the extra strength to force the handle aside. Duan had let it move and hit him from the other direction.

The worst moment came when Su Fan thought he had found the pattern.

Duan changed it.

“You've done this before,” Su Fan said, rubbing his wrist.

“I told you. Gate guard. Four winters. Most of the work was standing in snow. A little was staying alive.”

“Were you good?”

“I became a smith.”

Su Fan considered that answer.

Duan rested the handle on his shoulder.

“Strength helps. Speed helps. Being difficult to knock down helps. None of them tells you where the next blow is coming from.”

“Can you teach me?”

“Some of it. Then you'll need somebody who stayed a guard.”

He took the wooden sword and showed Su Fan how to hold it without squeezing until his knuckles whitened.

“The point goes toward him. The handle stays with you. People complicate it from there.”

***

That day's work was buckles.

Su Fan had never resented a buckle so much. His fingers hurt when he held the tongs. Duan had chosen small work deliberately, though he denied it with such speed that the denial was useless.

“Can I change the order?”

“Yes. You can make the second buckle first.”

He worked until the small movements steadied him. The lesson returned in pieces: the handle coming from the end he had ignored; Duan stopping him from falling on a bucket; the mistake of treating one success as a discovered pattern.

At midday, Ah-Du asked to see the sword.

“No swinging it.”

“I know.”

“No testing it on the fence.”

“I know.”

“No standing behind me with it.”

The boy looked disappointed by the third condition. Su Fan gave him the blade anyway and watched him carry it with unexpected care. Ah-Du inspected the old chip, rubbed the grip and asked whether the previous owner had been tall.

“Why?”

“It's a long sword.”

“I don't know.”

Duan, eating near the forge, said the original iron one had belonged to a caravan guard who was shorter than Su Fan. The wooden copy had been made later.

“What happened to him?” Ah-Du asked.

“He stopped being a guard.”

“Like you?”

“No. He wasn't given the choice.”

The boy stopped playing with the grip.

Duan took a mouthful of rice before adding that he had kept the copy because a wooden blade allowed a man to learn more than one mistake. He did not supply a heroic history. Su Fan was glad. The worn place beneath his thumb felt different enough already.

That evening he tried the first step again, alone, without completing the circuit beforehand. He lifted the sword, moved his foot, stopped while he still had room to change his mind. It was less impressive than the stance he had shown Duan. It also left him less likely to trip.

When the neighbour came through with her washing basket, he lowered the point before stepping aside. She did not thank him. She should not have had to.

He practised once more after she passed, then put the sword away before tired fingers could make him careless. The urge to continue stayed with him all through supper. He disliked leaving something unfinished. Duan said that was a useful quality in a hinge and a dangerous one in a lesson.

For the next fortnight, Su Fan practised moving between the six stones.

He did not name the exercise.

Ah-Du did.

“Six-Stone Heavenly Escape.”

“No.”

“Duan's Invincible Finger-Smashing Art.”

“Closer.”

Tan Wei returned on his first free day and found them at it.

He carried rice, lamp oil and a small packet of sweet cakes. His shirt fitted better than the one he had left in. There was a new blue cord around his wrist, loose enough to turn.

Auntie Lu claimed the cakes as payment for years of emotional suffering.

Tan Wei let her take one.

Before they went down to the water, Tan Wei insisted on visiting the clinic.

Bao Shun was sitting outside with his injured arm supported on a folded blanket. Bao Mei had propped a painted board against the wall, where the light showed the colour properly. Tan Wei admired it without asking what a thirteen-year-old meant to do with painting.

“Can you make a fish?”

“I can make several fish.”

“A good one?”

“Can you pay for a bad one?”

He laughed and promised to come back when he knew the dimensions of the cupboard he wanted marked. The girl fetched a scrap of paper and made him write those dimensions as far as he knew them. His promise became an order small enough to be plausible.

Su Fan watched the exchange with an uncomfortable pleasure. He had bought a board partly to help. Tan Wei appeared to want a fish. Bao Mei knew the difference, even if she was glad of both customers.

Mother Wei asked to see the blue cord. Tan Wei turned his wrist freely. She examined the skin beneath it and asked what Han had told him to report.

He answered more seriously than he had answered Auntie Lu's demands for cake. Su Fan wanted to supply a question about the emergency term. He kept it behind his teeth while Tan Wei described his own understanding.

It was not exactly the understanding Su Fan would have chosen. It was also more informed than he had expected.

At the doorway, Mother Wei gave Tan Wei a small packet for chafed hands and told him to stop tightening the cord whenever he felt proud of it.

“How did you know?”

“Your wrist is telling on you.”

He loosened it another fraction.

They walked through the square with the cakes wrapped again, fewer now than when Tan Wei arrived. People stopped him twice to ask about the gate. Each time he stood a little straighter. Su Fan remembered wanting a grey work sash as a boy, not for what it meant but for the way people would look up before speaking to him.

At the river path, Tan Wei took off the sash and folded it carefully.

“Too grand for the reeds?” Su Fan asked.

“Too expensive for mud.”

They climbed down to the flat rock they had shared long before either had a reason to keep things from the other. Tan Wei tested the familiar loose edge with his heel, found it unchanged and sat with a sigh.

“That bed's better than mine,” he said. “This rock's better than the bed.”

“You could take it back.”

“Han would put it on my work allowance.”

They ate the rest beside the river.

He showed Su Fan what he had learned.

A thread of water lifted from the shallows. It bent around his finger, wavered and fell. The second attempt held longer.

“First stage,” he said.

Su Fan watched the drops slide from his friend's hand.

“Already?”

“Han says the opening is the easy part. The line remembers where to go.”

“Does it hurt?”

“Only when I do something stupid. So occasionally.”

Tan Wei glanced at the bruises on Su Fan's knuckles.

“You've found another method of that.”

“Duan is teaching me.”

“Good.”

He meant it without qualification.

A water beetle crossed the still shallows between them. Tan Wei followed it with his fingertip, trying to make the thread curl without touching the creature. The movement failed. The beetle continued, unimpressed.

“What do you want to do when you've learned it properly?” Su Fan asked.

“Get paid more.”

“After that.”

“Get paid regularly.”

Su Fan smiled. Tan Wei did not immediately join him.

“I'd like a room where the roof doesn't depend on somebody doing me a favour,” he said. “I'd like to go somewhere because I can afford the fare. Not because a load needs taking.”

“Where?”

“I don't know yet. That seems part of the pleasure.”

Across the water a fisherman lowered his net. The weights touched down in a row. Tan Wei watched the familiar work with a new interest, following the tiny corrections in the man's shoulders.

“Han says balance is what you do after you discover you weren't balanced,” he said. “I thought that was a joke until he made us carry buckets across the yard.”

“Sounds like paid work disguised as teaching.”

“It was both. The kitchen needed water.”

He held out the remaining cake. Su Fan broke it carefully and returned the larger half. Tan Wei noticed and exchanged the pieces without comment.

Su Fan felt the new circuit stir as he shifted on the rock. He had not summoned it. He could demonstrate something here, now, and change the afternoon. Tan Wei would be delighted before he had time to be anything else.

That was what made the silence difficult. It was not only fear of the office or Han or the sect. He would also have to explain why he had let his friend write and visit and speak so freely while offering a tidier, smaller version of himself in return.

Su Fan nearly told him then.

Instead he asked about the dormitory and listened while Tan Wei described a roommate who snored in two distinct pitches. He laughed at the right places. The afternoon passed pleasantly.

Before climbing back to the path, they threw the last crumbs into the shallows. A little fish came from beneath the rock, took one and vanished.

Tan Wei tried to carry another crumb toward it on a bead of water. The bead flattened. The crumb sank beside his boot.

“Ferocious art,” Su Fan said.

“I was thinking of charging the fish.”

“For what?”

“Delivery.”

He tried again and managed a short, trembling movement along the surface. The fish ignored it and took a different crumb. Tan Wei laughed without embarrassment, pleased enough by the attempt.

Su Fan remembered them doing this with ordinary sticks when they were children, inventing little boats from bark and declaring that the river would carry them to the sea. He had always insisted on building the better boat. Tan Wei had usually tired of the competition first and gone to look for frogs.

Now his friend wiped his hand on the grass, content to leave one unsuccessful trick behind. Su Fan gathered the empty wrapping and followed him up the path.

When Tan Wei left, he pressed a coin into Su Fan's hand.

“My half of Bao Shun's food.”

“You don't owe—”

“I know.”

His friend closed Su Fan's fingers around it.

For a while after he had gone, Su Fan sat with the coin hidden in his fist.

It was warm from another person's hand.

chapters.title: Passengers Without Tickets
chapters.text:
The attack began with a woman waving from the bank.

She stood beside a broken cart. One wheel lay in the mud. Two sacks had split, spilling pale grain down toward the water.

The woman waved with both arms, then pointed toward the cart as though the trouble might not be visible from the water. Her sleeve had slipped down over one hand. She pushed it back and waved again.

They were travelling through a reach where the river pressed close beneath the eastern bank. The towpath on the other side had vanished behind reeds. There was room for two boats to pass, but not much room for a mistake between them.

Su Fan had spent the morning learning how to anticipate Sun Lian's requests. He had the right line ready when she wanted it, moved a medicine chest before the sun reached its lid and remembered to leave the landing pole where she could seize it. The pleasure of becoming useful had made him careless about what happened beyond the deck.

Now the merchant in the yellow hat stood up before Sun Lian had decided anything.

“Over there.”

“I can see her.”

The other two passengers remained seated beneath the cabin overhang. A woman supported her grown son's foot on a bundle of clothes. His ankle was swollen above the sandal, and he watched the cart with the quiet attention of someone who had recently discovered how hard a journey could become.

Su Fan moved the fitting hammer farther from the cabin door so nobody would trip over it if they landed. His wooden sword lay wrapped in his bedding. He had brought it because Duan told him to practise while waiting for deliveries, not because anybody had hired him as a guard.

The boat's load sat lower than on his first trip. The new braces were heavy. He knew their weight because he had helped forge and carry them; the two medicine chests were much lighter and had cost more. Sun Lian had put them where spray would not reach, then added a second cover.

On the bank, the woman knelt briefly beside the cart and got up again. Su Fan could not see another person from this angle.

A floating branch passed the bow. It turned in a small eddy before sliding toward the shallows. Sun Lian watched it, shifted her grip on the stern oar and reduced their speed without surrendering the current.

Sun Lian slowed but did not turn in.

“Keep your hands where I can see them,” she called.

The woman raised both hands.

“My father's hurt.”

“Bring him to the edge.”

“He can't walk.”

Su Fan looked at the cart. Its axle pointed toward the river. If it had lost a wheel there, the grain should have spilled inland.

He moved beside Sun Lian.

“I see it,” she said quietly.

Their cargo this time included new braces for the lower gate, two chests of medicine and three passengers. Duan had insisted Su Fan accompany his work. Su Fan had insisted on being paid.

The negotiation had pleased both of them.

Now one passenger, a merchant with a yellow travel hat, leaned over the rail.

“We can't leave an injured man.”

“Then you may swim to him,” Sun Lian said.

The merchant drew back.

She pushed the stern oar, angling toward the deeper channel.

The yellow hat tilted toward him.

“You saw something?” the merchant asked.

“The grain fell the wrong way.”

“Grain falls everywhere.”

That was true enough to make explaining difficult. The cart leaned toward the water, but its broken wheel lay behind the axle, where a wheel might have been placed rather than thrown. The sacks had been opened near their tops. None of it proved anything by itself.

Sun Lian did not wait for proof. She put more of her weight on the oar.

The woman on shore lowered her hands. For a moment she looked angry rather than frightened. Then she glanced behind the cart.

Su Fan took one step toward the cabin.

“Sit down,” he told the merchant.

“I've paid for passage, not orders.”

“Then take the passage sitting down.”

The man's face hardened. Su Fan was already looking past him, at a reed that moved against the wind on the opposite bank. A hand appeared around its stem and disappeared.

He heard a wet scraping sound ahead. Sun Lian heard it too. Her head turned before anything broke the surface.

“Hold something,” she said.

He caught the merchant's coat as the man began an indignant reply.

A rope rose across the water.

It had been lying below the surface, weighted with stones. Four men on the far bank hauled it tight.

Sun Lian swore and let the current carry the bow sideways. The rope caught beneath the forward rail instead of striking them across the chest.

“Cargo down!” she shouted.

Su Fan pulled the merchant away from the edge.

Two arrows hit the cabin wall.

The passengers dropped. Su Fan crouched behind a timber stack and took the wooden sword from his bundle, then put it down again. Against arrows it was a particularly poor piece of wood.

He picked up Duan's short-handled fitting hammer instead.

The first arrow made less noise than the rail.

It struck the cabin wall with a dry tap. The second split a thin panel near the latch. The woman beneath the overhang pulled her son sideways and rolled his supported leg with both hands rather than drag it. He hissed through his teeth but did not cry out.

Su Fan pushed the merchant down behind the timber. The man tried to rise again, then saw the arrowhead protruding through the wood and stayed where he was.

Sun Lian called for the lower cargo line to be released.

He reached for it. The boat had caught crosswise against the rope, and the cargo's weight was making the roll worse. If the lashings all held exactly as he had tied them, the heavy braces might carry the deck down with them. He loosened only the line she named.

A beam shifted a hand's width and stopped against a bearing block. The boat settled enough for her to gain another fraction of the stern.

The woman on shore had vanished behind the cart. The broken sacks lay open in the mud, grain bleaching in the sun. Su Fan hated the neatness of it now that he could see the intention: a place where a helpful boat would come close, a rope beneath the surface, archers where the turning deck would expose its passengers.

He crouched beside the fitting hammer. His heart was beating so hard that he could feel it in his teeth. The warm circuit would not come when he called for it. He tried again, angrier, and it stayed gone.

Duan's broom handle returned to him with humiliating clarity. Waiting for strength was still waiting.

He took the hammer with both hands and looked for ordinary work it could do.

The rope boom had caught below the bow rail. Its tension passed through the cleat and into a small iron fastening. He had examined that fastening on the first journey, when Sun Lian asked him to check a seam. It was sound, but not designed to hold a boat sideways against the river.

Beyond the bank, more reeds parted. He counted men because counting was a thing he could still do.

Men emerged from the reeds. Six on the near bank. Four at the rope. One standing farther back with a pale staff.

The last man wore a damaged disciple's sash.

“Medicine chests,” he called. “Leave them on the landing and go.”

Sun Lian kept her hands on the oar.

“You can have the grain aboard. Not the medicine.”

“We didn't ask for grain.”

“Then you've planned a hungry evening.”

The man lifted the staff.

A thin skin of ice formed around the hauling rope.

Su Fan had seen frost tricks on the mountain road. He had never watched one used by someone who needed the result.

The rope tightened until the forward rail creaked.

“Third stage, perhaps fourth,” Sun Lian said under her breath.

“How many are you?”

“Four. Wrong sort.”

The water beneath the boat began to thicken with slush.

Earthwork could hold her joints together. It could not persuade frozen water to flow.

Su Fan looked at the bank, the rope and the cargo lashings. He could reach the bow under cover of the timber. If he cut the line before it froze solid, the current would take them past the landing.

It would also swing the passengers' cabin toward the archers.

“Can you lower the sail?” he asked.

“It's tied.”

“Lower it loose.”

She glanced toward the archers, understood and moved.

Sun Lian kept one foot braced against the stern bench while she pulled the sail's loose end clear. She could not simply let go of the oar. The current would turn them broadside and drive the low rail beneath the water.

Su Fan passed her the nearer rope. She caught it with her free hand and jerked once. A knot held.

“Up there,” she said.

He had tied that knot. He remembered being pleased with how neatly it sat.

There was no time to untie it. He took the little cutting knife from the tool roll and reached from the shelter of the timber. An arrow hit the rail above his arm. He dropped flat, waited for the shaft to stop trembling and reached again lower down.

The knife went through the thinner tie. The sail loosened, caught briefly on a protruding brace and hung ready above the exposed side. Sun Lian kept its lower corner in her hand. One pull would bring it down when he moved.

It would be cloth, not protection from an arrow. He needed it to hide where he crawled, nothing more. The timber still sheltered the passengers for the moment.

“Stay low,” Su Fan told the merchant.

The man nodded so violently that his hat came off. He caught it, then seemed ashamed of having done so.

The mother had put her own coat over her son's head. She kept one hand on his ankle, protecting the injury even now. Su Fan wanted to tell her where the guard station was, how long the next reach would take, something with an ending in it. He did not know whether they would reach the next bend.

He gave her the knife.

“Only the cargo cord if it pulls you under. Not the thick one by your foot.”

She took it without asking him to repeat himself.

On the bank, the staff struck stone. Frost spread along the hauling rope in a slow pale sleeve. The river carried the sound of men shouting to one another; Su Fan could distinguish an argument about when to pull from the words themselves.

Not all of them knew what the others intended. That was useful. It was also frightening. A frightened archer might loose without waiting for the man with the staff to finish bargaining.

Sun Lian looked once toward the bow.

Su Fan nodded, not to promise success but to show that he understood the only task she could spare him for.

He kept the hammer low and turned onto his hands and knees.

He crawled forward.

An arrow went through the timber stack and stopped a hand's breadth from his cheek. He pressed flat until the next shot struck higher.

The sail dropped across the open side of the boat.

It was cloth, not armour. But for three breaths the men on shore could not see where to aim.

Su Fan reached the rope.

The ice had spread around the bow cleat. He struck it with the hammer. Chips flew. His second blow cracked the iron pin holding the cleat.

Then the boat lurched.

Someone had climbed aboard at the stern.

Su Fan turned. Too late to help. Too far from the hammer's useful end.

Sun Lian caught the boarder's wrist with a measuring cord, stepped into him and drove her forehead into his nose.

He fell backward into the river.

The merchant made a high, astonished sound.

“Stay down,” she told him.

The man with the staff began walking onto the frozen shallows.

Su Fan hit the cleat again.

This time he completed the circuit as the hammer fell.

The pin sheared.

The rope tore away half the forward rail and the boat spun free.

He fell hard against the deck. His wrist burned. He had mistimed the return.

Sun Lian hauled the stern around, using the current to gain distance.

The broken cleat spun past them in a foam of splintered rail. Su Fan saw the iron pin still caught inside it and felt an absurd urge to retrieve the piece. Duan would ask how it failed.

The staff struck the water.

A white ridge raced toward them, caught the stern and lifted it. Every small, reasonable question vanished.

His shoulder hit the timber. One of the lashings snapped. A crate scraped across the deck, struck the gap in the rail and tipped over before he could reach it. It was fittings rather than medicine; the distinction brought relief and guilt together. Someone would still have to pay.

Sun Lian shouted for him to move aft.

He crawled instead of standing. The circuit had left his wrist burning and his fingers unreliable. He could not afford to discover that while holding the rail. Near the stern he used his shoulder against a loose sack and kept it from sliding into the oar's movement.

The boat came level by degrees. Slush dragged along the hull, then thinned into scattered pieces. A strip of ice knocked against the stern and broke.

The ice stopped growing. On shore the man with the staff bent forward, coughing. One of his own men reached for his arm. He pushed the hand away. The gesture was the first ordinary weakness Su Fan had seen in him, and it did not make the danger smaller. It made the short distance between them feel temporary.

Sun Lian got the sail clear of the river before it could fill and pull against them. Su Fan helped with his better hand. Wet cloth came aboard heavy as a soaked blanket. The merchant tried to assist, put his fingers in the wrong place, and snatched them back when she told him to.

The bend shut the bank from view.

They counted people. Three passengers. Sun Lian. Su Fan. The mother answered for her son when he could not stop coughing long enough to speak. The medicine chests remained under their second cover. The lower corner of one had been struck but not opened.

Only then did Su Fan see blood on Sun Lian's forehead. She wiped it with her sleeve and looked downriver, not at the cloth.

He had thought surviving the trap would bring a moment in which the boat became ordinary again. The torn rail, the wet sail and the ice still clinging to its boards disagreed.

The mother asked for a strip of clean cloth. Su Fan fetched one from the tool roll and found that she wanted it for the merchant's arm, where a splinter had torn through his sleeve. She had already settled her son against the cabin wall. The merchant offered to pay her; she told him to keep his elbow still.

Sun Lian examined the gap in the rail without relinquishing the oar. The remaining wood would hold a temporary line. It would not stop a passenger falling if the deck rolled again. Su Fan rigged the line low and warned the others away from it. His first knot shook loose under his own test. He made it again, slower, using the hand that hurt less.

The work gave him something smaller than the whole river to attend to. Once it was finished, there was still a broken boat beneath him and armed men somewhere behind the bend.

He looked at the medicine covers. He knew who had packed one chest. He did not know every person waiting for it. The merchant had put a hand over his bandaged arm and was watching those same boxes with a resentment that had survived the escape.

Nobody spoke for several breaths.

At last the merchant sat up.

“You should have given them the chests.”

Sun Lian looked at the shattered rail.

“Perhaps,” she said.

Su Fan had expected an argument. Her answer left the deck quieter than a rebuke would have.

Behind them, out of sight, somebody began ringing a hand bell.

Sun Lian listened.

“That landing wasn't the end of it.”

chapters.title: Ice Does Not Care
chapters.text:
They could not outrun a warning bell.

Sun Lian brought the boat into a narrow backwater before the next bend. Willows leaned over the water. The hull scraped mud and settled.

The merchant began protesting.

She put a finger to her lips.

From the main channel came the slap of oars. A smaller boat passed the mouth of the backwater. Three men aboard. One holding a net weighted with hooks.

Su Fan stayed beneath the willow branches until they had gone.

The small boat had no cargo and hardly any freeboard. Its rowers used short strokes to keep close to the bank. Su Fan watched the man with the hooked net trail one corner in the water, testing the depth beneath the reeds.

He would not need to see the whole boat. A clean scrape in the mud, a broken branch, a piece of white sail showing through leaves would do.

Su Fan pulled the wet sail farther under the timber with his good hand. The torn part caught on a nail. He stopped pulling before the sound could carry and worked it free a finger at a time.

Beside him the mother held her son's shoulder. He was sweating from pain and the effort of keeping quiet. The merchant had pressed his hat flat against his chest; its yellow brim was too bright even beneath the willow.

Sun Lian pointed at it. The man turned it inside out without argument.

For a few breaths the search boat slowed. One oar rested on the surface. Su Fan could hear the drip from its blade. Then somebody farther downstream called, and the rower pulled again.

The hooked net lifted clear. They passed the mouth of the backwater and disappeared beyond the hanging branches.

Su Fan counted several breaths before letting his own out fully. He did not trust the relief. The first trap had required enough preparation to suggest that the attackers knew where a damaged boat would hide.

Sun Lian leaned close enough for her next words to reach only the deck.

“There'll be a second,” Sun Lian whispered. “Maybe more.”

“Can we walk?” one of the passengers asked.

“Through the reeds. Not with the cargo.”

“Leave it.”

Sun Lian looked toward the medicine chests.

The labels named thirty-two gate workers due for examination. Mother Wei had packed one of the smaller cases herself. Su Fan recognized her way of tying the cloth handle.

“We can move the people first,” he said. “How far to the towpath?”

“Two hundred paces. Mud all the way.”

“Then I'll take them.”

Sun Lian caught his arm.

“Take the hammer too.”

***

The merchant lost a shoe in the first thirty paces.

Su Fan made him leave it.

The other passengers were a mother and her adult son. The son had a swollen ankle and walked with a stick. He apologized whenever he slowed them.

“Save your breath,” Su Fan said.

The mud changed with every step.
