Near the boat it held a crust firm enough to carry a foot if the foot landed flat. Beneath the reeds it softened into a black sucking paste. Su Fan tested the next patch with the hammer handle and made the others follow his prints rather than spread into an easier-looking line.

The son insisted that he could walk if his mother stopped taking so much of his weight. She said he could make that argument on dry ground. Between them they managed three more paces before his good foot slipped.

Su Fan caught him under the arm. The jolt went into the wrist he had mistimed on the boat. He said nothing, waited until the man had regained his balance, then gave him a long reed bundled with two others for a second support.

It bent. It did not break.

Behind them the merchant stood motionless, looking at the place where his shoe had vanished.

“Leave it.”

“It has my money in the lining.”

That changed the difficulty without changing the time available. Su Fan looked back toward the willow. No shout yet. No crack of an oar.

“How much?”

“Enough that I would like my shoe.”

Su Fan drove the hammer handle into the mud beside the man's ankle, felt leather, and levered upward. The mud released a brown bubble. The shoe did not come. He tried once more, then saw the merchant's face when he shook his head.

The loss was real. It was not made smaller by being ridiculous.

The man stepped out of the other shoe and pushed it into his coat. Barefoot, he moved more carefully and complained less. The mother offered him a strip of cloth for his foot. He declined, then accepted when a broken reed cut him.

They went on in a crooked file. Su Fan could not see the river anymore. He listened for the search boat and heard only water settling in the channels around them.

At the drier ground he turned the group uphill, away from the obvious track made by people reaching the towpath. The mother noticed and nodded. Her son kept his eyes on the next place he had to put his foot.

At the towpath he found a shallow ditch screened by broom grass. He put them there and showed them the direction of the nearest signal post.

“Don't leave until the boat passes, or you see uniformed guards.”

“Which uniforms?” the mother asked.

He had no answer he trusted.

“Two witnesses,” he said instead. “Don't go with a single man.”

He returned by a different line through the reeds.

Halfway back, he heard wood crack.

The frost cultivator stood on the grounded boat.

Sun Lian faced him from the stern, one hand bleeding. A second attacker lay on the deck with a broken oar across his legs.

The cultivator had recovered enough breath to frost the rail. Ice crept beneath Sun Lian's bare feet.

“Move away from the chests,” he said.

She shifted her weight. Brown light passed through the deck. The joints tightened, but the cold continued spreading.

Su Fan crouched behind a willow.

He could throw the hammer. At that distance he might hit the man's head. More likely a shoulder. After that he would be empty-handed and visible.

There was another possibility.

The boat had grounded bow-first. The stern still floated. Sun Lian could free it if the weight moved aft.

From behind the willow he could see the boat's angle more clearly than he had from aboard.

The bow pressed into a shelf of mud. The stern floated in darker water, drifting a little with each movement on deck. Sun Lian had left her long oar ready on that side. The frost man stood between her and the medicine, forcing her to defend something fixed while he could choose where to step.

The second attacker groaned beside the broken oar. His legs lay at an awkward angle, but his hands still moved. Su Fan could not count him out. A man unable to stand might still catch an ankle or pull a line.

There was no sign of the woman from the cart. That did not mean she had gone. Every place he could not see seemed to have acquired the weight of another possible enemy.

Sun Lian's bleeding hand slid against the rail. She adjusted her grip rather than look at it. The brown light tightened the deck under her feet, holding her boat together while the other man's ice spread across its surface.

Su Fan wanted to give her a signal. He had no agreed signal, no birdcall from childhood she would recognize, no clever way to make a sound that only she could hear. Throwing something might turn the man's head. If it failed, it would at least tell Sun Lian someone else was near.

He weighed the hammer in his palm. His hand still worked well enough to hold it. Throwing it would make that irrelevant.

The useful work lay in moving the cultivator's weight forward and giving the stern a moment to swing. There would be pain in reaching that moment. Su Fan looked at the strip of mud between himself and the bow and stopped trying to imagine a version in which nobody saw him.

A flat stone lay beneath the willow root, slick with water.

Su Fan picked it up and threw it into the water behind the cultivator.

The man turned only his head.

Not enough.

Su Fan stepped out and ran toward the bow.

The staff came around.

A white line crossed the mud in front of him. He jumped late. Ice closed around his left ankle.

He had expected cold to arrive from outside.

Instead it seemed to begin inside the bones. His foot had become a thing he knew by the absence of ordinary feeling. The white shell pressed into the leather above his heel, fixing him at the end of a step he could no longer finish.

He tried to drag the foot free. Pain stopped him. The ground under the ice would not yield, and the boot was held more securely than the flesh inside it.

The staff lifted again.

He had no fine plan now. He had a hammer, a trapped foot and a man watching to see whether fear would make him leave his face unprotected. Su Fan kept the handle between them as best he could and bent toward the ice.

Sun Lian said something from the stern. He could not spare enough attention to understand it. The cultivator could, apparently, because he glanced toward her before returning his eyes to Su Fan.

That glance was all the time available.

Cold drove through his boot.

He struck the ice with the hammer. It cracked but held.

The cultivator smiled.

For a moment Su Fan felt a second pressure, finer than the cold. It searched up his leg as though looking for a cord to pull.

His circuit contracted.

He stopped forcing it.

The searching pressure slid past without catching. The ice remained.

That distinction saved him from a worse mistake.

He did not try to walk through it. He hit it again.

This time the hammer landed true. The ice split. Skin tore beneath his boot as he pulled free.

The cultivator stepped toward the bow.

Sun Lian moved.

She drove the stern oar into the mud, put both hands against the deck and pushed. The boat flexed around its grounded nose.

The man's footing shifted.

Su Fan reached the rail as the staff descended. He met the wooden shaft with the hammer, not the ice gathering at its tip.

The impact numbed his arm.

The cultivator was stronger. Faster too. His next movement would have broken Su Fan's jaw.

But Sun Lian had already brought the stern around.

The man stumbled. Su Fan drove the hammer into his knee.

He fell, struck the rail, and landed in the shallows.

His staff went under the boat.

Sun Lian hauled Su Fan aboard.

Together they pushed off.

The cultivator reached for the rail with one hand. Su Fan could have crushed it. Instead he struck the plank beside the fingers.

The hand withdrew.

They left him sitting in water up to his waist, cursing with a concentration that suggested he was very much alive.

***

Sun Lian collected the passengers downstream.

The merchant saw Su Fan's bleeding ankle and said nothing about his shoe.

At the guard station, they gave statements. The officer knew the frost cultivator's name: Zhu Ke, expelled from a branch school, wanted for two previous attacks.

He promised a patrol.

Sun Lian accepted the receipt without pretending it was a rescue.

The guard station had a roof, a rack of spears and a clerk who wanted them to begin at the beginning.

Sun Lian began at the cart.

The merchant interrupted to explain the shoe. The mother interrupted him to explain the rope. Her son sat on a bench with his foot raised while a guard brought water and a cloth. Nobody offered to unload the medicine chests until Sun Lian asked who would be responsible if they warmed on the deck.

Then two guards came down to help.

Su Fan gave his account from the bow. He could describe where the arrows struck, how the cleat had failed and where the frost man landed. He could not say how many attackers had reached the river after them. The clerk kept returning to that question as if repetition might improve his view through the reeds.

“At least the ones we saw,” Sun Lian said. “Put that down.”

The officer examined the splintered rail and found the broken fastening. He asked whether the crew had cut it deliberately.

“Yes,” Su Fan said.

The question made him suddenly angry. He wanted someone to look at the frost on the deck, the blood on the boatwoman's hand, the passengers without shoes, and stop asking them why their own property was broken.

The officer listened to the anger without answering it. Then he pointed to the current beyond the station.

“I'm writing how you got free. The next boat may need to know.”

Su Fan looked down at the fastening and felt the heat leave his face.

He explained the sail and the cleat properly. The officer asked two sensible questions and drew the reach in the dirt with the butt of his spear. Sun Lian corrected the position of the backwater. The mother showed where they had waited on the towpath.

It was the first time since the attack that Su Fan saw the whole event from somewhere outside his own need to survive it.

The promised patrol assembled while the statements were copied. Not quickly enough to recover the lost crate, not certainly enough to make the next passage safe. But there were actual men preparing an actual boat.

The merchant asked whether anyone could retrieve his shoe. One guard laughed. The officer did not. He asked where it had been lost and wrote the location beside the other losses.

Sun Lian folded their receipt into the dry part of her papers. The mother thanked Su Fan before leaving for the station's waiting room. Her son thanked him too, then apologized for having been slow.

“You reached the path,” Su Fan said.

He had no better answer. The man appeared to accept it.

When the deck was finally clear, Su Fan sat on a low box and tried to pull off his boot. The leather did not move. He tried a little harder and found a patch where it had frozen to the blood.

Sun Lian watched him stop pretending that it was a small problem.

Later she sat beside Su Fan while he cut the frozen leather away from his ankle.

“You cultivate,” she said.

He stopped cutting.

“Yes.”

“What stage?”

“First.”

She looked toward the damaged bow.

“You should have told me.”

“Would it have changed the plan?”

“I don't know. I didn't have the information.”

He bent over the boot again.

She let him work in silence, but when his hand began shaking she took the knife and finished the cut.

chapters.title: What the Fire Leaves
chapters.text:
The last clearing of the Sealed Stack happened on a wet afternoon.

Rain soaked the top layer of the burn pile. The lower books still caught. Smoke rolled along the ground and made the porters cough.

Su Fan could smell the fire before he reached the old quarter. Wet cloth, spoiled paper, glue. The air felt greasy at the back of his throat.

He walked slowly because of the ankle. Mother Wei had wrapped it after examining the torn skin and the cold damage beneath. She had not agreed that being able to stand meant being fit for every errand. When Sun Lian came for the maps, she allowed him to help on the condition that the boatwoman made him sit when the foot began to throb.

Sun Lian had said she already made him sit when he became annoying.

At the Stack, a porter dragged a rope around a bundle of loose volumes. He pulled the knot hard enough to cut through the softened cover of the top book. Pages slumped out over his shoe.

He swore, gathered them with both hands and tried again.

“Those won't carry,” Su Fan said.

“Then they'll burn here.”

The man was not pleased about it. His sleeves were wet to the shoulder. He had been given a number of loads to move and no shelter in which to pack them. Every time he finished a bundle the rain made it heavier.

Sun Lian took a broken shutter from beside the door and laid it across two crates. The porter stared, then understood. He spread the loose books on it long enough to retie the rope around a dry board.

“Leave the shutter,” he said.

“It was yours to begin with.”

They went inside past the condemned shelves. Pale rectangles on the wall showed where wood had stood for so long that the stone around it had darkened. The room looked larger and less habitable.

Min stood near the back with a slip of authority in his hand. His coat was buttoned wrong. He had overlooked it, or decided that the arrangement of buttons was an argument he could afford to lose today.

Min had secured permission to keep three shelves.

He called this a victory with the exhausted expression of somebody who had counted what victory cost.

Su Fan arrived with Sun Lian to collect old river surveys.

Jiang had asked the archive for construction records. The request came after the cart had been loaded, but before the fire reached the waterproof map cases.

For once, the timing favoured them.

The clerk pointed at a stack beneath a tarpaulin.

“Anything with a blue tie.”

The clerk put a mark beside Jiang's request and asked how much room they had aboard.

“Enough for the surveyed records,” Sun Lian said.

“That isn't a quantity.”

“Show me what the quantity contains.”

He disliked that. Su Fan recognized the expression from the delivery stores. A category was easy to issue. Individual objects required somebody to look at them.

The map cases came in four sizes. Some held rolled paper. Some were flat boxes with swollen hinges. One contained nothing but a sheet of oilskin, the map it had protected gone long before the present clearing.

Sun Lian set the empty case aside rather than count it as a rescue. Su Fan worked through the small ones while sitting on a crate. His ankle burned when he let it hang too long. He put the foot on a lower box and hated how much the simple adjustment helped.

The first map he unrolled showed a reservoir with two names. One had been scraped away and rewritten. Min could date the newer hand only approximately; he identified the older water measurement by a unit neither of the others recognized.

“Can you translate it?” Sun Lian asked.

“Some.”

“All we need for the level?”

“I'd want another copy before promising.”

Su Fan had once thought a scholar read a thing and knew it. Min read, turned the sheet toward the light, looked for damage, and asked whether a mark was a number or a worm hole. The work seemed both smaller and more demanding than the certainty Su Fan had imagined.

They found two records that contradicted one another about a channel's width. Sun Lian put both into the keeper's pile. The clerk objected that one was obviously wrong.

“Then we'll need the other to tell us which,” she said.

Outside, a porter shouted for another cart. The fire hissed as a wet bundle was thrown onto its centre. Min's hand jerked at the sound. He went on sorting.

Su Fan noticed that the scholar kept touching the slip authorizing his three shelves. It could preserve only a certain amount of space. Even permission had a weight limit today.

Several ties had lost their colour. Min helped them sort by dates instead.

Sun Lian spread a map on a clean board. It showed Greywing as a series of brown ridges, the nine gates as squares, and the river below them dividing into a network of channels.

West of Mudgate, a wide pale line ran toward marshland.

“The Dry Cut,” she said.

Su Fan knew it as a strip of broken ground where children hunted lizards.

“It was a river?”

“An overflow. Look at the contour marks.”

She traced them.

The channel passed beneath the old quarter before turning west. Most of its upper section had been built over. A small square near the Stack carried an obsolete gate symbol.

Min leaned closer.

“Older than the present works.”

“How old?”

“The drawing is a copy. The original date was already illegible when this was made.”

“Does it still connect?” Su Fan asked.

Sun Lian folded one corner back.

“Stone fills channels. So do people. We'd need to walk it.”

Su Fan put a finger where Mudgate should have been.

The drawing gave the valley a different outline. A loop of river lay where the lower market now stood. The place he knew as the lizard ground was wide enough on the paper to take a substantial flow. He tried to imagine water there and found his mind supplying the current from the town's ordinary bank, too small for the pale channel.

“Could it carry what's above us?”

“Not from a drawing,” Sun Lian said.

“I mean if it were open.”

“So do I.”

She took out a measuring string and laid it between two known landmarks. The copied distances did not agree closely enough to calculate a useful capacity. A fold ran through the old gate symbol. When she pressed it flat, a piece of surface came away on her finger.

Min brought a clean scrap and copied the symbol before they lost more of it. He drew the uncertainty as well as the visible lines, leaving one corner incomplete.

“What did this square mean?” Su Fan asked.

“Some controlled opening. Perhaps a gate. Not necessarily one operated like the present towers.”

“And the mark near the Stack?”

“Could be a building. Could be a note placed where there was room.”

Su Fan leaned closer. The marks were tantalizing because they refused to be only one thing. Somewhere beneath the place where he had earned six copper opening clamps, old water might once have passed in a channel large enough to change the valley. Or someone might simply have drawn badly.

Sun Lian asked whether there were later records showing the overflow filled in.

Min named two shelves. One still existed. The other was an empty patch beside the door.

They searched the surviving shelf first. Su Fan found a list of road repairs, a damaged account for stone carts and a little chart of monthly rain. None settled the question. Sun Lian kept the chart and the road repairs because the dates might help them compare other records later.

The clerk returned to say the cart would leave soon.

“Then those,” Sun Lian said, indicating the chosen cases.

“And the loose sheets?”

“Wrapped inside.”

The limit had become a physical pile. Su Fan could see what they could carry and what they could not. He helped roll the Dry Cut map around a sound wooden rod, resisting the urge to tuck every unread sheet into his shirt. He would not save paper by tearing it against his own sweat and bandages.

Min put the copied symbol in the same case. He wrote where the copy came from before closing it.

They placed the map in the keeper's pile.

A porter came in carrying another bundle.

Min saw the top book and stood so quickly his chair fell over.

“Not that one.”

“It was on the condemned shelf.”

“Because your clerk moved it.”

The clerk looked up.

Min picked up the book. Its pages were written in two hands. One was his. The other belonged to a child who had carefully copied each character beneath the adult line.

“Personal property,” he said.

The clerk considered arguing, then saw Jiang's requisition seal on Sun Lian's papers and chose a quieter afternoon.

Min took the book into the back room.

Su Fan found him there a little later.

He was trying to wipe rain from a child's drawing of a bird.

“Yours?” Su Fan asked.

“My daughter's.”

Su Fan had not known he had one.

“She lives in Siltbridge. Copies contracts. Last I heard, she could charge more for a day than I earn in a week.”

“You must be pleased.”

Min's hand stopped.

“I am now.”

The answer explained less than it revealed.

He shut the book.

The bird had one wing much larger than the other.

Su Fan recognized the difficulty from Bao Mei's early boards: the first line took up less space than intended, so the rest of the creature had to grow to make use of the paper. The child's letters beneath it were carefully copied. The strokes pressed too hard in the places where a smaller hand had tried to match a confident one.

Min dabbed the damp edge with an unmarked cloth. He had stopped trying to rub the page dry.

“Should I fetch another board?” Su Fan asked.

The scholar nodded.

Su Fan found one under a stack of empty cases and wiped the grit from it before bringing it back. Min laid the exercise book flat, propped its cover open and held a clean sheet between two pages that threatened to stick.

Outside the back room, Sun Lian argued about whether a rope handle counted as packing material to be charged separately. The normal absurdity of the dispute made the little room feel unexpectedly private.

“I thought you had always been here,” Su Fan said.

“Most people do, after enough years.”

Min adjusted the cloth.

“Was she born here?”

The scholar's hand stopped. Su Fan wished he had chosen a different question. He was asking for a story because the book had made the existence of one visible, not because Min had offered to tell it.

“You needn't answer.”

Min gave him a brief glance, almost grateful, and returned to the page.

“She disliked copying my hand,” he said after a while. “Too many flourishes. Said I made ordinary words look pleased with themselves.”

Su Fan looked at the child's line. Its letters were plain and compact.

“She may have had a point.”

“She had several. I preferred discussing mine.”

The silence that followed did not ask Su Fan to improve it. He held the board steady while Min freed another page. The bird appeared again as a faint blue impression on the paper beneath, still lopsided, almost in flight.

When the book was laid safely aside, the scholar looked at Su Fan's bandaged foot and found a subject less difficult than his daughter's childhood.

“How is your reading?”

“Better than my ankle.”

Min looked at the bandage.

“Reading can have that effect.”

“I fought a third-stage man.”

The old scholar's face lost its humour.

“On purpose?”

“Not initially.”

“Try to retain that distinction.”

Su Fan described the pressure that had passed through him without finding a hold.

Min listened closely.

“The text calls the first condition Pure Breath,” he said. “No borrowed pattern. No chosen element. Suppression usually acts through what a cultivator carries.”

“So it doesn't work on me?”

“The particular pressure you felt didn't work as he expected. Don't turn one observation into a funeral invitation.”

Su Fan looked at his ankle.

“Then I should try it again?” Su Fan asked.

“With the same man?”

“Not necessarily.”

Min looked so offended that Su Fan almost smiled.

“You have one injured ankle and one incomplete account. You don't require a second opponent to make those interesting.”

“What can I test here?”

“That you can describe what happened without improving it in the telling.”

Su Fan went back through the encounter. The cold had caught his leg first. Then the finer pressure had moved as if seeking something beneath the skin. He had been forcing his own circuit to remain closed. When he stopped, the searching sensation slid away, but the ice held until he broke it with the hammer.

Min asked whether he had felt the intrusive pressure vanish entirely or simply cease to hold him. Su Fan could not be certain.

“Write the uncertainty.”

He had brought his notebook. The page shook a little on his knee because his foot hurt and the crate was uneven. He wrote the physical sequence, leaving room beside the part he could not distinguish.

Min watched without correcting the words. At the end he pointed to a sentence claiming that the enemy's method had failed.

“Failed to do what?”

“Stop me.”

“It stopped you long enough to hurt you.”

Su Fan crossed out the sentence. In its place he wrote that the second pressure did not hold his circulation as expected.

It was less triumphant and considerably more useful.

Sun Lian called from the doorway. The cart was loaded, the packing fee settled, and the weather making its own decisions about their departure. Min wrapped the rescued practice book and put it inside his coat rather than with the requisitioned maps.

Su Fan closed his notebook. He was glad that he had not written down the word *immune*. It had been waiting behind several of his questions.

“The ice worked.”

“Yes. Ice is still cold.”

Outside, another book fell into the fire. The wet cover snapped loudly.

Min looked toward the sound.

“There are things we can learn from what failed,” he said. “That seems an unfashionable reason to keep a library.”

At the outer door, a porter asked whether the three saved shelves should be taken down as well.

Min stared at him.

“The shelves?”

“For the wood.”

“No.”

The man held up both hands and went to another pile. Min stood between the surviving books and the doorway until Sun Lian had finished checking the cart. Su Fan understood that the permission would need someone to remain beside it. A paper could travel to an office; a man could still mistake a shelf for fuel.

He fetched the scholar's fallen chair and put it where the rain would not reach. Min sat only after the books had been counted again.

Sun Lian made Su Fan take the lighter map case. He started to argue, shifted onto the sore ankle and stopped. Together they lifted the remaining case between them, using the repaired handles rather than trusting the old ties.

They carried the maps out together.

At the doorway, Min handed Su Fan a folded letter.

“If you go to Siltbridge with that boatwoman, ask for Min Yao at the east copying house.”

“Do you want me to wait for a reply?”

“No.”

Then, after a moment: “Yes. But don't tell her that.”

chapters.title: The Seal in the Drawer
chapters.text:
Mother Wei found seventeen gate workers who should not have been working.

The first man told her he was merely tired.

He had come into the tent smiling, apologizing for taking a healer's time when there were people with real injuries. His hands lay open on his knees. One thumb kept moving against the pad of his forefinger, a small repeated action that continued while he spoke.

“What happens when you finish a shift?” she asked.

“I eat.”

“And when you lie down?”

“Sleep, usually.”

He said it too quickly. She waited.

“The breathing takes a while to settle.”

“How long?”

He looked at the open tent flap. Beyond it, men were changing places beneath the tower. The shared exhalation reached them as a sound like cloth drawn slowly through a hand.

“Longer lately.”

Mother Wei set down her brush and asked him to describe an ordinary night without deciding which parts mattered. At first he supplied a sensible account of supper, washing and a bed. Then he mentioned waking to turn toward a rhythm that was not in the room. He laughed at himself when he said it.

She did not laugh. Neither did she make the symptom into a tragedy he had to reassure her about.

The next worker had pain beneath the ribs when a gate stopped. The third had learned to eat in small mouthfuls because a full breath interrupted him. They came with work-hardened bodies and little private adaptations that allowed them to continue. Each adaptation made it easier for an overseer to say that nobody had actually failed.

Outside, someone asked whether the medical queue would finish before the next bell. A clerk said it would take as long as Mistress Wei required. Mother Wei heard the capital letter in his voice and disliked how recently he had acquired it.

She had put the seal in her bag before leaving home. She had not touched it yet.

The patients did not need a story about her past. They needed her to ask the right questions now, to notice the man who steadied his cup with both hands and the woman who apologized whenever her breath caught. She separated what she could observe from what required another examination away from the working formation.

One man asked whether a rest order meant he would lose his place.

“It means you need rest.”

“That isn't the same answer.”

“No,” she said. “It isn't.”

She sent the question with his paper rather than offer a promise outside her authority. By the time the thirteenth release lay drying on the table, the morning light had shifted clear of the tent wall.

She signed thirteen medical releases before the overseer came to the examining tent.

“Thirteen?” he said.

“Four more when I'm finished.”

“We can't run the lower station with that many absent.”

“Then arrange replacements.”

“There aren't seventeen replacements.”

Mother Wei put down her brush.

He entered with the duty slate under his arm and no escort. That made the conversation harder. Mother Wei could have disliked him more easily if he had arrived with guards.

He set the slate beside her papers. Names filled the available spaces. A few had been crossed out and written into different rows. In one position the same name appeared twice.

“Who is covering that?” she asked.

“I was going to ask him to take the end of the second shift.”

“He's one of the seventeen.”

The overseer looked down. His fingers tightened on the slate's edge.

A patient waiting near the tent flap heard enough to begin putting on his work shoes. Mother Wei stopped him.

“I can sit,” the man said. “They need someone in the position.”

“You came because you cannot stop responding after you leave it.”

“It's worse if they change the rhythm too quickly.”

He was trying to help. She could see that plainly. His neighbours depended on the gate; his friends would take the extra burden if he went home. Duty had been made into the lever that kept him at work.

She asked him to wait outside with the others and sent the clerk to make sure they had water. Then she turned the duty slate so the overseer could see it properly.

“What happens if three of these men fail during the same shift?”

“We lower the local demand.”

“Why not lower it while they recover?”

“Because the upper schedule—”

He stopped. She knew enough to understand that he did not control the upper schedule. He was expected to provide a working row regardless of the bodies available to fill it.

“I can put the recommendation in writing,” she said.

“They'll ask who authorized it.”

“Then you can show them.”

He looked at her ordinary coat and the table assembled from two crates. She had treated people in rooms grander than his office and in places worse than this tent. Neither had made their symptoms more or less real.

A bell sounded beyond the flap. The overseer's eyes moved toward it. His body had started to rise before he decided to remain.

The overseer was younger than the oldest of her patients. He had ink on his sleeve and a sleepless redness around his eyes. She recognized the look. Men inherited bad arrangements and were told that competence meant making them work.

She had once believed it herself.

“These people are compensating for a damaged return,” she said. “Their breathing continues after the gate stops asking. They need rest and an uncoupled examination.”

“That's your opinion.”

“Yes.”

“I need an authorized opinion.”

She reached into her bag.

The stone seal had not been used for twenty-six years. She had cleaned the grooves that morning with a needle and oil. Her old name was still legible.

Wei Suyin. Licensed circulation surgeon of the Lower Reed Infirmary.

She pressed it into the red paste, then onto the release papers.

The overseer read the mark.

His posture changed.

“Your licence was suspended.”

“Reinstated for this examination by Steward Jiang.”

He looked at the second document she placed beside it.

For several moments he said nothing.

Then he took the releases and left.

The papers did not make seventeen beds appear.

She spent the next hour helping the clerk separate immediate rest from the examinations that required a quiet room. The first man she had seen wanted to go back to the workers' houses. The woman beside him had a daughter coming to meet her at the lower landing and worried that nobody would tell the girl where she had gone.

Mother Wei asked for a runner. The clerk looked toward the office as though seeking permission in the doorway. Then he took off his outer coat and said he could go himself when the next group had been counted.

“Go now. I'll keep the order.”

He hesitated only long enough to write down the daughter's name.

One worker refused to surrender his cord until the supervisor explained how his position would be covered. Mother Wei did not pull it from him. She waited while the explanation was made, watched him decide, then marked what he had consented to. A forced interruption could hurt a body as thoroughly as a badly prolonged duty. She had come to stop one kind of harm, not replace it with another.

By afternoon, the duty row had changed. The interval between two cycles lengthened; the water in the service channel dropped slightly. Some scheduled work would wait. Someone elsewhere would complain that the gate was failing to meet its allocation.

She could live with a complaint.

She was less comfortable with the relief on the overseer's face when he returned to collect a second copy of her authorization. He now had a paper to put between himself and those questions. She had used paper that way before. It did not mean his gratitude was false, only that gratitude could serve several purposes at once.

At the end of the examining table lay a cup she had forgotten to drink from. A patient had placed a piece of coarse bread beside it. There was no note. She ate while reading the last account, then checked the name twice because fatigue made a careless sort of familiarity.

When she put down the brush, the joint beneath her thumb would not straighten easily. She pressed it against the table until the cramp eased. Nobody had seen. She was glad, and then irritated with herself for the same instinct she had spent the day asking other people to resist.

Mother Wei continued working until her hand cramped.

***

Su Fan met her at the landing.

He was supposed to help carry the chests. Instead he looked at her face and asked what had happened.

“Work.”

“You look—”

“Like someone who has done it.”

He took the heavier chest.

At the landing, the water smelled of wet rope and cooking fires.

Su Fan had arrived early. He stood where he could see the path down from the station, pretending to examine a loose board until she came into view. The bandage at his ankle was clean but his weight still favoured the other foot.

She looked down at his ankle, then at the chests, and evidently postponed the argument. Su Fan was grateful. He was less pleased when she pointed to the lighter handle.

Sun Lian had arranged a place beneath the overhang. A folding stool waited beside it. Mother Wei sat without insisting she could stand. Su Fan watched her hands tighten on the edge of the stool before they relaxed.

For part of the journey she slept. Su Fan put a folded cloth between the chest latch and her shin so it would not knock her whenever the deck moved. When she woke near Mudgate, she touched the cloth and left it where it was. He kept looking toward the bank.

At the quay they divided the weight. She made him take the heavier chest only after confirming he could carry it without turning the injured ankle outward. He made a face at being inspected. She made the same face back and won, which was the sort of victory still available at the end of such a day.

Auntie Lu saw them pass and called that there was food. Mother Wei thanked her without stopping. “Home first,” she said. Su Fan could picture the small patched chair beside her window. Nobody ever asked to borrow it, though it was the most comfortable seat in the clinic.

Su Fan collected the food while she unlocked the clinic. For once the waiting room was empty. A message beneath the door said a child from the upper lane had stopped vomiting and would come in the morning. Mother Wei read the message twice and set it upright beside the lamp. Su Fan caught the corner before it slipped. She gave him a small nod.

At home, she washed her hands twice. The water in the first basin was red from ink, not blood. She disliked how little difference that made to her.

Su Fan set food on the table.

He did not ask while she ate. She looked up once, caught him preparing a question, and pushed the second bowl toward him.

When she finished, she brought out the seal.

“I used to work for the regional infirmary.”

“I guessed.”

“Most guesses are less accurate than their owners think.”

He stayed quiet.

The name on the stone had been cut in narrow, formal characters.

Su Fan had read it at the station. Wei Suyin. He knew it was hers, yet hearing the overseer speak it had briefly made her seem somebody he had met only that afternoon. At home she was again the woman who disliked cold food and had mended his cuffs so often that he knew which basket held the thread.

She rubbed the worn edge of the seal, then stopped herself.

Su Fan looked at the stone without touching it.

“Was this the seal you used today?”

“Yes.”

“Will you keep using it?”

“For the work Jiang authorized. We'll see after that.”

He nodded and resisted the urge to ask what she might do after that. Her permission named a particular job. He had seen enough contracts lately to know that the difference mattered.

For a while he listened to the kitchen. A pot cooling. A cart going down the lane. Mother Wei folded the seal’s cloth into a square and unfolded it again. He could ask about the scar, or the name, or why she had kept a licence she never used. He was afraid that choosing a question would make her put the stone away.

“There is something I can tell you,” she said. “Not every detail. Some of those belong to people who never agreed to become a story about me.”

“All right.”

He drew his stool back from the table so she had room for her hands. She stared at the ink caught in the grooves of the seal. The kitchen sounds continued around them, quite indifferent to his effort to remain still.

“There was a gate failure. A smaller one than what people imagine when they hear the words. The water stayed in its channel. The people holding the circulation didn't.”

She turned the seal over.

“We had too few beds and too many patients. I was ordered to treat those with the best recovery prospects first. That part I could defend. Then someone changed the order to those with the strongest lineage claims.”

“Did you obey?”

“For one night.”

The kitchen felt unusually cold.

“By morning I had stopped. By then a young woman had died waiting.”

Su Fan looked at the old mark on her wrist. He had seen it all his life without asking what instrument left such a straight scar.

“Is that why you came here?”

“Partly. They suspended me when I changed the lists. I left when I realized how often I had agreed before anyone needed to threaten me.”

He wanted to say that she had saved many people since. He could hear how easily the sentence might turn into permission to stop remembering.

“What was her name?” he asked.

“Fen.”

“Did she have family?”

“A sister. I wrote to her. She did not answer.”

Mother Wei put the seal back in its cloth.

“Today's men get their rest. That is what this old stone was useful for.”

Su Fan nodded.

As he rose to clear the bowls, she caught his sleeve.

“The mark in your book. I saw something similar on Fen's medical chart. It meant her condition did not fit the recognized branches. I do not know whether the marks are related. That is all I can truthfully tell you.”

“All right.”

“You needn't look disappointed.”

“I wasn't.”

“Then you've acquired a second face.”

For the first time that evening, she smiled.

He carried the basin to the kitchen. On the shelf above it stood two jars she had asked him to label that morning. He had forgotten them in the rush to the landing.

“Those are still waiting,” he said.

“They will wait until morning.”

“I can do them now.”

“Do you know what is in the second one?”

He looked at its unmarked lid. “No.”

“Then it will still be waiting in the morning.”

He left it alone. The answer was so familiar that for a moment he could remember being fourteen and annoyed by the same refusal to let him guess at something she knew.

He brought her a clean cup instead. She took it without drinking, warming her fingers around the clay. He wanted to say Fen’s name once more, to show he would remember it. He could not tell whether that would be a kindness or something he wanted from her, so he let the room stay quiet.

He washed the bowls. She sat by the window with the seal in her lap until the light failed.

chapters.title: A Second Beginning
chapters.text:
The first stage became reliable in early summer.

Su Fan knew because it stopped feeling like an event.

He carried a sack, climbed a ladder, set down a hammer. The circuit remained. He no longer had to wait for stillness before finding it.

There was satisfaction in that, but less spectacle than he had imagined.

He first noticed the change while carrying a repaired hinge across the yard.

A week earlier he would have stopped at the threshold, found the movement inside his ribs and waited until he trusted it. That morning Ah-Du asked him a question about the hinge, a customer called from the lane, and the neighbour stepped through the back door with a basket. Su Fan answered, moved aside and went on carrying the weight.

Only after he put it down did he realize the circuit had remained with him.

He tried to repeat the moment deliberately and made it worse. Duan watched him pick up the hinge for no apparent reason, carry it three paces and set it down again.

“Are we charging for the journey now?”

Su Fan explained. The smith considered, then gave him another piece to deliver.

“I don't want an errand.”

“Then you're ready for several.”

By midday he had carried hinges, fetched coal, measured a gate bar and eaten half his meal before it went cold. The warmth accompanied him through most of it. He wrote the failures down that evening and found, for once, that they were fewer than the successes.

The ankle from the boat attack still pulled in certain movements. Nothing about the new reliability removed the need to clean and bind it. Mother Wei made him distinguish pain from the old protective habit before he began congratulating himself on learning to ignore anything.

“You're allowed to be stronger and still have an injury,” she said.

He knew that. He had also quietly hoped the two things would stop occurring together.

When he slept, the circuit no longer seemed to wait just beyond waking. It was there when he opened his eyes, faint and ordinary as the weight of his own hands. He felt a happiness too private to demonstrate. For several mornings he let himself enjoy it before finding something else he could not yet do.

The second stage was worse.

The scripture called for another route through the lower body, one that should meet the first without forcing either. The drawing was incomplete. The last part had been rubbed almost blank.

Min could identify two of the damaged characters. Mother Wei could tell Su Fan which interpretation was most likely to hurt him. Duan could tell when he had ignored her advice.

None could walk the route for him.

Min copied the damaged passage onto a loose sheet so Su Fan would stop rubbing the bamboo with his thumb.

The lost strokes did not grow clearer because he wanted them. In one place a later hand had crossed out an instruction; in another, the binding had worn away whatever had followed it. Min left spaces rather than supply the most convenient meaning.

“Could the correction be wrong?” Su Fan asked.

“Certainly.”

“Could the first hand be right?”

“Also certainly.”

“That doesn't help.”

“It prevents a kind of help you wouldn't enjoy surviving.”

Mother Wei looked at the copied diagram in the clinic. She recognized several positions from ordinary exercises and disliked the speed implied by one of the arrows. She changed nothing on the original. On Min's copy she marked where a turn could load the injured ankle and where Su Fan tended to compensate through the hip.

“Which route?” he asked.

“The one you can try without forcing that joint. Not the one that gives you the most impressive sensation.”

He took the sheet back to the smithy and laid it beside a page of his own results. There were too many pages now to pretend that every promising morning led directly to the next. Some days the warmth travelled farther and the work went badly. Some days nothing noticeable happened and he carried his loads without pain.

Duan asked him which day he would prefer to repeat if he had a paying customer waiting.

Su Fan chose the uneventful one reluctantly.

He began noting sleep and work beside his attempts. The extra words made his progress appear less like a secret road and more like a badly managed workshop account. Ah-Du found the page, saw a column headed *stopped here*, and asked whether Su Fan was planning a journey with very poor roads.

“In a manner of speaking.”

“Buy a mule.”

He wished it were that simple.

Outside, early summer thickened the weeds along the drain. The neighbour pulled them in the evenings and complained when Su Fan's stones trapped the roots. He helped her move two stones and found that the altered stance relieved an ache he had begun to accept as part of the exercise. It annoyed him that the discovery came from weeding. He wrote it down anyway.

He spent three weeks reaching the same point beneath his left knee.

At first he blamed the old injury.

Then he blamed the drawing.

Eventually he noticed that the route failed only when he expected his weight to arrive there.

He tried it sitting down. It worked as far as the ankle.

He tried standing with his hand against the wall. Farther still.

He was protecting the knee before it needed protection. Six years of carrying loads had taught him to distrust that side. The habit had kept him working. Now it interrupted the movement he was trying to learn.

The first useful comparison was embarrassingly small.

He rested two fingers on the wall and made the movement successfully. He lifted the fingers and failed. The wall had taken almost none of his weight. It had merely persuaded him that a fall could be interrupted.

Duan stood behind him while he tried again.

“Don't catch me unless I go over.”

“I hadn't intended to.”

The possibility of being watched made him tighten. He stopped, annoyed with both of them.

They moved the exercise to a patch of level earth beyond the yard, where there was nothing sharp to strike. Ah-Du carried the mat and immediately lay on it. Su Fan made him get up. The boy complained that the mat had been having an excellent afternoon before training arrived.

Su Fan tried the movement sitting, then with one knee supported, then standing with his fingers barely touching the wall again. The route did not extend in a steady improvement. It appeared in fragments. He could find it when surprised by an ordinary adjustment and lose it while preparing carefully.

Mother Wei told him to stop for the day when the muscles began shaking. He wanted one more attempt. She asked him whether the next result would tell him about the method or about his refusal to rest.

He put the notes away.

That evening he helped Bao Mei carry finished boards under cover before a shower. One slipped. He shifted his weight and caught it without tightening the old injury. The movement was brief, gone before he could admire it.

“Careful with the paint,” the girl said.

He looked at the blue smear on his thumb and laughed. She asked what was funny. He could not explain without making her board into a demonstration, so he apologized and helped her wipe the mark from its edge.

Later he noted exactly how he had stood. He did not try to reproduce the warmth by dropping another board.

The work of changing an old habit became a collection of such ordinary opportunities, with all the frustrations of having to live between them.

Changing it did not require courage.

It required repetition, rest and the irritating patience of people watching him refuse both.

***

Bao Shun's compensation had arrived on the seventh day after Jiang's visit, while Su Fan was still learning how often a first circuit could fail. He remembered that earlier afternoon clearly.

The clerk paid it in mixed coins and asked for three witnesses. Auntie Lu insisted on counting every piece. Old Pock counted behind her, out loud, and was struck with a spoon when his numbers disagreed.

Bao Mei displayed six painted boards outside the clinic.

By evening she had sold four.

Bao Shun managed the money with his good hand. He had not become cheerful about the injury. He had, however, stopped refusing to discuss next month.

On that earlier payment day, the coins had made a sound that changed the room.

Bao Shun listened while Auntie Lu counted, his injured hand held close beneath the table. The clerk wanted a thumb mark beside the total. The thumb she indicated belonged to the hand that had been crushed.

“Other one,” Mother Wei said.

The clerk looked embarrassed and moved the paper. It was a small mistake, corrected in a moment. Bao Shun stared at the empty space where his bad hand would once have rested, then pressed the good thumb down carefully.

The payment did not make the lost work disappear. It bought food. It made a debt to the grain seller a manageable conversation instead of one he had begun avoiding. It allowed Bao Mei to consider another tin of paint without calculating how many meals its price contained.

She put her boards where people coming to witness the payment would see them. Auntie Lu accused her of exploiting a public occasion. Bao Mei asked whether the soup stall had ever occupied a less profitable principle.

Old Pock laughed until she made him move his elbow off the wet edge.

Su Fan remembered the four boards selling one after another, the way Bao Shun began taking an interest in which design a customer chose. His bad hand lay still. His voice did not.

That was the afternoon Su Fan kept returning to whenever his own progress seemed too slow to count.

Su Fan watched them from across the square while practising a small transfer of weight beneath his clothes.

Mother Wei caught him.

“Stand normally for five minutes. Nobody is grading you.”

He obeyed.

Weeks later, Tan Wei came to another supper in the square with his first proper month's wages.

His blue thread was brighter now. He could carry a bucket of water without spilling it, even when Ah-Du ran into him deliberately.

“Second stage,” he said, quietly enough that only Su Fan heard.

By the later supper, the square smelled of frying onions and the first warm evenings of summer. Auntie Lu had moved two tables outside. Bao Mei's new boards hung beneath the awning rather than leaning against the clinic wall.

Tan Wei wore the same better-fitting shirt as on his earlier visit, now softened by washing. He put down the rice he had brought and complained that the boat fare had risen precisely when he began earning money for it.

“Your prosperity has altered the whole river,” Old Pock told him.

“I'll ask for a share.”

He sat beside Su Fan and talked about the ordinary duties before mentioning the stage. He had learned to carry a vessel through a turning boat without sloshing the contents into his own shoes. Han said the practice was improving. Qiu Lan said the shoes had simply given up.

Su Fan laughed, then watched the blue thread settle beneath his friend's wrist as he lifted his bowl. The motion was confident in a way it had not been by the river. Tan Wei was not merely repeating a first lucky drop. Work and training had changed what he could reliably do.

He wanted Su Fan to understand that. He did not say it as a challenge.

The quiet pride made comparison arrive before kindness could get between them.

Su Fan felt a quick, unpleasant pinch beneath his ribs.

Then he made himself look at his friend's face.

Tan Wei was happy. Tired and happy and proud of something he had actually worked for.

“Congratulations,” Su Fan said.

This time no part of it was a performance.

They ate until Auntie Lu threatened to charge them for occupying useful space.

As they left, Tan Wei asked what he had been doing with himself.

“Working. Reading.”

“And standing in mysterious ways?”

“Ah-Du talks too much.”

“He talks the normal amount. You supply less competition.”

Su Fan almost answered honestly.

A gate messenger called Tan Wei's name from the road. His return boat was leaving.

The moment passed.

***

Su Fan reached the second stage two mornings later while carrying a basin to the clinic.

His left foot landed on a loose cobble. He adjusted without tightening the old injury.

The lower circuit completed.

The basin did not move.

He had been expecting a careful morning, a dry yard and the right silence around him. Instead the basin was full, the cobble loose, and somebody behind him wanted to get past with vegetables.

For one step his body had solved the problem before he tried to tell it how. The pressure moved through the lower route and met the first without the familiar knot beneath the knee. He felt the completion as a steadiness, not a rush.

He stopped because he was surprised. The water trembled against the rim.

No light appeared. No bird stopped singing. The woman with the basket asked him to move out of the middle of the lane.

He stepped aside. The warmth held.

He almost lost it by paying too much attention. The basin began tilting; he corrected it, waited for the woman to pass, and went on. His old injuries still existed. A boy running from the well splashed his trouser leg. He had to wait for a cart before crossing to the clinic.

By the time he reached the door, he had carried the new steadiness through half a dozen things he could not have arranged in the yard. That mattered more than the moment on the cobble.

He used his elbow to lift the latch and set the basin where Mother Wei had asked. There was water on the floor, but only the ordinary amount he spilled on a morning when he thought about something else.

She was rolling clean bandages in the next room.

“Did you fetch the basin?”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you standing there?”

He told her. She put down the linen and asked him to come into the light, where she could watch him move. He found himself trying to arrange his shoulders impressively and stopped before she needed to point it out.

She checked him, made him sit, and put a cup of tea in his hand.

She let him finish the tea before asking him to stand again. The waiting was difficult. He wanted a number, a name, a statement that would make the last three weeks line up neatly behind this morning.

Instead she had him turn to reach the shelf, then sit, then move the empty basin into the kitchen. The route weakened while he anticipated her scrutiny and settled when she began asking about an ordinary delivery. It did not vanish.

“Write down what happened,” she said. “Not what you hope it means for next month.”

He had already begun imagining next month. He looked at the empty cup and pulled his mind back to the uneven cobble, the woman with vegetables, the weight of the water.

“How does it feel?”

“Steadier.”

“Good.”

“That is all?”

She regarded him over her own cup.

“Would you like a banner?”

He smiled.

Later, returning to the smithy, he saw Tan Wei's last letter on the bench.

He took a clean page.

*There is something I should have told you earlier,* he wrote.

He sat with the sentence for a long time.

Then a customer arrived, and he put it in the drawer unfinished.

chapters.title: The Ferryman's Return
chapters.text:
Tan Wei learned to stand on moving water by falling into it.

Han stood on the landing with a towel.

“Again.”

The other trainees tried not to laugh. Qiu Lan failed openly.

“You can have your turn,” Tan Wei told her, climbing out.

“I did. You were underwater for it.”

The exercise used a floating beam rather than the open current. A rope held it near the bank, where the water rose only to Tan Wei’s chest. This had sounded reassuring until his fourth attempt to get out while holding a bowl above his head.

The bowl was pottery. Han said wooden bowls taught people to trust the bowl instead of themselves. Tan Wei suspected the cook had simply refused to lend them six good wooden ones.

He wrung his shirt out over the reeds. His shoes waited on the landing, safely dry and of no assistance. Qiu Lan stood beside them with both hands on her hips, considering whether to put her own pair back on before her next turn.

“Bare feet,” Han reminded her.

“The splinter is improving my balance. I’m being very careful where I stand.”

“Then take it out before it improves your circulation.”

She sat down to work at her heel. Tan Wei picked up the bowl again.

He had carried water all his life. A full vessel on a familiar path was easy enough; even the uneven boards between the dormitory and the washhouse had become manageable. On the beam, every correction caused another movement beneath him. The Ferryman’s Return helped his body find balance after a step. It did not decide where a sensible step should go.

He knew this. Knowing had not kept his trousers dry.

This time he tried to move faster. One foot, then the other, before the beam could roll. The first two steps worked. On the third he saw the water opening beside his left ankle and leaned away from it. The beam rolled toward the side he was trying to escape.

He went in with a noise that brought the laundry women to the window.

Han caught the empty bowl before it could strike the landing.

“Better,” the teacher said.

Tan Wei surfaced with a reed across his mouth.

“In what respect?”

“You let the bowl go.”

“I could have drowned.”

“You stood up to tell me.”

Qiu Lan held out the towel. When he took it, she quietly removed the reed from his hair and placed it on the landing as though it were an item he had asked her to keep safe.

He laughed despite himself. The laugh loosened something the repeated failures had been tightening.

Han took the bowl away.

“Walk without it.”

Tan Wei reached the other end. He had no reason to look down until he arrived, so for once he did not.

“With an empty bowl.”

He crossed again. The vessel shook in his hands, but there was nothing in it to watch. He reached Han and began smiling too soon.

The teacher filled it halfway.

This time he got six paces before falling.

Qiu Lan applauded from the landing.

“Progress. Shall we tell the Court?”

Tan Wei splashed her. She threw the towel at him, missed, and was obliged to retrieve it from the shallows. Han watched the two of them ruin the last dry thing available before calling the next trainee.

They finished with a task less suited to an audience. Each carried an ordinary bucket from the washhouse to the cook, across a fixed plank wide enough to make a fall embarrassing rather than inevitable. Tan Wei completed the route with almost no spill. He had been doing it for weeks. Now he could feel the small corrections he usually made without noticing.

The cook examined the level.

“Where’s the rest?”

“There isn’t a rest. That’s all of it.”

“Then you’ve underfilled it.”

He took the bucket back, wondering whether water had always been this difficult or whether instruction had spoiled a perfectly good ignorance.

***

After the shift, Han remained on the landing to let his bad leg straighten. He had put the cane beside him and was working a knot out of a piece of old line.

Tan Wei sat two paces away. For a while he watched the knot. Han loosened one loop, found it tightened another and went back to the beginning without appearing personally offended.

“Am I becoming timid?” Tan Wei asked.

The teacher looked up.

“Were you especially brave before?”

“I didn’t think about my balance this much.”

“You didn’t cross a floating beam with a bowl.”

“It’s more than that.” Tan Wei touched the cord at his wrist. “I can feel where the old movement wants to go. When I follow, I stay upright. When I choose differently, I fall.”

Han laid the rope down.

“Show me your return.”

“Here?”

“Without the water. My supper’s nearly ready.”

Tan Wei stood, took one step and let the familiar movement bring him back. It settled through his hips with a certainty he still found comforting. Han asked him to do it again with his feet slightly farther apart.

The return pulled against his stance. He could complete it, but only by moving one foot inward before the other had finished taking weight.

“There,” Han said.

“What am I doing wrong?”

“Growing taller than the man who first learned it.”

Liang Sui had been shorter than Tan Wei and stronger through the hips. He had worked on boats with higher sides, where a ferryman could brace against a rail instead of crouching close to the water. His surviving lesson contained the habits of that work. They were useful habits. They were not Tan Wei’s body.

“Then why preserve it exactly?”

“Because changing what you don’t understand is expensive.”

“And once I understand?”

Han smiled.

“Then you can make yourself expensive in a more interesting way.”

The answer was less complete than Tan Wei wanted. He said so.

“Good,” Han replied. “Remember that when somebody offers you a complete one.”

He had Tan Wei repeat the step without asking the impression to finish it. Tan Wei wobbled. His own muscles took over awkwardly, neither lost nor suddenly expert. Han stopped him after a few attempts and pointed to the place where his heel had been dragging.

“That is one thing you can watch tomorrow. Don’t alter six others to prove you’ve understood me.”

From the cookhouse, someone rang the meal bell. Qiu Lan appeared in the doorway carrying a bowl she had filled before the call. She said the beans were unusually good and therefore unlikely to survive prolonged philosophical discussion.

Han accepted her warning.

Tan Wei gathered the old rope. The knot had finally loosened beneath the teacher’s hands, but the line was too worn for serious use. Han told him to put it aside for tying bedding, not back with the working lengths.

“Still useful,” Tan Wei said.

“Certainly. Just not for everything.”

He carried it upstairs after supper and tied his spare shirt into a neat bundle. The little act pleased him. He was beginning to acquire a place for things in a room that had at first felt borrowed from somebody else’s life.

***

Two days later, a supply raft caught sideways in the service channel.

Tan Wei heard the binding crack before he saw what had happened. He was carrying a basket of empty grease cups toward the stores. Beyond the landing, a timber platform had swung across the flow and jammed against the stone support of a small maintenance bridge.

Six workers stood aboard. There was no clear landing beside them. The channel’s walls rose slick from the water, and the gap to the nearest steps was wider than anyone could jump with confidence. The raft’s upstream edge had begun dipping under the current.

One man tried to push it free with a pole. The pole slipped and struck the support. His neighbour caught his coat before he followed it into the water.

Tan Wei put down the basket.

The proper response was to close the local return and wait for the level to fall. He reached the wheel before the others at the landing and pulled. It moved a fraction, then stopped hard. He reset his grip. The rim gave him enough leverage to hurt his shoulder, not enough to turn whatever had jammed below.

“Han,” he told Qiu Lan as she reached him.

She looked at the raft, then the wheel. She did not waste a question on whether he had tried it properly.

“Keep them still,” she said, and ran.

He shouted for the men to stop pushing. They heard different parts of the instruction. The man with the pole let go; another began moving toward the low edge, making it lower. Tan Wei called him back by the colour of his coat because he did not know his name.

That worked. The man turned, irritated enough to listen.

A sound line hung at the landing. Tan Wei pulled it free, passed it around the fixed post and asked the stores assistant to hold the spare length. Two other workers arrived and took positions behind him. The raft men could not catch a thrown loop reliably while standing together on the tilted deck. Somebody had to get the line to them.

The retaining wall ran along one side of the channel, its top just beneath the rising water. It ended near the trapped raft. Tan Wei had walked it during inspections when it was dry. Today he could see only the first few stones and the brown streak of water passing over the rest.

He did not try to cross upright.

The beam had taught him something useful about the price of looking brave. He crouched, put one hand against the higher wall and fed the Ferryman’s Return into the movement after each short step. The current struck his legs. He let it move his knee rather than fight it with a locked joint, then found the next stone by touch.

Halfway along, the raft lurched. A binding snapped. The sound drove every man aboard toward the opposite side, which was exactly what the platform did not need.

“Stay where you are!”

His own voice startled him. It carried across the water with more authority than he felt. Two men stopped. A third caught the fourth by the belt. That was enough to keep the deck from rolling farther.

Tan Wei reached its edge on hands and knees.

He pushed the line toward the nearest worker and told him to tie it around his waist. The man began thanking him. Tan Wei asked whether he could still make a knot while doing so.

The worker laughed once, breathlessly, and his fingers steadied.

They sent him first because he was already tied. The landing crew took the slack, holding him above the strongest part of the current while he reached for the retaining wall. A second followed with the free loop, then turned to help from the steps.

Tan Wei’s hands had gone numb. The useful warmth along his arm no longer seemed separate from fear and exertion. He could still tell when the return settled correctly beneath his hip. He used it to keep the platform’s movement from carrying him sideways while he passed the line.

The third worker was heavier than the others. He rose too quickly, slipped and fell across Tan Wei’s shoulder.

The borrowed movement tried to turn their combined weight as though Tan Wei carried only his own.

Pain flared through his hip.

For an instant the return offered the most convincing direction in the world. Turn, recover, place the foot. Except the foot would land beyond the raft, and the man against him would follow it into the channel.

Tan Wei grabbed the worker’s collar and let himself fall backward instead.

They hit the deck. Water closed over his ear. He heard the landing crew shout through it and could not make out a word.

Then the line tightened.

The heavier man rolled away, gasping. Tan Wei’s head came clear. He spat water, kept hold of the collar until the worker found the rope and realized that lying down had left them with somewhere to go besides the river.

“Pull,” he managed.

They pulled.

The remaining men crawled rather than stood. Each departure lightened the raft and altered the tilt; Tan Wei had to change where he braced his foot after every one. He could not pretend that a single clever movement had solved the crossing. His hip hurt more each time he moved it.

By the time Han arrived, all six workers were ashore. Tan Wei sat beside the landing post with both hands pressed against his side. The basket of grease cups lay where he had dropped it. One cup had rolled beneath the wheel.

Han knelt.

“Good choice.”

“Which one?”

“Falling down.”

Tan Wei laughed, then stopped because it hurt.

The teacher examined his movement before letting him rise. Behind them, the raft thumped against the support, empty now. Another operator had come to investigate the jammed return. Qiu Lan counted the workers again, apparently unwilling to trust a number supplied by people who had just spent several minutes shouting over water.

“You strained the return,” Han said. “Rest tomorrow.”

“I have a shift.”

“You have a replacement.”

He signed the release himself. Tan Wei watched the ink dry, oddly close to tears. He had expected to be asked why he had not waited. He had prepared several angry answers. None was needed.

Qiu Lan brought him his shoes.

“You’ve improved,” she said. “This time other people got wet.”

He was still laughing when she offered her shoulder to help him upstairs.

***

That night the dormitory smelled of damp clothes, liniment and the cook’s burnt onions. Tan Wei had eaten sitting sideways to spare his hip. The men from the raft had sent up a bowl of something sweet; he shared it because there was more than he could finish and because he did not know what to do with being thanked alone.

He thought about writing to Su Fan. The account would sound more deliberate on paper than it had felt. He put the page aside until he could decide how to describe the moment when his wonderful borrowed movement had almost carried two people over the edge.

Sleep found him before the lamp went out.

He dreamed of a woman waiting on a shore he had never seen.

She wore a green scarf. He knew it had belonged to her mother. There was a cracked cup in the kitchen behind her, and the door would catch against a loose stone if she tried to open it fully. He knew he was late.

The knowledge arrived without a memory of learning it. He was not watching a stranger. He wanted to call out to her, to explain the delay, and the wanting hurt with an old familiarity that had nothing to do with his own day.

When he woke, he reached toward the empty wall.

For a moment he could not remember which room was his.

The mat beneath him felt too narrow. The window was on the wrong side. He waited for the sound of water against a boat and heard a man snoring in two pitches instead.

Tan Wei sat up slowly.

The dormitory returned in pieces: his shoes beneath the bed, Qiu Lan’s repaired sleeve hanging from a peg, the bundle he had tied with Han’s old rope. Rain tapped the roof. His hip ached when he moved.

He could not remember the woman’s face as clearly as he remembered the scarf. That seemed reassuring until he realized he still knew where she kept the cracked cup.

He lay back but did not sleep well again.

By morning the dream had faded enough to seem ordinary. People dreamed strange things. He had strained a cultivated movement, swallowed half the channel and been fussed over by six grateful workers. There were plenty of reasons for a disturbed night that did not require another conversation about reducing his training.

He listened to the others getting up. Someone complained about the weather. Qiu Lan asked whether he could walk to breakfast or wanted it brought upstairs.

“I can walk.”

“Then get dressed before they give your bowl away.”

He reached for his shirt and remembered Han’s warning: habits and dreams should be reported, especially when a pupil wanted them to be unimportant.

The thought irritated him because it fitted so well.

He put on the shirt, left the unfinished letter on the bed and went to find his teacher before breakfast.

chapters.title: Water Shares
chapters.text:
The first field to go dry belonged to a widow who paid her irrigation dues early.

She brought the receipt to Auntie Lu’s stall and put it beside the soup pot.

“I paid,” she said.

Nobody disputed it.

The paper had been folded into a square small enough to fit beneath the lid of a household jar. Its corners were soft from being opened and closed, but the red mark remained clear. She flattened it with two fingertips, keeping the ink away from a splash of broth.

Su Fan was collecting the smithy’s midday meal. He knew her field: a narrow piece below the road, bordered by a pear stump and a fence that leaned outward because she could not spare the ground to straighten it. In wet months she grew vegetables along the raised edge. In dry ones she argued with the ditch keeper about whether the last opening had lasted as long as the schedule claimed.

This time there had been no opening to time.

“The local gate’s stuck?” he asked.

“It opens beautifully. You could admire it all morning.”

“And the water?”

She pushed the receipt toward him.

That was the question. What could payment do about a channel containing three inches of mud and no water?

Auntie Lu put a bowl in front of the woman. She began protesting that she had come about the ditch, not lunch. Auntie Lu said an argument on an empty stomach was less interesting to listen to and charged her for the bread instead.

By midday there were eleven receipts on the table.

They belonged to fields of different sizes and people with different reserves. One man could wait several days before his crop suffered. Another had planted recently because the office had announced a reliable release. A family whose plot stood farther down the channel had spent the morning carrying jars from the domestic tap and discovered that the neighbours objected to their vegetables drinking before the neighbours’ children.

Nobody’s claim sounded foolish when the claimant explained it.

Nobody’s explanation produced water.

Su Fan took the bowls back to Duan without eating his own. The smith listened while fitting a hinge pin, asked which gate they had actually inspected, and sent him to inspect it before anyone proposed smashing it.

Sun Lian was at the quay. She heard enough to fetch a measuring pole. Old Pock followed because he distrusted modern river work, by which he meant anything done after he stopped earning from it.

He brought his own stick and announced that measuring water was easy when somebody remembered to supply some.

***

At the lower sluice, the ditch keeper turned the wheel for them.

The gate rose. Its runners were clean, the wooden face unwarped. Water left over from the last release lay in a shallow pool above it. When the gate opened, the pool drained with a brief, discouraging enthusiasm and exposed the mud beneath.

“There,” the keeper said. “Still my fault?”

“No,” Sun Lian told him.

He looked so relieved that Su Fan wondered how many people had already shouted at him that morning.

They walked upstream. In the deeper shade beneath the road, the channel remained damp enough to hold footprints. Farther on, the surface had begun to pale and crack. Old Pock stopped beside a little hollow where minnows flickered in water no deeper than his thumb.

He scooped two into his cap and carried them to the main stream without making a remark. Su Fan followed with the next pair. Their business seemed important enough to pause for four very small fish.

At the dividing weir they found the cause.

Nearly all the flow went toward the higher fields. A new stop had been bolted across the lower opening, raising the level needed before water could spill into the town’s branch. The work was sound. Fresh iron, well-seated bolts, no obvious defect Su Fan could blame on a careless contractor.

He knelt and examined the threads. Someone had even greased them against rust.

Sun Lian read the notice tied to a post.

“Temporary rationing.”

“Temporary until when?” Old Pock asked.

No date appeared.

Su Fan could see how the stop came out. Two people with the proper tools could loosen it without damaging the channel. The knowledge was immediate and tempting. He imagined the first sheet of water spilling through, the dry ditch filling, the widow’s receipt becoming true again without another visit to an office.

Sun Lian set her pole across the weir and measured the difference in levels.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’ve inspected the bolts twice.”

He stood. Old Pock looked from one to the other and asked whether they intended to discuss the stop or marry it.

The deeper stream below the road still carried water. It lay too low to enter the irrigation ditch without lifting. Sun Lian walked down to look at it, pushing her pole into the bank at several points. The ground held. The current was modest but steady.

“Timber here,” she said, half to herself. “A shaft across this part. Buckets would need replacing often.”

“A wheel?” Su Fan asked.

“A possible one. First I’d like to know why we have to build it.”

They went to the collection house with the widow’s receipt and the measurements. Old Pock carried the notice copied onto the back of an old tally. His handwriting sloped in several directions. The absence of a date was unusually easy to reproduce.

***

Captain Shen Tu was younger than Su Fan expected, perhaps thirty-eight, with a clean-shaven face and a small scar through one eyebrow.

He wore a guard’s coat without ornament. His sword was well cared for. The men around him looked busy rather than afraid. At one table a guard bound a cracked spear shaft; at another, a clerk counted the planks assigned to a damaged bridge.

Su Fan preferred that to swagger. It made him more cautious.

The captain finished listening to a carter before calling them forward. The carter wanted an escort for a short stretch of road. Shen Tu could spare two men after the afternoon change, not four immediately. The carter argued. The captain listened, asked which load had attracted the threat, then moved the departure earlier by combining it with another journey.

It was a reasonable solution. Su Fan resented being made to notice that before presenting the dry fields.

Shen Tu read the widow’s receipt.

“Her payment is recorded.”

“Her water isn’t,” Su Fan said.

“The upstream works need reduced load while the fittings are replaced.”

“Why are the higher fields still receiving their full share?”

“Because their channels can’t be reopened easily once they dry.”

Sun Lian went to the wall map. She did not touch it until the clerk moved a stool out of her way. Then she traced the higher channels with the blunt end of her measuring stick.

“That is true for two of them. Not the other five.”

Shen Tu looked at her.

“You’re the boatbuilder.”

“Yes.”

“Your supply contract runs through this office.”

“So does the water. We can discuss both.”

For a moment Su Fan thought the captain might smile. Instead he held out a hand for the copied notice.

Old Pock supplied it.

“Where did this come from?”

“The post where your men put the real one.”

The captain looked at the crooked writing, then the empty space where a date should have been. He handed it to his clerk.

“Make sure the next notice names the office receiving petitions.”

“That still won’t name an end,” Sun Lian said.

“No. I don’t have one to give you.”

He turned to the map. The repairs had taken crews away from ordinary operation. Some channels needed a minimum continuous flow to avoid drying and shifting their banks; others could be fed intermittently. He explained the difference accurately enough that Sun Lian agreed with part of it.

Then she pointed again to the five higher branches.

“These can take turns too.”

“They have standing allocations.”

“So does the woman whose receipt you’re holding.”

The clerk stopped sorting his papers. Beyond the window a guard called for another length of timber. The captain waited until the noise passed before answering.

“The steward authorized temporary restrictions. Petition her for a revised schedule.”

“How temporary?” Su Fan asked.

“Until the work is complete.”
