He rolled the receipt and returned it. He did not sneer, threaten to tear it up or deny that the field existed. Su Fan found that he had arrived prepared to resist all those things and had much less ready for a man who treated the injury as a decision already made elsewhere.

“Can you release some today?”

“Not without changing another allocation.”

“Yes,” Sun Lian said. “That is what we’re asking.”

Shen Tu’s expression closed by a small amount.

“I’ve told you where to take the request.”

They left with the same receipt. Outside, Old Pock spat into the dry ditch.

“Fine crop of schedules we’ll harvest.”

Su Fan looked back through the window. A guard was describing the damaged bridge. The captain asked two questions and sent six men with timber.

He was not merely pretending to run the district. That made the water decision harder to dismiss and no easier to accept.

They returned the receipt before going to the schoolroom. The widow was crouched beside her lowest row, pressing soil around a plant that had begun to lean. She stood when she saw them and wiped her fingers on her apron before accepting the paper.

“No water?”

“Not today,” Sun Lian said.

The woman nodded once. She did not ask for the whole conversation immediately. She folded the receipt on its old creases, put it away and finished pressing the soil around the roots.

“Will that help?” Su Fan asked.

“It might keep the wind from loosening it.”

He crouched at the next plant. There were only a few that needed attention, and the work was done before he found anything useful to say about the captain. When they left, the row stood straighter. It would still need water.

She came to the meeting with soil beneath her nails.


***

The town gathered that evening in the schoolroom.

Auntie Lu arrived early enough to choose a chair near the door, where she could leave to check the soup without asking anyone’s permission. The widow laid out the eleven receipts. Two more people brought papers after the discussion began, but one belonged to a different branch and had to be set aside rather than added to a larger, more impressive pile.

That produced the first argument.

The widow would not put a false claim into the petition. The man whose receipt she excluded said his field was also dry. She agreed that it was. She said the remedy might be different. He said dry was dry.

Mother Wei asked how many days the crops could survive.

Nobody agreed.

The recently planted field needed water soon. Another owner wanted his money back before the office spent it. A rice farmer said the only sensible action was to open the weir by force and let the people with swords explain to thirsty fields why this was wrong.

Auntie Lu wanted everyone to stop stamping long enough to remember that the floorboards were weak.

Sun Lian waited for a gap, found none, and placed her measuring pole across two desks. The unfamiliar object silenced the nearest people long enough for her to speak.

“A lifting wheel. From the deeper stream below the road.”

She drew it with chalk on the back of a broken slate: a framework, a shaft, buckets raised by the movement of the current and emptied into a channel. Not enough for every field at once. Enough to preserve some water while they disputed the schedule.

It needed timber, iron and twenty workers to assemble it. The ground would have to be cleared. Somebody would need to keep the little channel from filling with silt. A wheel was not a thing they could build, applaud and forget.

Duan offered the iron at cost.

“Not free?” the rice farmer demanded.

“Free iron is lovely. Show me where to buy it.”

The farmer flushed. Duan let him, then named the pieces he could supply from offcuts without charging for new stock. The distinction cooled the room more effectively than generosity without a price would have done. People began asking useful questions about lengths and tools.

One family had two beams, but the beams were holding up a shed. Another had a wagon but needed it for work during the day. Old Pock could judge the placement in the current and claimed this was the first sensible use anybody had proposed for him in years.

“What happened to the last use?” Auntie Lu asked.

“I washed your bowls.”

“They needed washing.”

“Then stop calling them antiques whenever I break one.”

The laughter did not solve the shortfall. It made the next offer less difficult to hear.

Su Fan put his wages for the week on the table. Duan pushed half back.

“You eat too.”

“I have food.”

“For the week?”

Su Fan looked at Mother Wei and discovered that this was not a promising direction in which to seek support. He took the returned coins.

The widow counted what remained. It was enough to begin the frame, not enough to finish the wheel. She wrote the missing amount beside the promised labour so no one would leave believing the evening had purchased more than it had.

Su Fan copied Sun Lian’s sketch onto a cleaner board. His first version made the shaft too long for Duan’s available iron. She shortened the bearing span; Duan altered the support. Neither change was elegant. Both could be made with what they had.

The lamps burned low while people chose workdays. Some offered money because they could not leave their fields. Others offered labour because money had become the thing they needed the wheel to save. Two men who had begun by shouting at each other ended by agreeing to fetch the same timber.

The rice farmer did not withdraw his opinion of the weir. He did offer the use of a cart.

They emerged with enough commitments to start building and not enough money to finish. It was still more than they had entered with.

On the way home, Sun Lian asked Su Fan why he had not suggested removing the stop at night.

“Because they know who pays for these fields. They’d collect the cost from the same people.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

“You thought I’d suggest it?”

“I thought about suggesting it myself.”

He looked at her, surprised.

“Then I remembered I own a boat they can seize.”

They walked beside the dry channel. In the dark, the new iron stop was invisible. He could still picture the greased threads and the ease with which a proper spanner would turn them.

At the schoolroom, the widow stayed behind to gather the receipts. She had the smallest field and the neatest handwriting. She turned down Su Fan’s offer to write the petition for her, but asked whether he could bring a lamp with more oil.

He fetched one from the smithy.

When he returned, she had already begun. The first line gave the date of the payment and the field’s allocation. The next stated when the water stopped. There was no grand accusation, no promise to bring down the mountain. There was a woman naming the work she had paid for and asking when she would receive it.

By morning, the petition would be in her words, not his.

chapters.title: The Letter He Did Not Send
chapters.text:
Tan Wei found the unfinished letter when Su Fan asked him to fetch a whetstone.

It lay on top of the drawer’s contents. There was no envelope. Only one sentence.

He read it before he knew it was private.

Then he put it on the bench.

Su Fan looked up from the lifting-wheel axle. The iron lay across two blocks, one end marked with chalk where Duan intended to cut it. He had been filing the bearing surface while Tan Wei described a quarrel over laundry soap. He could still hear the joke’s unfinished beginning.

For a moment neither spoke.

“That’s an unfortunate beginning,” Tan Wei said.

“I meant to finish it.”

“So I gathered.”

Su Fan put down the file. The absence of its scraping made the smithy seem abruptly larger. Duan had gone to see the timber for the wheel; Ah-Du was helping at the bank. From the alley came the ordinary sounds of somebody emptying a basin and arguing with a hen.

There was room to say the truth. He had arranged no such room on any of the previous occasions when he told himself he was waiting for one.

“It was for you,” he said.

“I’d hoped. Otherwise I’ve brought a stranger’s trouble to the table.”

Tan Wei sat on the block beside the anvil. He was still moving carefully after the strain at the service channel. He had mentioned it almost casually on arriving, then become annoyed when Su Fan tried to take away the sack he was carrying.

The sack contained onions. Su Fan had made considerably more of the injury than the onions required.

Now his friend waited, one foot resting on the lower rung, with no idea what sort of admission had been left in the drawer.

Su Fan had planned this conversation in several forms. In one, he began with the risks. In another, he showed the stone. In all of them Tan Wei listened while Su Fan arranged the facts in the safest order.

With his friend standing there, those versions felt meaner than he had intended.

“I’ve been cultivating,” he said.

Tan Wei’s face opened in surprise.

“Since when?”

“Early spring.”

“What line?”

“None.”

The silence changed.

Tan Wei looked at the unfinished letter, then at Su Fan’s hands. There were little burns and a half-healed cut from ordinary work. Nothing about them announced what he had just been told.

“Is that a name?”

“No.”

“You’re going to have to give me more than that.”

Su Fan went to the place where he kept the bamboo slips. He had hidden them from rain and furnace sparks more carefully than from people. The ordinary wrapping looked inadequate when he brought it to the bench, as though a thing this consequential ought to have made itself harder to carry.

Tan Wei moved the whetstone aside without being asked.

Su Fan opened the cover.

***

Tan Wei read slowly.

At the first diagram he frowned. At the correction about the stain, he laughed. Then he went back to the beginning, tracing a line with his finger without touching the fragile edge.

“You bought this for a copper?”

“With other books.”

“I paid six silver to have strangers tell me how badly I breathe.”

Su Fan smiled.

Tan Wei did not. The joke had brought him only halfway to the feeling beneath it.

“Does Mother Wei know?”

“Yes.”

“Duan?”

“He knows I’m doing something.”

“Ah-Du?”

“He saw the first circuit.”

Tan Wei nodded, once for each answer. Su Fan wished the list had been shorter. He could explain every name individually: the healer because the exercise might hurt him, Duan because work made hiding impossible, Ah-Du because the boy was always where he had been told not to stand.

Together they made a different shape. A life at home continuing around a secret that had been kept most carefully from the person he had once told everything.

“Show me,” Tan Wei said.

They went into the yard.

The wash line was empty. Su Fan moved the neighbour’s bucket farther from the stones and felt foolish for doing it as if he were preparing a public demonstration. Tan Wei waited by the door. He had brought the bamboo slips and kept them beneath his arm, guarded from a stray drop falling off the eaves.

Su Fan picked up the third stone, completed the circuit and held the weight while Tan Wei watched his hands.

The familiar warmth passed through his chest and down the second route. He did not try to make the lift more impressive by holding it away from his body. The stone was heavy enough without theatre.

Tan Wei asked him to turn.

He turned. The lower route wavered, then steadied when he stopped trying to anticipate his friend’s judgment. He set the stone down before the uncertain part could become a strain.

At last Tan Wei touched his forearm.

“I can’t feel a founder.”

“There isn’t one.”

“You sound sure.”

“That’s the part the book is clearest about.”

“What isn’t clear?”

Su Fan looked at the bamboo cover.

“How much time have you got?”

That drew the first unguarded smile. Tan Wei asked about the stages, the margins, the ache in the elbow he had noticed on his last visit. Su Fan answered more readily now that the subject was what he had actually done rather than what he had chosen not to say.

He described the failures as well as the warmth. The black mark mistaken for an instruction. The nail that broke under a stronger blow. The loose cobble and the basin that had not spilled. Tan Wei interrupted at that point to say he had spent an entire week learning not to spill things, and it was offensive to discover that Su Fan had found another way of being irritating about it.

Tan Wei looked at the bandage just visible above Su Fan’s shoe.

“The men who attacked the boat. Did you use it there?”

“Yes.”

“Does Sun Lian know?”

“She saw.”

Another name joined the list between them. Su Fan wanted to explain how little choice he had possessed on a deck covered in ice. The explanation was true. It would also have made his friend responsible for understanding one more reason why other people could be trusted with a fact he had not been allowed to know.

Tan Wei set the book on his own knee, smoothing its wrapping so the old cover would not rest against grit.

“You told me you hurt the ankle getting off a boat.”

“I did hurt it getting off a boat.”

His friend looked up.

Su Fan heard himself and stopped.

“That was a bad answer.”

“It was very carefully bad.”

A cart rattled past the alley mouth. Su Fan waited until its wheels stopped drowning out the smaller noises of the yard. He could apologize without attaching a reason. He tried it.

“I’m sorry.”

Tan Wei nodded, but kept looking at the bamboo slips. He turned them over and examined the binding that Min had tied years before either of them had been born.

“It’s strange,” he said. “I’ve spent months wanting somebody to tell me there was another possibility. Now there is, and I’m angry at the person who found it.”

“You’re not angry about the book.”

“No.”

He handed it back carefully, making sure Su Fan had the weight before releasing it.

Then he stood back.

For several breaths he seemed to be deciding between joy and injury.

At last he slapped Su Fan’s good shoulder.

“You impossible bastard.”

The grin came suddenly. It was real.

Su Fan let himself return it.

They sat beside the stones and went through the first exercise. Tan Wei could follow the stance easily. Han’s lessons had made him attentive to where his weight rested and how an old habit could pull before he chose to move.

The breathing was different.

When he tried it, the blue thread in his wrist answered before anything else could. The familiar return drew toward its trained channel. He stopped at once and opened his hands, letting the attempt go rather than force two instructions against one another.

Su Fan was relieved by the decision. He had wanted to share the discovery so badly that he had not thought far enough about what sharing might require of somebody with a different practice already inside him.

“Did that hurt?”

“No. It objected.” Tan Wei rubbed his wrist, considering. “That would take some unlearning.”

“Perhaps.”

“Does it mean I chose wrong?”

Su Fan opened his mouth.

He had thought that often enough. The lease, the fees, the emergency clause. He had also seen Tan Wei lift water and heard about six men brought off a raft. The new ability had given his friend wages, a bed, people who expected him to improve and work he was proud to do.

None of those things made every cost harmless. None disappeared because a bamboo book offered something else.

“I don’t know,” he said.

Tan Wei watched him carefully.

Then he nodded.

“Better answer.”

They put the slips away before Duan returned. Not because Tan Wei demanded another secret, but because the axle still needed its bearing surface finished and the book had no business lying beside fresh filings.

Tan Wei held the work while Su Fan used the whetstone he had originally asked for. The motion gave their hands something familiar. When the iron began to turn in the clamp, Tan Wei caught it; Su Fan stopped immediately, adjusted the grip and asked whether his friend’s hip was hurting.

“A little.”

“Then we can leave this.”

“We can put another block under it.”

They did that instead.

***

They went down to the river with food.

The path was dry enough to crumble at its edges. Below them, the lifting-wheel crew had set two posts into the bank. One leaned. Three men stood around it offering different explanations. Tan Wei watched for a while, then asked whether the water in the ditch was expected to improve through argument.

“Only after they finish arguing over the wheel.”

“Good. A complete method.”

They found their rock and unwrapped the food. Auntie Lu had supplied more radish than either wanted. Tan Wei claimed the largest piece so Su Fan could not accuse him of neglecting the things that were good for him.

He described the raft rescue properly then.

He did not begin with the six men ashore. He began with the wheel that would not turn and the moment he saw the raft lean while he still had both hands on an unsuccessful solution. He admitted that the borrowed return had nearly turned the heavier man’s fall into a worse one.

Su Fan listened without interrupting. He had questions about the line, the wall and who inspected the closing wheel. They could wait until the account was finished.

“Han said falling was the good choice,” Tan Wei said.

“Was it?”

“I’m here to ask you, aren’t I?”

The answer carried more pleasure than defensiveness. He was still trying to understand a success that had not felt like mastery.

After a while he described the dream with the green scarf.

Su Fan’s hand stopped over the food.

“I reported it,” Tan Wei said before he could speak. “Han had told me to. He adjusted the training and kept me off the shared circulation for two days.”

“And the next night?”

“Ordinary. Someone snored. Qiu Lan complained that I had used all the dry linen. Nobody’s mother owned my scarf.”

“Was it Liang Sui’s memory?”

“Han said it could be an impression carried with the method. He didn’t pretend he could identify a woman from a scarf I barely remembered.”

Tan Wei looked toward the work downstream. He had not described the dream to frighten Su Fan away from his own practice. He was telling him something that had happened, as a friend should be able to do without immediately becoming an argument.

Su Fan made himself take another bite of radish.

“That sounds frightening.”

“It was. Less so after I said it aloud.”

They sat with that for a time.

“Why didn’t you tell me?” Tan Wei asked at last.

“Letters pass through the dormitory office.”

“I’ve been home.”

“I know.”

“Did you think I’d tell somebody?”

“I thought you might tell somebody without knowing what it meant.”

Tan Wei looked across the water.

“You could have told me what it meant.”

“Yes.”

The answer did not repair the hurt. Su Fan could see that. He had hoped, without quite admitting it, that admitting the thing would release him from the long interval in which he had not admitted it.

Tan Wei picked a grass seed from the wrapping and rolled it between his fingers.

“I told Han about you,” he said.

Su Fan’s stomach tightened.

“Not this. I didn’t know this. I told him you were learning from Duan, that you read, that you asked too many questions because you’d rather find the hole in a floor before somebody stepped on it.”

He threw the seed into the current.

“He said I was fortunate in my friend. I agreed.”

Su Fan could find no useful defence against that. He looked at the flat stone beneath his palm. They had sat here when both bowls stayed dark. It had never occurred to him then that one of them could leave the other behind while remaining in the same town.

“I was afraid,” he said.

“I know.”

“Of more than the office.”

Tan Wei nodded but did not help him finish the explanation. Su Fan was grateful and ashamed of wanting help with it.

A boat passed below the far bank. Its wake reached their rock in little delayed slaps. Tan Wei watched it until the last ripple flattened.

“I won’t tell,” he said. “Not because you’ve now explained me into silence. Because you’re my friend.”

Su Fan nodded.

“And don’t spend the next year deciding when I’m ready for the rest.”

There was still the bond letter.

Su Fan felt it behind his teeth.

He could say it now. He had asked the clerk for clarification before registration proceeded. The red delay mark had not simply descended from the office onto his friend’s life. His own words had helped put it there.

He imagined the conversation beginning again, the genuine joy in the yard becoming another thing Tan Wei would have to set aside to make room for what had been hidden. He told himself this was already difficult enough. He would explain the delay another day, when he had the steward’s reply and could show that he had meant to help.

The reason arrived smoothly. Too smoothly for him to trust it completely.

Tan Wei wrapped the remaining food and stood, testing his hip before taking the first step.

“Come on. Auntie Lu says you still owe for the cracked bowl.”

“That was settled.”

“She says settlements are temporary until inspected.”

They climbed the path. At the wheel, the three men had finally agreed to shift the leaning post. One asked for help with a brace. Tan Wei took the light end; Su Fan took the heavy one. For a few minutes they worked without needing to decide what the afternoon meant.

On the way back, Tan Wei imitated the expression Han wore when a trainee explained why falling should count as a successful crossing. Su Fan laughed. It was a good imitation, though he had not met the teacher often enough to know why he believed it.

They went on together, laughing about something that required no caution.

For the length of the walk, Su Fan almost felt forgiven.

chapters.title: Siltbridge
chapters.text:
Siltbridge had more bridges than Mudgate had streets.

Su Fan counted six before Sun Lian told him he was looking at a single district.

The city spread across three river branches. Houses stood on stone piers. Market boats jostled beneath balconies. Above the eastern roofs, a long train of freight cages moved through the air on a shining cable.

Not one cage had wings.

He watched until Sun Lian put a rope in his hand.

“Wonder later. Tie now.”

The mooring was narrower than it looked. A vegetable boat occupied half the landing, and its owner believed that unloading one more basket would justify every minute she remained. Sun Lian brought Honest Measure alongside without touching her hull, which seemed to Su Fan a greater feat than keeping the freight cages in the sky.

He threw the line toward a waiting boy. The boy caught it, looped it around a post and held up three fingers.

“For catching a rope?”

“For the berth.”

Sun Lian held up one finger. They discussed the matter while the boat settled against its fenders. The vegetable seller entered the debate on both sides and took her time deciding which would benefit her.

At last Sun Lian paid, received a wooden tally and told Su Fan to make the bow secure before they acquired a second bill for admiring the negotiation.

Bao Shun and his daughter came ashore behind them. Their luggage consisted of two blankets, a change of clothes and a crate of painted boards. Bao Mei had spent the entire journey asking whether people in a city would pay for boats painted on wood when they could simply look outside.

“They pay for pictures of mountains,” Sun Lian said. “Cities are full of hills.”

“That isn’t the same.”

“Then you already know more about art than I do.”

Bao Shun carried the crate by its lower edge with his good hand. Su Fan reached to take it. The man shook his head and asked him to hold the gangplank steady instead. Bao Mei took the other end once they reached the quay.

The division of work was less elegant than one stronger person carrying everything. It also left the painted boards in the hands of the people who had brought them to sell.

Duan had sent Su Fan to buy steel, tempering sand and a replacement measuring gauge. Sun Lian needed a steering shoe cast. Bao Shun hoped to find a stall willing to take his daughter’s work.

Everyone had a reason to be there that did not involve Su Fan’s secret.

He found that restful.

***

They rented two small rooms above a rope merchant.

The stairs leaned toward the canal. The proprietor assured them that the building had leaned that way for fifty years.

“Then it has experience,” Sun Lian said.

She took the room nearest the escape window and showed Bao Mei how its latch opened before they put down the blankets. In the other room, Bao Shun chose the bed beside the wall, where he could support his injured arm without being brushed by somebody passing.

Su Fan put his pack beneath the second bed. The floor sloped enough that a loose coin rolled toward the door. He retrieved it and asked whether that counted as a deposit.

The proprietor did not laugh. Sun Lian did, quietly, after the man had gone downstairs.

From the window they could see a lane scarcely wider than a cart, a canal beyond it and three levels of washing hung from balconies. A woman lowered an empty basket on a rope. Somebody below filled it with bread. She hauled the basket up while continuing an argument with a neighbour across the water.

Bao Mei watched the exchange as attentively as Su Fan had watched the freight cable.

“Does she do all her shopping like that?”

“Only the things she trusts not to climb out,” Sun Lian said.

They agreed where to meet before separating. Sun Lian marked the rope merchant’s sign on Su Fan’s purchase list. Bao Shun copied it onto the paper around his crate. The city had already demonstrated how many buildings could display a coil of rope while selling something entirely different.

Su Fan went first to the metal market because Duan’s written instructions occupied most of the page and a large part of his conscience.

There were more kinds of steel than he had expected. Some were better. Some merely had more names. He asked to see a cut edge, repeated the questions Duan had made him practise and discovered that a question sounded less impressive when the seller answered with three further questions.

He bought nothing from the first stall. At the second he found the tempering sand, inspected its grain and reserved a sack for collection. By the third he was beginning to feel competent.

That was when he bought the gauge.

***

His first mistake was paying the marked price.

His second was telling Sun Lian what he had paid.

They met near a fountain crowded with buckets, carriers and one indignant duck. She had finished discussing the casting and wanted food. Su Fan showed her the tool while explaining that the seller had assured him it was used by professional makers.

She turned it over, looked at the maker’s mark and asked which flag hung above the stall.

He described it.

“Come with me.”

“I have a receipt.”

“Excellent. We can carry the evidence of your education.”

At the stall she explained, pleasantly, that her apprentice had mistaken a ceremonial price for a commercial one.

The seller looked at Su Fan, who began to object to the apprenticeship and stopped when Sun Lian’s elbow touched his sleeve.

“The finish is very good,” the man said.

“The numbers had better be as good. This line hasn’t even been cleaned.”

She ran a fingernail over a rough division. The seller took the gauge, polished the edge with a cloth and began explaining the expense of bringing skilled work into the district.

Sun Lian listened to the whole explanation. Then she repeated what she was willing to accept back.

The bargaining had a rhythm Su Fan could not yet hear. He kept expecting one of them to become offended. Neither did. The seller disputed her assessment, she admired a different tool without offering to buy it, and at the end he returned a third of the money.

Outside, Su Fan put the coins away separately from Duan’s remaining purchase money.

“I am not your apprentice.”

“You are in bargaining.”

“You could have warned me.”

“You went shopping while I was busy. Did you want a city that waited?”

He did not. He had, however, hoped to arrive in it already knowing how to behave.

His third mistake was stopping beneath the freight cable to look up. A porter walked into him with a sack of onions.

The impact nearly took him off his feet. The circuit helped him recover, but it did not catch the onions that spilled when the sack’s tie came loose. They rolled between people’s ankles with an enthusiasm for travel that the porter did not share.

Su Fan helped collect them. One had gone beneath a market cart. He knelt, reached too quickly and felt the still-healing ankle protest. The porter waited while he adjusted himself, then accepted the rescued onion without thanking him for a problem he had helped create.

By afternoon Su Fan had learned to admire the city while moving out of its way.

The cable carried cages in a steady procession above the roofs. At a turning tower, each cage slowed while a worker guided its suspension through a curved section. A blue formation flashed along the metal. The worker still had to push a reluctant load through with a pole.

Su Fan liked that detail. It made the extraordinary thing neither less extraordinary nor entirely separate from work he understood.

Sun Lian bought a little fried cake from a passing tray and gave him half. He bit into it before asking what it contained. The filling was sour, sweet and hot enough to burn his tongue.

“Wonder later?” he asked through the mouthful.

“Chew now.”

***

There were cultivators everywhere.

A woman heated a brazier with two fingers. A thin man guided a flock of paper birds through the crowd, each carrying a message. Two children in red training jackets chased a wooden dog whose legs moved without joints.

The dog ran beneath a stall and refused to come out. One child tried ordering it. The other lay on the paving stones and offered it a sweet. Neither approach worked until a young woman arrived, turned a little fitting behind its ear and carried it away under her arm.

Su Fan tried to identify their lineages.

He failed almost immediately.

At home, a sash, a familiar colour and a few movements often told him enough to know whose path a practitioner carried. Here the brazier woman’s heat work appeared in a hand otherwise occupied with turning flatbreads. The paper-bird man wore an ink-stained coat without a visible founder’s mark. A porter shouldering two loads used a brown reinforcement quite unlike Sun Lian’s, and no one around him paused to notice.

He wanted to ask each of them what they were doing. Sun Lian wanted noodles.

The brazier woman supplied both opportunities. Her stall stood where a side lane met the canal. Six people waited with bowls, two more argued about whose turn it was, and a boy behind her washed spoons in water he changed whenever she looked at him.

Sun Lian ordered. Su Fan watched the flame settle beneath the pot.

“Which sect do you belong to?” he asked.

“None.”

“Your family teaches the method?”

“My uncle taught me the stove. I learned the heat work from a public school.”

“Whose founder?”

She looked at him.

“Which part?”

He did not know how to answer.

A customer called that his bread was burning. She lifted it with two sticks, examined the underside and asked whether he preferred his supper pale enough to take home and introduce to his ancestors. He laughed and accepted it.

Su Fan waited for her to resume the explanation. She did not. The next bowl needed filling. The boy had washed a spoon without removing what was stuck to it. A customer wanted credit because she had been paid late.

The woman granted the credit and refused to add extra meat. Then she passed Sun Lian their bowls.

They sat on a low wall, where the canal smelled less pleasantly than the food.

“You’re doing that thing again,” Sun Lian said.

“What thing?”

“Trying to fit every shop through the door of your village.”

He looked back at the steady flame.

“At home they’d say she was carrying an unregistered branch.”

“At home they sell registrations.”

“Is it really that simple?”

“No. Nothing that earns money stays simple. Eat before the noodles stick.”

He ate. The broth was good enough to interrupt his desire for a larger argument.

Across the canal, a man was arguing with a collector about his stall permit. A school advertised introductory lessons in three techniques and charged separately for supervised practice. The paper-bird courier had a customer insisting that a message arriving at the wrong balcony should not count as delivered.

The city had not abolished costs, mistakes or people who liked telling others where they belonged. It had simply made room for more ways of doing things than Su Fan had known how to imagine.

He was delighted by that. He was also embarrassed by how much he wanted to hide the delight from somebody who had seen cities before.

Sun Lian finished her bowl and asked whether he wanted another cake.

This time he said yes without pretending he was still hungry from work.

***

They returned to the inn before evening to leave the purchases.

Bao Mei had sold nothing yet. She had learned the prices of five pigments, two kinds of brush and a board primer that cost more than her father wished to discuss. Her disappointment and excitement occupied the same face.

Bao Shun had found one stall willing to take three boards on commission. He disliked the proposed share but had asked for the terms in writing rather than agree because the city made him feel slow.

Su Fan showed them the refunded coins. Bao Mei asked whether he had earned them by being cheated. He said that was one description of a commercial education. She wrote the phrase on a scrap beside her colour prices, apparently considering it worth keeping.

Sun Lian needed to check her casting arrangement again. Su Fan accompanied her as far as the Chain Bridge, carrying the gauge and the purchase list because he had become less willing to leave either where he could not see it.

The river below was crowded with lamps. Music came from a ferry moored beside a tea house. Labourers sat on the parapet eating fried dough. One had his boots off and was carefully removing a pebble from the inner sole while another held his food.

The evening traffic narrowed around a commotion at the far end.

A wagon wheel had sunk into a broken patch of road. The driver had unloaded the nearest crates, but the axle remained caught. Six men pushed at the back. The horse stamped and turned its head, receiving instructions from too many people.

An elderly woman stood beside the front wheel with the harness around her waist.

“Together,” she said.

They pushed. Nothing moved.

She told them to stop before the horse mistook their efforts for a reason to pull. Then she planted her feet, grunted and lifted the front axle clear of the ground.

The movement was brief and enormously plain. Her patched coat tightened across her shoulders. The harness creaked. The men shoved, the wheel found sound paving, and the wagon rolled free.

They cheered. The woman told them to chock it before congratulating the road for becoming level.

Su Fan stopped before he could help himself.

Her cultivation felt dense and settled, but he could find no lineage signature he understood. Her white hair stuck out in short, stubborn tufts. She rubbed her lower back and examined the horse with more concern than she gave the men praising her.

She caught him staring.

“You. With the expensive gauge.”

Sun Lian covered her mouth.

“Come and hold this horse.”

Su Fan did.

The animal’s breath warmed his wrist. It seemed unimpressed by any cultivation except the one that might supply supper. He loosened his grip when it tossed its head, remembering the difference between holding a thing securely and trying to stop it being alive.

The woman untied the harness and accepted a cup of tea from the wagon driver. He offered to pay her. She told him to use the money on a proper repair to the road before his wheel found the same hole tomorrow.

Then she looked at Su Fan over the rim of the cup.

“Now. What is it you were going to ask that will make my tea go cold?”

chapters.title: A Woman Who Wrote Her Own
chapters.text:
Her name was Hua Jun.

She told Su Fan this after he had held the horse long enough to qualify as useful.

The driver had gone to argue about the broken road. His helpers were replacing the crates they had unloaded, with less care than Hua Jun thought appropriate. She interrupted her tea twice to point out that a top-heavy wagon would not improve because its wheel was no longer in a hole.

Su Fan kept the horse’s head away from a basket of greens. The animal regarded this as the only injustice presently occurring in Siltbridge.

“Have you always been that strong?” he asked.

“Since this morning. Yesterday I was terrible.”

Sun Lian laughed. Su Fan felt the question begin to look foolish in his hands.

Hua Jun took pity on him, though not much. She was eighty-four, had entered Foundation at sixty-one, and considered that achievement less impressive than convincing her youngest son to leave home.

“He’s forty-seven,” she said. “Still brings his washing.”

Su Fan tried not to look startled by the ages.

“Greywing?”

“Yes.”

“Thought so. You people look at a Foundation cultivator as though we’ve all descended from a cloud. Most of us have bad knees.”

“Yours seem sound.”

“Mine are magnificent. I worked on them.”

She drank the tea. A strand of white hair had escaped the others and stood almost vertically above her ear. She flattened it with a wet finger; it rose again while she examined the wagon’s packing.

The driver returned with a promise that somebody would inspect the road. Hua Jun asked whether that somebody would bring stone or merely eyes. He did not know. She told him to place a visible marker beside the hole before he left.

He borrowed a broken basket and put it over the damaged paving. The horse was returned to its proper owner. Su Fan watched the wagon move away, expecting the extraordinary woman to become less accessible as soon as the practical reason for their conversation ended.

Instead she held out her empty cup to the tea seller.

“Again. This one had too much rescue in it.”

Su Fan offered to pay. She accepted without pretending that useful advice ought to have no cost at all. Sun Lian bought her own cup and leaned against the parapet, evidently content to watch him attempt a better question.

He asked about her method.

This time he did not ask for a founder first.

***

“Body refining,” Hua Jun said. “Started with a stonecutter’s exercise. Learned some medicine. Changed what didn’t suit me. Broke my wrist twice discovering that suitability isn’t an opinion.”

“You changed it yourself?”

“Who else has my wrist?”

Su Fan looked toward the river.

He had been prepared to encounter another secret. Another forbidden exception. A hidden teacher living carefully beneath the world’s notice.

Hua Jun stood in a public square complaining about laundry.

She saw enough of his expression to put down the cup.

“Your local order is strict about sources.”

“They say power comes through lineage.”

“Much of it does. A preserved path saves years. A good master can keep a pupil alive. There’s a reason people pay.”

“And the other ways?”

“Harder to standardize. Harder to tax. Harder to practise without hurting yourself. Sometimes better. Often worse.”

She held up her left wrist. The joint had healed slightly crooked. He examined it with the attention of a smith looking at a repaired tool, and she seemed to prefer that to his earlier stare.

“Did you know why it broke the second time?”

“Afterward.”

“Not before?”

“Before, I knew several reasons it wouldn’t.”

He smiled. She did not. The wrist had been a real injury, not a joke provided to make him less afraid of experiments.

Hua Jun turned her hand. The movement was strong but not perfectly smooth at its limit. She used the other hand to lift her cup.

“The stonecutter who taught me was patient,” she said. “He knew what the exercise did under a load. I wanted to know what it might do without one. Those are related questions, not the same question.”

“And the medicine?”

“From people who were less pleased than you to see me discovering things.”

Sun Lian asked whether the refinements helped with repeated reinforcement work. She had spent several long days holding boat joints through bad water. Her interest was neither forbidden history nor an escape from the sect’s understanding of the world. She wanted to know how not to exhaust her hands before the work ended.

Hua Jun asked her to show the calluses. She looked, made no attempt to diagnose her entire practice and suggested that the boatwoman watch how much of each hold was spent correcting a poor working position.

“Sometimes the work needs the position,” Sun Lian said.

“Then improve the work when you can. Or hire somebody to hold the other end.”

“I have one of those. He’s expensive in questions.”

Su Fan looked down into his tea.

Hua Jun laughed. “Keep the ones who ask before lifting.”

That did not describe every recent occasion on Honest Measure. Sun Lian’s glance made the omission clear without requiring an account for a stranger.

A porter passed carrying two balanced baskets. Hua Jun moved her foot out of his path. The gesture was ordinary, but Su Fan noticed how easily her weight transferred without the preparation he still needed for his own second circuit.

He tried to see which part of her did it. She caught him watching.

“You’ll learn very little staring at a finished meal. What are you cooking?”

“Breathing work.”

“Show me a step.”

He hesitated.

“No breath trick. Just walk to that post.”

***

The post stood a few paces away, beside a little shrine almost hidden by delivery notices. Su Fan walked to it. On the return he became too aware of the old knee and placed his foot more carefully than he ordinarily would.

Hua Jun watched his feet.

“Old left knee. Recent ankle. You’re compensating less than most. Your teacher is patient.”

“A book.”

“Books are wonderfully patient. Terrible at noticing you’re turning blue.”

Sun Lian said, “We have a healer.”

“Keep her.”

Hua Jun rose and motioned him closer. She took his hand, inspected the way he held the wrist and asked whether it hurt before applying any pressure.

“Not there.”

“Useful distinction.”

She pushed gently against his palm.

He completed the circuit by instinct. For a moment the pressure settled through his legs instead of folding the wrist. The stone beneath his feet felt particularly clear, its roughness reaching him through the worn soles of his shoes.

Her eyebrows lifted.

Then she changed the angle.

He stumbled. The expected support had been in one direction, and he tried to find it after the pressure had already moved elsewhere. She caught his sleeve before he hit the bridge rail.

The tea seller clicked her tongue and moved a basket out of reach of the next experiment.

“Interesting,” Hua Jun said. “You recover cleanly in one direction. Work on the others.”

“Can you feel what it is?”

“A young man improving an old injury. And something quieter under that.”

She released him.

“If you expected me to shout a prophecy, you’ve held the wrong horse.”

He laughed before deciding whether it was respectful. She grinned.

“Again?” he asked.

“Without the special part.”

He tried to receive the same pressure using only the posture he knew. She did not make it identical. The second push was lighter, from a different side. He moved his foot this time and discovered that moving was allowed.

“That one was less impressive,” he said.

“It didn’t need my hand on your sleeve.”

She asked him what he had expected the first time. He described the straight line through his arm and legs. She showed him how narrowly he had prepared for it, turning her own hand so the change was visible instead of making him suffer it again.

“I could have forced the circuit harder.”

“And what would that have done to the direction of my push?”

He considered, then shook his head.

“Perhaps something useful,” she said. “Perhaps it would have made the fall more enthusiastic. You don’t yet know. That’s why we’re doing it beside a tea stall instead of a cliff.”

Sun Lian pointed out that the bridge did have a drop. Hua Jun moved them away from the rail without defending her choice of metaphor.

They repeated the ordinary step twice. Su Fan found a place where the ankle pulled and stopped before trying to work through it. The older woman accepted the stop as part of the exercise rather than a failure to complete it.

He wished Mother Wei could have seen that. Then he realized she would mostly have asked why he required a stranger to make her advice seem persuasive.

Hua Jun sat again. She had neither revealed his hidden method nor dismissed it as impossible. She had found one thing he could do, another he could not, and no reason to make either into the whole of him.

He wanted to keep asking questions until she explained how to become that certain about something so limited.

A cold drop struck the back of his hand.

***

They moved beneath the bridge awning as rain passed over the city.

The tea seller shifted her brazier away from the runoff. Hua Jun carried two benches for her. Sun Lian helped pull the canvas tighter; Su Fan caught the water from one fold before it emptied onto a customer’s lap. For a brief, damp minute, their three different kinds of strength were less important than choosing the same moment to lift.

The awning filled with strangers. A messenger tucked his paper birds inside his coat. One escaped, softened in the rain and landed beak-first in a bowl. Its owner dried it with an expression that suggested the recipient would be charged for weather.

Hua Jun began talking about schools beyond the province while the city steamed around them.

Some taught inherited arts with care. Some invented new techniques and ruined promising students in the process. A northern order raised mountains with formations built by generations of scholars. A coastal house bred fish that could survive in clouds. A woman Hua Jun had once met cultivated by listening to insects and was either very accomplished or very good at avoiding conversation.

“Did you see the fish?” Su Fan asked.

“Yes.”

“In clouds?”

“In a tank. The cloud was inside it.”

“Could they leave?”

“One did. The owner seemed to consider the demonstration less successful after that.”

Sun Lian wanted to know what held the water together when the fish crossed the boundary. Hua Jun admitted that she had been more occupied with recovering her lunch from a creature that believed anything airborne belonged to it.

They laughed. Su Fan found himself picturing a whole coast of improbable trades and difficult animals, people learning to manage problems no one in Mudgate would even think to put on a work sheet.

The wider world did not become harmless in the telling. It became larger than his grievance.

That unsettled him more.

He had begun to think his path disproved the mountain. Now he met a woman who had been living beyond the mountain’s argument before he was born.

Hua Jun asked what he did besides breathing.

“Smith’s work.”

“Good. Keep a trade.”

“Because cultivation might fail?”

“Because people still need hinges when it succeeds.”

She told him about a school that produced impressive demonstrations and pupils who could not afford the medicines required to repeat them. She told him about a careful inherited teacher who refused admission to students he could not supervise, despite being offered enough money to repair his roof. These were people she had known, not rules she claimed every distant sect obeyed.

When he asked how to recognize a good teacher, she pointed to the crooked wrist.

“Some of us learned slowly.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No. Here is part of one. Watch whether they can tell you what you did wrong without needing you to believe they can do nothing wrong themselves.”

The tea seller, overhearing, said that sounded like an excellent way to choose a husband. Hua Jun advised her to test the washing arrangements first.

Rain rattled on the canvas. A small child was trying to catch the drips in a cup with a hole in its bottom. Su Fan almost told her about the hole, then noticed that she had deliberately placed it above another cup. She was making a tiny cascade and had no need of his correction.

He watched the water fall through three uneven levels, content for once to be somebody who did not know the purpose of a thing immediately.

When the rain stopped, Hua Jun took out a charcoal stub and wrote an address on a piece of wrapping paper.

“South-bank practice yard. Pay for the beginner’s class. You’ll learn more from being hit by people your own size than from wondering about me.”

He thanked her.

“Don’t thank me until you see the price.”

She had an errand of her own before the market closed. She collected a parcel from beneath the tea bench, checked that the rain had not reached it and stood. Su Fan offered to carry it.

“On your way?”

“I don’t know where you’re going.”

“Then find out before volunteering your afternoon.”

He gave her an embarrassed smile. She patted his shoulder, not unkindly.

As they parted, she tapped the gauge at his belt.

“And next time buy tools from the maker, not the stall with the nicest flag.”

Sun Lian waited until they had crossed the bridge before laughing properly.

Su Fan let her. He was thinking about the pressure in Hua Jun’s hand. She had found a weakness in one movement without dismissing the strength that came before it.

He wanted to learn how to do that.

The following morning he found the practice yard after taking the wrong turning behind the dye market. He arrived with a blue mark on his sleeve, a damp address and enough time to watch the students warming up before he committed his money.

There were two prices on the board: one morning and a block of lessons. He could afford the first without touching Duan’s purchase money. The second would require rearranging what he had set aside for books and food.

He stood there long enough for the woman keeping the register to ask whether he needed the figures read aloud.

“No. I’m deciding.”

“Then stand on this side. The next man has decided.”

He moved. A labourer paid, took a staff from the rack and went into the yard, still chewing the end of his breakfast. Two women arrived together and argued over which one had paid last time. A boy in a fine sash put down the wrong coin; the registrar returned it without pretending not to notice.

Su Fan looked past them. In the yard, an instructor stopped a pair of students and moved one foot with the end of his own staff. The student repeated the movement, lost balance and laughed at himself. The instructor did not laugh until the student did.

It was less magnificent than he had imagined a city practice school might be. It was also work he could see being taught.

He counted out the fee for one morning. If he needed more lessons, he would decide after learning what this one cost besides money.

The registrar noticed the bandage above his shoe and pointed to a place on the form where he should mark an injury. He wrote it plainly instead of making the words small.

Nobody at the gate asked him to explain his destiny.

They asked whether he had an injury the instructor should know about, whether he intended to use a staff or a padded sword, and whether he had brought the fee.

He paid it himself.

chapters.title: A Daughter's Address
chapters.text:
Min Yao worked behind a screen painted with cranes.

The cranes were poor. The handwriting on the fee board was excellent.

Su Fan waited while she explained to a merchant that a contract could not promise both exclusive delivery and unlimited freedom to use other carriers.

“Write it so it can,” the merchant said.

“I can write the sentence. I cannot make the two things agree.”

“Your competitor said he could.”

“Then you should pay him. I charge extra for arguments with the future.”

The merchant left without his papers.

He stopped in the doorway to tell Su Fan that a sensible man did business where people understood what he meant. Su Fan stepped aside rather than become a witness to an argument he had missed the beginning of.

Min Yao waited until the man’s footsteps had gone down the passage. Then she took the rejected page, marked the unapproved clauses and laid it in a tray instead of tearing it up.

“He’ll be back,” she said.

“Because the other writer can’t do it?”

“Because the other carrier will read it.”

She turned to him properly.

“What needs copying?”

She was about forty, with her father’s narrow hands and none of his hesitant manner. Ink darkened the side of one finger. A child slept on a mat behind the screen, one arm flung over a little wooden cup.

Su Fan had brought a list of things he might say about the archive in case she asked. He had rehearsed none of them aloud. In the room itself, with work drying on the table and the child breathing softly behind the badly painted birds, they all seemed like ways of arriving before her father’s letter did.

He gave her the envelope.

She recognized the hand immediately.

For a while she did not open it.

“Is he ill?”

“He coughs.”

“He has coughed for twenty years. Is he ill?”

Su Fan thought of the folded sleeve, the rests on the climb, the way Min had remained seated beside the books once they were safe.

“Yes.”

She drew the letter from its wrapping without breaking the fold. He looked at the fee board while she read. There was a different charge for a clean copy, a checked copy and a copy made from dictation. Someone had tried to scrape away the last price and written it larger beneath the attempt.

Her face changed so little that he could not tell which part hurt.

When she finished, she put the letter beneath a paperweight.

“Did he ask you to wait?”

“He said I needn’t.”

“That is what I asked.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him more closely.

“You’re Wei’s boy.”

“Su Fan.”

“He mentions you.”

“In letters?”

“In the letters he writes and then sends six months later because a sentence isn’t right.”

***

She reached beneath the desk and brought out a box of envelopes.

There were more than Su Fan expected. Some were old enough for the folded edges to have lost their colour. Others had clearly been opened recently. A narrow ribbon held one bundle together; the newest letters lay loose on top.

“I thought you didn’t speak.”

“We speak badly. It’s different.”

He looked again at the box. At the archive, Min’s daughter had arrived in his imagination as an absence: a rescued exercise book, a folded letter, a wish for a reply the old man could barely admit. Here she had invoices waiting, a child asleep, and years of sentences already received and answered.

He had mistaken the small part offered to him for the size of the relationship.

Min Yao put the box away before he could count the letters.

The child stirred. She rose, moved the cup clear of his cheek and covered him with a thin cloth. He asked a sleepy question about lunch. She told him when it would be ready. He appeared to consider the answer tolerable and went back to sleep.

She returned to the desk.

“He wanted me to stay in the archive. There was an apprenticeship waiting. A good one, for that district. I wanted to travel. He knew twelve reasons travel would hurt me and no reason wanting it mattered.”

Su Fan felt the words settle uncomfortably near his own unsent explanations.

“Was he wrong?”

“About the dangers? Often not.”

She took a clean sheet.

“That wasn’t the part I needed him to be wrong about.”

A customer appeared carrying a receipt that had been washed with his coat. Min Yao asked him to return after the next bell. He said the seller would close before then. She looked at the damp paper, at her unused reply sheet, then asked him to sit by the window while she checked which words could still be read.

Su Fan offered to leave and come back.

“You’ve waited this long. Sit.”

She placed the wet receipt between clean cloths and lifted away the surface moisture without rubbing. The motion reminded him of Min rescuing the child’s drawing. Her hands were steadier. The care was much the same.

“Did he keep any of my exercise books?” she asked while working.

“One. There may be others.”

“A bird on the page?”

“Yes.”

She smiled, very briefly.

“He told me the wing was wrong. I told him the bird intended to turn.”

“What did he say?”

“That intention didn’t alter anatomy.”

Su Fan could hear Min saying it. He could also hear how exhausting it might become to have every improbable wing corrected by somebody who loved you and wanted you to arrive safely at the shape he understood.

The damp-receipt customer asked whether the amount was still legible. Min Yao told him it was, but the date was not clear enough to copy as certain. He disliked that. She marked the uncertainty and gave him the damaged original along with the transcription.

The man paid and left, carrying a problem that had become smaller without entirely disappearing.

Min Yao returned to her father’s letter.

“Does he know you’re carrying the river records?”

“He helped us choose them.”

“Good. Then he’s still arguing usefully with somebody.”

“He asked me to read the corrections.”

“That sounds like him on a better day.”

She began writing. Su Fan turned his stool so he faced the notices rather than the page. It was not a conversation he had earned the right to read merely by carrying its first half.

***

A formation school offered evening lessons. A medical guild advertised examinations for independent practitioners. A public library charged less for a day’s reading than he had paid for the flawed gauge.

He copied the prices onto the back of his purchase list, making room between tempering sand and the measurements for Duan’s steel. The notes began to resemble the plans of someone who intended to live several different lives before their boat departed.

Min Yao noticed.

“Studying?”

“Trying.”

“Then don’t buy the broad introductory manuals. They promise ten arts and teach you how to pronounce eight.”

She marked three cheaper titles on his scrap. One dealt with movement and injury. One with river construction. The third collected failed cultivation experiments.

“They sell the successes in silk covers. The failures are where people admit what they actually did.”

He thought she and her father would have agreed on more than either enjoyed admitting.

“Do you cultivate?” he asked.

“Badly, on evenings when I haven’t copied somebody else’s finances until my eyes ache.”

“What method?”

“One whose teacher insisted I stop treating the lesson as something I could purchase once and then own without practising.”

He smiled. She pointed at the library notice.

“Start there. You can decide whether a book is useful before paying to take it home.”

He had brought the copied gate map in his pack. The old paper had begun wearing at a fold. He asked what she would charge to put it onto something that could survive a boat journey and a workshop bench.

Two copper, she said, provided he did not need her to certify the original measurements.

He spread the map beside her blotter. She examined the uncertain corner Min had left incomplete and asked whether it had been damaged or deliberately left open. Su Fan explained. She copied the gap as a gap, then wrote a small note distinguishing the missing portion from a white space in the landscape.

He watched the line of the Dry Cut appear beneath her brush. On clean paper it looked more convincing. The thought unsettled him enough to mention it.

“Then remember which certainty came from a new sheet,” she said.

She made him compare the finished copy against the original before rolling either. He found one landmark written too close to a channel and asked her to move it. She corrected it without defending the first placement.

By the time she sealed the reply to Min, the child was awake and examining the cranes on the screen. He wanted to know why one bird had three legs. Min Yao said one was a reed. He disagreed. She told him he could improve it after lunch, with a brush small enough to leave the rest of the wall intact.

She handed Su Fan the sealed envelope.

“Give him that. Don’t tell him I cried.”

“You didn’t.”

“Good. Easier instruction.”

The child climbed onto a stool while his mother put away the ink. He showed Su Fan a paper boat made from a clean offcut. One side stood higher than the other, and the bottom had been pinched so tightly that it would probably tip the moment it touched water.

“Will it float?” he asked.

“For a little while.”

“How long?”

“I don’t know.”

Min Yao brought a shallow washing bowl from behind the screen and told him he could find out after clearing the receipts from the end of the table. The boy moved them with exaggerated care, making a business of every sheet. She corrected which tray held them but left the boat alone.

It floated for three breaths, turned in a slow circle and sagged at the low side.

The boy looked offended. Then he lifted it out before it dissolved completely and began making the higher side lower to match.

Su Fan almost suggested a different fold. Min Yao was already carrying lunch from the covered pot, and the boy was intent on his own repair. Neither had asked him to take over.

He said goodbye instead. The boy waved with the wet boat. A drop struck the floor between the cranes, and Min Yao told him to fetch a cloth before the next customer sat in his river.

He paid the two copper without bargaining and put the reply in the dry inner fold of his pack. She charged him nothing for the titles. Before he left, she corrected his copied library address. He had confused the word for the east entrance with the word for a locked entrance.

“That would have been a discouraging introduction,” she said.

***

At the library, Su Fan waited for someone to ask whose permission he carried.

A young clerk asked instead whether his hands were clean.

He showed them. There was old iron dust beneath one nail. The clerk pointed to a basin, gave him a scrap of cloth and told him where books on bodily practice were kept. He paid the reading fee and entered with the peculiar feeling that an important part of the procedure had been omitted.

The room held tradesmen, students and two people asleep over tables. Nobody appeared scandalized by the sleepers. A woman making notes nudged one gently when his sleeve approached the inkstone.

Su Fan found the first title on Min Yao’s list and read its opening twice. The writer described an injured labourer’s changed gait before discussing any cultivation at all. The drawings were clearer than the scripture’s, though clarity did not make the two methods the same.

He noted where the author distinguished a movement that spared pain from one that merely hid it until the next task. Mother Wei had been trying to make him observe that difference with fewer words for months.

In another book he found a body method that widened the channels without assigning an element.

For several pages his pulse quickened.

The early descriptions seemed close enough to his own experiences that he began comparing phrases rather than reading what followed them. A circulation without a visible colour. A return through the legs. Increased steadiness before dramatic strength.

Then he reached the implanted bone charm.

He stopped, went back and read from the beginning. The charm was not an optional aid mentioned after the real teaching. The whole route depended on its stabilizing action. The apparent similarity had been assembled out of details he wanted to recognize while leaving their cause behind.

Different method. Different cost.

He copied an observation about weight shifting, but left the practice diagram alone. Beside the observation he wrote that its circumstances were not his own.

Another text described a breathing discipline that reduced waste but depended on a patron’s seal to stabilize the return. A third warned that apparent emptiness could indicate severe injury rather than refinement.

He copied that warning in full.

The collection of failed experiments was less orderly than he expected. Some writers had recorded careful measurements. Others had explained their own brilliance at such length that Su Fan had trouble discovering what had actually failed. In one account, a marginal note by a second hand contradicted the conclusion. He smiled when he saw it and then read the objection just as cautiously as the claim.

A useful correction could be wrong too.

He worked until the position of the light changed across the table. His ankle began aching where it hung beneath the stool. He placed the foot on his pack, drank the water he had forgotten beside his elbow and discovered that the questions on his page had become better than the answers he had hoped to buy.

How could he separate support from compensation? What did a lineage-testing bowl actually respond to? Which part of a return depended on the movement that came before it? How could he test direction without turning a failed attempt into another injury? What made a circuit persist during ordinary work? What signs distinguished quiet circulation from damaged channels? Which observations from another method remained useful when its source of power was removed?

Seven questions. No sudden missing key.

By closing time, he had discovered neither a duplicate of the Human Dao nor proof that it was unique.

The clerk came through gathering lamps. Su Fan began putting his books back too quickly and was told to leave them on the collection table rather than create a mystery for tomorrow’s readers.

“Back tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“Then leave your place marker. Saves hunting.”

Su Fan looked through the doorway at the book waiting on the table. Nobody was going to burn it overnight. Nobody required him to name its founder before opening it.

He left a scrap between the pages.

Outside, the city was preparing for supper. A delivery boy went past carrying a stack of empty baskets taller than his head. Somewhere a woman was scolding a paper bird that had landed in her bowl. The freight cable continued above the roofs, moving things from one place to another without asking whether the people beneath it had learned enough for one day.

Su Fan checked the sealed letter inside his pack and turned toward the leaning inn.

The ease of leaving a book safely behind stayed with him all the way there.

chapters.title: The Young Master's Left Foot
chapters.text:
Ruan Zhi beat Su Fan without using cultivation.

The first time, Su Fan blamed the difference in reach.

The second time, he blamed his injured ankle.

By the fourth, he had run out of explanations that were not embarrassing.

The padded tip rested against his ribs while he considered whether the third explanation, a poor grip, had been more dignified than the first two. Ruan withdrew the sword and waited for him to settle his feet again.

He wore training clothes that were simple and expensive. The seams sat where they belonged even when he moved. His hair had been tied by someone who understood how to make effort look accidental.

He was twenty-nine, ninth-stage Qi, and helping the instructor while waiting for a family appointment in Siltbridge.

Su Fan had disliked him for half a breath before he spoke.

That made losing more irritating.

The practice yard occupied a space between two storehouses. Its floor had been levelled with packed sand, except for a hard strip beside the wall where students walked to the water jar. A rack held padded swords, staffs and several shields whose edges had been repaired so often that the repairs overlapped.

None of it looked like the ornamental training grounds painted in cheap scrolls. Su Fan’s shirt was already gritty at the shoulder. He had learned more about the floor in a few exchanges than he wanted to know.

The instructor had paired him with Ruan after watching him move. Senior partners were to use no active cultivation in the opening bouts. Su Fan could keep the steadiness he ordinarily carried, but the object was a clean touch, not the hardest blow he could produce.

He had been relieved by that instruction until he discovered how much skill remained after power was set aside.

“You look at my shoulder,” Ruan said.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“It moves before you strike.”

“Sometimes.”

He struck.

Su Fan watched the shoulder, shifted to meet the blow and took the padded tip against the other side of his ribs.

Ruan’s left foot had moved first.

“Again,” Su Fan said.

They went again. This time he watched the foot. Ruan changed his grip and touched the shoulder he had left unguarded.

The instructor called for a break before the bruises became expensive.

***

Ruan offered him water.

Su Fan accepted because declining would have been childish and because he was thirsty enough to have accepted it from the man with the frost staff.

“Who taught you?”

“A smith.”

“He taught you to keep the sword. That’s more useful than several things people pay to learn.”

“You keep getting past it.”

“Yes. You’re guarding where the last blow came from.”

Su Fan drank. He wanted a more complicated problem. A defect in his circulation would have been private, interesting and connected to the unusual path he had found. Moving his blade to the wrong place was simply a thing he did badly in front of somebody dressed better than him.

Ruan watched another pair while he waited.

Two middle-aged women were practising staff work. One had trouble bringing the rear end around without striking her own elbow. Her partner stopped each time the mistake appeared, gave her space to reset and became impressively impatient only when she began apologizing instead of trying again.

Near the wall, a boy in a fine sash struggled against an older labourer with one missing finger. The labourer’s grip looked awkward until the sword moved. Then it was merely a grip belonging to that hand.

Nobody seemed to think the match beneath either of them.

Ruan sat on the edge of the platform and rubbed sand from his shoe.

“Where are you from?”

“Mudgate.”

“Greywing’s lower vale?”

Su Fan nodded.

“My aunt administers land there. I know the branch.”

Su Fan waited for a comment about its people.

“Does the lower ferry still sell garlic cakes?” Ruan asked.

It took him a moment to answer.

“Yes.”

“Good. My aunt says they’re unhygienic. She buys six when she travels.”

The laugh escaped before Su Fan could decide whether it would sound too pleased by a young master’s joke.

Ruan appeared not to notice the calculation. He stood when the instructor called them back and chose a place on the yard where the sand was even.

“Tell me when the ankle hurts,” he said.

“It’s all right.”

“Then tell me when that changes.”

He did not speak as though the injury were an excuse or a secret weakness he had cleverly uncovered. It was a fact relevant to the work they were about to do. Su Fan found himself less willing to lie about it after that.

The next exercise contained no strikes. Ruan approached with the padded point extended. Su Fan had to leave its reach without jumping backward into the wall or moving so far that he could not return.

He failed in quieter ways.

Sometimes he moved too soon, surrendering space Ruan had not yet asked for. Sometimes he waited for a reassuring sign and found the point already beside his collar. Once he stepped sideways cleanly and spoiled it by twisting toward the weapon after it had passed.

“Why did you turn?”

“To see where it was.”

“Where had you put yourself?”

Su Fan looked down. Safe from that straight approach, until he had moved back into it.

They repeated the exercise. The steadiness of his two circuits helped him recover from a poor step, but it did not make the step less poor. Ruan’s patient silence after each mistake was almost as difficult as Duan’s.

When the ankle began pulling, Su Fan said so. Ruan called the instructor over and changed the task to hand movement while Su Fan sat on the low platform.

It should have felt humiliating. Instead he learned something useful before the pain became the only thing he could notice.

***

He returned the next morning.

At the inn, Sun Lian asked whether the first lesson had made him want to buy a different profession. He said it had made him want to learn the profession he had already paid for. She gave him a piece of bread and told him not to practise on the stairs.

The yard changed from day to day. Different students came. A delivery cart blocked the usual entrance one morning, and everybody had to pass through a narrow side gate carrying the weapons end-first. A loose roof tile kept the pair nearest the wall from using one part of the sand until the owner sent someone to repair it.

Ruan treated these changes as part of the lesson rather than an offence against the ideal conditions Su Fan kept expecting.

“Leave yourself another direction,” he said when Su Fan backed toward the closed gate.

“The gate was open yesterday.”

“Then yesterday was more generous.”

Su Fan worked on distance. He stopped trying to turn a shoulder movement into a promise about the whole exchange. A shoulder could lie. So could a foot, especially after he had made it obvious that he was watching one.

Distance was less obliging. If Ruan could not reach him, a convincing feint remained a movement somewhere else. If Su Fan retreated so far that he could not answer, he had solved only the first half of the problem.

He began to notice the moments between those two mistakes.

On the third morning, the instructor made Ruan work with the woman who had been learning the rear-end staff turn. She was shorter than him and gave him less distance than he expected. He adjusted after the first exchange. After the second, she complained that he was being polite instead of useful.

Ruan looked toward the instructor, received no rescue and became useful.

Su Fan watched without the satisfaction he would once have taken in seeing a young master corrected. The woman wanted a partner who would make her improve. Ruan could do that, but only by letting go of the wish to appear generous every moment.

It was a familiar enough problem to make Su Fan uncomfortable.

He practised his own turns while waiting. When the warmth in the lower circuit caught behind the knee, he stopped and reset rather than push harder. The ankle remained a limit; a better step did not change the date on which the torn skin had healed.

At the end of that morning, Ruan had to leave for his family appointment. A messenger stood at the gate with the controlled impatience of someone paid to wait without seeming to wait. Ruan listened to the man, sighed and put away the padded sword.

“Land?” Su Fan asked.

“Accounts about land. The actual land is usually more agreeable.”

He left without pretending the duty did not belong to him. Su Fan stayed to help collect the equipment and discovered that returning a borrowed weapon neatly felt different after spending an hour being corrected by it.

***

On the fifth day, Su Fan landed one clean touch.

He watched distance. When Ruan stepped close enough to strike, he moved sideways, let the first feint pass and touched his sleeve.

For an instant the world arranged itself around the small pale mark on the cloth. He had done it. No clever revelation, no burst of power, just a movement placed correctly after enough wrong ones to make it feel unlikely.

Ruan looked at the mark.

“Better.”

Then he hit Su Fan in the chest.

Su Fan landed on his back.

“An exchange doesn’t stop because you are pleased.”

The instructor laughed from the shade. The laugh contained enough sympathy to make it worse.

Su Fan lay still long enough to distinguish injury from humiliation.

Humiliation. Mostly.

The sky above the open yard was very blue. A freight cage crossed a gap between roofs. Somewhere out of sight the city continued operating as though his first successful touch had not deserved a pause in ordinary affairs.

He got up.

Ruan bowed, not deeply, but without mockery.

The courtesy cost Su Fan more of his dislike than a compliment would have.

They worked once more, slowly. Ruan gave him the same opening and then a different one. Su Fan missed both while trying not to celebrate in advance. By the end he could see why a single success was evidence of a possibility, not ownership of a skill.

He was tired of evidence. He wanted lunch.

After class they washed the sand from the practice swords with damp cloths. The padding could not be soaked; it would dry badly and shift beneath the outer wrapping. Ruan was as careful with the shared equipment as with his own good clothes.

Su Fan asked about his inherited sword art.

“The Clear Reed,” Ruan said. “Three generations of revisions since the founder. My grandmother removed a turning cut that ruined the knees of taller pupils.”

“She changed an inherited method?”

“She was Foundation by then. People become surprisingly flexible about doctrine when a respected elder has aching joints.”

“Does the branch allow it?”

“The branch calls it restoration.”

They shared a brief smile.

Ruan laid the cleaned sword on the rack and picked up another whose wrapping had loosened. He asked Su Fan to hold the end while he retied it.

“My grandmother still made us learn why the older turn existed,” he said. “Removing it didn’t mean every person who used it had been a fool.”

“Did it work for her?”

“For a while. Then her body changed. Methods are irritating that way.”

Su Fan thought of Hua Jun’s crooked wrist and the crossed-out channel in the scripture. He had been collecting examples as though enough of them might settle an argument with Greywing. Ruan sounded more interested in whether the next pupil could still walk comfortably at sixty.

That was a smaller question, and not a small one.

Ruan’s gaze dropped to his hand.

“You use very little qi when you move.”

“I haven’t much.”

“That wasn’t quite what I meant.”

Su Fan said nothing. The quiet stretched for a few breaths, then Ruan tightened the final knot and let the subject go.

“Come back tomorrow. We’ll work on your retreat. You keep choosing a straight line.”

“Straighter than my purchases, apparently.”

Ruan glanced at the gauge in his tool roll and smiled.

“Everybody learns somewhere.”

***

Su Fan returned to the inn sore enough that Sun Lian made him carry the smaller shopping bag.

“Did the young master defeat you again?”

“Yes.”

“Was he insufferable?”

“No.”

“How inconsiderate.”

Bao Mei looked up from painting.

“Did you win at all?”

“Once.”

“He fell over afterward,” Sun Lian supplied.

“Then that doesn’t count.”

Su Fan accepted the judgment. He sat on the floor rather than the sloping stool because getting down once seemed preferable to falling unexpectedly. Bao Shun moved the lamp so he could see the bruise beneath his collar and said that paid instruction appeared to use a great deal of colour.

Bao Mei offered to paint something over it. Su Fan asked whether her blue was cheaper than Mother Wei’s ointment. She told him the blue would be more attractive, which was not an answer about either price or healing.

They ate the food Sun Lian had brought. Bao Shun described the stallholder who wanted to take the painted boards on terms that grew worse every time he explained them. He had not agreed yet. Bao Mei had found another seller willing to look, provided she brought examples rather than assurances about talent.

Su Fan listened. The room contained several kinds of difficult apprenticeship, none of which would be improved by his announcing that he had finally touched a ninth-stage cultivator’s sleeve.

Before the plates were cleared, Sun Lian asked how many more mornings he intended to buy.

Su Fan looked at the purse beside his knee.
