He had been counting the lessons as though paying for them one at a time made the total smaller. There were still meals, the inn, the return journey. Duan’s purchase money sat in a separate wrapping. He had kept it separate for a reason.

“Five,” he said. Then he counted again. “Possibly six.”

“And the books?”

He had found a shop selling a good copy of the exercise catalogue. He had imagined taking it home, putting his own notes between its pages and never having to ask permission to open it again.

“The library will still have theirs tomorrow.”

Sun Lian nodded. She did not congratulate him on making a choice with his own money.

He borrowed a sheet from the innkeeper and wrote to Duan. The steel had been bought; the casting was delayed. He set down what the purchases had actually cost, including the refund on the gauge. He nearly added an explanation of why the yard was worth the extra days, then stopped. He had not yet established how many extra days there would be, and Duan had asked for steel, not a report on his apprentice’s bruises.

Bao Shun checked the address while Su Fan folded it. A carrier leaving at dawn would take letters upriver for a small fee.

“Put the date on it,” the older man said. “Otherwise he’ll spend three days wondering which three days you mean.”

Su Fan added the date. It made the delay look less like a thought he could change and more like time someone else would have to work around.

Later he opened the notebook beside the scripture’s first movement diagram.

He began with what had failed: watching one clue, retreating too far, turning back into reach, stopping because he liked his own success. Then he wrote the correction in plain words.

He hesitated over the name.

If he wrote only the lesson, it would become one more thing he had discovered while improving himself. Ruan had spent five mornings making the discovery possible. There was no reason to make the page less honest than the yard.

He wrote clearly: *Ruan Zhi. Left foot. Distance before prediction.*

A useful lesson did not become a borrowed lineage merely because somebody else had learned it first.

He wished he had worked that out before paying to be hit twenty-seven times.

chapters.title: One Copper of Blue
chapters.text:
Bao Mei disappeared while her father was bargaining over a stool.

She had told him she was going to look at the colour seller. He remembered hearing it. He had also been counting coins with one hand while the seller explained why a stool with three sound legs was a bargain.

By the time he looked up, the girl was gone.

Su Fan found him outside the inn with his face grey.

“Which colour seller?”

“The one with the blue flag.”

There were five blue flags visible from the doorway.

Bao Shun turned toward the lane, then back toward the canal. His injured hand was tucked close against his body in the way he held it when he wanted nobody to notice it. The good one kept closing on the edge of his coat.

“She said the stall. I said—” He stopped. “I think I nodded.”

“How long?” Sun Lian asked.

“I don’t know.”

The answer frightened him more when spoken aloud. The bargaining had become an argument about the bad leg of the stool, then a search for change, then a discussion of delivery. Any one of those intervals could have held the moment when his daughter returned, failed to see him and went somewhere else.

Sun Lian divided the search before he could begin blaming himself through the whole sequence again.

She would take the canal landings. Su Fan would go with Bao Shun through the painting stalls. The innkeeper sent a boy to the bridge watch with a description of the girl and the name of the lodging house.

“Back here when you know anything,” Sun Lian said. “Not three people all running after the same rumour.”

Bao Shun nodded, impatient for movement. Su Fan took the rolled examples of Bao Mei’s work from the table. A child asking about paint might be remembered for what she carried better than for the colour of a shirt.

At the first stall the seller recalled no girl. At the second, the man said several children had passed and became annoyed when asked which direction. The third blue flag belonged to a shop selling dyed cord, not pigment at all.

Su Fan searched methodically at first.

He asked where Bao Shun had stood, where the colour stall had been in relation to the sun, whether the girl had carried money or only her questions. He kept the inquiries short because every extra sentence seemed to make his companion’s face tighter.

Then he saw a child’s sandal beneath a cart and felt his thinking narrow.

It was not Bao Mei’s.

He checked anyway.

The cart owner demanded to know what he was doing beneath the axle. Su Fan held up the sandal, heard himself asking whose it was and knew, even while asking, that its size and patched strap were wrong. The owner called to a child eating beside the opposite wheel. The child looked down, discovered one bare foot and accepted the sandal without apparent concern.

Su Fan stood too quickly and struck his shoulder on the cart.

Bao Shun was watching him.

“That isn’t hers.”

“I know.”

The man’s fear had become worse because Su Fan, who had been supplying order, had briefly shown him another thing to fear. Su Fan slowed his breathing and made himself return to the question they could actually answer.

Which woman had sold blue powder beneath a flag with a torn edge?

The shop beside the cord seller knew. They crossed a narrow bridge, waited for a handcart to pass and reached a stall with bowls of dry colour arranged beneath cloth covers.

The woman there remembered painted fingers and a child asking why mineral blue looked duller before it was mixed.

“She went to Master Zhen’s workshop.”

“Where?”

“Over the dye bridge. Two doors past the red shrine.”

“With whom?” Bao Shun asked.

“With me. My sister was showing the apprentices a wash.”

The woman’s expression changed when she understood why they were asking. She called to the boy working behind her and told him to watch the stall.

“I’ll show you.”

Bao Shun was already moving. He had begun limping faster, favouring a leg that had cramped during the search rather than the hand everybody expected him to protect.

***

They found Bao Mei standing on a box beside a long worktable.

An elderly painter was showing her how to spread a wash across primed wood. Three apprentices watched. A bowl of expensive blue pigment stood beside her elbow.

The room smelled of wet timber, binding paste and a faint sharpness from newly ground colour. Finished signs hung from a beam. One showed a bowl so convincing that Su Fan’s first absurd thought was that Auntie Lu would have objected to the portion.

Bao Mei held the brush differently from the way she had held her poor little tools at home. The older woman guided the angle without taking over the stroke. The girl’s shoulders were relaxed. She was listening with the complete attention that had made her forget how long she had been away.

Her father reached her before Su Fan could speak.

“What were you thinking?”

The brush jerked.

Blue spilled across the board.

Bao Mei’s face went white.

“I told you.”

“You said the colour stall.”

“The woman brought me here.”

“You went with a stranger?”

Master Zhen put a hand between them, palm outward.

“She came to see a demonstration. The stallholder is my sister.”

“You should have asked me.”

“I thought you knew.”

Bao Shun had been imagining the worst for an hour. His voice could not immediately return from it. The apprentices stared. One began wiping the spill and was told gently to leave it for the moment.

Su Fan touched the man’s shoulder.

“She’s here.”

“I can see that.”

“She’s safe.”

“I can see that too.”

But his breathing slowed.

Bao Mei looked at the blue spreading into the pale part of the board. She had been so close to understanding the stroke. Now her father was angry, the apprentices were watching and the colour she had been allowed to touch because somebody trusted her appeared to have ruined the work.

Tears gathered without falling.

Master Zhen took the brush from her and laid it across the bowl.

“Outside for a moment,” she told everyone except the girl.

Nobody argued with her.

At the door, the colour seller caught Su Fan’s sleeve and offered to send word to the inn. He thanked her and asked that the bridge watch and Sun Lian be told the child was safe. The woman sent one apprentice with the message, then returned to her stall with an expression that suggested she was considering how a generous invitation had become such a complicated afternoon.

Su Fan and Bao Shun waited beneath a narrow awning.

For a little while they listened to the traffic. Someone on the dye bridge shouted for more room. A carrier complained that the room had been there before everybody else arrived. Ordinary irritation continued around them, indifferent to the terrible possibilities that had occupied the last hour.

Bao Shun rubbed his damaged hand with the good one.

“I shouted.”

“You were frightened.”

“That doesn’t make her less frightened.”

Su Fan had no answer to that.

***

The workshop door remained partly open. They could hear Master Zhen speaking, though not clearly enough to make out every word. Bao Shun turned toward it whenever his daughter answered.

He had wanted to find her. Now that she was found, he could not work out what to do with the force of wanting still left in him.

“I should have listened,” he said.

Su Fan looked at the rolled painting in his hand. It showed a boat with a brown hull and more care given to the reflections than to the sky. Bao Mei had made it at a table beside her father’s injured hand, while other people were deciding what the injury meant for their household.

“She thought she had told you enough.”

“She didn’t know this place.”

“No.”

“Neither did I.”

That was the admission that quieted him. He had been bargaining fiercely over a stool because he needed to sit at a work stall and could no longer rely on standing all day while one arm throbbed. The price mattered. The girl’s question had arrived at the same time as the seller’s claim that a bad leg was easily repaired.

He had treated one thing as urgent and another as understood. It had been a mistake, not a mystery about how little he loved his daughter.

Su Fan wished mistakes became easier to repair when their intentions were good. Tan Wei’s face beside the practice stones suggested otherwise.

Master Zhen came out carrying the blue board.

It was not ruined, she said. Blue could become water.

She had lifted some colour while it was wet and used the rest to begin a wash along the lower edge. One small patch remained much darker. She had left it that way rather than pretend nothing had happened.

“The girl has a good eye and poor brushes. Those are problems of different sizes.”

Bao Shun looked through the doorway. Bao Mei sat on the box now, wiping the table with a clean cloth. She did not look up immediately when he moved.

“She may attend the morning class while you’re here,” the painter said. “You bring her. You collect her. We all know where she is.”

He nodded.

“What does it cost?”

“Two copper a morning.”

He swallowed. It was not an outrageous price. That did not make it a price he could stop considering.

Su Fan reached toward his purse.

Bao Shun caught the movement.

“No.”

“I was only—”

“I know.”

The refusal was not angry. It still stopped his hand.

Master Zhen studied them, then looked at Bao Shun’s injured arm.

“My delivery porter left last week. Can you count?”

“Yes.”

“Can you tell the difference between a boat and a shoe?”

His face changed.

“She showed you?”

“She did.”

He looked through the doorway at his daughter.

“I can learn.”

“Then we can discuss a temporary arrangement.”

The work was not all carrying. Finished boards had to be matched to orders, wrapped without spoiling the fresh surface and checked against what the customers had paid. He could manage the smaller deliveries. Someone else would lift the larger frames. The painter did not pretend the damaged hand was sound or that using the good one meant he had no useful work left.

She named what the arrangement would cover and what it would not. Bao Shun asked her to repeat the hours. He wanted to attend to his daughter’s possible stall as well. Master Zhen agreed to a short trial rather than turn one afternoon into a permanent promise.

Su Fan lowered his hand from the purse.

Bao Mei came to the doorway while they were discussing it. She looked first at her father, then at the board, then at the woman who had not let the spill become the only thing the afternoon contained.

“I can help clean after the class,” she said.

“You can clean after your own work,” Master Zhen replied. “That’s part of learning. Don’t offer to pay the same fee three different ways.”

The girl considered this and nodded seriously.

***

They walked back more slowly than they had come.

Bao Shun bought no stool. He said he would return to that argument after looking at the one offered for use in the workshop. Bao Mei carried the rolled example under her arm. The blue mark on her cuff looked startlingly bright beside the faded colour she had brought from home.

At the inn, the proprietor said the bridge watch had received the message. Sun Lian had come back from the canal, confirmed which workshop the girl had been found in and gone to inspect the boat. The search was over. Its traces remained in the tiredness of people who had spent an hour imagining a different ending.

That evening Bao Mei brought a small packet of blue to the table.

Master Zhen had charged one copper for a damaged batch. The colour was less brilliant than the good pigment, but brighter than anything the girl owned. It would need care in mixing. Bao Mei described that limitation as though it made the purchase more interesting rather than less valuable.

She put the packet down as carefully as Tan Wei had held his first eligibility paper.

Bao Shun sat beside her.

“I should have listened properly.”

“I should have come back.”

“Yes.”

He stopped there. The two truths were allowed to remain separate.

After a moment she unfolded the scrap on which Master Zhen had written the class time. Her father read it, then asked her to read it too. They agreed where they would meet afterward and what she should do if the class ended early.

Bao Mei asked the innkeeper for a broken saucer. The woman produced one so quickly that Su Fan suspected it had been waiting to become somebody else’s responsibility.

The girl shook a little blue into it. She added water from the end of a clean stick rather than pouring from the cup. Her father watched the pigment darken.

“That’s scarcely enough for a flower.”

“It’s enough to find out what it does.”

She tried a stroke on the back of a spoiled price slip. The colour gathered at one edge and left the other pale. She looked displeased, then adjusted the mixture and tried again beside it.

Bao Shun reached for the paper. She held it down with two fingers.

“Wait until it’s dry.”

He withdrew his hand.

On the third attempt the line sat evenly. Bao Mei turned the saucer and offered him the brush.

“With this hand?” he asked, lifting his good one.

“It’s the one you’ve got free.”

He made a short blue mark, broader than he intended. She showed him how little pressure the point needed. He tried once more, concentrating so hard that his lower lip moved. The second stroke was not much better, but it was different.

“That will sell for very little,” he said.

“It’s a practice sheet.”

“Ah. Then I’m already making a profit.”

She laughed. He set the brush down without wiping it on his sleeve.

Su Fan could not see a future business in the crooked marks. He could see the father waiting for his daughter to tell him whether the colour was dry. When she said it was, he picked up the paper by its bare corner, exactly as she had shown him.

It was a small arrangement, made after the frightened words rather than instead of them.

He went downstairs before they noticed him watching.

At the canal, Sun Lian was repairing a split in the forward rail. The damage from the attack had been made safe for the journey, not made good. She held a new plank against the old fastening and needed a third hand to see whether the line sat correctly.

“How is she?” she asked.

“Safe. Embarrassed. Going to take painting lessons.”

“An expensive combination.”

“Her father found some work at the shop.”

“Good.”

She nodded toward the plank. He took the other end.

For a while they worked together in the evening noise of the city. A ferry musician was practising the same difficult passage repeatedly. Somebody on the next boat had a different opinion of which notes belonged in it.

Sun Lian asked him to lift his end a little. He did. She checked the fit and told him when she was ready to take the weight.

When he needed to shift his grip, he said so. She waited.

It was an uncomplicated arrangement. He found himself appreciating it.

chapters.title: The Counterweight
chapters.text:
The casting house would not release Sun Lian’s steering shoe.

It stood on a bench behind the master caster, wrapped in oiled cloth with one corner turned back to show the maker’s mark. Su Fan could see the clean curve of the socket. After days of rejected measurements and promises about the next firing, it was an unusually attractive piece of iron.

The master caster laid a revised bill beside it.

Sun Lian read the bill. Then she read it again, more slowly.

Outside, a cart waited across the entrance to the yard. Its driver had left enough space for a person to squeeze past, but not enough for a person carrying a heavy casting. The apprentices kept looking toward it. One held the long tongs upright against his shoulder; the other had been brushing the same patch of furnace floor since they arrived.

“You signed this,” Sun Lian said.

Su Fan opened the original agreement on the clear end of the bench. He put a small weight on its corner so the draught from the furnace would not lift it.

“I priced the metal I expected to use,” the caster said.

“You used the metal I supplied.”

“The wastage was higher.”

“Show me.”

He pointed toward a scrap bin without turning around.

Sun Lian went to the bin. Su Fan followed her gaze over the pieces inside. Runners, broken mould braces, irregular scraps with different surfaces. Some had lain there long enough to gather red dust. There was no sensible way to distinguish what had come from her casting merely by accepting the direction of the man’s finger.

“Which pieces?” she asked.

The caster made a small impatient noise.

“We have other work.”

“So have I.”

She bent to look at a thick runner resting across the top. Before her hand reached it, he stepped between her and the bin.

Su Fan moved without properly deciding to move. A moment later he was standing in front of a man whose hands glowed faintly from years of heat work, holding a paper that was suddenly a poor thing to have between them.

“Let her weigh it,” he said.

The furnace door stood open behind the caster. Orange light fell across the side of his face. Su Fan could feel warmth coming off the man independently of the fire.

The warmth increased.

Then came a pressure that seemed to arrive through the ground and settle across his shoulders. It was meant to find his circulation and close around it. He recognized something of the unpleasant searching quality he had felt beneath Zhu Ke’s frost.

The pressure found little purchase.

The heat worked perfectly well.

Sweat sprang along his upper lip. His throat dried. He became acutely conscious of the agreement in his hands and the clerk’s signature on it, all those thin strokes made in a cooler room by someone who was not standing here now.

He kept his feet still. He did not mistake remaining upright for being able to win.

“We have the contract,” he said. “And the weigh receipt. There are cheaper ways to settle this.”

The caster’s eyes moved to the paper, then back to his face.

Sun Lian had stepped sideways. She was no longer behind him.

“Guild arbitration,” she said.

She drew another document from her coat and opened it over the bench, beyond the edge of the hot light.

“Your mark is on the register outside. The original fee includes the casting work. Supplied metal was weighed on your scales. I’ll accept a measured loss, identified against this job. I won’t accept a different price because my boat is waiting.”

The caster looked at the apprentices.

Neither looked back. The one with the brush seemed to have discovered a defect in the floor requiring all his attention. Su Fan understood why. They would still be here after the customer and her inconvenient papers had gone.

“Are you accusing me?” the caster asked.

“I’m asking you to finish the transaction you signed.”

The heat eased first. The pressure remained for another breath, then withdrew so abruptly that Su Fan almost relaxed too much. He set the original agreement flat before the trembling in his fingers became visible.

There followed a long, unpleasant silence.

From outside came the cart driver’s voice, asking whether anyone intended to load him before the street grew busy. Somewhere in the neighbouring yard a woman laughed. The ordinary noises made the silence inside harder to maintain.

At last the caster picked up the revised bill, folded it once and put it beneath a ledger.

“Original price,” he said. “Collect it.”

Sun Lian did not immediately reach for her money.

She inspected the socket, checked the bolt holes against her template and made him turn the casting so she could see the underside. Su Fan wanted to take it and leave. She appeared willing to spend the rest of the morning making certain they did not have to come back.

One hole needed a burr removed. The younger apprentice fetched a file. He worked with his head bent, passed the template over the edge and waited for her judgment.

“That fits,” she told him.

He nodded without smiling.

When the payment was counted, she asked for the receipt. The caster signed it with a hand that had stopped glowing quite so brightly. Only then did she cover the shoe and allow Su Fan to help lift it.

The air outside felt cold against his wet shirt.

They carried the iron to the shade of a neighbouring wall and set it on two blocks. Sun Lian looked at him. He had been hoping she would look at the socket.

“Don’t do that again without telling me.”

“Stand in the way?”

“Stand in front of a cultivator you’re hoping won’t hit you.”

“I wasn’t hoping. You had the guild paper.”

“I might have had the wrong paper.”

He considered that.

“Yes.”

She pulled the cloth straight over one corner of the iron.

“I might also have wanted to let him keep the shoe while I fetched an arbitrator. Or taken my complaint elsewhere. You gave us a different problem before I’d chosen.”

“I thought he was going to stop you.”

“He was.”

Su Fan looked down the lane. The caster had returned to the furnace. Both apprentices were working again, their movements quick and careful.

“He was fifth-stage,” Sun Lian said.

“I know.”

“You know now. I couldn’t tell whether you knew while you stood there.”

He had known enough to be afraid. That was not quite the same thing as having given her anything useful to work with.

“The pressure didn’t catch properly,” he said. “The heat did.”

“Then next time tell me both of those things before we need them.”

He nodded.

After a moment she adjusted her grip beneath the cloth.

“You’re improving at that answer.”

“Which one?”

“The short one.”

They lifted the casting together. The socket was sound, the price was settled, and his shirt would dry. None of that made the morning a clever victory.

***

At the dock they found the harbour lift broken.

A cargo platform hung halfway between the upper wharf and the landing beside the water. It leaned toward the river, one corner lower than the others. A bundle of metal bars had shifted against the low rail. The remaining cargo had been wedged around it so thoroughly that nobody could reach the bundle without first standing where the platform might move.

Their steel was among the waiting goods above. Sun Lian’s casting had arrived on a handcart at the same level. Honest Measure lay below.

The lift keeper sat on an upturned crate eating something from a bowl.

“Tomorrow,” he said.

They were due to catch the outgoing current at dawn.

“Who’s coming tomorrow?” Sun Lian asked.

“The repair man.”

“What is he repairing?”

The keeper gestured with his spoon toward the tilted platform.

Su Fan set down his end of the casting. He walked along the upper rail and looked at the gear, then down the side where the counterweight moved between its guides.

The weight was sound. Its chain had not jumped. A guide pin on the cargo side was bent inward, catching the frame as it rose. Three supporting ropes were carrying different shares of a load that should have been spread across the floor.

He crouched to see the underside. The keeper told him not to touch anything.

“I haven’t.”

“Good. Keep doing that.”

Sun Lian came to stand beside him. He pointed to the pin, then followed the line of the lowest rope with his finger.

“If we support this corner and shift the sacks back, the frame will clear. The pin needs straightening or replacing before it runs again.”

“Can you reach it from here?”

“Not safely.”

“Then where?”

He studied the fixed beam beneath the landing. There was space to build a temporary support from it, if the keeper had sound timber rather than the split lengths stacked by the water. They would need wedges, a second line and somebody at the brake throughout the work.

He described that part aloud. It felt slower than simply beginning. Sun Lian asked two questions that changed where he intended to brace the load.

They went to the keeper together.

“No,” he said when Su Fan asked for wedges.

“You have them in that chest.”

“I also have a job. If you break the lift, people come asking whose lift it was when you broke it.”

That was a reasonable fear, although the keeper was enjoying it more than he needed to.

Sun Lian asked what the repair man would charge merely to look. The keeper named a figure. She asked how much the platform’s cargo owners would pay for another day’s storage.

His spoon stopped.

At last she offered to answer for damage their work actually caused, provided he witnessed the present state and supplied the timber. Not the existing bent pin. Not the cracked rail. Not a claim written afterward for every tired rope in the harbour.

He considered the distinction. Then he put down his bowl.

They began by making the space below useless to everyone except the people working in it. A porter protested at the diverted route until Sun Lian pointed to the cargo hanging over his head. He chose another way with considerable dignity.

The keeper took the brake. Su Fan and a dockhand passed the extra line around a fixed beam, keeping it clear of the running gear. Sun Lian checked the timber before letting either man put a shoulder beneath anything. One length had a soft patch hidden under an old paint stripe. They rejected it.

Only when the support was seated did Su Fan climb onto the near edge of the platform.

It gave slightly beneath him. He stopped and waited. The second line held. The keeper, above, complained that he could not see what was happening.

“That’s why you’re holding the brake,” Sun Lian told him.

The first two bundles moved easily. The third sack had settled into a gap beside the metal bars. Su Fan put his hands under its lower edge and tested the weight.

Too much for an ordinary pull in that position. Not too much if his circuit carried the effort cleanly from the floor through his legs.

He told Sun Lian what he was going to do. She took the rope controlling the lower corner. The dockhand steadied the upper bundle so it would not follow.

Su Fan drew in a breath, set his feet and lifted.

The sack came free a hand’s breadth. Halfway through the movement, the lower circuit caught beneath his knee.

For an instant he felt the old, tempting answer: tighten harder, finish the lift, let the available strength solve the position. The sack was already moving. Stopping seemed like losing work he had almost completed.

“More weight on your line,” he said.

Sun Lian leaned back. The pressure changed.

He lowered the sack against his thigh, reset his foot and let the unnecessary tightening ease. It took two breaths. The dockhand did not rush him. Above, the keeper began a question and was told to keep holding.

When Su Fan lifted again, the movement ran through him without catching.

The sack slid into place.

They waited for the frame to settle before anyone changed position. The low corner rose enough to free the damaged guide. Sun Lian passed up the smaller hammer. Su Fan worked the pin only after confirming that it no longer carried the weight of the platform.

It was ordinary iron in an ordinary bracket. The skill he needed had come from Duan’s workshop. He found that reassuring.

They tested the lift empty first, then with a limited load. The keeper watched from above as the frame passed the damaged point without scraping. He looked almost disappointed when it reached the landing.

“Still needs the repair man,” Su Fan said. “That guide should be replaced.”

The keeper brightened a little.

“Tomorrow.”

“Before you put a full load on it.”

This was received less warmly. Sun Lian wrote the defect on the agreed record and made him acknowledge it before they moved their own purchases.

By the time the steel reached Honest Measure, Su Fan’s arms ached. No one had offered him a name for the technique with which he had shifted a sack. He had a splinter under one nail, a little money saved on delay, and a clearer idea of where his new strength stopped being useful.

***

That night Sun Lian counted her remaining money aboard the boat.

The steering shoe lay fitted loosely in place, waiting for a final check in daylight. A lantern hung beneath the cabin roof. Its light moved over the cloth on which she had arranged the coins in separate groups.

Su Fan sat nearby, copying the figures from Duan’s purchases. He had finally made the cost of the gauge agree with the money in its wrapping. The refund looked smaller when set among all the other numbers.

Sun Lian moved two coins from one group to another, considered them, then moved one back.

“Your boat costs more than it earns,” he said before thinking.

“This month.”

“Do you owe on it?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

She looked up.

He stopped. The question had come with the same confidence as his step across the casting-house floor: something looked wrong, so he had already begun placing himself inside it.

“You don’t have to tell me.”

“True.”

She returned to the coins.

He finished his own column. For a while there were only the small metallic sounds of her counting and water touching the hull. From the inn came a burst of laughter, then Bao Mei’s voice objecting to something her father had said about colours.

Su Fan put Duan’s money away. He did not ask another question.

After a while Sun Lian said, “The supply contract pays enough to clear the debt before next winter. That’s why I haven’t walked away from the river office.”

“And the collateral?”

She tapped the deck.

He looked along the repaired rail, the patched sail and the tools arranged beneath the cabin roof. He had thought of her as somebody who could leave whenever she chose. She untied a line, selected a channel, and a whole village went away behind her.

He had not asked what travelled with the boat.

“Does the damage change the agreement?” he asked.

“Some repairs are mine. Some losses can be claimed. A claim isn’t a payment.”

“Will the river office pay for the missing crate?”

“We’ve reported it. That’s as much as we know tonight.”

She gathered the smallest group into a purse, then wrapped the others separately. There was no dramatic last coin. There was enough for certain things and not enough for all the things that could go wrong. Su Fan recognized that arrangement even without knowing the amounts.

Sun Lian saw him understanding.

“Everyone on this river is carrying something,” she said. “Mine has a name painted on the side.”

She put the money away and took the lantern down from its hook.

“Port line first,” she said. “The water’s dropping.”

He followed her onto the narrow side deck. This time he waited for her to show him which knot to loosen and how much room the hull would need before morning.

chapters.title: Three Stones
chapters.text:
They stayed in Siltbridge twelve days longer than planned.

The extra time cost money. It also bought Bao Mei nine painting lessons, Su Fan eleven mornings in the practice yard, and Sun Lian a casting that actually fitted.

There had been a day when all three benefits looked doubtful. Bao Mei came back from the workshop declaring that blue was the least trustworthy colour. Su Fan could not turn his head without remembering a padded sword. Sun Lian set the steering shoe on the inn table and stared at it until the proprietor asked whether it wanted supper.

It had needed another careful adjustment, not another quarrel at the casting house. She made the adjustment herself, with a file borrowed from a boatwright and Su Fan holding the lamp where she asked. He had been relieved to be useful without having to guess what useful meant.

Duan’s reply to the letter about the delay contained only six words.

*Bring the steel, not more explanations.*

Su Fan read it twice. Then he folded it around the purchase figures. It was good to know exactly which part of the trip his master wished to receive.

Min Yao’s reply remained sealed in his pack. He had checked the wrapping whenever rain threatened the inn’s sloping window. He knew the shape of the packet and nothing of what it said. That ignorance had begun to feel like a small job he could do properly.

On the last afternoon, he went back to the practice yard.

The morning class had finished. A boy was collecting the padded weapons while the instructor argued with a supplier about the stuffing in a split shield. Ruan Zhi waited beside the water jar, his sleeves rolled up. He had already arranged for the use of a narrow strip of yard and explained to the boy which swords to leave out.

“One final lesson,” he said.

Su Fan took the offered weapon.

“I thought yesterday was final.”

“It was. You retreated into the rack. I disliked ending there.”

“The rack seemed satisfied.”

Ruan smiled and stepped away from it.

They checked the ground first. A loose chip of wood lay near the wall. Su Fan moved it aside. His ankle no longer hurt with every ordinary step, but it had not become something he could afford to forget merely because the city was ending.

“This time I’ll use a little qi,” Ruan said.

Su Fan tightened his grip, noticed that he had done so, and eased it again.

“How little?”

“Enough for you to feel the difference. I’m not testing what your bones can survive.”

They began slowly. The first exchange was familiar. Ruan’s shoulder shifted; Su Fan kept the distance rather than chasing the apparent opening. He moved across the line instead of backward and recovered his guard before admiring it.

Ruan nodded.

Then his next movement arrived differently.

Su Fan saw it. That was the worst part. He saw the shoulder, the foot, the small turn of the blade. Nothing was hidden. His body began the answer he had practised for days, and the padded point was at his throat before the answer existed in the world.

He stopped breathing against the cloth.

“Useful,” Ruan said.

“For you?”

“For your sense of scale.”

Ruan withdrew the sword.

Su Fan rubbed the place it had touched. He could have spent the next hour describing why he had lost. The explanation would not have moved his feet any faster.

“Again?”

“Once.”

This time Su Fan gave ground earlier. Too early. Ruan did not follow the first movement. He waited until Su Fan had used the space, then entered it from another angle. The second touch landed against the ribs.

The boy collecting swords glanced over, saw that nobody was about to do anything spectacular and returned to his work.

Ruan lowered his weapon.

“You can learn to make better choices with the time you have. You can also get stronger. Those are related jobs. They aren’t the same job.”

Su Fan nodded. He was thinking of a caster’s heat and the guild paper he had treated as though it could step between a fist and his face.

They returned the weapons. He thanked the instructor, who told him to keep practising the ordinary steps when there was no young master available to strike him for forgetting them.

At the gate Ruan paused.

“I’ll be at Greywing later in the year. My aunt wants me to inspect her tenant lands. Perhaps we’ll practise again.”

“Will you still charge?”

“I don’t receive the fee.”

“Then perhaps we can practise somewhere cheaper.”

Ruan laughed. They bowed to one another, less awkwardly than they had on the first day.

Su Fan walked back through the city without buying the exercise catalogue. He stopped once to look at it in the shop window. The book would remain there after he left, or another copy would take its place. For now he had paid for bruises, questions and a name written beside a useful correction. Those would have to travel in the same bag as the steel receipts.

***

The third stage came on the journey home.

There was no emergency to force it. There was not even a convenient stretch of empty deck. Sun Lian had forbidden training while the boat moved, and the cargo gave her several good reasons before she needed to mention his ankle.

“You can practise tying that,” she told him when he looked at a clear patch beside the mast.

He looked down at the rope in his hands.

“It’s tied.”

“It’s attached. We’re working toward tied.”

He retied it. Bao Mei watched from the cabin entrance, decided this was more entertaining than drawing the riverbank, and put down her brush.

The first day carried them away from the city’s stone edges and cable shadows. The banks widened. Traffic thinned into boats they could see coming from far enough away to argue about who ought to move. Bao Shun slept for part of the afternoon with his injured hand supported on a folded cloth. He had worked more in the city than he had expected. He had also been paid for work that he could still do.

Bao Mei carried her lesson sheets between two boards. She checked them whenever the boat bumped. Sun Lian inspected the new steering fitting at every stop until she was satisfied that the sound of it belonged to the movement rather than to another fault.

Su Fan waited for the mooring.

He had brought three stones from the Siltbridge riverbank, each a little flatter than the ones at home. They were not special stones. One had a chipped edge he kept forgetting to turn downward. He placed them in a triangle on a level patch above the water and began with the movements he already knew.

On the first evening he could carry the circuit through a turn only when he moved slowly enough to feel each adjustment. Speed brought back the old habit of bracing too soon. He spent most of the available light moving one foot, then the other, while mosquitoes found the parts of him that cultivation had not made interesting.

When Sun Lian called him, he stopped. He did not negotiate another ten breaths into an hour.

On the second evening he took out the library notes.

One method described a return through the lower body that resembled a question the scripture had left unanswered. The full method depended on an implanted charm. He had copied that warning beside the diagram in large enough characters to prevent himself from conveniently overlooking it.

He could not borrow its conclusion and discard its condition. He could look at the observations: where the weight fell, how an unnecessary tightening interrupted a movement, what the writer had measured before claiming success.

He tried those observations against movements he could already perform.

The result was mostly an untidy patch of ground. On one attempt he shifted too far onto the injured ankle and stopped at once. On another he discovered that he had been drawing the return as though both legs answered at the same time. His body disagreed.

He crossed out the line rather than persuade the body.

Bao Mei came up from the boat carrying her own board. She sat a little distance away and mixed a colour with the clean water she had brought for it. For several minutes they worked without speaking.

“What are you painting?” he asked at last.

“Not that tree.”

He looked at the tree in front of her.

“It keeps turning into the one at home.”

She scraped a small patch back. Su Fan looked at his corrected diagram and understood the difficulty without needing to discuss it.

On the third evening he made no progress he could trust. The ground was uneven, his back was tired from cargo, and every successful sensation vanished when he tried to repeat it. He wrote those circumstances down. They were inconvenient enough that leaving them out would have made the page more encouraging.

Sun Lian asked whether he wanted to walk into the nearby village for hot food. He looked at the stones, then packed them away.

They ate sitting on a low wall while Bao Shun compared the seller’s benches with a design he had seen in Siltbridge. Bao Mei tried to describe the difference between two shades of blue to a man who thought either would do for a boat name. Sun Lian defended the right of boat names to be painted in whatever colour their owner could afford.

Su Fan laughed more than the argument deserved. When they returned to the mooring, he went to sleep instead of taking the stones out again.

On the fourth evening, the return completed while he stepped backward.

He had been trying to carry the second circuit through an ordinary change of direction. His heel found the ground without his knee locking against it. The warmth continued through the soles of both feet, along the inner legs and up through the torso.

It did not surge. It did not announce itself as an answer to anything beyond the movement he was making.

The three circuits remained distinct. He could feel where they crossed, and for the first time they did not catch at the crossing.

He stopped.

The warmth stayed.

He picked up the nearest stone and moved it from one hand to the other. He turned, lowered it, lifted it again. On the second turn he overcorrected and felt the route narrow. He reset his feet rather than push. It opened again.

He had gained less raw force than he expected.

He had gained far more control.

Su Fan put the stone down and walked away from the triangle. He wanted to know whether the movement belonged only to the marks he had prepared for it. At the edge of the bank he bent to retrieve a fallen peg, turned with it in his hand and stood without losing the new return.

Then he sat down, because he was shaking slightly and did not intend to turn a good evening into another visit to Mother Wei.

The river moved past the mooring. Honest Measure creaked against its lines. He could hear Bao Shun and Bao Mei negotiating the portions of a fish below him.

After a while Sun Lian called.

“Something happened?” she asked when he came down.

“Yes.”

“Painful?”

“No.”

“Then wash your hands. Bao Mei thinks the fish is for her alone.”

He washed them. At supper he told them what had changed, and what he still needed to check. Bao Shun asked whether it would help carry the steel. Su Fan said it ought to. Sun Lian told him they would find out in daylight, with the boat securely moored and somebody else on the other end.

It was not the reception he might once have imagined for a breakthrough. He ate his share of the fish and found that he preferred it.

***

At Mudgate, the lower irrigation channel was running again.

Not at full volume. Enough to make the fields green at their edges. The water moved past new boards at the intake and through a channel from which people had cleared old roots and silt while he was elsewhere.

The widow’s petition had received a revised schedule. The lifting wheel filled the hours between releases. It turned with a creak that suggested several men had argued over its axle and eventually agreed to live with the same imperfect answer.

Someone had painted a goose on its side in tribute to Auntie Lu.

She denied being flattered while standing where she could see it.

“The beak is wrong,” she told Bao Mei.

“Too large?”

“Insufficiently respected.”

Bao Mei went to examine it. Within moments she and the original painter were discussing whether the wing could be improved without stopping the wheel. Bao Shun set down their bundle and watched her join a conversation that had begun without him.

Su Fan looked for the widow. She was farther along the channel, checking a small gate with a man whose fields took water after hers. They were arguing about the agreed hours, which was an improvement over arguing about a dry ditch.

She saw him and raised a hand.

“Did you bring Duan’s metal?”

“Yes.”

“Good. He’s been blaming you for everything he can’t mend.”

The town had not waited for him to return with a solution from the city. He could see where the work had been done and where it still fell short. The sight relieved him, then embarrassed him for the small part of himself that had wanted to be needed more visibly.

Duan checked the steel before greeting him.

He checked the gauge next, comparing its face with the old one and asking what Su Fan had actually paid. Su Fan gave both prices, the first foolish one and the corrected one. Duan grunted at the second and said nothing about the first, which was almost generous.

Then he watched Su Fan cross the yard carrying a bundle of smaller fittings.

“Boots hold up?”

“Yes.”

“Turn.”

Su Fan turned. Duan examined the movement of his ankle before pretending that the stitching had been his chief concern.

Mother Wei accepted the library notes, read three lines and said, “At last, someone has written down the risks before the promises.”

He told her about the third circuit. She asked when it had happened, what he had been doing, whether it stayed after sleep, and whether his appetite had changed. He answered without turning the questions into an examination he had to pass.

Min took his daughter’s letter into the archive without opening it in company.

Su Fan waited outside long enough to be certain the old man had somewhere dry to sit, then left him alone. The sealed packet had arrived. Whatever followed belonged to the people whose names were on it.

Tan Wei was waiting at the river rock that evening.

His work clothes were damp at the hems. He had brought a small packet of food and was throwing crumbs to a fish that appeared to find him unreliable.

Su Fan sat beside him and told him about the third stage.

He did it before Tan Wei had to ask.

His friend listened. Then he lifted a thread of water from the current. It curled around three stones and returned without spilling.

“Third,” Tan Wei said.

“Already?”

“Don’t start.”

Su Fan smiled.

They compared what had changed. Tan Wei could work longer and move water more precisely. Su Fan could carry his strength through a turn without losing it. One improvement had a visible shape the river could display. The other was difficult to distinguish from a man standing more comfortably until he had to lift something.

Neither knew how to measure the difference fairly.

So they stopped measuring for the evening.

Su Fan told him about the city’s cable cages, the woman who had lifted a wagon and the young master who had charged nothing personally for beating him with a padded sword. Tan Wei laughed at the gauge story and asked whether the garlic-chive buns in Siltbridge were better than the ones they knew.

“No.”

“You’ve thought carefully about that?”

“Extensively.”

They ate what Tan Wei had brought. For a while the conversation concerned only food and the ridiculous price of a good brush.

Far uphill, the eighth gate’s bronze reeds caught the last sunlight.

Su Fan looked from their bright faces to the channel below. For the first time since leaving Mudgate, he noticed how little water was reaching the ninth.

chapters.title: Work for a Man Without a Sash
chapters.text:
Captain Shen Tu came to the smithy to buy nails.

He brought no escort.

That was the first thing Su Fan noticed. The second was that the captain knew exactly which nails he wanted.

“Long shank. Square head. For wet oak.”

Duan had been arguing with Ah-Du about a missing punch. The boy claimed it had moved while he was working. The smith said tools generally moved in the direction of the hand carrying them. Both stopped when Shen Tu set a strip of old timber on the bench.

A rusted nail remained in it, bent near the head. The captain pointed to the bend.

“Not these.”

Duan fetched a sample from the storage rack.

Shen Tu examined the head, then bent the nail between finger and thumb. The iron resisted. It curved smoothly without cracking.

“Good.”

“You break it, you buy it,” Duan said.

“I’ll take four hundred.”

The order was large enough to make the smith check his irritation before spending it.

He took the bent sample back, tested the surface with his thumbnail and asked what lengths the repairs required. Shen Tu gave him two measurements, both close enough that a careless customer might have called them the same. They discussed how many of each were needed. Ah-Du, who had found the missing punch in his apron, quietly put it down and fetched the order slate.

Su Fan kept his own hands on the axle he was finishing.

It was difficult to decide how much attention a man could give a captain without appearing either frightened or discourteous. Shen Tu made the problem worse by behaving as though he had simply entered a workshop whose iron he intended to buy.

While Duan counted stock, the captain looked around. His gaze paused on the six stones in the yard, the practice sword leaning behind the door and the new steel from Siltbridge.

“You travelled.”

“Yes,” Su Fan said.

“Expensive place.”

“So I learned.”

The captain smiled faintly.

“I heard about Zhu Ke. My patrol found him with a ruined knee and a very unconvincing explanation.”

Su Fan’s grip tightened on the axle. He remembered the staff crossing the frozen deck, the weight of another man trying to make the boat a place from which nobody could leave.

“Did you arrest the others?”

“Three. The rest scattered.”

“Will he stand trial?”

“He will stand with difficulty.”

Duan made a reluctant noise of amusement from the rack. Su Fan did not join him. The joke had found the part of the story that was easiest to tell afterward.

“Sun Lian reported the stolen goods and the damage,” he said.

“I have the report.”

“Will she recover anything?”

“What we recover and what belongs to her will have to agree before I can give you a useful answer.”

It was not a promise. Su Fan preferred that to one which would be forgotten the moment the captain rode away. He still disliked needing the man to pursue the people who had attacked them.

Duan returned with two bundles of nails and the figures for the remainder. Shen Tu checked the count of one bundle without apology. Then he paid half the order in advance.

The silver was sound. Su Fan watched Duan weigh it.

Ah-Du wrote the quantities on the slate, stopped, rubbed out a number and wrote it again. Shen Tu waited until the boy was satisfied before putting his mark beside the order.

“I need someone who can read a supply tally and tell bad iron from good,” he said, turning back to Su Fan. “Six weeks at the lower works. Better pay than carrying sacks.”

Duan set the scales aside. He did not look up.

“Why me?” Su Fan asked.

“You noticed a problem my clerk missed.”

“Your supplier caused it.”

“My supplier is paying to replace it.”

He said this without visible offence. That left Su Fan with the offer rather than the quarrel he had nearly prepared for it.

Six weeks of better wages would cover the smithy’s remaining roof debt. There were tools Duan still borrowed, medicines Mother Wei divided carefully between patients, clothes Su Fan had repaired enough times to begin recognizing older repairs beneath the new ones.

The work itself was not foolish. He could read a tally. He could test fittings before they disappeared into a storehouse whose doors later became difficult to open.

He could also be put somewhere useful to the captain for reasons the written description did not name.

“What access?”

“Stores and loading. No formations. No operator ledgers.”

“Then I could count bad iron without knowing where it went.”

“You could do the work you were hired for.”

There was the boundary, stated without embarrassment.

Su Fan glanced toward Duan. The smith had begun counting the second bundle, although he had counted it before setting it down. He was giving Su Fan no instruction and no excuse to borrow one.

“Would I be working under your clerk?”

“On deliveries. Your findings would be recorded. Questions beyond the appointment would go through the office.”

“And if the office disagreed?”

“Then there would be a disagreement.”

Shen Tu rested his hand on the old strip of oak.

“You think I’m offering you a way to inspect everything that troubles you. I’m offering work. The works need sound parts even when you dislike the people ordering them.”

Su Fan looked at the bent nail on the bench. An honest task could still sit inside a dishonest arrangement. It could also be an honest task that he refused because refusal felt easier to understand.

He imagined standing at a stores table while a load went through a door he was forbidden to follow. If he asked where it went, he would be reminded of this conversation. The reminder would be accurate.

“I’ll stay here,” he said.

Shen Tu nodded once.

“Then we’ll pay your master to make what we need.”

No demand for gratitude followed. The captain collected the first bundle himself, settling it under one arm with a little adjustment to keep the heads from cutting his coat.

At the door he stopped.

“The river works are not a single machine, Su Fan. Move one piece and somebody downstream learns about it. Remember that when you look for a simple fault.”

He left before Su Fan could decide whether it was advice or warning.

For several breaths the smithy seemed unusually quiet. Then Ah-Du asked whether the captain had bought the bent sample as part of the four hundred.

Duan looked at the nail.

“He can have that one. For his generosity in testing it.”

***

The order changed the day’s work.

Two small repairs had to be finished before the stock could be cut for the remaining nails. Duan sent Ah-Du to ask a customer whether a hinge could be collected later. The boy returned with an answer that included a complaint about the last delay and a request for a cheaper price.

“Tell him no,” Duan said.

“To which?”

“The interesting part.”

Su Fan put the nail order on the wall beside the ordinary repairs. It occupied less space than the money it would bring and more than he wanted it to occupy in his thoughts.

Duan set the deposit in the cash box.

“You could have taken it.”

“He wanted me where he could watch me.”

“Possibly. He also needs somebody who can count nails.”

“You trust him?”

“I trust him to want nails.”

The smith took out four silver and placed them beside the forge account. He checked a figure, made a short mark and let out a breath through his nose.

“Suspicion is useful. It isn’t payment.”

Su Fan went back to the axle. He had spent part of the journey home imagining how the new third circuit would make familiar work feel. Now the most difficult thing in the room had no weight he could lift.

“Would you have let me go?” he asked after a while.

“For six weeks?”

“Yes.”

“I’d have wanted to know who was finishing that axle.”

“And after that?”

“We would have discussed the other work.”

Su Fan looked up. Duan’s face gave him no tidy judgment.

“You’re not a tool I leave on the wall,” the smith said. “But neither is your going away something that happens only to you. We can discuss both without pretending one cancels the other.”

The words were practical enough to be inconvenient. Su Fan had wanted either permission to feel noble or confirmation that he had been sensible. Duan appeared determined to give him an account of the work still waiting.

They tested the first new nail against a piece of wet oak. Su Fan held the wood; Duan drove the nail halfway, drew it, examined the shank and set it aside for further use. The point had held its shape. The head had not folded beneath the hammer.

“That will do.”

“The works should have bought these before.”

“Yes. Now they are buying them.”

Su Fan could not make better iron by resenting the order. He cut the next piece, heated it and worked until the head sat square. His third circuit helped him carry the repeated motion without wasting quite so much force. It did not prevent a careless angle from making a bad nail.

One went into the scrap tray. He left it there instead of disguising its defect with another blow.

By noon they had more finished work and less fuel. Ah-Du fetched food. Duan counted the remaining charcoal and sent the boy out again with part of the captain’s money.

Su Fan ate beside the open door. Turning down the appointment had felt clean. The meal in his hand, the charcoal coming for the furnace and the silver beside the roof account were less interested in that feeling.

***

Bao Shun arrived carrying a small painted sign.

He had wrapped the lower edge in cloth so his good hand would not rub the fresh colour. The other arm rested against his side. The damaged fingers could help steady a light object in certain positions now, but he had learned not to ask more of them simply because he wanted the improvement to be faster.

The sign read *Mei’s Boards and Useful Things*.

“Too long?” he asked.

“Useful things is vague,” Su Fan said.

“That’s the useful part. We can change what we sell.”

Bao Mei had painted the letters in a blue that was not quite the expensive colour she had admired in Siltbridge. She had found a way to make the weaker batch work against the pale ground. The corners carried small brown boats, each one recognizably afloat rather than resting on a convenient blue stripe.

Duan examined the back.

“Who joined this?”

“I did.”

“Good.”

Bao Shun straightened a little. The praise concerned the wood, not the injury, and therefore gave him something he could accept without explaining how he was managing.

The stall was borrowed space at the edge of the market. Its owner used it on the busiest days and had agreed to let the Baos try the quieter ones. They would have to pack everything away each evening. They had argued over what counted as everything before deciding where the sign could hang.

Duan found two nails without charging.

“Not from the captain’s four hundred,” Ah-Du said.

“From the astonishing reserve with which I remain a smith.”

The boy nodded solemnly and began searching for the hammer he had just put down.

Later, Su Fan carried the sign to the market while Bao Shun brought a crate. Bao Mei waited at the stall with a cloth spread over the boards. She had already moved the display twice to see which position caught the light without throwing a shadow from the awning across the painted faces.

“Higher,” she told Su Fan when he held up the sign.

He raised it.

“Too high.”

Her father said this was an excellent beginning for a trade in useful things. They had found an immediate use for somebody with two sound arms and no authority over the price list.

Su Fan held it where she pointed.

The timber above the stall had old nail holes in it. One looked convenient. Bao Shun tested the grain beside it with a small awl and shook his head. They shifted the sign a little, used sound wood and stood back before driving the second nail.

It was crooked.

Not much. Enough that Bao Mei’s face changed when she looked from the letters to the edge of the awning.

Su Fan reached for the hammer again. Her father stopped him and loosened the first fixing instead. They adjusted the sign together, quietly, until the girl nodded.

No one had been rescued. A sign hung straight. It had taken three people longer than any of them would mention to a customer.

Bao Mei arranged the painted boards beneath it. Her father laid out repaired handles, pegs and boat hooks he could finish one-handed. Some pieces had been made before his injury and altered afterward to suit the work he could do now. He had not hidden the repaired joins. He had smoothed the parts that would meet a hand.

The business looked small beneath its new name.

It also looked real.

Their first visitor wanted to know whether a board could be repainted when the owner married and changed households. Bao Mei explained which surfaces could be stripped and what a new coat would cost. Her father began to answer at the same time, stopped, and let her finish.

The woman did not buy. She promised to return, which might mean anything. Bao Mei marked the question on a scrap so she could think about offering that work deliberately rather than wait for somebody to ask again.

A man bought two pegs and tried to bargain for a third free. Bao Shun showed him the larger set at a different price. They settled on the two. The coins made a small clear sound in the dish at the back of the stall.

Su Fan had intended to offer to buy a board immediately. He waited. Bao Mei was busy explaining why a blue boat required different work from a brown one, and the person disputing this was her father.

“The customer won’t know how long it took,” he said.

“Then I’ll tell them.”

“Will they pay for the telling?”

“They might if you stop telling them brown is just as good.”

He laughed and moved one of the brown boats into better light.

Across the square, Shen Tu was buying a paper windmill from a travelling seller.

Su Fan noticed him because the captain had dismounted and was crouching beside the tray. The seller held up a red wheel, then a yellow one. Shen Tu chose neither until he had spun each with a breath and watched whether its axle caught.

He tested the little mechanism with the same attention he had given Duan’s nails.

Then he paid, put the windmill carefully inside his coat and rode uphill.

chapters.title: The Breathing House
chapters.text:
Min had mistaken one character for another.

The difference was a short stroke worn away beneath a damaged binding. He had spent the morning holding the slip toward the window, then away from it, apparently hoping that the light would eventually become more cooperative than the ink.

When Su Fan arrived, the scholar had arranged two readings on a clean sheet. Beside them lay a scrap from an old catalogue, a note in another hand and a cup of tea with a skin forming on its surface.

“For twenty-seven years,” Min said, “I have read this as *close the house*.”

Su Fan put down the basket of food Mother Wei had sent.

“And now?”

“The older form could also mean *complete the house*.”

He placed his brush beside the second reading rather than draw the lost stroke onto the original. Su Fan was relieved to see him leave the damage alone. A confident repair to the ink might outlive the reason for making it.

“One says seal everything,” Min continued. “The other says make the structure sound.”

“Which is right?”

“I don’t know yet.”

Su Fan sat opposite him. The archive smelled of damp paper and the dust brought up by workers repairing the lane. A square of cloth had been spread beneath the slips so neither grit nor crumbs would reach them. Min moved the food to another table before Su Fan could open its wrapping.

“Read the line before it.”

Su Fan did. He read the next as well, slowly, keeping his finger away from the characters. They described breath passing through the body’s routes without escaping into uncontrolled strain. The damaged instruction came between a warning against forcing the return and a diagram whose outer line had been corrected twice.

Closing every outlet would trap the movement. Completing the routes would let it return.

“The second,” Su Fan said.

“Because it is more comforting?”

“Because I tried the first and nearly fainted.”

Min considered that.

“A useful translation note.”

He wrote it down without making the language prettier.

Su Fan watched the brush. The admission looked less impressive on paper than a claim to have discovered a higher meaning. It was also something a later reader might use to avoid spending an evening on the floor.

Min asked exactly what he had tried, how long he had continued and which sensation had persuaded him to stop. Su Fan answered as well as he could. He corrected himself once. The warning had begun before the warmth, not after; he had remembered the warmth first because it was the part he had wanted.

The scholar crossed out his own earlier note and rewrote it.

“Does that settle it?” Su Fan asked.

“No. It gives us a reason to be careful with one reading. A badly attempted sound instruction can hurt you too.”

He pushed the tea away and drew the catalogue scrap closer.

They compared other uses of the character. In one passage it described finishing a roof. In another it meant shutting a gate before winter. Neither belonged to the same work as the scripture. Min refused to let the convenient example become a verdict merely because it fitted what they hoped the damaged line would say.

Min fetched a narrow strip of paper and asked Su Fan to write his own account of the failed exercise.

“Not a fair copy of mine. Yours.”

Su Fan described the posture, the attempt to hold the return and the dizziness. He reached the place where he wanted to say how long he had persisted, then stopped with the brush against the page.

“How many breaths?” Min asked.

“I wasn’t counting.”

“Then don’t discover a number now.”

Su Fan had been about to write one that felt plausible. He put down *longer than I should have*, frowned at how little that told another person, and added what he did remember: his jaw aching, the furnace’s last heat against one side of his face, the way the room had tilted when he finally let go.

Min read it without correcting the uneven characters.

“The next trial can have a count,” he said. “This one can have an honest gap.”

They placed the strip beside the older annotation. The hands looked very different. Su Fan’s letters leaned into one another as though trying to finish before the ink ran out. The earlier reader had left broad spaces, perhaps for corrections, perhaps simply because there had been more room then.

He wondered who had written the first warning about pain. He could tell where the brush had pressed hardest. He could not tell whether the writer had been angry, frightened, or merely using a poor brush.

Min did not supply a life to fill the missing name. He weighted the loose paper, checked that it would not rub the old ink, and returned to the passage they could actually read.

The surviving book contained no easy ladder.

Its earliest sections named Pure Breath and twelve degrees of refinement. Beyond those came references to a Silent Furnace, a Sealed Reservoir and conditions whose meaning Min could not responsibly claim to understand. Some lines might be headings. Others might be comparisons. One diagram had a caption in a different hand from the surrounding instructions.

Su Fan leaned closer despite himself.

“Twelve degrees,” he said.

“In this section.”

“And then the furnace?”

“Perhaps. Or the writer uses a furnace to describe something already happening. We haven’t earned a confident answer to the damaged word in front of us. Let’s not build a kingdom on the next page.”

For the present, three circuits were enough to occupy Su Fan. They held through ordinary movements now, but a difficult load could still make him brace against his own strength. The trouble had followed him all the way from Siltbridge and had not been impressed by the fact that he could name it.

He asked about the next passage rather than the distant headings.

Min spread the slips beside the copied library notes.

“This describes returning force through the whole frame. You have been moving strength around injuries. Now you must learn where the load actually goes.”

“Like the lifting wheel.”

“Perhaps. Bodies are less tolerant of replacing a bad pin.”

Su Fan described the dock lift: the sound counterweight, the bent guide, the unequal load. Min asked him to draw it. The first drawing made the mechanism look more orderly than it had been. Su Fan added the second line they had needed, then the temporary timber, then crossed out the space where he had initially imagined standing.

“That seems a less attractive machine,” Min said.

“It was.”

“Better drawing, then.”

They worked until the food was cold. Min ate a little while Su Fan held the notes far enough from the bowls to keep grease off the paper. The old man tried to return to the slips before finishing. Su Fan put the spoon back in his hand and said Mother Wei would ask what had been eaten, not what had been inspected.

“A formidable correspondent,” Min said.

“She sends short letters.”

“The dangerous kind.”

***

Outside the Stack, workers laid fresh stone over an old drainage crack.

They had lifted three slabs from the lane. One leaned against the wall near the shutter. Each hammer blow travelled through the room’s floor and shook fine dust from a ceiling seam above a row of bound records.

Min called through the window.

The nearest worker looked up with the weary expression of a man who had already been told that his work was too loud by people who would complain if the lane remained broken.

“Two paces away from the wall,” Min said. “The stone beneath you joins the shelf footing.”

The man tested the slab with his hammer, glanced through the window at the shelves and moved. The next blows sounded less intimate.

Su Fan went outside to help shift the loose stone before it damaged the shutter. The worker accepted the help, then warned him about the open gap beneath the lane. There was water in it, darker than the daylight above could explain.

“How far does that run?” Su Fan asked.

“Far enough to make this my third repair to the same place.”

“Blocked?”

“Maybe. Or the ground moves. Ask the people who keep drawings.”

Su Fan looked back at the archive window. Min was watching with an expression that suggested he had heard.

Inside, Su Fan took out the old river map.

The channel beneath the archive ran in the same direction as the crack. A line on an old survey did not tell them whether the present water followed the original route. It gave them a place to begin asking.

Min turned the sheet to match the lane.

“You live above a drain,” Su Fan said.

“Apparently we all do. Some are merely better concealed.”

They set the map beside the view through the window. Su Fan pointed to a junction whose later copy had made the branches look joined. On the older sheet a faded gap remained between them. Min marked the uncertainty on a separate scrap rather than let either version silently defeat the other.

“Don’t tell the clerk,” he said. “He’ll charge the books for waterfront storage.”

The joke made Su Fan smile. The damp smell from the open lane did not improve.

He helped move the lowest bundles onto spare boards before leaving. Some contained records nobody had wanted to keep. Some had been kept for reasons no living clerk could explain. Water would not distinguish between them.

A bundle near the floor had begun to soften at one corner. Min untied it while Su Fan cleared a dry space. Inside were ordinary maintenance notes, written by several hands over many years. Su Fan recognized the weary pleasure of a repairman who had found a better way to fit a stubborn hinge. The writer had drawn an arrow to the troublesome part and added a complaint about whoever would neglect it next.

He showed Min.

“A man after Duan’s heart,” the scholar said.

“Duan would say he should have used better iron.”

“Then a man whose shortcomings Duan could enjoy.”

They laid the pages out to dry. Nothing on them explained the scripture. Su Fan was glad they had moved them anyway.

***

Min Yao’s reply rested beside the lamp.

Its seal had been broken. Min had placed a small painted bird on top of it, cut from the old exercise book. The bird’s wings were uneven, one made broader to cover an error in the first brushstroke.

Su Fan had carried the sealed packet so carefully that seeing it open felt like entering a room he had previously passed without looking inside. He kept his eyes on the bird rather than the lines beneath it.

“Good news?”

“She has a son. I knew that. She has now informed me he is six, rather than the four I had somehow continued imagining.”

Min lifted the paper bird and set it against the lamp’s base.

“Two years is not a difficult sum. I make more elaborate ones for people who have been dead far longer.”

“Will you visit?”

“I wrote that I would try.”

“Will you?”

The old man looked up sharply.

Su Fan almost apologized. The question had come from the memory of a box under Min Yao’s table and the letters inside it. He had not been asked to bring an argument home with the packet.

Then Min lowered his eyes.

“She asked the same question.”

For a while the hammer outside was the loudest thing in the room.

Min smoothed one edge of the letter. There was a stain on his finger, old ink worked into the skin. It left no new mark, but he checked before moving his hand away.

“I was good at keeping things,” he said. “Books. Records. A room in order. I thought people would appreciate being kept safely too.”

Su Fan looked at the shelves. He had admired how much Min could find inside that crowded room. Now he could see the effort required to leave it, and the ways that effort might become an explanation offered so often that the person hearing it stopped asking.

“Her work is good,” he said.

“I know.”

“She has customers who come back. A child who knows which pages not to touch.”

Min’s mouth moved slightly.

“She was not always certain which pages not to touch.”

“Perhaps he isn’t either.”

That drew a quiet laugh. Then the scholar coughed, turned away and waited for the fit to pass before touching the letter again.

Su Fan did not offer to write an answer for him. He put the copied diagrams together and tied them with a loose cord so the edges would not bend.

Min folded his daughter’s letter.

“Take your drawings. I have a reply to finish.”

At the door Su Fan looked back once. The old man had drawn a clean sheet toward him. He was still holding the brush above it, but the letter from Siltbridge lay open where he could read it.

***

At the smithy, Su Fan built a small wooden frame.

It had four posts, three movable braces and a weight suspended from the centre. He used offcuts Duan had agreed could be taken and a cord too short for the lifting wheel. Ah-Du watched the first assembly, offered a theory about making it taller and was invited to make his own miniature disaster from different scraps.

The frame stood on the yard’s flattest patch. Su Fan moved the weight and watched which joints tightened. He wanted to understand how one part could carry a load without taking all of it, and how a correction at one corner could create a problem at another.

At first it worked exactly as he expected.

This should have made him suspicious sooner.

Duan examined it after supper. He stood with his bowl in one hand and looked down at the four little feet.

“Your crosspiece is wrong.”

“Where?”

“Here.”

He moved the weight farther than Su Fan had moved it.

One post lifted off the ground. The frame tilted, the cord swung and Ah-Du caught the weight before it struck the stone beside his foot.

“I found the weakness,” the boy said.

“Duan found it,” Su Fan replied.

“I caught it. Different service.”

They reset the frame. Duan showed him where the crosspiece encouraged two posts to act as one stiff side instead of sharing the changing load. Su Fan loosened the joint, altered the brace and tried again. The next trial held. The one after that revealed a different limit.

He marked both positions on the ground rather than keep only the successful one.

Later, when the yard had emptied, he tested a small part of the arrangement in his stance. The comparison helped him ask a question. It did not turn his body into timber or tell him what a damaged knee would tolerate. He moved slowly enough to stop when the joint protested.

The third circuit carried through one position and caught in another. He made the movement smaller, found where the tightening began and ended the session before wanting a result became a reason to ignore it.

This would take weeks. Perhaps months.

He put the model beneath the eaves. Ah-Du’s taller version stood beside it, leaning badly and decorated with a scrap of red cloth. The boy had declared it a lookout tower rather than admit it could not hold a weight.

Su Fan left it standing.

Before sleeping, he wrote a different note beside the damaged instruction in the scripture.

*Complete, not close. Still uncertain. Test carefully.*

He left room beneath it for someone to disagree.

chapters.title: Forty-Seven Names
chapters.text:
Mother Wei counted thirty-two men at the lower gate station.

The payroll named forty-seven.

At first she assumed the missing fifteen belonged to another shift. The overseer agreed readily enough. He had found her a stool, a clean cup and a place beneath the eaves where she could examine workers without making them walk all the way to Mudgate. He seemed to hope that good arrangements would shorten the examination.

They did not.

One man had been sent with his sleeve rolled down over a swelling. Another claimed to have eaten and could not remember what. A third wanted her to sign him fit quickly because his place on the return would otherwise be given to somebody he considered unreliable.

“Then let me decide whether there are two unreliable men,” she told him.

He sat.

She worked through the morning. The river kept moving beside the station, bright and apparently tireless. Men came away from its platforms with the rhythm of the work still caught in their breathing. Some settled after rest. Others needed longer. The difference interested her more than the overseer’s assurance that the usual allowances had been observed.

When she finished the first group, she drew a line beneath the last name and checked her count.

Thirty-two.

The payroll sheet lay under a stone beside her notes. She had asked for it so she could distinguish a worker she had missed from one she had already examined. Its neat columns contained forty-seven active positions.

“The rest are on the other shift,” the overseer said.

“Bring me their change time.”

He supplied it. She remained.

The other shift produced eleven men she had not seen. One was annoyed at being examined before he had begun working. Another was grateful, though he tried to express it as a complaint about being kept from his meal. She made them wait in the shade, checked each against the list and asked them to tell her their own names rather than answer to a pointed finger.

Forty-three men in all.

Four names remained.

The overseer looked over her shoulder. His cup had long since gone cold.

“Reserve operators.”

“Where are they?”

“Not presently on site.”

“When can I examine them?”

He began explaining how the reserve system worked. Mother Wei let him finish, then asked the same question again.

This time he said he would have to enquire.
