She folded the payroll carefully. It belonged to the station, so she copied the four entries instead of taking it away. The overseer watched her brush with more attention than he had given the men coughing beside her stool.

That evening she wrote to Jiang.

Her letter did not accuse anyone of inventing workers. It gave the count, the shift times, the names she had not examined and the answer she had received when she asked where they were. She left the last line plain: a medical release could not certify the capacity of a person she had never seen.

***

Three days later, Su Fan carried copies of the examination releases to the records house.

His job was not to investigate. It was to keep the paper dry and obtain a receipt.

Mother Wei had wrapped the sheets in cloth and shown him where each packet ended. She had also given him a note for the clerk so nobody would have to rely on his account of which office had requested them.

“Dry,” she repeated as he put them in the basket.

“The sky’s clear.”

“It was clear before the last time it rained.”

He tucked the cloth beneath the basket cover.

The records house stood above the road on a low stone foundation. Inside, a clerk had placed his writing table away from a leak in the roof. The bucket catching it was empty, but its position suggested the clerk trusted the weather no more than Mother Wei did.

Two men waited ahead of Su Fan. One had brought an allowance claim without the supporting tally. The other had the tally and had lost the claim. The clerk handled both with the patience of a man who would later be blamed if he made an exception to the rule somebody else had written.

Su Fan waited until the counter was clear. He laid out Mother Wei’s packets and the accompanying note.

The clerk compared them with a station sheet. His finger moved down a column, stopped, then returned to the top.

“These four are active.”

“Wei says she hasn’t examined them.”

“They’ve drawn station allowance all summer.”

Su Fan looked at the names where the man pointed.

One belonged to a worker who had moved to his daughter’s village after a chest illness. Su Fan remembered carrying the bedding to the ferry. The man had insisted on taking a cracked washing basin because he knew how to hold it so it did not leak.

Another name belonged to someone whose funeral Auntie Lu had cooked for two winters earlier.

Su Fan read the village entries before speaking. A familiar name by itself could lead a man into an embarrassing certainty.

“Could the names repeat?”

“They could.”

“Do the villages repeat?”

The clerk looked again.

The change in his face was small. He stopped resting his weight against the counter and stood upright.

“I’ll need to check.”

Su Fan waited.

Behind him, the man with the missing claim returned to ask whether there was a blank he could copy. The clerk told him to wait outside. Then he gathered the examination releases, the station sheet and Mother Wei’s note and carried them into the back room.

The doorway remained open. Su Fan could hear a cupboard being unlocked and papers moving. He could not see which papers.

When the clerk returned, the allowance sheet had gone.

“The office will examine the discrepancy.”

“Receipt,” Su Fan said.

The man looked as though he had expected a different demand. Then he drew a clean slip toward him and wrote the packet count, the delivery date and the office mark.

Su Fan checked the count before accepting it.

He wanted to ask where the allowance sheet had gone. He wanted to ask whose hand had added the names and where the money was paid. He could also see how easily his simple errand might become a dispute about whether an apprentice had refused to leave a records counter.

He put the receipt inside the dry cloth and left.

Outside, the returning claimant asked whether the clerk had found his missing document.

“I don’t know.”

The man sighed and went back to waiting. Su Fan walked downhill carrying less paper and more questions than Mother Wei had given him.

***

She read his account twice.

He had written it as soon as he returned, including what the clerk had actually said and what he had merely noticed. The second part looked less certain once it no longer had the man’s expression to support it.

“You were meant to carry paper,” she said.

“I did.”

“And ask questions?”

“The clerk asked me first.”

She looked tired rather than angry.

“Names are not proof. People move. Records lag.”

“One died.”

“Yes. That is why we ask carefully.”

They went to the dead worker’s house that afternoon. It stood beside Bao Shun’s, with a small shelf under the eaves where bowls could dry out of the reach of passing animals. His widow recognized Mother Wei and invited them in before Su Fan had worked out how to explain the visit without making it sound like bad news.

Mother Wei asked about the letters from the gate office.

The woman fetched a packet from the bottom of a storage box. She had wrapped it against damp twice, once in cloth and once in an old cover from a rice account. Inside lay a death record, a wage slip and two letters she had never understood well enough to answer.

“May we read them?” Mother Wei asked.

“That’s why I’ve kept them.”

Su Fan moved the cup away before opening the first sheet. The letter offered continuation of the worker’s residual gate credit. It referred to a service designation, a preserved assignment and a form that had apparently been completed years earlier.

The second letter deducted a handling fee.

“Credit for what?” he asked.

The widow shook her head.

“They said he had left something useful.”

Mother Wei read the first letter herself. Her mouth tightened at one phrase, but she did not explain it before reaching the end.

“How much have they paid?”

The woman showed them three copper.

The coins were not displayed as a fortune. They were not nothing. She had put them aside beside a little list of things that would have to wait until the next market day. Su Fan could read oil and salt before he looked away.

He took care not to speak as though the money were so small that losing it would be merely a point in somebody else’s argument.

“Did they call it wages?” Mother Wei asked.

“No. I knew he wasn’t working. They said the gate still had the use of something.”

The woman asked him to read the first letter aloud. He began too quickly, using the rhythm he would have used to get through a workshop order. She stopped him at the service designation.

“What does that part say?”

He tried again in ordinary words, then admitted which phrase he did not understand. Mother Wei explained what she could and left the rest as a question to take to Jiang. The woman fetched a piece of charcoal and marked the outside of the wrapping where the unresolved question would remind her to ask again.

Su Fan read the amount and the deduction separately. She checked them against the coins, then nodded. She had never mistaken three copper for a living husband’s wage. What she had lacked was a person willing to sit long enough to distinguish the promise from its complicated wording.

“And you signed another permission?”

“I marked what they brought. They read the amount to me.”

She found the matching copy. The conditions were brief enough to fit on one side, though not written in the language people used when they wished to be easily understood. Mother Wei asked permission to copy it, and the woman agreed after asking whether she would get the original back.

“Tomorrow,” Mother Wei said. “These papers remain yours.”

At the next house, the absent worker’s brother supplied a different explanation.

A portion of his brother’s saved lineage impression remained assigned to the gate while he recovered elsewhere. He had signed permission for its continued use. The brother had a letter from the daughter’s village and a copy of the assignment, both with dates that made sense together.

“He wanted to return,” the man said. “Then he found he could sit through a morning without coughing if he stayed where she put him.”

“Is he being paid?” Mother Wei asked.

“The credit comes through the village office. He writes when it’s late.”

There was no secret in the arrangement. The brother seemed more irritated by a missed payment than by the possibility that someone at the gate might be using a dead man’s name.

The documents explained two of the entries.

They did not explain why a dead man’s impression had been listed as a living worker receiving meals.

On the way back, Su Fan slowed beside the water tap. He had expected the facts to make the accusation cleaner. Instead they required him to separate several things he had been holding together: a family’s lawful credit, the survival of a useful impression, a meal that no one could eat, and a load someone living still had to carry.

Mother Wei filled the cup she carried for the walk.

“Write down the dates again before you forget which belongs to which,” she said.

He did it on the dry side of the wall, using the receipt as a firm surface beneath his paper. Straightforward anger would have been easier to carry home.

***

Jiang came to the clinic after dark.

She arrived carrying only a writing case and a folded station schedule. Mother Wei moved a bowl of sorted herbs off the table so the papers could lie flat beneath the lamp.

Su Fan remained because he had delivered the releases and could identify which document the clerk had shown him. He tried not to turn that narrow usefulness into permission to answer every question in the room.

Jiang read the widow’s letters first. Then she read the absent worker’s agreement, the examination list and Su Fan’s account of the counter.

“Residual impressions are permitted,” she said. “They smooth the station’s response between shifts. Listing them as living operators is not.”

“Is it only stolen wages?” Mother Wei asked.

“No.”

Jiang placed the two shift counts beside the payroll. She did not need to perform the subtraction twice.

“The safety load is divided by the number of active bodies. A preserved impression can guide a route. It cannot take a man’s strain.”

Su Fan remembered the operator coughing beside the bronze reed. He had thought then of a person compensating for a faulty alignment, his breathing doing work that the brace should have made easier.

“Then the real workers carry the difference.”

“Yes.”

“Could the reserve figures have been copied into the wrong column?”

“They could have been. That would still leave the load calculation wrong. Intent does not carry it either.”

Mother Wei pointed to her release dates. Several men should have been replaced or rested. If the count already included bodies that were not there, the useful words on the releases had less room in which to become an actual change of shift.

Jiang read the dates again.

“Who approved it?” Su Fan asked.

“That is the next question.”

“Shen Tu?”

“Possibly. Possibly someone above him. Do not choose the answer because you dislike the man.”

He looked at the captain’s nail order still folded inside his own work notes. Shen Tu had paid for sound iron. He had restricted access to operator ledgers. Both facts remained facts. Neither told Su Fan which signature would appear on the calculation.

Jiang took out two clean sheets.

They made copies carefully. Mother Wei read the names aloud; Su Fan checked the dates against the originals while Jiang wrote. When a candle guttered, they stopped rather than guess at the last figure. The little pause irritated Su Fan until he remembered how much of the evening depended on people not putting a convenient figure where an inconvenient gap should remain.

One set went with Jiang. One stayed in Mother Wei’s locked medicine chest. The original records were wrapped for return to the widow.

Jiang closed her writing case.

“Do not promise what the audit will find.”

“Will the workers be safe meanwhile?” Mother Wei asked.

“I will have the actual count checked against the next assignment.”

It was a specific action, not a claim that every danger had been removed. Mother Wei nodded and wrote it beside the date.

In the morning they returned the widow’s papers.

She counted the sheets before putting them away. Su Fan was glad she did, although he knew none was missing.

“Will I lose the three copper?” she asked.

Mother Wei sat down before answering.

“We don’t yet know.”

The woman looked at the packet in her lap. She did not thank them for the uncertainty. She asked them to tell her when there was something they did know.

They promised that much.

chapters.title: The Captain's Terms
chapters.text:
Shen Tu found Su Fan beside the lifting wheel.

The fourth bucket had begun to hesitate on its way up. It still emptied into the little channel, but the binding pulled at a different angle from the others. Su Fan had marked it with chalk and was waiting for the last agreed release to finish before stopping the wheel.

The captain watched three buckets turn before speaking.

“Good work.”

“Duan made the axle. Sun Lian designed the lift. Half the town built it.”

“And you prefer not to be thanked alone.”

“Not for their work.”

Shen Tu leaned against the rail. He carried no sword today. Su Fan distrusted the absence more than he would have distrusted a visible blade, then disliked himself a little for making either arrangement evidence of the same suspicion.

The captain’s boots had mud on them. Someone at the upper road had been clearing a ditch, and one cuff bore the pale dust of fresh stone. He looked like a man who had already conducted several conversations that morning and intended to finish this one without having to conduct it again.

“The station is being audited,” he said.

“So I hear.”

“You’ve heard more than that.”

Su Fan kept one hand on the wheel’s maintenance rope.

“I carried medical papers.”

“Yes.”

The fourth bucket rose, tilted late and spilled part of its load back into the stream. Shen Tu watched the lost water without commenting.

“Four ghost meals. Four allowances. A clerk with debts, an overseer who wanted his numbers to look better, and a reserve system stretched beyond its proper use.”

“Is that what happened?”

“That is what the evidence currently supports.”

“Your clerk?”

“My office.”

The admission surprised Su Fan.

The captain noticed.

“You expected me to deny the office exists?”

“I expected you to tell me it wasn’t my concern.”

“It isn’t your authority. That is different.”

He took a folded paper from his sleeve. The outside had been kept clean, although a corner had rubbed thin against the cloth of his coat.

“Bao Shun’s widow-neighbour keeps her residual credit. The dead man’s impression will be relisted correctly. The extra safety allowance will come from the contractor’s deposit.”

Su Fan did not take the paper immediately. Shen Tu held it out until refusing to touch it would have become a gesture with no useful purpose.

He read it beside the rail.

The order named the credit separately from station wages. It instructed the office to correct the entry and preserve payment while the larger accounts were examined. The distinction Mother Wei and Jiang had made at the clinic was there, written in an official hand with a mark that another clerk would have to recognize.

It did something useful.

That was irritatingly hard to dismiss.

“Will she need to travel to claim it?”

“No new journey is required.”

“And the workers carrying the additional load?”

“The actual count is being used for the assignment. The audit has not finished.”

“Then this isn’t the whole answer.”

“I have not offered it as one.”

Su Fan read the last line again. He looked for a condition that might take the credit back if the widow failed to sign something else. The captain waited without helping him find one.

“Why bring it to me?”

“Because you’ll show it to Wei. She’ll stop making the widow fear her three copper. And perhaps you’ll learn that a corrected problem need not become a war.”

“I haven’t declared one.”

“No.”

Shen Tu looked at Su Fan’s hands.

“But you are learning to hold yourself like somebody who might.”

Su Fan became aware of the rope beneath his palm, the way his weight had settled evenly between both feet. He did not know whether changing the stance would hide anything or merely confirm that the remark had found a place to land.

He left his feet where they were.

A farmer came along the bank carrying a hoe. He saw the captain and slowed, uncertain whether he could interrupt. Su Fan told him the wheel would be stopped for a short repair after the release. The farmer asked whether the water already in the branch would be enough for his last row.

“Check it now,” Su Fan said. “I can wait a little before I stop.”

The man went on. Shen Tu watched him take the narrow path toward the fields.

“You see?” the captain said.

“What?”

“The part you alter belongs to somebody else before the water has finished leaving your hand.”

He could have been repeating his warning from the smithy. He could have been pointing out something true. Su Fan was beginning to resent how often those possibilities arrived together.

Shen Tu pushed away from the rail.

“Show her the order.”

He left Su Fan holding a useful paper and an unanswered question about his own body.

***

After the captain had gone, Su Fan checked the lifting wheel alone.

He wanted a fault he could fix without discussing anyone’s motives.

The fourth bucket supplied one. Its binding had frayed where a rough edge of the frame rubbed it on every turn. Replacing the cord without smoothing the edge would merely set the same job farther along the week.

He waited for the farmer to call from the field. Then he secured the wheel and tested that the current could not move it while his hand was between the spokes.

The rope felt ordinary now. He had held it throughout the conversation as though it might have given him something steadier to do with his uncertainty. Its actual use required attention of a different kind.

He removed the worn binding, cleaned the contact point and fitted the new length. The knot sat awkwardly on the first attempt. He undid it rather than leave a lump that would strike the frame every time the bucket rose.

A girl came down to watch. She had been sent to see whether the water was coming again and appeared to consider this an excellent reason to avoid whatever work waited at home.

“Did the captain break it?” she asked.

“No.”

“Why was he here?”

“To give me a paper.”

“Does the paper fix it?”

“Not this bit.”

She accepted the distinction and watched him finish.

When he released the wheel, the repaired bucket rose with the others and emptied cleanly. He let it make another circuit. Then another. The girl ran to report the water before he found an excuse to inspect it for a fourth time.

He stayed longer than necessary.

There was no further fault within reach. He folded the captain’s order and went to the clinic.

***

Mother Wei read it after supper.

Su Fan had delivered the paper earlier, but a patient had arrived with a cut that could not wait for a discussion about accounts. He had held the lamp, fetched clean cloth and helped move a bench before there was room to sit down and talk.

By then he had repeated the captain’s last remark to himself enough times that it had begun to sound more definite than the words actually were.

Mother Wei read the order from beginning to end.

“This helps.”

“Is it enough?”

“For the widow’s allowance? Yes. For the station? We wait for Jiang.”

“He knew about my strength.”

She set the paper down.

“What did he say?”

Su Fan repeated it exactly. She asked him to repeat the sentence before it too. He did, including his own claim not to have declared a war.

“That isn’t knowledge,” she said. “It’s attention.”

“He notices too much.”

“You’ve generally considered that a virtue.”

He looked at his bowl.

She let him finish eating. The room’s smaller tasks continued around the silence. A lid had to be replaced on a jar. A length of used cloth belonged in the washing basket rather than beside the clean pile. Mother Wei dealt with both before returning to the subject, and Su Fan had no way to make her deliberation mean that she thought the problem trivial.

“You cannot become unusual and expect every competent person to remain incurious.”

“I know.”

“Then decide what you will do when someone asks properly. Not when they’re threatening you. When they offer something sensible.”

He had no prepared answer for that.

He could imagine a guard demanding the scripture. He had imagined it often, usually at night when every sound outside the smithy seemed more purposeful than it was. He could imagine refusing, hiding the slips or making an argument about the purchase receipt.

He had spent less time imagining a person offering equipment, instruction and money in exchange for questions that were not wholly unreasonable.

“What would you say?” he asked.

“To which offer?”

He almost described one in which all the important terms favoured the answer he wanted. Instead he said that he did not yet know.

“Then read it when it comes.”

“And if the terms are good?”

“Good for what you want, or good enough that you feel obliged to want it?”

She did not wait for him to answer. A man at the door needed to collect medicine for his father. Mother Wei rose, checked the name and explained the label in the same patient voice she used when she expected to be listened to carefully.

Su Fan moved the bowls off the table.

He did not put the scripture away that night feeling either safer or more threatened. He checked its wrapping and the receipt, then sat with the uncomfortable possibility that the next difficult choice might arrive politely.

***

The sensible offer arrived two days later.

A station clerk brought an invitation to an auxiliary assessment. Skilled labourers with unregistered cultivation could be certified for technical work without joining the sect.

The wage was twice Duan’s apprentice rate.

The clerk had come at an inconvenient time. A wagon fitting had to be finished before the driver returned, and Ah-Du had heated the wrong piece. Duan sent the boy to correct it, told the visitor where to wait and gave Su Fan the paper without offering an opinion.

“I can return for the answer,” the clerk said.

Su Fan thanked him and read.

The first part described work he recognized. Handling loads, identifying materials, assisting repair crews under instruction. The second described an assessment of practical ability. The third contained the obligations attached to certification.

There was a confidentiality clause.

There was also a requirement to disclose all training sources.

He read that line twice, then the lines around it. The requirement was not hidden in an obscure appendix. It did not pretend to ask only where he had learned to hold a hammer.

He took the invitation outside while Duan finished the wagon fitting. In the yard, the six stones lay where he had left them after practice. Ah-Du’s little red-topped model leaned beneath the eaves. The world around the paper was ordinary enough to make the doubled wage seem especially large.

He could imagine accepting.

Better food for the clinic. Tools Duan would not need to borrow. An assessment made by somebody who possessed more than an old weight, a damaged diagram and a guess about what warmth meant. Access to people who might help him understand what he was doing before he hurt himself badly enough to discover a limit by losing it.

He could also imagine the bamboo slips locked in a cabinet he could not open.

The invitation did not say that would happen. He refused to make the paper guilty of a sentence it did not contain. It did say he would have to disclose the source, and he did not know what would follow disclosure once the method was inside an office that had categories for everything except the part that mattered to him.

He asked the clerk whether a purchased text counted as a training source.

“Yes.”

“Even without a named founder?”

“Especially if its application is unassessed.”

“Would I be allowed to read the full conditions before the assessment?”

“They’re attached.”

The clerk showed him the second sheet. Su Fan read that too.

“Who would receive the text?” Su Fan asked.

“The assessor would record the source.”

“A description, or the book itself?”

“That depends on what has to be assessed.”

“Would I keep my own copy?”

The clerk hesitated. He looked down at the conditions as though checking whether the answer had been added since he last read them.

“I’m not the assessor. I shouldn’t promise that for him.”

The uncertainty was better than an invented reassurance. It did not make Su Fan more willing to put the only surviving copy he owned into the man’s case.

The clerk drew the unsigned form closer, then stopped short of taking it.

“You could attend and ask before beginning the assessment.”

“Would attending commit me?”

“Not by itself.”

Su Fan read the relevant line again. It agreed with him. The invitation was not a snare that closed the moment his foot crossed a threshold. He had wanted to find one clear defect large enough to carry the refusal for him. Instead he found a process whose next steps would expose him to questions he was not ready to answer.

He set the two sheets side by side.

The clerk waited without tapping his brush or reminding him of the wage. A fly settled near the inkstone. He moved the cover over it before the insect could become part of somebody’s name.

“Do many people take this route?” Su Fan asked.

“Enough to keep me carrying forms. Some want the work. Some want the certificate so other employers stop asking the same questions. Some decide the disclosure costs more than the wage.”

“And you record that?”

“I record the answer they give me.”

Su Fan looked at the man’s ink-stained cuff. He had made a living, so far, out of being useful to people who needed something repaired. It was easy to imagine every other kind of employment as an extension of that simple transaction. Here the work also asked for knowledge he did not know how to surrender in parts.

He could not settle that merely by proving the clerk civil.

Duan came into the yard carrying the repaired fitting. He saw the sheets spread on the bench and paused.

“Questions?”

“Several.”

“Ask them.”

“I have.”

“Then read the answers.”

The smith went back inside. Su Fan found himself wishing, unfairly, that one of the sensible adults in his life would order him to refuse so he could stop having to decide what he was keeping and what he was giving up.

He returned the paper unsigned.

The clerk accepted it without argument.

“May I record a reason?”

Su Fan could say he was needed at the smithy. That was true in a limited sense. He could say he had no useful cultivation, which would be a lie he had already outgrown even if other people had not noticed.

“I’m not ready to disclose the source.”

The clerk wrote exactly that.

He read the sentence back before closing the file. Su Fan confirmed it.

There was no final warning, no dramatic promise that the invitation would never be repeated. The man put the papers into his case and walked away carrying the refusal.

Su Fan watched until he reached the road. For once he had not disguised his answer as something smaller. It still left him with the next morning’s work and a method he did not fully understand.

chapters.title: The Truth Does Not Open a Gate
chapters.text:
Jiang’s audit found more than four false entries.

It found eighteen months of substitutions, deferred repairs, borrowed shifts and approvals signed against estimates nobody had checked on site.

Some were theft. Some were shortcuts. Several were decisions that had looked reasonable when the previous five decisions were accepted as facts.

Together they made the lower works unsafe.

Su Fan expected closure.

Jiang brought a map instead.

They spread it across the schoolroom floor because no table in Mudgate was large enough. The children had been sent outside with their slates. Two remained at the window, hoping that adults kneeling around a map might prove more interesting than the lesson they had escaped.

Jiang set a weight on each corner. Sun Lian removed her boots before stepping onto the clean edge. Duan stayed on the bare boards and leaned forward with one hand braced on a desk.

“The high lake is here,” Jiang said. “The upper channels feed these terraces. The eighth gate regulates the pressure reaching the ninth. Close the eighth abruptly and water backs into the east settlements. Open it fully and your lower fields disappear.”

She moved a wooden marker along the route. Su Fan followed it past names he knew only from delivery lists. Each name occupied a little rectangle on the map, so orderly that it was easy to forget houses stood there.

“Reduce the lake,” Sun Lian said.

“Through what?”

“The western overflow.”

Jiang looked toward the old channel on the copied survey.

“Blocked in three places. Built over in two. One outlet now lies above the current riverbed because the channel shifted a century ago.”

“Then clear it.”

“With what labour, while maintaining the existing gates?”

The question was not rhetorical. Jiang had brought figures.

Duan read the material estimates. Sun Lian checked the distances against the older map. Su Fan compared the flow marks with the little he had seen upriver, trying not to make his few visits carry more authority than they possessed.

The work was possible.

Not quickly.

One obstruction could be cleared with ordinary crews if a route for the spoil was prepared. Another required support before anyone went beneath it. The built-over sections were not empty marks waiting for an energetic man to erase them. People stored goods there. One wall carried the edge of another property. Removing it would produce a second problem before it produced a channel.

Su Fan asked whether the most dangerous work could be postponed while they opened the easiest section.

“It would give the water somewhere to begin going,” Jiang said. “Not somewhere safe to finish.”

He looked at the marker in her hand.

“Why wasn’t it done before?” the widow asked from the doorway.

Jiang looked up.

“Because the old gates kept working, and the money went elsewhere.”

The woman nodded as though the answer was familiar enough to be worse than a lie.

She came into the room and pointed to the field below her own. It was too small to have a name on the map. She described it by the fence, the pear stump and the place where water first crossed the road in a bad season.

Jiang listened and added a note.

The clean map became less clean. By the end of the evening it held local paths, doubtful levels and the names of people who would need to be asked before a line on paper could become a trench through their work.

***

They met for four evenings.

On the second, the discussion nearly ended over a cart.

The repair crews needed it to move timber. The owner needed it to carry his harvest. Someone suggested that saving the gate mattered more than a load of vegetables, and the owner asked which family would eat the importance after his crop spoiled.

Sun Lian made them set down the hours instead of the accusations. The cart could carry one load early, return for the field work and be used again after the market journey. That left a gap in the repair schedule. The gap had to be filled with another arrangement, not hidden beneath a speech about everyone making sacrifices.

Duan crossed out a delivery time and wrote a later one.

Su Fan offered to carry a smaller load by hand. Jiang asked how much, over which distance, and whether doing it would prevent him from completing the fittings on the list. He gave a less impressive answer after calculating it.

They used that answer.

On the third evening, they discussed the evacuation marks.

People had tolerated figures about the high lake while the figures remained far uphill. A painted line beside a home suggested that somebody had stood there and imagined it underwater.

The suggestion made them angry.

A man said the mark would frighten buyers away from his house. A woman asked whether it meant the office had already decided to abandon the lower street. Another wanted to know who would carry her mother to the quarry road if the warning came after dark.

Mother Wei wrote that last question down.

The marks did not solve it. They made it harder to avoid.

The woman’s mother could walk to the washing place on a good morning. The quarry road was another matter. Someone suggested a cart, and the cart owner asked how it would reach that lane when three other households were trying to leave through it.

They turned the map to look at the back path instead. It was narrower, but joined the upper road without passing the low bridge. Two neighbours agreed to walk it with the woman in daylight and see what could actually be carried through. Mother Wei wrote the arrangement beside the name, leaving space for the answer rather than recording it as a solved problem.

Su Fan had drawn that path too thin on the first copy. It had looked unimportant because no goods were normally delivered along it. He widened the line and marked the turn where a person carrying another person might miss the way in rain.

The woman bent over his shoulder to check it. She knew a stone step that did not appear on either survey. He put that in too.

By the fourth evening the town had a repair schedule, a ration schedule, a list of workers needed at the lower gate and routes marked toward higher ground. None of the lists pleased everyone. Several people who had argued hardest were also among the first to offer tools when the choices became specific enough to grasp.

Su Fan helped copy the routes in larger characters. His hand cramped before he finished. He kept wanting to add an assurance beside the marks, something that would make them less frightening without making them less visible.

Jiang told him to keep the instructions readable.

The following morning, Auntie Lu fed the painters before allowing them to continue past her stall.

“You’ll do crooked work hungry,” she said. “Then I’ll have a crooked flood to look at.”

She made them paint the highest mark on the wall opposite, where she could glare at it all day.

Children gathered to watch. One tried to stretch his hand as high as the brush. His mother pulled him back sharply, then apologized to the painter as though the man had chosen the height personally.

Su Fan carried a pot of pigment to the next corner. Bao Mei checked the first marks for visibility from the road. She suggested a darker border where pale plaster swallowed the colour. Nobody asked whether a girl her age should be giving instructions when the improvement was so easy to see.

At a doorway, an old woman refused the first proposed position because her washing would cover it. The painter looked irritated until she showed him. They moved the mark.

By noon the route could be followed from the lower street without anyone needing to remember a speech given in a crowded schoolroom.

It was useful work. Su Fan still hated seeing the line beside Mother Wei’s lane.

***

He helped measure the old overflow entrance with Sun Lian.

It lay below the archive quarter, behind a sealed stone door. Water seeped from the bottom and ran through weeds growing between the paving stones. The ironwork was older than Duan’s earliest tools. Several parts had been repaired over one another, each craftsman apparently hoping the next would appreciate how little space he had been given.

Sun Lian set down the measuring pole and listened with one hand near the stone.

“There’s space behind it.”

“How much?”

“Enough to sound expensive.”

They began with the outside. The door’s width. The level of the seep. The condition of the visible supports. Su Fan cleared a little dirt from an iron eye, stopped when he saw how the rust had joined it to the surrounding fitting, and left it alone.

A porter from the archive watched from the steps.

“Are you opening it?”

“No,” Sun Lian said.

“Good. My cart is above it.”

“Then don’t leave the cart there if we ever do.”

The man considered this and moved it before they had finished measuring. Su Fan could not blame him.

Jiang had approved a survey, not an opening. The difference mattered. Nobody knew how much water stood beyond the old door or what support the stone had been borrowing from the ground around it.

The tempting thing was to test the iron with strength and call the movement information. Su Fan kept his hands on the measuring line instead. A door giving way would answer several questions at once, and perhaps leave no one in a position to write the answers down.

They sketched the visible arrangement. Sun Lian corrected the angle of a support on his drawing. He measured again rather than defend the first line.

Min came down while they worked. He looked at the door, then up at the archive wall. He had brought an older reference copied from a maintenance list, not a claim that the old books made the present passage safe.

“Does it help?” he asked.

“It gives us another thing to check,” Sun Lian said.

He accepted that more readily than Su Fan would have done a season earlier.

They left the door sealed. The seep continued beneath it. On the steps, Su Fan could see the fresh evacuation mark farther down the street, bright against a wall whose owner had washed it only the week before.

***

Shen Tu’s office arrested the store clerk.

The overseer was reassigned pending inquiry. Two contractors lost their deposits. A third appealed through a family patron and continued delivering under supervision.

Mudgate argued over whether this counted as justice.

Bao Shun said it counted as rice if the compensation continued. He was standing behind the borrowed stall when he said it, holding a price slip down with a small repaired weight. His daughter had sold another board. The money from that sale and the money due for his injury did different jobs in the same household.

The widow said justice ought to count as more than rice.

Both were describing something real. The argument grew less useful when each began explaining the other’s need as though it were an error.

Auntie Lu interrupted to ask whether either intended to buy supper. They did. For a while the bowls required enough attention to stop the discussion from consuming its own participants.

Su Fan found the arrested clerk being led past the quarry road that afternoon.

The man had ink on his cuffs and a bruise beneath one eye. His hands were bound in front of him. A guard carried a small packet of belongings that seemed too ordinary for the amount of trouble surrounding it.

The clerk recognized Su Fan.

“My mother needed medicine,” he said.

The guard pulled him onward.

Su Fan stood aside to let them pass. He had expected, perhaps, a denial, an accusation, something that would allow him to decide which expression to wear. The sentence offered him another person whose needs were not visible from the road.

He had no way to know whether the explanation was true, sufficient or merely practised. He disliked that those were separate questions.

At the clinic he asked Mother Wei whether an old woman named Chen lived in the upper labour rows.

She did.

Mother Wei asked why he was enquiring. He told her what the clerk had said and no more. She checked what she knew about the woman’s treatment, took a packet from the shelf and considered whether a visit was needed as well.

“Does he owe for it?” Su Fan asked.

“That is a different account.”

They sent medicine through a neighbour, without a note. The neighbour agreed to tell Mother Wei if the woman could not manage the instructions or had grown worse.

Su Fan helped wrap the packet. He did not ask the woman to be grateful for an investigation that might remove the person she depended on. He did not take the medicine to the guards as evidence that the clerk’s explanation had become an excuse.

The evidence against her son remained where Jiang had put it.

When the neighbour left, Mother Wei returned to the next patient. Su Fan washed the cups. There was no clean feeling waiting at the end of the errand, but an old woman would receive what she needed that afternoon.

***

That evening he returned to the sealed overflow.

Rain had begun in the uplands. Down in Mudgate the air was merely heavy, but the water beneath the stone door had changed. The thin seep spread across a wider patch of paving before finding the drain.

He crouched to compare it with the mark they had made earlier. The difference was small enough that an impatient man could dismiss it and clear enough that he had to write it down.

He put his palm against the old iron.

A faint vibration reached his skin.

It was not a voice, a summons or an answer from the scripture. It was movement behind a door that had been sealed longer than he had been alive.

For weeks he had wanted the true account brought into daylight. Now the account lay on Jiang’s table, corrected and witnessed. People had lost offices, deposits and the freedom to go home at the end of the day. Other people had kept a small payment that belonged to them.

The water behind the door had not read any of it.

He remained there listening until Sun Lian arrived with a measuring pole and two small wedges for marking positions on the outside.

“Move,” she said. “I need the bottom mark.”

He moved and held the lantern.

They checked the old measurement first. Sun Lian made him read it aloud before taking the new one, so neither would unconsciously persuade a figure to agree with the other. The seep had risen. Not dramatically. Enough to matter beside tomorrow’s reading.

A drop struck the back of Su Fan’s neck. Another darkened the stone near his boot.

“Rain’s reached us,” he said.

“Then keep the paper covered.”

He folded his coat over the board and held it steady while she wrote.

Below them, people were taking washing inside and covering market goods. Someone called a child home before the path became slippery. The ordinary evening continued around the first light rain.

Sun Lian checked the pole once more. Su Fan lowered the lantern to give her a clearer view, and they began the next useful thing.

chapters.title: The Other Letter
chapters.text:
Master Han gave Tan Wei the complete bond file because Tan Wei asked for it.

There was nothing secret about the request. Han had told every recruit to read the papers. Most had nodded and trusted him instead.

Tan Wei had done both. He had read the first sheet, asked the questions that seemed important at the time and believed the teacher’s answers. Since then, new copies had been added behind the original application: assignment changes, training notes, receipts for deductions he had noticed and others he had accepted as part of being paid.

He wanted to see them in order.

The lower station had no timber to unload that wet afternoon. A delayed cart had left the labourers waiting under the store roof, where one man slept against a sack and another repaired a split in his sandal. Tan Wei asked Han whether he could use the time to look at his file.

“Of course.”

The teacher took it from a cupboard, checked the name on the cover and gave it to him.

“Keep it dry. Bring it back before the office closes.”

There was no hesitation to warn him that a difficult thing lay inside. That made the discovery worse later, though he could not have explained why at first.

He sat beside the window in the small records room. Rain blurred the view of the landing. The water below it kept moving while every sensible person nearby waited for something else to arrive.

The earliest pages were familiar. His name, his village, his eligibility. He remembered standing at the recruitment awning and asking what a man without six silver could do. He remembered how carefully he had held the answer on the walk home, trying not to let hope make him foolish before there was anything solid to hope about.

The delay note was clipped behind his first application.

He knew Su Fan’s handwriting.

The questions came first: what happened if a candidate failed to qualify, what remained if he became ill, how long an emergency extension could last. Those were the things Tan Wei had asked his friend to help him understand.

Then came the request.

*Please hold Tan Wei’s application for clarification before the registration is finalized.*

Below it, a clerk had written: *Held at interested party’s request. Candidate transferred to later intake.*

Tan Wei stared at the words until the room grew noisy around them again.

Rain on the roof. Someone moving a chair in the next room. The scrape of a box being pulled across the floor.

He had missed three weeks of wages.

More importantly, he had spent three weeks believing the office had found something wrong with him.

He remembered explaining the red delay mark to Su Fan. He had tried to make it sound like time he could use, an opportunity to earn a little more before going uphill. His friend had listened. He had offered no explanation that would have changed the shape of those three weeks.

Tan Wei turned back to the first page and checked the date. Then he checked the clerk’s entry. There was no complicated gap in the order of events, no second man with the same name who might have made the request for a different reason.

He could picture the brush moving. The careful pressure at the beginning of Su Fan’s words. The small correction squeezed above a line instead of wasting a whole sheet. They had sat together often enough for even the mistakes to be familiar.

He closed the file, then opened it again.

For a moment he wanted to take the page to Han and ask the teacher what it meant. The request was clear. What he wanted was someone to make it mean less.

He put the papers back in their order.

Before leaving, he told Han he needed to show one of the attached letters to its writer. The teacher looked at his face, then at the file.

“Do you want me to keep a copy here?”

Tan Wei considered it.

“Yes.”

They made one. Han did not ask questions Tan Wei had not invited. He gave him a dry wrapping for the file and told him when the records room would close the following day.

The walk to Mudgate took longer in the rain. Tan Wei could have hurried. He found that he did not want to arrive with breathlessness giving him another feeling to manage.

***

Su Fan was finishing a hinge when Tan Wei entered the smithy.

He looked up, smiled, and stopped smiling when he saw the paper.

Ah-Du noticed both faces. He put the bowl he was carrying on a shelf, took a small basket as though he had suddenly remembered an errand and went outside without being told.

Water ran from Tan Wei’s sleeve onto the floor. Su Fan reached for the dry cloth beside the cooling trough, then stopped when his friend moved the file away from his hand.

“For your sleeve,” he said.

Tan Wei looked at the cloth as though he had not noticed the rain coming in with him.

“Put it there.”

Su Fan laid it on a clear patch of bench. His friend wiped the outside of the wrapping himself, making certain the papers remained dry. The small task took several breaths. Su Fan knew which letter he was protecting now. He could not find a useful question that would postpone it without becoming another thing he would have to explain.

The stool was under the worktable. He began to pull it out.

“I’m not staying,” Tan Wei said.

Su Fan left the stool where it was. His hand remained on its back for a moment after he had stopped moving it.

“You asked them to stop my application.”

“I asked them to clarify the clause.”

“Read the line.”

Su Fan looked at it.

He did not need to read. He remembered writing the questions, feeling more useful as each uncertainty became a request an office might answer. He remembered the last sentence and the way changing *before registration* to *before the registration is finalized* had made the interference look smaller to the person holding the brush.

“I should have told you.”

“Before or after?”

“Before.”

Tan Wei put the paper on the bench. He avoided the patch of oil without looking at it. He knew the workshop well enough to protect the letter while being angry at the man who had written it.

“Why didn’t you?”

“The clause had no limit. I thought they might bind you through the whole season. I thought you were agreeing before you understood.”

“So you agreed for me that I shouldn’t.”

Su Fan could hear how bad it sounded.

He also remembered the genuine fear that had made the sentence seem necessary. Bao Shun’s injured arm. The foreman counting the losses. Tan Wei’s eagerness to accept a place that might cost more than the clerk had said aloud.

Both remained true: he had been afraid for his friend, and he had asked an office to interfere with his friend’s choice without telling him.

Neither truth supplied a better answer.

“I was trying to get you a safer contract.”

“I asked you to read it.”

“I know.”

“I didn’t ask you to stop it.”

“I know.”

“Then stop saying that as though knowing now is the thing I needed.”

Su Fan went quiet.

Rain ran from the repaired roof into Ah-Du’s old bucket. The bucket had finally become useful. Each drop sounded distinct in the pause between them.

Tan Wei looked around the smithy, at the stones and diagrams, the private work that had only recently been made visible to him.

“You had a path,” he said. “All that time. You were worried about mine while keeping yours to yourself.”

“They aren’t the same.”

“No. Yours was yours to choose.”

Su Fan took the rebuke without answering.

He wanted to tell Tan Wei that the first circuit had not been certain when the letter was written. He wanted to distinguish a frightened experiment from the settled path his friend now imagined. The distinction was real. It did nothing to change who had been allowed to make the frightened choice.

Tan Wei touched the clerk’s entry with one finger.

“I thought they’d looked again and decided I wasn’t worth the place.”

“They hadn’t.”

“I know that now.”

Su Fan looked at the words beneath his own. He had not seen the clerk’s note before. For months he had imagined the office holding a question while it worked out an answer. The line on the page showed another consequence: a person moved to a later intake, an explanation left for him to invent.

“When I told you about the delay,” Tan Wei said, “did you think I’d work it out?”

“No.”

“Did you think it no longer mattered because I was still getting in?”

Su Fan did not answer quickly enough to pretend otherwise.

Tan Wei drew back his hand.

“I kept wondering what I’d done wrong.”

The forge had cooled while they spoke. Su Fan could see the hinge losing its last warmth on the bench. A simple object waiting to be finished by hands that had suddenly become useless for the work that mattered.

“I’ll repay the lost wages,” he said.

Tan Wei’s face changed.

For a terrible instant Su Fan thought he might strike him.

Instead he laughed once.

“You think that’s the part I came here for?”

“No.”

“But it’s the part you can fix.”

Su Fan looked at his hands.

He had spent most of his life repairing things. A hinge either moved or did not. A sound pin held its load. If the price of damage could be counted, there was a place to begin and some chance of knowing when the work was done.

Here the price was not accepting his money.

He put both hands flat on the bench so he would stop trying to find something to do with them.

“I’m sorry.”

Tan Wei stood very still.

“I believe you.”

The words did not sound like forgiveness.

Su Fan waited. He had been quick to supply the next sentence in other difficult conversations. He could feel several arriving now: an explanation, a promise, a question that might make Tan Wei tell him what action would settle the hurt.

His friend had come to say what had happened to him. Su Fan had already made enough decisions about that without being asked.

Tan Wei took the file back.

“For now, don’t write to anybody about me. Don’t ask favours. Don’t make arrangements. Nothing.”

“All right.”

“And don’t make me feel cruel for wanting that.”

Su Fan shook his head.

Tan Wei checked the dry wrapping, folded it over the papers and tucked the file inside his coat. The care with which he protected it felt worse than if he had thrown it down. It belonged to his life. He was taking it away with him.

At the door he paused only long enough to see where the water ran off the eaves.

Then he stepped into the rain.

***

Ah-Du returned after a while with the basket still empty.

He looked at the bench, the cooled hinge and Su Fan’s face. He did not ask what had happened.

“Duan said the fitting should be finished before evening.”

“I’m finishing it.”

The boy nodded and went to the bellows. For once he worked without attempting to improve the mood through an opinion about something unrelated.

Su Fan heated the hinge, corrected the alignment and let it cool. The familiar steps should have helped. Instead his attention kept returning to the clerk’s line beneath his own letter.

He filed one edge too thin.

He saw the mistake before testing the hinge. For a moment he considered whether it could be concealed inside the joint. It would move correctly now. It might last. A customer might never know which small failure had begun in a room after a friend left it.

He put it in the scrap pile.

Ah-Du glanced at it and said nothing.

Su Fan started another piece. This one he measured twice, not because twice was always better but because the first measurement had barely reached his attention. He finished the rough work and left the final fitting for Duan.

The smith returned after sunset.

He inspected the scrap hinge, then the unfinished replacement.

“Expensive evening?”

“Yes.”

Duan sat on the anvil block.

Su Fan told him what had happened. He did not make the extension clause sound more dangerous than it had been. He did not make his letter sound gentler. When he came to the offer to repay the wages, he repeated that too, though he would have preferred to stop the account before it.

Duan rubbed his beard.

“Well.”

“That is all?”

“What else do you need from me?”

Su Fan had hoped for a judgment he could follow. An instruction. Even anger would have given the room a direction.

“I don’t know.”

“Then don’t manufacture a task just because you understand tasks.”

The smith stood and checked the replacement hinge without taking up a tool.

“Leave it. You aren’t making it better tonight.”

Su Fan put down the file.

He washed the grit from his hands. The water in the basin darkened. His skin bore small marks from the day’s work, none large enough to explain why he felt as though something had been taken apart and left where he could not reach it.

He almost asked Duan to speak to Tan Wei.

The request formed so naturally that he stopped with the cloth half lifted to his wrist.

Don’t ask favours. Don’t make arrangements.

He dried his hands instead.

***

The rain had eased to a steady fine mist when he left the smithy.

People were closing shutters along the lane. A cart stood with one wheel beneath a cloth, the owner having run out of covering before he ran out of things that needed to stay dry. Auntie Lu had drawn her soup stall closer to the wall. Steam rose under the awning and drifted into the rain.

She called that there was food if he wanted it.

He nodded, then stopped to buy a bowl rather than make her repeat the offer. Hunger had survived the afternoon. He ate standing beneath the edge of the awning while she argued with a customer about whether a larger bowl entitled him to more meat.

Nobody there knew what sentence he had written months ago.

The fact did not comfort him as much as he had expected.

On the upper path he could see the river rock through a gap in the trees. Tan Wei sat alone beneath a broad leaf shelter. He had arranged it badly against the drizzle. Water fell from one edge onto his sleeve, but he did not move.

Su Fan stopped on the road.

He could have gone down. He knew where to step without slipping. He knew the arguments, the apologies, the exact memory that might make his friend laugh despite himself. There was a place beside Tan Wei that had been his for years, and the familiarity of it made taking it seem almost natural.

Tan Wei had asked for nothing.

Su Fan stood until he was certain his friend had not turned to call him. Then he continued along the road.

He went home.

chapters.title: A Good Teacher
chapters.text:
Han did not ask Tan Wei what had happened in Mudgate.

He moved him to a different training pair and gave him work requiring concentration. Tan Wei resented the kindness until the work absorbed him.

The new exercise involved two cups and a length of sloping board. Water had to pass from the first cup to the second without touching the wood. The inherited movement supplied a route. The pupil supplied judgment about how much force to use.

Tan Wei emptied the first cup too quickly.

The second overflowed.

Qiu Lan, seated opposite, caught the spill in a basin.

“You’re trying to drown something small,” she said.

“Possibly you.”

“Then I admire the ambition.”

She set the cups back. The first had a chip in its rim that made pouring difficult even without cultivation. Han had selected it deliberately. Real work seldom waited until every vessel agreed to behave like the clean examples in a training room.

Tan Wei drew the water out again. This time he slowed the movement so much that the thread sagged onto the board. It broke halfway down the slope and ran along the grain.

“Now you’re watering it,” Qiu Lan said. “Perhaps the board will grow into a boat.”

He looked at her sharply. She raised both hands.

“My turn.”

Her first attempt reached the second cup, though not all at once. The water arrived in a series of little surges, each one forcing her to adjust the next. She frowned, tried to smooth the movement and spilled nearly as much as he had.

Tan Wei caught it in the basin. The ordinary fairness of the task gave him something to do with his hands besides hold them still around anger.

They exchanged places after every third attempt. The sloping board looked different from the other side. Tan Wei discovered that he had been blaming the first cup for a hesitation he brought with him wherever he sat.

Han passed behind them, watched one attempt and told him to use less water.

“I can move more than this.”

“Yes. We’ve seen it on the floor.”

The smaller amount was easier to control and more irritating to fail with. Tan Wei had no grand burst of strength in which to lose the error. He had to feel when the inherited movement wanted to continue after the second cup already held enough.

The return was good at finishing a familiar action. His attention had to remain on the cup in front of him rather than the satisfying completeness of the action itself.

Qiu Lan stopped the next attempt before he began it.

“The basin.”

“It isn’t full.”

“It will be if you repeat that last performance. Empty it.”

He looked down. She had been catching his mistakes while making her own corrections, moving the vessel closer each time the spill changed direction. He had treated the basin as part of the furniture, something that simply existed beneath his failure.

He carried it out and returned with dry hands.

“Sorry.”

“Apologize with better aim. I still have the stores count after this.”

He asked whether she wanted to finish early.

“I want to finish knowing why the last turn worked. Those aren’t always the same thing.”

They made the next attempts smaller. Qiu Lan asked him to call out when the far cup reached its mark rather than wait for her to look away from the moving thread. He did. When they exchanged places, she gave him the same warning. It was irritating to be told to stop a breath before he felt ready. It also kept the amount in the second cup from being decided by how satisfying the movement felt in his wrist.

They had found a way to give each other information soon enough to use it. Qiu Lan’s sleeve stayed dry for three attempts in a row, which she considered evidence worth recording before anyone claimed the improvement was accidental.

After a while the water moved cleanly.

He did it again. Qiu Lan checked beneath the board and announced, with great ceremony, that the floor had survived.

They carried the basin outside and emptied it where the station’s kitchen garden could use it. Tan Wei’s shoulders had loosened without his having decided to forgive anyone. He was glad of that. He did not want every improvement in his afternoon to become a verdict about Su Fan.

***

Afterward Han asked him to stay.

The teacher had set three contracts on the table. One was for ordinary labour. One for a temporary operating lease. The third was the permanent bond that allowed deeper training in the Ferryman’s Return.

Tan Wei stopped at the doorway.

“You don’t choose today,” Han said.

“Why show me?”

“So today isn’t the first time you’ve seen them when someone needs your signature.”

He sat.

Rainwater still dripped from the eaves. Han moved a bowl beneath the most persistent leak, then returned to the papers. His bad leg took time to settle under the stool. Tan Wei waited without offering a hand the teacher had not asked for.

They began with the ordinary labour agreement.

It paid less. Its work was less specialized, and leaving it did not require the careful withdrawal of a cultivated branch. Han pointed to the notice terms rather than call it freedom without conditions. A worker could still owe for goods advanced or fail to be paid promptly. An ordinary contract did not make every person handling it honest.

The temporary lease offered more training and restricted travel during assigned shifts. Its obligations followed the work. Tan Wei recognized several clauses from his own file, including the one whose uncertainty had led Su Fan to write the letter.

He read that part twice. Han waited.

“What happens when an emergency is declared?” Tan Wei asked.

“We ask who declared it, which duty it extends and when the extension is reviewed. You keep the answer.”

“And when nobody answers?”

“Then you know you have an unanswered condition. Don’t let someone call that the same thing as reassurance.”

The third agreement lay nearest the lamp.

A permanent bond joined the preserved branch more deeply to the body. It could support higher stages and steadier access to the Ferryman’s Return. It also required a careful withdrawal if the carrier later left the path.

“Careful,” Tan Wei repeated.

“Painful in some cases. Dangerous in a few. We keep records, not guarantees.”

Han showed him where the withdrawal process was acknowledged and where the document referred to supervised practice rather than describe it. Tan Wei asked to see the records before making any later choice. The teacher said that was a sensible request and named the office that kept the permitted copies.

He did not make one contract sound virtuous and the others foolish. Each gave something. Each asked for something. The difficulty was deciding which cost a person could live with before the benefit made that cost easier to ignore.

“Would you sign it again?” Tan Wei asked.

Han looked at his bad leg.

“Yes.”

“Even with that?”

“That came from a falling beam. The line kept it attached.”

Tan Wei had assumed otherwise.

Han saw that and smiled without pleasure.

“People prefer an injury to agree with their opinions.”

Tan Wei looked down at the agreement. He had wanted the teacher’s body to give him a simple warning or a simple permission. It had a history of its own.

“Were you certain the first time?”

“No.”

“Then how did you choose?”

“I knew what work I wanted to do. I asked what I could ask. I believed some answers that deserved it and perhaps some that didn’t. Then I lived long enough to learn which questions I had missed.”

He moved the three contracts into a row.

“You have more time to read these than I had. Use it. That doesn’t mean you can read away every risk.”

Tan Wei made notes on a separate sheet. He did not sign any of the contracts.

When he stood to leave, Han asked whether he wanted a copy to keep by his bed or preferred to use the records room. Tan Wei chose the copy. The teacher marked the sample so it could not be mistaken for a completed agreement and handed it over.

Outside, Qiu Lan was waiting with his supper bowl.

“I saved the good part,” she said.

“There is a good part?”

“Now you’ve offended me and the cook.”

He took the bowl. For the first time since the visit to Mudgate, he felt hungry before somebody reminded him to eat.

***

Ko Lin visited the station the following week.

He came on a family errand, stayed for supper and pretended he had not wanted to see the training room.

Tan Wei let him pretend.

His cousin’s sash was cleaner than the sleeves beneath it. He had taken care over the part people would notice first. His manner still carried the expectation that someone ought to be impressed before he did anything to deserve it, but the expectation seemed less secure than it had at the assessment.

He remained at the fifth stage.

He had reached it quickly with pills and a patron’s attention. Since then, progress had stopped. The patron’s attention had moved elsewhere.

Tan Wei had heard enough family talk to know that this was a subject everyone approached indirectly. They asked about the sect, about prospects, about who had been seen with whom. They avoided asking what Ko Lin did with the long days after another promising exercise failed to change anything.

At supper his cousin spoke about a new intake and a dispute over practice space. He did not mention his own stage. Tan Wei asked about the food at the branch, which produced a more sincere complaint than the rest of the conversation.

Afterward they passed the training room.

The two cups and sloping board were still on the table. Qiu Lan had been practising before the meal and had returned to clean the water marks from the wood.

Ko Lin looked at the arrangement.

“Children’s work.”

“Then you should be excellent at it,” Tan Wei said.

His cousin sat down.

Qiu Lan handed him the first cup without explaining how many times she had spilled it. Ko Lin drew the water up quickly and sent it across the gap in a clean-looking arc.

It struck the far cup too hard. Half went over the rim.

Qiu Lan slid the basin beneath the spill with practised efficiency.

Tan Wei did not laugh.

That seemed to annoy his cousin more than laughter would have.

“The angle’s wrong,” Ko Lin said.

“It’s a board,” Qiu Lan replied. “It has very little pride about that.”

He tried again. This time he sent less water but stopped too abruptly, breaking the thread before the last of it reached the cup. His fingers tightened around the edge of the table.

Tan Wei moved the basin back within reach.

“Take your time.”

“I know how to move water.”

“Yes.”

The absence of an argument left Ko Lin with the cups. He worked through another attempt more slowly. It did not succeed completely, but he saw where it failed. Tan Wei could tell by the way he looked at the first vessel rather than glare at the second.

Han came to close the room. He watched the final attempt and told Ko Lin the floor would still be there another day.

His cousin laughed too loudly, then thanked him in a quieter voice.

On the walk to the gate, Ko Lin asked whether Su Fan still lived behind the smithy.

“Yes.”

“He always had a way of looking at you as though he had decided what you should do.”

Tan Wei stopped.

Ko Lin looked pleased to have found agreement.

“He helped you when nobody else would,” Tan Wei said.

“I didn’t say—”

“I know what you said.”

He walked on.

Being angry with Su Fan did not make him available for other people’s contempt. Ko Lin knew too little about the argument to borrow it, and Tan Wei did not intend to explain it merely so his cousin could feel more justified in disliking somebody.

They reached the outer gate. The guard checked the visitor mark and told Ko Lin which path remained dry after the rain.

His cousin shifted awkwardly before leaving.

“Does Han teach outsiders?”

“For a fee.”

“How much?”

“Ask him.”

Ko Lin looked back toward the training room.

Tan Wei could have offered to ask for him. It would have been easy to make the invitation seem effortless, to save his cousin the embarrassment of returning after calling the exercise children’s work.

He left him there to decide for himself.

***

That night the dream returned.

The woman in the green scarf stood beside a boat. Water slapped its hull. Tan Wei knew a storm was coming, though the sky behind her was clear.

He wanted her to move away from the landing. He wanted to bring something ashore before the weather changed. The wants came with the weight of unfinished business, but he could not tell which part of it belonged to the boat and which to the woman waiting beside it.

This time she said a name.

It was not his.

The sound reached him with a familiarity he did not possess while awake. In the dream he almost answered. The instant before the answer formed was the most frightening part afterward.

He woke before dawn and sat on the edge of the bed.

For a while the room would not become the ordinary room quickly enough. He could see the window and know it was the right window, yet still expect light from somewhere else. He placed both feet on the floor and waited until the mat beneath his heels felt like the one he had used yesterday.

Wet boots. Soap. Old rice.

Those were the dormitory’s smells. He named them quietly, not as an exercise Han had prescribed but because ordinary things helped him remain where he had woken.

Someone turned over and complained at the draft. The familiar irritation loosened the fear a little.

Tan Wei found his copied contracts beneath the bed board. He did not read them. He checked the mark Han had put on the samples, then returned them to the same place. Nothing had been signed in his sleep. The thought was foolish and necessary enough that he let himself confirm it.

He reported the dream before the morning work began.

Han listened without supplying the name the woman might have said. He asked Tan Wei to distinguish what he remembered clearly from what had already blurred. The teacher wrote those distinctions into the note instead of making the account more complete than the dream had left it.

Then he checked the blue cord at Tan Wei’s wrist.

“The station return has been unsettled,” he said. “You’ll train off the shared line for a week.”

“Does that mean I’m failing?”

“No.”

Han said it firmly enough that Tan Wei believed him.

“What work will I do?”

“The work we can assign without that connection. We’ll write it down so the next overseer doesn’t decide you’ve simply forgotten your place.”

He opened the duty book and changed the shifts himself.

Tan Wei watched the old entry crossed out and the new one written beside it. It did not make the woman’s voice disappear from memory. It meant he would not have to pretend he had never heard it in order to keep his work.

chapters.title: The Empty Position
chapters.text:
The relief mechanism was ugly.

Sun Lian regarded this as evidence that they had stopped wasting money on its appearance.

Duan had built the frame. Su Fan had fitted the joints. Six townspeople carried it up the old channel on a cart borrowed from a man who insisted the wheels had been better before anyone touched them.

The cart lurched over a stone. Every man holding the load said something different. Sun Lian called for them to stop, checked the lashings and told the owner that his excellent wheels would survive longer if he allowed them to go around the largest holes.

“It went through them yesterday.”

“It was carrying turnips yesterday.”

The turnips, the owner implied, had shown more gratitude.

They reached the work site without losing either the mechanism or the argument.

The device could lift a stone shutter a finger’s width at a time. It could not open the sealed overflow against the full lake. That distinction was written on the work order in Jiang’s hand.

The old stone door remained untouched farther along the passage. Their test concerned the local drainage and a smaller shutter whose movement could be measured without releasing whatever stood behind the sealed entrance.

Sun Lian read the permitted work aloud before anyone put a hand on the winch.

One of the crew said he had heard it at the smithy.

“Then you can help me remember it if I become ambitious,” she told him.

They unloaded the frame onto the prepared ground. The first arrangement left one foot on a patch that looked firm until the weight settled. Su Fan saw the timber sink and called the others back before the upper beam shifted out of line.

They lifted it again, laid a broader support and tested the seat.

This time it held.

The work was slow enough that the men began discussing what they might have earned by remaining at their ordinary tasks. One had left a brother to finish a cart repair. Another had promised to be home before a buyer came for livestock. None had come merely to admire a machine.

Sun Lian listened, then assigned the first test so everyone knew where to stand and what would happen before they could leave. She did not promise that a doubtful result would become a good one to suit their afternoon.

The first turn went smoothly.

The shutter rose by the intended fraction. Water changed its sound below it, moving through the narrow opening with a brighter, harder rush. Su Fan watched the marks on the frame while another man watched the lower line. The two measurements agreed closely enough to continue.

The second turn exposed a crack in the support timber.

It began as a pale line near a knot. Then the line opened enough to catch a shadow.

“Stop,” Sun Lian said.

The man at the winch held his position. Someone else stepped forward to wedge the timber without being asked.

“Wait. Lower first.”

“We’ve barely begun,” the winchman complained.

“Good time to discover it, then.”

They reversed the movement carefully. The timber eased as the load came off, making the crack look less serious than it had a moment before. Sun Lian marked its end before anyone could convince himself the danger had been an effect of the light.

Su Fan crouched beside it after the shutter was seated.

He had looked at that timber in the yard. He had tested the visible faces. The defect had not appeared until the load changed direction through it.

“I should have—”

“Fetch the replacement,” Sun Lian said. “We can decide what to learn from the old one when it isn’t underneath us.”

They exchanged the support. The task cost time, sweat and part of the crew’s good humour. It did not require anyone to stand beneath a damaged beam to prove he had not made a mistake.

The man expecting the livestock buyer looked toward the road. Sun Lian noticed and asked how long he could remain.

“Until the next turn. After that I need to go.”

She rearranged the work rather than tell him the river mattered more than his sale. They would seat the replacement while all six workers were available for the heavy parts, then leave the smaller alignment work until the remaining crew had a safe arrangement for it.

Su Fan took the old support to the cart. Its owner objected to having a broken timber laid against his side rail. Su Fan shifted it onto two blocks so the split could not catch the wheel when the cart moved.

“Was that bad when you brought it?” the man asked.

“We didn’t see the crack.”

“Not what I asked.”

“No. It’s the part I can answer.”

The owner examined the opened grain. He had hauled enough sound-looking wood to understand the distinction, though he clearly disliked being denied someone convenient to blame for the delay.

They marked the failed piece and kept it. Sun Lian would need to show why a replacement had been used, and Duan would want to see what his original inspection had missed. Burning it for the evening meal would have made the accounting simpler and tomorrow’s timber no safer.

By the time the man with the livestock left, the new support was seated and the load lowered. He washed his hands in the channel, collected the cloth he had left beneath a stone and went down the road without anyone calling the departure a lack of loyalty.

Su Fan liked that about working with her. Stopping did not require a confession. A defect was a defect. Discovering it early was useful, even when it ruined the afternoon.

He was trying to learn the same attitude toward himself.

It was more difficult.

***

Jiang arrived with two formation assistants while the replacement was being seated.

They had brought measuring reeds and a small bronze vessel wrapped in felt. One assistant set the vessel on a level stone and tested its rim with a light tap. The other checked the work order against the position of the shutter.

Jiang inspected the cracked timber before looking at the new one.

“How far did it open?”

Sun Lian showed her the mark.

“And after unloading?”

“Less visible. Still there.”

The steward nodded and had the defective piece laid aside for the report. Nobody was instructed to conceal the lost time inside a successful test.

The bronze vessel sounded when a lineage current passed nearby. Different tones identified different branches. Su Fan heard a faint singing note when Sun Lian reinforced the frame, a vibration so clear that he looked toward the instrument before remembering where the sound came from.

It rang more strongly when an assistant checked the river seal.

The next lift needed the upper brace steadied while its pin was aligned. Su Fan took one end with another worker. The man shifted his grip. For a breath Su Fan carried more of the weight, letting the third circuit settle through his stance instead of wrenching the brace back toward his partner.

The vessel made no sound.

He saw Jiang notice.

She did not interrupt the work.

That was worse than an immediate question. He had time to imagine what she had seen, what the instrument should have done and how foolish an attempted explanation would sound when he had not been asked for one.

He kept his attention on the brace. His partner recovered the grip. They seated the pin and stepped clear.

The test continued through two small movements, then a return to the starting position. The marks held. The shutter came down without catching. The assistants recorded the response and covered the vessel while the crew loosened shoulders that had been tense for longer than any of them intended to admit.

Sun Lian asked Jiang what would be needed before the frame could be used beside the active works. The answer included another check under assigned conditions, not a claim that today’s success proved the device suitable for every load in the valley.

Su Fan helped secure the moving parts for the meal break.

When the crew left for lunch, Jiang asked him to stay.

***

“Lift that brace again.”

“It takes two people.”

“You lifted it while the second man adjusted his grip.”

Su Fan looked at the timber.

He could refuse. She had authority over the work and enough personal strength to make refusal expensive. She had also paid Bao Shun and removed sick operators from duty. The report she was preparing would include the cracked support they had found instead of pretending all the supplied material had been sound.

He disliked how little the facts resembled a simple enemy.

“Here?” he asked.

“On the clear ground. Not against the shutter.”

He set his feet and lifted.
