The weight came into his hands, down through his arms and into the stance he had practised beside the three stones. He did not attempt to make the effort look smaller than it was. His shoulders tightened. He corrected them, found the return and held the brace long enough for Jiang to watch.

The vessel remained silent.

Jiang watched his breathing rather than the bronze.

“Unregistered method?”

“Yes.”

“Source?”

“A purchased text.”

“Family?”

“No.”

“Patron?”

“No.”

She took the weight from him with one hand and set it down.

He felt the ease of the movement more sharply than he would have felt a boast. Whatever the vessel failed to say about him, the timber had no difficulty distinguishing their strength.

“How long?”

“Since spring.”

Jiang looked at him again.

“Has a healer examined you?”

“Wei.”

“Does she know the source?”

“Yes.”

The steward folded her hands behind her back. One of the assistants had moved away to check the lower marks. The other remained beside the instrument, trying to appear occupied without missing the conversation.

“I cannot certify what I cannot classify,” Jiang said.

“I haven’t asked you to certify it.”

“You’re working beside a formation network that can injure people when an unknown current enters it. Your request isn’t the only consideration.”

Su Fan absorbed that.

He had thought of the method as a thing happening inside his body, something an elder might seize because it was unusual or condemn because it lacked a recognized founder. He had spent less time thinking about what his private experiment might do while his hands rested on equipment joined to other people’s circulation.

“I haven’t touched the active return.”

“Good. Continue not touching it.”

“Does the silence mean it can’t affect the network?”

“It means this instrument has not identified a response. Do not make it answer a question I haven’t tested.”

The distinction was unwelcome and fair.

“What do you need?”

“For now, do not circulate inside an active gate coupling. Ordinary labour only. If the method causes pain, memory changes or loss of sensation, stop and tell Wei.”

He nodded.

Jiang asked him to repeat the work restriction so there would be no disagreement later about whether she had prohibited all labour or only the use of his method in a particular place. He did. She wrote it into the site note and showed him where the active boundary would be marked at the works.

She did not ask him to produce the book that afternoon.

The absence of that demand relieved him so much that he nearly missed her final question about who knew what he was practising. He named the people he had actually told or who had directly witnessed it. He did not include somebody merely because he suspected attention in a captain’s eyes.

“And Su Fan?”

“Yes?”

“Being absent from an instrument’s categories does not make you absent from the world.”

She covered the vessel and took it away with the rest of the measuring equipment.

When Sun Lian returned from the meal, she found him putting the brace back where the crew would expect it. He told her the work restriction before she assigned him another task. Her first question was whether it changed how they could move the frame.

It did, in certain places.

They altered the carrying arrangement rather than wait to discover the difference while a load was in the air.

***

He told Mother Wei that evening.

All of it.

She listened while arranging a row of clean cups on the shelf. When he reached the part about the silent vessel, her hand paused. She waited for the rest before asking anything.

“Have you left something out because it would worry me?”

He considered the question before answering.

“No.”

“Good.”

“She’ll report it.”

“She probably should.”

He looked up sharply.

Mother Wei held his gaze.

“A healer keeps a patient’s confidence. A river steward is responsible for everybody standing downstream. Those duties are not always comfortable together.”

Su Fan sat back.

He had arrived expecting her to share his fear of discovery. She did share it; he could see that in the way she asked what tests had been performed and whether Jiang had seen the text. She was not prepared to make that fear the only fact in the room.

“Will you tell her everything?”

“I will answer what is necessary about your condition and what I can honestly assess. I won’t invent certainty because she needs it, or hide an injury because you dislike the attention.”

He looked at his hands. The palms were rough from the frame, unburned, capable of ordinary work. He thought of the operators whose fatigue had become an entry in a calculation made elsewhere. They had reasons to want accurate information too.

Mother Wei asked him to describe the lifting test once more. She checked whether he had strained the old knee or the healing ankle. Neither had caused a fresh problem. That was a useful answer she could give without claiming the method itself had become safe in every circumstance.

“Can you keep to ordinary labour beside the couplings?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Then do it. You don’t need to prove everything you can do each time someone doubts it.”

Outside, Ah-Du was teaching the goose to chase a rolling hoop.

The goose understood only the chasing part and had extended the lesson to several uninvolved people. A woman shouted that she had not volunteered her laundry as an obstacle. Ah-Du explained, unconvincingly, that the bird was still learning direction.

The noise gave Su Fan a brief, absurd wish that his own problems could be solved by closing a gate on a bird.

Mother Wei heard it too.

“Go and rescue your apprentice.”

“He isn’t my apprentice.”

“Then rescue the goose. It has fewer bad habits.”

Su Fan went outside.

The hoop had fallen against a basket, and the goose was attacking its own reflection in a wet patch of paving. Ah-Du held a leaf in front of him as though vegetation might confer authority.

“Distract it,” the boy said.

“With what?”

“Something less important than me.”

Su Fan fetched the empty feed pan and let the bird see it. The goose followed him two paces before discovering the absence of food and expressing an opinion of the deception.

Ah-Du retrieved the hoop. The woman rescued her laundry. Su Fan found enough actual grain to finish the negotiation without being chased into the clinic.

When the yard settled, he returned the pan and washed his hands. Jiang’s questions remained unanswered in the places where neither he nor Mother Wei knew enough to answer them.

The goose, having eaten, appeared satisfied with the day.

chapters.title: Garlic-Chive Buns
chapters.text:
Su Fan turned twenty on the eighth day of Early Harvest.

He had forgotten until Mother Wei put two extra buns beside his breakfast.

The usual bun had split at the seam. Green chives showed through the soft white dough. The other two were still warm enough to mist the inside of the overturned bowl she had used to keep them covered.

He looked from the food to her.

“Eat before somebody decides to celebrate you publicly.”

“Who would do that?”

She looked toward the square.

Ah-Du had already borrowed a drum.

Su Fan reached the doorway before the first blow. The boy stood on an upturned basket with the drum hanging nearly to his knees. A red strip of cloth had been tied around his forehead. It had slipped over one eye, which apparently did not impair his confidence in his audience.

“No,” Su Fan said.

“I haven't started.”

“An excellent place to stop.”

Ah-Du raised the stick. Su Fan took it and then the drum, while two passing women complained that they had already arranged their errands to include the performance.

“It was going to be tasteful,” the boy said.

“You're standing in Auntie Lu's onion basket.”

“Elevation helps the sound.”

Auntie Lu emerged from behind her stall, examined the basket and asked whether the sound would help the onions recover. Ah-Du stepped down.

He demanded compensation for artistic suppression.

She gave him a bruised pear and told him to develop a cheaper art.

By the time Su Fan returned to the clinic, Mother Wei had begun eating one of the extra buns.

“You were slow.”

“You gave it to me.”

“I gave you an opportunity.”

He sat down and ate the remaining two before she found another use for them. Chives caught between his teeth. The filling was hot and salty, with more oil than she usually allowed herself to put in breakfast. He tried to remember whether he had mentioned that he liked them this way.

She pushed a cup toward him.

“Twenty,” she said, testing the number as though it were a questionable measurement supplied by a patient.

“So it seems.”

“You might begin acting it.”

“What changes?”

“The age I complain about.”

He laughed with his mouth full and had to turn away. She waited for him to recover, watching with the brief satisfaction she usually reserved for a fever finally breaking.

When he stood, she caught his sleeve to remove a loose thread. He held still while she worked it free. At eleven, he had been scarcely taller than her medicine table. He had stood in much the same way while she repaired a cuff he had torn trying to be useful with an axe.

Now he could see the fine grey hair at the crown of her head.

“Thank you,” he said.

“For breakfast? You can wash the bowls.”

He did.

***

Duan found a reason to be annoyed by the birthday before the morning was half over.

Three people had come to the smithy to congratulate Su Fan, and each had brought a small repair they claimed was merely on the way. A broken fastening occupied the space reserved for tomorrow's braces. A pot handle had been left beside the new stock. Someone's aunt wanted to know whether twenty was old enough to mend her gate without charging for an apprentice's mistakes.

“Tell her the mistakes cost extra now,” Duan said.

He waited until the visitors had gone, then placed a new file on the bench.

Su Fan recognized the maker's mark. He had admired the same kind in Siltbridge and calculated how much ironwork he would have to finish before buying one.

“This is a business expense,” Duan said.

“Of course.”

“The old one takes too long.”

“Certainly.”

“And if you ruin the teeth by leaving it where Ah-Du can mistake it for a pry bar, I will deduct it from your wages.”

Ah-Du protested from the furnace. He had used the old file as a lever exactly once. According to his account, the object beneath it had been unusually reluctant to move.

Su Fan rolled the new tool in his hand. The handle fitted his palm without the worn ridge he had become accustomed to pressing around. He tested it against a scrap, lightly, and felt the teeth cut cleanly.

Duan watched him discover the difference.

“Enough admiration. There are six hinge eyes waiting.”

By noon, six people had found reasons to visit.

Bao Mei brought a small board painted with a plain grey bird. It stood on a reed with one foot raised, looking cross. The background was mostly bare wood. She had used a dark line to suggest water beneath it, then stopped before the little picture became crowded.

“It's you,” Ah-Du said.

“It is a bird,” Bao Mei replied.

“Yes. But annoyed.”

She handed it to Su Fan before the boy could expand his interpretation. Bao Shun had cut a shallow notch in the back so it could stand on a shelf as well as hang.

Su Fan set it above his sleeping mat. From that angle the bird appeared to be considering the state of his blanket. He straightened the blanket before returning to work, and Ah-Du laughed hard enough to spill charcoal.

Old Pock arrived with advice about women.

Mother Wei interrupted from the doorway before it became specific.

“He's twenty, not desperate.”

“That is when the advice is useful. Later it becomes a report.”

She took the empty medicine jar from his hand and told him that his own report could wait until he had paid attention to its label. Pock followed her outside, still arguing that personal history ought to count as a service to the young.

Sun Lian came after the midday meal, with a whetstone wrapped in cloth.

“Your old one has a hollow.”

“You've been inspecting my things?”

“You leave them where people work.”

He unwrapped it. The surface was fine and even, its grain running in a direction he could see only when he turned it toward the light.

“This is good.”

“It would be a poor gift otherwise.”

“I meant—thank you.”

She seemed more comfortable once he began examining the stone rather than trying to find a sentence equal to it. She showed him where to wet it and how not to ruin the edge of a blade by trying to finish too quickly. He demonstrated on an old knife, and she corrected his wrist.

No cultivation was involved. The edge improved anyway.

Before she left, Duan asked about the relief frame. Tomorrow's fittings were laid out in order beside the bench. They checked the delivery list, discovered that Ah-Du had counted a washer twice, and settled the matter before returning to the less reliable business of a celebration.

“Come hungry,” Su Fan said.

Sun Lian glanced at the packet of buns Mother Wei had sent for the smithy.

“You're making a promising start on everyone else's behalf.”

***

The town held the harvest meal that evening, though there was less harvest than usual.

There had been an argument about cancelling it. Auntie Lu had listened until somebody suggested that a feast was irresponsible in difficult times, then asked him whether eating the same rice separately would make more rice.

It was not quite an answer to every objection. It was enough to get the tables carried out.

People brought what they could: beans, pickled greens, a little pork cut thin to travel farther, rice from several households, and three fish that Old Pock claimed had voluntarily surrendered.

“They heard what I was using for bait,” he said. “Preferred to get it over with.”

The lifting wheel stood quiet beside the channel. Lanterns hung from its frame. Sun Lian checked that the wheel was secured before allowing anyone to tie the cloth streamers to it, then turned to discover two children already exploring the spokes.

“Out.”

“We're not turning it.”

“Excellent. You can preserve that achievement from over here.”

When they tried returning by the other side, she threatened to make them count missing fingers before dessert. They decided the low wall offered better entertainment.

Su Fan helped carry a long table through the narrow space between the stall and the channel. The men at the far end wanted to turn left. He wanted to turn right. For several moments the table advanced nowhere while each end explained the obvious route to the other.

Bao Shun finally told them to put it down.

They did, moved a stool, and lifted it again without further heroism.

By sunset the tables were uneven, the lanterns almost level and Ah-Du had obtained the drum from whoever Su Fan had returned it to. This time he was allowed to play provided he stood at the far end of the square and stopped when people began eating.

The arrangement lasted four beats after the first bowl was served.

Auntie Lu sent him to fetch water. The drum mysteriously disappeared during his absence.

Su Fan was carrying a stack of bowls when he saw Tan Wei at the edge of the crowd.

He did not go to meet him immediately.

His friend spoke to Bao Shun, helped carry another table and accepted food from Auntie Lu. He seemed tired, but not in the rigid way he had looked in the smithy. The file with Su Fan's letter was nowhere in sight. That did not mean it had ceased to exist.

Su Fan put down the bowls. He adjusted the last one on the stack, then made himself leave it alone.

Tan Wei came over.

“Twenty.”

“So they tell me.”

“You still look nineteen. I expected more effort.”

Su Fan smiled.

His friend handed him a small packet. Inside were a needle, good thread and a replacement cord for his tool roll. The needle was long enough to pass through the doubled straps without requiring him to fight for a grip on its eye.

“You keep repairing everyone else's things,” Tan Wei said. “Your own roll looks diseased.”

“It closes.”

“Against its wishes.”

“Thank you.”

Tan Wei nodded and took the bowl Su Fan offered him. There was more to say. Neither tried to force it into the space between a gift and a meal.

They sat with the others.

Ko Lin had come in ordinary clothes. Without the sash, he looked younger and seemed unsure what to do with his hands when no one was asking about his training. Qiu Lan rescued him from one uncomfortable silence by starting another.

“Have you warned the kitchen?”

“About what?”

“Your handling of cups.”

He pretended not to hear.

A few minutes later, while she argued with Pock over the ownership of the largest fish, Ko Lin drew a thin stream of water from one bowl and settled it cleanly in another. He did it slowly. The last drop left the first vessel without shaking free and splashing the table.

Tan Wei saw. He nudged Su Fan with his elbow.

They watched Ko Lin examine the dry boards with badly concealed pleasure.

“Better,” Tan Wei said.

His cousin looked up at once.

“I wasn't demonstrating.”

“Then don't charge us.”

Qiu Lan glanced back and saw the bowls. She offered no applause, but she moved her own cup within his reach when it needed filling. Ko Lin managed the task without spilling a drop.

The improvement pleased both friends. For a little while Su Fan could share something with Tan Wei without measuring the hurt around it.

***

After the meal, Auntie Lu announced a contest to determine whose imitation of the quarry foreman was most accurate.

A boy opened strongly with a shouted demand for a receipt for the wood he was standing on. Someone else imitated the foreman inspecting a roof by looking at the person beneath it. The audience awarded points with a fairness that decreased as the wine jars emptied.

Duan won before entering.

He had merely looked into the last jar and said, “That wasn't in the estimate.”

The town insisted this qualified.

He protested that he was discussing an actual shortage. This strengthened his claim so decisively that Auntie Lu presented him with a piece of prize cake and refused to hear another word.

Ah-Du immediately began preparing an imitation of Duan.

“Consider your future,” the smith advised.

The boy changed to a convincing performance of an innocent apprentice who had never misplaced a tool. It was so unfamiliar that several people asked whom he was supposed to be.

Min laughed until he coughed.

Mother Wei brought warm water and stayed beside him while the fit passed. He tried to wave her away, then accepted the cup with both hands. Su Fan saw how thin the hands looked around it.

“Too much excitement,” Min said when he could speak.

“Too little water.”

“I prefer my diagnosis.”

“You can keep it. Drink mine.”

She remained until the colour returned to his face. He was embarrassed by the attention. She ignored the embarrassment and adjusted the cushion beneath his elbow.

Later Su Fan took a piece of cake to the low wall.

There was nothing orderly about the evening. Two men argued over a borrowed net. A child cried because her cake had broken, then cried harder when her brother offered to dispose of the damaged portion. Somebody began a song with three incompatible versions of its second verse. The singers resolved the disagreement by becoming louder.

Light from the lanterns trembled on the narrow channel. Behind the tables he could see an evacuation mark on a wall, its bright border half covered by a hanging cloth. He knew what it was there for. Tonight the cloth belonged to somebody keeping an extra bowl warm.

He liked being there.

Tan Wei sat beside him.

For a time they listened to the song. Su Fan had remembered a fourth version of the disputed verse and decided the square had enough difficulties.

“I'm still angry,” Tan Wei said.

“I know.”

“But you can stop looking as though you're waiting to be sentenced.”

Su Fan let out a breath.

“All right.”

His friend broke a corner from his cake. Crumbs fell between the stones. A small bird landed below them, reconsidered the gathering and departed without accepting the opportunity.

“Even that one thinks the singing is bad,” Tan Wei said.

“It may know the words.”

“That would make one of us.”

Far uphill, a line of blue lights flickered along the gates. One went out, then returned.

Tan Wei noticed.

“Shift test tomorrow.”

“Will you be on it?”

“Han keeps me off the shared line this week. Loading work instead.”

“Good.”

His friend glanced at him.

Su Fan corrected himself.

“I'm glad you'll be there when I deliver the braces.”

Tan Wei let that stand. He did not explain the entire arrangement, and Su Fan did not ask to examine it. They returned to the song, which had reached a verse nobody had previously claimed to know.

Below them, Auntie Lu discovered that the goose had eaten half the prize cake.

The bird stood beneath the contest table with icing on its beak. For one suspended moment it regarded the gathering as though prepared to defend the judgment that the prize had been poorly awarded.

Then Auntie Lu reached for a basket.

Duan moved his remaining cake out of the way. Ah-Du shouted contradictory instructions. Pock began taking bets. Tan Wei laughed so suddenly that Su Fan turned toward him before joining in.

The resulting pursuit carried the celebration well past midnight.

chapters.title: The Shift
chapters.text:
The test began at the sixth morning bell.

Su Fan stood behind the marked line with Duan's delivery receipt in his pocket. He had slept too little. A piece of chive from yesterday's breakfast had lodged somewhere in the sleeve of his clean work shirt, and Ah-Du had discovered it while helping him load the cart.

“You're carrying provisions,” the boy had said.

Now the cart was empty, the fittings counted and the morning cold enough to make the stone platform unpleasant through his shoes.

Sun Lian waited beside the temporary relief frame. Han supervised the operators. Tan Wei and three labourers handled the physical locks. Jiang had gone to the upper reservoir to coordinate the release, leaving instructions with the test overseer and assistants at the measuring stations.

Su Fan could see most of the works from where he stood.

The main channel came down from the east, struck the curved approach wall and narrowed beneath the eighth gate. Above the throat stood the operator platform, with its stools and bronze reeds arranged along the return plate. A lower work ledge gave access to the side shutter. Sun Lian's frame had been bolted there, its two uprights straddling the old stone housing.

Between the upper and lower levels, beside a short flight of steps, was the mechanical release.

Tan Wei had cleaned the lever's socket before the test. He had lifted the keeper pin, worked the lever through its permitted range with the station uncharged, and lowered the pin again. Su Fan had watched him check that the latch sat properly.

His friend had looked across once.

“Still glad to be here?”

“Ask me after the receipt is signed.”

Tan Wei had grinned and returned to the locks.

The overseer now took his place beside the signal board. He had not been the man who gave Mother Wei evasive answers about reserves. This one kept glancing at the instructions in his hand, not because he could not read them but because he seemed determined that the test should follow every line.

Han checked the workers individually.

One man shifted on his stool. Han asked whether the seat was wrong or his back was troubling him. The man admitted the back. A pad was fetched. Another worker had set his feet too close to the return rail; Han made him move them before allowing the assistant to charge the plate.

Tan Wei remained with the loading crew, outside the line of seated operators. The blue cord at his wrist was visible when he reached for a tool.

Su Fan stayed where Jiang had told him to stay.

A painter's pale stripe crossed the stone between him and the active coupling. The boundary did not look impressive. The consequences on its other side were another matter.

The first reed brightened.

***

For five cycles, everything worked.

Water moved through the eighth gate. The bronze reeds answered in sequence, blue gathering along their narrow edges before fading at the rest interval. The workers breathed, moved their hands when required and sat back when Han signalled them to release.

The new braces held their alignment.

At the end of the first cycle, Sun Lian checked a mark on the frame. Su Fan could see her mouth move as she counted. She looked up and gave the overseer the agreed signal.

The second cycle took more water. Foam travelled along the inside wall and broke into smaller patches beneath the gate. Tan Wei and the other labourers watched the physical locks. Nobody touched a fitting simply because it appeared to be waiting for a hand.

On the third, an assistant asked for a repeated reading. The overseer held the sequence while the measure was taken again. Han used the pause to have one operator drink. Su Fan watched the man hold the cup in both hands and remembered Mother Wei's forty-three actual bodies against forty-seven entries.

The fourth cycle passed without a disputed reading.

By the fifth, people had begun to move with the quiet economy of a job going well. A labourer adjusted the knot in his belt. The assistant at the lower gauge wiped his nose without looking away from the needle. The overseer tucked the instruction sheet beneath a stone so he could hold the next signal with both hands.

Su Fan found himself looking for something he had missed.

Not every successful test concealed a failure. He knew that. He had also been present when apparently sound timber opened along a hidden split.

He checked the frame, then the latch, then Sun Lian's feet on the lower ledge. Nothing gave him a reason to speak.

The fifth rest interval ended.

Han lowered his hand.

On the sixth cycle, a reed answered before its operator exhaled.

Su Fan saw the light first. It ran down the metal in a bright, uneven line, faster than any of the earlier responses. The man on the corresponding stool still had his shoulders raised for the breath he was supposed to release.

Han lifted his hand at once.

“Hold.”

The overseer repeated the order.

Three workers stopped.

The fourth did not.

His chest continued moving in the old rhythm. His eyes widened. He tried to turn toward Han and managed only a small movement of his chin.

Then the next reed answered.

***

The sound was not louder than the ordinary station note.

It was too even.

Each return should have carried a living hesitation: one man releasing, another taking the load, the little intervals in which a body remained a body rather than a part of the machine. Now the notes came together, smooth enough to make Su Fan's teeth feel close and hard in his mouth.

Blue cords tightened around wrists.

A pressure passed through the platform. It carried no words. Su Fan nevertheless felt an impulse to remain where he had been placed, to keep the movement going, to complete what had already begun.

He shifted one foot.

The pressure remained, but the foot moved.

Across the stripe, an operator's fingers whitened against the edge of his stool. The man was looking directly at Han. He could see the raised hand. He was trying to obey it.

His chest would not stop.

“Break the return,” Han said.

The assistant at the signal board reached for a control. Light caught his sleeve. His arm halted midway, trembling as though he had thrust it into a current too strong to pull free of.

Han stepped into the line and pressed his cane against the return plate.

For an instant the station note faltered.

Su Fan thought the teacher had caught it.

Then Han's own cultivation answered.

The old man stood perfectly still, one hand on the cane, the other extended toward the nearest operator. The tendons in his neck rose. A thin line of blood ran from his nose and reached his upper lip before he could draw breath to speak again.

“Mechanical release.”

Tan Wei moved before the overseer had repeated the words.

He reached the lever and caught the handle. Immediately he let go. The sound he made was short and furious. He wrapped the handle in his sleeve and pulled again.

The sleeve smoked.

The lock did not move.

Below them, Sun Lian started the relief frame.

Its first turn changed the noise under the platform. Water that had been striking the closed side shutter found a narrow route and tore through it. The pressure against the main works eased enough for the upper timber to stop shuddering.

Then the relief frame began to creak.

Sun Lian set both hands against its control beam. The stone beneath her boots darkened. Her earth current passed into the frame, reinforcing the supports Duan had built without making them any straighter or stronger than the arrangement could bear.

“Keep clear below!” she shouted.

One labourer hauled the gauge assistant up from the lower stair. Another kicked a tool box out of the runoff before it jammed against the shutter housing. The third went toward Tan Wei, saw the smoke from the sleeve and seized a wooden bar from the rack.

He pushed it against the lever.

The wood skidded. One end caught beneath the rail, and the next pulse of water snapped it near his hand.

Su Fan remained behind the line.

The instruction had not been foolish. He could see why Jiang had given it. Every recognized route on the platform was being drawn into the station's return. Another unknown current might make the pattern worse rather than free anyone.

He could also see the mechanical lock.

Tan Wei had tested it before the station was charged. Lift the keeper pin. Then turn the lever.

Now steam rose from the fitting. The upper part of the handle glowed with reflected blue, and the smaller pin was half hidden behind the smoke from Tan Wei's sleeve.

He was pulling against the keeper.

“Keeper first!” Su Fan shouted.

Tan Wei looked, saw it and reached.

The blue cord at his wrist tightened.

His hand stopped above the metal.

***

He had been kept off the shared line.

He still carried the same branch.

Tan Wei's face changed as he understood it. His arm remained extended, his fingers parted around nothing. He tried to look toward Su Fan and could not turn his shoulders.

The labourer beside him caught his belt, thinking he had lost his balance. He pulled once and stopped when Tan Wei cried out.

“Don't move him like that,” Han managed.

The teacher's voice was thick with blood.

Su Fan looked at Sun Lian. Both her hands were on the relief frame. She had lowered her stance until the control beam pressed across her shoulders. The muscles beside her jaw stood out beneath wet skin.

If she let go, the shutter would fall and the lower platform would flood.

The remaining assistants were caught or too far from the release. The ordinary workers could still move, but the wood they had tried was broken. The metal was already burning through Tan Wei's sleeve.

There was no other free cultivator close enough to bear even a brief contact with the heat.

Su Fan took a cloth from the wash bucket.

He squeezed it once, leaving it wet enough to drip, and folded it across his palm. His fingers shook while he did it. A drop struck the stripe at his feet and darkened the paint.

“Su Fan,” the overseer said.

He had seen the movement. His mouth opened around an order he did not finish.

Su Fan crossed the line.

The command struck harder inside the coupling. It ran across his chest and down the familiar routes the inherited branch expected to find. His own circulation contracted around the pressure, uncomfortable but still his to move.

He took another step.

The command failed to hold him.

The heat did not.

He could feel it against his face before he touched the fitting. Tan Wei stood close enough that Su Fan saw a fine tremor running through his trapped fingers. Sweat had gathered at the end of his nose and would not fall until it grew heavy enough.

“The pin,” Su Fan said. He did not know whether he was speaking to his friend or himself.

He gripped it through the cloth.

Steam burst between his fingers. The fabric did not make the metal cool. It gave him a moment before the pain reached the centre of his palm, bright and immediate.

He lifted.

The pin moved, caught and dropped back when he let go.

He breathed once.

His hand wanted to close. He forced the fingers open and folded the wet fabric thicker. One corner had already browned. He turned the cleaner side toward the iron.

At the lower frame, something knocked against its stop.

“Soon,” Sun Lian said through her teeth.

Su Fan lifted again.

This time he turned the pin as he raised it, easing the roughened shoulder past the socket instead of hauling it straight against the burr. Duan would have cursed anyone who used force where a little movement could free the fitting.

The pin cleared.

It struck the stone with a sound he would remember later, although at the time he barely heard it.

“Tan Wei. Pull when it loosens.”

His friend's face strained. He could not answer.

Su Fan put his shoulder against the lever.

***

The first effort accomplished nothing.

The handle trembled. The whole housing seemed to tremble with it. Su Fan could not tell how much of that was the station and how much was his own body trying to escape the task.

He completed all three circuits.

The movement returned through his back, hips and legs. He had practised this with stones in a yard. None of those stones had been joined to a river. None had stood beside his oldest friend while the friend's own breath refused to belong to him.

He pushed.

The lever moved a finger's width.

Something tore in his palm.

He made a sound and nearly stepped away. The cloth had shifted against the handle; the injured skin had followed it. He could feel heat under the pain now, spreading farther than the place he held.

No insight removed it.

He looked down.

His rear foot was slipping on wet stone. He had been pushing from a narrow position, trying to keep his body clear of the frame while asking his arms to do what the footing would not support.

The base of the release housing rose beside his boot.

He moved the foot against it.

One circuit broke when he changed position. He let it, took the breath again and rebuilt the movement from the ground rather than demand that it survive a bad stance.

The next push went into the lever instead of backward through him.

A hard click reached his shoulder.

The lock released.

Tan Wei staggered forward.

His hand struck the handle beside Su Fan's. He pulled, cried out at the heat and kept pulling. Between them they turned the lever far enough for the release to take its own weight.

The bronze reeds went dark in a broken sequence.

One snapped against its mounting. Another gave a thin, declining note that ended in a clatter. Men fell from their seats. Han caught the nearest operator and went down with him, his cane scraping along the return plate before it fell free.

Su Fan stumbled into the rail.

Tan Wei caught the back of his shirt.

For several breaths there was only water, coughing and the groan of Sun Lian's frame.

The ordinary workers moved first. One dragged a fallen operator away from the runoff. Another knelt beside Han, who waved him toward the man he had caught. The overseer shouted for a healer and received an answer from somewhere up the stairs.

“Hands,” Tan Wei said.

Su Fan looked down as though the word belonged to someone else.

The cloth stuck to his palm. He did not pull it away. Tan Wei's sleeve was black where it had touched the lever, and his fingers were red along one side.

“Frame,” Su Fan said.

Sun Lian was still holding it.

They turned toward her together.

Then a pressure greater than the station's settled over the works.

The river flattened.

It did not stop. The flow continued beneath a surface pressed smooth by an unseen hand. Foam that had been jumping against the wall stretched into pale, narrow lines. The trembling in the relief frame eased.

Sun Lian looked up before allowing herself to change her grip.

A man in a dark blue robe stood on the upper stair.

He had arrived without any sound Su Fan could remember hearing. His robe was dry. In the broken, steaming works, that small fact seemed almost as impossible as the smooth water.

The older workers tried to kneel. Several could not get up far enough to do it properly.

“Elder Pei,” the overseer whispered.

Pei Gang looked at the injured men, the open lock and the smoking cloth around Su Fan's hand.

His eyes rested on Su Fan longest.

“Who released the station?”

Tan Wei straightened beside his friend.

“We did.”

The elder's gaze did not move.

“I saw you after the command broke.”

Su Fan let the loose part of the ruined cloth fall. The part against his skin remained.

“I lifted the keeper.”

Pei Gang descended one step.

Around them, water climbed the channel walls in a thin, perfectly level band.

“How,” he asked, “were you still able to move?”

chapters.title: A Pebble in a Bowl
chapters.text:
Pei Gang examined Su Fan in a room with no windows.

The room had a table, two chairs and a basin fed by a narrow stream of water through the wall. The basin drained through a slot beneath its rim. There was no visible tap. Water entered at the same quiet rate at which it left, maintaining a surface so still that Su Fan could see the lamp reflected in it.

Nothing else needed to be there.

His wet shoes marked the clean floor. He could not hold his hands naturally. The right palm hurt when he let the fingers fall, and the left hurt when he tried to make it carry the weight of the right.

Jiang stood beside the door.

She had reached the works after the station was disconnected. Su Fan had seen her speak to Sun Lian, then to Han, who sat with a cloth beneath his nose and an operator leaning against his shoulder. The steward had looked at the keeper pin on the stone before turning toward him.

She had not asked why he crossed her line. Not yet.

On the walk to the room, she had told him that Pei Gang was three hundred and eighty-two years old.

Su Fan had no useful place to put the number. He could imagine twenty because he had become it yesterday. He could imagine Duan as a younger man, or Mother Wei before the grey in her hair, although those pictures were mostly things he had invented from stories. Three hundred and eighty-two required him to discard the people he knew and begin counting again several times.

The elder looked neither frail nor particularly interested in his own age.

He sat down and left the second chair for Su Fan.

Mother Wei arrived before the examination began.

An attendant tried to explain that the elder was conducting a preliminary assessment. She opened her medicine case and asked whether the preliminary burns intended to wait for a final assessment before damaging anything important.

Pei Gang looked at Su Fan's hands.

“Treat them.”

She took the second chair for the work and made Su Fan sit on a low chest brought from the passage. Jiang remained standing. No one asked the elder to move.

The cloth came away slowly.

Su Fan watched the water in the basin instead of his palm. When Mother Wei had to pause, he could hear the small change in her breathing. He did not ask her whether the skin looked bad. He knew what she would say about questions whose answers were being supplied directly to his nerves.

“Did you pull it free?” she asked.

“Only the loose part.”

“Good.”

The praise was small enough to make him feel absurdly grateful.

She dressed both hands, checked the movement he could tolerate and told him which fingers not to force closed. Pei Gang waited without impatience. That did not make Su Fan feel less like a man being inspected. The elder had time to spare that no one else in the room possessed.

When Mother Wei finished, she stood beside him rather than put away her case.

Pei set a bowl of water on the table.

“Your method has no lineage response.”

“No recognized response,” Jiang corrected.

The elder glanced at her.

She did not lower her eyes.

“Quite,” he said.

***

“Place your hand beside it.”

Su Fan laid his forearm on the table and kept the dressed palm clear of the wood.

Pei watched the adjustment.

“Is that comfortable?”

“No,” Mother Wei said. “It is possible. Those are different.”

The elder inclined his head and moved the bowl closer so Su Fan did not have to reach.

A reed-shaped light rose from the water. It turned once above the rim, so fine that Su Fan could see the table through it. Then it pressed toward his wrist.

He felt the station's command again.

This version had no confusion in it. It did not arrive tangled with frightened men, broken notes and the roar of water. It found the edge of his breathing with an exactness that made his body want to anticipate it.

His breath paused.

The three circuits drew inward.

He could feel the pressure searching for a familiar turn, the place where an inherited current would answer a direction it already knew. His own movement did not supply that place. The light slid across his skin, lingered near the wrist and returned to the bowl.

Su Fan discovered that he had pressed both heels into the floor.

Pei watched without changing expression.

“Again. Do not assist it. Do not oppose it.”

“How will I know which I am doing?”

“Tell me what you attempt. I will compare that with what occurs.”

The answer did not promise safety. Su Fan glanced at Mother Wei.

She was watching his face, not the light.

The second test lasted longer.

At first he tried to reproduce the way he had stood on the platform. That brought the heat back into memory so sharply that he moved his injured hand before the light touched it.

Pei stopped.

“Pain?”

“Memory.”

“Of pain.”

“Yes.”

The elder asked him to keep the hand in a position it could bear. They began again.

His pulse quickened. Sweat gathered at his temples. He could breathe, but breathing had become something he noticed too closely, as though he had been asked to walk normally along a narrow wall while several people described the drop.

The pressure was real. The part intended to seize a named route could not find one.

That did not make the rest pleasant.

When the test ended, he kept his hand still through effort rather than calm. Mother Wei put her fingers against his uninjured forearm and waited before announcing that there would be a pause.

Pei allowed it.

An assistant entered to record the interval. The young man had a brush already wet with ink. He looked at Su Fan, then at the silent bowl, and wrote a line that Jiang asked to see.

She read it over his shoulder.

“Absence of branch capture. Not absence of response.”

The assistant corrected the line.

Su Fan stared at the amended words. Someone could have turned his frightened, sweating body into an untroubled exception simply by choosing the shorter description.

Pei lifted a small pebble from the basin's rim.

“Catch.”

He flicked it.

Su Fan saw the movement of his fingers. He saw nothing useful between that movement and the crack behind his head.

The pebble struck the wooden wall hard enough to bury itself.

His hand rose after it was over.

Mother Wei stood.

Pei raised a hand.

“A distinction, not a threat.”

“Make the next distinction with your own head.”

The room became very quiet.

Su Fan felt cold beneath his ribs. He had never heard anyone speak to an elder that way. He wanted to say something that would move the attention from her, and could think of nothing that would not make the room worse.

Pei looked at her for a long moment.

The bowl's surface remained still.

Then he inclined his head.

“The patient remains physically ordinary in that respect. Your objection is recorded.”

Mother Wei did not sit down.

The elder turned back to Su Fan.

“Pressure is not force. You understand that?”

“Yes.”

“Many gifted young men fail to.”

Su Fan could not decide whether the warning had required the pebble or whether the pebble had required a respectable description afterward. Both possibilities remained in the wall behind him.

***

Pei put the bowl aside.

“Where is the text?”

“Stored safely.”

“I did not ask whether you had put it in a puddle.”

Su Fan met his eyes for less than a breath. There was no triumph to be gained by pretending they were equals.

“I purchased it from the archive clearance. I have the receipt.”

Jiang shifted slightly beside the door.

Pei noticed.

“A lawful purchase is not a lawful licence to practise every dangerous thing it contains.”

“No.”

“Nor is it proof of danger,” Jiang said.

The elder looked at her again.

“You are protective of an unknown variable.”

“I am protective of an accurate report.”

He seemed to accept the distinction, though not necessarily the motive.

The assistant took another sheet. Su Fan was asked where he had learned to read, whether the book had a living teacher, whether the corrections belonged to one hand or several. He answered what he knew. When he did not know, the elder sometimes waited as though patience might produce more information.

It produced the same answer, said less steadily.

“Did you choose a founderless practice deliberately?”

“I chose to try an exercise.”

“Because the lineage assessment rejected you?”

“Because it was there. Because I could read it. Because it seemed possible to test part of it.”

“All three?”

“Yes.”

Pei considered him.

“People often discover a cleaner reason after the result.”

Su Fan looked at the bandages. His own latest result had left very little room for cleanliness.

The examination continued until afternoon.

He lifted measured weights in ways that spared his palms. He walked marked lines. He was asked to stand, turn, bend and repeat the movement while an assistant watched from the other side. At first the ordinary tasks relieved him. He knew what a weight was. He knew when his foot had left a line.

Then Pei asked why his right shoulder moved before his left when he became tired.

Su Fan did not know.

The elder had him repeat the turn without adding more cultivation. The uneven movement remained. Su Fan recognized it from difficult forge work, though he had never thought of it as something anyone could learn about him from a room's length of walking.

Jiang recorded the observation. Mother Wei recorded fatigue.

They were looking at the same man and asking different questions.

When a proposed lift required Su Fan to close his injured hand around a handle, he refused.

“I can't do that without straining the dressing.”

Pei looked at Mother Wei. She confirmed it.

The next lift used a sling around the forearm. Su Fan could manage that, but only with a small weight. He said so before the assistant added more.

Later, when the elder asked for a demonstration of the release movement against resistance, Mother Wei refused before Su Fan could answer.

“He has described it. You have the lever. You can inspect the injury it produced. There will not be a second one for comparison today.”

Pei did not become angry.

He became more attentive.

That frightened Su Fan more.

The questions returned to the station. Where had he stood when the first reed answered? What had he felt before crossing the line? Had he known Tan Wei would be caught through his branch? What exactly had he expected the cloth to accomplish?

“No,” he said to the question about Tan Wei.

The word came out harder than he intended.

Pei waited.

“I thought he was outside it. He was on loading work.”

“And then?”

“Then I saw his wrist.”

“Did you expect immunity for yourself?”

“I expected to be able to take a step. I had moved when the pressure reached me before.”

“One step did not prove you could reach the release.”

“No.”

“Yet you went.”

Su Fan remembered Sun Lian under the beam, Han bleeding beside the plate, his friend's hand suspended above the keeper.

“Yes.”

The elder did not praise him for it. He asked the assistant to bring a sketch of the platform.

They marked the positions. Jiang corrected the location of one measuring vessel. Su Fan moved the labourer with the broken wooden bar farther from Tan Wei than the first drawing had placed him. The distance mattered. A hand close enough to help one task had not been close enough to perform another.

When the map was finished, his crossing occupied the width of two fingers on the page.

He could still feel every step in his palm.

***

Food arrived while the last measurements were being copied.

Su Fan had not realized how hungry he was until the smell reached him. Mother Wei broke his bread into pieces he could lift without closing his fingers. He wanted to tell her he could do it himself. He was too hungry to spend the time.

Pei ate nothing.

A messenger came to the door. The elder listened to a brief report about the injured operators, asked which had been moved and gave an instruction concerning the next inspection. He did not consult the bowl or the model drawing. The works continued to occupy his attention even while Su Fan sat in front of him.

It would have been easier if curiosity had been the elder's only motive.

At the end, Pei dismissed Jiang to inspect the failed return and asked Mother Wei to wait outside for one minute.

She refused to go far.

He let her remain at the open doorway, where she could see Su Fan and hear anything said above a murmur. She took her medicine case with her but did not close it.

Pei folded the platform sketch.

“You believe I intend to confiscate the method.”

“I don't know what you intend.”

“A careful answer. Here is an easier fact. You crossed a command return that immobilized an experienced twelfth-stage instructor. That can save lives. It can also bypass safeguards designed to prevent one man from opening the wrong gate.”

Su Fan said nothing.

He had spent the morning thinking of being caught. The elder was thinking of places where he could not be caught by the usual means. Neither thought removed the burns.

“Your work today stopped a dangerous return,” Pei continued. “If another man with the same capacity entered the works to damage them, the measures that stopped Han would not stop him.”

“I didn't enter to damage them.”

“I am discussing a property, not accusing you of a purpose.”

Su Fan looked toward the open door. Mother Wei stood where she had promised to stand.

“If you practise secretly,” Pei said, “I must treat you as an uncontrolled hazard. If you practise under observation, we may learn something useful.”

“Observation by whom?”

“Me.”

The word carried the quiet certainty of a locked door.

Su Fan thought of the yard, the little timber frame, the notes that admitted when he did not know what he had done. He also thought of instruments he could not buy, physicians who understood injuries Mother Wei had only begun to study, and questions he might never answer by repeating an exercise beside a smithy.

The offer had not yet been written. Already it possessed several ways to hold him.

“I would need to know the terms.”

“You will.”

Pei stood.

The examination was over because he had decided it was over.

***

Outside, Mother Wei took Su Fan's elbow.

He thought she was steadying him until he noticed her own hand tremble.

The corridor had windows. Afternoon light fell across the floor, bright enough to make him blink after the enclosed room. Somewhere below, a servant was arguing with a porter about where to leave a crate. The ordinary annoyance sounded startlingly free.

Mother Wei stopped at the first step.

“Slowly.”

“For me or you?”

“Both, since you've decided to notice.”

They went down together.

He wanted to thank her for the objection, for staying at the door, for speaking as though the elder's attention did not make an injured hand less important. The words tangled with his fear that she had spent something on his behalf he could not repay.

She squeezed his elbow before he managed to speak.

“Don't make a speech. Save it for the people who will want one.”

At the bottom of the steps, Su Fan looked back.

Through the open doorway he could see the pebble still buried in the wooden wall.

Pei Gang had not retrieved it.

He had no need to.

chapters.title: A Place Prepared
chapters.text:
The proposed agreement gave Su Fan a room, a stipend and access to a physician trained in cultivation injuries.

The room had a bed with a mattress thick enough that he could not feel the boards beneath it. He knew because an attendant showed it to him before anyone gave him the agreement. There was a desk beside the window, a covered water jar and a cupboard with an empty shelf.

He thought of the grey bird above his sleeping mat at the smithy.

The attendant asked whether the light would be sufficient for reading.

“Yes.”

“We can move the desk.”

“It is sufficient.”

The man nodded, pleased to have solved the question he had been sent to solve.

Su Fan followed him back to Jiang's table.

The agreement also gave the sect the right to examine his method, retain copies of his records and restrict his movement during active study.

The term was ninety days.

Renewal rested with the supervising elder.

Su Fan read that sentence four times.

His hands were still dressed. He turned the sheet by catching its corner between two fingers that did not hurt as much as the others. Jiang waited across the table, her own copy weighted with an ordinary stone.

“You can request a fixed end,” she said.

“Will it be granted?”

“Perhaps.”

“And the copies?”

“They will not remove that clause.”

He looked back at the first page. The stipend was more than he earned at the smithy, and it would not depend on how many customers paid late that month. Meals were included. So was medical attention. Someone had thought of the things he currently lacked and put them in the first few lines.

“When does study end?” he asked.

“At the end of the term, unless it is renewed.”

“I mean each day.”

“That would depend on the work.”

“Would I be free to go down to Mudgate?”

“Outside active sessions, unless the supervising elder required observation.”

He found the line. It was there, almost the same answer in more formal language.

The proposed room was comfortable. Comfort did not tell him when he would be allowed to leave it.

He folded the paper, then unfolded it because the crease made reading harder.

“What happens if I refuse?”

“Your work within the active formations stops. Your unregistered cultivation remains subject to review.”

“Detention?”

“Not currently ordered.”

He heard the room left inside that answer.

Jiang leaned forward.

“You are not obliged to believe this is kindness. You should understand that it is not the worst offer you could receive.”

“I do.”

“Good. Understanding an offer is not accepting it.”

Outside, someone carried a tray along the passage. A spoon rattled against a bowl. Su Fan heard the attendant giving directions to another worker about the room with the newly moved desk.

He had not asked for the desk to be moved.

“Does everyone think I've agreed?”

“The room can be used by someone else.”

“That isn't what I asked.”

Jiang glanced toward the door.

“No. Some people have been told to prepare. Preparation is easier to order than consent.”

For a moment he thought she regretted saying it so plainly. Then she lifted her own copy and pointed to the place where a response could be recorded.

“Read everything before writing there.”

***

Pei Gang showed him the station model that afternoon.

It occupied an entire chamber. Water ran through silver channels mounted on a dark wooden platform. Small carved figures marked operator positions. Some held their hands in shapes Su Fan recognized from the eighth gate. Others stood beside junctions he had never been allowed close enough to inspect.

At the centre sat an empty socket.

Su Fan stopped near the doorway.

He had expected a diagram, perhaps a better version of the maps Jiang carried. This was a working thing. Water fell through narrow weirs and gathered in little reservoirs. Fine threads ran beneath the silver channels, crossing and returning in patterns too dense to follow all at once.

An assistant adjusted a measure at the far end. Another recorded the change. Neither touched the central socket.

“This is the lower system?” Su Fan asked.

“A model of several relevant returns. Not the whole river.”

Pei walked beside it without stooping. The chamber had been arranged for someone who wanted to see the entire machine while other people moved individual parts.

“The old system assumes a recognized current at every junction,” he said. “That lets one pattern coordinate many bodies. It also lets an error travel farther than it should.”

He touched one of the figures.

Blue light moved through the nearest channel. The next figure brightened, then the next. Water passed under a raised silver shutter, filling a reservoir whose level made a tiny wheel turn.

Su Fan leaned forward despite himself.

At the damaged junction, the light doubled back.

The first figure brightened again before the last had gone dark.

He felt his burned hand close a little. Pain made him open it.

“All linked to the same instruction,” he said.

“Within the station, yes.”

“Separate the returns.”

“That requires rebuilding the root formation. We are already doing so. It will not be complete before the rains.”

The assistant at the far end changed a setting. The doubled light now reached two adjoining figures. Their little shutters moved out of order, and water overtopped one of the channels into a collecting tray.

Pei stopped the sequence with a touch.

The assistant emptied the tray. There was no alarm, no damaged village below this spill, no man whose chest continued moving after he tried to stop.

“Why not isolate the faulty junction?” Su Fan asked.

The elder pointed to the adjacent returns.

“Because it receives part of their correction and supplies part of theirs. You can remove a wheel from a cart. You cannot assume it will then travel as a better three-wheeled cart.”

Su Fan studied the crossing lines. He had seen the obvious place to cut and not what depended on it.

“I don't understand this part.”

“Few people outside the formation office do.”

Pei named two routes, then indicated where one carried timing and the other carried a correction to the load. Su Fan could follow the difference when the elder demonstrated it. He could not have rebuilt either from the explanation.

That, too, was part of the offer.

***

Pei took a plain iron piece from a padded box.

It was smaller than Su Fan's palm, without the elaborate carving of the surrounding components. Its edge had been worn bright where it fitted into a holder. An assistant brought the holder forward and kept a cloth beneath it until the elder had taken the weight.

“A neutral interval,” Pei said.

He placed the piece in the empty socket.

The blue sequence began again.

Light travelled through the first channel and into the next. At the plain iron, the founder's pattern ceased to carry across. Water continued moving.

Su Fan watched the far side.

The next return began from its own place instead of inheriting the error behind it. The tiny shutter rose. Water passed through at the expected level. The little wheel turned once and settled.

“It works.”

“For this interval.”

Pei waited.

The iron piece began to tremble in its holder. A note too high to be comfortable came from somewhere beneath the model. The assistant at the measuring station raised a hand.

The elder stopped the test before Su Fan could decide which change mattered most.

“The fragment is costly and unstable,” Pei said. “It is not an answer we can multiply across the system merely because it behaved usefully for a short demonstration.”

The assistant lifted it with the holder. He did not touch the iron directly. A faint darkening remained around the socket after it was removed.

“You may be capable of providing a living equivalent.”

Su Fan looked at the empty place.

“A gate fitting.”

“A technician.”

“Would I be able to leave it?”

“Once we knew how to disconnect you safely.”

The model's water whispered through its channels.

Su Fan had lifted a hot pin for seconds. He remembered the moment before entering the coupling, when he had looked for another person free to act and found Sun Lian holding the shutter, Han trapped and Tan Wei unable to move.

Pei was proposing that he occupy a useful place deliberately, for as long as the works required him.

“What happens if the return catches me after all?”

“That is among the questions the study would answer.”

“While I am connected.”

“Under controlled conditions before any full assignment.”

The conditions might be controlled. He could see the collecting trays, the instruments, the people whose work was to notice changes before a failure spread. He could also see how much of the proposed safety depended on information the study did not yet possess.

“How many people have you tested?”

“None with your properties.”

“That wasn't my question.”

The elder's gaze sharpened.

Su Fan had spoken too quickly. He felt the mistake in the room before he decided whether it was a mistake he should withdraw.

He left it there.

“Twelve candidates,” Pei said. “No fatalities. Three lasting injuries. All compensated.”

Su Fan was glad Mother Wei was not in the chamber to hear the last two words standing together.

“What injuries?”

“Damage to circulation. Loss of reliable use of the affected routes. The medical records can be made available to the physician responsible for your assessment.”

“To me?”

“With explanations you would need to understand them.”

He was not refusing the question. That made Su Fan angrier in a less convenient way. There was no hidden cruelty he could expose with one brave sentence and leave the entire proposal discredited.

“Did they know it could happen?”

“They consented to experimental work.”

Su Fan thought of a desk by a window, a mattress thicker than the boards below, and a stipend whose size made ordinary worries grow quiet while a man read the first page.

He also thought of the operators in the station. Refusing the socket would not make their return safer.

“Why me, rather than another fragment?”

“Because you maintained independent movement in a captured system. Because your route sustained useful force afterward. Because you learn, adapt and recover in ways a piece of iron does not.”

The description sounded almost flattering until Su Fan heard the recovery included among the properties being offered to the works.

He studied the model until he could speak without anger.

“I won't sign this.”

Pei took the paper from him.

“Not today,” he said.

Su Fan could not tell whether the distinction was patience or possession.

***

By the time he reached Mudgate, the offer had improved considerably.

Auntie Lu's version included an estate, three servants and a marriage to an unspecified niece.

“Which niece?” she demanded.

“There is no niece.”

“Then the rest of the offer had better be excellent.”

“It is a room.”

“A room in an estate?”

“A room in a building.”

“With servants?”

“People work there.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You have a gift for making news disappointing.”

He laughed because he needed to. The laugh surprised him with how tired it sounded.

Pock wanted to know whether the elder had recognized a rare founder in him. A neighbour asked whether the position meant the household levy would be reduced. Someone else had heard that he was going away that evening and came to claim a repair before departure.

Su Fan gave the answers he had. No founder had been discovered. He had not accepted a position. He did not know what would happen to the levy. The pot handle still belonged at the smithy, and he would not be repairing it with a newly burned hand.

The owner looked at the bandage and apologized.

That ordinary correction nearly undid the composure he had managed before Pei.

At the clinic, Mother Wei read the agreement after checking his dressings. She asked what the model had shown him. He described it, including the unstable fragment and the three lasting injuries.

She sat very still at that part.

“Did you sign?”

“No.”

“Good. Now tell me what you understood, not merely what you disliked.”

It took longer.

He could describe the doubled return. He could explain why the neutral interval stopped one instruction from travelling onward. He could not explain the root formation or say whether another design would work better.

Mother Wei did not fill the gaps with reassurance. She wrote down the questions he would need answered if the offer returned.

He left the clinic carrying the agreement and a separate sheet that made it no easier to decide what the system ought to do without him.

***

At the smithy, Duan read slowly.

Ah-Du had been told not to interrupt and therefore found three quiet errands directly behind the smith's chair. On the third journey, Duan handed him a bucket and named a distant water tap.

The boy went.

“Renewal at their choice,” Duan said.

“Yes.”

“That's not ninety days.”

“No.”

The smith turned back to the first page. He did not dismiss the wage. He read it, looked toward the stock that had to be made into saleable work, and read it again.

“What do you want?”

Su Fan almost answered with what he wanted to prevent. Confiscation. Binding. A lifetime attached to a machine whose failures would become reasons to keep him longer.

Duan waited.

“I want to learn this properly,” Su Fan said. “Enough that I don't have to guess every time. I want work that pays. I want to be able to go somewhere without somebody's leave.”

The smith nodded.

“Then keep those things separate. An offer can give you one and take the other two.”

“Do you think I should refuse it?”

“You already have, for today.”

“And later?”

“Later you should know what you're saying yes to. Or what you're giving up by saying no.”

Su Fan looked at the new file on his bench. He had used it for less than a morning before burning the hand meant to hold it. The tool did not reproach him. It simply waited for the next job, which was more than he could say for most of the questions arriving from uphill.

Duan pushed the agreement back.

“Get another reader.”

“Wei has read it. Jiang helped me with the terms.”

“Someone who doesn't have to work in the same room as the man offering them.”

Su Fan thought of Min Yao, her little shop and the way she had asked what he was actually trying to accomplish before copying a document.

He took the agreement to the temporary correspondence address used for her work. The clerk there could send a copy with the next packet for Siltbridge. Su Fan paid for the copying as well as the carriage, because he wanted the original available if another messenger came from Pei.

Holding the brush awkwardly between his less injured fingers, he added a note.

He did not ask her to prove that the offer was a trap.

He asked which obligations continued after the stated term, which choices remained his and which phrases a reasonable reader might mistake for promises they did not contain.

The clerk sanded the wet ink and set the sheet aside to dry.

“Reply to the smithy?”

“Yes.”

“Not the upper residence?”

“The smithy.”

Su Fan stayed until the address had been copied correctly. Then he went home, leaving the question with someone who did not need him to choose a particular answer.

chapters.title: The Meeting at the Schoolhouse
chapters.text:
The town did not agree about Su Fan.

He had known that in principle. It was less pleasant in a room full of people he had carried water for.

The schoolmistress had cleared the children's work from the longest table. She had left one drawing pinned to the wall, a careful picture of a duck with four legs. Old Pock examined it while people came in and said he had seen worse things brought out of the river. The schoolmistress moved him away from the drawing before he could explain.

Su Fan sat beside Duan. His bandaged hands rested on his knees. He had brought a copy of the elder's proposed agreement because the widow had asked to read it, not because he wished to spend an afternoon defending his refusal to everybody in Mudgate.

That distinction lasted until the rice farmer arrived.

“Someone from here, in there,” the farmer said. “That's how things improve.”

He had taken the place at the table where Su Fan expected the water map to go. He spoke to the room rather than to Su Fan.

“We complain that they don't know us. Now they want one of ours, and we complain about that.”

“They want his method,” the widow said. “Show me the terms.”

Su Fan pushed the paper toward her. She held it close to the window. The farmer waited, tapping a finger on the table with the impatience of a man whose best point had already been made.

Bao Shun stood at the back because the narrow benches pressed against his injured arm. His daughter had come to copy the names of labour volunteers. She had brought good paper and was guarding it from a cup somebody had set too near the edge.

“Will the study increase the river-work levy?” Bao Shun asked.

“I don't know,” Su Fan said.

“Is the stipend paid from the works?”

“I don't know that either.”

The farmer made a small dissatisfied sound.

“You might learn these things by going.”

A young mother, seated nearest the door with a sleeping child against her shoulder, shifted the child's weight.

“What about sanctions? They say an unregistered method can make a place answerable for harbouring it.”

“Who says?” Duan asked.

“My brother heard it at the storehouse.”

“From whom?”

She looked irritated, then tired.

“I don't know. That's why I'm asking here.”

Duan lowered his voice.

“So are we.”

Nobody asked Su Fan whether he wanted to be discussed. The agreement passed from the widow to the man beside her. Someone at the far end asked how much the stipend was. When he heard, his eyebrows rose.

“It would pay for a proper roof,” he said.

“Whose?” Auntie Lu asked.

The man spread his hands. “I was only saying.”

Su Fan looked toward the window. In the yard, two children were trying to throw a loop of string over a low branch. Every unsuccessful attempt was followed by an argument over whose turn it had actually been. He envied the smallness of their dispute.

Mother Wei waited until the room had spent some of its noise.

“He is not a public fitting,” she said.

The rice farmer reddened.

“I didn't say he was.”

“Then phrase your proposal so it doesn't require him to become one.”

“I have fields below the eighth gate. So do other people here. If he can help—”

“You can ask him.”

“I am asking.”

“You've been asking everybody except him.”

The farmer turned. Su Fan wished Mother Wei had let the argument continue without bringing him back into it, which was an unreasonable wish after everything he had resented about being left out.

“Wouldn't it be worth trying?” the man asked.

“The appointment can be renewed without my agreement,” Su Fan said. “They want copies of the source. They don't yet know how to disconnect the proposed work safely.”

“Perhaps they'll learn.”

“Perhaps.”

“And you won't help them learn?”

Su Fan pressed his palms against his knees and felt a warning pull beneath the dressings. He lifted them again.

“I haven't agreed to let them learn with me fastened to the thing.”

A few people looked away. The young mother's child stirred. She rocked him without taking her eyes off the paper.

Deng spoke from beside the door. The widowed ferryman had arrived late, carrying a bench he said needed repair. Auntie Lu said it had needed repair before he began carrying it around the town.

“What work is the elder offering?” he asked.

“Study,” Su Fan said. “Possibly gate operation.”

“Paid?”

“Yes.”

“Leave at the end?”

“Not necessarily.”

Deng nodded.

“Then we have the answer to the part we can vote on. Nothing.”

The farmer began again, but Deng held up a hand.

“We can vote on our water. Our labour. Our taxes. Not his body.”

Su Fan felt grateful enough to dislike it. He could hear the room settling around an answer supplied on his behalf, and part of him wanted to make clear that he could speak for himself. Another part knew that Deng had just made it easier for him to do so.

The widow saved him from saying something stiff.

“Then stop discussing his body and tell us about the evacuation marks.”

She folded the agreement along its original crease and returned it to Su Fan.

“The end clause is bad,” she said quietly. “That doesn't make the farmer's fear imaginary.”

“I know.”

“Good. We have enough imaginary things on the levy sheet.”

***

The water map took the farmer's place at the centre of the table.

It had to be turned twice before everyone agreed which corner represented the schoolhouse. Old Pock insisted the bend beside the ferry had been drawn too generously. The schoolmistress placed a stone on that corner and asked him to identify the houses rather than improve the river.

They divided the low quarter into lanes.

At first everybody named somebody else to do the checking. The cooper's neighbour was good with doors. The reed-cutter's eldest knew every house. Bao Shun could remember who lived behind which shop.

Bao Shun raised his damaged hand a little.

“I can remember from here. Don't put me down to lift anybody.”

Bao Mei drew a line through the task beside his name. Her father asked her to leave the checking work. They argued briefly about whether checking implied opening swollen doors. The schoolmistress wrote two separate headings, and the argument became something they could use.

Each lane needed two people, not one person who might already be carrying a relative uphill. Mother Wei unfolded a smaller sheet from the clinic. Some patients could walk with help. Some required a cart. Three would have to remain flat while moved.

“Three carts?” asked the farmer.

“Three people,” she said. “The carts are what we haven't found.”

The young mother put her child down on a blanket beside the wall. She knew of a handcart behind a grain shed, but its wheel had a split. Duan made a note. Another woman offered two lengths of sound cloth and then asked whether they would be returned. Nobody laughed at the question. Cloth was expensive, and a rescue plan that began by pretending it was not would remain a plan on paper.

Auntie Lu volunteered her storehouse as a food point.

“It has shelves. The shelves are above the last mark. Before somebody asks, no, that does not mean you can leave sacks in front of my stove.”

Deng said the stove would be a useful place to warm wet people.

“It would be a useful place to cook food, if people stopped explaining my own stove to me.”

Duan offered the smithy for tools and heavy stores.

Then his eyes went back to the map.

The newest mark passed through the workshop's yard. It sat above the level of the lowest stock rack, above the place where good steel waited wrapped in oilcloth until a customer could pay for it.

For a moment he looked old.

“We'll move the good steel higher,” Su Fan said quietly.

“Tomorrow.”

“No. Tonight.”

Duan turned toward him with the beginning of a familiar expression. He had work to finish. The higher store was borrowed space. Moving everything meant finding it again when a job came in.

He looked at the map and stopped.

It was one of the few disagreements Su Fan won without enjoying it.

At the other end of the table, Deng and Old Pock had begun arguing over boats.

“Eight,” Deng said.

“Six comfortably.”

“We're not taking them out for pleasure.”

“Then they won't mind arriving alive.”

Sun Lian, who had been comparing the landing places with the proposed routes, put down her brush.

“Which eight?”

Deng looked at her.

“Eight people.”

“Children? Patients? Adults carrying their bedding? Eight of him?” She pointed at the rice farmer, who looked offended before deciding whether the remark might be flattering. “And who rows?”

Old Pock began explaining his six. Sun Lian listened, then asked the same questions again.

They left the map weighted on the table and went down to the landing with sacks.

***

The demonstration attracted people who had refused to attend the meeting.

One man said he had always known the boat could take more. Another said it sat too low before anything had been put into it. Old Pock told both to stand where their opinions would not obstruct the rope.

Sun Lian had the sacks carried aboard in stages. Deng stood where he would work the oar. A second man sat in the place proposed for someone unable to balance without help.

With the first load, the boat seemed reassuringly steady.

With the next, a little water came through a seam Deng had expected to remain well above the surface.

“That one needs work,” he said.

“Yes,” Sun Lian replied. “And you have put your passenger over the loose board.”

The man shifted. The boat rolled enough to make the spectators' amusement turn into a brief, collective intake of breath. Nobody was in danger of being swept away at the tied landing. That did not make the movement pleasant.

Deng steadied them with the oar and looked at the remaining sacks on shore.

“All right,” he said.

Old Pock smiled.

Then they tested his boat.

His estimate had been optimistic too.

The rice farmer helped remove the sacks afterward. He said nothing about Su Fan's appointment. When one of the loads caught against the landing, he lifted his end without waiting to be asked and stood holding it while the knot was freed.

Sun Lian marked the usable capacity beside each boat's name. The figures were smaller than the numbers offered in the warm schoolroom. She added the places where another trip would be needed and asked who would remain with the people waiting.

That question produced a longer silence than the first one.

Su Fan watched the ferry bump gently against the landing. He could hold more weight than he had in spring. He could not turn two journeys into one by wishing to be useful. His bandaged hands would not even let him take an oar properly that afternoon.

He carried the list back instead.

At the schoolhouse, the schoolmistress read the changed figures, moved two names to a different route and asked for another volunteer.

This time somebody offered his own name.

***

Qiu Lan came to collect a list of labour volunteers for the upper works.

She found Su Fan outside, copying the final names while the adults argued over whose handwriting was least likely to be misread in the rain. Bao Mei had already produced the cleanest copy. She let them argue until they noticed.

“Tan Wei says you're good at iron,” Qiu Lan told him.

“Duan is.”

“People can praise two men without one losing a share.”

He accepted that with a nod and gave her the list.

She checked the days offered beside each name. One man had promised a whole week although his wife had already explained that he would be away selling reed mats for three of those days. Qiu Lan asked which part of him the works were expecting to receive while the rest travelled.

The man amended his offer.

She had finished her temporary training and intended to return to her father's repair shop after the season. The gate wages would buy a new grinding wheel. She described the old one to Duan when he came out: a stone worn unevenly enough that her father had begun pretending the rhythm of its turning was useful for particular jobs.

“I've heard that explanation,” Duan said.

“Does it ever become true?”

“Not on the occasions I used it.”

They walked to the water-lift axle stored beside the shed. Qiu Lan knelt to inspect the fit and asked what had happened when the shaft first took its working load. Su Fan started with the successful arrangement. She asked what they had changed before reaching it.

He told her about the earlier problem.
