“That is the part I needed,” she said. “I can't afford your finished version. I need to avoid paying for your first one.”

Duan offered her a price on a spindle. She asked whether that included finishing the shoulders to her drawing. He said it depended on whether her drawing deserved to be followed. She took out a folded sheet.

By the time they had finished, she had a price she could consider and Duan had a promise to send customers from her village. Neither was obliged to admire the other's cultivation for the arrangement to work.

As she left, Qiu Lan asked whether Su Fan was keeping the next day free for the upper crew.

“I've been told to keep my hands out of work.”

She glanced at the dressings.

“Then keep them out. We need somebody who can read the marks too.”

He nearly said he could manage a little lifting. The tightness beneath the cloth answered before he did.

“I'll ask Wei.”

“Ask her what work you can do, not whether she thinks you mean well.”

He laughed. Qiu Lan looked surprised, then pleased, and went to catch the departing ferry.

***

They moved the good steel before dark.

Duan had to unwrap each bundle to identify it. He had meant to mark the covers properly months earlier. Now he stood in the yard naming each length while Ah-Du wrote on scraps and Su Fan checked the list against the space available uphill.

Bao Shun lent them a handcart. Two of the meeting volunteers helped push it. The route was short and steep enough to make everybody revise what they had expected one journey to accomplish.

Su Fan walked beside the load with a lamp he did not yet need. He wanted to put his shoulder behind it. Instead he warned the men at the bend, moved a loose stone with his foot and kept the list dry when a jar tipped in the borrowed storeroom.

Duan stood looking at the empty lower rack when they returned.

“Feels robbed,” he said.

“It's in the store.”

“I know where it is.”

Ah-Du began sweeping the newly exposed floor. Beneath the rack were old scales, two bent nails and a small iron wedge nobody admitted losing. Duan picked up the wedge and put it in his pocket. The movement restored something familiar to his face.

Su Fan went back to the schoolhouse for the last chairs.

He found Auntie Lu and Deng arguing over the broken bench.

“I said repair the leg,” she told him.

“I did.”

“You've made it shorter.”

“Only the broken one.”

“What am I meant to do with a bench that leans?”

“Sit uphill.”

She looked ready to hit him with it.

Then she laughed.

Deng reached for the bench again, smiling despite his effort to look offended. Su Fan lifted the lightest chair by its back and took it outside, leaving them to decide which end of the bench was going to be uphill.

chapters.title: Medicine
chapters.text:
The burns became infected along the edge of Su Fan's right palm.

He had kept the dressing clean. He had also gone back to work too soon and sweated through it. The distinction had seemed less important when he was standing beside work that needed doing.

Mother Wei removed the cloth and asked him not to explain.

“I hadn't begun.”

“Your mouth had.”

He shut it.

She set the dressing aside. He watched her expression rather than the wound, which was a habit she disliked because it made him answer questions she had not asked.

“How long has it hurt like this?”

“Since yesterday.”

“And before yesterday?”

“It hurt differently.”

She looked up.

He explained the difference. This time he gave her the dull ache during the steel move, the heat beneath the cloth afterward and the sharper pain that had woken him. He did not improve the sequence by placing the useful work before every foolish choice.

Mother Wei listened to the end.

“That's an answer,” she said. “We'll keep it.”

The clinic's shutters were open. Outside, a man was trying to persuade his child that a splinter could not be negotiated out of a foot. The child proposed going home and waiting for it to change its mind. Su Fan would have preferred that arrangement himself.

Mother Wei cleaned the wound while he stared at the ceiling.

There was a patch above the lamp that had been repaired with a slightly different colour of plaster. He had meant to finish smoothing its edge. Now he found himself examining the join so intently that he almost asked where she kept the scraper.

“Don't look for work up there,” she said.

He brought his eyes down.

A new bottle stood beside her instruments. Its seal came from Siltbridge. The wrapping was better than anything the clinic normally bought for a single patient, and the little box had been fitted to stop the glass striking its sides in transit.

“What's that?”

“Medicine.”

“What sort?”

“The expensive sort.”

He studied the seal. There were marks he could read and one he could not. In the city, sellers used seals to establish provenance, status and occasionally the size of the price they hoped an ignorant visitor would accept. He had learned not to confuse the three.

“Does it contain a cultivation impression?”

Mother Wei paused. When she answered, the teasing had gone from her voice.

“No. Prepared ingredients, no embedded lineage. It supports the healing tissue. It won't advance your realm.”

“I wasn't asking that.”

“I know. I was answering the fear beneath the question.”

He looked at the bottle again.

“Has it been used here before?”

“Yes.”

“With burns?”

“Yes.”

She let him ask the remaining questions. She could tell him what the medicine was intended to help and what she would be watching. She could not tell him the exact morning on which he would regain an ordinary grip. Nor did she promise that his own circulation would make the treatment easier.

When he had finished, she waited.

“Use it,” he said.

The relief was slow. That helped him trust it more than an immediate miracle would have, though he knew that preference was not evidence. His suspicion of an impressive result was no more reliable than somebody else's hunger for one.

He kept his hand still while she worked.

The child outside began crying. The father apologized through the doorway before anyone had asked him to. Mother Wei told him there was no need. Then she finished Su Fan's dressing and went to see them.

Su Fan sat with his hand raised where she had put it. Through the doorway he saw her crouch to the child's height. The boy had hidden his foot behind his father's leg. She did not drag it out. She asked him to show her where he had been walking, and he began a long account that included the unfairness of another boy owning better shoes.

By the time she returned, the crying had stopped.

She held out the bill.

Su Fan looked at the sum.

“How much?”

“You heard me.”

“I could have waited.”

“For the infection to become cheaper?”

He had kept part of his Siltbridge earnings in a little cloth purse apart from the ordinary workshop money. He knew what he had imagined buying with it. None of those purchases had involved sitting very still while somebody explained how much trouble he could cause by refusing to sit still.

He took out the purse.

The knot resisted his left hand. Mother Wei did not reach for it immediately. She waited until he asked, then loosened it and put it back where he could count.

He paid.

“Will that cover the next dressing?” he asked.

She showed him what was included.

He read the bill again, folded it and put it inside the emptied part of the purse. He was angry at the expense, at the wound, at himself for having made the wound more expensive. None of those feelings offered a better treatment.

Before he left, Mother Wei wrote down the work he was not to do.

He read the list.

“This leaves very little.”

“Then you'll have a short day.”

***

Duan took the list without comment.

That was worse than the comment Su Fan had expected.

The smith read it once, put it beside the day's orders and moved two jobs to a different part of the slate. One needed work Su Fan could usually do alone. The other had been promised for the following afternoon.

“I can mark the lengths,” Su Fan said.

“You can tell Ah-Du which marks are yours. He has already cut one piece to a measurement you never wrote down.”

The boy looked up from the bench.

“It was the sensible length.”

“For a different customer.”

Su Fan sat beside him and went through the order. The task should have been simple. It took longer because he had to explain where he had kept information in his head, why one shoulder needed extra material and which old drawing should no longer be followed.

Ah-Du listened, asked two questions and then pointed at a line Su Fan had forgotten to change.

“This one too?”

“Yes.”

“So I was nearly right.”

“You were right to ask.”

“That sounds like a smaller reward.”

“It is.”

The boy grinned and returned to the metal.

By midday Su Fan had watched other people complete work he wanted to take back. Duan did not permit him to make himself useful by hovering over every blow. When he corrected Ah-Du for the third time, the smith sent him to sort the delivery slips on the dry bench outside.

“There's nothing wrong with watching,” Su Fan said.

“There is when somebody has to keep stepping around you.”

He moved.

The yard was warm. He sorted the slips slowly with his left hand and held them down with the smallest of his practice stones. The old weights looked absurdly innocent beside the bill in his purse. He had used them to measure what he could do. He had not used them to measure how little he could leave alone.

A customer arrived for the delayed job. Su Fan told her it would not be ready at the promised time.

She glanced at his hand and softened, but only enough to avoid raising her voice.

“I arranged to be here today.”

“I know.”

“I can't come back tomorrow.”

They found another day. It cost her a different journey and Duan an inconvenient place in the work order. Su Fan wrote the new arrangement down instead of promising to finish it secretly after the forge cooled.

That evening he began a list of the cost of being injured.

Medicine came first because it was easiest to count. Lost work followed. Extra food. Bandages. He reached other people's time and stopped.

Mother Wei had spent part of a morning on him. Ah-Du had done work that would otherwise have taught him something different. Duan would stay later to finish the shifted order. The customer had altered her plans.

He could not turn all of that into a fair total by inventing prices.

He wrote the tasks and names instead.

The list was longer than he liked. It did not tell him how to repay anyone. It kept him from pretending the bottle had been the whole cost.

He put it away with the bill.

***

The next days were made of small restrictions.

He learned which fastenings he could manage one-handed and which would remain half-tied until somebody noticed. He became remarkably interested in whether cups had handles. He discovered that a book which lay flat on the table was easier to read than one he had spent months binding too tightly for its own good.

The scripture stayed closed during the worst of the pain. He did not want every uncomfortable sensation to become evidence for a theory he already preferred.

Mother Wei changed the dressing and asked ordinary questions. Had he slept? Had he eaten? Had he used the hand when told not to?

The third answer required more care than the first two.

At the lifting wheel he was permitted to observe the fit and carry a wrench. He could point out a damaged binding, but somebody else had to tighten it. The work still progressed. This was a relief and, at certain embarrassing moments, an annoyance.

Ruan Zhi found him there near the end of the week.

Su Fan had the wrench in his left hand and was holding it as though a man carrying such a small object might be mistaken for a person at leisure.

“I hear you met Elder Pei,” Ruan said.

“Briefly.”

“His interest is rarely brief.”

Ruan looked at the bandages.

“Those from the meeting?”

“From before it.”

“Good.”

He did not sound entirely convinced.

“The keeper at the gate,” Su Fan said. “You heard about the shift test?”

“I heard five versions. In one, you fought the elder. In another, you were already his disciple. I assumed both had been told by people standing a useful distance away.”

Su Fan put the wrench back where it belonged.

“Neither is true.”

“That improves the afternoon.”

They walked along the channel. Ruan had dust on his boots and a folded report tucked into his sash. He had come to inspect his aunt's tenant lands and had found the upper fields receiving more water than the revised schedule allowed.

“I ordered the excess diverted back,” he said.

“Did she agree?”

“Not yet. I wrote first. It gives her something to be angry at in the correct order.”

“Will she reverse it?”

“She may. Then I'll have to decide whether I prefer her money to being able to sign my own reports.”

He said it without asking Su Fan to admire him.

They passed a narrow inlet where a boy was clearing reeds from the mouth. Ruan stopped to watch the water run after the obstruction came free. The boy looked up, saw the sash and began explaining who had told him to work there.

“We're not inspecting you,” Ruan said.

The boy looked relieved and then mildly disappointed. He had done the work properly and had been ready to say so.

Ruan noticed.

“Good clearance.”

The boy nodded with sudden gravity and went back to his bundle.

“You could have put the excess down as a mistake,” Su Fan said when they had gone on.

“It was a mistake in the allocation. That doesn't mean it moved the water by itself.”

“And the tenants?”

“Some were grateful. Some wanted me to decide after their next turn. One spent a long time explaining that his cousin's land had received too much last year, which he seemed to think made the water ours now.”

Su Fan smiled.

“What did you say?”

“That I would include his cousin in the report if he wanted.”

“Did he?”

“No.”

Ruan stepped over a washed-out place in the path. Su Fan followed, slightly late, and had to alter his next step to avoid bringing his hand against the bank.

Ruan looked back.

“Oh, that will never do.”

***

He drew his practice sword beside a stone marker.

“Feet only. Your hands are a disgrace.”

Su Fan looked at the blade.

“Here?”

“The ground won't flatter you.”

“I wasn't expecting a lesson.”

“Neither was I. Then you tried to walk through a hole.”

Su Fan took his place with his injured hands kept clear. Ruan did not begin with a flourish. He asked him to move back, turn beside the marker and stop before the slope carried his weight farther than he intended.

The first attempt was ordinary enough. Su Fan made it harder by wanting it to look easy.

Ruan touched the side of his coat before he had finished correcting his stance.

“Again.”

Su Fan used the circuits to recover more quickly on the next attempt. The recovery was indeed quicker. Ruan's blade arrived during it.

“You are very fast at being late,” he said.

They slowed down.

The lesson was humiliatingly useful. A root changed where Su Fan could place his foot. A loose edge forced him to choose whether to shorten the step or turn sooner. When he treated the bank like the flat yard behind the smithy, he spent strength repairing a decision he could have avoided.

Ruan gave him time to see the difference. Then he changed the direction of the approach so Su Fan could not merely repeat the successful answer.

On one turn, Su Fan stopped a little too hard. His shoulder moved toward the marker. He caught himself with a step rather than the hand, but the shock pulled at the dressing.

Ruan lowered the sword immediately.

“How much?”

“Enough to stop.”

“An astonishing answer. You should use it more often.”

They rested beside the channel. Ruan sat first, making it unnecessary for Su Fan to decide whether sitting looked like surrender. A leaf travelled past them on the water, turned twice in an eddy and escaped downstream.

When they resumed, Ruan shortened the exercise. Su Fan placed his foot well once, then twice. The difference in their speed mattered less when he did not begin by giving away the place he needed to stand.

Not little. Less.

He still could not get past Ruan simply by noticing where the root was. The other man had noticed it too and had considerably more practice at making that knowledge unpleasant.

They stopped when Mother Wei appeared at the end of the lane.

Ruan bowed with the instinct of a well-raised man approaching danger.

She inspected Su Fan's hands, then Ruan's sword.

“No gripping?”

“No,” Ruan said.

“No falling?”

“Very little.”

She looked at him.

“None worth mentioning,” he corrected.

Mother Wei took Su Fan home. She did not forbid him to think about his feet. She did insist that he give his hands the rest they had failed to receive while he was congratulating himself on not using them.

At the clinic door, Ruan called after him.

“I'm glad the medicine helped.”

Su Fan touched the edge of the new dressing with his sound fingers.

“Are you?”

“Yes. It would be tedious to win forever because you couldn't close your hand.”

For the first time all week, Su Fan laughed without feeling the sound catch on something sore.

chapters.title: Iron Step
chapters.text:
The fourth stage did not arrive because Su Fan understood himself better.

It arrived after forty-three days of correcting the same movement.

The count began in his notebook, with an untidy drawing of a foot and a complaint about the old injury above it. Some of the following days contained measurements. Some contained only a description of what had gone wrong. During the worst of the burns, there were gaps marked *rest*, written more firmly by Mother Wei than the surrounding entries.

He had not enjoyed counting those days as part of the work.

He counted them now because leaving them out would make the result look easier to repeat than it had been.

From the beginning, he had misunderstood the transfer of weight. He sent force down the leg he trusted instead of through the frame supporting him. Standing still, he could disguise the difference. Under a changing load, his body tightened along a familiar route and twisted the place it was trying to protect.

Sun Lian's relief mechanism helped him see it.

Duan's blunt criticism helped him accept it.

Ruan's practice sword ensured he could not hide from it.

None of them had given him the completed movement. Each had shown him a different part of the same bad habit. Su Fan had spent the days between their observations discovering how readily a correction made in one situation disappeared in another.

He could stand well in the yard and step badly onto a bank. He could carry an ordinary load without waste and ruin the arrangement as soon as someone watched closely enough to make him want to demonstrate it.

The scripture gave the movement a plain name: Iron Step.

He had expected something more impressive for the amount of work it required.

Ah-Du offered to improve the name for a fee.

“What would you call it?” Su Fan asked.

“That's the part you pay for.”

“Then I'll keep the old one.”

The boy considered this an unfortunate example of poverty obstructing art.

They were in the yard, where the little four-post frame still stood beneath the eaves. Ah-Du's version had lost its red flag and acquired a second purpose as a place to dry cleaning cloths. It performed that work considerably better than it had carried weights.

Su Fan moved the model's hanging load with his sound fingers. One brace tightened. Another loosened. He watched the feet rather than the weight.

Duan came out carrying a length of timber.

“If you're going to test yourself,” he said, “we'll do it where the ground is sound.”

Su Fan looked up.

“I thought you wanted me to stop.”

“I wanted you to stop choosing tests whose result was whether somebody could fetch Wei quickly enough.”

“That wasn't the result.”

“It became an important part of it.”

***

The test used a suspended log.

Duan would not allow a boulder. Mother Wei would not allow Duan's first proposed log. She regarded it, regarded Su Fan's hands, and asked whether they had mistaken the clinic for a place with empty beds and unlimited cloth.

They compromised on a timber heavy enough to bruise Su Fan and light enough that two ordinary men could stop it.

Sun Lian tied the safety line. She had come to inspect a fitting and found the yard occupied by people selecting an object with which to strike somebody they liked.

“This is a practice,” she said. “Nobody earns extra respect for making the healer busy.”

She checked the timber's course, moved a stool that had no business being anywhere near it, and made Ah-Du stand where he would not be tempted to help by darting between the load and the person stopping it.

He objected to the assumption.

“Then you won't find the position difficult,” she said.

Su Fan stood on dry earth. His palms were protected, but the exercise did not require him to catch the log. Duan showed him the part of the timber that would meet his shoulder and upper body. They tried the path at a harmless distance first, with Su Fan stepping aside while the safety line took the movement.

He noticed how much he disliked stepping aside in front of an audience.

That was useful to know before they increased the load.

The first swing pushed him back three steps.

He stayed upright. Ah-Du made an approving noise. Duan stopped the timber and shook his head.

“You held your breath before it reached you.”

“I knew it was coming.”

“Yes. That was meant to help.”

Su Fan reset his feet. The earth carried three clear scuffs behind him. He had spent the last step saving himself from the correction he made during the first.

On the second swing, he decided too firmly where he intended to remain.

His knee buckled.

The safety line tightened. Duan and the second man brought the timber away before Su Fan's attempt to rise could put him beneath it again. Sun Lian kept her eyes on his leg.

He straightened slowly, felt along the movement without pressing on the injury, and stepped out of the marked space.

“We stop,” he said.

Nobody argued.

That surprised him more than it should have. He had imagined his own reluctance would need to be defeated by somebody else's authority. Instead they simply lowered the timber and made room for him to sit.

Mother Wei checked the knee. The old injury had protested; he had not earned the right to ignore it merely because the protest was familiar. She asked him to describe the point at which he had felt the movement catch.

“Before the weight came through,” he said. “I locked it because I expected the push.”

Sun Lian knelt beside the marks in the earth.

“And then you tried to send the whole load down that side.”

He nodded.

She drew a short line with a twig, then another.

“Your frame does the same thing when you tighten this brace too far.”

“My frame has fewer opinions.”

“It also doesn't pretend it can stand on one corner because it's embarrassed about the other three.”

Duan gave Su Fan water. They rested long enough for the excitement to leave the exercise. Ah-Du lost interest in waiting and began discussing whether Iron Step would be improved by the addition of the word *thunder*.

Mother Wei told him that thunder was usually a warning to go indoors.

He withdrew the proposal.

They adjusted the timber's height before trying again. Su Fan looked at the ground, the line, the men holding it and the place where he could step away. None of those things had become less necessary because he had understood his mistake.

This time he did not attempt to become immovable.

He let the arriving load travel through the route he had trained, down into the ground and back through a small, controlled bend. The tightening that usually caught above the old injury began, faltered and loosened without his forcing it open.

A fourth return joined the others.

The log struck.

His boots dug two shallow trenches.

He remained upright.

Pain ran through his calves. Not the sharp pain that had stopped the previous attempt. The ordinary pain of muscle doing difficult work. His shoulder ached where the timber had met it, and his breath came out in an ugly sound he was glad nobody immediately repeated.

Duan stopped the log.

Su Fan stood very still, afraid that moving too quickly would turn what had happened into something he had only imagined.

“Step out,” Mother Wei said.

He did.

The new circuit did not disappear when he bent his knee. He could feel where the return passed, incomplete in places but connected. He wanted to follow it again at once, to prove it with a weight, a stride, anything more impressive than standing while a healer examined his pulse.

Mother Wei kept hold of his wrist.

“Stay here.”

He stayed.

Nobody cheered until she finished checking him.

Then Ah-Du cheered enough for everyone.

***

The marks in the earth were smaller than Su Fan expected.

Two shallow trenches. A broken crust of dry soil at one heel. They looked like the evidence of an awkwardly moved cart rather than something he had spent forty-three days trying to do.

He crouched beside them carefully.

Sun Lian was loosening the line. Duan and the other man lowered the timber onto blocks. Already the yard was becoming a place for ordinary work again. Someone would need the rope later. The stool had to go back indoors. Ah-Du had a half-finished task he had been permitted to abandon while the test occupied everyone else.

Su Fan wanted to ask for a heavier log.

The desire arrived with such immediate confidence that he almost admired it. He had barely finished discovering one limit before wanting an object large enough to make the discovery look worthy of the effort.

He recognized it quickly enough to sit down instead.

Duan noticed.

“Good choice.”

“I hadn't said anything.”

“You were looking at the woodpile.”

Su Fan looked away from the woodpile.

He wrote the result down after eating. The first two failures occupied as much space as the final trial. He included the safety line, the rest, the changed height and the way his boots had moved.

At the bottom he wrote that the route remained present during ordinary walking across the yard. He did not write that he could stop a cart or stand against a higher cultivator. Neither had been tested.

Ah-Du read over his shoulder.

“You left out the cheering.”

“It didn't affect the circuit.”

“It improved the occasion.”

Su Fan gave him the brush. The boy added a small note in the margin, then returned it without trying to rename the technique.

Duan took the timber back to its place. It would become part of a repair. Su Fan liked that. He had no wish to keep the thing that had struck him as a monument in the yard.

***

Pei Gang's assistant came that evening.

Su Fan heard the footsteps before he saw the man at the gate. He had been stretching his sore calves with the care of someone newly convinced that a successful exercise could still leave him limping through supper.

The assistant carried a folded notice, not another copy of the study agreement.

“Your refusal has been recorded,” he said.

Su Fan stood.

The elder would allow continued practice under limited conditions while Jiang completed an observational report. No unauthorized entry into active formations. No teaching at scale. No departure from the district without notice during the review.

Su Fan read the last line twice.

“Notice,” he said. “Not permission.”

“That is the wording.”

“Whose wording?”

“Steward Jiang's revision.”

Duan had come to the doorway. He said nothing. Mother Wei was not there to argue over the paper, and Su Fan found that he could read it without waiting for somebody else to tell him which part ought to frighten him.

Min Yao's returned copy of the earlier agreement lay wrapped with his notes. Her comments had not transformed him into an expert. They had taught him to look for the difference between receiving a document and agreeing to everything it resembled.

He fetched the copy and compared the language.

The assistant waited with increasing stillness.

“I am acknowledging receipt,” Su Fan said. “Not accepting the study appointment.”

“The notice does not say you are accepting the appointment.”

“Then we agree on that.”

He marked the acknowledgment clearly and kept the copy left for him. His damaged hand made the writing slow. The assistant did not offer to make the mark on his behalf.

At the gate, the man glanced at the disturbed ground beneath the suspended rope.

“Practice?”

“Yes.”

“Record what you find.”

“I am.”

The assistant gave no indication whether the answer pleased him. He left with the signed receipt and the same measured steps with which he had arrived.

Duan waited until he was beyond the lane.

“That's a leash.”

“Yes.”

“Longer than the other one.”

“Yes.”

The smith looked at the marks outside.

“Don't confuse its length with its absence.”

Su Fan put the notice beside the refused agreement. They belonged together, though neither made the other simple.

***

He told Tan Wei about the fourth stage the next time they met.

He did it before his friend had to hear a rumour at the works or discover a new bruise whose explanation had been kept carefully short. Tan Wei listened while eating, then asked which movement had finally changed.

Su Fan showed him with an ordinary step rather than another swinging log.

Tan Wei watched twice.

“That looks easy.”

“It wasn't.”

“I assumed. You look offended enough.”

His friend was nearing the fifth stage through the lease. The pace made Han cautious and Ko Lin uncomfortable, though for different reasons. Tan Wei had begun learning which advice was meant to keep him well and which merely made the person giving it feel less troubled by his progress.

“I've been told to slow down,” he said.

“Will you?”

“I am slowing down. That's why I'm here eating instead of training.”

Su Fan nodded.

He had an opinion about the pace. He also knew that Han had actually watched Tan Wei work, while Su Fan had mostly imagined the consequences from a distance. He asked what slowing down meant in practice.

“Fewer ambitious attempts. More ordinary turns. Han says if I cannot repeat something when I'm bored, I haven't learned it as well as I think.”

“That sounds unpleasant.”

“It is. You'd be very good at teaching it.”

They ate beside the yard. Tan Wei inspected the remaining marks from the test and the place where the safety rope had been fastened.

“Can you stop a cart?”

“Depends how much cart.”

“A small cart.”

“Probably.”

“A rude cart?”

“More willingly.”

They smiled.

The friendship had not returned to its old ease. It had begun acquiring a different one, with pauses neither of them could pretend away. Sometimes Su Fan found himself considering a helpful suggestion and then asking whether it had been requested. Sometimes Tan Wei noticed the pause and looked annoyed that an ordinary conversation had become work.

They continued having the conversations anyway.

Tan Wei told him about an argument over the dormitory window. One recruit wanted it open, another believed the night air would undo every benefit of the day's practice, and Han had finally ordered both to change beds. Neither had liked discovering that the instruction did not establish who had been right.

Su Fan laughed and gave him the last piece of bread.

As Tan Wei left, he turned back.

“Tell me before the next dangerous test.”

“Why?”

“So I can help with the rope. Not so I can stop you.”

Su Fan took a moment before answering.

“All right.”

The following morning he opened the notebook to the next planned trial. Beneath the proposed weight, the place and the things he still did not know, he wrote Tan Wei's name.

chapters.title: The Wrong Side of Silence
chapters.text:
The new return housing hung above the platform, turning a little whenever the wind came through the gate.

Sun Lian stood where she could see both the crane and the receiving bed. She had already sent one man out of the narrow space beneath the load. Another waited with wedges in a tray. The old housing lay farther up the platform, its corroded edge wrapped so nobody would cut a leg against it while watching something overhead.

Su Fan guided the last span with a pole.

The iron was sound. Duan had inspected the fittings before they left the workshop. There were proper marks on the receiving bed and a clear place to withdraw when the housing came down. The work looked reassuringly ordinary after the arguments that had surrounded almost everything else at the eighth gate.

No cultivation inside the coupling. Ordinary labour only.

Su Fan had obeyed.

He shifted his grip on the pole. The skin beneath his dressings still disliked pressure, but he was not taking the load in his hands. Sun Lian had given him a position from which a small correction would be enough. If it ceased to be enough, he was to let the pole go.

The labourer beside him asked whether the housing would fit without further dressing.

“It should,” Su Fan said.

“Should?”

“We'll know when it is down.”

The young man smiled nervously. He was Ren Bo's nephew, sent over with a crew whose regular work had been interrupted by the new schedule. He had spent part of the morning telling Su Fan which relative was responsible for which piece of equipment, as though establishing those connections might make him less likely to be blamed for something he did not yet understand.

Su Fan had told him to watch the load instead.

Sun Lian raised a hand.

The housing descended another little distance.

Then the upper chain broke.

Later, three offices would disagree about which part of the routine had been authorized.

At the time, Su Fan saw only the load begin to turn.

The sound was a hard crack, followed by the scrape of iron against iron. The housing dropped on one side and swung toward the platform. The pole kicked against Su Fan's palm.

He released it.

The stone support stood behind him, broad enough to shelter two people if they got close and stayed low. He moved toward it without waiting to discover whether the remaining chain would hold.

Ren Bo's nephew did not move.

The young man's eyes were fixed on the place where the load had been. His hands remained open in front of him, prepared to help guide an object that was no longer approaching in any useful way.

Su Fan caught his belt and pulled.

The labourer stumbled against him. Together they struck the stone.

The housing hit the rail.

Iron burst outward.

A fragment struck the right side of Su Fan's head.

The world flashed white.

He found himself on one knee with somebody's boot near his face. Water washed across the platform. The boot moved, vanished and appeared somewhere he had not expected it to be.

He could hear shouting from very far away, though mouths moved close enough to touch.

He tried to stand.

The ground went sideways.

A hand pressed him down.

Sun Lian's face appeared above him. Her lips formed his name. He knew the shape of it before he could find any sound to match.

On the right, there was nothing.

***

He remembered being moved in pieces.

A shoulder under his arm. A cloth against his head. The labourer repeating something about the belt. Somebody asking for a board, then another voice saying that the wider one was already coming.

Su Fan tried to explain that he could walk.

He did not know whether the words came out clearly. Sun Lian shook her head with enough force to make the answer unmistakable.

The sky tilted when they lifted him. He shut his eyes and discovered that the movement continued behind the lids. A deep rolling sickness rose through him, quite separate from the pain beginning along the side of his head.

He wanted the platform beneath his feet. He wanted a wall he could identify by putting his hand on it. The certainty that had usually arrived with a familiar place would not settle.

At some point he heard the river again.

It seemed to be on the wrong side.

He opened his eyes to look for it and saw only the underside of a carrying board, the edge of a sleeve, a patch of sky passing between roofs.

“Keep still,” somebody said.

He recognized Mother Wei's voice only when she touched his shoulder.

That frightened him more than the blood.

***

She cut the matted hair away from his ear.

Su Fan lay facing a wall whose plaster he knew. The familiarity helped until he turned his head and the room moved without permission.

“Don't do that again yet,” Mother Wei said.

“What happened?”

“A piece of the rail struck you.”

“The other man?”

“Out. Alive.”

He tried to ask about the housing. She told him Sun Lian was dealing with it. Then she asked questions he thought she already knew the answers to and waited until he answered them himself.

A small piece of the outer edge of his ear was missing. The deeper damage worried her more. She did not say that in the satisfied voice of someone naming a problem she could therefore solve. She watched his eyes, listened to his answers and made him follow a moving finger.

When he tried to sit, she supported him and waited through the sickness rather than demanding he demonstrate how little it troubled him.

It troubled him a great deal.

“I can hear you,” he said.

“From here.”

She moved.

He heard a sound, faint and strange, but did not know where to turn until he saw her again.

“Don't keep testing it,” she said when he tried to follow her next movement. “I need to know how you are. I don't need you to win an argument with the room.”

She put him in a darkened space behind the curtain and told everyone to stop making him prove he was awake.

Duan's voice came from outside. Su Fan caught his name, the word *chain*, then a quieter exchange he could not separate into sentences. He lifted his head to listen and immediately wished he had not.

Mother Wei came back without being called.

“Rest.”

“The link—”

“Will remain broken while you sleep.”

He let his head settle.

Sleep did not arrive cleanly. He drifted into it, woke with his heart beating as though the housing were still swinging toward him, and found the same dim cloth above the bed. Sometimes there was a hand near his shoulder. Sometimes he was alone.

The room rang.

The sound had no source. It continued when he covered his ears. It grew more noticeable when the clinic quieted, when the last conversation moved out into the lane and the bowls stopped touching one another in the kitchen.

He listened for a change that would tell him it was a pipe, a loose fitting or an insect trapped somewhere near the bed.

There was none.

He had spent years trusting small sounds. The forge told him when air stopped reaching a part of the fire. A load told him when its binding began to shift. Footsteps warned him which person was likely to come through the doorway before he looked up.

Now one sound would not leave, and the others would not stay where they belonged.

***

Tan Wei sat beside the bed when Su Fan woke again.

He had not heard him arrive.

His friend had a bowl on his knees and was trying to decide whether it was useful to remain motionless beside a person who might be sleeping. When Su Fan opened his eyes, Tan Wei moved too quickly and caught the bowl before it tipped.

“You're awake.”

“So they keep telling me.”

“Sun Lian says you dragged Ren Bo's nephew out.”

“He was in reach.”

“Still counts.”

Su Fan looked toward the door. Somebody had spoken there, but the voice seemed to have come from behind the curtain on the other side. He turned his head, felt the room begin to slide and stopped.

Tan Wei noticed.

“Right side?”

Su Fan nodded.

His friend moved the chair to the left without commenting.

The small action nearly undid him.

He concentrated on the bowl instead. It contained food he could manage without much chewing, and Tan Wei had brought a spoon that did not require an ambitious grip. Neither detail was announced as kindness.

“Did you eat?” Su Fan asked.

“Yes.”

“What?”

Tan Wei looked offended.

“You sound like Wei.”

“Answer.”

He named the meal, then added the thing he had bought afterward because it smelled better than the meal. Su Fan believed him. It was too ordinary an admission to have been invented for his benefit.

They sat quietly while he ate.

Tan Wei did not ask him to describe the accident again. He talked about the people waiting outside instead: Ah-Du, who had brought something from the smithy and had been told it was not needed; Duan, who had wanted to inspect the bandage as though the injury might submit to an argument about poor materials; the rescued labourer, who could not find a way to go home without saying thank you once more.

“Tell him he can go,” Su Fan said.

“I have.”

“And?”

“He seems to think leaving will undo the part where he survived.”

Su Fan closed his eyes.

“Don't send him in yet.”

“All right.”

Tan Wei stayed until the bowl was empty. When he stood, he moved into Su Fan's view before speaking.

It was such a deliberate thing. Su Fan wanted it to be unnecessary. He was grateful that it was done anyway.

***

Jiang came with the broken chain link.

Mother Wei let her enter after making her leave two accompanying questions outside with the clerk who had brought them. Su Fan sat supported against folded bedding. He had asked to be upright for the visit and was trying not to show how much of his attention the arrangement required.

Jiang placed the link on a cloth where he could see it without turning.

The fracture looked less dramatic than the damage it had caused.

A mark remained on the iron near one end. Su Fan recognized its purpose before she explained the record that went with it.

Replacement.

“The crane had been cleared for a lighter load,” Jiang said. “Not the housing used that morning.”

“Sun Lian was given the lowering.”

“Yes.”

“And the load?”

“A schedule revision combined two jobs. The regional inspector was due before the main rains. The office wanted both completed.”

Su Fan looked at the small mark again. It had been put there by someone who knew the link was no longer something to trust. The knowledge had survived. It had simply failed to govern what happened next.

“Who signed the revision?”

“Shen Tu's works officer. Confirmed by the captain.”

For a moment Su Fan heard the captain discussing wet oak and nail heads. He remembered the careful attention given to a paper windmill in the market. The recollection did not make the signature less real. It made the person behind it harder to place at a comfortable distance.

“Did they know it was marked?”

“That is one of the questions being examined.”

“Will it matter?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

Jiang looked at the bandage.

“I won't tell you a punishment before the inquiry. That would make me as careless with the record as they were with the crane.”

He disliked the answer. He knew why she gave it.

“Will the work stop?”

“The damaged lifting gear is out of service. The work that can be done safely elsewhere will continue.”

“And who decides safely?”

“The people whose decisions must now be checked against the actual equipment.”

He looked away. It was an answer about what should happen, not proof that it would. Jiang did not try to make it sound like more.

She asked for his account of the last lowering. He gave the position of the pole, Sun Lian's raised hand, the turn of the housing. At the flash he stopped.

“After that, I'm not certain.”

“Then that is where your account stops being certain.”

She marked the break in her notes.

The link went to Duan afterward, kept as evidence rather than thrown into scrap. Su Fan was glad he would not have to look at it every time he opened his eyes.

***

A week later, the dizziness had eased.

The ringing remained.

Mother Wei told him some hearing might return. She could not promise how much. She also told him that reaching a cultivation milestone was not a treatment plan.

He had not asked.

She knew him well enough to answer anyway.

He had tried following the four circuits while lying still, carefully, looking for a place where the movement might find the damaged part and make it whole. He had found sensations he could not interpret and a growing willingness to interpret them in the way he wanted.

He told her that.

She listened without ridicule. Then she asked him to stop experimenting on an injury whose changes he could not yet distinguish from the effects of his own effort.

He agreed, unhappily.

On his first walk outside, the lane seemed almost normal.

The sunlight hurt less than he expected. Somebody was washing a board beside the well. A customer argued with Auntie Lu about the size of a bowl, and Su Fan could hear every word of the complaint. He felt an unreasonable lift of hope. Perhaps the trouble was less than the dark room had made it seem.

A cart approached from the damaged side.

He heard it behind him and turned the wrong way.

The driver shouted. Tan Wei caught his shoulder and moved him clear.

A wheel passed close enough that Su Fan felt the brush of air against his trousers. The cart stopped beyond them. The driver began angrily, saw the bandage and lost the shape of the reprimand halfway through it.

Su Fan stood in the lane, breathing too fast.

He could still hear most things.

He no longer reliably knew where they were.

Tan Wei kept a hand on his shoulder until he asked him to let go. Neither mentioned the arrangement of the chair at the clinic. Su Fan had understood that kindness. This was the same need, made suddenly larger by a moving wheel.

They walked home by the quieter lane.

That evening he moved his sleeping mat so the wall protected his right side. He put the things he needed where he could find them without reaching behind him. The changes were small enough that anyone entering the room might not notice.

He noticed every one.

Before dark he went outside and practised looking over his right shoulder before crossing the lane.

He stopped at the edge. Looked. Turned enough to see the approach rather than trust where he thought a sound had begun. Waited for a woman carrying a basket to pass.

Then he crossed.

The motion was simple.

He hated needing it.

chapters.title: The Warning Marks
chapters.text:
Rain began in the hills while Mudgate's sky remained clear.

At first people treated this as a rumour. A carter had heard it from a man who had come down the northern road. A reed merchant said the upper crossings were slow. Someone else's cousin had seen worse rain in a drier year and did not understand why everyone was making a subject of it.

Then the river rose without local rain.

It carried branches from trees that did not grow in the valley. One lodged beneath the ferry landing, its leaves still green and a pale strip of root turning in the current. Old Pock examined it, pushed it clear with a pole and went to look at the marks on the wall.

By midday, people were visiting the same marks for different reasons.

Some wanted to know how much time they had. Others wanted proof that they had more time than their neighbours were saying.

Jiang ordered the first evacuation preparation.

Not an evacuation. Preparation.

The distinction kept half the town arguing for a day they could not afford to lose.

A man who would have left under an order refused to move his grain on a warning. The miller wanted to finish the batch already paid for. A woman said she could not carry her bedding uphill, bring it back, and still do the work that would pay for supper if the water went down again.

Su Fan understood all three. He also watched the river reach the next stone while they explained.

He helped move medicine chests to the upper schoolroom.

His head still rang. The first man who took the other end of a chest stood on his right and asked a question while looking away. Su Fan heard enough to believe he had understood and nearly lifted before the man was ready.

“Wait,” he said.

He set the chest down.

“My hearing is damaged on that side. Face me when you speak, or come to my left. If we're carrying together, I need to see when you start.”

The man looked at the bandage and nodded. He did not ask how badly. He moved where Su Fan could see him and repeated the question.

Saying it aloud felt worse the first time than the fifth.

By the fifth, it had become something he needed to tell people so a box would reach its destination without being dropped. The hurt pride remained, but it no longer had the entire task to itself.

At the schoolroom, Mother Wei made three lists: patients who could walk, those who needed a cart, and those who needed to be carried flat. Bao Mei copied the names onto separate boards so rain would not destroy the record.

She read each one back before setting it aside.

An old man objected to appearing on the cart list. He had walked to the clinic and could walk away from it. Mother Wei asked whether he intended to make the same journey while the road was moving beneath his feet.

He wanted to argue with the description. Then he saw two men carry in the first medicine chest and asked where his blanket should go.

***

At the smithy, Duan refused to abandon the furnace.

“Nobody is abandoning it,” Su Fan said. “We are moving the tools.”

“If the water comes that high, the tools won't be the only loss.”

“No.”

The smith looked around the workshop.

Every rack had been made to fit a particular hand's reach. A burn on the far beam marked the winter Su Fan had learned to judge furnace draught. Ah-Du's height scratches climbed the doorpost in uneven steps, some honest and one made while he stood on the edge of a board.

Duan knew about the dishonest one. He had left it there.

A new nail held the order slate. The old nail had snapped and remained in the wood beside it. Su Fan had passed that small repair every working day without once thinking of it as something that could be lost.

Duan took his best hammer from the wall.

“Start with the steel.”

“Most of the good stock is already higher.”

“Then start with the pieces we brought back to use.”

They wrapped the remaining working lengths and checked the stored bundles against the list. The borrowed upper shelf was sound and dry. Su Fan returned to the workshop with that fact, hoping it would persuade Duan to leave the other work more readily.

The smith was fitting the small tongs into a cloth roll.

“There should be room for the gauge,” he said.

“There is.”

“Not against the hammer. Put something between them.”

Su Fan did.

Ah-Du stood beside the anvil with an expression nobody had given him permission to wear. He had been eager to help until the jobs became a list of things to remove from the place in which he expected to grow up.

“What about this?” he asked.

Duan looked at the anvil.

“Not on that cart.”

“Another cart?”

“We'll see what we can get.”

The boy nodded, but his eyes stayed on it.

Su Fan carried a roll of tools outside with a man on his right who now knew to wait for his signal. Behind them, Duan put a hand on the furnace wall and left it there for a moment before following.

***

Ruan Zhi returned from the upper fields with three carts.

His aunt had sent them for harvested grain.

He put patients in two and grain in the third.

The drivers disliked the change until Mother Wei showed them who would be travelling. Then they disliked the arrangement of the bedding, the narrow turn near the school and the amount of help available at the far end. These were problems they could actually improve, and they became busy with them.

“Will she object?” Mother Wei asked Ruan.

“Certainly.”

“Will you blame us?”

“I'll blame the water. It has poor manners.”

He helped the old man from the cart list settle against a folded blanket. The man explained that he had never left his house overnight. His own bed was better than this. His daughter knew where his shoes were kept, and if they went now she would come to an empty house and think something had happened.

Ruan listened until the man reached the end of the worries he could name.

“We'll tell the lane checkers where you are,” he said. “They'll tell your daughter. Show me which board has your name.”

The old man pointed. Ruan read it aloud, then asked the man to confirm it.

That helped more than telling him the cart was comfortable.

Tan Wei and Qiu Lan brought station workers to carry the heavier patients. Han had released everyone not required at the gate. He kept the active crews rotating rather than letting one group exhaust itself in a heroic display.

They arrived already knowing which people needed flat transport. Qiu Lan checked the boards against Mother Wei's instructions. Tan Wei lifted one end of a pallet, waited for the person at the other end to be ready, and gave Su Fan a glance before moving so he would not need to locate the command by sound.

It was competent work.

It was still too little for the amount of water gathering above them.

The carts had to return. The carriers had to rest. One patient became sick on the slope and another discovered that the bedding everyone had agreed to leave behind contained the medicine she took at night.

They dealt with each difficulty. None of the solutions made the river pause.

When the third cart climbed past them with its grain, Su Fan was briefly angry at the space it occupied. Then he thought of the people gathering at the schoolroom and the meals they would require after the first hot broth had been shared out.

Ruan walked beside the loaded axle, keeping it clear of a rut. He was not solving one problem instead of another. He was being forced to keep both in sight.

***

By the second evening, the warning mark opposite Auntie Lu's stall was wet at the bottom.

People who had used the mark to reassure one another now crossed the lane to look closely at it. The dark patch was small. It would have been easy to call it splash if the next stone had not begun darkening too.

The goose had been moved to the schoolroom before most people.

Auntie Lu refused criticism of this priority.

“It complains louder. Easier to locate.”

Deng secured her cooking pots in a cart. He put cloth between the larger ones so they would not batter one another on the climb. She inspected the load and moved a ladle to a place from which she could reach it without untying everything.

“You aren't cooking on the road,” he said.

“Then nobody will need the ladle. A useful arrangement for both of us.”

Old Pock inspected the rescue boats and refused two as unfit.

“They float,” the owners protested.

“So does a corpse. I require more.”

One had a split that could be repaired with the timber and hands available. The other had too many failing places for an honest patch to become a rescue boat by sunset.

Su Fan helped with the first. He checked the fitting, marked the replacement and let somebody with a steadier grip drive it into place. The hammering confused him when he turned away from it. He looked before moving, irritated each time and unwilling to let the irritation put him beneath another man's swing.

The second boat was pulled apart for useful timber.

Its owner watched a familiar plank come free and said it had carried his father for years. Old Pock stopped working long enough to ask whether the father was still alive.

“Yes.”

“Then let's keep him that way.”

The man made an angry sound, took the freed plank and carried it to the repair without being asked.

At sunset, Shen Tu arrived with an official order.

The lower quarter had to be cleared by midnight.

No exceptions for property.

People read the seal before the words. Pei Gang's authority was unmistakable.

The rice farmer stood in his doorway with two chests behind him. He had spent the first day explaining why he could not move grain on a warning. Now he had more reasons to move and less time in which to do it.

“Where do we go?”

“Upper road,” Shen Tu said.

“And after?”

“We handle tonight first.”

It was a practical answer to an impossible question.

Su Fan hated how often that was becoming necessary.

The guards did useful things after delivering the order. They carried, directed carts and stopped one man from trying to bring an animal through a lane already crowded with patients. They also spoke to people as though the command to leave ought to remove every difficulty in leaving.

A woman shouted at one of them to carry her mother before explaining the seal again.

He carried her mother.

Su Fan found himself grateful to him and angry on her behalf at the same time.

Bao Mei met him at the lane junction with one of the boards against her chest. Her father had been sent ahead with their remaining goods. She was trying to find out whether a family marked as departed had actually reached the upper road.

“The door is shut,” a neighbour told her.

“That isn't what I asked.”

“They took a cart.”

“Which road?”

The neighbour pointed toward the ferry, then hesitated. Su Fan knew the passage he meant. It divided behind the basket-maker's shed; one branch climbed, and the other led to relatives nearer the bank.

“I'll ask at the corner,” he said.

Bao Mei shook her head. “You're taking medicines. Give him the question.”

She meant the neighbour, who had begun looking for a reason to leave now that his answer had become less useful than it sounded.

He went to ask. He returned with another man who had helped push the family's cart uphill and could name the person waiting to receive them.

Bao Mei changed the mark beside the house.

Su Fan looked at the board. Some names had a single stroke, others two. The difference was not tidy handwriting. It was the distance between seeing somebody leave and knowing where they had arrived.

“Who taught you to do that?” he asked.

“Wei told me not to put people where I hadn't seen them.”

She wiped a wet thumb on her skirt before touching the board again.

“I'd like them all to have two.”

“So would I.”

She went on to the next lane.

***

After dark, the town filled with the sounds of things being carried badly.

A chest scraped against a door too narrow for it. A crate broke on the stones and someone began picking up the spilled contents until a neighbour pulled him toward the road. Animals objected to being led where they could smell fear and unfamiliar bedding.

The river made less noise than Su Fan expected.

In places it merely appeared, darkening a floor, lifting a loose board, closing a route that had been open on the previous journey. The quiet made him look more often. He could not trust the absence of a warning he might not hear from the right.

At the clinic, two patients remained to be moved.

One could travel in a cart with enough support. The other, an old woman whose hip had healed badly, needed to remain flat. Mother Wei was arranging the order when a shout came from the next lane.

A woman had returned to her house for a wedding chest.

Her neighbours called after her. She kept going. The water outside her door had reached the place where the lower step disappeared.

Su Fan saw her from the corner.

He could run in and carry the chest out. He could also spend the time needed to get the clinic's last patients onto a road that was becoming more crowded and less certain with every trip.

Deng was closer to the nearest boat.

Su Fan called his name, waited until he had his attention and pointed.

“She's gone back. The house beside the reed shed. Can you get her?”

Deng looked at the water, the doorway and the people shouting instead of moving.

“Take your patients,” he said.

He went for the boat.

Su Fan returned to the clinic without knowing whether he had sent the right man in time. He helped secure the first patient in the cart. He listened from the left while Mother Wei explained what the men at the schoolroom needed to know. Then he walked beside the wheel through the wet lane.

At the slope, the cart stuck.

Two people pushed while another shifted the loose material beneath the wheel. The patient apologized for being heavy. Su Fan told him the cart had no opinion about the matter, which was not especially funny but made the man stop apologizing for a breath.

They got it moving.

The upper road was crowded with possessions that could not be taken indoors and people unwilling to move farther from the place they could still see their homes. Somebody had lit a lantern too close to hanging cloth. Su Fan moved it before finding a carrier to take his patient the last distance to the schoolroom.

Nearly an hour had passed before he saw the woman with the wedding chest.

She stood beside it, wet to the waist, arguing with Deng.

He had lost an oar. He was furious with her. She appeared to believe that admitting the danger would allow him to confiscate the chest after all.

Su Fan found himself laughing once, shakily, at the sight of two people alive enough to quarrel.

Deng saw him and pointed downhill.

“Still one at Wei's?”

“One.”

“Then go. I'll come behind.”

Su Fan turned toward the clinic.

The next warning bell rang.

This time nobody waited to count it.

chapters.title: A Floor Gives Way
chapters.text:
The clinic's last pallet would not fit through the back door.

They had brought it in through the front. The front room was now waist-deep in brown water, and something large had lodged against the steps outside. Every time the current moved it, the door shook in its frame.

Su Fan reached the rear passage as Tan Wei and Qiu Lan turned the pallet for the second time.

The old woman lying on it gripped the edge of her blanket. Her hip had healed badly years before. She could manage a familiar room with time and support. She could not be lifted upright and folded through a narrow doorway because the river had made the ordinary route inconvenient.

“Don't tip me again,” she said.

“We aren't going to,” Qiu Lan told her.

“You said that before.”

“We were wrong before.”

Mother Wei looked from the patient to the doorway.

“Take the doorframe.”

Duan had come with a crowbar and the expression he wore when a thing he had repaired was about to be destroyed for reasons beyond the repair. He tested the lower joint, then asked everybody to move their feet.

Su Fan set his shoulder against the wood.

“Your head,” Mother Wei said.

“Clear of it.”

“Keep it clear.”

Duan worked the crowbar beneath the joint. The first pull loosened plaster but not timber. Su Fan felt the frame shift against his shoulder and stopped pushing until the smith changed the angle.

Tan Wei held the pallet steady. Qiu Lan kept the old woman from trying to help by dragging herself toward the doorway.

“Everyone is busy,” she told the patient. “Your assigned task is complaining.”

The woman performed it with spirit.

Outside, a boatman called that the water was rising in the rear lane. The broad workboat had been brought for the patients who could not sit. It waited against a temporary rope, bumping softly where the current reached around the building.

The sound came from Su Fan's damaged side. He turned to see the man before answering and was glad he did. The boatman had asked how much longer, not whether they were ready.

“Frame first,” Su Fan said. “Then the pallet.”

Duan pulled again.

A strip of wood split away from the lower corner. Water seeped beneath the floorboards around Su Fan's boot. He had stood in this passage with fever, with a burned hand, with baskets of herbs he had not known how to name. He knew which board creaked beside the wall.

Now all of them seemed to move.

Mother Wei gathered the last things from the nearby shelf. She left a chipped bowl, a heavy jar and the little stool Su Fan had repaired twice. She took the packet of patient names and put it inside her clothing where the water would not reach it first.

“Again,” Duan said.

Su Fan leaned with him.

The frame loosened.

For a moment there was enough space. Qiu Lan saw it and shifted her grip. Tan Wei lifted his end of the pallet. The old woman drew a sharp breath and held it, determined not to provide another sound anybody could mistake for permission to turn her.

Then something struck the outside wall.

The floating cart hit broadside, driven by the new current. The impact travelled through the clinic with a deep wooden complaint. Dust fell from the partition above Duan's head.

Su Fan saw the beam move.

“Back!”

Duan turned toward him instead.

The timber dropped.

The smith went down beneath it. Su Fan caught the beam before it reached his chest, hands and shoulder finding places he would not have chosen if there had been time to choose them.

The fourth circuit locked into its trained route.

For one breath he held it.

Then the floor beneath his left foot broke.

His strength had nowhere sound to go.

He sank to the knee. The beam dropped another hand's width. Duan cried out, a short sound that stopped Su Fan thinking of anything except the weight and the man beneath it.

He shifted, trying to find the stone foundation through the broken boards. His boot met something, slipped and filled with cold water. Pain ran through his leg. His damaged ear filled with a roar that might have been water or might have been inside his head.

He could not hold long.

“Tan Wei,” he said.

His friend was already moving.

Qiu Lan had taken the pallet's weight onto the remaining sound boards. Mother Wei kept the patient from rolling while Tan Wei stepped into the water reaching through the front room.

A band rose around his wrists.

It passed through the doorway and pressed beneath the fallen cart outside. Tan Wei did not try to stop the flood. He caught the returning movement around the hull and turned enough of it aside to change what the cart was doing to the wall.

The Ferryman's Return found water where Su Fan had found no ground.

The cart shifted.

Pressure eased against the partition.

“Now!”

Su Fan heard the shout from close to his left. He moved the beam just enough for Qiu Lan to catch Duan beneath the good arm and pull him clear.

The effort tore a cry from the smith. He tried to help with his left hand and could not make the arm obey.

Mother Wei reached him, checked his breathing and pointed toward the pallet.

“Out. Everyone.”

Su Fan let go.

He fell backward through the broken doorway as the partition collapsed behind him.

The timber struck the place where his knee had been. Water burst through the gap, carrying plaster, a strip of shelving and one of Mother Wei's cloth rolls into the rear passage.

He scrambled up on the sound threshold and reached for the pallet.

The old woman was still complaining. He could have wept with relief at hearing it.

***

They carried her into the boat first.

Qiu Lan stepped down carefully, keeping the pallet level while Tan Wei and Su Fan passed the weight toward her. The boatman held them against the wall long enough to settle the load. Mother Wei made sure the blanket had not twisted beneath the woman's hip, then turned back for Duan.

The smith had lost consciousness.

His left shoulder was bent at an angle Su Fan would not look at twice. They moved him as Mother Wei directed, slowly where every instinct demanded speed. The current tugged at Su Fan's legs. He had to watch the others' hands because the words came to him unevenly through water, ringing and the hammer of his own breath.

Duan's good arm slipped from the cloth beneath him.

Su Fan caught it and felt the familiar weight of the smith's hand, the thickened skin, the old small scars across the fingers. He had watched that hand turn hot iron into a useful shape a thousand times. It seemed impossible that the rest of the man could be carried so helplessly beneath it.

They got him aboard.

Mother Wei settled beside him. Qiu Lan moved toward the bow, making space for the last crossing. Su Fan climbed in and turned back to help Tan Wei.

His friend had one foot on the boat's edge and one in the water.

A blue line tightened at his wrist.

The distant station had called for more support.

Tan Wei stopped.

It was not the hesitation of a man deciding where to put his weight. His whole body went rigid around an instruction that had found him at exactly the wrong moment. His eyes remained open. He seemed to be looking through the boat toward somewhere farther upriver.

The current pulled against his standing leg.

Su Fan took his belt and hauled.

For an instant he had no useful grip. Wet cloth slid beneath his fingers. He caught the folded part at Tan Wei's back, braced himself against a sound board and pulled again while the boatman held them off the wall.

Tan Wei fell into the boat.

The blue line slackened as Han's answering signal reached the lower crews. His shoulders jerked. He gasped and rolled onto his side, coughing river water he had not quite swallowed.

“I'm here,” he said.

Su Fan held his shoulder.

“I'm here,” Tan Wei repeated, this time looking directly at him.

The boat moved.

Behind them the clinic's rear wall settled with a sound like somebody slowly tearing cloth. Su Fan watched the doorway disappear behind the angle of the neighbouring house. He wanted to count the people aboard again, although he could see them all.

Qiu Lan had one hand on the patient's pallet and the other on the boat's side. The old woman was asking where her shoes had gone. Mother Wei bent over Duan. Tan Wei was breathing beside Su Fan, his wrist hidden against his chest.

The boatman swore at something in the water and changed their course.

They were all there.

That was not the same as being safe.

***

The upper landing had become a place made of hands.

People reached down before knowing what they were being asked to take. A lantern moved over faces. Somebody called for room. Somebody else said there was no room and was told to make it anyway.

Su Fan tried to stand before the boat stopped moving. Tan Wei caught his sleeve.

“Wait.”

He waited.

The old woman went ashore first, still flat, with Qiu Lan walking beside her and repeating the instructions the receiving men needed. The patient wanted to know who had her shoes. Qiu Lan said she would ask when there were fewer people trying to step on their own feet.

It was not a promise that the shoes had survived. Su Fan noticed that and was grateful for the care of it.

Duan came next.

Mother Wei examined him beneath a borrowed lantern on the upper road. The light shook until she asked the holder to rest his hand against a post. Su Fan stood where he could hear her, wet clothes dragging against his skin.

The shoulder was badly damaged. So was the upper arm. He would live if they kept him warm and got him to a stable bed.

Su Fan heard only the first part at first.

Then he saw Mother Wei's face when she looked at the smith's working hand.

“Can he—”

“Not now,” she said.

He stopped.

She did not know what he had been going to ask, or perhaps she knew every possible version of it. Either way, there was work before the answer.

They found dry cloth. A man removed his own outer coat and laid it over Duan's legs. Somebody brought a board from a dismantled shelter. Su Fan helped lift, keeping his right side toward the people who knew to touch his shoulder before changing direction.

The road climbed more steeply than it had on all the ordinary days he had walked it.

He watched the man ahead of him place his feet. He counted the places where they could stop without blocking the route. The fourth circuit could give him more strength than he had possessed in spring. It could not make the board easy to carry without jolting the person on it.

Duan woke before they reached the schoolroom.

His good hand moved against the cloth, searching for something to hold.

“The furnace,” he muttered.

“Still there,” Su Fan lied.

Duan caught his sleeve.

The grip was weak. Su Fan felt it as though the smith had put the whole weight of himself into the fingers.

“Don't.”

Su Fan swallowed.

“I don't know.”

The old man closed his eyes.

They carried him on.

***

Ruan cleared a place on the schoolroom floor.

He did it without announcing whose place it had been. Bedding moved. A family gathered their bundles a little closer. The young mother from the meeting shifted her sleeping child so there was room for Mother Wei to kneel.

Bao Mei brought dry cloth.

She stopped when she saw Duan's shoulder, then brought the cloth the rest of the way. Mother Wei took it, gave her another task and waited until the girl had understood before turning back to the smith.

Ah-Du stood in the doorway.

He looked at Su Fan as though one of them must possess an explanation fit to be given to the other. Su Fan had none. He could say the beam had fallen. He could say the floor had broken. Neither sentence contained what had happened to the place the boy expected to find tomorrow morning.

“Bring his tool roll,” Su Fan said instead. “The one we moved earlier. He may ask for it.”

Ah-Du nodded and went.

Duan did not need the tools that night. The boy needed a task that belonged to the smith rather than to the flood.

Tan Wei sat beside the wall with his wet sleeve pulled back. The blue line had faded again. He watched it for a while, then covered it before Su Fan could decide whether to ask.

“Han answered,” he said.

“I saw.”

“I wasn't on the active crew.”

“I know.”

His friend stared at the floor.

“There was water everywhere.”

Su Fan sat beside him. He did not say that the same water had saved Duan, although it had. Tan Wei had been there. He knew what he had done and what had nearly taken him away from it.

After a while Qiu Lan came back from settling the old woman. She had found one shoe caught beneath the pallet cloth. The other remained missing. She placed the recovered shoe beside the patient with a seriousness that made Su Fan turn his face away for a moment.

Small things were still being returned to their owners.

Mother Wei asked for a better light. Ruan moved the lantern. Duan made a sound from the bedding and the conversation beside the wall ended at once.

***

Auntie Lu put a cup of hot broth beside Su Fan.

He had not noticed her approach. That happened often enough now to frighten him in a new way each time it mattered.

“Drink.”

“I should—”

“You are no use dead on your feet.”

His hands had begun shaking too hard to argue. He took the cup with both of them, resting its base against his knees until he trusted himself to lift it.

The broth was salty. He could taste it through the dirt and river water in his mouth. For several breaths, that was all he did: hold the cup, drink, lower it without spilling.

Around him, people made temporary places for themselves. A man tried to hang wet clothes where they would not drip on a child. Someone asked whose blanket had been taken by mistake. The schoolmistress moved the children's slates to a high shelf and spread bedding beneath the table where they had argued about the evacuation marks.

The map was still pinned against the wall.

One corner had curled away from the plaster. A dry line showed the road outside the clinic, the turn by the smithy, the market crossing. Su Fan could find every place on it. He could no longer safely walk between them.

He looked toward Duan.

Mother Wei was still working. The smith's good hand lay outside the cloth. Ah-Du had put the tool roll where he would see it if he opened his eyes.

Su Fan finished the broth.

Outside, the river struck the lower houses one after another.

The sounds arrived through his good ear and the ringing in his head, some close, some impossible to place. He stopped trying to locate them after a while.

Each impact sounded like a separate thing ending.

chapters.title: The Cut Bank
chapters.text:
The decision to breach the low embankment was made at the eighth gate.

Su Fan was not in the room.

He learned of it when workers began carrying powder charges down the west road and Jiang came to the schoolroom with a map she no longer had time to spread carefully.

One corner caught beneath a cup. She pulled it free, spilling cold broth onto the floor, and did not stop to apologize until Mother Wei moved the bedding out of the way.

“Below this line must be empty,” Jiang said.

Mother Wei looked at the mark.

“The whole lower quarter.”

“Yes.”

“Tonight?”

“Before dawn.”

The schoolroom quieted in pieces. People near the table stopped talking first. Those farther away noticed the silence and tried to hear what had produced it. A child began asking why the adults were looking at the same sheet again.

Jiang's face held anger so tightly that Su Fan could not tell whom she was angry with. Her sleeve was wet above the elbow. Mud had dried in a pale band across the front of her coat, then been wetted again by something splashed against it later.

The high lake had risen faster than the new returns could handle. The upper settlements stood behind retaining walls older than their current foundations. If the head gate failed, the flood would arrive without channels or warning.

Pei Gang was holding the pressure stable.

He could not hold it indefinitely.

Opening the low bank would send the excess across Mudgate's lower quarter and into the unfinished western cut. Homes would be lost. The main system might survive.

“Was there another plan?” the widow asked.

“There should have been,” Jiang said.

Nobody mistook that for an answer about tonight.

The widow put her hand on the table. Su Fan had seen her use that gesture to stop a clerk turning a page before she finished reading it. This time there was no page to keep in place that would improve what it said.

“Who is still down there?” she asked.

They brought the lane boards.

A single stroke meant a house had been left. A second meant somebody had confirmed where its people had gone. There were gaps between those two kinds of knowledge. In a quiet afternoon they might have been corrected by walking to a neighbour's door. Now the roads between the questions were filling with water.

Mother Wei checked her patient list against the boards. Her last patient was beside the wall, demanding to know why a borrowed blanket smelled of fish. Duan lay beyond her, pale under the lantern. Both were accounted for. That did not account for the houses around the clinic.

Jiang asked for a final search crew.

Su Fan stood before deciding whether standing was sensible. Mother Wei looked at his bandage, his wet trousers and the way he kept his weight slightly off the leg that had gone through the floor.

“No entering where you cannot get out,” she said.

“I know.”

“You know many things after somebody has to fetch you. Know this one before.”

He nodded.

He went with a partner who could hear the calls from his right and had no difficulty telling him when he had missed one. They took a lantern, the current house marks and instructions clear enough that exhaustion would not improve them into an adventure.

Their job was to check the houses marked empty.

It was not to argue with the people laying the charges.

***

The west road was no longer a road all the way down.

In places the paving remained visible through shallow water. Farther on, the current hid its edges. A cartwheel turned slowly against a wall, held by a tangle of rope. The lantern showed only one part of the obstruction at a time.

Su Fan followed the route they had used on the earlier evacuation. He turned his head deliberately before crossing each open space. The ringing in his ear made distance uncertain, and he refused to compensate by moving faster.

Ahead, men were clearing the bank under the direction of someone holding a shielded lamp. Their loads stayed covered. A guard pointed the search crew toward the houses and told them which path would be withdrawn first.

Su Fan looked at the bank.

He had neither the authority nor the power to stop the breach. Even if he could, water still stood above thousands of other people. It would not become harmless because he could see his own home more clearly than theirs.

Knowing that did not make the painted marks easier to pass.
