At the first house, they called through an open shutter. Nobody answered. The man beside him checked the rear room while Su Fan watched the entrance and the current. A basket floated near the hearth. Something soft moved beneath it and turned out to be a cloth bundle, not a person.

They marked the door and went on.

The second house was locked.

A neighbour had said the family left before sunset. The rear opening was wide enough to look through, and the rooms beyond were empty of people. Their possessions remained arranged for a return: a bowl upside down on a shelf, a folded mat above the wet floor, firewood stacked where it would not have been reached by an ordinary rise.

Su Fan felt as though he was trespassing on their confidence.

His partner called him away.

The smithy stood dark behind a stronger current.

The furnace roof had collapsed.

Su Fan could see one corner of the tool rack through the broken wall. The rest had gone. Water moved through the space where Ah-Du usually stood with the bellows handle. A strip of roof timber rested against the bench, lifted at one end each time the current caught beneath it.

He took a step toward the gap before his partner touched his arm.

“Can anybody be inside?”

“No.”

“Then leave it.”

Su Fan stayed where he was.

He looked for the anvil and could not see it. That did not mean it had moved. The dark hid more than it showed, and the water had no interest in presenting a useful inventory.

He had promised Duan only that he did not know.

Now he knew about the roof. He wished knowledge had arrived in a form he could choose not to carry back.

They moved on.

***

At Bao Shun's house, a shutter banged against its frame.

The sound came to Su Fan from the left although the shutter was ahead and to his right. He stopped trying to use it for direction and watched the wood move in the lantern light.

The painted shop sign floated inside, face down.

It had been portable because the stall was borrowed. Bao Mei had taken it home after closing, as she did each evening. The back, which her father had joined so carefully, showed above the water. One fixing still held a scrap of cord.

Su Fan checked both rooms.

The Baos were uphill. He had seen them. He called anyway, because certainty about one family did not tell him whether a neighbour had sought shelter in an empty room.

There was no answer.

He marked the door.

His partner held the lantern while he did it. The chalk dragged over wet wood and left a weaker line than he wanted. He made the mark again, pressing until it was visible from the lane.

“Is that enough?” the other man asked.

“It will have to be.”

They left the sign where it turned slowly in the water.

Farther down, a dog barked from a ledge and then fled past them when the light moved. Su Fan watched it scramble toward the upper route. He could not tell whether it belonged to one of the families already waiting there. He hoped somebody would know it when it arrived.

At the last house, they found a man sitting beside an empty bed.

The room had been built a little higher than its neighbours. Water had entered through the rear wall and spread beneath the bed, but the man kept his feet on a low wooden rest as though this were an inconvenience he could outwait.

“My wife,” he said when Su Fan came in.

“She's at the schoolroom.”

“I know.”

“Then come.”

The man looked around the room.

“We built this.”

Su Fan stood in cold water up to his thighs. He could see where the wall changed colour above the bed, where a shelf had been removed and hung again at a better height. A pair of cups stood together in a small recess. The ordinary arrangements of two people who had expected to go on knowing where things were.

“She'll be looking for you,” he said.

“I told her I'd follow.”

“Then follow.”

The man rubbed both hands over his face. He did not seem confused. He knew where his wife was. He knew the water had come. He could even explain the promise he had made. What he could not seem to do was stand up and let the room become a place he had left.

Su Fan could not offer a sentence that would make leaving fair.

He held out his hand instead.

The man looked at it for a long time.

Then he took it.

His feet were stiff when he put them into the water. Su Fan supported him while the other searcher found the clearer part of the threshold. The man turned once toward the bed and stopped so abruptly that Su Fan thought he would go back.

“Nothing else,” his partner said, not harshly.

The man swallowed and came with them.

***

They reached the upper steps as the last searchers were being called in.

Deng stood near the turn, directing people toward the schoolroom rather than letting them gather where they would obstruct the route. He took the man's other arm and asked whom they should find for him.

“My wife,” the man said again.

“This way.”

Deng did not require a better answer before helping him climb.

Min met them above the steps carrying a small box.

Su Fan expected books.

Inside were letters and a child's drawing wrapped in oilcloth. The box was light enough to carry easily, but Min held it against his body as though a sudden wind might take it away.

“The archive?” Su Fan asked.

“The old quarter is higher. The lower store isn't.”

“You left it?”

“I locked it.”

“That won't stop water.”

“No.”

Min leaned against the wall to catch his breath. His coat had caught on something and torn near the pocket. He had not noticed, or had noticed and found it unimportant beside the things that could still be chosen.

“But I have spent enough years confusing a lock with an answer,” he said.

Su Fan took the box.

He did not open the oilcloth farther. The letters belonged to a conversation he had helped carry, not one he had acquired the right to read.

Min accepted his arm for the climb. Halfway up, the scholar stopped and looked back toward the lower store. Su Fan waited. He knew the look now. He had worn it outside the smithy a short while earlier.

“Did you bring the maps?” he asked.

“The copies we were using are above. Some older papers are still below.”

“Can anyone—”

“No.”

Min said it quietly, before Su Fan could finish making the loss into another task.

They climbed the remaining steps.

At the schoolroom, the widow found a place for the old man from the last house beside his wife. She had been asking for him. When he sat, she took his hand and began scolding him in a voice too low for Su Fan to hear clearly.

He was glad she had the opportunity.

Ah-Du sat near the door with his knees drawn up. He had fallen asleep holding a piece of the smithy's wrapping cloth. When Su Fan passed, the boy woke and looked toward the empty space behind him.

“Did you see it?”

“The workshop?”

“The anvil.”

“No. I couldn't see that part.”

“So it might still be there.”

“It might.”

Ah-Du began to stand. Su Fan put the box on a bench and caught his sleeve with the hand that was not carrying Min's weight.

“Not tonight.”

“I wasn't going tonight.”

The answer came too quickly. They both knew it.

Su Fan waited until the boy sat again. He wanted to promise they would bring the anvil back. He could offer neither a safe route nor proof that it remained where they had left it.

“Wait until somebody can see the ground,” he said. “Then we ask the people who know how to move it.”

Ah-Du looked at the cloth in his hands and nodded.

Min retrieved his box without asking Su Fan to choose which of them needed him more.

***

The road filled before dawn.

People had been told to stay farther back, but they wanted to see. Some stood because sitting down would make their exhaustion impossible to resist. Others held bundles they could have put on the dry ground and did not.

Su Fan found Tan Wei beside the railing.

His friend gripped it with both hands. The blue cord around his wrist had gone pale. He had not been asleep. Neither of them asked the other whether he intended to try.

“The last crew?” Tan Wei said.

“Back.”

“All the houses?”

“The ones on our list.”

It was the most Su Fan could truthfully say.

Far below, lamps moved away from the bank. A signal passed along the road. People near the front drew closer together without taking a step.

The first charge went off before dawn.

It sounded smaller than the damage it began.

Earth lifted from the embankment. For a moment the dark hid the result, and Su Fan thought absurdly that perhaps the bank had refused. Then the second blast opened the weak section.

Water pushed through the gap.

It paused against the obstruction of its own broken channel, climbed over it and widened the opening by force.

The current turned through the market.

Auntie Lu's stall went sideways. The frame held together for a little distance, recognizable by its crooked roof and the board where she had chalked prices. Then one side caught, the other continued moving, and it ceased to be a stall.

The lifting wheel spun once in the wrong direction.

Su Fan watched the motion with the helpless attention of someone who knew exactly which joint was not intended to take it. He had worked on that wheel. He could remember the sound of the first useful turn, the complaints about the handle, the argument over where a child might get a hand caught.

It broke apart.

A roof drifted past with a clay pot still standing on it. For a ridiculous moment, the pot remained upright. Su Fan found himself waiting for it to survive, as though one unbroken household object could change the thing he was seeing.

Then it tipped and vanished.

Nobody spoke.

The water did not rush on to somewhere else and leave the town behind. It occupied the lanes, deepened them, found the spaces between foundations and continued using them.

Tan Wei's fingers tightened on the railing.

Far above, Pei Gang stood on the eighth tower beneath a crown of moving water. At that distance the elder was a small figure within a work too large to mistake. The high lake pressed against the system, and he held it from falling on the people below.

Su Fan looked from the tower to the market and back again.

Pei Gang's work was real. So was the road disappearing beneath it.

Below him, the town paid for the years before this one.

chapters.title: The Upper Road
chapters.text:
They counted the missing three times before calling them dead.

The first count was wrong because two families had gone to relatives without reporting. A boy came back for a bundle, found his mother's name on the board and became so frightened that nobody could get a sensible answer from him until Bao Mei put down her brush.

“Where is she?”

“At my aunt's.”

“Which aunt?”

He told her. Somebody went to check. When the answer returned, she crossed out the mark beside the family and wrote the place clearly enough that nobody would have to frighten him with the question again.

The second count was wrong because a rescue boat had landed beyond the ridge.

Its crew had helped their passengers uphill by another route. They had spent the night finding dry space, warming a child and arguing over whether the boat could be brought back. They had not known that people at the schoolroom were waiting for their names.

When the message arrived, the widow read it twice before letting anyone alter the board.

The third count left fourteen.

Mother Wei would not let the names be read aloud until the search parties returned.

“They have been gone too long,” someone said.

“Then we'll be ready to hear them when they come.”

The waiting changed shape each time a figure appeared on the road. People who had been sitting stood. Someone would call a name too early. Then the arriving person had to answer questions before putting down whatever he had carried back.

Some brought belongings.

Some brought bodies.

Su Fan helped carry those they found. He worked beside people who knew to speak from his left or touch his arm before changing direction. Once he forgot and turned toward a sound on the wrong side, almost losing his grip. The man at the other end waited without making it into another thing that needed to be forgiven.

Su Fan knew several of the dead by face rather than name.

A man who repaired nets behind the ferry stall. A woman who always bought the smallest measure of oil. Two workers who had arrived that spring and never been more than familiar backs in the quarry queue.

He had shared the road with them. He had moved aside for their loads, heard them complain about prices and once borrowed a length of cord from the net-mender without remembering until now exactly whose hand had given it to him.

Their families supplied the rest.

One woman corrected the spelling on the board. She did it with an impatience that made Bao Mei's lips tremble until the girl understood that the impatience was not entirely for her.

“I'll change it,” Bao Mei said.

The woman watched until it was right.

When the last search parties returned, there were still fourteen names.

Some bodies had come back. Some had not.

Mother Wei listened to the reports. She asked where each search had ended and what the returning people had actually seen. Then she sat down for the first time that morning and allowed the list to be read.

At the schoolroom, Bao Mei wrote the names on clean boards.

She used no blue pigment.

***

There were things to do after the count, and Su Fan resented them for continuing to exist.

Water had to be carried. Wet bedding had to be hung where it would not drip on people who had finally fallen asleep. The youngest children were hungry before the adults had decided who was responsible for the next meal.

Auntie Lu had brought fewer pots than she wanted and more than anybody now thought she should have left behind. She made room around the largest one and sent people away with tasks before they could explain why they were willing to help but did not know how.

Su Fan carried fuel from a dry stack. He caught himself listening for the familiar crack of Duan testing a piece of charcoal between his fingers.

There was no forge fire here.

The schoolmistress had put the children's work in a covered box and turned the long table into a place for clean cloth. The four-legged duck still hung on the wall. Someone had moved a lantern so it would not scorch the paper.

Su Fan looked at it while waiting for an empty bucket.

The picture had survived without being useful to anyone. He was glad of that in a way he could not have explained without making it sound foolish.

Duan woke properly on the second day.

Su Fan was outside when Mother Wei called him. He came in too quickly, caught his shoulder on the doorframe and stopped to let the dizziness settle before approaching the bedding.

The smith saw him do it.

“How's the head?”

“Still attached.”

“Don't let that become your measure for everything.”

His voice was weak. The attempt at irritation was familiar enough to make Su Fan sit down before his knees decided the matter for him.

Duan asked about his hand before asking about the smithy.

Mother Wei told him the arm would mend badly if he tried to use it too soon. Even with careful treatment, heavy hammering might never be possible again.

The smith listened without interrupting.

“Never?” he asked when she finished.

“Might not. I won't make a certainty out of the best result or the worst one.”

“What can I do now?”

“Rest. Let me look after it. Tell me when something changes instead of deciding whether the change is convenient.”

Duan glanced at Su Fan.

“She gives everybody that speech?”

“Apparently.”

Neither of them laughed for long.

The smith's good hand lay on the blanket. He rubbed one finger against a patch worn smooth by years of work, as though checking whether the life in that hand still belonged to him.

Then he looked at Su Fan.

“How much steel?”

“Most of the good stock is on the upper shelf.”

“Dry?”

“Yes. We checked the covers.”

“Tools?”

“The best hammers. Two files. The gauge. Your small tongs.”

“The big tongs?”

Su Fan shook his head.

Duan stared at the ceiling.

The list was better than nothing. It was much better than nothing. Su Fan knew how deliberately they had carried those things uphill, how many turns of cloth had kept an edge from striking another tool. He wanted the list to be enough to bring the smith back to the business of being relieved.

Duan lay still.

After a while he said, “We can make tongs.”

His voice broke on the last word.

Su Fan stayed beside him. He did not turn toward the doorway or pretend he had missed the sound through his damaged hearing.

Mother Wei moved the cup within reach of the smith's good hand and left them for a moment.

Duan closed his eyes. Su Fan watched the breathing, waited through one uneven breath and then another, and found no useful sentence he was obliged to say.

Ah-Du came in carrying the tool roll.

He had been waiting for the smith to wake, and waiting had given him time to decide exactly how the surviving tools should be arranged. He unrolled the cloth on a dry board beside the bedding. The two files lay together. The gauge was wrapped separately. He had wiped the hammer heads so carefully that one still carried a pale thread from the rag.

Duan opened his eyes at the sound of the board being set down.

“Not on the floor,” he said.

“It isn't.”

“Good.”

The boy pointed out each piece, although everyone in the room knew the names. Su Fan let him finish. He had wanted the same list to do more than a list could do.

At the small tongs, Ah-Du stopped.

“I couldn't find—”

“I know,” Duan said.

The boy folded the empty part of the roll inward.

For a while the smith looked at the tools without touching them. Then he asked Ah-Du to turn the gauge so the edge would not press against the file teeth. The boy obeyed at once, relieved by an instruction whose meaning he understood.

Duan thanked him.

That was less familiar than the instruction. Ah-Du looked at Su Fan, then back at the smith, and said he would leave the roll where it could be seen.

When he went out, Duan closed his eyes again. The tools remained beside him. They had not made him well, and nobody asked him to pretend that seeing them had been enough.

***

Shen Tu's guards established a ration point beside the upper road.

Their order helped. Their insistence on household papers did not.

Half the papers were underwater.

The queue formed before the tables were ready. People held bowls, sacks, folded cloth and whatever else had survived in a shape that could carry food. A guard tried to make them stand in households. Two families who had spent the night together could not agree whether that made them one household for the purpose of the grain measure.

Su Fan carried sacks to the dry side of the table.

He could hear the instructions when the guard faced him. When the man turned away and pointed elsewhere, he had to ask again. On the third occasion, the guard became impatient.

“Over there.”

“Speak where I can hear you.”

The guard looked at his bandage, then at the space beside the table.

“There. Against the boards. Not the wet ground.”

Su Fan put the sack where it belonged.

He disliked the man's tone. He disliked being given orders by a uniform while people he knew waited with empty bowls. He also knew why the sack had to stay dry and why leaving it in the passage would make the next load harder to carry.

The old resentment returned with the work.

Then he looked at the people waiting to eat and carried the next sack.

At the front of the queue, the widow refused to move aside.

“My papers are in the house.”

“You need proof of household.”

“The house is in the river. Would you like proof of that?”

The clerk behind the guard kept his brush poised over an empty line.

“Names can be claimed twice,” he said.

“So can people be refused twice. Which one are we arranging today?”

Others began speaking behind her. A man held up a packet whose ink had run into a single dark patch. A woman said her papers were at a relative's house on a road the guards had closed. The guard tried to lower the noise by repeating the requirement.

The widow waited until Shen Tu came over.

She did not begin with an accusation about the river. She pointed at the wet packet, the empty line and the people who had already been waiting since before the tables were set out.

“Two neighbours,” she said. “Let two neighbours witness the claim. Record their names as well if you need somebody to hold responsible.”

The captain asked the clerk what record they could keep under that arrangement.

It took longer than the hungry people wanted. It took less time than sending them all to recover documents from flooded houses.

He allowed it.

Mother Wei added patients' names. Deng organized the boat crews into food carriers. People who had been standing in the queue became witnesses for the households beside them. The clerk's brush began moving again.

The system did not become generous or simple. It began allowing more people to eat.

Su Fan took a filled measure to a woman who could not leave the bedding where her husband lay. She thanked him and asked whether the next distribution would happen in the same place.

He found somebody who knew rather than give her the answer he hoped was true.

When he returned to the sacks, the guard faced him before speaking.

Su Fan nodded and took the next load.

***

Jiang came down from the gates at sunset.

Her coat was stiff with dried mud. There were burns around one wrist. She had wrapped them badly enough that Mother Wei noticed from across the room, but the steward went first to the boards beside the wall.

She read the fourteen names.

Su Fan stood near the doorway holding an empty bowl. He watched her reach the end of the first board, return to one line and read it again. He did not know whether she recognized the person or was making certain of the spelling.

She removed her official belt before entering the room where the families sat.

One of the people inside looked up sharply. Another kept staring at the floor. The steward sat where she was directed, not at the place nearest the lamp.

Su Fan did not hear what she said.

The ringing grew louder when he tried to separate her voice from the other sounds in the room. He stopped trying. The conversation was not a report he had been asked to witness.

He saw that she stayed.

Later, Mother Wei brought her a fresh dressing and a cup. The belt remained folded beside the door.

***

On the fourth day, the water began to settle into its new course.

The lower quarter did not reappear.

Some roofs emerged. Broken walls stood like teeth above the brown current. The breach had deepened the channel, and the river now preferred the road it had been given.

Su Fan walked with Sun Lian to a place from which they could see the old market turn. She carried measurements and a line stained by the water. Her clothes had been washed, but the mud had left marks that ordinary washing would not easily remove.

“Can we put it back?” he asked.

She knew what he meant.

“With a new embankment, dredging, a proper overflow and more money than anyone here has.”

“How long?”

She did not answer quickly.

He appreciated that until the waiting became a place in which he could imagine a better answer.

“Not before winter,” she said.

He looked toward the smithy.

He could identify the taller wall by the angle of its broken top. The yard lay beneath a smooth stretch of current. Somewhere under it were the marks from the log test, the place where he had practised the first circuit, and the little hollows made by moving six stones between one arrangement and another.

He had spent weeks treating the coming danger as a problem that could be solved well enough to preserve the arrangement around it.

Better fittings. Honest lists. A stronger stance. Enough attention in the right place.

Some of those things had saved lives. He knew that because the people were here, waiting for food, arguing over shelter, asking what work there would be next.

The road under the water had been his route home.

He could not walk it now.

Sun Lian put away the line. She did not tell him the river would give everything back eventually. She asked whether Duan was awake and whether the tools needed another dry covering.

He answered both questions.

They began walking toward the schoolroom.

A familiar voice called from behind them.

“Where should we put it?”

Ah-Du stood beside two exhausted men and a cart that leaned badly under its load.

The salvaged anvil sat on the boards, dark with water. Mud filled the shallow marks along its foot. A rope had left a clean stripe across one side where it had been dragged tight enough to do its work.

Su Fan stopped.

The boy's face was pale with effort and bright with a pleasure he seemed afraid to show too openly beside everything they had lost.

“We waited until they said the way was clear,” he said before Su Fan could ask.

One of the men shifted his grip on the cart.

“Then we discovered how heavy the thing remained.”

Ah-Du looked toward the schoolroom again.

“Where?”

For the moment, that question had an answer.

“Under the schoolroom awning,” Su Fan said. “Dry side. I'll help.”

chapters.title: A Roof on Credit
chapters.text:
The relief vouchers arrived before the timber.

A clerk brought them in a dry case and laid them on the schoolroom table. Outside, people stood in coats that had not dried properly since the night of the breach. They watched the case opened with the attention they would have given a cart of food.

Each household received a numbered sheet entitling it to materials, grain and temporary shelter. The district would recover the cost through future labour or adjusted levies.

The word *relief* occupied the largest space on the page.

The repayment terms occupied the smallest.

Min read them beneath the awning while people waited in the cold. He wore a scarf someone had persuaded him to accept. It made him look both warmer and more annoyed than usual.

“Interest?” the widow asked.

“Not called interest.”

“What is it called?”

“Administrative continuation.”

Auntie Lu made a sound that startled the goose.

The clerk explained that the form was standard. That made the people who could read it less reassured than he expected. A standard form had room to anticipate the trouble it described. This one seemed chiefly to have anticipated the district's difficulty in being paid back.

“What happens if the work isn't available?” a man asked.

“The levy can be adjusted.”

“Up or down?”

The clerk looked at the paper.

Min held out his hand for the relevant sheet and found the part everyone else had missed. He read it aloud without making the language kinder. The explanation was useful. It did not make the timber arrive.

Su Fan took a copy for Min Yao.

He no longer expected an intelligent reader to make an unfair agreement fair merely by describing it accurately. But he wanted to know what they were being asked to carry, and he wanted someone outside the immediate shortage to have the same words before the words acquired another meaning.

The widow kept her own sheet flat against a board. Her house had been wet when she left it. Now the paper describing the cost of replacing it had to be protected from a drop falling through the awning.

Deng moved the board out of the drip.

“Thank you,” she said, without looking away from the terms.

The clerk began calling the next names.

***

The first argument concerned kitchens.

Private cooking fires would use too much fuel. A common kitchen would feed more people with less wood. It would also require everyone to agree about portions, work and the ownership of pots.

Auntie Lu set her largest pot on three stones and invited the people with opinions to move it somewhere better.

Nobody did.

A woman wanted food prepared earlier because her children would otherwise wait through the morning. A carrier needed to eat before leaving for work. Mother Wei needed hot water that would not become the kitchen's property merely because it had been heated near the same fire.

Deng found another vessel for the water. Somebody objected that it had been intended for washing. Auntie Lu asked whether they wanted a clean pot or an argument about the history of pots.

They cleaned it.

Su Fan helped bring the first load of fuel. He put it on the dry side and asked where the next stack should go. Before the flood he would have chosen the place himself. Now there were three people already using the ground for things he had not thought to ask about.

The arrangement changed twice before noon.

People who had promised to help discovered that the tasks were not all the pleasant business of stirring something warm. Somebody had to wash vessels in cold water. Somebody had to carry the wet waste away from the places people slept. Somebody had to remain after the last portion was served and put the fire safely to bed.

Auntie Lu listened to the proposed division of work.

“I'll manage it six days out of seven,” she said.

“What happens on the seventh?” someone asked.

“You discover gratitude.”

Deng volunteered to take the other day.

Several people looked at him.

“I can boil things.”

“Until they stop resisting,” Old Pock said.

“That is usually the point.”

Auntie Lu considered the offer with the solemnity of a woman deciding whether to place a town's digestion in hostile hands.

“Nothing complicated.”

“I wasn't planning anything complicated.”

“Your last soup had opinions.”

“It had pepper.”

“It had ambitions.”

They agreed he would take the seventh day. Nobody trusted his cooking, but several trusted him to arrive, keep the water boiling and remain until the washing was done. Under the circumstances, those were not small qualifications.

The first meal exposed a difficulty nobody had put on the list.

A woman collected two portions and left without her own. When Deng called after her, she shook her head toward the shelters. Her father could not manage the walk. She had brought one bowl for him and one for the child, and intended to return after both had eaten.

“Then yours will be cold,” he said.

“It will still be food.”

A man behind her complained that she had been given two turns in the queue. The child, hearing the complaint, tried to hand his bowl back. Broth spilled over the rim and ran down his fingers.

Su Fan caught the bottom of it before the boy dropped it.

Auntie Lu came around the pot. She took the child's wrist, looked at the reddening skin and told him where Mother Wei had put the clean water. Then she turned to the man in the queue.

“Would you prefer the old fellow carried here?”

“I didn't know there was an old fellow.”

“You could have asked before upsetting his dinner.”

The man looked at the woman. She was wiping the child's sleeve with a corner of her own, her face closed against the prospect of being made grateful in front of everybody.

“I'll carry the other bowl,” he said awkwardly.

She considered him, then handed it over. He followed her down the line of shelters, holding the food very carefully.

They returned together later. The bowl was empty. The woman had eaten after all, and the man said there were two more people at that end who would need meals carried. He offered to do it while the food was hot, provided someone kept his own place.

Deng took a piece of charcoal and added a duty beneath washing.

“Deliveries,” he read aloud.

“Put names against it,” Auntie Lu said. “I won't have everybody claiming to be delivering when the pots need cleaning.”

Su Fan fetched a shallow tray. Its edge was split, but a cloth folded beneath the bowls stopped them sliding. The boy with the wet sleeve insisted on carrying the spoons. On the next trip he walked ahead of the man who had complained, announcing each shelter as though they were bringing a feast instead of thin broth.

Nobody argued about the second bowl again that afternoon.

Auntie Lu asked for the fuel list. She marked the days she would work and handed it back before anybody could quietly turn six into seven.

***

The next argument concerned Duan's anvil.

It occupied dry space beneath the schoolroom awning that could have held bedding. When they brought it up, the immediate problem had been getting it out of the weather. Since then another family had arrived from a crowded room farther along the road, and the place beside the wall was the only dry corner they had been offered.

Su Fan saw the bedding laid near the anvil and knew there was going to be an argument before anyone began one.

Duan offered to move it outside.

Su Fan objected before the old man finished speaking.

“The tools will rust.”

“A sleeping family will be cold,” the widow said.

“We need the forge to repair the carts.”

“We need the families to live long enough to use them.”

Neither proposition removed the other.

The woman whose bedding lay in the passage held a pair of small shoes against her coat. One was dry. The other had not had time to become so. She did not take part in the argument at first, which made it easier for Su Fan to speak as though the choice were between a useful workshop and an inconvenient patch of cloth.

Then she asked how long the anvil would remain.

He had no answer.

Duan sat with his damaged arm supported. His good hand rested on the edge of the tool roll.

“I said move it,” he told Su Fan.

“You'll need shelter to work.”

“Yes. You haven't discovered a need I don't possess.”

The rebuke stung because Su Fan had been defending something real. He wanted that to excuse how quickly he had defended it at someone else's expense.

Sun Lian arrived while they were still failing to improve either side of the problem.

She looked at the awning, the anvil and the open ground beyond it.

“I have old sailcloth,” she said. “Not enough for a proper building. Enough to keep rain off tools.”

“How much timber?” Duan asked.

She measured with her eyes, then walked the space rather than pretending the first estimate was sufficient. Some of the sound pieces from the dismantled boat could be used. The arrangement would be temporary and would have to be moved if they shifted camp.

“That is more roof than we have now,” the widow said.

They put it up that afternoon.

Su Fan carried poles and steadied them while Sun Lian fastened the sail remnants. Duan told them where the anvil had to stand for somebody to work beside it without striking a support. His arm remained bound. Nobody suggested that being anxious about the tools entitled him to lift them.

The cloth had old patches, a seam darkened by years of handling and a place where the weave had thinned enough to show light. Sun Lian put that part where it would not carry the greatest strain. When the wind lifted an edge, the whole lean-to seemed to inhale.

It stayed up.

The family took the dry corner beneath the schoolroom awning.

Su Fan helped move their bedding and said nothing about how quickly he had made the anvil more important than people. The woman thanked him for carrying the bundle. She did not thank him for the argument, and he did not need her to.

That night he wrote the incident down privately. He kept the description short enough that it did not become a defence of everything he had intended.

***

Winter ground was available at the disused upper quarry.

The stone was poor. That had made it useless to the sect and potentially useful to everyone else.

Jiang obtained permission for temporary occupation. Permanent settlement would require drainage, a road and a new levy agreement. The word *temporary* appeared often enough that Su Fan asked which of those requirements had to be completed before people could put up anything more solid than cloth.

“Those are the terms we still have to negotiate,” Jiang said.

“After we move?”

“While you decide whether to move. The ground does not become better because I pretend the permission is more than it is.”

Temporary, Su Fan had learned, could mean anything from one night to the rest of a life.

They walked the quarry together.

A shelf of rock offered shelter from the north wind. Below it, the floor sloped south through old spoil and patches of stubborn grass. In dry weather it looked almost ready for houses. Sun Lian crouched beside a channel cut by the last heavy rain and showed them where the same ground would send water when it became wet.

“Not there,” she said when someone chose the flattest place for a doorway.

“It looks level.”

“That is why the water will stay.”

A spring lay above the site. They could bring water down if they laid a pipe and protected it from frost. The slope would help. The exposed places would not. Every useful feature seemed to arrive with work attached to it.

Su Fan had been looking at the approach.

A narrow entrance could be watched. The rock shelf gave a view of the road. A place for stores near the centre would make it harder for someone to take a chest without being seen.

He described the entrance first.

Bao Shun asked where the shops would go.

The widow asked where children would learn.

Mother Wei asked where waste would drain.

Sun Lian asked how a cart carrying timber would turn through Su Fan's narrow entrance while somebody else tried to bring a patient out.

He looked at the route again.

The space he had imagined as a place to defend was already becoming a place people would need to enter and leave for reasons that had nothing to do with an attack.

“Wider,” he said.

“How much wider?” Sun Lian asked.

They used the width of an actual cart rather than the comfort of a word.

Bao Shun wanted his shop near the path. Bao Mei wanted light enough to paint by and somewhere she could set boards without people treading on them. The schoolmistress wanted a roof before she wanted a wall, and a wall before anybody promised her a fine doorway. Mother Wei wanted the water route kept away from the waste route even if that spoiled the neatest row of buildings.

Jiang stood listening, adding conditions where the permission required them. She did not draw a whole town with one stroke of a brush. The people who would live there kept interrupting the drawing.

By the end of the walk, Su Fan understood why a settlement could not be planned by the person most worried about an attack.

He still wanted an entrance they could watch.

He also wanted the cart to get through it.

***

They began with the things that could be moved twice without being ruined.

Cloth shelters. Bedding. Covered stores. The clinic's table and the water vessels people kept borrowing and failing to return to the same place. The old sail roof could come apart and be raised again. Duan disliked that prospect, but less than leaving his tools out in the weather while other people debated a permanent lease.

Su Fan worked until the light began to go.

He was tired enough that the ringing in his head seemed louder. He had learned to tell people when he needed a command repeated. He had not yet learned to do it without sometimes hearing impatience in voices that were merely hurried.

At the slope, he found Tan Wei helping younger children move bedding.

The children had turned the job into a competition over who could carry the largest roll. Tan Wei had stopped the competition by taking the largest one himself and asking them to show him the route. They were now arguing about which of them had been appointed guide.

Su Fan took a corner that had begun dragging in the mud.

His friend had been paid an emergency bonus for the flood work. Most of it had become grain before reaching the camp. Su Fan had seen the sacks delivered and had immediately begun calculating what Tan Wei ought to retain for his own needs.

“Keep some,” he said.

“I did.”

“Enough?”

Tan Wei looked at him.

Su Fan stopped.

“Sorry.”

His friend shifted the bedding higher.

“You can ask. Just don't decide afterward.”

The distinction ought to have been easy by now. Su Fan found it remained easier to recognize after speaking than before.

“How much help do you need with this?” he asked.

“The other end. Not a speech about carrying.”

He took it.

The children ran ahead, found the wrong stakes and were recalled by a woman who had already moved her bundles once. Tan Wei waited while the route was settled. Su Fan looked at the ground, at the pegs that marked rooms no one could yet stand inside, and at the space where water would have to be brought before the cold deepened.

Nothing about the place looked finished.

A small boy came back to tell them where the bedding belonged. He spoke from Su Fan's left because Tan Wei had reminded him, and Su Fan thanked him for both the direction and the care without making either sound grand.

Together they carried the roll up the slope, past stakes marking houses that did not yet exist.

chapters.title: The Clinic Without Walls
chapters.text:
The new clinic began as a blanket tied between two posts.

Mother Wei placed her table behind it and told the wind that consultation was private.

The wind ignored her.

By the time Su Fan brought the morning water, one corner of the blanket had escaped its cord. It lifted whenever a patient approached, giving the waiting line a view of the table, the medicine chest and whoever had been persuaded to take off a coat.

Su Fan caught the corner and looked for a better knot.

“Don't tie it to the table,” Mother Wei said from behind him.

“I wasn't going to.”

“The last helpful person was.”

He tied it back to the post. The post leaned. He packed stones around its foot, tested it and found that the blanket would now stay in place unless the ground moved or somebody sat on the cord.

Mother Wei regarded the arrangement.

“An encouraging beginning.”

Patients queued along the quarry wall. Some had injuries from the flood: scraped shins, a foot cut on hidden debris, a shoulder strained carrying a bed. Others had ordinary illnesses made worse by wet bedding and too little food. These people sounded almost apologetic when asked what troubled them, as though a familiar cough had chosen a poor time to ask for attention.

One man wanted a charm against future rain.

“I have a roof fund,” Mother Wei told him. “Contribute to that.”

“I meant something to carry.”

“A roof is inconvenient that way.”

He explained that his neighbour's family tablet had stayed dry throughout the flood. His own had not. He had been wondering whether this signified something.

“Where did your neighbour keep it?”

“In a chest upstairs.”

“And yours?”

“By the door.”

“Try upstairs first. It is cheaper than the other explanation.”

The man considered this. He still looked disappointed when she asked about the rash on his wrist, which was the reason his wife had sent him.

Su Fan set the water down where Mother Wei pointed. Clean water on the raised board. Used vessels beneath the opposite end of the table. The two places were separated by no more than a few paces, yet people kept confusing them when they were tired.

He offered to paint marks on the wood.

“Bao Mei is doing signs,” Mother Wei said. “Your job is the water.”

“There are only three buckets here.”

“Four when you bring the fourth. Then you are going to Duan.”

He glanced at the queue.

She followed the glance without turning her head.

“The queue is not an instruction to you personally.”

“I know.”

“Then stop reading it like one.”

She had assigned him a set number of tasks each morning. Water, the heavier chest when it needed moving, and whatever small repair she had actually asked for. When those were finished, he had to leave and earn money beneath Duan's sailcloth roof.

She was just as strict with herself, less successfully.

A bowl of breakfast stood beside the medicine list. The surface had cooled into a pale skin. Each time Su Fan saw her reach toward it, another patient spoke and her hand went somewhere else.

He moved the bowl nearer.

She moved it away from the medicines.

He said nothing. There were limits to the ways a man could object to being supervised while supervising somebody else.

***

Duan hated being treated in public.

He arrived with Ah-Du carrying his small bundle, although the bundle was light enough for him to carry with his good hand. The boy kept offering to put it down and being told he would only have to pick it up again.

The blanket offered visual privacy. Everyone could hear the smith complaining when Mother Wei moved the damaged arm.

“You tell a man not to use it,” he said, “then spend an hour using it for him.”

“Would you prefer it to set solid?”

“I would prefer a different shoulder.”

“Bring one tomorrow.”

A woman in the queue smiled, then looked down quickly when Duan swore. Su Fan sat outside holding the old man's coat. Ah-Du had been sent back to watch the tools, with instructions not to interpret watching as trying them all.

The coat had a scorch mark near its lowest fastening. Su Fan remembered making it. He had been fifteen, hurried and certain that the iron had cooled enough. Duan had worn the coat afterward without repairing the mark, occasionally pointing to it when somebody claimed an apprentice had learned all there was to learn.

Now the left sleeve had been folded differently to make room for the binding.

Behind the blanket Mother Wei asked whether the pain had changed since yesterday. Duan answered the question he preferred, which concerned how long he would be unable to work.

She asked again.

He gave her a better answer.

The woman beside Su Fan shifted her basket from one knee to the other. Her own arm had healed badly years ago. She began to say that a neighbour knew a man who had recovered completely from something similar, then stopped when Su Fan looked at her.

“I was only going to say—”

“I know.”

He had made his voice too sharp. She turned the basket around in her lap.

“I am sorry,” he said after a moment.

She nodded. Neither of them supplied a prediction.

When Duan emerged, sweat stood on his forehead. He took the coat with his good hand, held it open and missed the sleeve twice.

Su Fan rose.

He caught the hanging fabric and guided it toward the old man's arm without asking first.

Duan jerked away.

“I can dress myself.”

The words came harder than necessary. The waiting woman bent over her basket as though it had suddenly become important to check every object inside.

Su Fan stepped back.

Duan tried again. The coat twisted. He could not get the left cuff far enough away without pulling at the shoulder, and each failed attempt left the fabric more awkwardly gathered. He stood breathing through his teeth.

Su Fan kept his hands at his sides.

He wanted to say he had only been helping. The words would have required Duan to apologize before he could accept any help at all.

After a moment the smith held the coat out.

“The left.”

Su Fan took only that sleeve. He held it open and waited while Duan decided how to move. When the hand came through, he released the fabric. Duan managed the rest slowly, fastening one toggle with his good hand and leaving the next undone.

They walked back to the anvil without speaking.

At the lean-to, Ah-Du was sitting on an overturned crate, examining a small heap of nails.

“Watching,” he said immediately.

Duan looked at the heap.

“Why are they sorted?”

“They were difficult to watch all mixed up.”

The smith sat. He took one nail, laid it against the next and asked the boy what difference he had found. Su Fan left them arguing over which irregularity mattered and went to fetch the work slate.

Duan had not forgiven the coat incident aloud. Su Fan had not asked him to. There was a bent hinge on the slate, and they knew how to begin with that.

***

Jiang brought medicine under a restricted emergency licence.

She came on foot with a carrier and two sealed cases. The waiting line made room when it saw the cases, then closed again behind her. A child followed the carrier as far as the table, hoping the boxes contained food.

Mother Wei checked the seals before opening anything.

Jiang gave her the licence.

The healer read it once, took a brush and crossed out the clause limiting treatment to registered workers.

Then she handed it back.

“I cannot alter the provincial supply rules,” Jiang said.

“Then keep the supply. I'll continue treating everyone with what I have.”

“You don't have enough.”

“I know.”

The two women faced one another across the table.

Su Fan had returned with a repaired stool. He put it down more quietly than necessary and found a reason to refill the water bucket. He did not leave far enough to miss the result.

Jiang placed the licence flat. The crossed-out line remained perfectly readable. It was a mistake, Su Fan thought, to imagine that because Mother Wei had drawn through it, the office which supplied the medicine would cease to count it.

“There are allocations attached to this,” Jiang said. “I cannot receive worker stock and record it as something else merely because you object to the category.”

“Then use a category that includes the people waiting.”

“I need authority for that.”

“And I need medicine for them.”

The carrier shifted his grip on one case. Mother Wei pointed to the clear ground beside the table and told him to put it down. Whatever happened to the paper, he did not have to hold the weight throughout the argument.

A little farther along the wall, a woman began coughing. Nobody used the sound as a point in the discussion. It continued until her husband brought her the drinking cup.

Jiang asked for a second sheet.

She wrote slowly enough that Su Fan could see she was calculating the consequence rather than searching for an attractive turn of phrase. Part of the stock would be assigned to the district's unregistered emergency population under her own office's liability.

Mother Wei read that sheet too.

“How much?” she asked.

Jiang showed her the quantities.

“That will not cover everyone.”

“No. It is what I can assign today.”

“What happens when it is used?”

“You request more and state what remains. As you do with the other stock.”

This was not a hidden passage through the provincial rules. The medicine would still be counted. The cost would sit in an account attached to Jiang's office, and somebody would eventually ask why she had put it there.

She drew two columns and had the carrier read the labels from the cases. Mother Wei checked them against the list. When the figures disagreed, they counted again before signing.

The disagreement concerned one small packet lodged beneath the packing straw. The carrier found it, held it up with relief and was told to put it with the rest rather than wave medicine over the table.

The moment let both women breathe.

Mother Wei signed for the stock.

“Thank you.”

“Keep complete records.”

“I do.”

“Then perhaps we will both survive the gratitude.”

Jiang sanded the wet writing. Mother Wei opened the first case only after the carrier had witnessed the receipt.

Su Fan had imagined a confrontation ending either with the cases carried away or with an official admitting the rule was wrong. Instead the medicine stayed, the rule remained, and Jiang took a second responsibility away with her.

He brought the stool forward.

“Is that repaired?” Mother Wei asked.

“Yes.”

“Then sit him on it.”

She meant the next patient. The man was trying to keep his weight off a swollen foot and had been standing too long while people discussed the supply.

Su Fan helped him sit.

***

The new medicines changed what could be offered. They did not shorten the line immediately.

Mother Wei checked the people she had postponed that morning. She asked questions again rather than assume that a fuller chest made yesterday's observations sufficient. The clean cloth ran low. The small cup vanished beneath somebody's folded coat. A woman who had been waiting quietly announced she could not remain because her children would be alone.

“Bring them,” Mother Wei said.

“I have three.”

“I have been warned.”

The woman came back with all three. The youngest disliked the blanket and attempted to look underneath it. Su Fan diverted him with the repaired stool until the owner of the swollen foot asked whether his furniture was now a public attraction.

By afternoon, Mother Wei's breakfast bowl had finally gone empty. Su Fan did not see who had made that happen. He was pleased without needing to find out.

Bao Mei arrived carrying three painted signs.

She had wrapped them separately so their surfaces would not rub. The boards were small enough for her father to finish one-handed, with holes bored before she painted. She unwrapped them on a dry cloth and asked where the red bowl should hang.

“Waiting area,” Mother Wei said.

“I know what it means. Where does the waiting area stop?”

The healer looked along the wall. Its boundary shifted whenever the sun, the wind or somebody's sore leg suggested another place to sit.

They chose the first post. The sign would mark the beginning rather than pretend the whole line could be kept inside a painted command.

The blue cup went above the clean water. A black cross over a hand marked the medicines nobody should touch without asking.

Su Fan held the boards while Bao Mei tied them. The red bowl had a small white highlight on its rim that made it look almost wet. The blue cup was brighter against the pale ground than it had been on the drying cloth.

A man walking toward the table saw the black sign and stopped with his hand half raised.

“What if I am asking?”

“Then you can use your mouth,” Bao Mei told him.

Mother Wei laughed.

“They're better than shouting.”

“Can I paint the wall when there is one?”

“Nothing that frightens the patients.”

“What about Auntie Lu's goose?”

“Especially that.”

Bao Mei ran to fetch more cord. One of the children followed, offering to help if there was anything he could carry that would not result in being told not to touch it.

The girl found him an empty basket.

When they returned, Mother Wei asked what she owed for the signs. Bao Mei named a price and then, seeing the open medicine case, began to reduce it.

“Was the first price wrong?” the healer asked.

“No.”

“Then use the first price.”

Bao Mei counted the coins into her palm. She looked at the red bowl again with an expression Su Fan recognized from Duan inspecting a repair that would be used after he walked away.

She had made something that worked.

The wind turned the signs on their cords. Su Fan shortened the loose end of the blue cup's tie after a gust spun it backward. Bao Mei made him leave enough cord for the board to move without striking the post.

“You want it hanging,” she said. “Not nailed to the air.”

He did as she asked.

For weeks he had thought about the lost buildings as though their absence were the whole loss. In the old clinic, he had known where to put a bucket without waiting for instructions. The bench had told people where to sit. The shelf had kept a child from reaching the stronger medicines. The door had made a private conversation possible without requiring anybody to announce that it was private.

Here those arrangements had to be made again, one at a time, among people who were tired of being told where to stand.

An old woman approached the red bowl, touched the painted rim and asked whether she should wait there.

“Yes,” Su Fan said. “Mother Wei will call you.”

“Will I hear her?”

He looked at the space beside the blanket.

“I'll ask her to come where you can see her.”

The woman sat. He placed her walking stick within reach, not against the far wall where it would have been out of everybody else's way.

Mother Wei called his name.

He turned the wrong way, corrected, and found her standing on his damaged side.

“Sorry,” she said, moving into his view. “Water, please.”

He brought it.

chapters.title: Men with Receipts
chapters.text:
The collectors came at noon, when most able workers were uphill clearing foundations.

There were four of them. Two carried sticks. One carried a seal. The last carried a ledger and seemed to believe that made the other objects unnecessary.

Su Fan saw them from beneath the sailcloth roof. He had a broken cart fitting on the bench and a piece of chalk in his hand. Duan was telling him the replacement needed another finger's width at the shoulder. The smith stopped speaking when the men turned toward Sun Lian's stores.

Their coats were dry. Their boots were not particularly muddy. They had come by the lower approach rather than through the ground everybody else had spent the morning clearing.

The ledger man asked which chest contained the cargo tools belonging to the owner of *Honest Measure*.

Sun Lian looked up from a length of damaged rope.

“Who is asking?”

He gave the name of an office and held out a paper. The man with the seal stood just behind his elbow, making sure she could see the authority he carried.

She wiped her hands before taking the claim.

Su Fan watched her read. At first her expression was merely attentive. She checked the second side, returned to the first and moved one finger down a line.

Then she laughed in a way he had never heard from her.

“You ordered the boat to stay.”

“The office ordered emergency service,” the ledger man said. “The lender did not waive repayment.”

Her supply contract had been suspended after the gate failure. A continuation fee had accrued while *Honest Measure* remained committed to emergency work instead of paid delivery. The claim counted those days carefully. The days the boat had spent carrying other people's possessions away from the water were particularly well represented.

“The lender is the contractor's brother.”

“That is not relevant to the amount.”

He might have been rehearsing the sentence for years.

Sun Lian unfolded the paper fully. She put the rope aside and walked to the cart where her smaller tools were kept. The collectors followed, evidently taking movement for agreement.

She opened a wrapped packet, found her own papers and placed them beside the claim.

“This is the instruction to retain the boat for emergency service. This is the delivery suspension. This is the outstanding account for work already performed.”

“We are not collecting that account.”

“I noticed.”

The man with the seal inspected none of the documents. He looked instead at a measuring chest strapped against the cart's side. Its corners were reinforced with old brass. Sun Lian had repaired one hinge herself, leaving the replacement pin slightly longer so it could be drawn without damaging the wood.

Su Fan knew the chest. He had once put a wet gauge back in it and been made to take every object out and dry the lining.

Sun Lian folded the claim along its existing creases.

“You can inspect the inventory. You cannot remove the tools until the district confirms the suspension terms.”

The ledger man opened his book.

“Refusal of—”

“Inspection is not refused.”

He hesitated over the line.

She turned the inventory so he could read it. The small difference mattered to her. She was not going to let him describe what she had said merely because he possessed the paper on which it would be written.

The man with the seal signalled the others.

One reached for the measuring chest.

Su Fan put down his chalk and stepped around the bench. He was aware of Duan looking at him. There was enough space beside the cart for three people if nobody tried to force a fourth through it.

He caught the chest's handle.

“Wait for the confirmation.”

The collector pulled.

Su Fan held it still. He did not drag the man toward him. He could feel how little effort would be needed to make this look different to anyone arriving late.

“Let go,” the collector said.

“Of her chest?”

The stick came down toward his fingers.

Su Fan released the handle and shifted out of the line of the blow. The weighted end struck the wood. He caught the shaft below it, turned his wrist and stepped close enough that the man could no longer use the length.

He kept the fourth circuit quiet.

The collector tried to pull the stick back. Su Fan changed the angle instead of pulling harder. The man's fingers opened. The stick came free.

Behind him, Sun Lian said something sharply.

He turned toward the sound.

The second man came from his right.

Su Fan heard the scrape of a boot on the wrong side, looked where his body insisted the movement was, and corrected too late. The blow struck his shoulder. Pain drove him against the cart. The disarmed stick fell beneath the wheel.

He could see the second man's arm rising again.

Tan Wei caught the wrist before the next strike.

Water flashed blue from the bucket beside the wheel. It wrapped the collector's ankle, no more than a turning band, but enough to shift his foot as Tan Wei pulled his arm the other way.

The man fell into the mud.

The bucket tipped. Water ran between the cart ruts.

For a moment the only movement was the fallen collector trying to keep his coat out of it.

“Stop,” Sun Lian said.

She had a hand on the first collector's chest and the inventory in the other. Her feet were set. He had discovered that trying to move her was not the easiest remaining part of his job.

The ledger man stepped backward.

“Assault on authorized agents.”

“Four witnesses saw the first blow,” Tan Wei said.

“Five,” Auntie Lu called from the kitchen.

Su Fan had not seen her come out. She stood with a ladle in one hand and a cloth in the other, looking offended in a way that did not depend on which man had lost his balance.

“Seven,” Deng said, arriving with two roof workers.

The number continued improving.

One of the men on the slope had seen a stick raised and come down to find out why. A woman who had been mending bedding said she had heard Sun Lian offer inspection. Duan supplied the exact point at which the collector reached for the chest.

The man with the seal looked from face to face.

Sun Lian removed her hand from the first man's coat.

“The tools stay.”

The ledger man said they would return with guards. He pinned the claim to the cart as though that restored something which had been lost.

They left by the same approach.

Tan Wei watched until they passed the bend, then righted the bucket.

Su Fan tried to lift his arm. The shoulder answered with a deep ache.

“Don't,” Tan Wei said. “Wei will ask you to do that often enough.”

“I heard him.”

“I know.”

“I turned.”

“The wrong way.”

There was no kindness in pretending otherwise. Su Fan looked at the muddy place where the second collector had fallen and felt his face grow hot.

Sun Lian unpinned the claim. The point had gone through a line of figures.

She smoothed the paper against the cart.

“Next time,” she said, “stand where you can see both of them.”

He wanted to say there should not be a next time. She was already checking whether the blow had damaged the measuring chest.

***

Shen Tu came before evening.

He examined the claim, heard the accounts and asked for the emergency-service instruction. Sun Lian laid out the same papers she had shown the collectors. This time the reader looked at them.

Su Fan stood behind her, his shoulder aching. Mother Wei had examined it and told him not to turn a bruise into something worse by repeatedly proving it hurt. He had obeyed until the captain arrived, when standing still suddenly became more difficult.

Shen Tu asked who had struck first.

The witnesses answered. He asked the same question of Su Fan, who described the hand reaching for the chest, his own grip on the handle and the stick.

“Did you use cultivation?”

“No.”

“On either man?”

“Neither.”

Tan Wei said he had used water from the bucket to stop the second blow. He did not claim the collector had slipped by himself.

The captain looked at the empty vessel, the mud and the mark on the chest. He had arrived late, but not too late to see useful things.

“The collectors will wait for review,” he said.

Sun Lian thanked him with no warmth at all.

He accepted the temperature of the thanks.

“Debt does not disappear because the weather was bad.”

“Neither does an order requiring the debtor to work without payment.”

“That is what the review will establish.”

He gathered the disputed copies. She kept her originals and made sure he understood which sheets he was taking.

“What do I show the next men who arrive?” she asked.

Shen Tu wrote a short instruction on a separate sheet and put his office mark beneath it. It stopped removal pending review. It did not cancel the amount or say when the boat's emergency service would be paid.

Sun Lian read the limits before accepting it.

The captain turned to leave, then paused beside Su Fan.

“You're easier to approach from the right.”

It was an observation a sympathetic man might have made.

The captain was not making it sympathetically.

Su Fan met his eyes. He could hear a hammer sounding somewhere above the camp and could not be certain which worksite it came from.

“Yes,” he said.

Shen Tu left with the disputed papers.

Afterward, Sun Lian put the measuring chest back against the cart. The stick had dented one corner but had not broken the lid. She drew the long hinge pin, opened the chest and checked the instruments one by one.

Su Fan offered to help.

“Hold the lid. With your other arm.”

He did.

The task gave him something he could manage without anyone having to tell him he had behaved well. One gauge had shifted from its padded place. Sun Lian checked its needle and set it back.

“You should not have had to do that,” he said.

“Which part?”

“Any of it.”

She looked at him over the open chest.

“That is a very large complaint. Hold it a little higher.”

He lifted the lid.

She finished checking the tools. Then she took the captain's instruction, wrapped it with her other papers and tied the packet tightly enough that the damp could not reach the folded edges.

“The review may still go against me,” she said.

“I know.”

“Good. I don't need you promising the boat what the captain didn't.”

The thought had been close enough to his tongue that he was relieved she stopped it.

***

That night, the mother of the arrested stores clerk came to the clinic.

She waited until the last patient had gone behind the blanket before approaching Mother Wei. Su Fan was carrying away a used water vessel. He recognized the woman from the upper labour rows and nearly asked whether the medicine had helped her.

Then he saw the cloth bag in her hands.

She held it against her stomach, both thumbs pressed along its opening as though she feared something might escape.

“My son,” she said.

Mother Wei put down the list she had been writing.

The clerk had died in custody during the flood evacuation. The notice said fever. It also said his confession had resolved the outstanding supply irregularities.

The paper had been folded into the same bag as his personal effects.

Mother Wei brought her a stool. The woman sat on its edge, not yet prepared to occupy all the space she had been offered.

“Were you told when?” the healer asked.

The woman showed her the notice.

Mother Wei read it without making her repeat what was there. She asked what she had been told about his belongings and whether anyone had accompanied the message. The answers were brief. There had been a delivery, a receipt for the bag and no conversation which had made the event more understandable.

Su Fan remained by the water vessels. He did not know whether she wanted him to hear.

Mother Wei looked at the woman before calling him over.

“Would you show him the schedule?”

She nodded.

Inside the bag were two letters and a copy of a delivery schedule bearing Shen Tu's office mark. The letters had been opened already. The woman kept them beneath her hand while she passed over the schedule.

Su Fan did not reach for them.

The copied figures were cramped. The clerk had fitted more into the margin than the original ruling permitted, shortening labels and carrying one line beneath another. Some of the entries were familiar. Su Fan had seen the corresponding dates while following the false operator accounts.

Beside each change, a superior's approval had been copied in the same tight hand.

He read the page twice.

A gust lifted the blanket behind them. Mother Wei caught its edge and secured it around the post. For a moment the clinic's lamp shone openly across the camp, illuminating three people bent over one small sheet while others walked past carrying supper bowls.

“What is it?” the woman asked.

“Part of the delivery record,” Su Fan said. “Some of these changes match entries we asked about before.”

“Does it show who told him?”

“It shows approvals he copied. They need to be checked against the originals.”

He wanted to say what it did not show before she had time to hope for more. The paper did not prove the captain had killed her son. It could not tell them who had known what during the evacuation, or whether the notice's description of fever was true.

It did show that the clerk had not been making every alteration alone.

The old woman spoke before he could turn the distinction into a speech.

“He stole,” she said. “I know he stole. Don't make him innocent to help me.”

Mother Wei sat beside her.

“What do you want?”

“I want them to stop saying he did it by himself.”

Su Fan looked at the schedule again. He had wanted the bad entries found, the men responsible named, the failures corrected. The notice in the bag was written as though the work of naming had ended conveniently with one man who could no longer answer questions.

“May I make a copy?” he asked.

The woman studied him.

“Will you keep this one?”

“Only if you ask me to. I can put it in a dry folder while the copy is made.”

“And the letters?”

“They are yours.”

She drew them closer. One edge had been worn soft by repeated unfolding. Whatever was written there was not evidence she had offered to the whole valley.

Mother Wei found a clean folder. Su Fan laid the schedule inside without smoothing it harder than necessary. He wrote the woman's name on the outside where she told him, then showed her the label before closing it.

She placed the notice beside the bag and sat back at last.

“Could I have some water?” she asked.

Mother Wei reached for the blue-marked cup.

chapters.title: What a Name Could Carry
chapters.text:
The new settlement required a list of households.

The old town had contained households, lodgers, apprentices, widowed relatives and people who slept where work left them. The form allowed a head of household and dependants.

Duan wrote Su Fan's name as a dependant.

Su Fan crossed it out.

The smith looked offended.

“You've eaten my rice for six years.”

“I've worked for it.”

“Badly at first.”

“Then charge arrears.”

Ah-Du stopped sharpening a piece of charcoal. He had been trying to make it fine enough for the small boxes on the page, and had so far produced a blackened thumb and a steadily shorter piece of charcoal.

“Can you charge for old mistakes?” he asked.

Duan turned toward him.

The boy put the charcoal down.

The form lay on the bench between the smith and Su Fan. Wind tugged at one edge. A weight from the scale held the other, leaving the crossed-out name plainly visible in the middle.

Duan had written it carefully. His usual hurried hand had been slowed by the awkward position of his damaged arm and the need to keep the sheet from moving. Crossing it out had taken Su Fan one quick stroke.

For a moment neither said anything.

Su Fan could remember the first bed Duan gave him. It had been behind a partition near the charcoal store, with a roof seam that let in cold air but no rain. Mother Wei had brought his folded clothes. Duan had said he would be useful once he learned which end of a broom made contact with the floor.

He had wanted so badly to be useful that he swept dust into corners the smith would not discover for another month.

Since then there had been wages, quarrels, bowls left warm beside the furnace and work entrusted to him when Duan was elsewhere. None of those things fitted neatly into either box on the form.

“You want your own plot?” the smith asked at last.

“I want my own name on the work.”

Duan put down the brush.

“All right.”

He sounded sadder than Su Fan expected.

The answer made Su Fan feel as though he had refused something that had not been described properly enough for him to accept or decline it.

“I wasn't saying I wanted to stop working with you.”

“I didn't say you were.”

“The space could be beside the shop.”

“It could.”

Duan looked at the form again. Su Fan wished the crossed-out line were less dark.

They asked the clerk what separate registration would require. The clerk was sitting on an upturned crate outside the awning, trying to keep four different households' papers from becoming one large household in the wind.

He explained that the applications could request adjoining spaces. The shop lease would belong to Duan if granted. Su Fan could rent a room and hold a separate work registration. The land agreement itself was still to be settled; writing a request did not put a roof on it.

“We understand that,” Duan said.

“People sometimes don't.”

The clerk pointed to the corrected name.

“I'll need this clear.”

Su Fan fetched another sheet rather than ask the clerk to interpret the crossing-out. He copied the ordinary details, left the disputed part empty, and turned it toward Duan.

The smith dictated the workshop requirements. Space for the furnace, safe access for fuel, room to carry a long piece of iron without striking somebody's doorway. He grew more like himself as the list became particular.

Su Fan added a small room beside it under his own application.

“Window?” Duan asked.

“If I can afford one.”

“A hole is inexpensive.”

“Keeping the weather out costs more.”

“Then learn a trade.”

Su Fan smiled and wrote the request.

Ah-Du remained an apprentice because he loudly refused to pay rent until someone proved adulthood profitable.

“You will want a place for your things,” Su Fan told him.

“I have a place.”

“You have several. Most of them belong to other people.”

“That sounds profitable.”

Duan asked him to find the small punch. The boy looked toward the row of sorted tools, then toward his own coat, and wisely went to search without further economic argument.

Su Fan sanded the two applications. When the ink had dried, Duan read the new sheet from beginning to end. He set his good hand beside the space reserved for the shop holder's mark.

“Adjoining,” he said.

“Yes.”

The smith nodded and signed.

A customer arrived before the ink had dried. He wanted the repaired strap from his cart and hoped the fact that he had been made to wait would reduce the price.

Duan pointed to Su Fan.

“He did it. Ask him.”

Su Fan fetched the strap. He showed the man where the old metal had cracked and where a new piece had been fitted. The customer bent it against the edge of the bench until Duan told him the repair had been made for a cart, not for an afternoon of trying to prove he should pay less.

They agreed on the amount already quoted.

“Whose name do I put down?” the man asked. He supplied a carrying company that wanted a record of every repair, partly so its drivers could not charge for the same one twice.

“Duan's shop,” Su Fan said.

“And who worked it?”

He glanced at the smith.

“You,” Duan said. “Unless the strap has changed its mind.”

Su Fan wrote his name. The sheet was damp at one corner and his first stroke spread wider than he intended. He finished carefully, sanded it and returned the receipt.

The customer took the repaired iron and went away. No new freedom announced itself. Su Fan still had work waiting, a place beneath someone else's sailcloth, and a shoulder that complained when he carried too much at once.

Duan checked the money, set aside the part belonging to the shop and pushed Su Fan's share across the bench.

“Don't spend it on a window before you have a wall.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“You looked as though you were considering a very fine one.”

Su Fan put the coins away with the application. Then he took up the next piece of work.

***

The evening meeting was held where the common kitchen's warmth reached the edge of the sheltered ground.

People brought stools, crates and things they hoped could be sat on without breaking. Auntie Lu objected to anyone placing a paper within splashing distance of the pot. Deng moved the pot farther away and was told the fire could not move with it merely because a meeting needed room.

They moved the meeting.

By the time Tan Wei arrived, the widow had sorted the relief copies into a packet. Bao Shun was describing the difference between storage for finished boards and storage for damp wood. Both needed cover. Keeping them together might ruin the work they intended to sell.

Tan Wei waited until the discussion reached a pause.

“I have a proposal.”

Su Fan looked up from the material list.

The gate office needed permanent technicians for the winter repairs. The rate was higher than seasonal labour, and bonded technicians could earn housing credit for relatives or designated dependants.

Tan Wei wanted to use the allowance for a storehouse and two rooms beside the new clinic.

Auntie Lu set down the bowl she had been holding.

“How much of a storehouse?”

“Not the entire building. Enough to begin the frame and roofing, with the other materials already promised.”

Sun Lian asked which part of the credit could be used for transport. Tan Wei showed her the terms he had brought. He had marked the relevant line before coming, and Su Fan saw how much preparation had taken place without his advice.

Mother Wei waited until the practical amount was understood.

“What would you owe in return?”

“Three years at the station, with training and wages. Emergency extension applies while actively coupled. Withdrawal rights remain between cycles.”

“Supervised?”

“Yes. Han insists on that part.”

She asked what the supervision involved. Tan Wei answered what he had been told and admitted what was still to be confirmed in the final copy. He did not behave as though naming a benefit made every remaining question rude.

“Have you read the original?” Su Fan asked.

“Yes. Han has too.”

“Who copies the agreement?”

“An independent scribe. I asked.”

Su Fan felt relief, followed by the uncomfortable recognition of how his friend had anticipated him.

He looked at the blue cord on Tan Wei's wrist. The temporary arrangement already gave him strength Su Fan could not reproduce. It had also called him into a shared return beside a boat full of frightened people, when he had needed to remain himself for one more step.

Three years sounded different when Su Fan looked at the cord.

The widow asked whether the town would owe Tan Wei anything.

“No. The credit is mine to assign.”

“Would it be lost if you left the work?”

“There are conditions. I want the scribe to explain exactly how they apply to the assigned building before I sign.”

“Then we should decide whether to accept it,” she said, “not whether to permit your employment.”

Tan Wei nodded gratefully.

Su Fan lowered the question he had been about to ask. It was a question about risk, but it had begun to sound in his head like an argument for postponing everything until he was satisfied.

The meeting discussed the storehouse.

Sun Lian wanted the roof supported properly before goods were placed beneath it. Bao Shun asked for a dry shelf that could be reached without moving every grain sack first. Mother Wei wanted the clinic rooms close enough for a sick person to be brought under cover, not so close that the medicine storage became a public passage.

“Who keeps the keys?” Deng asked.

That question occupied more time than the height of the roof.

People who trusted one another to carry patients through floodwater still wanted to know who would open a store when a person responsible for it was elsewhere.
