The widow suggested a record of what went in and out. Auntie Lu asked who would be available to write it when somebody needed a cooking pot before dawn.

They worked toward an arrangement which left neither all the keys nor all the blame with one person.

Tan Wei listened. When a question concerned the limits of his allowance, he answered. When it concerned how the building should be used, he gave an opinion and let other people disagree with it.

Su Fan found this harder to watch than a dramatic sacrifice would have been. A sacrifice could be praised, refused, argued over in large words. Here was a friend offering something valuable and then staying while people discussed where the door should go.

The proposed two rooms remained beside the clinic. The exact dimensions would wait for the final allocation and the measured ground. Nobody counted timber they did not yet have as though it were already dry and standing.

When the meeting ended, Tan Wei gathered his papers.

Su Fan asked him to walk.

His friend looked at the unfinished work, then at the path.

“All right.”

***

They stopped above the flooded quarter.

Lights moved along the new river edge where search workers still checked debris. The old road no longer supplied a reliable guide. A familiar line of houses lay somewhere beyond the darkness, but Su Fan could not fit the remembered doors to what he could see.

Tan Wei leaned against a post on his left.

For a while neither spoke.

The cold reached through their coats. From the common kitchen came the sound of someone dropping a lid and being told, at considerable volume, that lids did not improve through repeated dropping.

“Do you want the bond?” Su Fan asked.

Tan Wei considered the wording.

“Yes.”

“Or do you want what it pays?”

“Both.”

It was an answer Su Fan could not separate into a good part and a dangerous part without doing violence to what his friend had actually said.

“The dreams haven't stopped.”

“No. They are being watched.”

“That doesn't mean—”

Tan Wei looked at him.

Su Fan stopped. He could hear the sentence continuing without his mouth: that did not mean they were safe, that did not mean Han knew everything, that did not mean a signed promise would remain stronger than a frightened office when the river rose.

All those things might be true.

They were also things Tan Wei had lived closer to than he had.

“I can't tell whether I'm asking because it matters,” Su Fan said, “or because I need you to reach my answer.”

Tan Wei rubbed rain from the post with his thumb.

“Then stop at the question.”

Su Fan did.

A search lamp moved between two other lights. Someone called across the water. The reply took longer than Su Fan expected, and he had to turn his head before he could understand where it came from.

He remembered Tan Wei beside the assessment hall years before, saying nothing on the walk home. He had assumed then that because they shared the silence they meant the same thing by it.

After a while Tan Wei spoke again.

“I like the work when it works.”

Su Fan looked at him.

“I like understanding why a boat stays level. I like seeing water move because I asked it properly. I like being taught by someone who knows more than I do.”

“You already have that.”

“I have the beginning of it.”

Tan Wei held his hands apart, looking at the space between them as though there might be a basin there.

“When Han first had us lift a drop, I thought it was a foolish thing to spend an afternoon doing. Then I couldn't. I kept making more water move than I meant to, or nothing at all. Qiu Lan could do it before I could. That annoyed me so much I stopped listening.”

Su Fan smiled despite himself.

“You are enjoying this part.”

“A little.”

“Good. Remember it next time you explain something to me twice.”

Tan Wei lowered his hands.

“The first time I got it right, I knew why. Not every part, but enough to do it again. I wanted to keep learning. I still do.”

The account sounded uncomfortably familiar. Su Fan could have offered a different setting, a small stone, an imperfect circuit and the same pleasure.

“You found something that suits you,” Tan Wei said. “It doesn't make everything that suits someone else a trap.”

“It may still be a trap.”

“Yes. And yours may kill you because half the instructions are missing.”

Su Fan let out a breath that almost became a laugh.

“That is fair.”

“It's unpleasantly fair.”

They stood beside the water until the cold made remaining still feel deliberate.

Su Fan wanted to ask what he could do if things went wrong. He could hear how easily the question might become a request to be appointed responsible in advance.

Instead he asked when Tan Wei expected the final papers.

His friend told him. The appointment still depended on the registrar and the independent scribe being present. Han wanted the medical supervision arranged separately from ordinary shared work.

“Will you come when I sign?” Tan Wei asked.

Su Fan looked at him.

“As a witness,” his friend added. “Not a guardian.”

“Yes.”

Tan Wei nodded and pushed away from the post. His sleeve caught on a splinter. Su Fan reached automatically, then saw his friend had already freed it.

They went back by the wider path.

At the kitchen, Deng had saved two bowls under an upturned basin. The broth was still warm. He said they could thank him by carrying the washing water when they were finished.

Tan Wei took the bowl on the left and handed Su Fan the other.

Neither had to ask whose decision it was to sit and eat.

chapters.title: The Hand He Chose
chapters.text:
Tan Wei signed at a table with four chairs.

He had insisted on the fourth.

One for himself. One for Han. One for the station registrar. One for the independent scribe who would keep his copy outside the gate office.

Su Fan stood behind the last chair.

The room smelled of old ink and recently dried clothing. Someone had put a brazier near the doorway, where it warmed the person entering and did little for anyone obliged to remain beside the window. The scribe moved his chair once, tested the light on the page and moved it back. He preferred cold fingers to missing a small character.

Tan Wei had washed his hands. There was still a faint dark line beneath one nail from helping lift wet timber the evening before. He rubbed at it while the registrar arranged the papers, then stopped when Han put a cup beside him.

“Drink before we begin,” the teacher said.

“I have.”

“Then you may ignore me. It will be useful practice.”

The remark made Tan Wei smile. Su Fan had expected Han to treat the occasion solemnly. The teacher instead checked whether the chair would support his bad leg and asked the registrar which copy he intended to read.

They compared the opening lines before going further.

The registrar read aloud. He had done this often enough that some phrases came quickly, almost as single long words. At first Tan Wei followed without interrupting. His eyes moved between the spoken line and his own copy.

Then he raised a hand.

“The address of the housing credit.”

The registrar stopped.

“It is assigned to the clinic site and common storehouse under the new application. That is the old location.”

The man looked at the entry, checked a second sheet and nodded. The scribe watched the correction made on each copy. He did not merely write the right address on his own and assume the others would acquire it later.

Su Fan had been preparing to point out the error. He let his hand fall back to his side.

The reading continued through wages, training, duty periods and the conditions under which a permanent impression could be withdrawn. Tan Wei interrupted a second time.

“The window between return cycles. Read that again.”

A bonded operator could begin uncoupling between scheduled returns, provided a qualified supervisor managed the process and the station was not under an active emergency seal.

“What qualifies as active?” Tan Wei asked.

The registrar pointed to the definition.

A declared, logged condition. Signed by the supervising elder. Limited to the specific station and event.

“Not simply a difficult shift?”

“A difficult shift is not a declaration.”

“And I may see the entry?”

“The entry is part of the operating record.”

Tan Wei turned to the scribe.

“Copy that paragraph separately as well.”

The scribe made a note. Han waited while the registrar explained where the declaration would be recorded and which supervisor could arrange an uncoupling. When the explanation became broader than the words on the page, the scribe brought them back to the words.

Su Fan said nothing.

He could feel questions rising in him with the familiar urgency of work he had not yet finished. What if the qualified supervisor was absent? What if an emergency lasted beyond the event which began it? What if somebody called an ordinary day difficult enough to require a different interpretation?

Some questions belonged here. Some had already been asked. Some could not be answered by interrupting his friend until no uncertainty remained.

Han looked once toward him, not warning him away, simply acknowledging that he was there.

Tan Wei reached the last page.

He read it for himself before turning it over. The registrar waited with the brush ready. Outside the window a labourer called for a hand with a cart. The room remained ordinary enough that Su Fan could almost persuade himself the act before them was another employment arrangement, no different from the one Shen Tu had offered him.

Then Tan Wei moved the blue wrist cord out of the way.

He signed his name.

His handwriting had improved since the first letter from the dormitory. The characters no longer leaned into one another so urgently. He had left room around them.

The scribe checked the copies, sanded the wet ink and wrapped his own document separately. Su Fan watched him secure it inside a case which would leave the gate office with him.

Nobody applauded.

Han stood carefully and asked whether Tan Wei was ready to go to the other room.

His friend looked at the signed page once more.

“Yes.”

***

The permanent impression entered through the wrist cord.

Han supervised in a quiet room away from the shared formation. There was no line of operators on either side of Tan Wei, no gate wheel waiting for a timed return, no body of water whose movement depended on the next breath.

A basin stood on a low support. Two healers had arranged what they needed within reach. One asked Tan Wei about the recent dreams and had him describe when they occurred rather than merely whether they frightened him.

Su Fan remained near the door until the question of his presence had been settled.

“May I stay?” he asked.

Tan Wei looked toward the healers, then back at him.

“Yes. But don't stand where I have to look around you to see Han.”

He moved.

The teacher checked the cord and asked his pupil to sit as he had practised. Tan Wei adjusted his feet. His knee had begun bouncing, and he put a hand on it until the movement stopped.

“You can be frightened,” Han said. “I need you to tell me what changes.”

“I am frightened.”

“Then we have begun honestly.”

Su Fan remembered his own first circuit and the misleading comfort of doing something dangerous alone. There had been nobody to watch him make the wrong movement except a boy who did not know what it meant. He had called the absence of witnesses privacy. Here the presence of witnesses made the risk harder to pretend away.

The blue thread brightened.

Tan Wei inhaled, then stopped halfway.

His eyes fixed on something beyond the wall.

Su Fan took half a step before he understood that he had moved. One healer had already shifted closer. Han spoke his pupil's name.

“Here. This room. This year.”

Tan Wei's fingers spread on his knees.

The basin's surface trembled. A thin line of water rose at one edge and fell back. Nothing in the room had moved enough to cause it.

“Tan Wei.”

His friend's eyes found the teacher.

“There,” Han said. “Stay with that.”

The movement returned to Tan Wei's chest. He drew another breath, shorter than the one he had begun, and let it out unevenly.

A healer asked a question Su Fan could not hear clearly from where he stood. He nearly leaned toward his good side, then remembered he had been asked not to obstruct anyone. Tan Wei answered. Han heard him and altered the position of his own hand beside the cord.

For several minutes the borrowed routes settled against the ones his pupil had already trained.

From outside, the process looked almost gentle. There was no blazing column, no shattered floor. Sweat ran down Tan Wei's face and darkened the neck of his shirt. He had stopped trying to look composed.

Su Fan unclenched his own hands.

The burn scars in his palms pulled as his fingers opened. He watched them for a moment, using the small discomfort to keep himself from following every change in his friend's breathing with a movement of his own.

He could intervene if something went wrong.

He could also make something go wrong by moving because he was afraid.

Han glanced at him once and returned his attention to the patient.

Tan Wei spoke a name Su Fan did not recognize, too softly for him to be certain he had heard it correctly. Han asked him to describe the room. He named the basin, the window and the person beside his left hand. The healer nodded.

His voice became steadier.

The blue thread no longer seemed to lie merely on his skin. Three narrow lines held above the wrist where its shifting light had gathered. Tan Wei looked down and then deliberately back toward Han, as though looking too closely at the mark might pull his attention away from something he needed to keep doing.

At last his breathing settled.

The teacher waited longer than Su Fan wanted him to wait. He asked ordinary questions. He had Tan Wei turn his hand, rest it and speak again. One healer checked his responses while the other watched the mark.

Only then did Han move the basin closer.

A ring of water rose and held its shape without trembling.

Tan Wei looked at it with exhausted delight.

“Still spill it when I laugh?”

“Less now,” Han said.

His friend laughed weakly. The ring wavered and fell, splashing the basin's edge.

“Some,” the teacher amended.

Su Fan found he was smiling. He had not given himself permission to do so, and for once the omission was harmless.

***

After the healers left, Tan Wei asked for a mirror.

Han found a small one with a handle worn smooth by use. The permanent mark was modest: three blue lines above the wrist, like reeds reflected in water.

Tan Wei turned his hand to see them from another angle.

Su Fan watched his face rather than the mark.

“Hurts?”

“Yes.”

“Badly?”

“Bearably.”

“Do you want—”

Tan Wei looked up.

Su Fan stopped, then finished carefully.

“Water to drink.”

His friend smiled.

“Yes. That kind is safe to decide for me.”

Su Fan brought the cup. Tan Wei took it with his unmarked hand and drank slowly, making a face when he discovered it had cooled.

“You control water now,” Su Fan said. “You can complain to it.”

“Han hasn't taught that part.”

“An omission.”

“A serious one.”

They sat without speaking for a while.

Tan Wei seemed neither triumphant nor defeated. He was tired, sore and quietly pleased. A person who had made a consequential choice and now had to live through the afternoon after it.

The registrar's room was being used for something else already. Through the wall Su Fan could hear a dispute over a missing delivery. Whoever had signed last was apparently not the person who had received the goods. Ordinary work continued around the act which had occupied all of Su Fan's attention.

Han returned with the instructions for the next few days. Tan Wei listened, repeated the parts he needed to remember and asked whether he could go home by himself.

“You can go with your witness,” the teacher said. “Let him do something inexpensive.”

Su Fan offered his arm when they stood.

Tan Wei tested his balance first, then took it.

Outside, the light seemed too bright after the quiet room. A recruit passing them looked at the new mark and straightened, impressed. Tan Wei did not have enough energy to reward the expression. He nodded and kept walking.

They stopped once on the road.

Su Fan had expected a moment like this to fill itself with questions about the future. Instead Tan Wei asked whether there was anything left from the common kitchen or whether they would arrive after Deng had begun experimenting.

“I think Auntie Lu is cooking.”

“Good.”

He looked at his wrist again, then let his sleeve fall over it.

***

The housing credit arrived five days later.

It came as a receipt and a quantity of authorized materials, not a rain of silver. Somebody still had to arrange collection. Somebody had to check that the pieces delivered could do the work drawn for them.

Sun Lian examined the timber before the frame was raised. Duan, sitting with his arm protected, objected to one joint on the proposed doorway and explained why until the people holding the pieces could see it too.

The storehouse began rising beside the clinic site.

Townspeople carried timber, laid stone and complained about the weather. Bao Mei painted the doorway before the wall had been completed. She said the timber was easier to reach now. Her father said this was true but did not justify painting the place where he still had to fit a brace.

They settled the boundary with a chalk line.

Tan Wei helped after his shifts. He arrived smelling faintly of the river, put down his work bag and asked which task was waiting. Nobody gave him command of the building because his credit had helped pay for it.

Su Fan worked beside him.

The frame was awkward enough that strength alone did not make the lifting simple. A beam had to be turned before it could be raised, and the available ground sloped away beside the temporary supports. Sun Lian marked where each person should stand and had them try the movement without the weight first.

Ah-Du declared the rehearsal much easier than the work.

“Then remember it when the work arrives,” she said.

They lifted together.

Halfway through the turn, the blue lines on Tan Wei's wrist tightened. His grip changed into a shape Su Fan did not recognize. His thumb moved along the wood as though searching for a different handle.

Su Fan kept his own end steady.

Then his friend blinked and loosened the unfamiliar grip.

“Hold,” Sun Lian called.

They rested the beam on the waiting support before anyone asked a question.

“What happened?” Su Fan said.

“An old movement. Han says to mark when it occurs.”

“Will you?”

Tan Wei took a small notebook from his bag and wrote the time. He added what he had been doing when the movement came. After a moment he crossed out one word and chose another.

He did not hide the occurrence. He did not turn it into a performance of courage either.

Sun Lian asked whether he needed to stop lifting.

“For a little while,” he said.

Another worker took his place. Tan Wei held the alignment cord and watched the beam rise from the ground. The job continued without punishing him for having answered.

By dusk, the storehouse had a roof.

Its walls were unfinished. Rain could still come through several places if the wind chose the right angle. For the moment, the first drops fell straight down, tapping the new covering while people carried grain sacks underneath.

Auntie Lu came with a bowl balanced inside a basket and announced that a building whose first occupants were sacks should make room for people soon.

They crowded beneath the roof.

Someone stood too close to an open edge and discovered the limit of the shelter. Everyone laughed when he stepped inward, shaking water from his hair with an expression of deep personal betrayal.

Su Fan laughed too.

He could hear the rain clearly on his left and less clearly on his right. He turned enough to see Tan Wei across the room.

His friend stood beneath the roof his decision had helped pay for, rubbing his marked wrist with his other hand.

chapters.title: The Elder's Burn
chapters.text:
Pei Gang's right hand had not healed.

Su Fan noticed it during the second review. The elder kept the hand below the table, but a dark line crossed the visible wrist. Water gathered there and evaporated without heat.

Holding the high lake had cost him something.

Su Fan was glad to know the cost existed. He was not glad enough to confuse it with the cost paid below.

Jiang conducted the examination. Pei watched.

They began with movements Su Fan had performed before. Lift, carry, stand, turn. A weight which felt manageable at his side became less so when he held it away from his body. Jiang marked the difference and asked him to repeat the turn without preparing so long beforehand.

He tried.

The fourth circuit held. His right foot moved farther than he intended, correcting a balance he should not have lost in the first place.

“Again?” he asked.

“After you rest.”

An assistant exchanged the weight for a heavier one. Su Fan disliked the small courtesy with which the man asked whether he was ready. It sounded too much like permission to fail politely.

He took the load.

For a short time he managed it cleanly. Then his shoulders began taking work which should have passed through the rest of his frame. He could feel the old effort gathering in the familiar places.

He set it down before Jiang told him to.

“How long could you have continued?” she asked.

“Longer. Badly.”

She wrote that rather than the answer he might have preferred to give.

During the rest, the assistant noticed a dark scuff beneath Su Fan's heel and began rubbing it away with a cloth.

“Leave it,” Jiang said.

He looked up.

“I want to know where the foot moved.”

Su Fan put his shoe beside the mark. The sole was wearing unevenly. He had known that when walking, but the shape left on the floor made the habit harder to dismiss as discomfort belonging to an old pair of shoes.

“Those are the ones you work in?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Keep them for the next test, then. Don't return in new shoes and tell me the method has changed.”

The assistant brought a stool. Su Fan sat and loosened the lace that had been pressing the side of his foot. He wanted to correct the posture at once, while the error was visible. Jiang had him leave the weight alone.

“Describe what you felt before you decide how to repair it.”

He began with the strongest sensation, the load across his shoulders. Then he remembered the heel moving first, and amended the account. The assistant marked the two places on the floor rather than erase the earlier one.

Pei watched this small exchange without comment. When Su Fan stood again, he was painfully aware that a powerful man had spent several minutes looking at the way his shoe wore down. It was less flattering than being called an anomaly, and probably more useful.

The injured hearing had not improved enough to change the footwork assessment. When an assistant approached outside his right-hand view, Su Fan turned late. He managed the second approach better because he knew to expect it.

“That is anticipation of this test,” Jiang said. “Not yet a reliable answer to the difficulty.”

“I know.”

“I am recording it for someone who may not.”

He looked at her page. She had distinguished the two attempts. His irritation subsided a little.

At the far end of the room, Pei moved his left hand over a document. The right remained below the table. Su Fan had first known the elder as a presence that seemed to make other people's movements smaller. Seeing him avoid a simple motion was unsettling in a different way.

He wondered whether the injury hurt constantly or only when the hand was used.

He did not ask.

Jiang finished the report. The fourth circuit remained stable under ordinary pressure. Under a heavier load, Su Fan could maintain it only briefly. The bodily injuries and hearing deficit continued to limit what he could safely be expected to do.

The elder listened to the end.

Then he dismissed the assistants.

One collected the weights. Another wiped a damp ring from the table where a vessel had rested. They left without looking at Su Fan, and the quiet after the door closed felt more deliberate than the quiet during the tests.

Pei put a different document on the table.

“A registration,” he said.

***

Su Fan read the opening line twice.

The paper named him correctly. It identified the district correctly. It described the practice under a source he could not accept.

A lost outer teaching of the Hollow Reed tradition. Recovered and restored under Pei Gang's supervision.

“That isn't what happened.”

“It is a form the regional office can recognize.”

“The method has no connection to your founder.”

“The text was housed in our archive. The possibilities are broader than your present knowledge.”

Su Fan looked at Jiang.

She did not rescue him from the decision.

He read farther. The proposed status was not merely a new title to put beside his name. It would give him a recognized place in work that currently required explanations and exceptions. He could use materials through an established programme. He could receive instruction without every request becoming another inquiry into the absence on his original assessment record.

He imagined carrying the document to a gate office and being admitted because the person at the door knew what box to put him in.

The desire was immediate enough to make him ashamed of how quickly he had dismissed the offer before reading all of it.

“What would I receive?” he asked.

“Legal standing. Training resources. Freedom to work within the district as a certified technical cultivator.”

“And you?”

“Responsibility for a recovered method and credit for identifying it.”

There was no attempt to hide the exchange.

Pei turned the paper slightly so the source line faced him more directly.

“You have already needed people to explain you to offices which have no category for your work. This gives them one. It gives me responsibility for the tests still required. It also means that a mistake will be investigated under a recognized supervision instead of treated as an unauthorized practice whose very existence demands an answer.”

Su Fan could hear the value in it. That made the source line harder to push away.

“Would the text be called yours?”

“The recovery would be supervised under my name.”

“And the people who wrote the corrections?”

“Their names, when established, can be recorded.”

“When established.”

“Yes.”

Su Fan thought of Min's mismatched annotations. The unknown person who had written that an exercise hurt. The next person who had corrected the drawing. The damaged character which might mean close or complete, and the space Min had left beneath his own uncertain reading.

Whatever the book had once been, it had survived because several hands refused to let a wrong line remain unquestioned.

The line before him was undamaged. It would be easy to copy. There would be no visible reason for a later clerk to doubt it.

“Could it say the origin is unconfirmed?”

“Not under the category being offered.”

“Then a different category.”

“That is the review you are already undergoing.”

Pei did not sound impatient. Su Fan almost wished he would. Anger would make the choice easier to describe afterward.

The elder rested his left hand on the table.

“You have a skill that may be useful. You have a text you do not fully understand. You have people depending on work you are not yet qualified to perform in several places where it is needed. I am offering you a route through those difficulties.”

“With a source neither of us has proved.”

“With a source our archive may reasonably claim as part of what it preserved.”

“It was being sold for fuel.”

For the first time Jiang looked up from the paper.

Pei's expression changed only slightly.

“A failure of custodianship does not settle the origin of the thing neglected.”

That was true. It did not make the proposed origin true as well.

Su Fan read the source line once more. He imagined signing it because it would let him do useful things, then finding reasons not to correct it because people had already relied on what he signed.

He pushed the paper back.

“I won't sign a source I can't verify.”

Pei looked at him for a long time.

“You accept an old book on evidence you cannot fully verify.”

“I test what I practise. This asks me to state the untested part as fact.”

The elder's injured hand closed beneath the table.

Jiang heard the small movement. Her eyes shifted toward it.

Pei opened the hand again.

“Your accuracy may prove costly.”

“It already has.”

Su Fan regretted the answer as soon as it left him. It sounded like a challenge he could not support, and worse, like a claim that the town's loss belonged uniquely to his refusal to lie.

The elder did not take it as a challenge.

“Yes,” he said. “I have seen the lower town.”

The silence which followed was not an agreement.

Jiang gathered the examination report. The registration remained unsigned on Pei's table.

***

On the way out, the elder stopped beside the station model.

Su Fan recognized the channels and small representations of the linked returns. Since his earlier visit, somebody had added marks showing the damaged reaches and the provisional arrangements holding the water. Some lines were neat. Others had been made quickly enough that the brush left uneven edges.

Pei touched none of those with his right hand.

“You think another arrangement was possible,” he said.

“Before the rain? Yes.”

“And during it?”

Su Fan looked at the channels.

He remembered the current through the market, the roof turning, the long pale line of light holding against the high lake. He had been on the upper road. He had not seen every gauge, every damaged return, every choice considered in the room before Jiang brought the order down.

“I don't know.”

Pei seemed to prefer that answer to the earlier refusal.

“Good. Keep the two questions separate.”

He pointed to the old command route with his uninjured hand.

“The next flood will not wait for us to agree about the last one. I need a way to interrupt this without losing the water.”

He followed the route to the place Su Fan had been shown before. The model made the gap look small. The actual system would contain people, uneven repairs and a body of water large enough to erase their mistakes along with their houses.

“You can help me build it,” Pei said, “or you can remain outside and hope our other candidates survive the work.”

Su Fan felt the intended pressure.

He also knew there were real candidates. They did not become imaginary because the elder had mentioned them at a moment designed to make refusal uncomfortable.

“What are you asking me to agree to now?”

“To recognize that remaining outside is also a choice with consequences.”

“I recognize it.”

“Do you?”

The question was quieter than Su Fan expected. He could not tell whether Pei was thinking of him, the people on the model's routes, or a choice the elder had already made and could no longer alter.

He looked at the physical channels instead of trying to answer the man's whole life.

“Let Sun Lian inspect the bypass. Give Jiang the materials she requested. That would help now.”

“It is already authorized.”

“Then let it be funded.”

For the first time Pei's expression hardened openly.

“You have not seen the entire ledger.”

“No.”

“Remember that.”

Su Fan bowed because leaving safely mattered more than winning the last sentence.

He had no wish to be made useful by an invented origin. He also had no complete answer to the system drawn before him. Both remained true when he followed Jiang out of the room.

Behind them, the elder returned to the table. Su Fan heard a cup placed down, then the faint scrape of paper being moved with the wrong hand.

***

Jiang walked with him to the lower stair.

“You asked for the right materials,” she said.

“Will we get them?”

“Some.”

“Because I asked?”

“Because I've been asking for six weeks. Don't give yourself credit for arriving at the end of an argument.”

He accepted the correction.

It was uncomfortable to discover how quickly he had made a private confrontation the explanation for a public result. He had seen Jiang's requests on tables before this visit. He had helped carry drawings for work whose cost had been discussed long before the elder offered him registration.

“Does some mean enough to begin?” he asked.

“It means enough to do specified work. Sun Lian knows which parts are funded.”

“And the rest?”

“I continue asking.”

She paused at the next landing to speak to a clerk waiting with a packet. Su Fan stepped aside. The conversation concerned a delivery already late, a load that had been divided and a receipt from somebody who had not been where the driver expected.

He had nothing useful to contribute.

When Jiang finished, she turned back to him.

“Your report will distinguish the tests from the proposed registration. You refused the latter. That does not erase the former.”

“Thank you.”

“Don't thank me for keeping two documents separate. Read the copy when it arrives.”

She went uphill again.

Su Fan descended alone, keeping the wall on his right where the stairs allowed it. He could feel the ordinary fatigue of the tests in his legs. There had been no great duel, no revelation which made the elder's pressure dissolve. A document remained unsigned. Some materials were finally coming.

At the camp, the first cart of timber funded for the work arrived before dusk.

It was not the same allocation as the housing credit which had begun the storehouse. Sun Lian checked its destination against the list and stopped a man from carrying one of the longer pieces toward the clinic roof.

“That one is for the frame.”

“The clinic needs cover too.”

“It does. This piece has already been bought for another job.”

They argued, then found which shorter lengths could be spared without making either plan fictional. Su Fan stood by the cart until she told him what to unload.

One end of a beam was split. The driver said it had been like that when loaded. Sun Lian marked it, set it apart for a use which did not depend on the damaged end, and had the driver witness the note before he left.

Su Fan took the next piece with another worker.

The man's hands slipped on wet bark. They lowered the timber, changed grips and lifted again. He was tired enough to be grateful for a task with an immediate, visible destination.

Duan called from beneath the sailcloth roof, asking whether there was a straight length suitable for a support. Sun Lian answered that she would check what remained after the assigned pieces were counted.

Nobody asked Su Fan what had been said upstairs.

Later they would. He would tell Mother Wei about the examination and the offer. Min would need to know how the source had been described. His own account would have to be as careful as the report he wanted Jiang to preserve.

He did not tell the workers that Pei Gang's hand was burned.

It was not information he had been given for sale.

He helped shift the last beam off the cart and stayed to cover the stack before the light went.

chapters.title: The Wrong Sound
chapters.text:
Ruan Zhi hung six small bells around the practice yard.

Su Fan disliked him before the lesson began.

The first bell went on a cord beneath the shelter. The second hung from a post near the path. Ruan put the others at different heights, testing each with a finger and listening as though selecting instruments for a performance nobody had asked to attend.

“Where did you get those?” Su Fan said.

“Places where people keep bells.”

“Did they agree to part with them?”

“Most were pleased to stop hearing them.”

He adjusted the lowest cord so the bell would not strike the stone beneath it. One was brighter in tone than the others. Another produced a dull little clank that sounded apologetic about the effort required to ring it.

Su Fan had expected sword practice. He had brought the plain practice blade and set it beside the wall. Ruan had not touched it.

“Find the one I ring,” he said.

Su Fan closed his eyes.

A bell sounded.

He pointed left.

“Right rear.”

He lowered his hand.

Again.

He pointed behind him.

“Right side.”

He opened his eyes.

“I know there's a problem.”

“Then stop solving a different one.”

For weeks Su Fan had trained harder at his old movements, hoping improved skill would cover the missing information. Ruan had watched him turn late three times before bringing the bells.

Su Fan looked at the one behind his right shoulder. Now that he could see it, its position seemed so obvious that his error felt wilful. He knew it had not been.

“Once more,” he said.

“Why?”

“To be certain.”

“Of what?”

He had no answer he liked.

Ruan rang the dull bell while standing plainly in front of him. Su Fan watched the clapper move. The sound reached him with a wrongness his eyes corrected before he could name it.

“That,” Ruan said. “Use what is still telling you the truth.”

He made Su Fan practise with his eyes open.

Turn first. Confirm. Move.

The sequence was slower than instinct.

It was also correct more often.

***

The first exercise required nothing more ambitious than walking across the yard.

That made it particularly irritating to fail.

Ruan placed a stool on the right-hand side of the path Su Fan usually took. He rang a bell behind it. Su Fan turned, saw the stool and went around it. The second time, Ruan rang from farther back. Su Fan moved before looking and caught the stool with his heel.

He stopped before falling.

Ruan waited.

“I saw it.”

“After you chose where to put your foot.”

Su Fan set the stool upright. He wanted to move it out of the way. Ruan watched him decide against that very convenient solution.

They tried again.

The next several attempts were better. Then Ruan spoke instead of ringing. Su Fan answered and turned toward the voice at once, undoing the careful sequence he had managed for the bells.

His friend sighed.

“The world is unfortunately allowed to contain people.”

“I had noticed.”

“Notice them in the useful order.”

Su Fan looked toward the path. Two workers were carrying a basket of stone past the yard. One called a warning to the other. A child laughed farther uphill. The sounds overlapped, and he could not pull them apart with the confidence he remembered having.

He was angry with Ruan for making him attend to it.

He was angrier with the part of himself that would have preferred another hour striking a target hard enough to pretend the work had addressed the problem.

Ruan waited while he reset the stool.

“Eventually you'll do it without arranging every step,” he said. “For now, arrange them.”

For a few attempts Su Fan improved so quickly that he began to mistrust it.

The bright bell was behind the left post. The dull one hung near the wall. He had learned their voices, and his hand was beginning to answer the remembered arrangement before his head turned.

Ruan noticed after the third correct choice.

“Stay there.”

He exchanged two bells.

The next answer was wrong.

Su Fan opened his mouth, then closed it. He had not meant to cheat. He had found information he could use and mistaken the ease of using it for the skill they were practising.

“That would work in this yard,” he said.

“Until I move a bell.”

“It could still be useful to recognize a sound.”

“Of course. Recognizing my voice does not tell you which side I am approaching from.”

Ruan put the bright bell in Su Fan's hand and walked around him, speaking ordinary nonsense about the quality of the beans and the likely price of repairing the torn sleeves on his practice coat. Su Fan could recognize him throughout. Several times he still turned toward the wrong place.

When Ruan stopped, Su Fan looked at the bell in his palm.

“I want a problem that gives me a better answer when I work harder.”

“I noticed.”

“An irritating quality in a friend.”

“Bring a stranger tomorrow. See what he charges.”

Su Fan handed the bell back. This time he waited to see where Ruan placed it and used the position only as one piece of information, not a promise that nothing would change.

They worked through the afternoon.

Su Fan learned to keep obstacles on his damaged side when doing so left him a useful view of the open ground. He learned to glance right before committing to a retreat. He also learned that a good position in one exercise could become a trap when Ruan changed where he stood.

“Don't worship the wall,” his friend said after driving him into it with three ordinary advances.

“You told me to use it.”

“I told you it could prevent an approach from that side. I did not tell you it would move out of your way afterward.”

Su Fan rubbed his elbow and changed position.

A shallow basin near the shelter reflected a strip of sky and the movement of anyone crossing behind him. He used it once to catch Ruan approaching. The next time a gust disturbed the water, and the reflection told him almost nothing.

Ruan tapped his shoulder with two fingers.

“Not every day is a still basin.”

“No.”

A polished piece of metal gave a different, narrower view. They tried it, discovered what it showed and moved it aside when the angle became misleading. Su Fan resisted the temptation to arrange the entire yard into a place in which his injury would never matter.

He would have to leave the yard.

None of these exercises restored what he had lost. Each gave him a little more room to live with it.

By mid-afternoon his neck ached from all the deliberate turning. Ruan called a halt before Su Fan admitted he needed one.

They sat beneath the shelter. Somebody had left a bowl of roasted beans on a crate. Ruan took a handful, discovered they were harder than expected and ate the next few with less confidence.

“Excellent training,” Su Fan said.

“For what?”

“Patience.”

“I came to teach you patience. I have brought nothing suitable for teaching it to the beans.”

Su Fan laughed. The laugh loosened something in his shoulders which an hour of being told to relax had failed to persuade.

Ruan drank, wiped his hands and looked toward the practice blade.

“We can do something you enjoy disliking now.”

***

The padded target had survived many ordinary blows.

Ruan held it against his chest and told Su Fan to strike.

He did.

The target thudded. Ruan shifted half a step and looked at him.

“Again. You stop your breath before the shoulder arrives.”

Su Fan reset his feet.

The scripture's next exercise was called True Strike. Its name had initially encouraged expectations the surviving instructions did little to support. There was no promise of a great blast. The passage asked for the shortest sound route between effort and impact.

He had been making that route in pieces.

Prepare the circuit. Plant the foot. Move the hand. Release the force.

Each separate part could be done reasonably well. Between them, he kept inserting small acts of resistance: a tightening before the turn, a pause at the shoulder, a grip on his own breath as though he feared it might escape without finishing its work.

Ruan had noticed the last of those without needing to know the scripture's language.

“Less preparation,” he said.

“I need the circuit.”

“You have it. You look as though you are asking it to apply for admission.”

Su Fan tried a smaller movement.

The target made a less impressive sound.

He scowled.

“Better,” Ruan said.

“How?”

“You stayed balanced after the blow.”

The next attempt struck too early. The one after that carried his weight past where he could recover it. Ruan moved enough to make him step, then pointed out that a stationary pad was being kinder than an opponent would be.

Su Fan slowed the movement. He traced the route without trying to make the impact important. His fourth circuit remained steady through the stance. The difficulty lay in what he did on top of it.

A breeze lifted the bells. None rang loudly enough to distract him.

He stepped, turned and let the hand arrive with the rest of him.

The blow landed without a visible aura.

Ruan slid backward across the yard.

The padded target split along one seam.

Both men stared.

A small tuft of stuffing hung from the tear. Then another fell onto Ruan's boot.

He lowered the target and touched his chest.

“That,” he said carefully, “was different.”

“Are you hurt?”

“Bruised. Deeply offended. Not dying.”

Su Fan moved toward him anyway. Ruan held up a hand, took a measured breath and made an even more offended face at the result.

“Still the first answer.”

Su Fan looked at his own hand.

There was no pain in the wrist. No leftover jolt in the elbow. The effort had gone where he meant it to go. He had not acquired another circuit between one breath and the next. He had used the strength already available to him without spending so much of it obstructing the movement.

The distinction did not make him less excited.

He wanted to try again.

Ruan saw the look.

“On wood. I like you, but not at unlimited expense.”

“I wasn't going to—”

“You had already begun imagining the second attempt. Give me the courtesy of making it against something without ribs.”

Su Fan took the target from him. The split seam exposed tightly packed layers beneath the outer covering. He could see where the stitching had held and where the pressure had found the weakest place.

Ruan sat on the crate.

For a while neither spoke. Su Fan waited until his friend had stopped holding his chest before allowing himself to smile at the broken pad.

“Don't look so pleased,” Ruan said.

“I was looking at the stitching.”

“A famously joyful subject.”

***

Duan examined the broken target later.

He laid it across his knees, keeping the injured arm out of its weight. With his good hand he pressed the stuffing and drew one loose thread from the seam.

“Too much stuffing,” he said.

Ruan gave him a wounded look.

“That's your diagnosis?”

“I make tools. You two make reasons to use bandages.”

“The bruise is not imaginary.”

“Neither is the bad seam.”

The smith asked Su Fan to describe the blow. He listened to the account, then asked Ruan what he had felt. The two descriptions agreed in some places and disagreed in others. Su Fan had thought the force arrived smoothly. Ruan described one sudden arrival, with less warning in the shoulder than usual.

Duan looked at the practice ground.

“Show me on a block.”

They suspended a piece of wood where it could swing without striking anyone. Ruan checked the clearance and moved the crate out of the path. Duan objected to the first fastening, which would have made damage around it too easy to mistake for damage caused by the strike alone.

They altered it, though the grain around the hole remained a possible weakness. The smith pointed that out before any testing began.

Su Fan made one slow rehearsal and an ordinary first blow. The block swung.

On the second attempt, he tried too hard to recover the exact feeling of the successful strike. His shoulder tightened. The block moved weakly and his knuckles hurt.

He shook the hand once.

Duan saw.

“Wait.”

Su Fan waited. He walked to the water, drank and came back before touching the block again.

On the third attempt, the timing met.

The impact cracked the grain around the fastening hole.

Duan stopped the trial.

“Enough. You found a thing. Don't ruin the hand finding out how excited you are.”

Su Fan sat down.

Ruan caught the block and turned it. The crack was plain. So was the weakness where it began. They had evidence of a changed strike, not a measurement from which to announce how many walls Su Fan could break.

For a while the three of them discussed alignment, load and the difference between a striking surface and a supporting joint.

Ruan showed how an opponent might move before the hand arrived, spoiling the clean route Su Fan had found. Duan asked why his grip encouraged one angle of contact and resisted another. Ruan answered, considered the question and changed the grip slightly to demonstrate a distinction he had not needed to explain before.

“You would lose reach,” he said.

“You might keep your wrist,” Duan replied.

“Depends what is being struck.”

“Yes.”

They tried the positions without impact. Su Fan watched their hands. The smith could not offer a full fighting lesson; the swordsman could not tell every kind of iron how to survive a bad load. Between them, the exercise became more useful and less magnificent.

Su Fan wrote down the failed attempt as well as the successful one.

Ruan read over his shoulder.

“Include the part about the target holder's generous service.”

“I have written that you moved backward.”

“Under protest.”

He added the words. Duan asked whether protest altered the distance and was told the matter had not yet been tested.

They left it there.

***

That evening Su Fan hung the six bells at the edge of the quarry yard.

They had to be placed where people would see the cords before walking into them. He moved one away from the path after a carrier asked whether the new settlement intended to charge him for announcing every load.

Ah-Du immediately asked whether the school was charging admission.

“Not yet,” Su Fan said.

“What does admission include?”

“Turning your head before walking into a stool.”

“That sounds like something I should be paid to learn.”

“You are describing your apprenticeship.”

The boy considered this and began making a sign anyway.

Su Fan heard the charcoal scraping from inside the shelter. He left him to it and took up the practice blade. There would be no more force tests that evening. His knuckles were sore, and one useful strike was not permission to ignore a second, bad one.

He walked the yard instead.

Turn. Confirm. Move.

On the fourth crossing he forgot and turned late. He stopped, looked where he had meant to go and began again without starting the whole exercise from the beginning as a punishment.

A bell sounded behind him.

He looked first.

Ruan stood at the path with the torn target beneath his arm.

“I am taking this to be repaired,” he said. “You may consider your contribution.”

“Money?”

“Unless you have developed a founderless art of stitching.”

Su Fan laughed and went to fetch his purse.

Above the shelter entrance, Ah-Du held up the unfinished sign to see whether there was room for another word.

chapters.title: Min Yao Comes Home
chapters.text:
Min Yao arrived with a child, two cases of paper and a bill for travel.

Her father noticed the bill first.

“You didn't need to come.”

“I needed to collect three copying fees, inspect a disputed contract and see whether you were dying. The order varied during the journey.”

Min looked toward the boy.

The child looked back solemnly.

“This is Jin,” Min Yao said. “He is six. We covered that in the letter.”

“I remember.”

“Good. I was beginning to worry the ages were moving in opposite directions.”

Min tried to smile. The effort turned into a cough.

His daughter put down the paper cases.

She did it without asking him whether the cough was serious. He had already started making the small dismissive movement she must have known from years earlier. Seeing that she had no intention of accepting it, he stopped.

Jin waited until the fit passed, then held out a wooden bird.

“Mother says you know letters.”

“A few.”

“Can you write this one's name?”

“Does it have one?”

“Not yet.”

Min took the bird with both hands.

It had been carved simply, with wings indicated by two shallow cuts. One side was smoother than the other where a child's thumb had rubbed it. The old man turned it over, studying the flat place beneath its belly.

“What would you like it to be called?”

Jin looked toward his mother, then back at the bird.

“I thought you knew.”

Min Yao closed her eyes briefly.

“He has been saving that question.”

“A difficult commission,” Min said.

Su Fan stood beside the luggage, uncertain whether to introduce himself again or let the family remain inside the moment. Min Yao saw him and nodded toward the heavier case.

“That one is clean paper. Please keep it clean.”

He lifted it.

The case was heavier than he expected. Paper gathered weight quietly, page by page, until it became a burden which needed both arms. He remembered carrying one rescued basket down the mountain and wondered how much Min Yao's livelihood fitted into the case he held.

Jin asked whether the bird might have two names in case it disliked the first.

“People manage with one for years,” Min said.

“Do they all like it?”

“No.”

“Then two.”

The scholar considered this with proper seriousness. He said he would need a brush and a place to sit. The boy took his free hand as though these were difficulties best addressed together.

Min Yao watched them start up the path.

For a moment her expression changed so quickly that Su Fan could not name it. Then she took the second case and asked him which route would keep them out of the wet ground.

***

He carried their luggage to the small room beside the surviving archive.

The higher old quarter had escaped the worst water. That was the fact Min had put in his letters. The lower storeroom still smelled of damp paper, and the room in which he slept contained fewer dry things than his daughter had been encouraged to imagine.

Min Yao set her case down and looked around.

She inspected the bed, the food cupboard and the medicine bottle.

She said nothing for several minutes.

That silence frightened her father more than a lecture would have.

“You may speak,” he said eventually.

“I am deciding which subject deserves the first argument.”

“Perhaps none.”

“An ambitious proposal.”

Jin had found a stool near the lamp. He sat with the bird on his knees, waiting for the promised brush. Min looked toward him with visible relief.

“Names first,” he said.

“Food first,” his daughter answered.

“I ate.”

“What?”

The question sounded enough like Mother Wei that Su Fan nearly smiled. He avoided doing so when Min Yao looked at the bowl beside the bed and found it empty in a way that did not establish when it had last been used.

She unpacked food from a separate cloth. Her father protested at the expense of bringing provisions from the city when there were people cooking nearby.

“Yes,” she said. “People you can assure you have already eaten.”

He surrendered that argument.

Su Fan moved the paper cases where she pointed. The dry place beside the wall was occupied by a bundle of books. Min began shifting them one-handed. His daughter caught the other side before the bundle tipped.

For a moment they worked together without speaking.

The books had been tied after getting wet. A pale line marked where the damp had reached them. Min Yao ran a finger above it, careful not to rub the softened binding.

“How many?”

“I haven't finished counting.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“It is the answer I have.”

She looked at him, then set the bundle on boards rather than return it to the floor.

He had lost more than he had admitted. There were empty places among the shelves and other places filled too tightly because dry room had become more valuable than any old arrangement. His daughter knew the room well enough to notice both.

Su Fan put the last case down and started toward the door.

Min Yao stopped him.

“The relief contracts. Bring all versions, not the one everyone has already agreed is worst.”

He nodded.

“And the boat claim.”

“Sun Lian has it.”

“Ask whether she'll let me read it.”

The phrasing was deliberate. Su Fan heard that and accepted it without resentment.

“Today?”

“When she has time. And when I have fed my father enough that he cannot use faintness to escape the next subject.”

Min said he had never fainted to avoid an argument.

“No,” she replied. “You have only made it seem increasingly possible.”

Jin looked up from the stool.

“Will you still write the bird?”

Min held out his hand for it.

“Yes.”

The child brought it over. Min Yao moved the food bowl close enough that her father could alternate between the two tasks without choosing one permanently over the other.

Min Yao began taking the papers she would need from the smaller case.

Jin noticed at once.

“Are we going again?”

“I am going to work for a while. You are staying here.”

He looked at the unfamiliar room, the narrow bed and the old man holding his bird.

“How long?”

“Until before supper.”

The answer did not satisfy him. He had been patient throughout the arrival, and the patience was beginning to show its cost in the way he pressed his mouth closed.

Min Yao knelt beside him. She told him where she would be, pointed out the food she had left and asked him not to open the paper cases without her. He nodded at the last instruction because it was familiar. The first two remained a negotiation with a place he did not know.

Min drew a clean scrap toward the lamp.

“Can you draw the bird while I write beneath it?”

Jin looked at the scrap.

“Mother says not on clean copying paper.”

“This one has a damaged edge. See?”

He turned it to show the small tear.

The boy inspected the damage gravely. Then he sat down and asked for a piece of charcoal rather than the brush, which he said was still difficult to make stop.

Min Yao watched him settle. She did not tell her father that this meant everything was well between them. She moved the water where the child could reach it and asked Min whether he would call for help if the coughing became worse.

“Yes.”

She waited.

“Yes,” he repeated, less lightly.

Only then did she lift her papers.

Su Fan left them deciding where the letters should fit.

***

Min Yao worked at the clinic's spare table.

Mother Wei gave her the table for a limited part of the afternoon and took away the medicine list before a disputed levy could become attached to a patient's name. Sun Lian arrived with her papers wrapped against damp. The widow brought the household versions. Su Fan carried the copies he had collected.

Min Yao asked where each had come from.

Not which seemed fairest. Not which everybody preferred. Where it had been obtained, when it had been handed over, and whether the person presenting it had signed that version.

The questions sounded simple until people answered them.

One sheet had been copied from a notice. Another had been supplied with the first material vouchers. A third had been read aloud to a family who had understood it to be the same agreement their neighbours had received.

It was not.

Different offices had attached different continuation charges. One version counted emergency service as paid work. Another treated it as a pause in ordinary employment without suspending the loan against it.

“They cannot all be the same agreement,” Sun Lian said.

“They aren't. They have been treated as though they were.”

Min Yao placed two sheets side by side. She marked the conflicting lines on a separate page rather than spoil anyone's original. Her hand moved quickly, then slowed whenever a word had more than one possible reach.

“Can you undo it?” Sun Lian asked.

“I can show where the promises conflict. Somebody with authority must choose to correct them.”

Su Fan had learned enough not to be disappointed by the limit. Sun Lian looked as though she had known it before asking and disliked it just as much afterward.

“The collectors had a very simple account of the matter,” she said.

“They had one claim to enforce. You have several promises which were made as though they would never need to be read together.”

Min Yao asked permission to copy the boat documents. Sun Lian agreed and kept the originals within sight until each copy was checked.

The widow wanted to know whether signing for the grain had also accepted a charge printed on a different sheet.

Min Yao did not answer immediately. She read the receipt, the attached terms and the later notice. Then she explained the argument the office might make and the points on which it could be disputed.

The explanation did not please anyone.

It did, however, keep them from sending a demand whose strongest sentence depended on pretending one of the documents did not exist.

Outside the blanket, a patient asked whether the table was a clinic or an office.

“Both for another little while,” Mother Wei said. “If the office becomes contagious, I will put it outside.”

Min Yao checked the time and gathered the papers that could wait. She left space for the healer's next task instead of treating the importance of her own work as a claim to the whole room.

The most serious difficulty emerged from Tan Wei's station agreement.

His individual withdrawal window remained intact on his copy: a supervised procedure between scheduled return cycles, except under a declared emergency limited to the specified station and event.

A copy of a broader operating order had reached them afterward. It spoke of active operators across linked stations.

“Is this the complete order?” Min Yao asked.

“It is the copy we were given,” Su Fan said.

“That is not necessarily the same thing.”

She compared the heading and the closing lines. There was a reference to an operating record, but the material before her did not establish when the full order had been issued.

Tan Wei had signed on a known date. They knew when this copy had been supplied. Those were different facts.

Su Fan looked at the space she left on her comparison sheet.

“So we need the date?”

“We need the authenticated order and its date. And an answer about which promise they intend to apply to him.”

“It came after he signed.”

“This copy did. Do not make that tell us when the order began.”

He stopped.

The distinction was unpleasant because he had already begun building a reassuring answer on the sequence in which they had learned things.

Min Yao tapped the broader wording.

“It says it applies to all active operators.”

“That can't—”

“It can be written. Whether it can be enforced is the dispute. Don't confuse an unjust sentence with an ineffective one.”

Tan Wei had wanted the agreement he understood, not an argument between different offices conducted inside his body. Su Fan felt an urge to go to him at once with everything the paper might mean.

He asked Min Yao what they could responsibly say now.

“That there is a conflict which needs a formal answer. Not that he has lost every right, and not that we have already proved the broader order cannot touch him.”

She copied the known dates onto a separate page and left the issue date unfilled.

“First, we ask for a formal reconciliation. Calmly. In duplicate.”

“Why calmly?” Sun Lian asked.

“Because I want them answering the question, not reporting our behaviour.”

“And if they don't?”

“Then we will have their failure to answer a question which can be shown clearly.”

Sun Lian looked at the papers.

“I would prefer my boat paid.”

“So would I,” Min Yao said. “That is why I am trying not to give them an easier subject.”

The afternoon's light shifted off the table. Mother Wei returned for the space she had lent. They wrapped the originals, labelled the copies and stopped before tired eyes turned a small error into another argument for someone else to untangle.

***

At dusk, Su Fan carried the paper cases back to the archive room.

Min Yao had collected one of the fees she had come for. The other two remained somebody else's explanation of why payment would be more convenient later. She spoke of that while setting the case down, not as a complaint requiring Su Fan to rescue her, but as part of the work waiting when she returned to Siltbridge.

Jin sat near the bed with his wooden bird.

It now carried a small written name beneath its belly and, on a scrap tied to its leg, a second one. Min said the bird had not yet expressed a preference.

The child disagreed. It preferred the one that sounded less like an old man.

Min accepted the judgment with a solemn nod.

Su Fan left before supper. He had work to finish and no wish to become another person the daughter had to feed while trying to see her father.

Later, passing the archive window, he heard Min reading aloud.

The story involved a fox that kept borrowing chickens and insisting it was a temporary arrangement.

Jin objected every time the fox returned.

“Why did they give him another?”

“He promised the first would be returned.”

“Then they should wait for the first.”

“A reasonable difficulty.”

Min changed the fox's explanation.

On the next visit, the fox said the first chicken was engaged in important work and needed a second to assist it. Jin asked what work a chicken could do which required leaving the coop at night.

Min considered.

“Inspection.”

“Of what?”

“The fox's house.”

“Does the chicken want to?”

The old man coughed, recovered and gave the chicken a more definite opinion than it had possessed at the beginning of the story.

By the fourth visit, the fox had become a provincial official with an exceptionally poor seal. It produced a document which explained that the chickens were not missing, merely assigned elsewhere.

Jin said that was the same thing if their mother wanted them home.

Min Yao laughed from the other side of the room.

It was brief and unguarded. Her father paused, and Su Fan could almost hear him choosing not to make the laugh into an occasion she would have to defend.

The fox returned with a worse document.

Su Fan continued down the steps before anyone saw him.

He had expected the daughter to arrive bearing answers.

He was glad she had also brought someone who wanted a story.

chapters.title: Ground for a House
chapters.text:
The settlement vote took place in the half-built storehouse.

Rain dripped through a gap in the roof. Deng moved a bucket beneath it without interrupting the argument.

He had already moved the bucket twice. Each time he found where the drops were falling, the wind changed and persuaded the roof to leak somewhere else.

“We should decide the ground before the roof decides to leave it,” Auntie Lu said.

The available choices were not generous.

They could accept a five-year lease on the quarry ground, with levies tied to occupied plots, or remain temporary refugees under annual review. One gave them a longer claim to a place that needed roads, drainage and houses. The other gave them less immediate obligation and no secure answer about the following year.

Neither returned the old homes.

Min Yao explained the terms. She read the parts concerning the land, then the parts concerning the buildings they intended to put on it. When someone asked whether a five-year term meant nobody could interfere for five years, she pointed out the conditions rather than let the number become a stronger promise than the words.

Jiang answered questions about the road. Sun Lian explained drainage. Mother Wei spoke about the danger of another winter in shared tents.

The widow asked each household to say what it could actually pay.

The answers made everyone quieter.

Some could contribute labour sooner than coin. Some had tools, a few materials, a little grain. Others had lost the person whose work usually paid for all three. Promises which sounded easy when spoken for the whole settlement became smaller when attached to a particular family.

A man near the door offered more days of labour than his wife thought possible.

“You still have the cart work,” she said.

“I can do this afterward.”

“In the dark?”

“If I must.”

She did not argue with the bravery of that answer. She asked when he intended to mend their own shelter and collect the grain already promised to another household in exchange for help.

He looked at the floor.

The widow moved the list closer to him.

“We need the days you can give,” she said. “Not the days you will be ashamed to tell us you cannot.”

He reduced the offer.

No one thanked him less. Su Fan was glad of that, then caught himself doing a similar calculation on his own page. He had put down work time which also appeared in the workshop's repair promises. The same afternoon had been sold twice without either buyer knowing.

He crossed out one line before his turn came.

Beside him, Bao Shun counted tasks his injured hand would allow. He could finish pegs, repair light handles and help record deliveries. He could not raise a wall because the settlement needed him to be able to do so.

Bao Mei added her painting work separately.

“Not every day,” her father said.

“I know. There is school.”

“And eating.”

“I can paint between bites.”

“Do not put that in the agreement.”

The small laugh which followed made the figures easier to look at. It did not increase them. Min Yao waited until each correction had been heard before continuing, leaving enough blank space beside the promises for later changes to be visible.

Su Fan looked at the list he had prepared.

He had counted savings and expected work. He had also written down a workshop, a protected store and a practice yard, drawing each as though the space between buildings cost nothing.

Now the widow asked who would pay for the drains crossing those spaces.

Sun Lian put a finger on the slope.

“The water will use them whether we account for them or not.”

A man said the sect ought to pay for everything after what had happened below.

Jiang did not ask him to lower his voice.

She told him what had been authorized, what remained disputed and which costs were attached to accepting this ground. He did not like the answer. Neither did several people sitting near him. The answer did not change because they disliked it.

Min Yao set the two forms beside each other.

“We are deciding between these terms,” she said. “You may continue disputing the responsibility for the flood under either. Do not sign one because you have imagined a third agreement which nobody here can grant.”

Deng caught the bucket before a child kicked it. He emptied it outside and came back wet to the elbow.

The roof still needed mending. Everybody could see that. It was an oddly useful fact to have above them while they discussed the next five years.

When Su Fan's turn came, he described the common workshop, the store and the yard.

The widow asked who would supervise the work.

“Duan and I.”

Duan raised his good hand.

“I supervise. He does the lifting.”

People laughed. The smith waited until they finished and added that he would require someone to listen before lifting, a service which had become rarer since Su Fan grew stronger.

Someone proposed making Su Fan head of the whole works committee.

He began refusing before the sentence ended.

Min Yao looked at him.

“Which part can't you do?”

He stopped.

“All of it at once.”

“Then don't agree to all of it.”

That should have been obvious. Su Fan had heard the size of the responsibility before he heard that it could be divided.

They worked through the jobs.

He took tools, materials and the work yard. Sun Lian took drainage and transport. The widow took accounts. Deng took the road crews. None could change another's allocation without bringing it back to the group.

Su Fan began adding a delivery sequence to his materials list.

Sun Lian leaned over.

“That cart is already moving stone on the day you want it.”

“I thought the timber should come first.”

“It may. We can discuss it. You cannot give the same cart two mornings because your list has more room.”

He crossed out the date and left the load.

The arrangement was clumsy enough to require talking. It offered no single person the pleasure of having everybody else obey promptly.

They accepted it anyway.

The five-year lease was chosen. Questions remained about individual plots and the timing of payments, but the settlement would no longer be planned around the hope that an annual review might kindly leave them where they stood.

Min Yao kept the marked copy apart from the unsigned versions. Jiang explained which papers still had to be entered at the office. The widow collected the household promises without treating the larger ones as evidence that their owners mattered more.

Before they dispersed, Sun Lian climbed onto a low support and examined the roof gap.

“An overlap,” she said. “Not another political question.”

Deng handed up the material she needed.

For the first time that evening, a problem was solved while everyone who had discussed it remained in the room.

***

Construction began with a ditch.

Ah-Du complained that every hopeful enterprise in his life had begun with a ditch.

“School?” Bao Mei asked.

“The school roof leaked. We dug a ditch.”

“Apprenticeship?”

“Coal drain. Ditch.”

“Your first wages?”

“Dropped them in a ditch.”

She laughed so hard she spilled the water she was carrying.

Su Fan let them waste the minute. There would be enough cold work afterward.

The ditch had to pass ground where several people had already imagined doors. Moving a line on Sun Lian's drawing took a finger. Moving the line in the quarry took bodies, tools and the discovery that soil which looked loose could contain stone placed there by somebody who had long ago lost interest in whether it inconvenienced them.

They worked around one buried slab and lifted another.

Su Fan took too much of the second load at first. The other man released his share unexpectedly, and the weight shifted before Su Fan could set his feet. He caught it without falling, but the corner struck his shin.

He swore.

“Shall I go away?” the man asked.

“No. Tell me before you let go.”

“You looked as though you had it.”

“I looked wrong.”

They reset their grips and moved the slab together.

Being stronger had not made other people able to read his intentions. He knew that. The bruise gave the knowledge a fresh place to live.

Duan sat beneath an awning drawing the new furnace.

His left arm remained bound. He held the brush awkwardly in his right hand, swore at the lines and refused Su Fan's first offer to copy them.

“The curve is wrong,” the smith said.

“I can see where you mean—”

“Then I have managed to communicate despite the catastrophe.”

Su Fan went back to the ditch.

By afternoon, Duan asked Bao Mei to draw the curves.

She sat beside him, listened to what each part needed to do and copied the line. Her first version was too smooth. Duan pointed out a change in the passage which she had rounded away because it looked accidental.

She put the bend back.

“Less pretty,” she said.

“Less likely to smoke us out.”

“A useful form of beauty.”

He made a noise which might have been agreement and showed her the next part.

She did not tell him how brave he was to continue designing with one arm. She asked whether a dimension included the thickness of the lining. He answered at once, pleased to be asked something about the work.

Su Fan watched from the water stack.

The difference between his own offer and hers was not simply that she had waited longer. Bao Mei had found a way to make Duan's knowledge necessary while her hand did something his could not presently do.

Then she blotted a corner, said a word Auntie Lu would have objected to, and asked for a clean scrap.

Duan laughed.

The lesson became less tidy and more useful.

***

The first permanent wall rose beside the clinic.

It was crooked.

At a distance, Su Fan thought it looked sound enough. Up close, the upper course wandered where the crew had followed an uneven edge rather than the line set for it.

Sun Lian made them take it down and lay it again.

The men groaned.

One said the wall would still keep rain out. Another said nobody in the old town had possessed a wall so fine that its upper edge needed to be admired by boatbuilders.

Sun Lian gave them a straight piece of timber and asked where the next part would sit.

They looked.

The upper course came down.

Su Fan carried the removed pieces to where they could be reused. He had been tempted to defend the day's progress because the stones were already in place and everyone was cold. The temptation weakened when he saw how much more work the next crew would inherit if they left it.

They laid it again.

The wall improved.

By the time they stopped, the mortar on Su Fan's fingers had dried into pale lines. He washed at the marked water place and discovered a small cut he had not felt while working. He wrapped it before picking up another stone, partly because Mother Wei was watching from the clinic and partly because he was beginning to understand that her irritation could be anticipated usefully.

Bao Mei came to inspect the wall she had been promised a chance to paint one day.

“Not yet,” Sun Lian said.

“I know.”

“You have a brush.”

“I brought it to discourage anyone from making it crooked again.”

Duan, passing with Ah-Du carrying his drawings, said this was the most efficient supervision he had heard proposed all day.

They left the wall to stand without decoration.

At dusk, the goose escaped.

It walked along the new masonry with an authority nobody had granted it, placing each foot carefully and pausing at the corner as though considering whether the workmanship deserved approval.

“Get it down,” Sun Lian said.

Auntie Lu approached with a bowl.

The goose looked at the bowl, then at the height beneath its feet. It lowered its neck and hissed at the possibility that the route down might require assistance.

Ah-Du offered a theory involving a board and was told to keep the board away from the fresh work.

Deng placed a low crate beside the safer end. Auntie Lu moved the bowl. The goose considered both people unreasonable, then stepped down with as much dignity as the arrangement allowed.

“Inspection complete,” she declared.

Sun Lian checked the edge where its feet had been.

“Next inspector waits until it is set.”

The bird began eating as though the argument concerned somebody else.

***

Later, after the workers left, Su Fan stood in the outline of his room.

Four low walls. A doorway. Space for a mat, a shelf and a chest.

The dimensions looked different when he could stand between them. On paper the room had seemed small enough to apologize for. Here it contained the place where he would sleep, put his notes, remove wet shoes and close a door if he needed to be alone.

There was no door yet.

He stepped through the opening twice, deciding how the chest could be placed without blocking it. The right-hand wall would give his sleeping place a protected side. He could keep the clearer approach where he was more likely to notice it.

He wished he had been choosing entirely for other reasons.

He had paid for his share. Not much. Enough that the receipt carried his name and the number matched the place beneath his feet.

The receipt was folded inside his coat. He took it out, checked it for no practical reason and put it away before anyone arrived to see him admiring a piece of paper.

Mother Wei came up beside him.

“Which way will the bed face?”

“Wall on the right.”

She nodded.

She did not tell him it was sensible in the voice people used when congratulating him for accepting something he had not chosen. She looked at the doorway and asked where he intended to put the lamp.

“Near the shelf.”

“Not beneath loose papers.”

“I know.”

“I have seen your papers.”

“They are organized.”

“By the depth at which a person gives up looking?”

He smiled.

She stepped into the room. The low wall made it easy to enter anywhere, but she used the doorway anyway. Su Fan noticed that and was unexpectedly grateful.

From here the flooded lower quarter lay hidden behind the ridge. He could see the direction without seeing the water. The absence felt different when he had to remember it deliberately rather than look down at it whenever he lifted his head.

“I thought I'd feel worse about building somewhere else,” he said.

“You may tomorrow.”

He accepted that.
