Mother Wei looked at the ground just beyond the opening, where the afternoon light had reached before the cold took it. She took a small packet from her sleeve and placed it in his hand.

Garlic-chive seeds.

“For the doorstep.”

“There isn't a doorstep.”

“There will be.”

The packet weighed almost nothing. He turned it over, found the fold which would let him open it, then resisted doing so with dirty fingers.

“Will they grow here?”

“We will find out when there is a place to plant them.”

No guarantee. No instruction to be cheerful. A small task waiting for a season he had not yet reached.

He put the packet safely inside his coat, beside the receipt.

Mother Wei went back toward the clinic before the path grew too dark. Su Fan watched her pass the new wall and call to someone who had left a water vessel in the wrong place.

Then he stood a little longer in the doorway.

chapters.title: Three Scraps of Iron
chapters.text:
They lit the new furnace on the coldest morning of the year so far.

The first draught failed.

Smoke rolled back into the workshop. Ah-Du abandoned the bellows and stumbled toward the doorway with both hands over his face. Su Fan followed, coughing hard enough to lose the insult he had intended for the weather.

Duan blamed the wind, then his own drawing, then the apprentice who had built exactly what the drawing showed.

Su Fan waited until the list was complete.

“Move the lower vent?”

“Two fingers left.”

They moved it.

That required letting the first heat die back enough to work near the opening. Ah-Du objected to having risen before dawn merely to discover that dawn had been a more sensible time to remain asleep. Duan told him he could pursue that theory after the furnace worked.

The second attempt drew differently.

Su Fan felt the air move before he saw the fire settle. The smoke thinned. The little flame which had been trying to enter the workshop found a more useful direction.

They stood watching longer than necessary.

The new walls were still pale. Damp mortar darkened the joints nearest the warmth. Overhead, the roof timbers had not yet acquired the soot which would make the building smell permanently of its trade.

Duan stood before the furnace with his injured arm tucked into his coat.

He said nothing for so long that Ah-Du stopped making jokes.

Then the smith picked up a hammer with his good hand.

He struck the anvil once.

The sound carried across the quarry settlement.

Su Fan saw the slight movement in the old man's face before the hammer was set down. One blow was not a return to the work he had done all his life. It was one blow, and he had chosen to make it.

Outside, someone called to ask whether the furnace was working.

“It is now,” Duan answered.

He sat where he could see the fire and began telling them what needed doing next.

***

Su Fan's sword used the best of the salvaged plain steel.

Not all of it. They still needed tools more than symbols.

Duan laid out the stock and made Su Fan choose the amount before discussing the blade's shape. A piece good enough for a weapon was also good enough for parts which would earn money or keep another worker's hand away from a dangerous load.

“You can have a longer sword,” he said. “Tell me which order waits.”

Su Fan chose the length they could afford.

Ah-Du thought it looked disappointingly modest.

“A dragon along the back would make it seem longer.”

“No dragon,” Duan said.

“A small one.”

“Make a sound blade first. It can disappoint the dragon later.”

Duan designed the balance for Su Fan's hand and the footwork Ruan had taught him. They used a plain wooden length to consider the reach before committing the steel. What felt impressive standing still became awkward when Su Fan turned too late or had to recover from a short step.

The smith watched him move.

“Again. Without looking as though somebody is painting you.”

Su Fan lowered the wooden blade and started over.

The final design had no decorative grooves. No ancestor's name would be cut into it. Su Fan had thought he might miss the chance to give the weapon a distinction people could recognize at a glance. By the time the work began, he cared more about whether it would follow his hand without asking for a different body to carry it.

The work took days.

Duan directed. Su Fan did the hammering. Ah-Du worked the bellows and offered opinions at moments when the furnace made pretending not to hear him unusually convenient.

They stopped for paid repairs. They stopped when the light was poor. They stopped when Su Fan's tired hands began accepting small errors because another pass would mean doing more work.

The steel did not care how badly he wanted the blade finished.

At one stage the surface looked better than the shape beneath it deserved. Duan made him set it against a straight edge. The line revealed an irregularity Su Fan had been trying not to see.

“You noticed,” the smith said.

“Yes.”

“Before or after I asked?”

Su Fan did not answer quickly enough.

Duan looked at him until he took the work back.

The first temper was wrong.

Su Fan wanted to call it nearly right. He could find reasons for that description, all of them more attractive than the time needed to correct it. Duan examined the part which concerned him and refused to let fatigue turn a near success into a weapon that might fail when needed.

“Would you sell it?”

“No.”

“Then don't make yourself the customer who is too embarrassed to complain.”

They reworked what had to be reworked.

Ah-Du said the dragon would have distracted people from the trouble.

“It would not have distracted the steel,” Duan replied.

The boy considered this and turned the bellows without further artistic advice for almost an hour.

When the sword was finished, it looked ordinary.

A straight, undecorated blade. A plain guard. A grip wrapped in dark cord.

Su Fan took it into the yard.

The first basic cut felt strange because he expected more resistance. He made the second too quickly and had to recover his footwork. Then he slowed, turned his head to check the space on his right and began the sequence again.

The blade followed his hand closely enough that he stopped noticing its weight.

That pleased Duan more than admiration of its appearance would have.

“Bring it here,” he said.

He checked the grip after the movement, not merely while it lay on the bench. Su Fan had wrapped one part tightly enough to look neat and poorly enough to shift beneath a damp palm. They corrected it before anyone called the weapon complete.

Ruan came to see the result.

He moved it through a short, controlled sequence, returned it hilt-first and asked whether Su Fan intended to apologize for its lack of ornament.

“No.”

“Good. It would have been a long apology.”

Su Fan took it back.

For a moment he felt the foolish desire to ask whether it was worthy of the method he practised. Then Duan told him to wipe it, put it away and finish the hinge waiting beside the furnace.

The sword could wait while he remained a smith.

Carrying it proved to be another small skill he had not acquired by making it.

The first time he wore the plain scabbard through the workshop, it caught against a stool. He turned to free it and struck the doorpost with the other end. Ah-Du watched with an expression of rapidly growing professional interest.

“Do not say it,” Su Fan told him.

“I haven't chosen which thing yet.”

Duan asked for the small tongs.

Su Fan reached past the bench, discovered that the sword was still in the way, and finally took it off before handing over the tool. He hung it where it would not be struck by a carried load and returned to work.

Later, Ruan showed him how to settle the scabbard when sitting and how to keep its presence in mind while moving through a crowded space. The lesson involved no qi and very little dignity.

“You have carried longer iron than this,” Ruan said.

“Usually in my hands.”

“Then stop expecting your hip to know what your hands learned.”

By evening Su Fan could cross the room without announcing the weapon against every piece of furniture. He still put it aside before moving the supper bowls. Ah-Du said this was a promising arrangement for a school whose first enemy appeared to be the workshop itself.

***

The armour came from scraps too.

Sun Lian had salvaged thin iron plates from a damaged cargo lining. She brought them wrapped in cloth so their edges would not cut the person carrying them. Several were unsuitable. She separated those before Su Fan could become hopeful about the size of the whole bundle.

“These ones have already done more work than they should,” she said.

“Could they be straightened?”

“They can be made to look straight. That isn't what you asked me for.”

He put them aside.

Mother Wei inspected the edges of the usable pieces. She was less interested in how formidable the coat might look than in what its wearer would bring to her after falling in it.

Auntie Lu found heavy cloth.

It had been intended for another practical use and retained the outline of a seam which did not belong to a coat. She handed it over with instructions that Su Fan was to sew it himself.

“I have fed you,” she said. “I am not also dressing you for every bad decision.”

“I can sew.”

“I have seen the evidence.”

“That is unfair.”

“It is very visible.”

He sewed until his fingers ached.

Fitting the plates into the cloth required more care than arranging them on the bench. When he sat, one pressed in the wrong place. When he reached, another caught against its neighbour. A layout which covered more of him while he stood still could restrict the movement he needed to avoid being struck.

Sun Lian watched him try the coat and told him to climb onto a low step.

He did.

“Now get down without thinking about the armour.”

He caught an edge with his wrist.

They altered that part.

The result protected his torso without pretending to make him invulnerable. It was heavier than an ordinary coat and less elegant than Su Fan had secretly imagined. The visible patches reminded him that several people had supplied it and none of them had promised to make him look impressive.

Ruan tested it with a blunt thrust.

The breath went out of Su Fan.

He sat on the nearest crate and concentrated on getting it back.

“Better than a hole,” Ruan said.

Su Fan agreed after he could speak.

“You might have warned me.”

“I said I would test it.”

“There was room for greater detail.”

Ruan crouched and checked the struck section. The plate had done useful work. So had the cloth beneath it. Su Fan's body had done the rest and wished to complain about the distribution.

Mother Wei examined him afterward and told both men that a successful test was not an invitation to repeat it until she acquired another patient.

Ruan said he had no such intention.

Su Fan was glad she had said it before he could discover one.

***

The last piece was an iron ring made from an offcut of the new gate stock.

Duan had bent the small piece while checking the metal's consistency. It was not large, and the force required did not make his injured arm available for work again. He had used his good hand and the bench, cursing at the inconvenience as frankly as he praised the stock afterward.

Su Fan asked to keep the ring.

“For what?”

“Weight training. Grip work. Something to measure against.”

The smith handed it over.

It had no inscription. One edge still needed smoothing. Su Fan worked it until it would not catch a cord or cut his fingers, then weighed it against something he knew and wrote the result with his practice notes.

The measurement mattered more to him than a name would have.

Ah-Du looked at the sword, the patched coat and the ring.

“Three scraps,” he said. “A fearsome inheritance.”

Su Fan turned the ring in his hand.

“Mind the furnace.”

The boy grinned and obeyed.

Later, alone in the yard, Su Fan hung the ring from a cord and touched it lightly to see how it moved. He did not yet have an exercise settled for it. The swing was simple enough to reveal when he had pushed unevenly.

He tried once more, then left it hanging.

There was food to carry inside.

***

That evening the new workshop held its first shared meal.

There were no tables yet. People sat on blocks, tool chests and the floor. A clean board across two supports held the bowls until somebody discovered that one support was shorter than the other and corrected it before supper slid toward the door.

Deng brought a pot whose contents Auntie Lu inspected before allowing anyone near it.

“What is that?”

“Food.”

“A category, not an answer.”

He told her what was in it. She tasted a little, frowned with the concentration of a person reluctant to surrender a useful opinion, and said it could be served.

Deng looked pleased enough that she immediately warned him against making the same thing every seventh day for the rest of the winter.

“I had not reached that far in my planning.”

“You were moving quickly.”

Tan Wei arrived after dark and placed a sack of grain beside the door. He washed his hands, took a bowl and stayed to eat. The blue lines above his wrist showed when he pushed up his sleeve. Nobody made them the subject of the meal.

He asked Su Fan about the sword.

“Plain,” Su Fan said.

“I can see that. Does it work?”

“So far.”

“An encouraging review.”

Ruan, sitting within hearing, said the weapon had shown admirable restraint during construction. Su Fan threw a folded cloth at him and missed because the throw had been made chiefly to object rather than to hit.

Ah-Du announced that this proved the school needed more pupils.

Min came with his daughter and grandson.

He tired quickly. The walk had taken more from him than he wanted to admit, and Min Yao selected a place where he could sit without anyone having to watch him be helped into it. He accepted the bowl she brought and ate before beginning his inspection of Ah-Du's sign.

The sign above the practice yard contained two spelling errors and one unsupported military claim.

“The last one is advertising,” the boy said.

“The first two are advertising something else.”

Jin wanted to know whether correcting the letters would make the military claim true.

“Unfortunately,” Min said, “scholarship has limits.”

Ah-Du said the sign had never been intended for experts.

Bao Mei offered to repair the lettering if he stopped adding words before the paint dried. He said the words had been carefully chosen. She asked him to read one of them aloud.

The discussion occupied them for most of a bowl.

Outside, frost gathered on the new roofs.

Inside, people's coats steamed faintly near the warmth. The workshop did not smell like the old one yet. Fresh timber, damp mortar, new clay drying around the fire. The familiar iron smell was there, but it had not had years to settle into everything.

Su Fan sat beside the furnace with the plain sword within reach and the ring hanging from its cord on the wall.

His patched coat lay folded away from the sparks. It looked less like the armour of a dangerous cultivator than a garment whose owner expected to mend it again. He found that he liked it.

Jin fell asleep against Min Yao's side.

She adjusted his weight without interrupting what Sun Lian was saying about a transport fee. The child slept through a dropped spoon, a laugh and Ah-Du's indignant defence of the sign. Min watched him for a moment, then returned to his own food.

Duan leaned back and closed his eyes.

Su Fan nearly asked whether he was tired.

The old man's good hand rested on his knee. His face had lost the guarded look it often wore when someone approached with a question about his arm. Around him, people argued about supper, work, spelling and the placement of a shelf they had not built yet.

For once, nobody asked whether his shoulder hurt.

He listened to them talking around his anvil.

chapters.title: The Winter Account
chapters.text:
Before the firewood came, the settlement began burning things that had once had other purposes.

The first were the ugly pieces. A cracked door, two chair backs without chairs, a shelf whose owner had been promising to mend it since before the flood. People could laugh while carrying those to the common kitchen. They told Auntie Lu the shelf had finally found useful employment. They asked whether she would charge less for broth cooked over furniture they had supplied.

By the third cold morning, a woman arrived with the end of a child's bed.

Su Fan was repairing the kitchen's smoke hood when he saw her standing beneath it. She had wrapped the painted end in a piece of sacking. One blue flower remained visible beside her wrist.

“Where do you want this?”

Auntie Lu stopped stirring.

“Has the child somewhere to sleep?”

“With us.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“It is what I've got.”

The woman set the wood beside the other fuel. She spoke without anger, which made Su Fan wish Auntie Lu had been less direct. Then he wished the woman would be angry. Anger, at least, would give him something familiar to stand beside.

Auntie Lu examined the wood.

“Painted,” she said. “Not under the soup pot.”

“I can scrape it.”

“Put it behind the shed. We'll see.”

The woman looked from the stove to the bowls waiting on the board. Her expression said she knew the difference between an objection and an excuse. Nevertheless she carried the bed end where she was told.

Su Fan climbed down from the stool.

“I could take that to Duan.”

“What for?”

“Make something from it.”

“Will making something warm her room?”

He had no answer ready.

Auntie Lu pointed her spoon toward the hood.

“Fix what you came to fix. I can be useless about one bed without help.”

The hood had been made from overlapping pieces of thin iron. Heat had twisted one edge away from the next, letting smoke into the room whenever the wind pressed down the chimney. Su Fan had brought two clamps and a narrow strip to cover the join. He had not brought a place for a cold family to sleep.

He climbed onto the stool again.

Below him the morning went on. Deng arrived with the water pails and announced that the path behind the clinic was ice all the way to the bend. Auntie Lu told him that water was not usually improved by bringing it back to water.

He put the pails down.

“The path. Not the well.”

“Then say the path.”

“I did.”

She handed him a bowl.

Their quarrel continued more quietly while he ate.

Su Fan loosened the first fixing. The iron sprang against his thumb. He stopped, adjusted his grip and made the remaining fixings take the load before trying again. Working overhead was less forgiving than standing in the practice yard with both feet where he had chosen to put them.

The smoke stung his eyes. He could hear the kitchen on his left and, on his right, the familiar thin ringing that made every enclosed room slightly false.

“Someone behind the stool?” he asked.

“Me,” Deng said.

“Don't move it.”

“I was hoping to climb on your shoulders.”

Su Fan turned far enough to see him before reaching down for the strip.

He hated needing to do that. He did it anyway.

The repair took longer than it should have. One piece of old iron had torn around its hole; tightening it would only make the tear longer. He moved the fastening to sound material and left the bad one visible rather than hide it beneath the new strip.

When he finished, Auntie Lu opened the door a hand's width and watched the smoke draw.

“Better.”

“For now.”

“For now is what I ordered.”

She gave him broth and half a bun. Payment would be entered with the kitchen repairs, she said. The bun was not payment. It was to stop him standing there looking at the child's bed.

He ate by the doorway.

The woman had gone. The blue flower still showed beneath the sacking.

***

Duan was trying to turn a coat inside out when Su Fan returned.

The injured arm lay against his body. He had the collar caught under his chin and one sleeve between his knees. A stool stood close enough to hold the rest of the garment, but the coat kept slipping from it.

Su Fan stopped just inside the smithy.

Duan looked up.

“You may laugh.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“Then you're wasting an opportunity.”

A seam had opened beneath the good arm. The smith wanted to show Ah-Du how much room to leave in the repair. Ah-Du had instead sewn the gap so firmly shut that Duan could no longer raise his elbow.

The boy stood beside the bench with a needle in his mouth and the expression of a man whose careful work had been shamefully misunderstood.

“It won't split again.”

“It won't move again.”

“You said strong.”

“I said strong enough.”

Su Fan set his tools down.

Duan looked at the coat, then at him.

“Hold this edge. Only the edge.”

He held it. Duan worked the other sleeve free with his good hand and spread the seam across the bench.

“There,” he told Ah-Du. “Room for the body first. Then make the stitching hold the room.”

The boy took the needle from his mouth.

“You could say that before I sew.”

“I believed a coat was a sufficient clue.”

Su Fan laughed. Duan allowed himself a small smile and sent him to count the remaining charcoal.

There was less than the morning board claimed.

He counted again. The sacks at the back were not all full. One contained the broken pieces swept from beneath the bin, useful for keeping a fire alive but poor for getting it started. He brought the smaller number to Duan.

“Kitchen?”

“And the clinic. The brazier in Min's room has been going out.”

The smith looked at the unfinished work on the bench.

They had paid for this charcoal. It was not the settlement's supply. Without it they would miss orders, and missing orders would eventually leave them buying neither charcoal nor food.

Su Fan knew all of that. He also knew which people were coughing on the other side of the lane.

Duan tapped the account book.

“Tell me the amount.”

Su Fan did.

“How many firing periods if we keep to the repairs already promised?”

He gave the answer he hoped was right.

Duan waited.

Su Fan took the slate and worked it through properly. The correct answer was less comfortable.

They could spare a bag if they delayed the new fittings and used the larger furnace only when enough work was ready together. That would mean a longer day later. It would also mean asking the customer rather than simply deciding on his behalf.

“I'll speak to him,” Su Fan said.

“Speak. Don't tell him the infirm are waiting to see what kind of man he is.”

“I wasn't going to.”

Duan raised one eyebrow.

Su Fan looked back at his calculation.

“I might have mentioned the clinic.”

“Mention it. Leave him a choice after you do.”

The customer was a miller whose grain had begun to freeze together in the damp store. He wanted the fittings because a shutter would not close. Su Fan had expected a merchant annoyed about a date on an order. Instead he found a man lifting spoiled meal out of a barrel with both hands.

They moved the work forward, not back.

Su Fan returned to the smithy with a different plan. He could finish the shutter fittings while the fire was hot for the hinges, then use the remaining heat for the small pieces. The new order he had meant to begin would wait. He would explain that delay to its owner.

Duan examined the revised list.

“That will do.”

The arrangement did not produce more fuel. It only meant the available fuel would serve several kinds of cold before it was spent.

Su Fan filled the bag for Min's room.

Ah-Du returned Duan's coat with a looser seam and an excessively large patch.

“Room,” he said.

Duan put it on.

For the first time that morning, the sleeve moved when he did.

***

Outside the clinic, a station labourer was warming his hands around an empty cup.

Su Fan knew him by sight. He had helped carry bedding uphill after the flood, then disappeared into the shifts that kept the surviving gates working. Now he wore an operator's discarded outer coat over ordinary clothes. The sleeves hung past his fingers.

“Is Wei in?”

“With a patient.”

“How long?”

“I don't know.”

The man turned the cup between his palms.

Su Fan lowered the charcoal bag beside the wall.

“Something wrong?”

“My boy has a cough.”

“Bring him.”

“He's there.”

The man nodded toward the screen inside. A small boot protruded from beneath the blanket on the nearest pallet.

Su Fan looked away from the door.

“Then she'll see him.”

“She is seeing him.”

For a moment they stood in mutual embarrassment.

The man drew a folded paper from his coat.

“I was going to ask about something else.”

He worked at the fold until Su Fan offered to hold the cup. The paper was a request for a different shift. At the bottom, below the official spaces, somebody had written that his wife could not manage both the child and the household work without help.

“I thought you might know which words they listen to.”

Su Fan read it.

The request was plain. It said what was needed, for how long, and which worker had offered to exchange part of the duty. There were no threats and no claims about rights the man could not explain.

“What did they say?”

“Not refused. Sent back for a clearer reason.”

Su Fan looked again at the sentence about the child.

“Did they tell you what wasn't clear?”

“No.”

He could think of sharper words. He could write a sentence that made the clerk appear cruel, or one that invoked an office the man might never have visited. He could make the page sound more important than the person holding it.

Then he remembered a smaller letter he had once written for Tan Wei.

“What do you want changed?” he asked.

“The shift.”

“On the paper.”

The man considered.

“I don't want them thinking I'm leaving. We need the pay. I want them to stop making me choose every morning which one of us is going to be angry.”

Su Fan read the request a third time.

They added the proposed exchange worker's name where the clerk could not miss it. They separated the dates from the explanation. The labourer insisted on keeping the sentence about his wife, although Su Fan thought the form would be stronger without it.

They kept it.

When Mother Wei emerged, the man rose so quickly that water slopped from the cup she had filled for him earlier.

“Sit,” she said. “He has more breath than you seem to.”

She explained what she had found and what she wanted him to watch. Su Fan picked up his bag before the discussion could turn into something he had no right to hear.

The labourer stopped him.

“Will this work?”

He meant the paper.

“It says what you're asking more clearly.”

“That wasn't my question.”

“No,” Su Fan said. “I don't know whether they'll grant it.”

The man folded it carefully.

“All right.”

He did not sound grateful. He sounded like someone who had obtained one small useful thing and still needed a much larger one. Su Fan found that easier to bear than gratitude he had not earned.

At the bend he looked back. The man had gone inside. The empty cup remained on the wall, catching a few grains of sleet.

***

The lane to Min's room had been swept, but the water beneath the grit was beginning to freeze again.

Su Fan kept the charcoal high against his hip. Carrying it close helped his balance; it did not make the ground less treacherous. At the narrowest point he stopped and let a woman with a laundry basket pass. They turned awkwardly together, each trying to make space for the other, until she told him to stand still and let her be courteous by herself.

From the common kitchen came a burst of laughter.

Deng had found a use for the child's bed end. With its painted side facing the wall, it made a backrest for the bench nearest the stove. The woman who brought it was sitting there while her child ate.

The wood would burn eventually if nothing else came. For the moment it was still a bed doing something other than burning.

Su Fan did not stop to praise the arrangement. Auntie Lu saw him looking and shook the ladle at him.

He lifted his free hand.

At Min's door he paused to brush the coal dust from his sleeve. Inside, he heard Jin asking whether a fish would get tired of never being able to lie down.

Min's answer was too faint to catch.

The boy laughed.

Su Fan waited until the laughter had ended before knocking. He had carried fuel uphill, arranged two repairs and helped rewrite a request. None of it had answered the question waiting on Tan Wei's paper.

He was beginning to understand how much of a day could be useful without settling the thing that mattered most.

***

The answer arrived with the firewood.

Both had been delayed, and both were less useful than promised.

Auntie Lu counted the cart's dry logs while Min Yao unfolded the letter from the river office. The first page acknowledged her query. The second explained why a full answer required another office. The third charged her for the first two.

“Three coppers,” she said.

“For what?” Tan Wei asked.

“For knowing who won't tell me.”

He took the letter and read it beside the newly built stove.

Su Fan watched from the doorway. He had brought a bag of charcoal for Min's room. The old scholar was sleeping inside, one hand visible above the blanket. Jin had laid a paper fish on the pillow beside him.

Tan Wei read the second page again.

“The district order includes every active operator,” he said. “My agreement says a specific station.”

“Yes.”

“Can they do that?”

“They have done it. Whether they may is the question they have charged us to send elsewhere.”

Tan Wei folded the letter along its existing creases.

“I'll speak to Han.”

Su Fan nearly said he would come.

Instead he shifted the charcoal against his hip.

“Do you need a copy?”

“Two.”

***

Winter work changed the settlement's sounds.

There was less hammering before dawn and more coughing through the walls. Frozen mortar waited for noon. Men who had once complained of the heat at the old kilns now crowded around Duan's furnace pretending to discuss orders.

Su Fan worked until his clothes steamed, then trained in the roofed yard.

His fourth-stage circulation had grown reliable. That did not make the fifth close. When he pushed more qi through his legs, his shoulders tightened. When he relaxed his shoulders, the force escaped before reaching his hands.

He marked the failures on a scrap of board.

Duan studied it.

“Those marks mean what?”

“Where the movement broke.”

“How many movements?”

“Six.”

“How many things were you trying to correct?”

Su Fan looked at the crowded board.

Duan went back to filing a hinge.

For the rest of the afternoon, Su Fan practised one step.

***

Han came down after supper.

He had brought the station's current operating register, carried openly beneath his arm. Tan Wei walked beside him. Neither looked angry. That worried Su Fan more than anger would have.

Han sat near the stove. His bad leg took time to settle.

“The flood declaration remains active,” he said. “It has been extended to cover the linked stations during restoration.”

“For how long?” Min Yao asked.

“Until restoration is complete.”

“And whose finding completes it?”

“The supervising elder's.”

She laid Tan Wei's contract beside the register.

Han looked at the two pages for a long time.

“I witnessed this,” he said at last, touching the contract. “I explained it to him.”

“Yes,” Tan Wei said.

The teacher's fingers stayed on the paper.

“I believed the station limitation would hold.”

“I believed you.”

Han nodded once. He did not defend himself against a statement that was true.

Su Fan looked away to give them what privacy the small room allowed.

From the bed, Min stirred.

“Read the dates,” he murmured.

Min Yao turned toward him.

“Father, sleep.”

“The dates first.”

She read them aloud.

The district order had been issued nine days before Tan Wei signed.

For a moment, only the stove made a sound.

Tan Wei reached for his own copy.

“So they already knew.”

***

Later, Su Fan found him outside under the lean-to.

Snow had begun, too thin to settle on the hot roof.

“I'm not leaving the method,” Tan Wei said before Su Fan spoke. “I like what I can do. I like the work when they let us do it properly.”

“I know.”

“I want the agreement I signed.”

Su Fan nodded.

Tan Wei watched the flakes disappear against the furnace chimney.

“Would you help me get that?”

“Yes.”

“Without deciding what comes after?”

Su Fan let the question stand long enough to answer it honestly.

“I'll try. And you can tell me when I start.”

Tan Wei held out the folded contract.

“Start by reading this. The whole thing.”

chapters.title: The Price of a Cart
chapters.text:
Sun Lian refused the passenger before she refused the cargo.

The passenger stood on the landing with a travelling chest, a rolled quilt and a little brass cage containing nothing that Su Fan could see. He had dressed for a journey on which other people would be cold. Fur lined his collar. His gloves were soft enough that the rope he was holding had left no mark on them.

“I paid for passage,” he said.

“You paid for yourself and that chest.”

“The cage is hardly anything.”

“Then it will be easy to leave behind.”

The man glanced at Su Fan, perhaps hoping for the ordinary sympathy of one male stranger watching another be inconvenienced.

Su Fan looked at the boat instead.

The Honest Measure lay low beneath the landing. It was not overloaded, but every useful stretch of deck already had a purpose. Two crates of fittings sat beneath a cover. Spare timber ran along the port side, lashed clear of the walkway. A bundle of tools occupied the space where Su Fan would have put the passenger's quilt.

Something moved inside the cage.

Not an animal. A patch of pale light shifted against the bars, then gathered itself into a small cloudy lump.

“What is it?”

“A warming spirit.”

Sun Lian held out her hand.

“The containment certificate.”

“It isn't dangerous.”

“The certificate.”

The passenger took a folded paper from inside his coat. Sun Lian read it, turned it over, then held it where Su Fan could see a line near the bottom.

Land transport only.

The man sighed.

“That is a recommendation.”

“It has a seal.”

“Everything has a seal.”

“Then you won't miss this one on the landing.”

He began explaining how much the spirit had cost.

Sun Lian waited until he finished.

“That sounds like another reason not to sink it.”

The light struck the cage again. A faint smell of hot dust reached Su Fan. He could not tell whether the thing inside was alive, cultivated, or merely something a seller had found a profitable name for. Neither could Sun Lian. That was the point she seemed to be making.

The passenger hired a boy to carry the cage back to the inn.

Before the boy left, Sun Lian asked who would be responsible for receiving it. The passenger gave a name. She made the boy repeat it.

Only then did she take the man's chest aboard.

“People mind the refusal more than the danger,” she said quietly.

“Because they can see the refusal.”

She glanced at Su Fan.

“Don't make that into a saying. Help me with the timber.”

He smiled and took the end she indicated.

***

Winter changed the loading work.

A plank that had been trustworthy in dry weather now carried a thin skin of ice beneath its coating of grit. Rope stiffened. Fingers lost their sense of pressure before they lost their willingness to grip. Men who knew a knot by touch had to look at it.

Su Fan preferred the cold to the smothering heat of the old quarry sheds. He had said so the first morning.

By the second, he stopped saying it.

They moved the timber one piece at a time. Sun Lian checked the lashings after each shift in weight. When Su Fan suggested moving three pieces together, she asked where he would put his feet while the deck changed beneath him.

He showed her.

She stood in the proposed space.

“Now where will I stand?”

He looked down at the gap between the crates.

“That would be awkward.”

“It would be wet.”

They moved the pieces separately.

The ferryman helping them had a cough he tried to hide by turning away. Sun Lian noticed. She shortened his part of the carry and gave him work on the landing instead of making a public ceremony of his breathing.

He objected once.

“You can still count,” she told him. “Nobody's replacing you with a child.”

He accepted that more readily than concern.

At the next crate, Su Fan felt a fixing shift beneath his hand. The lid rose slightly, though it should have been secure.

“Stop.”

They set it down.

Inside were copper collars nested in straw. One had been packed against a rough nail. During the cart journey it had rubbed a bright groove into the metal.

The supplier's porter said it would not matter.

Sun Lian lifted the collar out and held it in the light.

“Where will this sit?”

“In a pump.”

“Where in a pump?”

The porter did not know.

“Then neither of us knows whether it matters.”

She marked the damaged piece separately on the receipt. The porter wanted her to accept the whole crate and argue later. She declined.

“We're already arguing now. It will cost less.”

Su Fan fetched a thin strip of wood and helped repack the remaining collars. He had spent much of his life hoping that a better understanding would make arguments unnecessary. At the landing, understanding often meant knowing which argument could not safely be avoided.

The passenger watched from a bollard.

“We will miss the tide.”

Sun Lian did not look up.

“The tide isn't paying for a damaged fitting.”

“It is paying for my arrival.”

“No. You are. That's why I want you to arrive.”

The ferryman coughed into his sleeve and laughed at the same time.

***

An old woman came down the steps carrying a covered bowl.

She wore three layers of ordinary clothing and had tied a strip of cloth over her ears. A younger woman followed with two bundles. Neither carried the comfortable certainty of someone whose name was already on a passenger list.

Sun Lian went to meet them before they reached the gangplank.

The old woman wanted a bowl taken to a nephew upriver.

“What is in it?”

“Soup.”

“How far upriver?”

She named a place beyond the intended stopping point.

“It won't be soup by then,” Sun Lian said. “Not soup I'd make a nephew eat.”

“He has a fever.”

The younger woman set the bundles down.

“It isn't only soup.”

The bowl contained a small sealed medicine jar, wrapped in cloth to keep it upright. The old woman had put it among the food because, she explained, her nephew distrusted medicine but would never refuse her cooking.

Sun Lian took the jar out.

“Does he know it's coming?”

“He knows I worry.”

“That doesn't answer.”

The women exchanged a look. The younger one admitted that a messenger had come down two days earlier. They had no money for another special journey, and the regular carrier had gone before the jar was ready.

Su Fan looked toward the passenger's chest. There was room for one small bowl.

He almost said so.

Sun Lian was asking for the exact house, the name of the person who would meet the boat, and what should happen if nobody came.

The old woman repeated that her nephew was ill.

“I believe you,” Sun Lian said. “I'm trying to get this to the ill man rather than leave it on a quay while everyone remembers how kind we were.”

They settled on the nearer landing. A shopkeeper there knew the family and could keep the jar until it was collected. The younger woman wrote the name on a scrap and tied it to the wrapping.

Sun Lian charged the ordinary small-parcel rate, not a special fee.

Su Fan waited until the women had gone before asking why she had not waived it.

“Because they asked me for work.”

“They were worried.”

“Yes.”

He looked at her.

She put the parcel in a dry compartment.

“I carry some things without charging. That doesn't mean every frightened person who reaches my boat must be made to accept a favour.”

The passenger cleared his throat.

“Then perhaps, since we are discussing fairness—”

“No,” she said.

“I haven't asked.”

“You were about to discuss my price.”

He considered denying it, then went back to watching the water.

Su Fan helped the younger woman retrieve a dropped glove from between the landing boards. She thanked him as though he had done precisely one useful thing.

It was a pleasant change.

***

Before departure, Sun Lian handed him a short piece of chalk.

“Mark what you can reach without stepping over a line.”

He thought she meant the cargo.

She meant everything.

The oar. The loose end of the forward rope. The place where a passenger might sit without obstructing the cover. The bucket that would be needed if water came aboard. The knife used for cutting a snagged line. The second knife, because the first could be dropped.

He moved around the deck and made his marks.

She inspected them.

“This one.”

“What about it?”

“You can reach it with your left hand while you hold that brace with your right. Can you reach it the other way around?”

He tried. His shoulder struck a crate.

“No.”

“Then don't promise yourself you can.”

She erased the mark.

They had worked together long enough that he no longer heard every correction as a judgment on his usefulness. That did not mean he enjoyed all of them.

At the stern she asked him to stand where he would be able to see both her hands and the forward landing.

“That puts you on my right,” he said.

“I know.”

“I won't hear—”

“You won't always hear. That's why I want you to see the signal.”

They tried it. She raised one finger, then two, then closed her hand. He repeated the meanings before moving. The first time, he looked at the rope instead of her and missed the change.

“Again,” she said.

The ferryman on the landing offered an elaborate gesture of his own, which meant either that he wished them good passage or that somebody owed him money.

Sun Lian told him to keep it for the man who did.

They rehearsed until the signals could be given without becoming a performance.

Su Fan had wanted his damaged hearing to be something he managed privately. Each practical adjustment made that less possible. It also made the work safer in ways he could not honestly resent.

When they finished, she gave him the chalk again.

“Keep it dry.”

“For the marks?”

“For whatever I forgot.”

That pleased him more than praise would have.

***

Duan's bundle was waiting at the top of the steps.

It contained two samples of good iron, a bent fitting and a list of prices the smith wanted checked whenever there was a chance. He had written the list with his good hand. The figures were clear. The letters had the look of men standing too close in a queue.

Su Fan read them twice.

At the bottom was an instruction about the bent fitting.

Do not let them sell you a new one until they have looked at this.

He could hear Duan saying it.

Ah-Du had added a second line in smaller letters.

Ask whether they have a hammer that finds its own way home.

Su Fan folded the paper.

He had left a list of his unfinished work at the smithy. Beside each item he had written what remained to be done, which tools were needed, and whether the customer had already paid. The list had seemed embarrassingly thorough until Duan asked a question it did not answer.

Who had promised the woman with the stove hinge that it would be ready tomorrow?

Su Fan had.

Then he had better speak to her before leaving.

He had gone. She had been annoyed. The conversation had not become an inspiring example of mutual understanding. She had accepted another collection time and told him not to make a habit of discovering his journeys after making promises.

Now the revised date was on the slate.

The boat was waiting.

For a moment he stood with the bundle against his chest and felt the strange pull of leaving a place that was not finished. The new workshop still needed plaster along one wall. A brace on the practice frame had to be replaced. There were two letters he had not answered and one conversation with Tan Wei he kept imagining could be made simpler by finding a better sentence.

None of those things would arrange themselves neatly behind him.

From below, Sun Lian called his name.

He turned before answering, putting her on the side where her voice came clearly.

“Coming.”

The passenger had finally sat down. His quilt was folded beneath him. Without the cage, he looked less imposing and more like a man who hoped the journey would justify the trouble of beginning it.

Su Fan stepped aboard with Duan's bundle.

Sun Lian checked the parcel once more, tested the rope against her palm and looked up the river. She had her own customers, her own damaged fittings, her own promises that could not be carried merely because someone else wanted to be helpful.

He took the position they had agreed.

When she gave the signal, he saw it.

***

Ruan Zhi's aunt came to the quarry in a covered carriage.

The wheels struck a rut deep enough to tilt the cabin. Her driver swore. From inside came a cooler voice telling him the rut was unlikely to apologize.

Ruan met her beside the practice yard.

Su Fan had seen him face an armed smuggler with less concern.

Lady Ruan was small, silver-haired and dressed for a warm room rather than a quarry. She took in the half-built houses, the timber stacks and the stove smoke without changing expression.

“Your account,” she said, handing Ruan a folded sheet.

He read it.

“These were evacuation carts.”

“They were my evacuation carts. Apparently they continued evacuating sacks of lime for another six weeks.”

“The road was impassable for the hired teams.”

“And you found it easier to use mine than ask.”

Ruan glanced toward Su Fan, who immediately regretted being present.

Lady Ruan noticed the glance.

“He is not paying this for you.”

“I wasn't going to ask him.”

“Good. He looks expensive to feed.”

Su Fan bowed. He could think of no safe reply.

***

She walked the settlement before leaving.

At the clinic, Mother Wei asked whether her knee still troubled her in damp weather. The lady looked irritated that somebody knew. She sat down anyway.

At the storehouse she checked the locks. At Bao Shun's workshop she ordered six shelves and refused a discount. At the kitchen she tasted the soup and asked why there was so little oil in it.

Auntie Lu told her what oil cost.

By the time she returned to the carriage, a boy had been sent to purchase two jars.

Ruan approached with his account still open.

“I can pay half now.”

“You can pay all of it over time.”

“Aunt.”

“Generosity does not become yours because you borrow somebody else's cart.”

She climbed inside, then opened the curtain again.

“The shelves are for the clinic. Make certain he knows the height before he cuts them.”

***

That afternoon, Ruan fought badly.

He attacked too directly and corrected too hard. Su Fan slipped one cut, stepped inside the second and landed a short strike against the padded ribs.

Ruan stumbled.

It was the first clean opening Su Fan had made against him without an agreed drill.

He lowered his hands.

Ruan looked at him.

“Don't.”

“You were distracted.”

“Yes. Will you ask every man trying to kill you whether his aunt has upset him?”

Su Fan lifted the practice sword again.

The next exchange put him on his back.

***

They sat afterward with cups of hot water.

Ruan rubbed the place where True Strike had gone through the padding. The force had not been large. It had arrived without the warning swell he expected from a fourth-stage practitioner.

“You don't announce it,” he said.

“I still move.”

“Yes. And your right shoulder rises before your second cut. I don't need to feel your qi if you keep doing that.”

Su Fan marked the observation on his board.

Ruan watched him write.

“I cannot go to Siltbridge with you.”

Su Fan looked up.

“I haven't asked.”

“You have a contract dispute, a boatbuilder with unpaid freight, and a scribe whose best contacts are there. You will go.”

“Probably.”

“My family has been called to account for the lower fields. My aunt expects me to attend. So do the tenants.”

There was embarrassment beneath his formal tone. Su Fan recognized it because he had heard it in himself when admitting that something else mattered.

“Then attend.”

Ruan glanced at him, almost suspicious.

“I owe those people an explanation,” he said.

“You don't owe me one.”

They drank their water.

After a while Ruan reached for the training sword.

“Before you leave, we should do something about that shoulder.”

chapters.title: The Closed Window
chapters.text:
Tan Wei had invited him to supper, not to a meeting.

Su Fan remembered that distinction when he saw the papers on the table.

He had brought a clean copy of the request and a second copy with room for notes. He had also brought the piece of dried fish Auntie Lu insisted was too small to sell. Now he stood in Tan Wei's doorway holding all three while his friend tried to rescue a pot that had begun burning at one side.

“Put the fish down,” Tan Wei said.

“The papers?”

“May also sit, if they behave.”

The room was warm near the stove and cold everywhere else. A coat hung over the window gap. Two bowls waited beside a heel of bread. Someone had carved a game board into the table long before Tan Wei acquired it; one corner of the pattern disappeared beneath a repair.

Su Fan set the papers on the dry end.

Tan Wei tilted the pot. A smell of scorched grain filled the room.

“Is that recoverable?”

“Everything above the bottom is innocent.”

He divided the innocent part between the bowls. The guilty part remained in the pot for later consideration.

Su Fan sat where he could hear him.

For a little while they ate without discussing contracts. Tan Wei told him that a station runner had fallen asleep while standing against a wall and continued answering questions for several breaths before anybody noticed. Su Fan described Ah-Du's attempt to make a tool roll that could be tied with one hand.

“Did it work?”

“For the hand doing the tying.”

“And the other?”

“Became part of the roll.”

Tan Wei laughed with his mouth full and had to put his bowl down.

The laugh changed the room. Su Fan had spent so long anticipating difficult conversations with him that an ordinary laugh felt briefly like permission to stop guarding every word.

Then he saw his friend rub the marked wrist against his sleeve.

“Does it hurt tonight?”

“Sometimes.”

“Should you—”

Tan Wei looked up.

Su Fan stopped.

“Should I move the bowl nearer?” he finished.

“That would be an unusual treatment, but yes.”

They ate the fish with their fingers. Tan Wei said it was better than the expensive pieces because the expensive pieces had expectations.

Su Fan was about to tell him what Auntie Lu had charged when someone knocked.

Qiu Lan entered carrying a small earthenware jar.

“Not medicine,” she said when Tan Wei saw it. “Before you become tragic.”

Pickled vegetables. Her family made them with more pepper than the common kitchen allowed.

She took the third bowl from the shelf without asking where it was and inspected the pot.

“You burned it.”

“Only underneath.”

“Where the fire is. A difficult place to avoid.”

She scraped a little onto her bowl anyway.

Su Fan moved the papers to make room.

Qiu Lan saw them and sighed.

“I said supper.”

“So did I,” Tan Wei replied.

Neither looked at Su Fan, which was worse.

He folded the copies and put them beneath his coat.

***

The discussion began only after they had washed the bowls.

Qiu Lan asked to see the exact words in Tan Wei's agreement. She had read them before, but wanted to compare them with a notice at her own station.

Su Fan fetched the copies.

They bent over the table. Tan Wei kept his original near his elbow. Qiu Lan followed the lines with a dry finger, pausing where the office language changed from a named place to a linked system.

“Here,” she said.

“Yes.”

“That is what they showed us after the flood.”

“After,” Tan Wei repeated.

The word carried more than a date. Su Fan heard the old anger in it, but also something tired. A man could spend a day being furious about a decision and still have to report to the work shaped by it the next morning.

Qiu Lan sat back.

“I don't want my impression removed.”

“No one asked you to.”

“I know. I'm saying it before somebody decides it is the answer to every question.”

Su Fan looked down at the paper.

“I haven't written that.”

“Good.”

She did not apologize for asking.

Her family had sent money for training when they could barely afford the journey. She could now do work that would have required several ordinary labourers. She liked the skill. She liked being trusted with it. She also disliked being treated as though liking the work made every arrangement around it acceptable.

Tan Wei nodded.

“That.”

“What?”

“Put that in.”

“Not in those words,” she said.

“Why not?”

“Because it sounds like me arguing over supper.”

Su Fan took up his brush.

“It might be clearer than the first paragraph.”

She leaned over to read what he wrote.

He did not turn her statement into a declaration that all operators agreed. He put her name beside it and left a space for her to change the wording.

She changed the wording.

Then she changed it again.

The third version was shorter than his.

Tan Wei watched, smiling faintly.

“You're enjoying this,” Su Fan told him.

“I spent years listening to you finish other people's sentences. It's pleasant to see one survive.”

Su Fan could have defended himself. He knew several examples in which he had merely saved time. Instead he sanded the ink and moved the sheet where Qiu Lan could see it.

She read it aloud.

When she reached the last line, she nodded.

“That is what I mean.”

***

A younger operator arrived later with a cracked sandal and a question about the next shift.

He stopped when he saw the papers.

“Have you found a way?”

“A way to ask properly,” Tan Wei said.

The young man looked disappointed.

He had thought a written complaint was something handed to the right person which then changed the next day's work. Su Fan had once thought much the same about evidence. He could not decide whether age consisted mostly of acquiring better questions or learning how slowly anyone answered them.

The operator sat near the door. His heel showed through the sandal.

He wanted to leave the stations entirely.

Qiu Lan wanted a narrower duty and a clear withdrawal process.

Tan Wei wanted the agreement he had signed to mean what it said.

For several minutes they tried to make these into the same request.

They were not the same request.

“If we put all of it together,” the young man said, “they can't ignore it.”

“They can answer the easiest part,” Qiu Lan replied. “Then say they answered us.”

“Separately, they'll say there are only three of us.”

“Then we should find out who else wants which thing.”

The young man frowned.

“That will take longer.”

“Yes.”

He looked at Su Fan.

Su Fan had been waiting for this moment without admitting it. The two stronger opinions paused, and somebody asked him to make them fit. He could arrange their words into something neat. He could decide which demand mattered most and let the others appear beneath it.

He set the brush down.

“I can make three copies.”

The operator stared at him.

“That isn't an answer.”

“No. It is something I know how to do.”

Tan Wei rested his marked hand on the table.

“Tell us why you want to leave.”

The young man began with the shifts. Then he spoke of his father, who had lost a fishing net in the flood and could no longer work a boat alone. His mother needed help carrying water. The station pay was better than the ferry work, but the station did not ask the same questions when somebody failed to come home.

He had not put any of that in his first request.

By the time he finished, Qiu Lan was no longer arguing about the order of their paragraphs.

They wrote down the work he would return to, the people depending on it, and the question he needed answered. It did not make his case identical to theirs. It made it his.

***

The sandal broke when he stood.

The strap pulled free of its fixing and left him balanced on one bare heel, clutching the stool.

Tan Wei laughed before he could help it.

The young man looked so offended that Qiu Lan began laughing too. Then the stool shifted and all three caught him at once.

Su Fan found a leather scrap in Tan Wei's tool bundle. He asked before taking it.

“Use the ugly end,” Tan Wei said.

“Which one?”

“That is why I kept the whole piece.”

They repaired the sandal on the table after moving the papers well away. The young man insisted he could have walked home without it. Qiu Lan told him to save his courage for a problem that wanted it.

Su Fan cut a new hole and tested the strap.

Too tight.

He loosened it.

Tan Wei held the shoe steady with his good hand and watched the needle go through the leather. The movement was simple. No lineage was needed. No one took that as an argument against the work he had spent months learning.

When the sandal was finished, the young man tried it on, took three steps and came back to complain that it was now more comfortable than the other.

“We can damage it a little,” Tan Wei offered.

He left with the separate request folded inside his coat.

After the door closed, Qiu Lan returned to the notice.

“He may still be refused.”

“Yes,” Tan Wei said.

“He should know that before he starts telling his father he'll be home.”

“I'll speak to him at the station.”

Su Fan nearly said he would make the wording stronger.

The brush remained on the table.

***

Qiu Lan left before the room grew cold.

Tan Wei put the copies in order. He counted them, then made Su Fan count them as well. They had already discovered how easily a useful page could disappear among papers that looked almost the same.

One copy was missing the final sentence.

Su Fan had stopped writing when the sandal broke.

He took the page back and completed it.

“That's why,” Tan Wei said.

“I know.”

“I wasn't accusing you.”

“I know that too.”

He did not, quite. Being watched over a mistake still felt uncomfortably close to being judged by all his previous ones.

Tan Wei seemed to recognize it.

“I want someone checking my copies as well.”

Su Fan looked at the pile beneath his friend's hand.

“All right.”

They exchanged pages.

Tan Wei's handwriting was less elegant than the scribe's and clearer than Su Fan's. He had left enough space between clauses that an addition could be seen as an addition rather than squeezed into a sentence after the fact.

Su Fan found a date copied incorrectly.

Tan Wei corrected it without making a joke.

The smallness of the exchange was what made it difficult to dismiss. Trust was not being restored by an eloquent apology. It was being asked to perform an ordinary task and having that task checked.

When the copies were dry, Tan Wei put the originals away.

“Now.”

“What?”

“The game.”

He cleared the carved board and fetched a handful of unequal pieces from a cup. Two were beans. One was a button. A small dark pebble represented a piece missing long before either of them acquired the table.

Su Fan had not played in months.

Tan Wei won the first game while continuing to complain about the burned grain.

He won the second after announcing his plan aloud.

During the third, Su Fan realized he had been guarding a square Tan Wei no longer needed.

“You're thinking about tomorrow,” his friend said.

“So are you.”

“Yes. But I'm also taking that.”

He moved the pebble.

Su Fan looked at the board, then at the papers no longer lying on it.

For once, there was no useful sentence to add.

***

Han scheduled the uncoupling examination for the last return of the month.

It was an examination only. Tan Wei had not decided to withdraw. He wanted the condition of his channels recorded by somebody other than the office that benefited from his remaining bound.

Mother Wei attended. So did the station healer and a clerk with the emergency register.

Su Fan waited outside.

He found that waiting required more discipline than training.

Through the thin wall came the scrape of a chair. Water being poured. Han's low instructions.

Then Tan Wei said, “That's not my hand.”

Su Fan stood.

The next sound was Han's voice, firm and close.

“Look at it. Tell me where you are.”

“Eighth station.”

“What year?”

Tan Wei answered.

“What did you eat this morning?”

A pause.

“Too much turnip.”

Mother Wei said something Su Fan could not hear. Tan Wei laughed once.

Su Fan sat down.

***

The examination found no immediate tearing and no irreversible replacement of Tan Wei's channels.

It also found that the return cycle had become more frequent since his permanent bond.

Han compared three readings.

“They shortened the interval.”

“The shared formation requires additional support during reconstruction,” the clerk said.

“That is an explanation for the schedule. I am asking who approved the load.”

The clerk referred him to a signature at the bottom of the page.

It belonged to the district office. A broad approval, three lines long, covering improvements to emergency operation.

Mother Wei asked Tan Wei to hold a cup.

His fingers assumed a neat, unfamiliar arrangement around the handle. He frowned and shifted them.

“How often?” she asked.

“More when I'm tired.”

“Dreams?”

“The woman. The same house. Sometimes I know which door opens into which room.”

“Do you know that now?”

He closed his eyes, then opened them quickly.

“Yes.”

Han took the cup from him.

“We reduce his station hours.”

The clerk turned another page.

***

By noon they had permission to reduce Tan Wei's hours for seven days.

They had no permission to test a full withdrawal.

The distinction came on two separate pieces of paper, each requiring its own seal.

Outside, Tan Wei sat on a wall and watched Qiu Lan teach a younger trainee how to lay a water sheet over a leaking joint. The boy kept making it too thick. Qiu Lan let him waste the strength twice before changing his grip.

“I still want this,” Tan Wei said.

Mother Wei sat beside him.

“The method?”

“The work. The skill. I don't want to spend the rest of my life being frightened of something I chose.”

“You may keep what you have learned,” Han said. “The permanent impression can be separated from parts of it. Not all. Not without loss.”

“How much?”

“I don't know yet.”

Tan Wei looked at the blue marks on his wrist.

Su Fan stood a little distance away. He kept his eyes on the practice basin until his friend called him over.

“I want the full assessment,” Tan Wei said. “If they refuse that, I want to leave the permanent bond. I won't decide whether to stay in a room whose door they won't let me test.”

Su Fan felt the old urge to agree too eagerly.

He restrained it.

“What do you need?”

***

Han knew where the original return schedules were kept.

The contractor maintained them in Siltbridge, with the commissioning charter and the old station diagrams. Current offices held extracts. The extracts no longer agreed.

Min Yao wrote a request for inspection.

Sun Lian added her own freight claim. Several unpaid deliveries were listed against the same records house. As a contracted carrier, she had a right to inspect the receipts.

They waited nine days.

The answer denied access because the files were under active review.

On the back, somebody had written a smaller instruction intended for the local clerk.

Superseded originals to be destroyed after spring renewal.

Min Yao held the paper toward the lamp.

“They've sent us the filing copy,” she said.

Tan Wei read the line twice.

“When is renewal?”

“The first full return after the thaw.”

chapters.title: The People in the Boat
chapters.text:
By the time Su Fan reached the lower turn, he was carrying more requests than luggage.

Duan wanted prices. Mother Wei wanted to know whether a particular supplier still sealed its powders in waxed paper. Bao Mei wanted a scrap of blue cloth held beside the merchant's best pigment, not his cheapest, so she could judge how much further her own mixture had to go.

Ah-Du wanted a story in which somebody respectable fell over.

“That one may take longer,” Su Fan had told him.

“I can wait.”

The papers lay together in an oilcloth packet. They did not weigh much. That made it easy to pretend he could add another.

A woman at the settlement edge asked him to look for her cousin. A man wanted a debt collected. Someone else had heard that a city teacher accepted students who could not produce a family tablet, and hoped Su Fan might arrange an introduction for his daughter.

He had said yes too quickly to the first request.

At the second, he stopped.

“How would I know whether the man owes it?”

“I've written it down.”

“Has he?”

The conversation became less friendly.

By the time he reached the turn, Su Fan had promised to deliver two letters if the addresses were on his route, ask one question at a named office, and bring back no money belonging to somebody else.

The man with the debt had called him careful in a tone usually reserved for cowardice.

Su Fan was still thinking about it when Old Pock hailed him from the ferry steps.

He did not hear.

Pock threw a small pebble at the road in front of his boot.

Su Fan stopped and turned sharply.

“Don't do that.”

“Don't ignore me.”

“I wasn't.”

Pock looked at the right side of his head, then shifted his place on the steps.

“Here, then. Come and be useful where I can see you.”

The ferry's stern line had frozen into a knot.

***

It was a small problem, which meant everyone had an immediate solution.

A man waiting with a basket of eggs proposed cutting the rope. The ferryman asked whether the man would like to buy the replacement. A woman suggested hot water. Pock asked what she intended to carry that water in, since she appeared to have brought only complaints.

Su Fan knelt beside the bollard.

The knot was hard, but the rope itself had not frozen through. Someone had hauled the wrong end under load and tightened the inner loop until grit worked into the strands.

“Give me some slack.”

“I have,” the ferryman said.

“From the boat.”

“That is slack.”

Su Fan looked down.

The river had moved the ferry while the line remained fixed. The weight still rested on the very loop he was trying to open.

He stood.

“Push her off a little.”

“With what?”

Pock handed him a pole.

The landing was narrower than it looked from the road. Su Fan placed his left foot where the stone was dry and his right against the step. He set the pole into the ferry's reinforced side, not against the thin boards.

The boat moved.

The man with the eggs cheered as though the ferry had been rescued from a siege.

“Enough,” Pock said.

Su Fan held the boat where it was while the ferryman worked the loop free. His circulation helped him keep the pressure steady. It did not prevent the pole from slipping when a wake touched the hull.

He had to move his feet.

The egg man stopped cheering.

“Easy,” Pock said.

Su Fan brought the pole lower and let the ferry return part of the distance rather than fight to preserve an exact position. The load eased. The knot opened.

The ferryman held up the rope.

“There.”

Nobody applauded the knot.

Su Fan handed back the pole and brushed mud from his sleeve.

“You could have done that,” he told Pock.

“Yes.”

“Then why call me?”

“You were going to ride.”

It was difficult to argue with that.

***

On the ferry, the woman who had suggested hot water sat opposite him.

She carried a bundle of household linen tied in a cloth, and a pair of small shoes looped through the knot. She watched the river with the rigid attention of someone trying not to look afraid.

Su Fan put the packet beneath his coat.

The egg man began explaining that the lower crossing had once been quicker. Pock told him that the lower crossing was now a place where a roof occasionally appeared at low water.

“I know what happened.”

“Then stop asking the river to apologize.”

The woman tightened her grip on the bundle.

Su Fan wished Pock had been gentler. Then he noticed the ferryman looking at her hands.

“First crossing since?” he asked.

She nodded.

“Keep your eyes on the opposite steps. Not the water.”

“I know how to ride a boat.”

“So do I. I'm still telling you.”

She looked toward the steps.

The advice helped. Not enough to remove the fear, but enough that her fingers loosened slightly.

Su Fan did not ask which house she had lost. He had become tired of the way people sometimes sought a name before deciding how much sorrow to allow a stranger.

Halfway across, a cart upstream struck a loose board on the temporary bridge. The sharp crack came from his right.

He turned the wrong way.

The woman saw it. So did Pock.

Su Fan corrected himself and felt heat rise in his face.

The ferryman said nothing. He simply pointed with two fingers toward the sound's actual source, then returned his attention to the current.

It was the right kind of help.

Su Fan watched the bridge crew wave the cart back. No one had fallen. Men were already fetching a replacement board. The ferry moved on.

The woman opposite breathed out.

“Every noise,” she said.

Su Fan looked at her.

“Since the flood. Every noise sounds like the beginning of something.”

He could have told her that some noises now had no trustworthy place at all.

Instead he said, “The board held long enough for them to stop.”

She watched the opposite landing.

“Yes.”

They travelled the rest of the way without forcing the conversation to become comforting.

***

At the far side, a carrier was arguing with a boy over a sealed packet.

The boy insisted that it belonged in the basket going to the city. The carrier said the address was incomplete.

“It says where.”

“It says behind a place that burned down.”

“The house didn't burn.”

“Then write the house.”

“My mother wrote it.”

“Your mother isn't carrying it.”

Su Fan waited until the carrier had set down the basket before approaching.

“May I look?”

The boy held the packet away from him.

“Not inside.”

“Only the address.”

He read the cover. A familiar market name appeared beside a lane he thought he remembered. There were several possible houses behind it.

He asked the boy which entrance his mother used when she visited.

“She doesn't. Her sister comes here.”

“Does she know someone else in that lane?”

The boy began to cry, silently and furiously, as though tears were another part of the transaction being held against him.

The carrier looked uncomfortable.

“I can't deliver it to guessing.”

“I know.”

Su Fan crouched so the boy did not have to look up.

“What is your aunt's work?”

“She mends baskets.”

“Does she sell in the market?”

“Sometimes.”

“What does she put on the stall?”

“Baskets.”

Pock, coming up the steps behind them, made a small approving noise.

Su Fan tried a different question.

“Does she have a sign? A colour on the awning?”

The boy wiped his face with his sleeve.

“Three white strips. Because the old cloth tore.”

The carrier leaned closer.

“Near the dye sellers?”

The boy nodded eagerly, though Su Fan could not tell whether he knew or merely wanted someone to have found the answer.

They wrote both the business and the possible market location on a separate slip. The carrier agreed to ask at the basket sellers, not to promise delivery.

Su Fan made him say that part again where the boy could hear.

The boy paid the ordinary fee with coins so warm from his fist that they left damp marks on the carrier's palm.

After he ran back toward the ferry, Pock looked at Su Fan's oilcloth packet.

“How many?”

“Requests?”

“Things you intend to bring back.”

“A few.”

“Count them.”

Su Fan did.

Pock listened, then pointed to the city-teacher question.

“That one sounds like a journey by itself.”

“I only agreed to ask.”

“Then only ask.”

***

At the road shelter, Su Fan unfolded his list.

He had written it by person. Duan. Mother Wei. Bao Mei. The woman with the cousin. The father with the hopeful daughter.

Now he copied it by place.

Iron sellers. Medicine stores. Pigment lane. A named office. Two addresses that might or might not be near his route.

The rearrangement made something embarrassingly obvious. Several errands that had sounded small from the settlement would require travelling across the city and back. He had imagined fitting them between his own work, as though every street would conveniently lead toward the next obligation.

He marked the requests that depended on available time.

Then he stopped.

The woman with the cousin had heard him say yes. He had not said “when convenient.”

He could send word back from the next stop. It would cost a little and make him look less dependable than he had looked at her door.

He found a clean scrap.

Pock watched from the shelter entrance, eating something wrapped in a leaf.

“Changing the promise?”

“Correcting what she thinks I promised.”

“What did you promise?”

Su Fan looked at the scrap.

He began again.

The second version did not improve his appearance. It said he had agreed too quickly, described the route he expected to take, and asked whether delivering the letter to a carrier would be acceptable if the house lay too far away.

He folded it before finding a way to make it sound like the woman's misunderstanding.

Pock finished eating.

“That one will travel.”

“You haven't read it.”

“I watched you stop enjoying it.”

Su Fan put the scrap aside for the return ferry.

The old man offered him the remaining piece from the leaf. It was a hard sweet made from nuts and syrup. Su Fan took it.

For several breaths neither spoke.

A loaded cart creaked past on the upper road. The driver sang badly and with great confidence. Pock identified the song, then explained that the driver had misplaced both the tune and the woman for whom the tune had supposedly been written.

Su Fan laughed.

The journey ahead had room for that, too.

It did not have to consist entirely of making himself worthy of having left.

***

Before moving on, he checked the packet's wrapping.

The paper edges were dry. Bao Mei's cloth scrap had slipped between the price list and the medicine question. He moved it into a separate fold so a wet pigment sample would not damage Mother Wei's instructions.

Duan's bent fitting had worn a mark through its covering. Su Fan padded it with another strip and tied it where it would not strike his hip at every step.

He had brought more than he needed for himself and less than everyone else might need from him. That was not a problem he could solve by tightening the knots.

At the shelter door, he looked back toward the ferry.

The boy with the packet was visible on the far landing, pointing out something to his mother. Pock had gone down to help with a handcart. The frightened woman was climbing the opposite steps with her linen bundle held against her chest.

Each of them had crossed for a reason that did not belong to Su Fan.

He put the corrected promise into the return basket and gave the carrier its small fee.

Then he took the road.

***

They made the plan in Sun Lian's cabin.

She insisted on the cabin because she owned it. If people were going to risk her boat, they could at least sit somewhere that reminded them of the fact.

Su Fan, Tan Wei and Min Yao crowded around the little table. Han remained at the station to arrange Tan Wei's medical leave. The reduction in working hours gave him seven days away from active duty, provided he reported to the Siltbridge healer whose name Mother Wei had supplied.

It was a legitimate journey.

The rest was less certain.

Sun Lian put a drawing of the records house on the table.

“Front office. Receiving yard. South warehouse. Carrier's counter here.”

She tapped each place.

“The old papers?” Su Fan asked.

“Either the stone room or the loading gallery. I saw sealed chests in both when I delivered the winter brass.”

Min Yao had a contact among the temporary copying staff. The woman could tell them which files were scheduled for destruction. She could not open the archive.

“We start with my freight receipts,” Sun Lian said. “We do not begin by breaking a door.”

Su Fan nodded.

“And we do not end by burning the place down.”

“I wasn't considering it.”

“I am saying it while the boat is still mine.”

***

They discussed what each person would do if refused, separated or arrested.

Su Fan proposed that Tan Wei stay outside the records house.

Tan Wei leaned back.

“Why?”

“Your contract. They can hold you more easily.”

“They can hold you as an unregistered practitioner more easily. Are you staying outside?”

Su Fan looked at the map.

Min Yao waited without rescuing him from the question.

Finally he said, “No.”

“Then find me a useful job.”

Tan Wei knew the return schedules. He could distinguish a current operator roster from a commissioning diagram without standing there reading every heading. His fingers still remembered knots learned at the gate.

He also knew when the borrowed memories were becoming intrusive.

“If I say I'm done, we leave,” he said.

“Agreed.”

“If she says the boat is in danger, we leave.”

Sun Lian looked pleased.

“If you say the route is closed, we don't send you through it because you're difficult to sense.”

That last condition made Su Fan pause.

Then he agreed to it too.

***

Min Yao's task was to obtain copies with dates, seals and a witness to their origin. A stolen page might be true and still be useless at a hearing.

Her contact would take a risk by helping.

“I pay her,” she said. “Out of our travel account. Not after some future victory.”

Su Fan counted their coins.

The payment left little for trouble.

Duan lent them another string. He called it a loan, then refused to specify the interest. Auntie Lu packed food. Mother Wei packed medicine and gave Tan Wei a separate set of instructions that she would not allow Su Fan to inspect.

Jin cried when his mother explained she would be away.

Min Yao knelt and told him the truth: six or seven days, perhaps more if the river froze. His grandfather would read with him. Bao Mei would help with his sums.

The boy asked whether the water would take their house again.

“No,” she said, then stopped.

She looked at the new roof, the high quarry wall beyond it.

“We built much higher this time.”

***

Before they left, Su Fan went to Min.

The old scholar listened to the plan with his eyes shut.

“Take blank paper,” he said.

“We have some.”

“More.”

“Why?”

Min opened one eye.

“Every fool thinks he knows which page he came for.”

Su Fan added another packet to their supplies.

chapters.title: The Fifth Measure
chapters.text:
The most encouraging result of the week came from a damaged weight.

Su Fan discovered that on the morning he intended to write it down as progress.

He had suspended the weight beneath the practice frame and marked how far it moved when he struck the padded arm. For three days the mark had travelled farther along the board. His circulation felt smoother. His feet settled more quickly. Even the ache around his shoulders seemed less troublesome.

He brought Duan out to look.

The smith stood beneath the eaves, his injured arm protected inside his coat.

“Show me the weight.”

Su Fan showed him the marks.

“The weight.”

He lowered it.

A seam in its outer casing had opened. Fine grit trickled onto the ground.

Duan tapped it with one fingernail.

“Lighter.”

Su Fan stared at the little pile beneath it.

“How much?”

“Enough that you should stop looking pleased.”

They took it to the bench and compared it with the workshop's ordinary weights. The difference was not large enough to explain every improvement. It was large enough to make the tidy series of marks useless.

Su Fan wiped them off the board.

Duan stopped him.

“Why erase them?”

“Because they're wrong.”

“The result is real. Your explanation was wrong.”

He handed back the chalk.

Su Fan wrote beside the marks: *weight leaking; comparison invalid*.
