Ah-Du came out to inspect the ruined triumph.

“Can we still say it moved farther?”

“Yes.”

“Excellent. I was going to tell people that part.”

“Tell them the other part as well.”

The boy looked disappointed.

“That makes the story longer.”

Su Fan almost laughed. Then he saw how much he had wanted the shorter version himself.

***

He began again with a plain stone.

The stone had no convenient hook and no smooth surface on which to write a number. It was simply heavy, awkward and unlikely to leak unless he broke it.

Duan approved.

“Less impressive.”

“More troublesome.”

“Good combination.”

Su Fan wrapped it in a sling and tested the knots. He stood beneath the frame without using his circulation and let the load settle through his arms.

The body answered in familiar ways.

His right shoulder tightened. His left knee turned slightly inward. The old habit near his hip pulled him away from the position he intended to hold. Correcting one part made another insist on its own protection.

He could force the arrangement into place for a breath.

He could not remain there without making the correction itself another source of strain.

The scripture's drawing showed a clean returning line. His body supplied a less elegant argument.

He set the stone down.

From the workshop came the rasp of Duan's file. Ah-Du was working the bellows in short bursts, stopping whenever the smith asked. Neither sound cared whether Su Fan had found the correct name for the obstruction.

He changed one thing.

Not the amount of force. Not the depth of the breath. He moved the sling so the weight hung closer to the centre he could actually support, rather than the centre the diagram seemed to promise.

The next attempt lasted longer.

It also hurt.

He stopped before deciding that pain was evidence of importance.

At the table he drew his own rough figure beside the copied one. The shoulders were uneven. The feet looked more like two misplaced leaves than feet.

Under it he wrote where the pull began.

Then he went back to paid work.

The gate fitting waiting on the bench still needed a square edge. No one would accept a crooked one because the man making it had spent his morning asking a difficult question of his ribs.

***

By midday he had become careless in a different way.

The first fitting was sound. The second almost sound. On the third, the tool slipped and cut a shallow line across the edge he had meant to preserve.

He swore.

Duan looked over.

“Hungry?”

“No.”

The smith said nothing.

Su Fan examined the damage, put the tool down, and realized he had not eaten the bun beside his elbow.

He ate it standing.

“That isn't resting,” Duan said.

“I know.”

“Then sit.”

Ah-Du cleared a place on the stool with exaggerated ceremony.

Su Fan sat.

For a while the three of them ate in the warmth beside the furnace. The boy described a quarrel in the kitchen over the proper size of a serving spoon. Duan said the proper size was the one that put food in his bowl.

“That is what Auntie Lu said.”

“An intelligent woman.”

“She was talking about the other bowl.”

“Less intelligent than I hoped.”

Su Fan laughed with them, then found himself looking toward the practice frame.

Duan followed his gaze.

“You're still there.”

“The sling position was wrong.”

“Then it will be wrong after you finish eating.”

He wanted to explain that a sensation could disappear if he waited too long. He also knew how often he had chased one until he could no longer tell what he was feeling.

He looked at the damaged fitting instead.

The cut was repairable. It would cost time. He marked it for correction before putting it with the finished work.

Ah-Du noticed.

“You could have turned that side down.”

“Yes.”

“Would anyone know?”

“They might.”

“That isn't what I asked.”

Su Fan looked at him.

The boy held his gaze for an instant, then grinned.

“Duan says that to me.”

Duan lifted his bowl.

“He occasionally listens.”

***

The afternoon's experiment was humiliatingly ordinary.

Su Fan walked across the yard carrying two buckets.

One held water. The other held stones of roughly the same weight.

He had expected the changing water to be the harder load. It was, but not for the reason he had written down. The stones made him brace against a fixed pull. The water punished that bracing differently at every step.

When he attempted to correct both with the same response, the buckets swung in opposite directions.

He got wet.

Ah-Du, sitting on the wall, said nothing.

That restraint lasted longer than Su Fan would have credited.

Then the boy asked whether the exercise was meant to wash the yard.

Su Fan lowered the buckets and laughed despite himself.

“Come here.”

“To carry them?”

“To tell me when I begin leaning.”

Ah-Du's expression changed. He climbed down.

The next trial lasted only six steps before the boy shouted.

“Already?”

“Your head moved.”

“My head can move.”

“Then tell me which part of you is forbidden.”

They argued over what he was supposed to observe. Su Fan had asked for a judgment without giving the boy a usable question.

He tried again.

“Watch the distance between my shoulder and that seam in the coat. Tell me when it closes.”

Ah-Du watched.

This time his call came before Su Fan felt the tightening himself.

They repeated the walk twice, then stopped. The boy had other work. Su Fan's wrist was beginning to complain, and the water had found its way into one boot.

The useful discovery was smaller than the one he had hoped to make. An observer could see the correction beginning before he recognized it from inside.

He wrote that down.

He did not write that he had solved the next circuit.

***

Mother Wei found the wet boot beside the furnace.

She looked at it, then at him.

“River?”

“Bucket.”

“A formidable opponent.”

She had come for a repaired latch. He gave it to her and tried not to offer an account of his practice before she asked.

She asked anyway.

He showed her the notes.

She read the observation about the shoulder and the leaking weight. At the drawing of his uneven stance she paused.

“Did you put that difference in because you saw it, or because somebody told you it ought to be there?”

“I saw it in the reflection. Ah-Du saw it from the wall.”

“Good.”

She returned the sheet.

“Does good mean safe?”

“It means you answered the question I asked.”

He had deserved that.

She checked the old injury around his hip with a few careful movements and told him which complaints she wanted reported. She did not name a cultivation stage. She did not promise that a better route would make the damaged hearing useful again.

Su Fan was grateful for her caution until he remembered how much he had wanted certainty from her.

At the door she turned.

“Have you written to Tan Wei?”

“We spoke.”

“That was another question.”

He fetched the unfinished letter.

It concerned ordinary matters: a missing cup, a price Duan wanted checked, the way Ah-Du had repaired a stool so that it now leaned in a more reliable direction. He had stopped at the sentence in which he meant to describe the practice.

Mother Wei read only what he held out.

“Why stop there?”

“I don't know whether it is progress yet.”

“Then tell him that.”

She took the latch and left before he could turn the advice into something more difficult.

***

Tan Wei came by near dusk.

He brought no lesson and asked for no demonstration. He wanted to borrow a small punch and return a bowl that did not belong to him.

“How did you acquire that?”

“I was given food.”

“And the bowl?”

“Came with it. I assumed this was the usual arrangement.”

Su Fan found the punch.

Tan Wei saw the buckets, the stone sling and the board of cancelled marks.

“A prosperous day?”

“I became less certain of several things.”

“Expensive?”

“One fitting. Half a morning. A wet boot.”

“Moderate, then.”

Su Fan told him about the weight.

Tan Wei laughed first at the faulty casing, then at Su Fan's expression when he admitted how pleased he had been.

“You could have kept using it.”

“Until it became light enough for Ah-Du to make the same progress.”

“Then you'd have founded a school.”

They were both smiling when the joke ended.

Su Fan waited for the familiar inward movement that tried to turn a friend's pleasure into proof they had returned to how things used to be.

It came.

He let it pass without asking anything of it.

Tan Wei picked up the punch.

“I have an early shift. Not a shared trial. Ordinary work.”

“You don't need to explain it to me.”

“I know. I wanted to tell you.”

Su Fan nodded.

He handed over the unfinished letter as well.

“There is a sentence missing.”

“Will I recognize the place?”

“It is where the writing stops.”

“A subtle method.”

Tan Wei tucked it into his coat.

After he left, Su Fan returned to the yard.

The light had gone from the lower stones. He could still see enough to put the equipment away. That was not the same as seeing enough to attempt another test.

He loosened the sling and rolled the stone beneath the eaves.

On the board, the invalid measurements remained beside the better observation. The result he wanted had not arrived. The work had nevertheless become more exact, and more difficult to flatter himself about.

He covered the board against the night damp.

Tomorrow's attempt would have to begin there.

***

The river froze at the edges, leaving a narrow black lane through its middle.

Sun Lian steered with both hands on the tiller. She disliked the sound of ice against the hull and disliked people asking whether it was serious even more.

Su Fan trained on the forward deck when she allowed it.

No stamping. No weapon swings near the sail. No striking any part of her boat to discover whether his cultivation had improved.

He hung the iron ring from a short cord and moved it with the back of his fingers.

The task looked easy. Ah-Du had laughed at it before they departed.

The ring had to travel without twisting. Su Fan had to step, turn and move it again while keeping the same circulation through his feet, abdomen and hand. Any unnecessary tension drew it sideways.

For weeks, the error had appeared in the turn.

On the second day upriver, he finally felt where it began.

His left hip locked before he changed direction. The rest of his body had been compensating for it since the crane accident, bracing to keep his damaged ear away from what he could not hear.

He stopped the exercise.

Correcting it would expose that side again.

He looked toward the stern.

“Tell me when the pole moves,” he said.

Sun Lian glanced at him.

“Which pole?”

“The spare, behind me.”

“Why?”

“So I stop pretending I can watch it myself.”

She studied his stance, then nodded.

***

It took the rest of the morning.

Twice his balance failed. Once the ring struck his knuckles hard enough to draw blood. He stopped before exhaustion made the results worthless and returned after eating.

Tan Wei watched for a while.

“Your shoulder,” he said.

“I know.”

“You know after you move it. Try knowing before.”

Su Fan gave him a look.

Tan Wei grinned and went back to the schedule copies.

Late in the afternoon, the circulation passed through the turn without bunching.

The change was small enough that Su Fan almost missed it.

Then the pressure completed a second route beneath the first, joining at the lower abdomen without forcing either aside.

He stood very still.

The ring swung once and settled.

He did not attempt another turn.

He sat down, breathed normally and waited to see whether the new circulation held when he was no longer concentrating on it.

Sun Lian glanced over her shoulder.

“Something broken?”

“No.”

“Good. We cannot afford that today.”

***

At the next landing, he tested it on shore.

A porter had dropped a loaded handcart into a rut and was trying to free it without unloading the jars. Su Fan helped from the rear.

He could have lifted hard enough to impress the man.

Instead he placed one foot, put both hands beneath the frame and let the new route carry a steady force through his body.

The wheel rose.

The porter shoved a board beneath it.

Together they rolled the cart free.

No trembling in Su Fan's legs. No sharp drain after the effort. The fifth stage held under work.

He smiled before he remembered anyone was watching.

The porter offered him a copper.

Su Fan accepted it.

***

That evening he bought four sesame cakes.

Min Yao ate hers while comparing the dates on the district order. Sun Lian examined the copper he had earned and suggested he lift enough carts to pay the boat's debt.

Tan Wei waited until the others were occupied.

“Fifth?”

Su Fan nodded.

His friend broke the last cake in half and handed part back.

“For the extra appetite.”

Across the river, Siltbridge's lamps were appearing one by one.

Su Fan ate his share while the city grew around them: cranes above the warehouses, bells from the evening market, a furnace chimney throwing sparks into the cold.

At the customs pier, two guards waited beside a notice board.

Sun Lian guided the Honest Measure toward them.

The nearer guard looked at her cargo mark and took out a paper already folded to the right place.

chapters.title: The House of Receipts
chapters.text:
The room cost more because it had a window.

Su Fan asked whether the cheaper room had a roof.

The innkeeper looked at him for a moment, then laughed hard enough to disturb the cat sleeping beneath the desk.

“Both have roofs. Only one has daylight.”

“Then why did you show me the expensive one first?”

“Because you looked tired.”

He could not decide whether that was kindness or trade. In Siltbridge, he was learning that the two often occupied the same doorway.

The cheap room had a pallet, a shelf and a wall thin enough to pass a quiet quarrel from the room beside it. Someone had scratched a boat into the plaster. Beneath it another traveller had added legs.

Su Fan set his bundle on the pallet.

The innkeeper waited.

“What?”

“The roof has met your standards?”

“For tonight.”

“Pay for tonight, then.”

He paid. The sum was not ruinous. It was simply more than a night had ever cost when he slept under somebody else's leaking roof and repaid the privilege in work.

Outside, Sun Lian was speaking to a carrier. She held one of her cargo papers flat against a post while he read it. His finger stopped at a line; hers stopped him from turning the page before he had answered.

Su Fan remained by the inn door.

He had offered to help twice already. She had accepted once and declined once. He was trying to make both answers feel equally ordinary.

When the carrier left, she folded the paper.

“Room?”

“Yes.”

“Bed?”

“Of a kind.”

“Lice?”

“I haven't asked their price.”

She smiled.

He wanted to ask where she would sleep. He also knew the question could come out sounding as though he intended to approve the answer.

“Have you found what you need?” he said instead.

“For the night. Not for the work.”

“Anything I can carry?”

“Tomorrow.”

She pointed down the street.

“Eat before you discover another errand.”

***

The eating house had no sign.

It had a window full of steam, three benches and a woman who knew Sun Lian by the way she put her tools down.

“You're late.”

“The river disagreed.”

“The river always disagrees. Sit.”

Su Fan followed her to the end bench. A basket maker moved his unfinished work out of the way. Nobody asked about his sash, his lineage or the scar beside his ear.

For several minutes the absence of those questions felt like freedom.

Then a man at the next table asked him to fetch more broth.

Su Fan looked up.

The man had mistaken him for someone working there.

Sun Lian opened her mouth. Su Fan reached for the empty bowl before she could speak.

The owner took it from him.

“He's eating.”

“I only asked—”

“Ask me. I sell it.”

The man apologized, awkwardly enough to suggest that he had not intended an insult and had not expected to be made aware of one.

Su Fan sat down.

Sun Lian watched him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You had a face.”

“I own several.”

He looked at his bowl.

The first warmth of the city had vanished. He was annoyed with the stranger, then with himself for being annoyed, then with the fact that fetching a bowl could feel like agreeing to a place in the world.

The owner put food before him.

“Eat before you appoint yourself to something.”

Sun Lian laughed.

The broth was sharp with ginger. Under it lay thick noodles and a small portion of fish. He ate too quickly at first, then slowed when he realized no one was about to take the bowl away.

At the other table, the man who had made the mistake was explaining a delivery dispute to his companion. He spoke gently about a sick daughter and harshly about a merchant who had changed the weight of an order.

Su Fan disliked him less.

It did not make the first moment disappear. It merely made the man harder to contain inside it.

***

The basket maker asked whether Duan still worked in the valley.

Su Fan looked at him.

“You know him?”

“Bought hinges from him years ago. Before my second wife. She objected to the cupboard, not the hinges.”

“Both survived?”

“Not together.”

He examined Su Fan's hands.

“Apprentice?”

“Smith's assistant.”

“Then he'll have taught you to charge for the nails people tell you are too small to count.”

Sun Lian leaned back.

“That lesson is continuing.”

The basket maker showed them a broken clasp he had kept in his pocket because every repair shop he passed seemed inconveniently far from the next place he needed to be.

Su Fan turned it over. The pin had worn thin at one side, but the body was sound.

“Replace the pin.”

“The last man said replace the clasp.”

“He may have seen something I haven't.”

“Will you replace the pin?”

“Not here. I haven't the tools.”

The man looked mildly disappointed.

It was a small refusal. Su Fan felt the familiar urge to make it disappear by finding a clever method with whatever lay on the table.

He handed the clasp back.

“The shop near the ferry sells that size. Ask them to show you the replacement before they cut the old one.”

The basket maker accepted the advice.

He did not become offended. He did not decide Su Fan was worthless. He put the clasp away and returned to his meal.

Su Fan wondered how much effort he had spent throughout his life avoiding a catastrophe that often did not occur.

Sun Lian had begun speaking with the owner about a carpenter she needed to find. Their conversation moved through names, debts, favours and the difference between a man who could do good work and a man who would finish it before the season changed.

He listened.

He knew almost none of these people.

That pleased him until he realized it also meant he could not judge them for her.

***

After supper they walked through the covered market.

The cloth awnings held the day's damp. Lamps made small warm islands beneath them. A seller of sugared seeds called to Sun Lian, who refused him without slowing, then stopped six stalls later to buy a much smaller packet of something more expensive.

“What is it?”

“Food.”

“I had gathered.”

“Then your education is advancing.”

She gave him one.

The sweet was sour at the centre and made his jaw ache.

He tried not to show it.

She watched him until he swallowed.

“You can dislike it.”

“I don't dislike it.”

“You look as though it has asked you to marry it.”

He laughed and admitted that he would prefer another kind.

“Then buy another kind.”

He did.

For a little while they stood beneath the same awning eating different sweets. It was a pleasure so ordinary that he might once have hurried past it toward whatever useful errand came next.

Across the lane, a boy tried to persuade a little girl that the wooden tiger in his hand was worth two painted birds. She rejected both his valuation and his description of the tiger.

“It looks like a dog.”

“An old tiger.”

“A sick dog.”

Sun Lian watched with interest.

“She's right about the carving.”

“Would you tell the seller?”

“She is telling him.”

The boy turned the animal around, as though its other side might improve his case.

Su Fan looked at Sun Lian in the lamplight. She was tired. There was a mark on one sleeve where she had rubbed against the landing wall. She was also enjoying herself, independently of whether her work had gone well or he had made the journey easier.

He had known this about people in principle.

It was different to stand beside it without trying to become the cause.

***

Back at the inn, the woman changing the bedding asked him to lift the pallet.

He put down his bundle and did.

Underneath lay a broken hairpin, a coin too worn to read and a strip of paper with a name written on it.

She gathered all three.

“Lost things?”

“Sometimes.”

“What do you do with them?”

“The owner keeps a box.”

“Do people come back?”

“For the valuable things. Occasionally for the important ones.”

She took a clean cloth from her basket and spread it over the pallet frame.

Su Fan held the end while she tied the corners.

The work was quick and practiced. She knew which knots would hold a restless sleeper and which would merely look secure until the first turn of the body.

“Do you do every room?”

“Most.”

“Every day?”

“When occupied.”

He looked at the basket, the wet cloths beneath the clean ones, the cracked skin across her knuckles.

He nearly offered to carry it downstairs.

Instead he asked.

She said yes and told him where to put it.

Downstairs, the innkeeper was adding figures by lamplight. The cat had moved onto the ledger.

“Does it help?”

“It discourages unnecessary arithmetic.”

Su Fan set the basket beside the washroom door.

The innkeeper glanced up.

“Your companion said you're asking about fittings.”

“Some.”

“There is a dealer by the west market who'll sell you a fine specimen and deliver its poorer relatives.”

“Do you know a better one?”

“I know where not to buy. That is a different service.”

Su Fan smiled.

He wrote the warning beside Duan's list, clearly marked as one man's account rather than a proved fact.

The innkeeper noticed.

“Careful fellow.”

“I've been wrong recently.”

“That can be expensive.”

“So can not noticing.”

The cat put one paw across the next column. The innkeeper sighed and moved the ledger instead of the animal.

***

In the room, Su Fan unpacked only what he needed.

He placed his notes on the shelf and the sword where he could reach it without striking the wall. The room's best position put the solid side to his right. He moved the pillow accordingly, then remembered that walls did not make every danger approach conveniently from the left.

He checked the door.

Once was enough.

Outside the window he had not paid for, someone began singing. The sound came through the thin dividing wall, blurred by plaster and distance. He could not locate it properly, but he could hear that the singer was cheerful and not very good.

He found a clean sheet for Duan.

The first lines concerned prices and the broken clasp. Then he wrote about the eating house, the basket maker who remembered the old hinges, and the sour sweet he had pretended to like.

He stopped before turning the letter into a report of his own improvement.

Duan did not need a lesson from the city. He needed useful figures and enough ordinary news to know the person carrying the figures was still a person.

Su Fan sanded the page.

In the next room the quarrel had ended. Somebody was laughing quietly. The singer outside forgot a line and began again from a place that seemed unlikely to help.

Su Fan lay down.

For tonight, the roof met his standards.

***

The paper was a lien notice.

Sun Lian read it with the boat hook braced beneath her arm.

“The delivery was accepted.”

“The payment has been disputed.”

“By the people who haven't paid me.”

The guard looked uncomfortable. It did not prevent him tying a red cord around the tiller.

The Honest Measure could remain at the commercial pier. It could not depart until the account was settled.

Sun Lian put the notice into her coat.

“Touch the hull with that iron hook and I will dispute your teeth.”

The guard changed hooks.

***

They went to the records house the next morning.

It stood behind the bonded warehouses, a square stone building with an ornamental roof and no ornament near the doors. Clerks moved between counters carrying boxes. Porters brought in sealed ledgers and took out bundles of old paper.

Min Yao noticed the bundles first.

Some still had silk ties. One carried an obsolete station seal.

She said nothing until they reached the carrier's counter.

Sun Lian laid down her delivery receipts.

“I need the acceptance record.”

The clerk inspected the seals.

“Under review.”

“The debt against my boat depends on whether this delivery was accepted. You have detained the boat. Produce the record.”

Her voice remained even. People at the next counter looked over.

The clerk fetched a supervisor.

Min Yao stood slightly behind Sun Lian, apparently another impatient customer. Across the room, a woman sorting damaged ledgers looked up once, then returned to her work.

That was their contact.

She had placed a strip of yellow paper beneath the third bundle on her table.

The originals were in the loading gallery.

***

They spent the morning arguing.

By noon Sun Lian had obtained a copy of the acceptance receipt. It carried a mark confirming the brass had been received in good condition forty-three days before the contractor claimed it was defective.

The supervisor refused to release the boat until the accounts office reconciled the dates.

The accounts office would reopen tomorrow.

Min Yao bought lunch for four at the stall opposite the records house.

Her contact joined them carrying a basin of washing.

“Tonight,” the woman said softly. “The disposal wagon comes tonight. They moved the date.”

“Can you certify a copy?” Min Yao asked.

“Of a page I have handled. Not a chest I have never opened.”

Sun Lian put down her chopsticks.

“How long does the wagon stay?”

“Until the last ledger is counted.”

***

They changed the plan together.

No entry through the front office. No attempt to carry a chest through guarded doors. The disposal bundles would pass through the gallery into a covered yard.

Sun Lian knew the loading hatch. She had delivered through it.

Su Fan would enter from the adjoining roof and lift the wooden latch. Tan Wei would identify the records they needed. Min Yao and the copying clerk would work in the rented room across the alley, with Sun Lian watching the yard.

They would return every bundle before the wagon left.

It was still unlawful. The originals were still the contractor's property. Min Yao made certain nobody confused the usefulness of the evidence with permission to take it.

“Anything we copy may be challenged,” she said. “The witness helps. It doesn't make the entry disappear.”

Tan Wei tapped the schedule already in his pocket.

“Leaving lets them destroy the only version they haven't rewritten.”

Su Fan looked at each of them.

Nobody asked him to decide for the group.

***

At dusk, the gallery lamps were extinguished.

Su Fan crossed the adjoining roof on his hands and feet. Frost made the tiles slick. He carried no sword, only a small knife, rope and the padded hook Duan had made for lifting roof panels.

Through the loading hatch he could see the wrapped chests.

He listened with his good ear turned down.

Nothing.

He tested the hatch, felt the latch move and lowered himself into the dark.

Someone at the far end of the gallery struck a flint.

chapters.title: Ordinary Stones
chapters.text:
The practice court charged spectators less than participants.

Su Fan regarded that as evidence of unusually sound judgment.

A painted board listed the fees, the permitted weapons and the injuries for which the proprietor would accept no responsibility. The last section was longer than the first two combined.

He read it twice.

A woman beside the entrance watched him.

“Most people look for the prize.”

“I was looking for what the prize might cost.”

“You'll enjoy the cheap seats.”

Inside, a rectangle of hard-packed earth lay between two low platforms. One side had been spread with sand. The other was bare and slightly damp where the awning leaked. Nobody had corrected the difference.

Two young cultivators were sparring with padded staves.

The taller one moved beautifully. His sleeves barely stirred. Each step ended where it appeared to have been intended before he began it. Pale light followed the staff when he turned.

The shorter one looked as though he had learned to fight while carrying furniture through narrow rooms.

He won.

The tall cultivator stepped into the damp patch, made a small correction, and found the other staff already occupying the space to which his hands needed to return. A shoulder met his chest. He landed sitting down.

The spectators applauded.

Su Fan looked at the uneven ground.

The woman at the entrance saw his expression.

“It isn't a mistake.”

“The floor?”

“We mend holes. We don't promise the world will be level.”

He paid to watch another bout.

***

The shorter fighter returned to the side platform and began repairing a loose tie on his wrist guard.

He was not especially young. Up close, Su Fan could see the lines at the corners of his eyes and a patch of old scar tissue near the ear. He had a working man's hands and a cultivator's careless familiarity with small impossible movements.

The cord slipped.

He swore in an entirely ordinary way.

Su Fan offered to hold the guard.

The man accepted without asking his name.

“Good bout,” Su Fan said.

“Depends which end you watched from.”

“The last one.”

“That was the good end.”

He pulled the tie tight.

“Did you wait for the wet patch?”

“I waited for him to decide the wet patch was beneath his notice.”

The man flexed his wrist.

Su Fan looked back at the court.

“I thought his return was fast enough.”

“It was.”

“Then—”

“He returned to where I wanted him.”

It sounded simple after the fact. Su Fan distrusted that simplicity. He had listened to enough descriptions of repairs to know that the easy sentence usually omitted the broken part.

The fighter seemed to recognize the look.

“Stand up.”

“I haven't paid to participate.”

“Then don't hit me.”

He placed his padded staff across Su Fan's forearms and asked him to push it away.

Su Fan did.

The staff moved easily. Then the fighter changed its angle, and the pressure Su Fan had supplied carried his own elbows outward. Before he could correct them, a thumb touched his ribs.

“Again.”

Su Fan pushed less.

The fighter stepped closer.

The thumb touched the same place.

“Now you're protecting the mistake rather than making it.”

A bell rang at the entrance. The man glanced toward the court.

“That's mine.”

He took back the guard.

Su Fan remained standing with the sensation of the two failures still in his arms.

Neither had required the other man to overpower him.

Neither meant power would not matter if the staff were iron.

***

The proprietor's assistant brought out a different set of practice weapons for the next group.

These were shorter, with weighted ends and padded striking surfaces. A girl carrying the rack told the entrants not to choose by appearance unless they intended to fight somebody equally impressed by it.

One young man chose the largest anyway.

Su Fan watched him turn it in his hands.

The girl looked at Su Fan.

“You want a turn?”

“To choose?”

“To discover something.”

He should have left. He had errands waiting and a limited amount of money set aside for the day.

Instead he asked the price.

The woman at the entrance gave it without lowering her voice for his benefit.

He considered the unfinished repairs in the settlement, the papers in his bag, and the way the tall cultivator had looked at the wet patch after landing in it.

“One round.”

The assistant handed him a plain practice staff.

“Name?”

“Su Fan.”

“School?”

“None.”

She wrote the name and left the other space empty.

No one laughed.

He had prepared himself for that possibility so thoroughly that its absence briefly left him without a useful response.

His opponent was a woman in a faded blue jacket. She tested her staff by pressing one end against the ground.

“Anything I should know?”

“My hearing is poor on the right.”

She nodded.

“Do you want a different position?”

“I want you to know before I fail to answer a call.”

The assistant moved the signal bell where both could see her hand as she rang it.

The woman in blue did not promise to ignore the weakness.

Su Fan respected her more for that than he enjoyed it.

***

He lost the first exchange by treating the padded weapon as though pain were the greatest possible consequence.

The woman struck low. He withdrew his leg, kept his balance, and felt satisfied until the second end of her staff touched his throat.

The assistant called a point.

Su Fan looked at the padding.

A real blade would not have asked him to reconsider.

He reset.

The second exchange lasted longer. He kept his right side closer to the court boundary and watched the woman's shoulders rather than her weapon. His circulation helped him change direction without the old heavy delay.

She noticed.

Her next attack tested the edge of that response rather than repeating what had failed.

He met it and drove her staff aside.

For one instant he had the opening.

Then his own follow-through carried him over the line.

The assistant called the point against him.

“I touched first.”

“You stepped out first.”

The woman in blue had already lowered her weapon.

Su Fan looked down.

His heel was beyond the chalk.

He had read the rules. In the middle of the exchange, he had quietly replaced them with the contest he preferred.

He stepped back into the court.

The last exchange began with no hurry.

The woman moved toward the damp side. He did not follow directly. She tested his reach, drew back, then changed the angle of her hands without changing the distance between them.

He saw the movement.

He misunderstood it.

Her staff caught his below the centre, lifted, and forced him to choose between releasing the weapon and letting his wrist take a bad twist.

He released.

She stopped the padded end short of his face.

The assistant rang the bell.

Su Fan bowed.

The woman returned it.

“That last choice was sensible,” she said.

“Dropping the staff?”

“Keeping the wrist.”

He was still disappointed enough that the praise annoyed him.

Then he flexed the hand he needed for work and understood what she had meant.

***

Outside the court, the shorter fighter was eating a pear.

“How expensive?”

“One round.”

“I meant the lesson.”

Su Fan sat on the low wall.

“I thought the opening mattered more than the line.”

“Sometimes it does.”

“Not here.”

“Not in the thing you agreed to do.”

He took another bite.

Su Fan watched the next pair enter. The woman in blue was speaking with the assistant about a loose fastening on one of the weapons. She had not remained to explain his weaknesses. She had other work.

“What do you do?” he asked the man beside him.

“Besides being admired by strangers?”

“Before you come here.”

“Hauling. Some teaching. Some work I explain differently to different employers.”

“Does the court pay?”

“When I win. Less when I don't.”

“Then why show me the grip?”

The man looked at him.

“Because you held the guard.”

It was a smaller answer than Su Fan had expected.

He found he liked it.

The fighter offered him the pear. Su Fan declined, then asked where the fruit seller stood. The man pointed without turning.

This time Su Fan checked the direction with his eyes before following it.

***

On the street, he bought a small length of cord and sat beneath an awning to repair the tie on his own protective coat.

The coat had seemed less impressive after seeing the woman stop a padded staff at his throat. That did not make it useless. It meant he had to stop asking it to protect things it did not cover.

He worked the cord through the fastening and tested how the cloth shifted when he raised his arms.

Too tight, the shoulder caught.

Too loose, the plate moved away from the place it was meant to guard.

He settled on a position that did neither particularly well and marked it for Sun Lian to examine when she had time.

Across the lane, two children were using a broken hoop as a boundary for a game. One kept stepping outside it, then claiming the hoop had moved.

Su Fan laughed aloud.

The child looked at him angrily.

He raised both hands in surrender.

A seller nearby asked whether he wanted the hoop repaired.

“It isn't mine.”

“That rarely stops people giving advice.”

He put the needle away.

The disappointment from the bout had not vanished. It had become more specific. He had not been defeated because founderless cultivation was secretly worthless, nor because the woman possessed a mystery his method could never meet. He had been defeated in three different exchanges for three different reasons.

That was less comforting than a grand explanation.

It also left him something to practise.

He wrote the reasons down without naming the woman an enemy or himself a fool.

Then he added one more line.

*Released the staff. Wrist sound.*

The sentence looked embarrassingly modest beside his notes on circulation.

He kept it.

***

When he returned to the place where his belongings were stored, he tried the first exchange again without a partner.

The movement worked beautifully.

That proved almost nothing.

He moved a stool into the space his opponent had occupied and discovered that his imagined opening depended on her becoming conveniently narrow. He laughed, shifted the stool back and tried a smaller movement.

A second attempt caught the edge of his coat.

He stopped.

Practice alone could answer some questions. It could also let him choose an opponent who never objected.

He took a scrap of chalk and marked the boundary on the floor.

At the next step his heel crossed it.

He did not erase the line.

From the adjoining room came the noise of someone arguing over a washing fee. Farther away, a cart driver shouted for people to move clear. The city went on spending effort on things no manual thought worth drawing.

Su Fan put the stool back where it belonged.

The next time he entered a court, he would know a little more.

That was not the same as knowing who would win.

***

The first thing Su Fan saw was his own rope.

It lay across the floor beside the hatch. Someone had cut it after he descended.

The second was Captain Shen Tu, standing beneath a lamp with his sword still sheathed.

“You made four written requests,” the captain said. “Then arrived on the carrier whose account you attached to the fourth.”

Su Fan shifted toward the nearest chest.

Shen Tu watched the movement.

“You are difficult to sense. You are not difficult to expect.”

A bolt crossed the room.

Su Fan dropped behind the chest. The shaft struck its lid and drove halfway through the wood.

No qi had announced it. No inherited pressure. Just a crossbowman in the dark.

Su Fan drew his knife.

***

Outside, Sun Lian saw the gallery lamp and gave the agreed signal.

Two taps against the drainpipe.

She waited for an answer.

There was none.

Tan Wei started toward the yard.

Sun Lian caught his arm.

“Front gate first.”

“He's in there.”

“And six men are going through that gate to help keep him there.”

She pointed.

Tan Wei stopped.

Across the alley, Min Yao had already opened the rented room's shutter. The copying clerk stood beside her, pale and furious.

“They knew,” the woman whispered.

“They knew someone might come,” Min Yao said. “We decide what they learn next.”

***

Shen Tu did not enter the narrow aisle between the chests.

He ordered two men to turn over a brazier instead.

Hot ash spread across the floor. Smoke rose through the gallery. Su Fan pulled his sleeve over his mouth and crawled toward the hatch.

A stone hit the floor beside his hand.

Another struck his right shoulder.

He turned too late.

The captain had used no technique. He stood beyond easy reach, throwing pebbles taken from a weighted curtain bag.

Su Fan moved left, placing the chests between them.

Shen Tu advanced to keep his injured ear toward the archers.

It was precise, unpleasant work.

“Give me your hands,” he said. “You will leave with them attached.”

Su Fan glanced up at the roof beams. The smoke was thickening. The archive beneath them held generations of accounts. A spreading fire would kill evidence and possibly clerks asleep in the lower rooms.

He shoved the overturned brazier away from the paper stacks.

Shen Tu moved then.

His palm struck the chest beside Su Fan and broke the corner inward. Wood hit Su Fan across the ribs. His patched coat took the splinters. It did little against the force.

He fell through the gap into the next aisle.

His knife spun out of reach.

The captain drew his sword.

***

Su Fan had prepared for a man who would try to suppress his cultivation.

Shen Tu had prepared for Su Fan.

The difference became clear when the next strike broke the beam he used for cover.

Su Fan caught the falling length of wood and thrust it at the captain's knees. Shen Tu stepped over it, cut twice and forced him back toward the crossbows.

A bolt passed through his coat above the left hip.

He felt the hot line of it after he hit the floor.

He could not win this exchange. Fifth stage, sound steel, no ancestral grip for the captain to seize: none of it supplied the missing distance, speed or years of fighting.

He drove his palm into a loose floorboard.

True Strike split it along the grain.

He tore it up and dropped into the space beneath the gallery.

A blade followed, opening the cloth across his shoulder.

Su Fan crawled through dust and old brick while boots moved above him.

Ahead, a stone partition blocked the passage.

Behind him, someone lowered a lamp into the hole.

Then water began to run under the wall.

chapters.title: The Other Exit
chapters.text:
The paper seller had put the damaged sheets underneath.

Su Fan discovered them while helping to lift the stack from the cart. The top edges were clean, the corners square. Halfway down, damp had turned several sheets the colour of weak tea.

The seller took the stack from him.

“Packing paper.”

“You charged for writing paper.”

“I charged for the bundle.”

Min Yao stood in her doorway with the receipt in one hand.

“The receipt says writing paper.”

“The receipt says paper.”

She held it closer.

The seller looked.

For a moment Su Fan expected him to apologize. Instead he explained that paper came in several useful conditions and that a person who understood the trade would know this.

Min Yao listened without interrupting.

When he finished, she untied the bundle and separated the damaged sheets.

“These can be returned. These can stay.”

“That breaks the bundle.”

“Yes.”

“It changes the price.”

“Show me the price for each.”

The man glanced at the cart driver, who was already looking toward his next delivery.

Su Fan felt the old pleasure of a dispute that seemed simple enough to settle. There was a receipt. There was bad paper. The right answer ought to stand directly between them.

Then the seller said there would be no more paper delivered here until the account was settled.

Min Yao needed the good sheets.

Su Fan could see them through the doorway: jobs laid out on boards, clean spaces waiting for copies, a drying rack with more pegs than pages.

She considered the threat.

“I will pay for what I keep,” she said. “You may choose whether to sell it.”

The seller complained all the way back to his cart.

He took the damp paper.

He also took payment for the rest.

When he had gone, Min Yao shut the door and leaned against it.

Su Fan waited.

“That was irritating,” she said.

“I thought you handled it well.”

“I did. It was still irritating.”

She handed him the smaller stack.

“Inside, please. Before I begin improving my character at its expense.”

***

The shop was arranged around things that must not touch each other.

Wet ink and fresh paper. Grinding pigment and finished copies. A cup of tea and anything valuable. Jin and the tray of sealing wax.

The last separation was proving difficult.

“I am only looking,” the boy said.

“You look with your fingers.”

“They are closer.”

Min Yao moved the tray.

Su Fan set the paper where she showed him and waited for a clear place to put his own packet. The table seemed to consist entirely of other people's unfinished intentions.

A man arrived with a document that needed copying before midday.

He wanted four copies. Then three. Then four again, provided the fourth cost less because the words had already been written three times.

Min Yao named the price.

The man objected to the charge for checking.

“I can see whether the words are there.”

“Then you may pay for copying without checking.”

“Will you guarantee it?”

“No.”

He looked at Su Fan, who found sudden interest in a pot of paste.

The client paid for checking.

When he left, Min Yao put a small mark beside the job.

“What does that mean?”

“That he has changed the requested number twice.”

“So you remember?”

“So I don't trust myself to remember only the version that annoyed me most.”

She pulled a clean sheet toward her.

Su Fan had thought of records as things that made other people accountable. Here they also prevented the person keeping them from quietly making herself right.

***

The document concerned a hire agreement.

Su Fan recognized some of the language. The surface promises were straightforward: work, accommodation, payment at stated intervals. The difficult part began where the agreement described circumstances under which ordinary arrangements could change.

He leaned closer.

Min Yao covered the lower half with a blank sheet.

“This isn't yours.”

“I know.”

“Then read only what you need to move the weights off it.”

He sat back.

The correction was mild. That did not make it pleasant.

“I wasn't going to tell anyone.”

“You weren't asked to know.”

Outside, someone called for the paper seller. The cart rattled away.

Su Fan looked at the packet under his hand. He had carried letters, contracts, private accounts. Their owners had sometimes trusted him to read them and sometimes only to keep them dry. He had not always noticed how easily concern made him feel entitled to cross the difference.

Min Yao removed the covering sheet and went on working.

She did not insist on his confession.

After a while she asked him to hold a ruler steady while she ruled a clean margin. He did. The task was useful and narrow. It did not restore a privilege he had never been given.

Jin watched from the floor.

“Why do you leave so much space?”

“For the person who changes his mind.”

“Does everybody?”

“Enough.”

The boy considered that, then left a large blank patch around the bird he was drawing.

***

A fastening on the drying rack failed while Min Yao was finishing the second copy.

The upper crossbar slipped. Three wet pages folded inward toward one another.

Su Fan caught the bar.

He caught it too hard.

The old joint creaked beneath his grip.

“Don't straighten it,” Min Yao said.

He stopped with his hands already beginning the wrong movement.

She took the lower pages away one at a time. A corner had touched another sheet. The ink transferred in a faint reversed smear.

Jin stood very still.

“It wasn't me.”

“Nobody said it was.”

“I was here, though.”

Min Yao put the salvaged copies flat on a clean board.

“Su Fan, lower the left end. Slowly.”

He did.

The rack settled against the wall without collapsing.

He looked at the joint. A small wooden peg had split along an old line. He could replace it easily. He could not make the wet ink return to the page it belonged to.

“I'll pay for—”

“First help me see what is spoiled.”

They examined each sheet.

One could be used as a checking copy. One would have to be rewritten. The third had escaped with a mark outside the usable area.

Su Fan fetched an offcut from her repair box and shaped a replacement peg. Min Yao checked the fit before allowing the rack to take weight again.

He wanted the repair to cancel the mistake.

It did not.

She worked through the next part of the morning without a break to recover the lost time. He asked whether he could grind ink or trim paper. She gave him both jobs.

The client returned early.

Min Yao told him when the copies would be ready.

He complained.

She did not tell him that a visitor had damaged the rack. She had accepted the work. She would deliver it.

Su Fan respected that and disliked being protected by it.

When the client left, she glanced at him.

“You can stop looking as though I have sentenced you.”

“I made more work.”

“Yes. You are doing some of it.”

“That doesn't—”

“No. It doesn't make everything even. Most mornings don't.”

She returned to the copy.

***

At midday Jin asked whether they were going to eat before the ink ate them.

Min Yao put down her brush.

They moved the finished work to the safest part of the room and laid a board over the table. The meal was bread, vegetables and a little hot soup brought from a neighbouring stall.

Jin gave Su Fan the chipped cup.

“It doesn't leak.”

“Thank you.”

“It did. Mother fixed it.”

Min Yao looked at the boy.

“Changed it. I changed the leaking cup for this one.”

“That is fixing the drinking.”

Su Fan laughed.

The child asked what the quarry settlement looked like.

Su Fan began with the workshop.

Jin wanted to know whether there were dogs.

He began again.

There were dogs, though not all of them agreed about who owned which doorway. There was a goose that behaved as though the disagreement was beneath it. There were children who had found new hiding places around unfinished walls and adults who kept discovering why those places should not be used.

“Does Grandfather know the hiding places?”

“Probably some.”

“Then he will tell.”

“He might ask what books you took there first.”

Min Yao smiled into her soup.

Su Fan did not tell her that the old scholar missed her in a way he did not always know how to say. He had no permission to turn one person's silence into another person's obligation.

Instead he described the paper fish Jin had once made and the care with which fragile drawings were kept.

The boy listened, pleased and embarrassed at once.

Then he asked whether a goose could be taught to carry letters.

“No,” Min Yao said immediately.

“You haven't tried.”

“I have met geese.”

***

After the meal, the hire-agreement client returned with a correction.

He wanted a sentence changed in the copies.

Min Yao put the original beside the requested alteration.

“That changes the obligation.”

“It clarifies it.”

“Then the original must be amended and acknowledged.”

“The other party already agreed.”

“Where?”

The man tapped his own forehead.

She waited.

He grew angry, then embarrassed by how quietly she was refusing him.

Su Fan stood near the repaired rack and said nothing.

The man offered extra payment.

Min Yao told him the price of making a clearly marked proposed amendment.

“That isn't what I asked for.”

“No.”

The client took the copies as originally ordered. He did not thank her. She checked the payment, gave him a receipt and returned to the next job.

Su Fan watched her close the account.

“Will he come back?”

“Perhaps.”

“Will you take his work?”

“Perhaps.”

He had expected a cleaner answer.

She sorted the damaged sheets into a scrap pile.

“If he asks for honest copying, I can do honest copying. If he asks for something else, I can refuse that. I don't have to decide his entire future every time he enters the shop.”

Su Fan thought of the captain, of suppliers, of men whose useful actions did not remove the harm they had done.

He said nothing.

Min Yao looked at the peg he had fitted.

“Will that hold?”

“The rack should. Not a person leaning on it.”

“Jin.”

“I heard.”

The boy had already moved away.

***

Before leaving, Su Fan brought out his packet.

The pages he had permission to show her were placed separately. The sealed letters remained sealed. He explained whose question each document contained and where he did not know the answer.

Min Yao asked him to leave two of the copies for closer reading.

She did not promise a result.

She gave him an account of the copying work he had actually caused, offset by the work he had done and the repaired fastening. One damaged sheet remained on his side of the reckoning.

He paid for it.

The sum was small. The exactness mattered more than the sum.

At the door, Jin offered him the bird drawn inside the large blank space.

“For changing your mind.”

Su Fan took it carefully.

“Thank you.”

The boy looked up at him.

“Not too much. Then the bird won't fit.”

On the street, Su Fan put the drawing between two dry boards in his packet.

There were many things he would have liked to carry back from Siltbridge: an answer no office could evade, a tool that made every repair possible, enough money to let the people he cared for rest without calculating the cost.

For the moment he had paid for a spoiled sheet, repaired a rack, and been given a bird with room around it.

He carried those things without improving their description.

***

Tan Wei could not see through the wall.

He had to trust Sun Lian's description of the yard drains, the map she had made from memory, and Su Fan's repeated complaint that people confused moving water with knowing where it went.

He placed both hands in the inspection basin.

The drainage channel was nearly dry. A thin skin of dirty water ran beneath the gallery toward the river.

Tan Wei sent a pulse through it.

Not enough to break stone. Enough to carry movement around a corner.

He felt the return against his fingers.

Two short interruptions.

Su Fan was there.

***

“Again,” Sun Lian said.

Tan Wei repeated the pulse.

A hand appeared behind the iron grille at the base of the wall.

Su Fan's fingers closed around a bar. Blood darkened the sleeve above them.

The grille had been set into sound stone. Pulling it free would take time they did not have.

Sun Lian looked up.

“Receiving door.”

“It opens into the yard.”

“Yes.”

“Six men.”

“Fewer now.”

From the street came a woman's voice demanding to know why the contractor was burning occupied premises.

Min Yao had found the night watch.

She had also found two nearby warehouse owners, who were less interested in disputed documents than in the smoke rising beside their stock.

The first guard at the yard gate turned to answer them.

Sun Lian moved.

***

She drove a timber wedge into the receiving door's hinge and struck it with the heel of her hand.

Earth qi passed through the wood. The wedge swelled and split the rotten socket around the pin.

The door dropped crookedly.

Tan Wei caught its weight in a sheet of water before it could fall on them.

Inside, Su Fan was trying to stand.

His face had gone grey.

“Roof route closed,” he said.

“We noticed,” Sun Lian replied.

They got his arms over their shoulders.

At the far side of the yard, Shen Tu appeared through the smoke.

He saw the broken door, the night watch at the gate, and Min Yao standing in full view with the copying clerk beside her.

His expression barely changed.

“Three thieves,” he called. “Stop them.”

The nearest watchman hesitated.

Sun Lian shoved the acceptance receipt toward him with her free hand.

“Detained carrier. Injured passenger. And your fire bucket is empty.”

It was not a defence that would survive a hearing.

It bought three breaths.

Tan Wei used them to overturn the inspection basin.

Water rushed across the yard in a low sheet, lifting ash and soot. The watchmen stumbled. A guard reached for Su Fan and caught only his torn coat.

Sun Lian led them into the alley.

***

They left by the river steps, not the boat.

That had been Sun Lian's condition from the beginning: the Honest Measure would not serve as the obvious refuge for anyone chased out of the records house.

A hired skiff waited two streets away. It had cost nearly all their remaining travel money.

Min Yao reached it first with the copying clerk. She had brought the woman's work satchel because leaving it would identify every commission she had handled that day.

Tan Wei lowered Su Fan into the bottom of the skiff.

The woman's breathing was fast and uneven.

“I haven't copied anything,” she said.

“I know,” Min Yao told her.

“I can't go back.”

“I know.”

Sun Lian pushed them off.

Across the water, lanterns gathered around the Honest Measure.

A man cut the red cord from its tiller and replaced it with a heavier chain.

Sun Lian watched until the bend hid the pier.

She did not look at Su Fan.

***

They spent the night in a cooper's shed upriver.

Tan Wei held the lamp while Min Yao cleaned the wound above Su Fan's hip. The bolt had grazed him. The ribs were worse.

When she pressed them, he lost his breath entirely.

Sun Lian sat outside.

He called her name once.

She answered without entering.

“Not tonight.”

chapters.title: What They Had Lost
chapters.text:
Su Fan bought the wrong lantern.

He did not know it was wrong until Sun Lian began laughing.

The seller had assured him that the painted boat was traditional. It had a broad red sail, a cheerful yellow hull and a figure at the stern holding what Su Fan took to be an oar.

“That isn't an oar,” Sun Lian said.

He looked more closely.

It was a spoon.

“The Hungry Ferryman,” she said. “For children who steal food before the festival meal.”

The seller, a woman with ink on both thumbs, folded her arms.

“He asked for a boat.”

“I did.”

“And I sold him a boat.”

“You did.”

Sun Lian laughed again.

Su Fan considered exchanging it. Then a child beside the stall pointed at the lantern with such open longing that he felt embarrassed to have been concerned about owning it.

He kept it.

The child asked the seller for another Hungry Ferryman. The woman produced one from beneath the table, where several respectable river vessels had been hiding a much less respectable fleet.

“I thought it was traditional,” Su Fan said.

“It is,” she replied. “Children have been stealing food for years.”

***

The festival occupied three streets and part of a square.

No one agreed on where the boundaries were. Sellers extended their stalls whenever the crowd thickened. Musicians moved toward whichever doorway gave them the best sound. A man attempting to maintain a clear passage for carts had begun carrying his sign instead of planting it, since people kept putting bowls on its base.

Su Fan followed Sun Lian through the crowd.

At first he tried to listen for her steps. The noise made that useless. He could hear laughter, drums, a child crying and the sharp call of someone selling fried dough, but the sounds seemed to move independently of the people producing them.

Sun Lian looked back.

“Too much?”

“Not too much. Badly arranged.”

She stopped beside a shuttered shop.

“How shall we do this?”

He appreciated the question.

“Stay where I can see you. If you need me to turn, touch my left shoulder.”

“Not the right?”

“I might turn the wrong way.”

“Then the left.”

She demonstrated once, lightly, and waited for him to nod.

It was a small agreement, made without pity. In the crowd it became more useful than any speech about adapting bravely.

They went on.

The lantern swung above his shoulder. Twice its spoon struck him in the ear. He moved the carrying stick to the other hand before Sun Lian could suggest that the ferryman was attempting to feed him.

She suggested it anyway.

***

At a game stall, people were throwing wooden rings over painted posts.

The largest prize was a stuffed animal whose maker seemed uncertain whether it was a tiger or a goat. The smallest was a paper packet of roasted seeds.

Sun Lian examined the posts.

“The near ones lean.”

“The rings are round,” the stall keeper replied.

“That doesn't answer.”

“It is the answer included in the price.”

She paid.

Her first ring caught a post, bounced twice and fell off.

Her second landed neatly over a farther one.

The keeper gave her the seeds.

“What happened to the animal?” Su Fan asked.

“You have to hit the red post.”

“The one leaning away?”

“The one included in the larger price,” the keeper said.

Su Fan took a turn.

He had no intention of using cultivation. The game should have been simple. Distance, weight, release. He had spent months studying all three.

His first ring went too far.

The second struck the ground in front of the post.

Sun Lian ate a seed.

“Your theory?”

“Unreliable equipment.”

“An excellent beginning.”

He missed the third.

A girl no higher than the stall table threw after him and won the uncertain animal. She carried it away by one horn, which settled at least part of the question.

Su Fan looked at Sun Lian.

She held out the packet.

He took a seed.

For once, failure did not cost anyone blood, wages or the right to leave. It cost a little money and made someone he liked laugh.

He found that he could bear it.

***

They stopped near the musicians.

One played a reed instrument while another struck a shallow drum with the patience of a man who had heard this tune more often than the gods intended. The singer knew most of the words. Where memory failed, he supplied confidence.

Sun Lian began singing quietly with him.

Su Fan looked at her.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You keep saying that when your face is busy.”

“I didn't know you sang.”

“I didn't know you bought children's lanterns. We are both learning.”

She continued.

He recognized the tune after a while. It was sung in the valley with different words, some of which would not have suited the children standing near the musicians.

Sun Lian knew those words too.

She did not sing them.

The drummer saw their expressions and grinned.

A woman beside them started clapping off the beat. Her companion tried to correct her. She corrected him by clapping more loudly.

The argument drew enough people that the musicians moved farther into the square.

Su Fan shifted with the crowd and almost lost sight of Sun Lian.

A hand touched his left shoulder.

He turned.

She was there, holding two cups of hot drink.

“Which is mine?”

“The one you take.”

He took the nearer one. It was sweet and smelled faintly of toasted grain.

The Hungry Ferryman watched them with his painted spoon raised.

***

The child who had been crying was now shouting.

Su Fan noticed because the rhythm changed. The noise of the square continued around it, but the child's voice had become hard with panic.

A woman was trying to speak to him. He pushed her hand away.

“Not that way!”

Su Fan moved closer, then stopped outside the small circle that had formed.

The boy's younger sister had disappeared.

Someone said she had gone toward the water. Someone else said the sweet sellers. The boy insisted she had been beside him, as though repeating the last known fact might bring her back to it.

Sun Lian knelt.

“What was she carrying?”

He stared at her.

“Was she carrying anything?”

“A cup.”

“What colour?”

“Blue. She wanted to keep it.”

Sun Lian looked at Su Fan.

“The drink stall.”

He nodded.

They did not run in opposite directions. Sun Lian stayed with the boy while Su Fan went back along the short route they had just taken. At the stall, he asked whether a little girl with a blue cup had returned.

The seller pointed behind him.

She was sitting on an empty crate, carefully holding the cup upright with both hands.

“I spilled it,” she said before Su Fan asked anything.

“Somebody is looking for you.”

“I wanted another.”

The seller had given her water while trying to find out whom she belonged with. She had supplied a brother's name that seemed to apply to half the boys in Siltbridge.

Su Fan crouched.

“May I walk with you to him?”

She looked at his lantern.

“Hungry Ferryman.”

“Yes.”

“You stole food.”

“I bought the wrong boat.”

She considered that distinction and accepted his hand.

When they reached the square, the boy shouted at her so furiously that she began crying. Sun Lian waited until his fear had used up enough breath for him to hear himself.

“She's here,” she said.

He looked at the girl, then at the cup.

The girl offered him a drink.

He took it without knowing what else to do.

They left together, holding each other's sleeves.

Su Fan watched until they were clear of the musicians.

No one called him a hero. The seller returned to his cups. Sun Lian finished her drink.

That seemed right.

***

Later they found a quieter part of the quay.

Lanterns drifted on the water in shallow trays. Some bore names. Others carried wishes, jokes or drawings that only their makers would recognize.

Su Fan had not intended to set his boat afloat. He liked it more now that its dignity had been settled.

Sun Lian leaned against a post.

“When I was learning to fit a keel,” she said, “I once argued with a man for half an afternoon because his line was crooked.”

“Was it?”

“Yes.”

“Then?”

“The line was crooked because the hull was crooked. I had measured from the wrong edge and produced a perfectly straight instruction for making it worse.”

“What did he say?”

“Very little. He made me remove the piece.”

“And fit it again?”

“After I carried it back to the yard and explained why it couldn't be sold as straight stock anymore.”

Su Fan looked at the lanterns.

“That sounds expensive.”

“It was.”

“Did he let you forget?”

“Eventually. I made different mistakes.”

She smiled at a memory that did not require him to improve it.

He told her about the leaking weight.

She laughed, then asked a precise question about how it had been hung.

He answered.

For a few minutes they discussed the experiment as workers. Then a lantern struck the quay below them and turned over, spilling its little flame into the river.

Neither tried to make that mean anything.

***

A man came along selling paper and a brush for wishes.

Sun Lian declined.

Su Fan bought a small strip.

He stood with the brush poised above it for longer than the man considered commercially reasonable.

“Health?” the seller suggested.

Su Fan thought of his hearing, Duan's arm, Sun Lian's tired hands, all the bodies people asked the world to return unchanged.

“Money?” the man offered.

“Does the river prefer one?”

“It has accepted both without complaint.”

Su Fan smiled.

He wrote a line, then crossed it out.

The first wish had been too large to belong to a strip of paper. The second had sounded like an instruction to people who had not asked for one.

Finally he wrote Tan Wei's name and, beneath it, a description of the ridiculous lantern.

“That isn't a wish,” the seller said.

“No.”

“Then it's a letter.”

“Yes.”

“You'll need an envelope.”

Sun Lian began laughing before Su Fan could answer.

He paid for the envelope.

The seller departed in excellent spirits.

***

On the walk back, Sun Lian stopped at a doorway to speak to someone she knew.

Su Fan waited a little way off.

The conversation was about work at first. Then it became private. He could tell by the way the other woman touched Sun Lian's sleeve and lowered her voice.

He did not move closer to hear.

The lantern warmed his hand through its thin paper. Its painted ferryman had acquired a crease along the hull, and one corner of the sail was beginning to curl.

A child passing with his father pointed at it.

“Hungry Ferryman!”

Su Fan inclined the little boat in acknowledgment.

When Sun Lian rejoined him, she looked neither particularly happy nor unhappy.

“Ready?”

“Yes.”

He did not ask her to report the conversation.

At the inn, they separated to their own arrangements.

Su Fan set the lantern where it would not scorch the shelf and finished the letter to Tan Wei. He wrote about the ring game, the missing child, the singer who lost his words and the seller who transformed a wish into a postage expense.

Only at the end did he mention the work.

Then he put the brush down.

For one evening, life had supplied enough to write about without demanding that he justify why any of it mattered.

***

Su Fan woke when somebody moved the lamp to his left.

For an instant he thought he was back beneath the gallery.

He reached for the knife that was no longer at his belt.

Tan Wei caught his wrist.

“Here. Cooper's shed. This morning.”

The words sounded familiar in a way Su Fan disliked.

He let his hand open.

***

They counted the cost after breakfast.

One boat seized. One copying clerk unable to return to her employment. Three people accused of unauthorized entry. A torn coat, a lost knife, cracked ribs and a wound that would make ordinary work difficult for weeks.

No original charter.

No uncoupling diagram.

The acceptance receipt remained useful, but it would not free the Honest Measure until a hearing. The contractor now had grounds to argue the vessel had facilitated a crime.

Su Fan looked at Sun Lian.

“I'll repay—”

“Don't finish that sentence.”

He stopped.

She set a broken buckle on the table. It had come from the boat's spare harness, the one she had taken for their luggage.

“You cannot repay a boat with three strings of copper and a promise to work yourself dead.”

“I know.”

“No. You say that when you mean you haven't found the way yet.”

He had no answer.

Min Yao drew a line through their remaining travel budget.

“We need transport home. And a room for her until she decides where to go.”

The copying clerk was named Zhen Su. Until that morning, Su Fan had known her only by her function in their plan.

He looked at her properly.

She had two children staying with an older sister. She could write three hands, calculate freight faster than Min Yao and had been paid irregularly for months before they arrived.

She had taken their money because she needed it.

That did not make her less brave. It made the cost less abstract.

***

Sun Lian went back to the city with Min Yao.

They did not hide. They filed separate statements with the municipal watch and lodged the acceptance receipt with an independent registrar.

The watch would investigate the smoke, the assault and the entry. It would not promise an outcome.

The boat would remain detained.

Min Yao deposited a bond for their appearance. It consumed the emergency money Duan had lent them.

When they returned, Su Fan was standing beside the shed with his hand pressed against his ribs.

Tan Wei stood several paces away, looking furious.

“He tried to practise.”

“I was checking whether I could travel.”

“You were checking whether pain had begun respecting you.”

Sun Lian walked past them into the shed.

A moment later she came out with Su Fan's sword.

“I'll keep this until we reach home.”

He looked at the wrapped blade.

Then he nodded.

***

They returned on a grain barge.

Sun Lian paid her passage by helping with a damaged steering brace. Tan Wei worked the lines. Min Yao wrote statements for passengers who needed letters carried home.

Su Fan lay beneath a blanket and hated every hour of it.

He could see work that needed doing. He could hear strain in the barge's timbers. He could do almost nothing useful without making the injury worse.

At dusk Zhen Su sat beside him.

“I chose to help,” she said.

“That doesn't make what happened acceptable.”

“No. But don't take my choice away because it ended badly.”

He looked at her.

She was sorting the contents of her work satchel into dry and damp piles.

“You're all very concerned about who owns people,” she said. “Try letting them own their mistakes as well.”

She returned to the papers.

Su Fan watched the river slide past the low gunwale.

When Tan Wei asked him to hold a loose end of rope, he did that and nothing more.

chapters.title: The Duplicate
chapters.text:
The first maker promised that his valve would solve their difficulty before Sun Lian had finished describing it.

The second asked what the difficulty was.

They stayed with the second.

His shop occupied the space behind a public mill. Everything in it carried a fine coating of flour, including a sign asking customers not to touch the finished work with dirty hands. A girl sat at a desk near the door, recording orders while the mill shook the ink in her cup.

The maker listened to Sun Lian, then looked at Su Fan's drawing.

“This is a copy.”

“Yes.”

“Of what you saw, or what somebody told you was there?”

“Both. Marked separately.”

He leaned closer.

For the first time since they entered, his expression changed from politeness to interest.

“Who corrected that channel?”

“She did.”

Sun Lian pointed to the place.

“The first drawing put the branch behind the housing. It isn't.”

The maker nodded.

“A good correction.”

Su Fan had once hoped to produce a drawing so accurate that no one would need to correct it. Now he was beginning to suspect that the visible corrections were among its most useful parts.

The maker read the notes twice.

Then he pushed the paper back.

“I can't promise you a valve.”

The girl at the desk looked up.

“You usually promise them an invoice first.”

“This one may require both.”

***

He took them into the mill.

A wooden wheel turned behind a screen. Its motion passed through a set of gears to the grinding stones. At one corner, a small metal housing clicked every few turns.

The maker stopped beside it.

“Listen.”

Su Fan moved so his left ear faced the mechanism.

The click came again.

“Loose tooth?” he asked.

“Not there.”

“Load change.”

The maker nodded.

He asked the miller to alter the feed. Grain fell more slowly. The sound changed.

The little housing did not govern the whole machine. It dealt with one consequence of the work, under a narrow range of conditions. Outside that range, the miller had to stop and adjust it.

“It doesn't know what the mill is for,” the maker said. “It knows what reaches it.”

Sun Lian folded her arms.

“Our difficulty is what reaches it from more than one direction.”

“Yes.”

“And a load that changes because the people carrying it change.”

“Yes.”

The simplicity of his answers was less reassuring than the first seller's confident explanation. It was also more useful.

He removed a cover from the housing.

Inside, polished surfaces met worn ones. One spring had been replaced recently. A second was old enough to have lost its shine.

“Why not replace both?” Su Fan asked.

“The old one still behaves as expected.”

“And the new one?”

“We're learning.”

The miller, standing behind them, made a dissatisfied noise.

“We're paying.”

The maker accepted the correction.

***

At the workbench, they compared three samples.

One moved smoothly under Su Fan's hand. The second caught halfway. The third felt almost too loose to serve any purpose.

He chose the first as the best.

The maker put all three in a shallow frame and applied pressure from the opposite side.

The first jammed.

The second moved.

The third struck its stop hard enough to make the girl at the desk look up.

“Which is best now?” the maker asked.

“For what?”

The man smiled.

Sun Lian sat on the nearest stool.

“Now we can discuss an order.”

They did not order the successful sample. Its range was too narrow, and the material would not tolerate the conditions described in the drawing. They discussed what could be tested in a smaller frame and what would remain unknown until the actual structure was surveyed.

Su Fan wrote while the two makers argued.

At first he tried to make every sentence fit into a neat column. Soon the page filled with arrows, crossed-out dimensions and questions whose answers depended on other answers.

He started a second sheet.

The girl brought him a board to lean on.

“You're making it look easy,” she said.

“I am?”

“On paper. Wait until they want the price.”

The price came.

Sun Lian asked what was included.

The maker named the materials, the shaping, one revision after the first test, and no promise that the test would justify building anything larger.

“And if it fails?”

“You will own a failed test.”

“Useful failure?”

“If you ask a useful question.”

She looked at Su Fan.

He understood why she had brought him. Not to approve her purchase. To be responsible for the question he kept insisting needed an answer.

***

They ate beside the mill while the maker prepared a small demonstration.

The girl brought them a pot of tea and asked whether the valley was truly rebuilding above the old quarry.

“Yes,” Su Fan said.

“Is the ground sound?”

“Some of it.”

“That sounds like an expensive answer.”

Sun Lian laughed.

“What are you studying?” she asked.

“Accounts.”

“By choice?”

“Partly. I like knowing when someone has mistaken being busy for making money.”

She nodded toward the workshop.

Her father pretended not to hear.

Su Fan looked at the order books. The columns contained ordinary hopes in a form he understood: a promised delivery, an unpaid balance, materials that had arrived and materials still expected.

“How many customers want a guarantee?” he asked.

“All of them.”

“How many get one?”

“For the part being the shape we agreed? Most. For the world remaining the shape they described? Fewer.”

She took away the empty cups.

The mill continued turning.

Outside, a carrier shouted that someone had left a cart blocking the grain entrance. Inside, a man who could explain a complicated pressure return could not find the little hammer he had put down moments earlier.

Sun Lian found it beneath his drawing.

He thanked her without embarrassment.

***

The demonstration used no spirit stone.

Su Fan noticed that first.

The maker had arranged two containers at different heights, a length of ordinary tube and a small weighted shutter. The object was not to imitate the river. It was to expose a mistaken assumption before the mistake became expensive enough to drown someone.

The first release went smoothly.

The second made the shutter chatter.

On the third, Sun Lian changed the angle of the return tube. Water struck the frame and splashed across the bench.

The maker reached for a cloth.

“Good.”

The girl at the desk said, “Not for the floor.”

He handed her the cloth and took another.

Su Fan examined the wet mark.

He had expected a steady opposing force. Instead the return came in pulses, each changing the next movement.

The drawing had hidden that.

He could imagine a person trying to answer those pulses with breath and posture. He could also imagine a device that behaved well in a model because nobody had asked it to endure the irregularity of actual work.

Sun Lian put one finger on the shutter's edge.

“Could this be made to stop here rather than rebound?”

“Perhaps.”

“What would carry the next pulse?”

The maker looked at the frame.

“That is the question.”

They changed the stop.

The shutter ceased chattering. A joint farther back began to leak.

Su Fan watched the water gather.

The problem had moved.

It had not disappeared.

***

For a moment he wanted to take hold of the frame and steady it with his own circulation.

He knew he could remove some of the vibration. He could feel where the movement accumulated. A small correction through his hands might let the demonstration continue long enough to observe the rest.

Then he imagined the maker recording a successful test without knowing what had made it successful.

“Stop,” he said.

Sun Lian looked up.

He explained.

The maker took his hands away from the frame.

“Would you be doing that in the finished structure?”

“I don't know.”

“Then don't do it invisibly here.”

Su Fan stepped back.

They reset the apparatus without his help.

The same joint leaked.

It was an ugly, consistent result.

The maker marked it.
