Afterward he allowed Su Fan to steady the frame while the girl recorded that a practitioner was supplying additional support. The leakage changed. The shutter's movement changed as well. Neither result could be compared cleanly with the earlier one until they accounted for the added force.

Su Fan had wanted his method to make the world simpler.

It kept making his responsibilities more exact.

***


The first seller was waiting near the mill entrance when they came out.

He had improved his offer.

The price was lower, the delivery earlier, and the guarantee now written on a narrow slip with an impressive red seal.

Sun Lian read it.

“What does the guarantee cover?”

“Failure.”

“Of the valve?”

“Of course.”

“Not the installation.”

“That isn't our work.”

“Not damage caused while replacing it.”

“That depends on the installer.”

“Not the people depending on it.”

The seller spread his hands.

“We cannot insure every use.”

“No,” she said. “You cannot.”

She handed back the slip without accusing him of anything he had not actually promised. The guarantee covered replacement of a failed object. It did not transform uncertainty into safety. Once Su Fan saw that, the first man's confidence became less mysterious and less useful.

The seller lowered his voice.

“The other maker will charge you for telling you he doesn't know.”

“He told us which things he doesn't know,” Sun Lian said.

“That is a comfortable trade.”

“So is selling the answer before hearing the question.”

They walked on.

Su Fan expected her to be angry. She seemed mostly tired.

“He may have a good valve,” he said.

“He may.”

“Then why not buy a sample?”

“Because today we needed to learn what a sample would have to survive. Tomorrow's purchase can be tomorrow's argument.”

At the next corner she stopped to examine a split in her glove. It had opened while they were moving the test frame. Su Fan offered her the needle from his tool roll.

She accepted it, sat on a low step and repaired the glove herself.

He stood beside her holding the papers out of the damp.

The distinction seemed worth keeping: another person's help could be useful without turning the work into his.


They left without a miraculous component.

They carried a written estimate, a small drawing of the demonstration frame, and a list of measurements that would be needed before the maker would consider a larger design.

Sun Lian seemed satisfied.

Su Fan was not.

“We spent most of the afternoon proving that the first idea wasn't enough.”

“Yes.”

“We could have known that in the valley.”

“Did we?”

He looked at the papers.

“No.”

“Then the afternoon did something.”

They stopped beneath a bridge while a cart passed overhead. The timbers shook. Dust fell into the water.

Su Fan looked up at the joints.

The bridge had been strengthened in three different periods by people who had used different methods and left different weaknesses. It remained standing. That did not mean any single repair explained why.

Sun Lian followed his gaze.

“Don't start.”

“I wasn't going to climb it.”

“You had the face.”

He smiled.

She took the estimate from him and folded it along the marks the girl had made.

“We will have to decide what we can afford to test.”

“And what we can't afford not to?”

“Also what we don't yet know how to test. Don't leave that one out because it makes the other two less impressive.”

The river passed beneath them, carrying flour dust, leaves and the reflected light from windows.

***

At their lodgings, Su Fan copied the maker's questions.

He did not copy the answers more confidently than they had been given.

The unstable return remained unstable. The old drawings remained incomplete. A model could show a failure without proving the safety of an alternative. A person supplying hidden support could make a bad idea look better than it was.

He drew a box around that last point.

Then he added a practical instruction beneath it.

*Record every hand on the frame.*

It was less grand than naming a technique.

It might save someone from trusting the wrong result.

Before putting the papers away, he wrote to Duan about the three samples. He described why the smoothest one had jammed and why the ugly one had moved under the opposite load.

At the bottom he added that the maker's daughter understood the accounts better than either visitor and had charged them for the spilled tea only after deciding whose fault it was.

He could imagine Duan's answer.

Probably a question about the invoice.

Su Fan put that beside the letter so there would be no need to invent it later.

***

Zhen Su found the diagram on the fourth day home.

It was inside her work satchel, folded around a packet of damaged receipt slips. She had used it to keep the smaller papers together because one side was blank.

She brought it to Min Yao without ceremony.

“This seal belongs to your river.”

Min Yao opened it on the table.

The drawing showed nine stations, their connecting returns and a tenth line running west beneath an older seal.

Su Fan recognized the turn beside the Sealed Stack.

Sun Lian recognized the missing dimensions.

Neither spoke until Zhen Su finished explaining where the page had come from.

A copying commission six months earlier. The contractor had wanted a clean version for its engineer. This sheet had been rejected because the ink bled through at the bottom. She had kept it as waste paper, as the office allowed.

“Can you swear to that?” Min Yao asked.

“Yes.”

“Can you identify the engineer?”

“Yes.”

Sun Lian leaned over the table.

“The west line has no return conductor.”

“Because it isn't a station,” Su Fan said.

“It is a drain.”

***

They took the page to Jiang.

Su Fan walked slowly. Mother Wei had forbidden him to lift anything heavier than a kettle, and had made the order clear enough for Tan Wei to repeat it whenever necessary.

Jiang studied the drawing beside the older map recovered from the Stack.

The two matched at the bend. The new dimensions supplied what the ancient survey omitted: the depth of the outflow chamber and the position of an isolation collar above the ninth return.

“A manual bypass,” she said.

Sun Lian nodded.

“Not enough to drain the high lake. Enough to take the lower return out of service while we separate the active branch.”

“How long?”

“We need measurements.”

“Condition?”

“We need access.”

“Authority?”

Nobody answered immediately.

Jiang put the papers down.

“These are not the same question. Stop treating a good answer to the first as an answer to the last.”

***

The village meeting took place two evenings later.

Sun Lian explained the proposed inspection. No promises of a miracle gate. No claim that ancient masonry would survive because it had survived this long.

They would clear the upper approach, take levels and examine the sealed chamber before considering a flow test.

The work needed labour, timber and money.

Auntie Lu asked whether the settlement would lose drinking water during the survey.

No.

The widow asked who owned the western marsh.

Two farms, one abandoned holding and a disputed common.

Bao Shun asked whether men with damaged hands could work on the fittings above ground.

Yes.

Tan Wei asked what happened if the bypass worked but the elder still refused an uncoupling window.

Sun Lian folded her drawing.

“Then we will have a working bypass and another decision.”

The meeting approved the survey, not the opening.

Su Fan voted with everyone else.

***

Afterward, he found Sun Lian outside the workshop.

“I should have taken the written requests more seriously,” he said. “They told him where we would be. I thought getting past the lock was the hard part.”

She nodded.

It was not forgiveness. It was agreement.

“I cannot promise you a new boat.”

“No.”

“I can keep an account of what I owe.”

“So can I.”

She handed him the first survey measurements.

“Check these. Sitting down.”

Su Fan took the paper.

Through the window he could see Duan showing Zhen Su's older child how to square a block of wood. The family had arrived that afternoon. There was no room ready for them yet. Auntie Lu had already begun arguing about beds.

Su Fan sat beneath the lamp and checked the figures one at a time.

chapters.title: Beneath the Thaw
chapters.text:
The survey began with a cabbage.

Sun Lian wanted a stake driven beside the lower wall. The man who owned the patch wanted to know why the stake had to occupy the only cabbage that had survived the last frost.

“Not through it,” she said. “Beside it.”

“Beside it has roots.”

“So does the wall.”

“The wall isn't my supper.”

Su Fan held the stake while they argued.

He had expected the difficult part to be the old stone, the water below it, the uncertain drawings. Instead they were standing in a narrow strip of soil between a damaged house and a path, discussing a plant whose outer leaves had been eaten by something with very little respect for property.

The owner looked at him.

“You're the one from the smithy.”

“Yes.”

“You moved my stove.”

“With two other men.”

“You may remember it was heavy.”

“I do.”

“Then remember I cooked on it. Things can be small on your drawing and still be where somebody lives.”

Sun Lian took the stake from Su Fan.

“Show me where you would allow it.”

The man pointed to a patch near the corner.

She measured from the proposed place, checked the line of sight and shifted one of the other markers.

“That works.”

He looked suspicious.

“Then why didn't you choose it first?”

“Because I hadn't asked you yet.”

The answer pleased him less than it should have. He continued watching until the stake was in.

When they left, he gave them a cabbage leaf for the goose.

“Payment?” Su Fan asked.

“Removal of waste.”

Sun Lian put it in the cart anyway.

***

They carried the instruments in a borrowed handcart.

Some belonged to the survey office. Some had been made at the workshop. The difference mattered when something was lost, but less when all of it had to be kept out of the mud.

Su Fan checked the lashings twice.

Sun Lian noticed.

“It isn't a river crossing.”

“It has wheels.”

“A convincing distinction.”

The road descended toward the older structures. New repairs stood beside old ones without agreeing on the direction of the ground. A step that had once met a doorway now led into the lower part of a wall. In one place a channel crossed beneath the path and emerged at an angle no current builder would have chosen.

They stopped there.

Su Fan unfolded the copied drawing.

The line on the page was straight.

The visible channel was not.

“Bad copy?”

“Perhaps.”

“Ground movement?”

“Perhaps.”

“Someone altered it.”

“Perhaps.”

He looked at her.

She smiled without much pleasure.

“We can collect possibilities all morning. Measure what is here.”

They did.

The channel's current position could be recorded. Its depth could be estimated only as far as the accessible opening allowed. Beyond that, the water disappeared under stone.

Su Fan wrote *unknown* beside the covered stretch.

It looked like an omission.

He was learning to leave it visible.

***

At the next marker, two assistants had obtained different readings.

The older one wanted to repeat the younger one's work for him. The younger one insisted he had checked twice.

Sun Lian asked when each measurement had been taken.

“Before the shift change.”

“After.”

She looked toward the works.

The water level had altered.

The two measurements did not disagree about the same thing. They described different conditions.

Su Fan had been ready to inspect the younger man's instrument.

He closed the case again.

They added the times to the record and took a third reading under the present load. The result fell between the first two.

The older assistant grunted.

The younger one tried not to look pleased.

“You may still have made an error,” Sun Lian told him.

“I didn't.”

“You may have. Keep that possibility available. It costs less than defending every mark.”

The older man looked at her.

“That advice has an age limit?”

“No.”

Su Fan bent over his own notes to hide a smile.

***

The difficult passage lay beneath a low roof of old stone.

They did not enter it.

The opening was wide enough for a person who wanted badly enough to fit. That was not a useful measure of whether a person should go through.

Sun Lian knelt outside and examined the visible joints.

Su Fan held the lamp where she asked.

From within came the sound of water striking something hollow, then returning through a narrower space. On his damaged side the noise seemed to spread everywhere at once. He turned his head slowly until the stronger ear gave him a more reliable direction.

“What can you hear?” she asked.

He described it, then added what he could not tell.

She nodded.

The younger assistant leaned forward.

“I could crawl as far as—”

“No,” Sun Lian said.

“Only to look.”

“Then we need a way to look without making you part of the obstruction.”

They used a small mirror on a pole. The first angle showed nothing but reflected lamplight. The second revealed an edge of iron and a dark gap beyond it.

Su Fan moved the lamp.

The iron was not where the old drawing placed it.

That might mean the drawing was wrong. It might mean they were looking at a different fitting. It might mean the visible piece belonged to an alteration nobody had recorded.

He wanted it to be the useful answer.

Sun Lian wanted another view.

They obtained it by moving the mirror, not the stone.

The second view made the first less clear.

The younger assistant sighed.

“Worse?”

“More honest,” Su Fan said.

Then he regretted making it sound like a lesson.

“It could still be useful,” he added.

Sun Lian kept working.

***

At midday the farmer from the cabbage patch came down with a covered pot.

He claimed his wife had made too much.

The pot contained enough for four people who had been working and one person who intended to watch them admit they were hungry.

They ate on a dry section of wall.

The farmer asked whether the old channel could be reopened.

Sun Lian answered carefully.

“Some part may be usable. We haven't established where the rest carries water.”

“Could it take water away from the lower road?”

“Possibly.”

“Could it put water under my house?”

“Possibly.”

He looked at the pot.

“Then I prefer the cabbage argument.”

Su Fan laughed.

The farmer did not.

His house had survived damage that took neighbouring rooms. He had repaired one wall with stone borrowed from a boundary that no longer mattered in the same way. The old channel, if altered, could make that repair useless.

“You people say away,” he said. “Away always belongs to somebody farther down.”

Sun Lian set down her bowl.

“We need the downstream part on the drawing before anyone opens anything.”

“Will the people deciding read that part?”

She did not promise they would.

She told him who would receive the survey and which pages would be copied for the settlement.

He listened.

Then he asked for his house to be marked by the name of the lane, not by his own name.

“Why?”

“People forget names. The lane is where the water goes.”

Su Fan wrote it that way.

***


Before leaving the wall, the farmer asked whether they wanted to see the earlier marks.

Su Fan put down his bowl.

“Earlier?”

“Men came through when the upper path was repaired. They left stakes for a season.”

“Where are they?”

“In people's stoves, mostly.”

The older assistant made an impatient sound.

“They should have been left.”

“Then somebody should have said whose wood they were, and how long mostly hungry people were expected to admire them.”

The farmer took them to a corner behind his house. One stake remained, not because anyone had understood its importance but because a climbing bean had grown around it and made removal inconvenient.

Sun Lian inspected the top.

The mark was damaged. They could not use it as a trustworthy reference.

Su Fan felt a brief, disproportionate anger at the missing stakes. Then he looked at the repaired wall, the narrow patch of food, the pot whose contents the farmer had brought to strangers.

The old survey had left useful things without leaving a usable explanation.

They recorded the remaining stake's location and condition rather than pretend it restored the earlier measurements.

The farmer watched Sun Lian write.

“Will yours stay?”

“We'll identify them.”

“People will still burn them if it gets cold enough.”

“Then we'll keep references that don't all depend on loose wood.”

He considered that.

“Good.”

It was not praise for cleverness. It was approval of a plan that had finally made room for the people who would encounter it after the planners went home.

On the way back to the pot, Su Fan asked whether the bean had survived.

“No,” the farmer said. “Bad soil there.”

“Then why leave the stake?”

The man shrugged.

“Habit.”

Su Fan looked once more at the remnant of an official measurement preserved by an unsuccessful bean.

He added that to no report.


The afternoon turned colder.

The assistants began packing the instruments before Sun Lian had finished the last observation. She stopped them and asked which readings could no longer be trusted because their fingers had gone numb.

Neither wanted to answer.

Su Fan looked at his own hand. He had been gripping the lamp handle hard enough to make the knuckles ache.

He put it down.

“We should check the last two.”

The younger assistant looked relieved. The older one looked irritated at being relieved.

They repeated the readings.

One changed.

Not much. Enough that using the first figure to set a fitted part would have created a problem nobody could see until the part arrived.

Sun Lian crossed it out with a single line, leaving the original legible.

Su Fan had once admired clean records. He still did, but he no longer thought cleanliness meant concealing the path by which the figures became trustworthy.

While they worked, the younger assistant found a carved mark on a loose stone.

“Here.”

Everyone turned.

The mark looked old until the lamp came closer. Its grooves were fresh beneath the dirt.

A child on the upper path called down.

“That's mine.”

“What is it?”

“A horse.”

They examined it again.

The stone became a horse with some difficulty.

The farmer, who had not yet left, said it was a better horse than the one that had carried the survey office's last notice.

The child looked pleased.

Su Fan put the stone back where it had been.

No ancient answer emerged from it.

The afternoon improved a little.

***

At the cart, they divided the wet tools from the paper.

The cabbage leaf had suffered in transit. Sun Lian held it up.

“Your promised cargo.”

“The goose won't mind.”

“The goose minds everything.”

They wrapped it separately.

Su Fan checked the list of observations. He had expected the day's work to make the proposed route clearer. It had, in some places. In others it had revealed that clarity had been imagined rather than measured.

He showed Sun Lian the page containing the old drawing and their new marks.

“We have more questions than we began with.”

“We have fewer places where a question is pretending to be an answer.”

She watched his face.

“That was a saying. You may dislike it.”

“I was going to ask whether you charge for them.”

“Only when they save material.”

They started uphill.

The cart caught in a rut. Su Fan took more of its weight through his arms. The circulation steadied him, but the wheel remained caught.

Sun Lian told him to stop pulling.

She moved a stone, changed the wheel's angle, and let the cart roll free.

He could have forced it. He might even have succeeded without breaking anything.

The easier method still required someone else to see it.

***

Back at the workshop, Su Fan laid the papers out to dry.

Duan examined the drawing without touching the wet edges.

“Which part can I make?”

“None yet.”

The smith nodded.

“An improvement over making the wrong part twice.”

He studied the visible fitting beneath the low roof.

“That might not be a valve.”

“What might it be?”

“A fastening. A guide. A piece left from something removed.”

Su Fan added the possibilities to the margin.

Duan frowned.

“Don't list them as though I saw more than your drawing.”

He amended the note.

Later, when the instruments were clean and the borrowed cart returned, Su Fan copied the survey for the people who would have to live beside the proposed work.

He marked the cabbage patch.

He marked the house below the channel.

He marked the places where nobody had yet looked.

The blank stretches were still blank.

This time they had reasons written beside them.

***

The first thaw exposed a roof in the old riverbed.

For two days, people on the high road believed it belonged to a house. Then the water fell farther and revealed a row of pale curves beneath the broken tiles.

Ribs.

Each was taller than a cart.

Sun Lian took the survey crew down at low water. Su Fan went with them, carrying a measuring line rather than a hammer. His ribs had knit, but Mother Wei had insisted that pain after exertion still counted as pain.

The creature lay beneath what had once been a small river shrine. Its skull pointed upstream. Stone had grown through the empty eye sockets.

Ah-Du stepped into the open jaws.

“Don't,” Sun Lian said.

“It's dead.”

“So are most of the bridges that fall on people.”

He stepped out.

***

The exposed bones made a useful landmark.

They also explained why the old survey curved west instead of taking the shortest route. The builders had laid their channel around the buried skeleton rather than cut through it.

Su Fan ran his hand over a rib. The surface was smooth and faintly warm despite the cold water.

“Dragon?” Ah-Du asked.

“Something with teeth,” Sun Lian said. “Write down what we can measure.”

They worked until the tide began to turn.

The first eel came out of the skull.

It looked like a strip of glass pulled through muddy water. Su Fan saw the stones beneath it, then the stones vanished behind a mouth full of hair-thin teeth.

It struck the end of the measuring pole and bit through the wood.

Ah-Du jumped backward.

“Up the bank,” Su Fan said.

Three more shapes moved among the ribs.

***

The eels did not care about lineage.

They hunted warmth, following the crew's legs through the shallow water. Su Fan drew his sword and cut at the nearest head.

The blade struck a rib.

The eel was already past him.

A burning line opened across his calf.

He turned, too quickly on the soft mud, and felt the old injury in his chest complain.

Sun Lian slammed her pole into the ground. Earth rose in a low ridge between Ah-Du and the water.

“One side!” she called. “Get them all on one side.”

Su Fan backed toward the skeleton. The bones narrowed the approach. He watched the mud instead of the transparent bodies.

A ripple lifted against the current.

He thrust downward.

This time the sword caught flesh. The eel twisted around the blade, its body becoming visible where blood filled it.

The second came over the first.

Su Fan stepped into it and used the flat of the sword with a short, clean release.

True Strike snapped it against the stone.

The force jarred his wrist. He had used too much.

Behind him, Sun Lian hauled the last worker over the bank.

“Now!”

Su Fan climbed after them.

An eel hit the mud wall hard enough to leave a long wet dent.

***

They returned the next day with baskets, long hooks and a fisherman who knew the animals.

The fisherman called them lantern eels. He said the flesh was unpleasant but the bladders fetched good money from lamp-makers.

“Why are they here?” Su Fan asked.

“Warm bones. Small fish. People who put their feet in.”

The answer was sufficient.

By noon they had caught six and driven the rest farther upstream. The survey resumed.

Ah-Du found an old mason's mark beneath the shrine foundation: a crooked boot beside three dots.

He copied it carefully.

Later, when Sun Lian checked his notes, she found he had also drawn himself standing inside the creature's jaws.

He had made the teeth larger.

She left the drawing in the survey book.

chapters.title: Inspector Wen
chapters.text:
Su Fan's first account was too good.

He realized it when Duan asked him where he had been standing.

“Beside the frame.”

“Which side?”

“The side nearest the return.”

“Then you couldn't see the far fastening.”

“I saw it afterward.”

“That isn't what you said.”

Su Fan looked at the page.

He had not invented an event. He had arranged the events into a shape that made his part easier to understand. The result was smoother than the morning had been and less true.

He crossed out the sentence.

Duan sat on the stool with his injured arm supported against his body. He had agreed to listen while Su Fan prepared a statement, provided the listening did not become a substitute for finishing the customers' work.

They had already stopped twice to answer the door.

Now a pot mender waited outside with a borrowed tool.

Su Fan put the paper aside.

Duan watched him go.

The delay was irritating. It was also useful. When Su Fan returned, the sentence he had wanted to defend looked less important than the difference between seeing something fail and being told afterward why it failed.

He rewrote the paragraph.

This time it contained a gap.

***

The people asked to give accounts did not arrive in a useful order.

A worker came before his shift. Another after, half asleep and smelling of wet wool. A woman brought her small son because no one could watch him. A porter had left his spectacles at the works and could not read the copy put before him.

The collecting clerk wanted names first.

The people wanted to know whether they would be paid for the time.

Nobody had told the clerk.

Su Fan could see the morning preparing to become another argument in which each person defended the only part they had been given.

He fetched stools.

The clerk said that was not necessary.

The woman with the child sat before he finished speaking.

Duan asked the clerk to put the unanswered question at the top of his notes.

“Which one?”

“Whether these people lose wages by telling you what you asked to hear.”

The clerk hesitated, then wrote it down.

It did not settle the wages. It stopped the question from being treated as an interruption.

Su Fan went to the kitchen for water.

When he returned, the porter was describing a noise.

“Like a chain slipping.”

“Was it a chain?” the clerk asked.

“I didn't see.”

“Then why say chain?”

“Because that's what it sounded like.”

The clerk looked dissatisfied.

Su Fan set the water down.

“Write that it sounded like one. He isn't claiming he saw it.”

The porter nodded.

The clerk made the correction.

A useful distinction survived without requiring either man to become foolish.

***

By midday the accounts disagreed in three places.

Su Fan expected the clerk to choose the version supported by the greatest number of people. Instead the man drew a rough map and marked where each witness had stood.

Two had heard the same event through different walls. One had arrived after the first alarm and mistaken the second for the beginning. A fourth had been repeating something his brother told him.

The disagreements became smaller.

They did not all disappear.

The woman with the child could not remember whether a shouted instruction came before or after a particular movement. She had been watching the path, afraid somebody would fall into the water.

The clerk asked her to try harder.

She tried.

Her answer became more detailed.

Su Fan recognized the danger before he knew how to phrase it.

“Are you remembering that,” he asked, “or deciding it must have happened?”

She looked at him sharply.

Then at the clerk.

“I don't know.”

The clerk began to set down his brush.

“Write that,” Duan said.

The woman rubbed her palms against her knees.

“I don't want to make trouble for anyone.”

“You can tell us what you know,” the clerk said. “You needn't supply the rest.”

It was the most useful thing he had said all morning.

Her shoulders lowered.

The child, who had been drawing with a burnt stick on a broken tile, looked up.

“Mother said the sound was horrible.”

The room went quiet.

The clerk did not write that as evidence of a mechanism. He asked whether the boy had been there.

“No. She told me when she came home.”

The boy returned to his tile.

His mother's hand settled briefly on the back of his head.

***

Su Fan gave his own account after the others.

He placed the corrected copy on the table.

The clerk read it, then asked him to begin without looking at the page.

He started with the work he had been assigned.

The questions came steadily.

What had he been permitted to touch?

What had he touched?

What had he understood at the time?

Who had warned him?

What had changed between the warning and his decision?

He could answer most of them.

The ones he disliked were not necessarily unfair.

At one point he began explaining what would have happened if he had done nothing.

The clerk stopped him.

“Did you know that then?”

“I believed it.”

“On what basis?”

Su Fan looked toward the yard.

He could describe the load, the movement, the time available. He could describe earlier failures. He could not turn a belief made under pressure into a certainty merely because the eventual outcome had been better than the one he feared.

He said so.

The clerk wrote more slowly.

“And your method?”

Su Fan gave its name.

The brush paused.

He described the exercise as far as it related to the action being examined. He did not pretend to understand every part of it. He also did not use uncertainty as a way to avoid describing what he had deliberately done.

When the clerk asked whether a lineage holder could have performed the same action, he answered that he did not know.

The man looked up.

“You did not test that?”

“No.”

“Then we will not write that they could not.”

Su Fan felt the objection rise in him.

He let the sentence remain.

The method's usefulness did not require him to prove everybody else's uselessness.

***

During the break, a second packet arrived.

It bore the clinic's mark.

The messenger put it beside the statements and asked for a receipt. The clerk reached for the cord.

Mother Wei, who had come to collect Duan's medicine bowl, took the packet first.

“These are patient records.”

“They were requested.”

“For whom?”

The messenger showed the instruction.

The names were right. The destination was not.

A copying error had sent the records with the general accounts rather than to the person authorized to examine the medical details.

The clerk looked embarrassed.

Su Fan had already seen the first name through a gap in the wrapping.

He turned his eyes away.

Mother Wei did not make a speech about trust. She retied the packet, corrected the destination and told the messenger whom to find.

Then she looked at Su Fan.

“You have washed?”

“Yes.”

“Since carrying the coal?”

He looked at his fingertips.

“Not sufficiently.”

She handed him the bowl.

The clerk watched her leave.

“Does she speak to everyone that way?”

“Only people she has met,” Duan said.

The room relaxed.

It did not make the error unimportant.

***

Outside, Sun Lian was examining the map the clerk had drawn.

She had not attended every conversation. She had come for her own statement and would not sign an account of things she had not witnessed.

A line near the lower corner troubled her.

“This path is behind the wall.”

“The porter said he came down it.”

“He could have. Then he couldn't see the wheel until here.”

She marked the point.

The clerk compared it with the porter's account.

One of Su Fan's assumptions changed.

He had believed the porter saw him act and could confirm the sequence. The man had seen the aftermath instead.

Su Fan felt the loss of a supporting witness before he felt the value of a clearer account.

Sun Lian noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

She waited.

“I thought he saw more.”

“He saw what he saw.”

“I know.”

“Then let him keep it.”

She returned the brush.

The clerk corrected the map.

Su Fan looked at the gap where his imagined confirmation had been. He would rather have had the witness. Wanting it did not put the man on the other side of a wall.

***

The woman with the child returned near the end of the afternoon.

She had remembered something.

Everyone became attentive, which immediately made her less certain.

“It may not matter.”

“Tell us,” the clerk said.

A bucket had been moved from the path before the first shouted instruction. She remembered because she had nearly tripped over it, then seen it beside a post when she looked back.

The clerk asked where the post stood.

They put it on the map.

The detail did not prove anyone innocent. It did not identify the cause of the larger failure. It helped place two people at a particular moment.

The woman looked disappointed when no dramatic consequence followed.

“That was all.”

“It is useful,” the clerk said.

“Enough?”

He considered the question.

“For what you remember, yes.”

Su Fan liked him better for not promising more.

The child offered Duan the tile he had drawn on.

It showed a large wheel, several stick figures and a goose that had not been present at the event.

Duan examined it solemnly.

“Who is this?”

“Me.”

“Were you there?”

“No. I wanted to be in the drawing.”

Duan nodded.

“A privilege of drawings.”

The clerk laughed, then glanced at his map.

***


The question about lost wages remained on the first page.

The clerk had not forgotten it. He had also not found an answer by virtue of remembering.

He asked which people had missed paid work and for how long. The answers were awkward. One man had traded a shift. Another had been promised payment only if the job was finished before dark. The woman with the child had lost no formal wage, but had left laundry unfinished for a customer who would not care that her absence had been useful.

The clerk wrote separate descriptions instead of forcing them all into the same column.

“Will they pay?” the porter asked.

“I can submit the account.”

“That's not payment.”

“No.”

Su Fan wanted to offer the missing money from the workshop. The impulse was immediate and generous and used money that was not entirely his.

He looked at Duan before speaking.

The smith shook his head once.

Not a refusal to help. A refusal to have help announced before its cost was discussed.

They spoke privately while the clerk packed his papers. Duan agreed that the workshop could advance a small amount against an acknowledged receipt, but only where the person wanted that arrangement. They would record it separately. A delayed reimbursement might remain delayed.

Two workers accepted. One refused because he did not want another person waiting on his account. The woman asked whether the workshop could finish the damaged handle on her laundry basket instead.

Duan looked at it.

“Yes. Tomorrow.”

Su Fan wrote the promise beside the other work.

The arrangement did not make the official silence fair. It let the people who had spent the day answering questions choose what immediate assistance would actually help them.

When the clerk returned for the final signatures, the lost-wage question was still visible at the top of his page.

He did not cross it out because someone else had softened the consequence.


When the accounts were finished, he read each one aloud to its owner.

The porter corrected a word.

The tired worker asked for a whole sentence to be removed because it described what another person had said, not what he knew.

Sun Lian added a limitation.

Su Fan changed nothing in his final version, but only after listening to it without quietly substituting the version he preferred.

They signed or marked the pages.

The clerk counted them and made a separate list of the questions still unanswered. He left a copy at the workshop.

It was not a verdict.

It was not even a complete explanation.

The day's work had produced something less satisfying and more durable: a record in which an uncertainty was not automatically a lie, a useful act was not automatically permission, and an honest witness did not have to remember more than a person could reasonably remember.

After the clerk left, Duan put the child's tile beside the account book.

Su Fan looked at the goose.

“That part is inaccurate.”

“Yes,” Duan said. “Fortunately it isn't testimony.”

Then he pointed at the unfinished hinge.

“The customer for that has been accurate about returning twice.”

Su Fan picked up the file.

***

Wen Zhao arrived without an escort large enough to impress anyone.

He was seventy, early Foundation, and annoyed by the mud on his boots. He told the man carrying his case to stop wiping them because they would become muddy again before reaching the next building.

Jiang received him in the temporary office.

Su Fan was summoned after lunch.

He found three chairs, a basin of water and a stack of statements bound in blue thread.

Wen Zhao pointed to the empty chair.

“Sit. You may ask to see anything I refer to.”

That was a better beginning than Su Fan expected.

It did not remain comfortable.

***

“Did you enter the contractor's records house without permission?”

“Yes.”

“Did you damage its floor?”

“Yes.”

“Were you attacked before or after that damage?”

“Before.”

“Did you remove records?”

“No.”

“Did you intend to?”

Su Fan looked at the blue-bound statements.

“Yes. Temporarily, to copy them.”

Wen Zhao wrote something down.

“Your purpose is relevant. It is not a denial.”

“I understand.”

“Your captain says you attacked an officer conducting a lawful investigation.”

“His men fired first.”

“Your companions say the same. None could see the first shot.”

Su Fan had known this. Hearing it spoken by a neutral voice made it worse.

The inspector turned a page.

“The night watch recovered three crossbow bolts from the gallery. One was buried in a chest facing away from the entrance. That is useful.”

He did not look pleased by the prospect of vindicating anybody.

***

The next questions concerned Su Fan's cultivation.

Wen Zhao asked him to place a hand beside the basin, then above it, then beneath it.

He measured the movement of water and the heat at the skin. He watched the floor beneath Su Fan's feet. Only at the end did he take out a lineage-reading strip.

The strip remained pale.

“You began with a text from the Stack?”

“Yes.”

“Who gave it to you?”

Su Fan explained the disposal shelves, the keeper and the clamp repairs.

“Was the keeper authorized to dispose of material?”

“Yes.”

“Can he attest to that?”

“He is ill.”

“That was not my question.”

Su Fan looked up sharply.

Wen Zhao met his gaze.

“I can go to him.”

***

They visited Min that afternoon.

The old scholar was awake and in a foul mood because Jin had beaten him at a counting game. He said the child had changed the rules. Jin said the rules had been wrong.

Wen Zhao listened to the argument before asking his questions.

Min produced the disposal authorization. He had kept it folded into a catalogue no one else had thought important enough to save from the flood.

The inspector checked the dates and seal.

“Why this particular text?”

“Because he asked about it.”

“Did you know he would cultivate from it?”

“I suspected he would try.”

“Did you understand the method?”

Min coughed into a cloth.

“Less than I pretended. More than was comfortable.”

Wen Zhao waited while the coughing passed.

He asked no question about the stained cloth.

***

Outside, the inspector gave Su Fan a copy of his preliminary finding.

There was no current basis for treating the scripture as stolen sect property.

The unauthorized entry in Siltbridge remained under investigation. So did the contractor's conduct. Su Fan's unregistered method required a regional assessment that Wen Zhao lacked authority to complete alone.

“This doesn't make me lawful,” Su Fan said.

“It makes one accusation unsupported.”

Wen Zhao closed his case.

“You have been dealing with men who confuse those two things. Don't begin helping them.”

chapters.title: A Yard with No Master
chapters.text:
Ruan Zhi brought a sack of beans to the practice yard.

Su Fan looked at it.

“Is this a lesson?”

“It may become supper. That depends on you.”

He untied the mouth and poured a small pile onto the ground between the stones. The beans rolled into cracks, settled against the wall and made Ah-Du look up from the bellows.

“Are those paid for?”

“Yes,” Ruan said.

“Then I approve.”

The exercise appeared simple. Su Fan was to cross the yard, lift a weighted bundle, return it to the bench and put down the small cup of water he carried without spilling it.

The beans lay where his most convenient steps would have fallen.

He looked at Ruan.

“You could simply tell me not to use the same path.”

“I did. You used it more carefully.”

“That isn't the same thing.”

“Show me.”

Su Fan took the cup.

The first crossing was easy. He watched the ground, kept the weight close and let his circulation support the change in balance.

Ruan moved the bench.

Su Fan stopped.

“Don't.”

“People do.”

“The exercise was—”

“The exercise has changed.”

Ah-Du found a better place from which to watch.

***

On the second crossing, Su Fan concentrated so hard on the beans that he failed to see Ruan move his own foot into the intended path.

He checked his step before colliding.

Water spilled.

Ruan looked at the cup.

“Again.”

“Will you keep changing it?”

“Yes.”

“Then this isn't a repeatable test.”

“No. It's practice for things that don't repeat.”

The distinction annoyed him because it was useful.

They set the weighted bundle farther from the wall. Su Fan chose another path. This time he watched Ruan's shoulders, the cup, the bench and the ground in a sequence that became too complicated to maintain.

He stepped on a bean.

It shifted beneath his heel.

His cultivation caught the change before he fell, but the sudden correction threw the water against the cup's rim.

Ah-Du made a sympathetic noise.

Ruan offered him the cloth.

Su Fan dried his hand.

“You enjoy this.”

“Very much.”

“Is enjoyment part of the method?”

“Only for the teacher.”

He tried again.

***

After several attempts, Duan came to the doorway.

“Are you practising movement or making a mess?”

“Both,” Ruan said.

“Which is paying?”

“Neither yet.”

The smith examined the beans.

“Get them out of the furnace path.”

Ah-Du protested that moving them would spoil the lesson.

“Good. I need the path.”

For a moment the exercise had to make room for the work whose yard it occupied.

Su Fan and Ruan gathered the loose beans. Some had fallen into damp cracks and could no longer be considered supper. Ah-Du was appointed to separate those from the clean ones, a task he described as a punishment for supporting education.

Duan carried a light fitting to the bench with his good hand.

Su Fan moved to help.

The smith looked at him.

“Ask.”

“Do you want—”

“No. Move the stool.”

He moved it.

Duan sat, set down the fitting and adjusted his injured arm before reaching for the file.

The movements were slow and particular. There was no dramatic flow through the body, no sudden liberation from resistance. There was a man arranging the world so that the work he could still do remained possible.

Ruan watched without speaking.

Then he returned the cup to Su Fan.

“Smaller load.”

Su Fan began to object.

Ruan shook his head.

“Not because you can't carry the weight. Because I want to see what you do before strength makes the correction.”

They changed the exercise.

***

With less weight, Su Fan could feel the mistake sooner.

He had been holding his ribs as though the next movement were a blow. His legs were trying to move a body whose upper half had already prepared to resist them.

The correction was not to collapse.

He had learned that painfully enough.

It was to let one part stop answering a danger that had not arrived, while the rest remained capable of meeting the danger that did.

He moved.

The cup stayed level.

Ruan did not praise him.

He stepped closer and touched Su Fan's elbow.

The water spilled.

Su Fan laughed once, sharply.

“There must be an end to this.”

“When you decide the cup matters less than the elbow, perhaps.”

He looked at the small bruise beginning beneath the sleeve.

“A real strike would—”

“Yes.”

The cup had been a task, not a moral obligation. Saving every drop while allowing a limb to be trapped would be a foolish victory.

On the next attempt, Ruan moved to catch the elbow again.

Su Fan let the cup go.

Ruan caught it before it struck the ground.

Ah-Du applauded.

Duan asked whether they had finally invented serving drinks.

***

Qiu Lan arrived carrying a narrow wooden wheel.

It was not the grinding wheel she had once discussed. It was a small model whose paddles had been cut from scraps, meant to show a relative how a particular arrangement might fit beside an existing channel.

One paddle had split.

She wanted a better fixing.

Su Fan examined it.

“You could make the whole wheel heavier.”

“And then the available water would spend more of itself moving the wheel.”

He looked at the frame.

“Yes.”

Ruan leaned closer.

“Could your method drive it directly?”

“It could. I don't intend to stand beside it forever.”

The answer was so practical that Su Fan smiled.

She noticed the beans.

“I won't ask.”

“Wise,” Duan said.

They repaired the paddle with a lighter fitting. Qiu Lan tested the model using water from an actual pail, guiding a small stream through the channel she had built.

The wheel turned.

Su Fan watched the steadiness of the flow. His own method could make his body more efficient at lifting the pail. It could not do what she was doing with the water.

No one needed to turn that into a contest.

When the wheel caught, she reduced the flow, examined the resistance and began again.

The second attempt was better.

“Why make a model?” Ruan asked.

“Because my uncle agrees with every drawing until the wood arrives.”

Duan laughed.

“An experienced customer.”

***

Qiu Lan asked to see the cup exercise.

Ruan explained it.

She watched Su Fan cross the yard, then took his place.

Her first attempt was worse.

The water responded to her attention and moved when she wanted the cup to remain ordinary. She spilled half of it while trying to prevent a smaller spill.

Ah-Du looked delighted.

She pointed at him.

“You next.”

The boy immediately discovered urgent work with the bellows.

On her second attempt, Qiu Lan carried the cup without using her art.

Ruan shifted the bench.

She stopped, put the cup on the ground and moved the bench back.

“That isn't allowed,” he said.

“You didn't say.”

Su Fan laughed hard enough that the ringing in his ear seemed briefly less important.

Ruan considered the new rule his own carelessness had produced.

“Now it is.”

“Expensive teacher,” Qiu Lan said. “Changes the lesson after the answer.”

She picked up her repaired wheel.

The exchange had not humiliated her. She had failed at an unfamiliar exercise, found a loophole, and returned to work she understood. Su Fan envied how little time she spent making the failure explain her entire worth.

Perhaps that, too, required practice.

***


Before leaving the first time, Ruan had asked Duan a question of his own.

The padded staff he used for training had begun to turn slightly in his grip after a hard impact. He had blamed the binding and replaced it twice. The trouble returned.

Duan held it against the light.

“Which end do you think this is?”

“The striking end.”

“That explains the wrapping. It doesn't answer the grain.”

He showed Ruan a narrow line near the centre. The wood had been chosen for its straightness from one direction. Under a different load, the line encouraged it to twist.

“Can it be repaired?”

“For light practice.”

“For what I use it for?”

“No.”

Ruan looked genuinely annoyed.

“It was expensive.”

“Then don't make it expensive twice.”

Su Fan watched him weigh the answer. The young man could afford a replacement more easily than anyone in the yard, but that did not stop him from wanting the object he had bought to be the object he had intended to buy.

He left the damaged staff with Duan for cutting into smaller useful pieces.

“Will you show me how to choose the next one?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

Duan named an ordinary teaching fee.

Ruan paid it without turning the payment into generosity.

Later, when Su Fan mentioned that he had never expected to see Ruan being corrected over a stick, his friend looked at him with amusement.

“You imagine I wake knowing everything that will embarrass me by evening?”

“No.”

“You make it sound convincing.”

Su Fan thought of the effortless way Ruan moved in a bout. He had been seeing the result and inventing a life in which the result had never been absent.

The next time Ruan told him to begin again, the words sounded a little different.


When the others left, he repeated only the first part.

Lift. Turn. Carry. Set down.

No beans. No moving opponent. No demand that the whole day be justified by a breakthrough.

He could feel the returning circulation more clearly when the task was small enough that he did not need to force it. At the difficult point near his shoulder, the old tightening still began.

He shortened the movement.

It eased.

He lengthened it too quickly.

The tightening returned.

He marked the two positions separately.

A smaller successful movement was not proof that the larger one would succeed. A larger failed movement was not proof that the smaller one had been imagined.

He had once expected cultivation to make the body obey a better idea.

Increasingly, it required him to learn what the body was actually doing before offering it another instruction.

The thought was useful for three breaths.

Then a customer called from the gate and he nearly dropped the cup while turning.

He put it down before answering.

***

The customer had brought a door latch and a complaint about the draught through her sleeping room.

Duan was occupied. Su Fan took the latch.

The mechanism was sound. The door had shifted.

He could repair the latch until it shone and still leave the room cold.

They walked to the building. He examined the frame, listened to the woman's description and asked whether the trouble changed after rain.

It did.

He made a temporary adjustment that would let the door close without forcing the frame farther out of line. He explained that the wall movement still needed attention.

The woman asked whether the temporary repair would last.

“For ordinary use, while the ground remains as it is.”

“That is a very careful promise.”

“It is the one I can make.”

She tested the door.

It closed.

For the moment, that was enough.

On the way back, he saw a child carrying a bowl with both hands. The child walked slowly, tongue caught between his teeth, eyes fixed so firmly on the contents that he nearly struck a post.

Su Fan called a warning from the side the child could hear.

The child stopped, looked up, then carried the bowl around the post.

No lesson was necessary after that.

***

At dusk, Ruan returned for the empty sack.

Ah-Du had saved the clean beans and written a bill for sorting them. The figures were absurd. The final line charged extra for seeing too much failure.

Ruan read it solemnly.

“I will dispute the final item.”

“On what basis?”

“That you enjoyed it.”

The boy considered the argument.

“Half price.”

They settled for a promise to share the cooked beans when Auntie Lu agreed they were fit for a pot.

Su Fan gave Ruan the cup.

“I found where the movement begins to break.”

“Good.”

“I haven't corrected it.”

“Then you have tomorrow's work.”

“And yours?”

Ruan rolled one shoulder.

“To stop assuming I can change every rule after Qiu Lan answers.”

They stood for a moment in the cleared yard.

The little ordinary objects remained: cup, bench, stone, a damp cloth hanging over the wall. None looked capable of carrying the weight Su Fan had tried to put into them that morning.

Perhaps they never had to.

They only had to show him the next mistake accurately enough that he could stop defending it.

***

Ah-Du wanted a sign.

He had already cut the board. That was how Su Fan knew the question was not whether there would be a sign, but how much argument would precede its installation.

“Practice Yard,” Su Fan said.

“People know it's a yard.”

“Then write Practice.”

“People know that too.”

“Apparently we need no sign.”

Ah-Du looked betrayed.

Bao Mei took the board from him and painted the opening hours.

***

The yard began with six people.

None received Su Fan's breathing method.

His restriction against teaching unassessed cultivation remained in force. More importantly, he did not yet know how to separate the method's reliable instructions from the guesses he had survived.

He could teach footwork. He could teach how to lift a load without twisting the back, how to fall, how to keep a blade from entering one's own leg.

The last lesson attracted more interest than the first two.

Bao Shun came to learn movements he could manage with one damaged hand. Qiu Lan came between shifts. Two porters came because they had seen Su Fan free a cart and assumed he knew something worth stealing.

Ah-Du arrived late carrying the painted board.

Su Fan made him warm up before touching a practice sword.

“You are already behaving like a sect,” the boy complained.

“Put your feet farther apart.”

***

The first argument concerned a shoulder.

Su Fan corrected Qiu Lan's stance. She tried it twice, frowned and returned to her original position.

“That puts the pull through my neck,” she said.

“It should go through the back.”

“It doesn't.”

He demonstrated.

She watched, then pointed to the difference between their reaches.

“Your arm is longer.”

Su Fan started to explain the principle.

Then he stopped and moved the hanging target closer to her.

The next strike landed cleanly.

Qiu Lan raised an eyebrow.

Bao Shun laughed.

It took several minutes to restore anything resembling discipline.

***

Duan watched from the workshop door.

Later he asked what Su Fan had taught.

“Basic cuts.”

“What did you learn?”

“That I have long arms.”

The smith nodded solemnly.

“A useful discovery. Expensive to miss.”

Su Fan rolled his eyes and carried the practice swords inside.

***

Tan Wei joined them on the third evening.

He had returned to reduced duty after the Siltbridge journey. The medical leave had ended. The district had denied Han's request for a full uncoupling assessment, citing the coming spring return.

He said none of that in the yard.

Instead he showed Bao Shun how to turn a bucket without lifting its full weight. The movement came from ordinary ferry work rather than the inherited method.

Soon everyone was trying it.

Su Fan watched from beside the rack.

Tan Wei caught his eye.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You look offended.”

“I spent an hour getting them interested in footwork.”

“This has a bucket.”

“That appears to be the difference.”

***

When the others left, they practised together.

No qi at first. Then a little, under agreed limits.

Tan Wei had reached the fifth stage and learned to use it. His water changed direction more quickly than Su Fan expected. It did not announce its intention merely because Su Fan had known him since childhood.

One turn caught Su Fan's ankle and put him on the ground.

Tan Wei offered a hand.

Su Fan took it, laughing despite the mud down his collar.

Above the gate, Bao Mei's sign dried in the evening air.

OPEN AFTER THE LAST WORK BELL.

BRING YOUR OWN BUCKET.

chapters.title: The Western Chamber
chapters.text:
The old drawing did not show the house.

This would have been a minor inconvenience if the proposed line had not passed through its kitchen.

Sun Lian spread the drawing on the table while the householder stood behind her with flour on both hands. A pot simmered near the hearth. Three children watched the visitors with the cautious hope that official work might delay their own chores.

“The wall is here,” Sun Lian said.

“The wall has always been here,” the woman replied.

“On this copy, the line runs behind it.”

“Then the copy can go behind it.”

Su Fan looked at the hearth.

The building was not old enough to appear on the earliest survey. It was old enough to contain several lives that had no reason to consider themselves temporary.

They had not come to order its removal.

That was the first thing Sun Lian explained.

The woman listened, then asked why the visitors had not begun with that.

Sun Lian accepted the complaint.

They measured from outside instead.

***

The lane curved around the building and narrowed between two walls.

One had been repaired with mismatched stone. The other carried old water stains above the height of Su Fan's shoulder. A line of weeds grew from a seam near the ground, bright green despite the cold.

The assistant carrying the rod wanted to put it against the cleaner wall.

Sun Lian chose the stained one.

“Why?”

“Because the stain is part of what we're here to understand.”

Su Fan held the lower end while the assistant read the mark.

He tried to imagine the water that had left it. Not a story about it. The actual height, the direction, the places it could have reached.

The old survey offered one explanation.

The present buildings offered several objections.

They recorded both.

A child from the kitchen followed them carrying a small stool. He set it down wherever the visitors stopped, then sat as though he had been appointed to supervise.

“What are you looking for?”

“Where the water used to go,” Su Fan said.

“Down.”

Sun Lian nodded.

“An excellent starting point.”

The boy looked pleased.

His certainty lasted until they showed him a channel whose lower end now sat above the place the old drawing called its entrance.

“Then the drawing is wrong.”

“Or the ground has changed,” Su Fan said.

“Then the ground is wrong.”

They left him with that possibility.

***

The exposed stone near the covered passage had been worked by more than one set of hands.

Su Fan could see the difference in the cuts. Some were broad and patient, made when the surface was accessible. Others were narrow corrections added around fittings already in place.

A later builder had widened one opening and closed another.

The reasons were not written on the wall.

He wanted to recognize the pattern. The scripture had trained him to look for places where effort opposed itself, where an old correction created a newer strain. It was tempting to see the same answer wherever work looked complicated.

Sun Lian stopped him before he spoke.

“Describe the stone first.”

He looked at her.

“You have the expression you get when you recognize something before knowing what it is.”

He almost objected.

Then he pointed to the actual cuts.

“This edge is older. That fixing crosses it. The lower opening was reduced.”

“Good.”

“The flow may have—”

“May.”

He nodded.

They copied the visible arrangement.

It was enough work to keep both of them occupied without naming the vanished builder a master or a fool.

***

The small slab moved when they thought it was secure.

They had not intended to remove it. The assistant was clearing loose grit from the edge so the joint could be measured. He leaned on what looked like a sound upper surface.

The slab tilted.

Su Fan caught the assistant's sleeve and pulled him back.

Sun Lian put a brace against the lower edge.

For several breaths the stone remained poised between two positions, neither safe.

“Don't hold it with your hands,” she told the younger man.

“I wasn't—”

“You are reaching.”

He stopped.

Su Fan could have added force through the brace. He waited until Sun Lian told him where that force would go.

They eased the slab back into its bed.

It settled with a dull knock that seemed louder than it should have been in the narrow lane.

The assistant sat on the child's stool.

The child objected, then saw the man's face and said nothing more.

No one had been crushed. One hand was scraped. A knee would bruise.

The absence of a disaster did not make the movement acceptable.

Sun Lian examined the joint again from outside its possible fall.

“We stop here.”

“We've hardly begun,” the assistant said.

“Yes.”

He looked at the tools.

“The office expects—”

“Then the office will receive a description of what nearly happened.”

Su Fan took out a clean sheet.

This was not the thrilling discovery he had imagined beneath old stone. It was a loose slab, a frightened worker and a limit that needed to remain a limit after the frightened worker felt better.

***

The householder brought water for the scrape.

She also brought the child's second stool, so he could stop conducting a private injustice from beside the first.

The assistant thanked her.

She shrugged.

“You were going to bleed on the path.”

Sun Lian washed the grit away and bound the hand with a clean strip. She did not offer a diagnosis beyond what she could see. If it worsened, Mother Wei would examine it.

The householder watched the slab.

“Will that fall into my wall?”

“Not from what we have seen. We will leave a mark and keep people away until it is secured.”

“Keep whose people away?”

The question was not hostile. It was practical.

They agreed on a barrier that would not block the household's only route to the well. The woman insisted that the warning be drawn as well as written.

“My youngest can't read.”

“Neither can half the men who hurry,” Sun Lian said.

The woman laughed for the first time.

Su Fan drew a simple barred hand and an arrow indicating the safe side.

The child studied it.

“That's a bad hand.”

“It is a warning hand.”

“It still has too many fingers.”

He was right.

Su Fan corrected the drawing.

***

They finished the accessible measurements before leaving.

The old channel could not be treated as empty merely because no one was using it. Water sounded somewhere beyond the covered section. A draught came through one seam and disappeared when the pressure at the works changed.

The changes were recorded with times.

The assistant, recovering his confidence, suggested that the sound proved an open route.

Sun Lian asked him to imagine three connected chambers, one blocked passage and a narrow crack between them.

He frowned.

“The sound could still travel.”

“Yes.”

“Then it proves water is somewhere.”

“Yes.”

He looked disappointed.

Su Fan understood the feeling. It was difficult to work all morning for an answer that refused to become larger merely because they needed it.

They placed the mirror again.

This time the lamp revealed a patch of old metal behind the opening. Its edge was too obscured to identify.

Su Fan drew only what he could see.

He left the rest blank.

The blankness no longer felt empty. It held the possible costs of being wrong.

***

On the way back, they passed a mason repairing a step.

He asked whether they had found an ancient treasury.

“A loose slab,” Sun Lian said.

“Valuable?”

“Only if it stays where it is.”

The mason offered to look at it when his current work was finished.

He had no cultivation worth announcing. He knew how stone failed beneath load, which was the knowledge the morning had lacked.

Su Fan described the visible joint.

The mason asked about the bed beneath it.

“We couldn't see.”

“Then I'll bring wedges.”

“Can you make it safe?”

“I can make it safer to examine. Don't sell the second promise before I've done the first.”

Sun Lian arranged the visit.

The mason returned to his step. He had a customer waiting, a limited amount of mortar and no interest in being recruited into a grand story about lost knowledge.

Su Fan liked him.

It did not make the proposed work cheaper.

***

At the workshop, the drawings acquired another set of hands.

Duan compared the visible metal with ordinary fittings he knew. He suggested two possibilities and rejected a third after Su Fan clarified the angle.

The assistant began writing the first possibility as a label.

“Question mark,” Duan said.

The young man added one.

“Larger.”

He enlarged it.

Ah-Du came to look.

“What is it?”

“We don't know.”

“Then why draw it?”

“So we can ask better people.”

The boy looked at Duan.

The smith pointed at the bellows.

“An excellent question for later.”

Su Fan copied the revised plan. He marked the house, the loose slab, the safe approach and the limit of the mirror's view. He added the mason's planned inspection as future work, not as work already completed.

Near the bottom he wrote the sound observations.

He did not write that the passage was open.

***


The assistant caught Su Fan outside the workshop before the drawings were copied.

“Does the report need my name?”

“Yes.”

He stared at the scraped hand.

“I was told to clear the edge.”

“You were.”

“And now it will say I loosened the stone.”

“It will say what happened. Including where you were told to work.”

The young man looked toward Sun Lian, who was discussing the brace with Duan.

“Will she write that?”

Su Fan did not answer for her.

He asked her to come over.

The conversation was uncomfortable. Sun Lian had directed the examination. The assistant had leaned where he had not been told to lean. Neither fact erased the other.

She put both in the report.

The assistant read it, then asked for one phrase to be changed. He had reached toward the slab after it moved because he thought another person was in its path, not because he believed he could hold the whole weight.

“Who?”

“Su Fan.”

Su Fan remembered pulling him backward. He had not noticed that the man was trying, in the same frightened instant, to help him.

They added the explanation without calling the action safe.

When the page was finished, Sun Lian signed her part first.

The assistant's hand shook as he made his mark. He was still afraid of what the office might do with the account. No honest wording could promise that authority would behave well.

But he no longer had to choose between concealing the danger and accepting a version in which he alone had caused it.

Afterward he asked Duan where to buy a better pair of work gloves.

Duan examined the old ones.

“Repair those first. Spend money when it buys protection, not merely the feeling that tomorrow will be different.”

The assistant smiled weakly.

He sat beside Ah-Du while the boy showed him which seam had opened.


That evening, he took out the scripture.

The open-centred mark on its cover was familiar enough that he rarely looked at it properly anymore. He traced it with his eyes, keeping his hands away from the worn surface.

It would have been easy to make the morning's old stone part of the same mystery. The temptation was not only curiosity. A connection might justify his presence, make his small method relevant to a structure too large for his present strength.

He could hear Min warning him about a damaged character and a confident reading.

So he compared the actual lines.

He found no proof.

He closed the slips.

Outside, someone was trying to persuade the goose away from a basket. The argument had reached the stage at which both sides appeared to believe volume could establish ownership.

Su Fan went to help move the basket.

The goose stayed.

He returned to the table with a nick on one knuckle and a clearer understanding of his influence over living things.

The old drawing waited beneath a stone weight.

Tomorrow the mason would examine the slab. After that, they might learn enough to ask what lay beyond it.

For now, keeping a worker from being crushed and a household from losing its path had been sufficient work for one day.

***

They reached the sealed door after seventeen days of clearing.

The work had used thirty-two people, six hired carts, two replacement winch ropes and every dry timber the settlement could spare without stealing from its own roofs.

Nobody called the discovery fortunate when they were the one hauling spoil uphill.

Su Fan entered first with Sun Lian behind him.

Their lamps showed a passage wider than the old survey suggested. Mineral threads hung from the roof. Water dripped upward from a broken bronze plate, gathered in a trembling bead beneath the stone and fell when the bead became too heavy.

Ah-Du stared.

“Is that cultivation?”

“Old formation work,” Sun Lian said.

“Whose?”

“We don't know.”

He waited for more.

She moved on.

***

The door had no handle.

A wheel stood beside it, half buried in pale deposits. Above the wheel was the open-centred mark Su Fan had seen in the scripture.

He felt no recognition from the book. No warmth in his chest. Nothing chose him.

He wiped grit from the mark and leaned closer.

It was smaller here, cut beside a row of ordinary maintenance symbols. Whoever made it had also drawn an arrow showing where to grease the axle.

Sun Lian knelt at the wheel.

“Don't turn it.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“Tell everyone behind you.”

Su Fan did.

***

The chamber beyond could be inspected through a narrow opening near the floor.

They sent a lamp through on a pole.

A circular gate stood within a stone throat. Its hinge had seized. One of the upper braces had cracked. Beyond it, darkness sloped toward the western marsh.

The bypass existed.

It could also fail violently if they opened it under the present head of water.

Sun Lian lay on her stomach and dictated measurements. Min Yao wrote them down. Bao Shun, working above ground, would use them to prepare wooden models of the missing fittings before Duan committed good iron.

Su Fan stayed beside the opening, steadying the lamp.

After an hour his forearms began to shake.

He changed hands rather than pretending they did not.

***

They found three names on the inner wall.

Not founders' titles. Not the promises of immortals.

Names, days worked, quantities of stone.

One entry had been crossed out. Beneath it, in a different hand, someone had written that the first crew had charged for a full day and left before noon.

Min Yao laughed so abruptly that dust fell from the roof.

Ah-Du copied the complaint into the survey book.

Su Fan stood beneath the open-centred mark and wondered how many people had worked here before the Hollow Reed had a name.

There was no answer available in the chamber.

For once, that enlarged the place rather than diminishing it.

***

When they emerged, Wen Zhao was waiting with his preliminary report.

The contractor had altered receipt dates. The municipal watch had confirmed that the fire in the records house began with an overturned brazier used during the interception. The initial force used against the intruders would require further examination.

Sun Lian's commercial claim would proceed separately from the criminal case.

Her boat remained detained.

Su Fan's entry remained unlawful.

Neither finding changed the condition of the gate beneath them.

Sun Lian read the report, folded it and put it away.

“Come back tomorrow,” she told the inspector. “You can watch us measure how long it takes to move the collar.”

Wen Zhao looked at the mud on their clothes.

“Will I need different boots?”

“Yes.”

chapters.title: Twelve Minutes
chapters.text:
Bao Mei would not paint the names until somebody checked the spelling.

The board stood against the workshop wall, pale wood beneath a coat she had mixed herself. There was room for fourteen names and a little space around them. No flowers yet. No river. She had decided that decoration could wait until the people were right.

Su Fan brought the copied list.

She read the first name and shook her head.

“What?”

“That character.”

“It is the one on the register.”

“It isn't the one his wife uses.”

The distinction stopped him.

He had carried the list as though the work of counting had made everything on it final. Fourteen dead. Searches completed as far as the searches could be completed. Names recorded, claims begun, absence made legible to offices.

Now a girl with a paint stain on her thumb was telling him that one of the dead men had a name the office had not written correctly.

He took out a clean sheet.

“Who should we ask?”

“His wife.”

“Is she—”

“Here. She comes for the small repairs.”

Bao Mei pointed toward the market.

Su Fan went.

***

The woman was mending a torn basket.

She did not look pleased to see the paper.

“Another form?”

“A name.”

She took the sheet, read it and made a small impatient sound.

“They always used that one.”

“Did he correct it?”

“Sometimes. When it mattered.”

“Does it matter here?”

She looked up at him.

He wished he had asked a better question.

“Yes,” she said.

She wrote the character herself. Her hand was slower than the clerk's and more certain.

“He was named for his mother's village. Not for the mountain.”

Su Fan copied it carefully beneath hers.

The woman watched.

“Will this change the account?”

“No. This is for the board.”

“Then change the account as well.”

He hesitated.

He could take a correction to the office. He could not guarantee that the office would accept it without further proof, or do it quickly, or refrain from charging for the alteration.

He explained that.

She listened without rewarding the explanation.

“Take it anyway.”

He did.

Before leaving, he asked whether she wanted anything written beside the name.

“What sort of thing?”

“His work. Something people should know.”

She looked at the half-mended basket.

“He disliked cold rice.”

Su Fan waited.

“He said nobody was poor enough to deserve eating it without complaint.”

She smiled unexpectedly, then stopped.

“You don't have to put that on the board.”

“I can remember it.”

She returned to the basket.

“That will do.”

***

They checked the other names over the next several days.

Some people wanted only the name. Some wanted an age. One family disagreed about which household should be mentioned. A brother asked for an honorary title the dead man had never used. His sister crossed it out.

“He would have laughed at that.”

“He would have liked it.”

“Then he can like it without us lying.”

Su Fan sat between them with his brush untouched until they settled on the plain name.

The work took longer than carrying fourteen boards would have taken.

It required less strength and more willingness to remain in a room after the useful questions were finished.

At one house, a child wanted to know whether the name would keep a person from being forgotten.

Su Fan did not say yes.

“It will help people ask who she was.”

“What if nobody knows?”

“Someone knows now.”

The child considered that.

Then she told him about a song her aunt used to sing while washing clothes. She remembered only the last line and sang it three times, each with a different tune.

He wrote the words on a separate scrap.

Not for the memorial board.

For the person who would one day want to know which line she had remembered.

***

Bao Shun built the frame.

His damaged hand could steady the light pieces if he placed them correctly. It could not clamp them with the old easy force. He arranged wedges on the bench and used his good hand to bring the joints together.

Su Fan offered to hold one side.

Bao Shun accepted.

The work was slow. The man examined each join before moving to the next. Nothing about the frame was ornate. It needed to remain straight through damp weather, not prove how much grief its maker could carve into wood.

Bao Mei painted the corrected names in black.

She used blue only for a narrow line at the bottom.

Her father looked at it.

“River?”

“Perhaps.”

“Perhaps?”

“It is blue. People may do the rest.”

Su Fan liked that answer.

He had spent too much time lately wanting every mark to carry an explanation. The simple line allowed room for what the people looking at it would bring.

When the paint dried, they wrapped the board in cloth.

Ah-Du helped carry it.

He was unusually quiet.

At the first bend he asked whether it would be mounted near the new houses or near the path that looked down toward the old town.

They had not agreed.

“Both groups asked,” Su Fan said.

“There is only one board.”

“Yes.”

The boy looked at the wrapped shape between them.

“We could make another.”

Su Fan almost praised the solution.

Bao Shun shook his head.

“We could. Then we would have two places to look after. Ask before you give people more work in the name of making things easier.”

Ah-Du nodded.

They carried the one board to the meeting place.

***

The discussion about where to hang it became a discussion about who passed which path.

Older people wanted somewhere they could reach without climbing. Workers wanted it near the road they used each morning. One man thought a memorial ought to require effort from those who visited it.

Auntie Lu asked whether he planned to carry everyone unable to satisfy that principle.

He withdrew the suggestion.

They chose a sheltered place near the upper path, where the board could be seen without obstructing the work of the settlement. It was not the grandest location. It was a place people actually used.

Deng checked the roof above it.

A leak would ruin the names before philosophy improved the arrangement.

He repaired the gutter.

Su Fan helped mount the frame.

When the cloth was removed, people stepped closer, then left space for others. There was no single moment at which everyone became quiet. Small conversations faded at different times.

A woman touched one name.

A boy asked which was his uncle's.

Someone corrected the boy's pronunciation gently.

The board did not answer any of them.

It remained where they had put it.

***

Su Fan had expected to feel something clearer.

He stood with his hands empty and found himself thinking about the fixings. Whether the upper one had enough sound timber behind it. Whether rain would reach the lower edge. Whether Bao Mei would need to repaint the black letters before the blue line.

The thoughts were practical. They were also a way of not looking too long at the names.

Tan Wei stood beside him.

Neither spoke for a while.

Then Tan Wei pointed to a name near the bottom.

“He taught me to tie a ferry knot.”

“You never said.”

“You never asked where I learned it.”

The words were not an accusation. That made them harder to dismiss.

Su Fan remembered the man as someone who shouted about boat loading and charged for things other ferrymen lent freely. Tan Wei remembered a patient lesson on an afternoon when he had been too young to be useful.

Both memories belonged to him.

“I thought he was mean,” Su Fan said.

“He was. About rope.”

Tan Wei smiled.

“He said wasted rope was stolen time.”

Su Fan looked at the name again.

A person was difficult to preserve honestly in a sentence.

That did not mean the attempt was useless.

***

There was food afterward.

Auntie Lu had insisted on it before anyone could make the gathering so solemn that hungry people were expected to admire their own restraint.

The meal was not a feast. It used what could be spared without making the next day worse. People brought bowls and, where they could, something for the pot.

Deng moved a bench so an older woman could sit out of the wind.

Auntie Lu told him it blocked the path.

He moved it again.

She brought him food before he had finished the second adjustment.

Su Fan watched them and said nothing.

The life continuing around the board did not feel disrespectful. It felt awkward, necessary and occasionally funny. A child dropped a dumpling. The goose arrived with alarming speed. Three adults attempted to prevent a theft already completed.

Someone laughed, then looked toward the names as though laughter required permission.

Bao Mei kept laughing.

The child who lost the dumpling was not amused.
