Tan Wei gave him half of another.

The child considered the exchange and decided the half was larger than the lost whole.

No one corrected him.

***

Later, Su Fan returned with the tools.

Most people had gone. The woman who corrected the first name remained near the board.

She asked whether he had taken the correction to the office.

“Yes.”

“What did they say?”

“They need to compare the household record.”

“Of course they do.”

“I left the copy you made.”

She nodded.

He wanted to offer a deadline. He had none to give.

Instead he told her when he intended to ask again.

“That will do,” she said, using the same words she had used at the basket.

This time he understood that they did not mean the matter was settled. They meant he had described one act she could reasonably expect from him.

She looked down toward the lost quarter.

For a while neither moved.

“I keep thinking of something I should have brought out,” she said.

Su Fan thought of the old forge, the tools Duan asked for after waking, the large tongs nobody could produce.

“Yes.”

“Then I remember I brought myself.”

He waited.

“That was what he told me to do.”

The wind moved beneath the shelter.

Su Fan did not tell her she should be grateful for being alive.

After a while she turned toward the houses.

He walked with her as far as the fork, carrying the unused hammer.

***

At the workshop, Bao Mei was cleaning her brushes.

The black water in the basin looked darker than the paint had on the board.

“Did people like it?” she asked.

“They read it.”

She considered the answer.

“Good.”

He told her about the corrected record still waiting at the office.

She asked for a copy of the accepted spelling, then placed it with the account for the work.

“Why there?”

“So if the board needs repainting, nobody copies the wrong one again.”

Su Fan looked at the small practical bundle.

The memorial would not preserve itself. Someone would have to keep the paper dry, repair the roof, check the fixings and remember which character a woman had written with her own hand.

He had wanted the finished board to do more than any board could do.

Bao Mei was already planning how to help it do the thing it could.

He put the hammer away.

Before leaving, he asked whether she had been paid for the extra blue.

She gave him a look remarkably like her father's.

“It was in the price.”

***

They tested with sand instead of water.

Bao Shun's model stood in the workshop yard: a wooden throat, a weighted gate, two narrow return channels and a sliding collar that could separate one from the other.

Ah-Du poured the sand too quickly on the first attempt.

Everything jammed.

Sun Lian made him empty it, clean the grooves and begin again.

On the fourth attempt the collar moved, the western channel took the flow, and the lower return emptied without disturbing the upper passage.

Duan watched from a chair.

“Now put a broken brace in it.”

They did.

The gate twisted and threw sand across the yard.

***

The elder came while they were cleaning up.

Pei Gang had healed enough to stop wrapping his burned hand. The skin across the wrist remained shiny and tight. He held that arm closer to his body than before.

He examined the model without touching it.

“What is your estimate?” he asked Sun Lian.

“Twelve minutes to lower the chamber enough to isolate the returning branch. Longer if the throat takes less flow than the survey suggests.”

“How long will the repaired brace bear?”

“Twenty at the measured load. That estimate has a margin. The masonry does not.”

“And when the main return crosses the old chamber?”

“The strain changes.”

“Doubles,” Pei said.

Sun Lian glanced at Jiang.

The steward nodded reluctantly.

The elder had noticed the part of the problem they had not solved.

***

He moved the model's upper channel with one finger.

“A living neutral interval would take the strain during that transition. Your bypass and my study are not competing proposals.”

Su Fan stood beside the timber pile.

“You require control of the interval.”

“I require reliability.”

“You require a renewed oath at your discretion.”

“Because a man can walk away. A gate cannot.”

Pei's voice held no anger. That made the offer harder to dismiss.

Jiang leaned over the model.

“A mechanically locked collar could hold the separation.”

“If you have a sound foundation beneath it,” Pei said. “You have not yet exposed the lower bearing.”

He looked at Su Fan.

“You may dislike my terms. Do not confuse that with having completed the work.”

***

They exposed the lower bearing three days later.

It was damaged.

For an hour, nobody said much.

Then Duan asked for the dimensions.

He drew with his good hand, crossed out the first design and began another. The new brace would transfer load sideways into the passage walls. It needed more iron than they possessed and stonework they had not planned.

Jiang found half the iron in a decommissioned upper station.

Ruan obtained permission to quarry the rest of the stone from his family's western holding. This time he obtained it in writing.

Sun Lian recalculated the timing.

Twelve minutes remained the fastest safe interval.

***

That night Su Fan returned to the chamber alone to collect a forgotten measuring cord.

He stood at the opening and listened to the water on the far side.

With his good ear toward the stone, he could hear the high pressure as a steady hiss. Beneath it came slower knocks, irregular and distant.

He imagined the people connected to that movement. Tan Wei. Qiu Lan. Han. Operators he had never met who had signed agreements they might still trust.

For a moment the elder's prepared room seemed terribly easy.

A bed. Supervised training. One person's body in place of an unfinished mass of iron and stone.

Then he heard footsteps behind him.

Sun Lian had come for the same cord.

She took one end from his hand.

“Hold that,” she said. “I don't trust the last measurement.”

Together they measured again.

chapters.title: The Green Scarf
chapters.text:
The man who wanted the testing work had read only the pay.

He admitted that readily.

“The rest is for people who expect to be injured.”

Su Fan looked at the paper.

“Does expecting it change whether it happens?”

“No. It changes whether I sleep tonight.”

The man made handles for tools. He had a narrow face, a loud laugh and a habit of smoothing his sleeve over a scar near the wrist. Su Fan had bought a hammer handle from him once and complained about the price.

The handle had outlasted two cheaper ones.

Now the man's ordinary orders had slowed, and work at the stations offered money sooner than customers offered payment for things they already owed.

He wanted to assist with a controlled test.

He did not want Su Fan to improve his life by explaining why the money mattered less than safety.

“I know I need both,” he said. “I haven't found the office that sells them together.”

Su Fan put down the paper.

“Then let's find out what work they are actually asking you to do.”

“That would be useful.”

The answer carried a warning.

He listened to it.

***

The description of the job was longer than the description of the risks.

That did not make the job clearer.

One paragraph referred to supporting the return. Another to maintaining an assigned position. A third allowed the supervisor to alter duties as required by the test.

“Supporting what?” Su Fan asked.

The man shrugged.

“Something they don't want falling.”

“Physically?”

“Would there be another kind?”

There would.

Su Fan did not attempt to explain every possibility. He wrote the question on a separate sheet.

He also wrote down the point at which the man could stop, who could order the test ended, and whether leaving before completion changed the payment.

The man watched the questions accumulate.

“At this rate they won't hire me.”

“They might answer.”

“They might hire somebody who doesn't ask.”

That possibility sat between them.

It would have been dishonest to pretend the questions cost nothing. They could cost the work. The absence of questions could cost something worse.

Su Fan asked which points the man wanted taken forward.

“All of them,” he said after a while. “But don't put words in my mouth about leaving the stations forever. I am asking about this job.”

They used his wording.

***

At the testing yard, the supervisor was irritated before they arrived.

A delivery had failed to come. One of the assistants was absent. The apparatus had taken longer to set than expected, and the people paying for the trial wanted a result before the weather changed.

Su Fan could see all of this in the half-finished arrangements.

He could also see how easily it might become a reason to avoid questions.

The handle maker presented his sheet.

The supervisor read it, frowned and handed it to an assistant.

“Ordinary support work,” he said. “Nobody is asking him to join a formation.”

“Then put that beside the duty,” Su Fan replied.

The man gave him a cold look.

“Are you applying?”

“No.”

“Then let him speak.”

Su Fan stepped back.

The correction was fair.

The handle maker cleared his throat.

“I want to know which weight is mine and who tells me to put it down.”

The supervisor's expression altered.

Those were questions he could answer without defending the entire institution.

He took them to the frame.

***

The assigned support was a lever with a marked travel range.

The man would help keep it within that range while the test applied a changing load through another part of the apparatus. He would not supply qi. He would not be coupled to an operator's impression.

Su Fan checked that the words on the paper now said both.

The handle maker inspected the grip.

“Too narrow.”

“It is standard.”

“My hand isn't.”

He showed the supervisor where the pressure would fall after several minutes.

An assistant offered a cloth wrapping.

The man rejected it because the cloth would shift.

Su Fan expected another argument.

Instead the supervisor told the assistant to fetch two wooden pieces and let the applicant demonstrate what he wanted.

He made a temporary grip while the others checked the frame.

It was not elegant. It fitted his hand.

When he took the position again, his wrist remained straighter.

“There,” he said.

The supervisor tested the lever.

“Acceptable.”

For a moment the conversation had become work rather than status.

Su Fan watched the man's shoulders loosen.

He had not been saved from the job. He had been allowed to make the job more possible.

***

The stopping signal was less satisfactory.

A raised hand meant hold. A closed fist meant reduce. Two calls meant release.

The handle maker stood where he could see the nearest assistant but not the supervisor.

“If the assistant looks away?”

“He won't.”

“If he does?”

The assistant became offended.

Sun Lian, arriving to examine a fitted section, looked from one man to the other.

“He will look away,” she said. “People look away. Decide what the worker does then.”

The supervisor stared at the frame.

They moved the assistant's station and added a physical stop marker the worker could see. If the lever crossed it, he was to call and release according to the agreed sequence rather than wait for a hidden instruction.

Su Fan asked how the call would reach a person whose hearing was unreliable.

The supervisor looked at him.

Sun Lian answered before the discussion became personal.

“He isn't the only person who may miss a word beside moving water.”

They added a visible signal.

It did not make the test safe in every possible condition. It removed one avoidable way for a sensible instruction to become useless.

The handle maker practised the sequence twice.

On the third attempt he made a mistake.

They practised again.

No one called the repetition a failure of courage.

***

Before the trial, the man stepped aside to speak with Su Fan.

“You think I shouldn't do it.”

“I think you should know what you're doing.”

“That isn't quite an answer.”

Su Fan considered.

He had seen enough harm around the stations that refusing this work felt like the cleaner choice. He had also never had to live inside this man's accounts.

“I would want the answers you asked for.”

“And now?”

“Now you have more of them.”

The man looked at the amended page.

“Still not all.”

“No.”

He laughed without much amusement.

“My daughter thinks I'm too old to take advice and too young to stop needing money.”

“Is she right?”

“About whichever part annoys me that day.”

He folded the paper and put it inside his coat.

He chose to proceed with the limited work.

Su Fan did not congratulate him.

He wished him a good trial and asked where he wanted his spare coat kept.

“Somewhere you won't decide to mend it.”

He grinned.

The joke made the boundary easier to hear without removing it.

***


His daughter came to the yard carrying a small roll of tools.

She had not come to collect him.

That was the first thing she said.

“I know,” he replied, much too quickly.

“You left the narrow knife.”

“I wasn't making handles.”

“You made a handle.”

He looked at the lever.

She put the tool roll on the bench.

Su Fan moved aside. The girl was older than Bao Mei, with a direct way of examining work that reminded him of her father before the man began joking about it.

She ran one finger along the temporary grip.

“This edge.”

“I know.”

“Then why leave it?”

“Because they were waiting.”

She looked toward the supervisor.

The supervisor, who had been complaining about delays all morning, said nothing.

The girl took the knife and eased the edge without weakening the part that carried pressure. Her father held it steady. They argued over the final shape in low voices that suggested the argument had begun years before and was not yet finished.

When she handed it back, he closed his fingers around it.

“Better,” he admitted.

She did not smile triumphantly.

“Bring the tools home. All of them.”

He nodded.

At the gate she stopped beside Su Fan.

“Did you read it?”

“The agreement?”

“Yes.”

“We went through it together.”

“Did he listen?”

“Enough to change several things.”

She looked back at her father.

“He listens. He just likes the person giving advice to suffer a little first.”

Su Fan laughed.

Her expression softened briefly, then became practical again.

“Don't let them call the grip a favour. It is work. He forgets to charge when someone says the word useful.”

She left before he could promise to manage her father's accounts.

Su Fan returned to the bench and repeated the message exactly.

The handle maker sighed.

“An expensive child.”

“A useful one.”

“That's how she catches you.”

He put the narrow knife away and added the tool-making time to the note beside his agreement.

No one had decided on his behalf whether he should take the job. Someone had remembered that his skill had a price even when the work was urgent.


The first run stopped because of a cramp.

Not a spectacular failure. Not a broken formation or a hidden betrayal. The handle maker's fingers tightened around the lever, and the grip he had improved could not make a tired muscle stop being tired.

He gave the signal.

The nearest assistant responded.

The load was eased.

The apparatus settled.

Several people looked annoyed.

The man stood rubbing his hand, embarrassed by the ordinary reason he had interrupted expensive work.

The supervisor asked whether he could continue.

“After rest.”

“How long?”

“I don't know yet.”

Su Fan expected pressure.

There was some.

The delivery delay, the absent assistant, the changing weather: all the morning's difficulties approached the same small hand and asked whether it might be convenient for it to stop cramping.

The man looked at the paper in his coat.

“I asked this before we began.”

Sun Lian moved her tools away from the frame.

“Yes,” she said.

The supervisor swore, not at the worker but loudly enough that the distinction offered little comfort.

Then he called a break.

They all stood down.

***

During the break, Su Fan brought water.

The man took it.

“Disappointing.”

“What?”

“My grand rebellion. A hand cramp.”

“You used the stop.”

“Yes. I expected to feel more impressive.”

“You look thirsty.”

“I am.”

They drank.

An assistant came over to ask how the altered grip had behaved. The handle maker explained the pressure point that remained. Together they moved one edge of the wooden addition.

The improvement did not erase the need for rest.

It made the next attempt different.

Su Fan watched the two men work without requiring either to apologize for being irritated.

The supervisor came by later.

The payment would remain at the agreed rate for the time assigned. The stopped run would be recorded as stopped, not as completed and not as abandonment.

The handle maker asked for that written on his copy.

The supervisor did it.

The ink was untidy.

It was legible.

***

Su Fan left before the later trial.

He had not been hired to supervise the entire day, and the man had not asked him to remain as a guardian.

At the yard entrance, Sun Lian caught up with him.

“You were waiting for him to choose the safer answer.”

“I was waiting for him to have an answer he could choose.”

“Both, perhaps.”

He looked back.

The handle maker was showing an assistant how to fit the spare wooden grip. He seemed less like a victim than he had when the agreement lay unread on the table.

That did not make him invulnerable.

“No method of asking questions can remove every pressure,” Su Fan said.

“No.”

“Then how do we know when—”

“We keep the questions specific enough that an answer can change something.”

She lifted her tool bag.

“Today it changed a handle and a stopping rule.”

He almost said that was too little.

Then he remembered the lever beneath the man's cramped hand.

***

At the workshop, he put the amended copy beside the ordinary accounts.

Not as proof that the stations had become trustworthy.

As a record of what one person had requested and what had been promised for one piece of work.

Duan read the description of the grip.

“He should make those for sale.”

“He may.”

“Did you tell him?”

“No.”

“Good. Let him finish this job before you found his next business.”

Su Fan laughed.

That evening the handle maker returned for his spare coat.

His hand was sore. The work had ended without the result the supervisor wanted. He had been paid for the agreed assignment.

He also had an order for two better grips, to be priced separately.

“Your daughter's verdict?” Su Fan asked.

“She says I should charge more.”

“Will you?”

The man folded the coat over his arm.

“I will ask what they need first.”

He left smiling.

The unfinished test remained unfinished.

A worker had nevertheless come home with his own account of the day intact.

***

Tan Wei dreamed of a woman washing a green scarf in a shallow river.

He knew her name.

He knew which tooth had broken when she was twelve. He knew she disliked pears, that she talked in her sleep, that she had once waited three days for him at a ferry crossing because he had promised to return before the rain.

The knowledge came with a tenderness so complete that he woke crying.

In the room beside his bed, Han was trimming a lamp.

Tan Wei sat up.

“Did I call out?”

“Yes.”

“What did I say?”

“A name.”

He wiped his face.

“She was real.”

Han put down the scissors.

“Yes.”

“That makes it worse.”

***

The preserved impression did not arrive as a villain.

It arrived with a way to knot a rope, an old preference for bitter tea, an affection for somebody who had been dead longer than Tan Wei's family had lived in Mudgate.

Some mornings he could separate the memories easily.

That morning he reached for his cup and expected it to have a blue rim. When it did not, he felt a small, unreasonable grief.

Han watched him set it down.

“The spring return will strengthen the connection.”

“How much?”

“I cannot predict it precisely.”

“Could I stop knowing which memories are mine?”

“Possibly. Not inevitably.”

Tan Wei turned his wrist.

The three blue reeds had grown darker since winter.

“I want out of the permanent impression.”

Han closed his eyes briefly.

“Are you certain?”

“Yes. I want to keep learning. I want the forms I can perform with my own channels. I don't want someone else's wife.”

***

They filed the request together.

Tan Wei wrote it himself. Han signed as supervising teacher. Mother Wei attached the medical observations and the dates of the involuntary movements.

The district response arrived within a day.

Withdrawal deferred until completion of spring renewal.

Han read it standing in the station courtyard.

Tan Wei watched his face.

“You knew they might refuse.”

“Yes.”

“So did I.”

Han folded the paper.

“I taught you how to enter this agreement. I will help you leave it.”

“Even if you lose the station?”

The old man's bad leg had begun to tremble. He shifted his weight before answering.

“I would prefer not to. That is no longer the only thing being asked of me.”

***

Su Fan found them at the clinic after the evening bell.

Han was explaining which routes could be retained after uncoupling. Tan Wei had drawn a rough body on the page and marked the branches as they discussed them.

Some were already his through practice. Others relied on the permanent impression to remain open.

He might lose one stage. He might lose two. There was a possibility of greater damage if the separation happened during a forced return.

“Then we need the interval,” Su Fan said.

“Yes,” Tan Wei replied. “Not a rescue in the middle of a panic. A planned interval, with people who know what they're doing.”

Su Fan looked at the drawing.

“I can work on the gate.”

“I know.”

“That is the part I know.”

Tan Wei's expression softened.

“Good.”

***

That night, Tan Wei wrote the woman's name in a separate book.

He added the green scarf, the broken tooth and the ferry crossing.

He did not tear out the page.

Whoever she had been, she had belonged to a life worth recording. He could acknowledge that without giving her his.

In his own notebook he wrote a different list.

The storehouse roof in the first rain. The smell of Auntie Lu's burned ginger. Su Fan falling into the practice mud. A girl at the river school who had laughed at his handwriting when he was nine.

The last memory made him smile.

He added her name before he forgot it again.

chapters.title: A Clean Blow
chapters.text:
Ruan Zhi took the padding off the practice blade.

Su Fan watched him.

“That changes the agreement.”

“Yes.”

“To what?”

“Looking at it.”

He laid the bare wooden blade on the bench. Beneath the cloth, a split ran from the fastening toward the middle.

Su Fan touched the edge.

“How long?”

“I don't know.”

They had both struck it. They had both trusted it because it looked like the same harmless object they had used the previous week.

Ruan turned it over.

“If it had opened during a bout, one of us would have called the other careless.”

“One of us would have been right.”

“About the wrong moment.”

Duan examined the split and cut the blade out of service. He did not permit a new wrapping to disguise the damage.

Ah-Du asked whether he could have it.

“For what?”

“A shorter sword.”

“Then cut it beyond the split.”

The boy regarded this as an excellent outcome. Everyone else's failed equipment improved his collection.

Su Fan and Ruan went into the yard with plain staves.

Neither looked quite as ready to begin.

***

The first bout was without cultivation.

Su Fan liked these less than he pretended.

Without the circulation's help, the weakness in his timing appeared quickly. Ruan did not need to move faster in every direction. He needed to arrive at the useful place first.

Su Fan struck high.

Ruan turned the staff and touched his ribs.

He tried to shorten the recovery.

Ruan stepped closer and took the space beneath his hands.

He tried to prevent the close approach.

Ruan made him retreat into the post.

After the third touch, Su Fan lowered his weapon.

“I know what you're doing.”

“Excellent. Stop me.”

Knowing did not make the next attempt better.

He anticipated the close approach and gave away the longer line. Ruan touched his shoulder with irritating gentleness.

The gentleness was deserved. A harder strike would have supplied pain instead of additional information.

Su Fan stood breathing through his annoyance.

Ruan waited.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You keep watching.”

“It is a useful habit in a bout.”

Su Fan laughed despite himself.

They began again.

***

With cultivation, the first exchange lasted longer.

The returning force made his movement less expensive. He could correct sooner, keep his balance under pressure and use a smaller motion to recover a line he had nearly lost.

Ruan changed the problem.

Instead of meeting force with force, he made Su Fan decide which movement deserved it.

A short feint. A withdrawn strike. A step close enough to suggest commitment, then no commitment at all.

Su Fan spent strength answering possibilities.

By the time the real attack arrived, he had already made his body busy.

He blocked it.

He could not use the block to do anything else.

Ruan pressed, turned and touched the end of the staff beneath his chin.

They stopped.

Su Fan could feel the useful route inside him. He could also feel the fatigue created by asking it to answer every suspicion.

The scripture had warned against frightened preparation long before he could produce a full circuit. He had understood the words in a quiet room.

The yard was less accommodating.

“How much of that was necessary?” Ruan asked.

“Yours or mine?”

“Mine was very satisfying.”

Su Fan wiped his face.

They repeated the exchange slowly enough that he could identify the first needless correction.

At full speed, he made it again.

That was the work.

***

Qiu Lan stopped at the gate on her way to the clinic.

She watched three exchanges, then asked why Su Fan kept looking at Ruan's left hand.

“Because he changes the grip there.”

“Does he always?”

“No.”

“Then he can make you look wherever he likes.”

Ruan bowed toward her.

“A valued observer.”

She ignored him.

At the stations, she said, a worker could become so accustomed to a particular warning that he stopped noticing the conditions before it. The signal remained useful. Dependence on that one signal became dangerous.

Su Fan listened.

He did not ask her to demonstrate a fighting technique she had never claimed to possess.

Ruan asked whether she wanted to try the exercise with a staff.

“No. I have work, and you look pleased enough already.”

She left.

Afterward Ruan held his left hand perfectly still.

Su Fan watched it.

The staff touched his ribs.

Ruan said nothing.

He did not need to.

***

They changed the exercise.

No scores. No attempt to win a whole exchange. Su Fan was to respond only when the attack crossed a particular distance, then stop as soon as the response had done its work.

The first attempts felt passive.

He disliked waiting.

He disliked allowing Ruan to choose the beginning.

He especially disliked discovering how often he had called an early movement readiness when it was simply an attempt to avoid uncertainty.

Ruan did not let the waiting become paralysis.

When Su Fan failed to answer a committed strike, the staff landed hard enough to make the lesson clear.

When he answered a feint, Ruan withdrew and let him feel the wasted motion.

Gradually the useful interval became easier to recognize.

Not easy.

Easier.

A customer passed the gate carrying a broken latch. Su Fan glanced toward him.

Ruan lowered his staff.

They stopped before the visitor entered.

The man apologized for interrupting.

“You brought work,” Su Fan said.

“I can wait.”

“So can this.”

He examined the latch while Ruan sat on the wall.

The interruption had cost them a useful rhythm. It had also prevented the practice yard from becoming a place where everyone else's ordinary need was treated as an offence against Su Fan's advancement.

Duan took the repair.

The men returned to the exercise.

They did not recover the rhythm immediately.

***

Rain began halfway through the next bout.

At first it was only a few dark marks on the ground. Then the earth changed beneath their feet.

Ruan stepped aside.

Su Fan followed too quickly and felt his heel slide.

He recovered through the circulation, but the correction put him close to the wall. He could not make the next retreat without choosing whether to strike the post or turn his weak side into the exchange.

He turned.

Ruan's staff stopped near his right shoulder.

“I didn't hear your step,” Su Fan said.

“I know.”

“I saw the first.”

“And expected the second.”

Su Fan looked at the wet ground.

The injury had not merely removed part of a sense. It had left him with expectations formed by a body that no longer reported the world in the same way.

He wanted anger to be useful.

For a moment it was not.

Ruan put down the staff.

“We can stop.”

“No.”

“Then we can change what we're doing.”

That was harder to reject.

They moved to a simpler exercise in the sheltered part of the yard. Ruan approached from different angles within Su Fan's sight. Su Fan practised turning before committing, not guessing the sound correctly.

It was slower than he wanted.

It was something he could actually practise.

***

Duan called them inside when the rain became steady.

The workshop was warm, smoky and crowded with things waiting to be repaired. Ah-Du had put his shorter sword on a shelf and was trying to convince the smith that sanding it counted as an apprenticeship task.

“It is wood.”

“The sword has a metal pin.”

“So does the door. Shall I give you a qualification for opening it?”

Ruan laughed.

Su Fan sat near the bench and found that his hands were shaking slightly from effort. The tremor annoyed him until he remembered that pretending not to see it had never improved a trial.

He drank water.

Ruan examined a bruised place on his own wrist.

Su Fan looked up.

“I touched you?”

“You did.”

“You didn't say.”

“You were busy explaining how badly it was going.”

The bruise was small. It did not turn the morning into a victory. It prevented Su Fan from making the opposite mistake of recording only his failures because disappointment felt more honest than a mixed account.

He wrote both down.

Ruan approved of the bruise receiving a whole sentence.

***

The next task was a drawer.

Its wooden side had swollen in the damp. Duan wanted it opened without breaking the papers inside or destroying a repair that could still be made.

Su Fan pulled.

It resisted.

He adjusted his grip and began to use the circulation.

Duan cleared his throat.

Su Fan stopped.

“Look first.”

The drawer had caught at one corner. More force in the present direction would twist it tighter.

He changed the angle.

It opened halfway, then stopped again.

This obstruction was different. A loose piece inside had fallen across the rear edge.

He could not solve both problems with the same pull.

Ruan watched from the stool.

“Familiar.”

“Very.”

They lifted the cabinet enough to shift the loose piece, then opened the drawer fully.

Inside lay ordinary records: purchases, repairs, old promises paid and unpaid. Nothing that justified breaking a cabinet to reach it a breath sooner.

Duan removed what he needed.

Su Fan dried the swollen edge and marked the place for later adjustment.

The comparison with fighting was obvious enough that none of them stated it.

Ah-Du did.

They all groaned.

***

After the rain, Su Fan returned to the yard alone.

He did not attempt to reproduce the bout.

He practised the smallest useful turn.

First too early. Then too late. Then without enough room for the following step.

He moved the starting place.

The turn improved.

He added the staff.

The shoulder tightened.

He removed the staff and found the simpler movement again.

This was slower than the story he had once imagined about cultivation. There was no clean ascent from knowing a principle to possessing it. The body learned under one condition, misunderstood under another, and tried to protect old injuries at inconvenient moments.

That did not mean the work was false.

It meant the work was specific.

At the end of the session he wrote the conditions beside the result.

Dry ground. Clear sight. No unexpected contact. One completed turn.

A useful beginning.

Not a claim about a fight.

***

Ruan returned for his coat before supper.

He found Su Fan covering the practice board.

“Better?”

“In one movement.”

“Good.”

“Not the whole exchange.”

“I heard you the first time.”

Su Fan smiled.

The young man stood at the gate with the repaired staff across his shoulders. He looked less effortless when he was tired. That was a useful thing to notice without taking pleasure in it.

“Do you ever get tired of beginning again?” Su Fan asked.

“Yes.”

“What do you do?”

“Complain. Eat. Begin again badly. Occasionally improve.”

It was not a polished answer.

Su Fan was grateful.

They arranged another practice only after checking the work waiting for both of them. Ruan had family business. Su Fan had the drawer and the latch. Neither obligation became less real because the practice mattered.

When he was alone, Su Fan put the leaking old weight beside the split blade.

Two objects that had once made a result look more trustworthy than it was.

He did not keep them as symbols.

Duan wanted the metal recovered and the sound wood used.

Tomorrow they would become parts of other work.

***

For twelve days, Su Fan failed to cut the rope.

It hung in the workshop yard with a wooden weight at its lower end. A child could have sliced it with a sharp knife. That was not the exercise.

He had to strike the weighted end, send force through the rope and break the weakened section near its upper knot without tearing the rest apart.

Duan had made the arrangement to test how evenly the new collar brace would bear a shock.

Su Fan had asked to use it after work.

On the thirteenth day, Duan told him he was wasting rope.

“I'll replace it.”

“With money, not promises.”

Su Fan paid for the next length before tying it up.

***

The problem was not strength.

He could break the wooden weight. He could rip the knot from its peg. He could throw the whole arrangement across the yard and achieve nothing useful.

The force needed to arrive in sequence.

His fifth-stage circulation completed two stable routes. When he joined them too early, the strike spread into his shoulders. Too late, and the impact had already passed.

He reduced the qi until the movement could barely sway the weight.

Then he practised the joining without striking at all.

Morning before work. Evening after it. Short sessions, stopped before fatigue changed the movement.

Ruan watched once and said the exercise looked intolerably dull.

Su Fan told him where the spare rope was kept.

An hour later, Ruan had paid for a replacement too.

***

The sixth stage came while Su Fan was lifting a brace into position.

He had no room to adjust his feet. Sun Lian needed the load held for another few breaths while a mason drove the wedge home.

Rather than force more qi through the same route, he let the returning pressure pass beneath it.

The two circulations joined and separated without obstruction.

His body stopped fighting the weight from both ends.

The brace remained heavy. Sweat still ran into his eyes. But the force reached the ground without collecting painfully behind his ribs.

“Wedge,” Sun Lian called.

The mason struck.

Su Fan lowered the load onto its seat.

He stood breathing for a long time afterward.

Sun Lian looked at him.

“Did something tear?”

“No.”

She pointed toward the daylight.

“Then go outside before you decide to test anything.”

***

That evening, the rope parted at the upper knot.

The wooden weight fell straight down.

Su Fan caught it before it struck his foot.

Duan inspected the broken fibres, then the unbroken lower length.

“Again tomorrow.”

Su Fan grinned.

The smith tried to maintain his severe expression and failed.

***

Ruan agreed to a controlled bout three days later.

He used enough qi to make the difference between their stages matter. Su Fan could no longer evade by recognizing the pattern alone. Ruan changed patterns. He feinted, withdrew and attacked from angles a diagram would not have supplied.

Su Fan lost the first exchange.

In the second he caught a thrust on the flat of his sword, stepped along the outside line and released a True Strike through the crossing blades.

Ruan's weapon jumped in his hand.

A small opening appeared.

Su Fan put the point against his padded chest and stopped.

Both remained still.

Then Ruan looked down at the point.

“That,” he said, “was inconvenient.”

***

He won the next three exchanges.

Su Fan left with bruises and a knowledge he had not possessed before: the distance to a ninth-stage opponent could be crossed in a particular moment, with the right position and no wasted force.

It could not be ignored.

He wrote both facts in his practice book.

Ah-Du saw the entry and asked which was more important.

Su Fan rubbed his shoulder.

“The one that hurt.”

chapters.title: The Wrong Flowers
chapters.text:
The copied page looked better than the original.

That was why Su Fan distrusted it.

The lines were straight. The figure stood evenly. The returning route passed through the body in a clean curve, untroubled by the crossed-out marks and cramped corrections that covered the older sheet.

A stranger could understand it at a glance.

A stranger could also hurt himself by following it.

Su Fan put the two pages beside each other.

The copyist waited.

“You asked for a clear copy.”

“Yes.”

“This is clear.”

“You left out the correction.”

“It made the line difficult to follow.”

“It made the line different.”

The young man leaned closer.

He had copied the shape of the first drawing and treated the later marks as damage. It was an understandable decision. The original page gave no tidy account of which hand should be trusted.

Su Fan could not solve that by pretending his own reading was certain.

He asked for a second sheet.

They would copy the disagreement.

The copyist sighed.

“That will be less handsome.”

“I know.”

***

They began with the marks whose order could be established.

The oldest line disappeared beneath a darker one. A note referred to an arrow that had later been moved. Another correction had been written where the page was already cracked.

These details did not tell them which instruction was right.

They told them which claims had come before others.

Su Fan had once read the scripture as though every surviving mark belonged to one patient intelligence leading him toward a hidden answer. Now he could see separate people disagreeing, trying, failing, and leaving evidence of both care and impatience.

The copyist asked whether the first writer had been a master.

“I don't know.”

“The second?”

“I don't know.”

“Then which name goes above the copy?”

“The title that is actually there.”

“And the rest?”

“Different hands. Order partly uncertain.”

He wrote the phrase on a scrap.

The copyist considered it.

“That sounds as though we haven't done our work.”

“We have done enough to know what we haven't done.”

The young man smiled faintly.

“A useful sentence for charging by the page.”

Su Fan laughed.

They agreed that the copy would distinguish the lines by their position and note where the order remained doubtful. No invented founder's name would make it easier to sell.

The decision cost another sheet.

Su Fan paid for it.

***

An old woman came to the copying table while they worked.

She wanted a recipe copied from a damaged booklet.

Not medicine. Pickling.

She was careful to explain that the recipe had belonged to her sister and that the last person who copied it had improved the amount of salt.

“The vegetables died.”

“They were already—” the copyist began.

“They died again.”

Su Fan moved his papers aside.

The woman unfolded the booklet. The missing edge contained part of a measurement. She knew roughly what it had said, but not enough to trust a neat reconstruction.

The copyist asked whether she wanted the gap filled.

“No. Leave a gap. I will try small jars.”

She looked at Su Fan's two drawings.

“You have a gap too.”

“Several.”

“Then don't pickle the whole harvest.”

The advice was ridiculous enough to make him laugh and accurate enough to remain with him afterward.

They copied the recipe as it survived.

The woman asked for wide margins.

“For changes?”

“For insults. If my sister's writing was the trouble all along.”

When she left, the young copyist shook his head.

“She knows exactly what she wants.”

“She knows what she can afford to lose.”

He looked again at the body drawn on his own page.

***

At the workshop, Su Fan tried to make the copied disagreement useful.

He did not attempt the disputed movement.

He set up a simple model of the load instead, using the small frame, a cord and a weight he had checked that morning. The model could show how a return pulled against a fixed point. It could not tell him whether a human joint should be asked to carry the same arrangement.

He wrote that limitation above the drawing before beginning.

Ah-Du read it.

“Very discouraging.”

“It is a model.”

“It looks like a model.”

“Then the warning should be easy to remember.”

The boy helped hold the frame while Su Fan altered the cord.

The first arrangement held.

The second shifted the load onto a narrow joint and made the wood complain.

The third looked wrong but distributed the force more evenly.

Su Fan marked the results.

Duan came over and moved the weight a finger's width.

The third arrangement failed.

Ah-Du caught the frame.

Su Fan caught the weight.

For a moment all three stood holding different parts of an argument.

Duan looked at the warning.

“Good that you wrote it.”

They reset the model.

This time they recorded the positions under which it worked, not merely that it worked.

***

The copyist arrived later with the corrected sheet.

He had come in person because he wanted to see why the difference mattered.

Su Fan showed him the model.

The young man watched the cord tighten, then glanced at the drawing of the body.

“That line is doing two things.”

“Yes.”

“I thought it was one continuous movement.”

“So did I, at first.”

“Which interpretation is right?”

“We haven't proved it.”

The copyist looked dissatisfied.

Su Fan recognized the feeling.

They compared the copied arrows with the model's limited movements. One arrow could describe direction. Another might describe a change in emphasis rather than motion. A third had no clear equivalent at all.

The copyist added a note in the margin.

He did not remove the uncertainty from the finished work.

When he left, he asked whether he could return to see the next test.

“Ask first,” Su Fan said. “It may involve something I shouldn't show without understanding it better.”

The man nodded.

That mattered too. Curiosity did not grant an automatic right to every experiment, and secrecy did not automatically make an experiment profound.

***

In the afternoon, Bao Mei borrowed the table to letter a small sign.

She examined the clean copy and the marked original.

“Which is yours?”

“The notes on the separate sheet.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“Then why are the letters different?”

Su Fan looked.

His earlier notes had been careful, cramped and slow. The recent ones were quicker. Some were less legible, written while a result remained fresh in his mind.

He had changed without deciding to change his handwriting.

Bao Mei pointed to a word.

“I would read that as something else.”

He asked what.

The mistaken reading would have reversed the meaning of the warning.

He corrected it immediately.

She watched him.

“You could make a sign for yourself.”

“What sort?”

“Write so another person can be frightened by the right thing.”

He laughed.

She returned to her own lettering.

The lesson did not require cultivation, and she did not know enough about his practice to be impressed by the fact that she had improved it.

That made the correction easier to trust.

***

Later, Su Fan sorted the papers he had begun treating as one collection.

They were not one collection.

Some belonged to the work at the gates. Some concerned his own practice. Some were copies given for a particular question. Others carried private observations whose owners had never agreed to make them part of a public theory.

He separated them.

A page with a family note on the reverse remained inside its covering. He knew the practical drawing on the front. He had no reason to read the other side.

Duan watched him make three piles.

“Moving the mess?”

“Giving it names.”

“A dangerous stage.”

Su Fan put the incomplete drawings in one wrapper and the verified measurements in another. The difference was not perfect. Some pages contained both. He marked those rather than forcing them into a cleaner category.

At the bottom lay an old attempt he had meant to discard.

The result had failed so completely that he had been embarrassed to keep it. Now he saw that it recorded a mistake he nearly made again during the morning's model test.

He put it back among the useful pages.

Not every failure was useful.

This one was.

He wrote why.

***

The question of copying the method for other people remained.

It would have been satisfying to imagine a clean manual placed in every hand that had been turned away from the sect's bowl. A path without a patron, a room full of ordinary people discovering that the old ceiling was lower than the sky.

It would also have been satisfying to forget how often his own hands had trembled after following an instruction badly.

He thought of the page whose beautiful line removed a warning.

He thought of the recipe and the whole harvest.

When a young worker asked whether he could borrow the slips for an evening, Su Fan did not answer with a declaration about secrecy.

He asked what the worker hoped to learn.

“Enough not to be useless.”

The answer hurt.

Su Fan could not make it safe by wanting to help.

He explained what he had actually tested, what he had not understood, and which early attempts had caused trouble. The worker listened with diminishing excitement.

“So you won't lend it.”

“Not as something I can tell you is safe to follow alone.”

“You followed it alone.”

“Yes.”

“And now you get to decide.”

Su Fan let the accusation stand.

He had no sentence that would make the difference pleasant.

He offered to show the ordinary load exercise that did not require opening a new route. The worker declined and left.

That evening, Su Fan recorded the conversation among the questions still requiring an answer.

He did not turn the refusal into proof that he was wiser than the man who wanted help.

***


He saw the young worker again two days later, carrying a borrowed training board.

Su Fan stopped.

The worker looked wary.

“I found someone else.”

“Who?”

“A teacher who explains what he will teach before asking for the fee.”

The words were pointed. Su Fan accepted them.

The board carried ordinary stance exercises used by an inherited school. No lineage fragment was being offered with the first lessons. The teacher expected pupils to learn balance, conditioning and how to stop before they injured one another.

“Is the fee manageable?” Su Fan asked.

“For now.”

“Have you seen the class?”

“Yes.”

He had asked the questions himself. Su Fan could hear the pride in the short answers and was glad he had not supplied them in a letter first.

The worker shifted the board under his arm.

“I still think you could have shown me more.”

“You may be right.”

That surprised him.

Su Fan continued before the admission became a promise.

“I don't know enough yet to settle the question by being certain either way.”

The young man considered him.

Then he asked whether the workshop could smooth a splintered edge on the board. It had caught his sleeve twice.

Su Fan took it inside, checked that the carved exercises would not be damaged and worked only the rough edge.

When he handed it back, the worker tested it against his cuff.

“How much?”

Su Fan named the ordinary small charge.

The man paid.

He did not ask about the scripture again.

Watching him leave, Su Fan felt the uncomfortable mixture of relief and disappointment that came when someone found a path without needing his approval.

He was pleased for the man.

He had also wanted to be the person whose answer mattered.

Both feelings were present. Neither improved the other by being denied.

He returned to the copied page and made the warning clearer.


Before sleeping, he placed the damaged original above the clean copy.

The clean version was easier to use. It was not more authoritative.

He added a note explaining which marks had been copied, which order they believed could be established, and which interpretations remained untested.

Then he signed his own contribution.

Not as a founder.

As the person who had made those particular claims.

Outside, the settlement quieted one household at a time. A door closed. Someone called for a child. The furnace was banked, and the last light from it softened the edge of the table.

Su Fan covered the papers.

Tomorrow somebody might find a better reading.

He wanted the page to leave them enough room.

***

Deng brought the wrong flowers.

Auntie Lu looked at the yellow bunch in his hand, then at the table where the marriage witness waited with his brush.

“Those are for funerals.”

“They were the freshest.”

“That is a poor defence.”

Deng studied them.

“I can get others.”

“You will miss your own wedding.”

He looked toward the door as though considering whether this would improve matters.

Auntie Lu took the flowers, put them in a jar and told him to sit down before she changed her mind.

***

The ceremony took place beneath the storehouse roof.

It had been Tan Wei's suggestion. Everyone knew where it was, the floor was dry, and no one could charge them for borrowing it without arguing with half the witnesses.

Bao Mei painted a red cloth with two birds that appeared to be disagreeing about a fish.

Deng said the birds looked happy.

Auntie Lu said one of them was clearly lying.

Old Pock drank before the reading and had to be reminded that the witness was not asking his opinion of marriage in general.

Min sat near the open door, wrapped in two blankets. Min Yao had agreed to bring him only after the place nearest the stove was surrendered.

Jin stood between his knees, keeping count of every dish that arrived.

***

Su Fan had been assigned chairs.

He fetched them from the clinic, the schoolroom and three houses. By the time he finished, half had been moved elsewhere. He considered returning them to their original arrangement, then noticed Mother Wei settling into one beside a woman who had lost her son in the flood.

He left them alone.

Ruan arrived carrying oil, salt and a sealed letter from his aunt.

The letter said she hoped Deng understood that Auntie Lu's kitchen belonged to her, regardless of marriage.

Auntie Lu read it aloud.

Deng nodded throughout.

“I had understood that before proposing.”

“Good,” she said. “Then at least one of us was thinking.”

***

During the meal, Tan Wei stole the crisp edge from Su Fan's bowl.

Su Fan moved the bowl away.

“You have your own.”

“Yours had more.”

“You counted?”

“I have been trained to observe water levels. The skill transfers.”

Su Fan tried to reclaim the piece and caught only a sleeve.

Across the table, Qiu Lan laughed so hard that she spilled her drink.

For a few minutes, nobody discussed contracts, the return or the old gate.

Sun Lian argued with Duan about whether a boat could have too many storage compartments. Bao Shun watched his daughter accept a commission without answering for her. Zhen Su's children joined Jin beneath the table and began conducting their own ceremony with two wooden spoons.

Mother Wei ate while her food was still hot.

***

Min asked to go home before sunset.

Su Fan helped him stand.

At the doorway the scholar paused beside the jar of yellow flowers.

“Appropriate,” he murmured.

Auntie Lu heard him.

“Say another word and I shall improve the match.”

Min laughed, which became a cough, which made Min Yao look sharply at both of them.

He apologized to his daughter and accepted her arm.

***

Later there was music.

The fiddle had survived the flood in a sealed grain jar. Its owner had not played it since. The first notes came unevenly. Nobody complained.

Deng held out a hand.

Auntie Lu stared at it.

“My knees.”

“Mine too.”

They moved slowly, barely leaving the place where they began.

Su Fan watched them from the wall.

Tan Wei leaned beside him, chewing the last of the stolen crisp rice.

“Do you think they'll be happy?”

Su Fan considered Auntie Lu correcting Deng's foot with her own.

“I think he'll be busy.”

His friend laughed.

When the tune ended, Deng bowed so low he nearly failed to straighten. Auntie Lu hauled him upright by the collar.

The whole room applauded.

chapters.title: The Missing Word
chapters.text:
Min could no longer hold the scripture for long.

He managed the first three slats before his fingers began to shake. Su Fan pretended to be looking for a place to put his coat. By the time he turned back, the old man had lowered the bamboo onto his knees and was studying the cord as though its knot had offended him.

“The stand,” Min said.

Su Fan brought it from beside the window. One foot was shorter than the others. He folded a scrap of paper beneath it, set the scripture against the rest and waited while Min found the angle he wanted.

“Less light.”

He moved it.

“More than that.”

He moved it back a little.

“There. You could have done that first.”

“I was saving it.”

Min gave him a small, unwilling smile.

Outside, Jin and Bao Mei were trying to persuade a kite to rise in a wind that kept changing its mind. Bao Mei held the frame above her head. Jin ran whenever she shouted, whether or not she had let go. The kite had already travelled farther along the ground than through the air.

The old scholar watched them for several breaths.

“He needs a longer tail.”

“Jin?”

“The kite. Though a tail might slow the boy sufficiently for instructions.”

Su Fan opened his practice book on the stool between them. The room had become crowded since Min Yao arrived. A child's shoes stood beside a case of legal papers; clean washing hung above a trunk of damaged books. There was a bowl under the window to catch rain from a seam nobody had yet managed to mend. Someone had put a bright pebble in the bowl. Jin's contribution, probably. It made the drip sound different.

Min turned away from the window.

“You found the mark underground.”

“Yes.”

“Beside instructions for grease?”

“Yes.”

“I had hoped for something less dignified than a temple.”

Su Fan unfolded his drawing. He had brought the copy made from his own measurements, with the uncertain parts left in lighter ink. The open-centred mark appeared beside the maintenance wheel. Below it were the tallies and the later complaint about a crew leaving before its work was done.

Min leaned forward too quickly. A cough interrupted him. He held up one finger while Su Fan reached for the water, insisting on finishing the cough before accepting assistance with it.

“Now,” he said, when he could. “From the entrance.”

Su Fan began with the tunnel. He described where they had set the lamps, the narrow passage into the chamber, the wheel and the repair marks. When he reached the broken plate and its strange upward drip, Min stopped him.

“Upward from what?”

“The lower edge.”

“Toward the plate?”

“For a little distance. Then it fell.”

“How far?”

“I didn't measure it.”

“Did it happen before you touched the wheel?”

Su Fan considered. He could remember the small bright movement very clearly. The order around it was less certain.

“I noticed it afterward. That doesn't tell us when it began.”

Min nodded and pointed to the blank beside the drawing. Su Fan wrote the distinction there.

The questions continued. Was the mark cut above the grease instruction or beneath it? Did the tool marks cross? Which repair had covered which tally? Su Fan answered some. For others he had only the drawing, and the drawing had recorded what he had thought important that day.

By the time they finished, it looked less complete.

Min seemed pleased.

“I should have taken another rubbing,” Su Fan said.

“Perhaps. You might also have had a wall fall on you while obtaining it. There are limits to what a scholar can reasonably demand from somebody else's head.”

“You used to demand rather a lot.”

“I was younger.”

“Last month?”

“A vigorous period.”

The kite struck the shutter. Jin shouted an apology to the house. Min closed his eyes and listened until the child had retrieved it.

***

The passage they wanted lay near the end of the scripture's first section.

A piece of the bamboo had split away. Enough ink survived to prove there had been a character there; not enough survived to tell them which character. Min's older translation treated the line as a warning against receiving power from another person. Beneath it, in smaller writing, he had proposed a second reading and then crossed half of that out.

Su Fan held the slat steady while Min placed two slips beside it.

“The first assumes this refers to the source,” the scholar said. “Where the power comes from. The other may refer to the pattern entering the body, and what it replaces.”

He tapped the surviving words with the dry end of his brush.

“Receiving another's strength. Receiving an arrangement already completed. Similar enough for a careless reader to feel satisfied. Different enough to matter.”

“Those are not the same instruction.”

“No.”

“Which is right?”

“I don't know.”

He said it without the little flourish that had once made uncertainty sound like something he was permitting for Su Fan's benefit.

Su Fan studied the missing place. At first, when he had scarcely managed a warmth beneath his ribs, he had wanted the scripture to tell him that every refusal he had ever received was wrong. A prohibition against borrowed power would have been easy to cherish. It would also have made Tan Wei's choice seem simpler than it was.

“The first reading would forbid learning almost anything.”

“It might refer only to transferred cultivation.” Min paused for breath. “It might be a poor reading. It might even be poor advice.”

“You think the scripture could be wrong?”

The old man glanced toward the window. Bao Mei was tying a strip of cloth to the kite while Jin supervised with intolerable confidence.

“I have spent my life correcting books. It would be a strange respect to stop because one helped you.”

Su Fan sat back.

The stool rocked. He caught himself, then looked down at the stone someone had placed beneath its loose leg. He had been sitting on a repair without asking who had made it or whether their name deserved his trust.

Min followed his glance.

“An excellent chair,” he said. “Until you lean that way.”

“I was thinking about the correction.”

“Then you have found its practical application.”

They returned to the words. Min asked Su Fan to read the preceding instructions aloud. On the first attempt he read what he remembered. Min stopped him at a changed ending.

“On the bamboo.”

Su Fan began again, slower.

The surviving passage described a route that could be held open by an arrangement elsewhere. It warned of a return finding an easier path than the one the practitioner intended. Whether that warning condemned all such arrangements or demanded that their costs be understood remained beyond the missing character.

Su Fan thought of Han, whose knowledge had not been enough to preserve the terms he had explained to Tan Wei. He thought of the blue cords of the cheap charm around the quarry wheel. Both belonged to inherited cultivation. He could not make the rescued hand disappear merely because he disliked what had followed.

“Could we test the two meanings?” he asked.

“We can test particular effects. A test cannot recover ink that is gone.”

Min drew a shallow bowl on a spare sheet. He added a line entering it, then another leaving.

“This could tell a mason not to use water from his neighbour. Or it could tell him to inspect the channel before accepting the neighbour's whole supply. Show me one wet foundation and I still cannot tell you which sentence the original builder wrote.”

“But I could learn which channel flooded it.”

“Yes. That would be useful work.”

The brush slipped. A dark streak crossed the bowl.

Min stared at it. Su Fan waited, uncertain whether to offer a new sheet.

“Now the drawing is more accurate,” Min said. “Somebody has made an error in the middle of the explanation.”

He laughed, then coughed until he had to put the brush down.

Su Fan gave him the water. This time Min took it before being asked.

***

They stopped working on the scripture and opened Su Fan's practice record instead.

It was an untidy collection. He had added pages when money allowed, stitched others to a surviving edge and wrapped the whole thing in cloth after medicine ruined part of a drawing. The clean copies were useful, but this was the book he actually carried to the yard. Grit lodged in the fold beside his account of the first circuit. A flattened insect had acquired a permanent place beneath a failed rope trial.

Min inspected that page with particular interest.

“Another practitioner?”

“It flew into the ink.”

“A regrettable commitment.”

Su Fan turned to the comparison between his early circulation and the joined routes that had settled at the sixth stage. He explained the rope exercise, how arriving with more force had broken the wrong part, and how he had reduced the movement until he could tell where its timing failed.

Min asked to see the failures.

Su Fan found them. There were more than he remembered, though several had been reduced to an angry line across the page.

“When was this one?”

“Before the first clean strike.”

“I had inferred that much.”

“Three days before. Perhaps four.”

“And this?”

“The same week.”

Min laid his fingers on the edge of the sheet.

“You should date the failures.”

“I date the successes.”

“You may need to know which mistake preceded which success.”

Su Fan borrowed a brush. He could establish some dates from the work accounts: a trial made after a delivery, one interrupted by rain, another on the day Duan had made him replace the rope with money rather than a promise. For the rest he wrote the uncertainty. It was irritating to discover how much he had forgotten about evenings he had considered important while living them.

Min drew one of his own notebooks from beside the bed.

“Here.”

It fell open at a paragraph bracketed in red. Beside it stood the word *wrong*, followed by nothing at all.

“Why?” Su Fan asked.

“If I knew, I would not be showing it to you.”

The notebook was old. The judgement had been made with the certainty of a man who expected to remember his reasons forever.

“I thought you kept everything.”

“I kept the paper.”

Su Fan looked from that omission to his own crossed-out drawing. He added a sentence beneath it, explaining what had gone wrong rather than what he had thought of himself afterward.

Outside, Jin gave an enormous shout. The kite had risen above the roof at last. Its new tail swung behind it, and for a few moments the frame held steady against the pale sky.

Min watched with his mouth slightly open.

Su Fan left the brush resting across the ink dish. He did not ask the next question until the old man's eyes returned to him.

They made a separate note about the open-centred mark. Su Fan had seen it on the scripture's cover and beside the chamber wheel. That was all he could establish. It might have belonged to a craft, a place, an office or a tradition neither of them knew. Its repetition did not supply a founder's name.

Min asked him to leave space beneath the note.

“For another occurrence?”

“For anything that makes this one less impressive.”

Su Fan smiled and left the space.

***

Min Yao came in with soup and took possession of the stool before either man could call the work nearly finished.

The bowl smelled of greens and softened grain. Min made a face while it was still in her hand.

“You complain before you know,” she said.

“Experience.”

“Eat.”

She moved the scripture out of reach, covered the ink and put the bowl where the reading stand had been. Her father's protest concerned the displaced pages rather than the meal. She arranged them in precisely the order he indicated and waited until he could find nothing else to correct.

Su Fan began putting his notes away.

A sheet beneath Min Yao's elbow caught his attention. It carried a small table of variant characters in a hand he recognized from the contract copies she had made. One of the forms matched the damaged passage.

“Did you learn those from your father?” he asked.

“Some.” She looked at Min. “The useful ones. The rest I learned after leaving.”

The scholar lifted his spoon. The small movement of his mouth might have been a smile or the effort of accepting a statement he would once have contested.

“Can you look at the missing character?” Su Fan asked.

“After he has eaten. And I will need the surrounding pages, not only the two readings you prefer.”

He had not realized he had selected them that way. He placed the relevant copies with the others.

Min Yao examined the book cover while he tied his parcel.

“That cord is cutting the edge.”

“I'll loosen it.”

“Use a wider one.”

Her father closed his eyes.

“An entire household of critics.”

“You taught us to read.”

“I see the defect in the arrangement now.”

The soup was still warm when he began eating.

At the door, Su Fan looked back. Min Yao held the bowl while her father steadied the spoon. Neither remarked on the division of work. She asked whether he wanted more salt. He said the food had been over-salted in anticipation of his complaint. She put a small pinch on the side anyway.

Su Fan left before his presence turned their ordinary argument into something they had to perform for a visitor.

***

The kite was caught on a beam.

Jin stood beneath it with the string wrapped around both fists. Bao Mei had gone to fetch a longer stick. Every pull made the kite's upper corner fold more tightly against the wood.

“Stop,” Su Fan said.

“I almost had it.”

“I know. Let me hold this.”

Jin surrendered the string reluctantly. Su Fan asked him to fetch the low bench, then climbed only high enough to reach the trapped corner. The paper had torn beside a rib. He lifted the frame free instead of dragging it along the rough wood.

On the ground, Jin inspected the damage.

“Can you mend it?”

“Bao Mei can mend the paper better than I can.”

“Can you make it fly higher?”

“Probably not.”

The child looked disappointed in the amount of cultivation he had purchased by asking.

Su Fan sat on the step. The line had formed a dense knot where Jin had wound it around his hands. He loosened the first loop with his smallest finger.

“Are the marks in the tunnel magic?” Jin asked.

“Some may be.”

“Can you read them?”

“Not yet.”

“Grandfather can.”

Through the open window, Su Fan saw Min Yao adjusting the blanket across her father's knees. Min had put down the spoon. He was watching the bowl as though it contained something he meant to remember.

“He can read some,” Su Fan said.

“More than you.”

“Much more.”

Jin considered this answer, then sat beside him. Their shoulders were nearly level because the child had chosen the upper step.

“Will he teach me all of them?”

Su Fan worked another loop loose.

“I think he would like to.”

The child accepted that as enough for now. He began describing the kite's flight in a version that gave himself credit for most of the wind. Su Fan listened until Bao Mei returned, out of breath, carrying a stick too long to turn through the narrow gap beside the house.

“You've got it down,” she said.

“Yes.”

She looked at the stick, then at Jin.

“You could have shouted.”

“I did shout. When it was flying.”

Bao Mei set the stick against the wall and went to inspect the tear. Jin watched her for a while, then held out the worst of the tangled line.

“Can you do this one?” he asked.

Su Fan took it. One end was free, and he could see where the first loop passed under the second.

He began there.

chapters.title: First Water
chapters.text:
The First Water notice went up beside a list of missing buckets.

For a little while, more people read the buckets.

Auntie Lu had written the list herself, with descriptions sufficient to distinguish a household vessel from one borrowed by the kitchen and subsequently claimed as ancestral property. The ceremony notice was handsome, crowded with seals, and less specific about what anyone was expected to return.

Su Fan stood behind Tan Wei while the clerk smoothed its corners against the board.

Seventh day of the planting month. First morning bell. All nine stations to take their assigned positions for renewal of the shared formation.

Below the principal order, a smaller paragraph continued the emergency declaration through renewal and the subsequent stabilization period.

Tan Wei read that paragraph twice.

“No date,” he said.

The clerk, who was carrying a pot of paste and had no authority over either time or water, pretended to misunderstand.

“The seventh. At the top.”

“For the end.”

“I only brought the notice.”

“I know.”

Tan Wei stepped aside so the next person could read. He did not make the clerk stay to defend the entire river office. That restraint left him looking angrier than a quarrel might have done.

Five weeks had passed since Su Fan's sixth circuit settled. He had spent the mornings in the yard and the days at the western chamber, returning with stone dust in his hair and a new difficulty to discuss over supper. The joined circulation no longer surprised him whenever it held. It took work all the same. A long day could leave him clumsy enough to miss the hole in a buckle.

The chamber had become more familiar too. A straight brace now occupied a place he remembered as a dark gap. The collar moved through its dry trial without catching. A mason had scratched a small fish in the mortar beside the entrance, then rubbed it out when Jiang arrived with her measurements.

None of that amounted to water passing safely through it.

“Six days,” Tan Wei said.

Su Fan nodded.

Behind them, a farmer asked whether the ceremony meant the upper channels would open on time. His seedlings were ready. A woman wanted to know whether the delegates would buy provisions locally or bring everything with them. Two children were interested only in the drums.

First Water had been held at the beginning of planting for eighty-three years, with exceptions for drought, war and a season Old Pock remembered with delight, when the supervising elder had misread the calendar and everyone below him had been required to call it an adjustment.

The ceremony meant something beyond the order at the bottom of the page. It meant channels running, fields supplied, boats moving without scraping their bellies along mud. Su Fan could not look at the people gathering beneath the notice and wish the river would fail merely to prove its keepers wrong.

A messenger found him there.

The upper station requested his presence. Jiang was already on her way.

Tan Wei read the message over his shoulder.

“Bring back what they actually say.”

“I will.”

“And eat before you go.”

Su Fan looked at him.

“Mother Wei has help now?”

“She is expanding.”

***

The prepared room stood open.

Su Fan recognized it from the earlier offer. The walls had been washed. A narrow bed now occupied the space beside the inner door, with a folded blanket and a covered tray waiting on a stool. The coupling rings had new padding where they would touch a seated body. Another channel ran from the lower frame to a separate vessel on the floor.

He stopped at the threshold.

Jiang had arrived before him. She was examining the added channel, one hand holding the end of her measuring cord. Wen Zhao stood near the window with a writing board against his forearm. He nodded to Su Fan, but did not give the reassuring smile of a man who could guarantee the meeting's result.

Pei Gang waited beside the chair.

His injured hand was covered. The other rested on a length of polished wood fixed to the frame.

“I have addressed the injury risks identified in the earlier trials,” he said.

“Some,” Jiang replied.

“Those for which we have measurements.”

The elder did not sound offended. He sounded as though he had already spent considerable money answering a criticism and expected that fact to be acknowledged.

Su Fan walked around the chair without touching it. The new padding would prevent one kind of injury. It also made the rings look more comfortable than their purpose allowed. He crouched beside the added channel.

“Where does this discharge?”

“Into the isolated vessel during separation,” Pei said. “The return is reduced before the subject is released.”

“Who reduces it?”

“The supervising practitioner.”

“From here?”

Pei indicated the control on the arm of the frame. Su Fan traced the route with his eyes, from the seated position to the coupling and away toward the floor. A person in the chair could see the control. He could not reach it with both rings closed.

The elder watched him discover that.

“An operator in distress cannot be required to perform the separation himself.”

It was a sensible answer. Su Fan hated how sensible it was.

“Will I be allowed to stop?”

“If stopping does not endanger the river system.”

“Who decides?”

Pei looked at him.

“We have already had this discussion.”

“Yes.”

Outside the window, workers were assembling the delegation's reception shelter. A length of cloth snapped in the wind. Someone called for another ladder, then called again when the first request produced only advice.

Su Fan stood. His right ear caught the hammering as an uneven pressure rather than a useful direction. He turned until the elder remained on his left.

Pei noticed. His gaze passed over the damaged ear and returned to the frame.

“There will be a healer present throughout.”

“Chosen by whom?” Jiang asked.

“By agreement.”

“Mother Wei?” Su Fan said.

“If she accepts the assignment.”

The answer was another improvement. He made himself register it rather than dismiss everything in the room because he wanted to leave.

Wen Zhao wrote a short note. When Su Fan glanced at him, the inspector said, “I am here to observe the terms offered and the response. Operational command remains with the elder.”

He had stated the limit before anybody had to discover it at the wrong moment.

Su Fan wished more than ever that the limit were different.

***

The new agreement was shorter.

One spring return. A defined period of supervised use. Payment to the quarry settlement. An independent record of Su Fan's method rather than an attribution to an unverified founder. Examination afterward by a healer acceptable to both parties.

Pei let him read without interruption.

That made it harder to behave as though the paper were merely a trap laid by a man unwilling to hear him. Some of the earlier objections had been answered. The record of his method would remain his. The initial period had an end. The settlement would receive real money with which to buy materials already being argued over.

Jiang moved to his side when he reached the continuation provision.

Where necessary to preserve operational stability, emergency extension could be ordered until safe separation was possible.

Su Fan put one finger beside the words.

“How long could that be?”

“We do not expect an extension.”

“That isn't a duration.”

Pei's covered hand tightened against the table edge.

“The maximum cannot be established before we know the response.”

“So the part that tells me when it ends depends on the part we haven't tested.”

“It depends on whether ending it at that moment would injure the people you intend to help.”

Su Fan looked toward the chair.

A cup stood on the bedside stool. It was an ordinary glazed cup with a chipped base. Someone had stocked the room in the expectation that a man would sit there, become thirsty, drink, and continue. The thought frightened him more than the polished rings.

“You do not know whether the system can release me once it begins using me.”

“We have designed a separation.”

“You have designed one for a thing you have never operated.”

Pei's gaze sharpened.

“So have your friends.”

Su Fan had an answer ready and lost it before speaking.

The mechanical collar had passed its dry trial. They had shifted weights, checked the walls, rebuilt a support whose first version had looked sound. The western throat had not carried the actual spring return. Sun Lian's calculations were careful. Care was not a result that had already happened.

He heard the hammer outside strike several quick blows, pause, then resume at a different place.

Jiang took the agreement from the table and laid it beside her own drawings.

“That is why we have asked for a partial flow test.”

Pei did not look away from Su Fan.

“Then let us discuss the same standard for both proposals.”

They did.

It was an unpleasant discussion, and more useful than the one Su Fan had prepared in his head on the walk uphill.

***

Jiang spread Sun Lian's latest measurements across the table.

The drawings included the errors. One stone seat had shifted between surveys. A timber had been replaced after splitting under a lower load than expected. The proposed limit was marked in red beside the throat, not hidden in a separate account that only the person making the claim would read.

Pei studied the sheets in silence.

“The collar has passed its dry-load test,” Jiang said. “The wall braces are seated. We need permission for a partial flow before renewal.”

“And if it damages the chamber?”

“We close the upstream isolation.”

“If the closure holds.”

“If the closure holds,” she agreed. “That is why the test is partial and the crew remains outside the bearing recess.”

Su Fan watched the elder's good hand move over the drawing. It stopped at a junction he had helped expose. Pei asked about the depth behind the repair, and Jiang gave him the measurement without consulting her notes.

“And the north wedge?”

“Replaced. Two supports behind it.”

“Different loading during transition.”

“We have allowed for it.”

“You have calculated for it.”

“Yes.”

The distinctions became exhausting without becoming meaningless. Su Fan could see how a man might eventually agree to anything simply to stop having each useful word taken apart. He could also see the narrow places where a careless answer would matter to the people below.

“What duration?” Pei asked.

“Twelve minutes of controlled flow for the full interval. The preliminary test is shorter.”

“And repairing the chamber afterward?”

“Two days of station service,” Su Fan began.

“Three,” Jiang corrected. “Allowing for inspection.”

He had repeated the best estimate and left out the part nobody enjoyed paying for. He felt his face warm. Pei gave him a level look and then returned to the sheet.

The elder lifted one corner of the drawing. Beneath it lay the list of operators who had requested relief from their permanent impressions. He did not pick that up.

“Could the test be completed before the delegation arrives?” Wen Zhao asked.

“Not with time to repair and inspect a failed result,” Jiang said.
