For a moment Su Fan thought Pei might agree anyway. The elder had found faults worth discussing rather than rejecting the work out of hand. He had begun asking the questions of someone deciding how a mechanism could function.

Then he touched the First Water order.

“The regional delegation is already travelling. The repairs have been certified ready. I will not interrupt renewal for an unproven alternative whose principal advocate refuses a supervised examination.”

Jiang stood very still.

“The date can move.”

“It will not.”

A strip of reception cloth blew across the window. For a moment it hid the workers outside and filled the room with a pale shadow.

Wen Zhao lowered his brush.

“The refusal of a partial trial will be included with the objection.”

“Include the proposed interruption to service,” Pei said.

“I will.”

“And the available supervised alternative.”

“That too.”

No one had been shouted into silence. The door remained open. Su Fan could leave without agreeing to the chair, and the absence of an immediate threat did nothing to reduce the pressure of what would happen in six days.

He slid the unsigned agreement back across the table.

Pei watched his hand.

“You may reconsider before the return.”

Su Fan did not promise an answer different from the one he had just given.

***

Under the station's outer roof, Jiang stopped to roll her drawings.

Her fingers had left damp marks on the paper. Su Fan took the lower end while she found the cord. For a while neither spoke.

Wen Zhao joined them with his board beneath his arm.

“I can record your objection,” he told her. “I cannot command the gates.”

“I know.”

“A record may change what follows.”

“It will not lower the collector during the ceremony.”

“No.”

The inspector looked tired. Su Fan had wanted him to produce some authority neither of them had considered, a phrase that would require the elder to stop. Wen offered no invented power to make their departure easier.

“Send the final measurements,” he said. “And the operating limits. Not only the reasons you believe it can work.”

Jiang nodded.

Su Fan looked down the valley. The quarry settlement showed as a cluster of roofs above the pale scar where Mudgate had been. Farther west, the clearing crews had exposed a dark line through the marsh. Men looked very small against the ground they had moved.

“You heard him,” Jiang said as they started downhill.

“Which part?”

“The part about our own design.”

“Yes.”

“Bring it to the meeting.”

“I wasn't going to hide it.”

“I did not say you were. But there is a difference between admitting risk when somebody asks and putting it on the table first.”

He disliked the correction because he could already imagine himself delivering the meeting's most satisfying news: Pei had refused them, the date would not move, the good people below must act. It was a clean account. It omitted the untested chamber and the three days an unsuccessful trial would cost other workers.

They passed a cart carrying painted boards for the ceremony. Its driver asked Jiang which platform they belonged to. She read the delivery mark, gave him the correct turning and stepped aside so he could take it.

The work of the ceremony continued to need sensible answers.

***

At the workshop, Sun Lian was testing a loop of measuring cord against the marked beam. She saw Su Fan's face, finished the comparison and put the cord away.

“How much time?”

“Six days.”

“The partial test?”

“Refused.”

She waited.

He told her about the room, the improved separation channel and the better agreement with the same uncertain end. He repeated Pei's objection to their untested mechanism. He included Jiang's correction from two days to three.

Sun Lian listened without interrupting. When he finished, she asked whether the elder had identified a particular fault.

“The north wedge under transition. Jiang showed him the added supports.”

“We'll inspect it again.”

He had expected anger. There was anger in her face, but it did not relieve her of the need to look at a wedge.

Duan came to the doorway. Ah-Du stood behind him, holding a piece of iron in tongs and trying to appear as though he had a legitimate reason to listen.

“Put that back before you lose the heat,” the smith said.

The boy went.

Sun Lian pulled a clean board onto the bench. She drew three headings and left space beneath each.

“What is that?” Su Fan asked.

“Who needs to hear the failure cases. Who has already heard them. Who we're assuming knows because we are tired of explaining.”

She considered the third heading, then underlined it.

“Call the others.”

Su Fan went out into the yard. From the upper road he could hear the announcement bell being tested, one bright note at a time. A child near the kitchen tried to copy its rhythm by striking a spoon against a bowl.

He found Tan Wei at the water tubs and told him the meeting would begin after the evening shift.

“Did you eat?” his friend asked.

Su Fan opened his mouth.

Tan Wei pointed toward the kitchen.

“Start there. Then tell me what they actually said.”

chapters.title: Those Who Stayed
chapters.text:
They met without Su Fan at first.

Sun Lian had asked for it while he was still carrying bowls back from the kitchen. The people taking the greatest risks needed to speak without looking at him every time somebody mentioned the purpose of the work.

He had said he understood.

Now, sitting in the workshop while voices moved behind the closed storehouse door, he was discovering how little understanding changed the desire to know what they were saying.

Duan was fitting a handle to a small plane. The wooden body stood clamped to the bench. His injured arm rested in a sling that no longer looked temporary, and he held a narrow rasp with his good hand, taking off a little wood at a time.

Su Fan watched three strokes before realizing the smith had paused for him to move his knee away from the drawer.

“Sorry.”

“An acceptable beginning.”

He shifted. Duan opened the drawer, took out a gauge and compared the handle with its mate.

“Will you tell me what they're saying?” Su Fan asked.

“I can't hear them either.”

“You know what I mean.”

The smith tested the handle with his good hand.

“Yes.”

He did not offer to go and listen.

Su Fan folded his arms, unfolded them, and reached for an axle fitting that did not need his attention. Through the open workshop door he could see Ren Bo's nephew waiting outside the meeting with two empty sacks. The boy had been sent to collect something and had allowed the errand to become an excuse to remain.

Su Fan recognized the arrangement. It did not make watching it comfortable.

“Hold this,” Duan said.

He placed the handle in Su Fan's palm and asked him to close his fingers as he would when working a plane. The grip pressed against the heel of his hand. Duan marked the place, took the wood back and removed another thin shaving.

“Who is it for?”

“A man with smaller hands than yours.”

“Then why test it on me?”

“To see whether you were capable of holding something without improving it.”

Su Fan laughed, reluctantly.

The smith's mouth moved. He set the rasp down and shifted the clamp. It took him longer than it would once have done. Su Fan waited until he asked for the loose screw to be steadied, then held only that.

A voice rose inside the storehouse. Another answered. He could not distinguish the words, but his body leaned toward them anyway.

Duan looked at him.

“Do you expect everyone to choose what you would choose?”

“No.”

“Good. They may not.”

Su Fan stared at the shavings on the bench. He had been ready to accept refusals nobly. That was already a way of placing himself at the centre of other people's choices.

He picked a shaving from his sleeve and put it with the rest.

Outside, the nephew abandoned his empty sacks and went to find food. Su Fan envied him the excuse.

***

When they called him in, the table had been cleared of everything except the gate drawing and three lists.

People leaving the lower work area before renewal.

People staying to operate the bypass.

People who had not yet decided.

Sun Lian had placed the undecided sheet as carefully as the others. It was not a small corner reserved for names somebody intended to move later.

Tan Wei stood beside Han. Qiu Lan sat with a cup of water between her hands. Jiang was at the end of the table, her outer coat folded beneath her board. Ren Bo had taken a place close enough to the door that he could leave without asking the whole room to move.

Su Fan found his own name beside the collar position. Tan Wei's was on the staying list, with Han's and Qiu Lan's. Several names appeared on a separate sheet concerning the retention of existing bonds.

Qiu Lan saw him looking.

“Mine is there too.”

“I see it.”

“Good. I am not signing one thing by being present for another.”

Han pulled the drawing toward him.

“We are not cutting every connection. The collar isolates the returning branch. Inside that interval, an operator may separate the permanent impression or remain linked through a local loop.”

He used two lengths of cord to show the difference. The cords were ordinary kitchen string, one stained where somebody had used it to hang dried peppers. Su Fan had seen enough impressive diagrams made from less useful material to find the simplicity reassuring.

“How many wish to leave the permanent impressions?” he asked.

“Eleven confirmed. Four still deciding.”

“How many keep them?”

“Most.”

Su Fan nodded.

Han watched the nod. The old teacher seemed to have been waiting for it, and that made Su Fan uncomfortable.

“You don't need my agreement about that,” he said.

“No,” Han replied. “But I need to know you understand which work you are assisting.”

That was fairer than the small argument Su Fan had almost made.

A woman near the window asked whether retaining a local impression meant retaining the district's entire emergency obligation. Min Yao turned the relevant page toward her. The answer was still disputed. The mechanism could make a separation possible; it could not guarantee that an office would describe the result as the woman intended.

“Then I want that uncertainty beside my name,” she said.

Zhen Su wrote it down.

Another worker asked about pay for the days already missed. Someone wanted to know who would tell a family if the passage had to be evacuated. These were not questions that could be answered by saying the work mattered.

Su Fan sat on the bench they had left for him and listened.

***

Sun Lian began with the ways the chamber could fail.

She did not stand beneath the lantern like a lecturer. She knelt beside the drawing, put a spare wedge at the throat and asked Ren Bo to hold the string representing the winch line.

“If the wall cracks before full flow, this closes.” She moved the little wooden gate. “We withdraw. Nobody goes back for a gauge. Nobody goes back because the crack looks smaller from inside.”

“What if the collar is halfway?” Ren Bo asked.

“We keep the western throat open and the upstream regulator reduced while the local crews stabilize. We do not force the collar the rest of the way because the drawing looks better with it there.”

“And if the upper return rises?”

Jiang placed her hand beside the red mark.

“Beyond this corrected reading, we abandon the separation and clear the chamber.”

A man who had helped build the new storehouse leaned forward.

“Even if some people have begun?”

“Han manages those already in the process,” Jiang said. “The rest wait. We cannot use the chamber after it ceases to be a place where people can work.”

The silence after that answer was different from the silence before it. It contained particular people imagining particular faces.

“Who calls it?” Ren Bo asked.

“I do,” Sun Lian said. “Jiang has the upstream measure. I have the chamber. Either of us can stop it.”

Su Fan raised a hand.

She looked surprised enough that somebody laughed. He had not intended the gesture to be funny, which made his face warm.

“If I think I can hold it longer?”

“You tell us. You do not keep everyone inside while you find out.”

“What if the signal doesn't reach—”

“Then we need to repair the signal. We do not replace it with guesses about how brave you feel.”

He put his hand down.

Tan Wei studied him without smiling. Su Fan was grateful. He had wanted to ask the question honestly, and an easy joke would have helped him pretend the answer applied to somebody else.

Sun Lian slid a second wedge under the drawn brace. The timber scraped the table.

“Now tell me what happens when this one goes.”

For the next part, the people who usually worked the lines did most of the talking. Ren Bo pointed out that a man holding the guide could not also signal the upper landing. Qiu Lan asked where an operator leaving the local loop would meet the healer. A labourer put his cup on the supposed retreat path and said that was where the spare tool crate had stood yesterday.

They moved the crate on the drawing. Someone was sent to move the real one before the correction became a reassuring fiction.

Su Fan had designed none of those questions.

***

They went down to the passage in small groups while there was still light.

The first crew stayed at the upper entrance. The second walked through with Sun Lian, who pointed out where the floor narrowed and which side of the winch remained clear when the line was under strain. Su Fan carried a lamp although it was not yet needed. He wanted his hands occupied.

Ren Bo's nephew followed them as far as the lower landing.

“You said you were only coming to hear,” he told his uncle.

“I came to hear.”

“And now?”

“I heard.”

Ren Bo stopped beside the lower winch. He knew the wheel well enough to stand out of its turning path without looking down. His nephew had been the man pulled from danger at the crane, the day Su Fan lost part of his hearing. The boy's glance moved from the winch to Su Fan's ear and away again.

“You could do the tally above.”

“Yes,” Ren Bo said. “And you will.”

The nephew opened his mouth.

“Not because you're useless down here. Because someone must know who has come out, and because you write more clearly when you're angry with me.”

“That isn't an answer.”

“It is the work I am asking you to do.”

The older man did not order his nephew to approve. He took the tally board from under his arm and held it out until the boy accepted it.

Sun Lian waited through the exchange. Then she showed Ren Bo the place from which he would call the sequence. He tested the reach to the line, frowned, and asked whether the guide could be moved a little. The answer required measurements, not reassurance.

Su Fan followed the retreat route back toward daylight. In a dry passage, with no pressure in the throat and everybody moving politely, it looked almost generous. He imagined a dropped lamp, a man turning back for another, someone unable to lift a foot high enough over the rough step.

He marked the step for repair.

He did not decide that marking it had finished the problem.

***

By the time they returned to the storehouse, Old Pock and Deng had developed a disagreement about boats.

It concerned a landing neither intended to use, which did not prevent them spending several minutes establishing who knew it better.

Sun Lian let them finish until the argument began producing facts they had already produced once.

“Western landing, Pock. Second landing, Deng. Show the boat crews the marks before morning. Argue somewhere dry afterward.”

Old Pock accepted the western work with an elaborate show of suffering. Deng took the second landing and immediately began listing what would have to be moved from it.

Auntie Lu said the upper kitchen would remain open.

“That at least is safe,” someone murmured.

She turned.

“Come cook for frightened people who all believe they are late for something. Then tell me about safe work.”

The man reconsidered aloud. She allowed him to carry the grain sack as evidence of his improvement.

Min Yao would take duplicate accounts to Wen Zhao and the municipal registrar. Zhen Su would remain at the quarry with the originals. They had already agreed which pages were public statements and which contained medical details that belonged only with the people responsible for them.

A woman asked why there needed to be so many copies.

“Because a copy in the same room as its original can burn with it,” Zhen Su said.

She had said it simply. No one requested an explanation of how she knew.

Ruan's place remained unfilled. His family expected him at the delegation reception, and no answer had yet arrived from him.

Su Fan looked at the empty space beside the outer passage.

“We plan without him until he answers,” Sun Lian said.

“Yes.”

He meant it, though he disliked imagining the narrow entrance without Ruan's sword there.

When the lists were read back, two people moved their names to leaving. One undecided worker asked for until morning, because his wife had gone to another settlement and he would not make a choice that would reach her only as a completed announcement.

Nobody called him cowardly.

Nobody praised the people staying as though the ones leaving had failed a test.

There was still relief, disappointment and a little resentment in the room. The lists did not abolish any of it. They gave the work a shape that the people doing it had actually seen.

***

Near midnight, Su Fan found Tan Wei fastening a new cord around his notebook.

His friend sat beneath the workshop eaves with an oilcloth wrapper spread over his knees. A lamp stood on an overturned box. The three blue marks above his wrist moved faintly with his pulse.

Su Fan sat on the step beside him.

“You've tied that too close to the edge.”

“I know.”

“Do you want—”

“I want you to hold the corner while I undo it.”

Su Fan held the corner.

From the storehouse came the last clatter of cups. Beyond that, the settlement was quiet except for a mule complaining at something in its sleep. Tan Wei threaded the cord through again, tested the knot and pulled it apart once more.

“Are you frightened?” Su Fan asked.

“Yes.”

“Me too.”

Tan Wei looked up.

“Of the gate?”

“Of making one mistake and calling it the only choice.”

His friend turned the notebook in his hands. Its pages had thickened where water once got into the binding. Some of the entries concerned work, some ordinary things he wanted to remember as his own. Su Fan knew that without needing to see them.

“Then listen when someone gives you another,” Tan Wei said.

Su Fan nodded.

After a while he added, “I won't always know I'm doing it.”

“No. You usually look very reasonable.”

He laughed, and Tan Wei's mouth softened.

They worked on the wrapper together. The first knot made it too difficult to open quickly; the second left a loose fold where water could collect. Tan Wei settled on an ordinary tie he used for clothes on a ferry journey.

“There.”

Su Fan tested the corner he had been holding. It stayed flat.

“You could have used that at the beginning.”

“I was saving it.”

The answer reminded Su Fan of Min and the reading stand. He almost repeated the whole conversation, then let the memory remain where it was for the moment.

Tan Wei put the wrapped notebook beneath his coat. He asked whether Su Fan had brought the spare release-tool binding back from the chamber.

“Yes.”

“Bring it here. Yours was coming loose.”

Su Fan went to fetch it.

When he returned, his friend had made room beneath the lamp. They sat shoulder to shoulder over the ordinary cord, neither of them pretending it could keep every dangerous thing out.

chapters.title: The Steward's Seal
chapters.text:
Jiang opened the station stores herself.

The keeper had the key ready, but kept his hand closed around it while he read her requisition. Su Fan waited beside the cart with two labourers and a coil of packing rope. They had been told to arrive early. The upper road was already filling with deliveries for the reception platform.

“These braces were assigned to the northern inspection platform,” the keeper said.

“The platform has three replacements. The western bearing has none.”

“The elder's order is attached.”

“I can see it. My order is this one.”

Jiang put the second sheet on top and pressed her seal beside the listed quantities.

The keeper looked at the mark, then at her face. He was an older man with ink on the sides of his fingers and a strip of cloth tied around one knee. Su Fan had seen him wave away demands from impatient disciples. He had also seen him count ordinary nails as though each would be missed personally by the man who paid for them.

“Will it protect us?” he asked.

“It records that I instructed you. Keep a copy.”

She did not tell him it was the same thing.

After a moment he opened his hand. The key turned reluctantly, then the door pulled free of its swollen sill. Inside, the warehouse smelled of old rope, oil and timber kept just dry enough to remain valuable.

The keeper fetched the copying board himself.

Su Fan steadied it while he took an impression of the seal. The man checked the copied quantities against the original before allowing the labourers through the door.

“Three braces,” he said. “Not the loose ends stacked beside them. Those have another assignment.”

“We want the sound ones,” Jiang said.

“I want everybody to remember which sound ones they received.”

She nodded. The argument had become a record they could both live with, though neither looked pleased by it.

***

They moved through the stores with Jiang's list.

Wedges. Good rope. Copper wire for the warning bells. A crate of ordinary lamps whose flames would not go out because an inherited command had interrupted the formation feeding them.

Su Fan checked the lamp catches while the keeper watched. One had been bent in storage. He set it aside instead of putting it beneath a good one where the defect would be somebody else's discovery after dark.

“That was serviceable when it came in,” the keeper said.

“Then it will be again after someone straightens this.”

He showed the damaged part. The keeper inspected it, marked the tally and fetched another lamp without being asked.

The rope took longer. Jiang wanted the coils unbound so the hidden lengths could be examined. The labourers exchanged a glance at the work. Then one spread a cloth over the rough floor while the other began feeding the first length across it.

By the time they finished, dust had reached everyone's sleeves. Jiang had found an old splice in a coil labelled new. The keeper crossed out the label in front of her.

He was angry now, but not only with the people taking his supplies.

The two pressure gauges came in separate padded cases. Jiang had checked their readings before, and checked their identities again. One would be mounted beside the working board. The second, with its polished metal face, would hang where the lower landing crew could compare the reading without crowding Sun Lian's station.

Su Fan lifted the case carefully. The polished surface caught his face for an instant, crooked and narrow through the open lid.

“Keep it upright,” Jiang said.

He adjusted his grip.

At the last shelf she stopped beside a smaller locked case.

The keeper's expression changed.

“Those are district instruments.”

“So are the gauges.”

“Those are issued against a named examiner.”

“Use my name.”

He had another key for that lock. When the lid opened, Su Fan saw thin needles nested in dark cloth, each inside a frame with small marked screws. They looked less impressive than the bowls used at the lineage assessments. There was no jewel at the centre, no place for a founder's name.

Jiang lifted one and checked that it moved freely.

“What does it answer?” Su Fan asked.

“Strain. Pressure in a channel, under specified conditions. It need not receive the operator's founder to do that.”

He looked at her.

“You had an instrument that could measure it?”

“We use them on broken formations and unclassified materials.” She watched his face. “They are inconvenient and expensive. That is not the same as impossible.”

He thought of the dark bowl, the ringing bronze classifier, the long effort to prove that what he felt was more than an error inside his own body. For a moment he wanted to be angry with everyone who had failed to place this little object in his hand sooner.

Jiang held it out, but did not release it until he had both hands ready.

“The frame has to be supported. The reading changes if you pull it out of position. That mark is a reference, not a cultivation stage. And if you force a great deal of qi into it to see whether you can, I shall take the repair cost from you personally.”

The warning restored it to the category of tools.

He rested it on the folded cloth she indicated and directed a small amount of qi beneath his thumb.

The needle trembled.

He stopped. It settled.

“Again,” she said.

He repeated the movement with less force. The needle moved a smaller distance.

Nothing about it supplied the scripture's history. Nothing declared him superior to the men whose sashes had once made the assessment hall seem larger. It registered a change where a change had occurred.

He found himself smiling.

Jiang took the instrument, closed the case and wrote its number on the requisition.

“Smile after you have carried the braces.”

***

Wen Zhao caught up with them at the loading yard.

He came without an escort and stood clear of the first brace while the labourers lowered it onto the cart. The inspector read the receipt the keeper handed him. Then he read Jiang's order.

“You are transferring district property to an unauthorized operation.”

“Yes.”

“Have you obtained an amended order?”

“No.”

He watched Su Fan place a timber pad beneath the second brace. The wood would keep it from grinding against the gauge case during the journey.

“I will have to include this,” Wen said.

“Yes.”

“You need not answer every question as though I asked whether it was raining.”

Jiang looked at him then.

“Would a speech make your duty easier?”

“No.”

“Then let us both do it.”

The keeper held his copy flat while the ink dried. A wagon for the reception platform stopped behind their cart, and its driver began complaining that they had occupied the best loading space. No one possessed sufficient authority to make two carts fit where one belonged.

Su Fan and the labourers pushed their load forward. Wen walked beside it until the road widened.

“Where are you going next?” he asked Jiang.

“To the chamber.”

“I'll come.”

She handed him the smaller case rather than ask whether he meant to stop them. He took it, checked its catch and settled it under his arm.

On the way down, a reception messenger hurried past carrying a sealed account of the stores' readiness. He bowed to Jiang, hesitated when he saw Wen carrying equipment, and continued uphill.

Su Fan wondered which version of readiness would reach the delegation first.

At the steep turn, one cart wheel struck a stone. The load shifted against its ropes. Both labourers braced while Su Fan caught the rear sideboard. The brace remained seated on its pad. The cases did not fall.

Jiang looked back from the front.

“That is why we tied it twice.”

The driver answered that he had been doing this longer than Su Fan had been alive. Then he stopped at the next level stretch and checked both ropes.

***

The western chamber was colder than the warehouse.

Water moved somewhere beyond the closed throat. It could be heard through the stone in places where the ear expected silence. Su Fan still disliked turning his damaged side toward the wall there; the dull vibration became difficult to separate from the ringing that sometimes arrived without an external cause.

Sun Lian met them at the upper landing. She inspected the new braces before speaking to Jiang.

“These are the northern platform stock.”

“Yes.”

She looked at the order, then at Wen.

“I know,” the inspector said.

The supplies went down one piece at a time. Nobody attempted to impress the observer by carrying an awkward load alone. Wen stayed where he could watch the crew's hands and the retreat path rather than in the centre of the landing, which made Su Fan like him a little more despite the record under his arm.

Han had come to inspect the local-loop fittings. He showed Wen the separate positions for operators retaining their impressions and those requesting withdrawal. Qiu Lan demonstrated how a willing practitioner could remain connected locally after the returning branch was isolated.

The inspector asked what would happen if the central pressure did not fall far enough.

“We do not begin the permanent separations,” Han said.

“And if it rises after you begin?”

“We stabilize those already under treatment. We stop taking new people into the inner line.”

“How certain is that stabilization?”

“Not certain enough for me to promise you no injuries.”

Wen looked up from his board.

Han's bad leg had begun to tremble. He shifted his weight and continued explaining. The possibility of losing a stage was not the worst of the risks. Some routes had been held open by the impression longer than an operator's own trained capacity could sustain. Under a forced return, the distinction became harder to establish in time.

“Then why proceed?” Wen asked.

Qiu Lan set down the empty basin she had been holding.

“Because being unable to promise safety is not the same as finding safety by doing nothing.”

The inspector considered her, then wrote her answer beneath Han's. He did not convert it into an approval.

Sun Lian took him along the wall braces. She showed him the repaired seat, the permitted travel of the collar and the paths that had to remain clear. When he asked about full-flow behaviour, she said they had not been allowed to test it.

He wrote that too.

Su Fan watched his brush and felt the old temptation to treat every written sentence as a gain for one side. The inspector's page contained risks they feared, actions they were taking and orders they had not obeyed. It would be an inconvenient document for everyone.

***

Wen found him later at the upper landing.

Su Fan was practising the manual release with a wooden substitute for the collar handle. The weight was wrong and he had written that on the board beside the model. The exercise taught reach and sequence, not what the actual return would feel like in his hand.

“Why are you here rather than at the office appealing the order?” Wen asked.

“We appealed it.”

“Again.”

“The return is in four days.”

The inspector glanced toward the tunnel. Two workers were moving the spare tool crate away from the retreat path. Behind them, Ren Bo argued with a man about whether a line could be reached without letting go of the wheel.

“That does not make this lawful,” Wen said.

“No.”

“It may make the order indefensible.”

Su Fan waited.

“That is not something I can decide before the evidence exists.”

He wanted to ask what evidence would be enough. A broken wall? A dead operator? Eleven people learning that their names had become conditions attached to a mechanism? The questions crowded together until they would have sounded like an accusation regardless of how he began.

Wen seemed to see the effort in his face.

“I did not say you must produce a disaster for me.”

“What can you do before one?”

“Record the measured risk. Carry an objection beyond the person who refused it. Attend when command is exercised.”

“And stop it?”

“If I acquire the authority. I have not acquired it by wishing.”

Su Fan looked down at the wooden handle. There were things he could do because his circulation differed from the inherited lines. There were many more things he could not do at all. It remained irritating to discover other people had limits too.

He went through the sequence once more while Wen watched.

The inspector asked why the spare wedge was on the opposite side of the bench from the hand that would reach for it. Su Fan moved it, tried the sequence again and found the reach easier.

Wen made no remark about having improved the plan.

***

Jiang stayed after the labourers went home.

She set the two pressure gauges side by side and compared them under the same small load. Their readings differed by an amount Su Fan would once have rounded away.

She did not adjust either dial to make them agree.

Instead she repeated the comparison, checked the instrument positions and marked both deviations on the board. Sun Lian leaned close to see the figures.

“We carry the difference in the reading,” Jiang said. “Not in our hopes.”

“If either changes from that?”

“We compare against the upstream signal and stop relying on the pair as a pair. A second number is useful only while we know why it differs.”

Su Fan helped mount the main gauge where Sun Lian could see it without leaving the brace. The polished auxiliary went higher on the landing. Its face reflected a narrow portion of the stair behind him. He noticed the movement there whenever he turned his head toward the main board.

Jiang lent him the independent needle for a short trial outside the active mechanism. He measured the pressure of his sixth-stage circulation at a few familiar points, then stopped when fatigue made his hand unsteady. The last reading was not something he wanted in his practice book. He wrote it down with the condition beside it anyway.

By the time he took the needle back, the temporary office was the only room still lit.

Jiang sat beneath a low lamp, writing on a sheet much smaller than the reports she usually used. She had reached the middle of the page. Then she stopped, rubbed her eyes and began again on another.

Su Fan knocked against the open frame.

She covered the letter with a sheet of calculations.

“The needle,” he said.

“Set it in the case.”

He did. She checked the catch, and he told her about the unsteady final reading. She nodded, apparently satisfied that he had noticed it rather than improved it in the telling.

At the door he nearly asked whether she had eaten. It was a reasonable question and also an excuse to remain close enough to learn something she had chosen not to show him.

He said goodnight instead.

As he walked away, the lamp's shadow moved across the window. Jiang had drawn the smaller page back toward her.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal
chapters.text:
The first full rehearsal failed because nobody could hear the bell.

Copper wire carried the signal cleanly from the chamber. The striker moved. The bell rang. Above it, six workers were dragging a brace across the stone floor, and the scrape swallowed the note so completely that Su Fan thought Jiang had not yet sent it.

He stood with his good ear toward the doorway, waiting.

Sun Lian came up the stairs and found three men still inside the marked area after they should have left.

“Stop.”

The men lowered the brace. The quiet afterward made the little bell sound absurdly clear when Jiang tested it again.

“We heard that,” Ren Bo said.

“Yes,” Sun Lian replied. “Now that we have stopped making the noise we will be making.”

One of the younger workers looked toward Su Fan's damaged ear. Su Fan felt the glance before turning far enough to meet it.

“I missed it,” he said. “So did you.”

The man nodded, embarrassed.

Nobody was in danger yet. That made it possible to admit the mistake without first deciding whose injury it would be blamed for.

They added a falling red board at the entrance, a pull cord along the wall and a second bell with a lower tone. Bao Mei had painted the board on both sides so a person turning from either stair would see it. The first place they tried left it behind a lamp. The second obscured the upper pressure mark. Sun Lian made them move it a third time.

Ah-Du climbed down from the ladder with red paint on his sleeve.

“If this falls on somebody, do we count that as a warning?”

“We count it as poor work,” Duan said.

“Then I shall make it a very polite board.”

He secured it again.

The next trial began with the same brace being moved across the same stretch of floor. Su Fan kept his eyes on the work instead of the signal, making himself behave as he would when his attention had a reason to be elsewhere.

The red board dropped into the edge of his sight.

He stepped back. The two men beside him followed. A moment later the lower note reached his left ear.

Sun Lian marked the result, then asked the men on the far side what they had seen. One had caught only the pull cord moving against the wall. That was enough to stop him, which was the point.

They began again.

***

The second failure came at the lower winch.

Ren Bo could operate it with two men, as planned. He could not do so after one of those men had to hold a slipping guide rope.

At first the problem disguised itself as an awkward worker. The young man on the line moved his feet, tried another grip and apologized while the wheel crept back. Ren Bo told him to stop apologizing and call for help. Then Ren Bo discovered that his own hands were occupied and the nearest free worker was on the wrong side of the travelling brace.

Sun Lian halted the trial before anyone attempted to climb across it.

“Again,” Ren Bo said.

“With the same missing hand?” she asked.

He looked at the line. The answer annoyed him enough that he released the wheel too sharply. It struck its stop, and everyone turned.

“Sorry,” he said.

Ah-Du opened his mouth, thought better of whatever had come to it, and carried the measuring cord down.

Bao Shun stood beside the landing wall. He had come to deliver a fitted storage box and stayed when the exercise began. His damaged hand rested against the box's edge. For several minutes he watched the rope change direction each time the winch took weight.

“A cleat under that turning point,” he said.

Ren Bo crouched to see where he meant.

“It would carry the guide while the man changes his hold.”

“And foul the spare line,” another worker said.

“Not if it faces this way.”

Bao Shun used his good hand to show the angle. Duan leaned over the rail and told Su Fan to fetch a piece of chalk. The two older men began arguing about the shape with the pleasure of people who had finally found a problem small enough to insult accurately.

The first drawing demanded a grip Bao Shun's hand could not make.

Duan rubbed out part of it.

“Open the approach. A man should be able to set the rope without closing every finger.”

“Then it can jump out.”

“Not with this shoulder.”

They tested the shape in scrap wood before anyone cut the final fitting. Su Fan held the model against the stone while Bao Shun fed the line one-handed. It caught on the first attempt, slipped on the second and held when they altered the lower edge.

They did not call it finished until someone unfamiliar with the argument could use it.

Ren Bo's nephew took that part. He had been recording the times above ground. His handwriting had become smaller and angrier with each interrupted attempt.

“Don't show me first,” he said.

He looked at the marks, placed the rope and drew it tight. The cleat held. He could release and reset it without reaching beneath the turning wheel.

His uncle nodded.

The boy tried not to look pleased.

***

The third rehearsal finished within thirteen minutes.

The crew stood breathing in the stillness after the final signal. Someone laughed, certain the long effort had finally bought them the result they wanted.

Sun Lian looked at the timing sand.

“One minute too long.”

The laugh died.

Su Fan leaned against the upper wall. His sixth-stage circulation had held through the movements. His shoulders ached anyway. He could imagine what the sequence would cost after climbing into the recess under actual heat and pressure rather than stepping between marked positions in an obedient chamber.

“We can move faster,” a worker said.

“We can sometimes move faster,” Jiang replied. “The window does not become larger on the day somebody is tired.”

They laid out the sequence on the board. The first waste was an exchange of signals that told two people what they had already seen. Removing it made the work clearer, not merely quicker. The spare wedge belonged beside the person who would use it, not on the neat storage rack. A lamp had to be raised so the winch caller could see the next worker's face without leaning into the path of a rope.

Su Fan wanted to hurry the next trial. He could feel everyone's attention beginning to fray. He could also feel how easily a good result would let them go home.

Sun Lian sent them outside for water instead.

The break produced complaints, then silence, then the sound of people drinking more than they had expected to need. Two workers sat on the warm stones and argued about whose turn it was to bring food. One had eaten his whole parcel before the first rehearsal and now regarded the empty cloth as evidence of somebody else's poor planning.

Su Fan gave him half a bun.

“You will want that later,” the man said.

“Probably.”

They ate without attempting to make the exchange important.

The fourth attempt took just under twelve minutes by Jiang's measure.

Nobody cheered this time.

Sun Lian walked the route after the crew cleared it. She found a discarded peg on the step Su Fan had marked for repair. The peg had not delayed anyone. It might have done.

She picked it up and put it in the appropriate tray.

“Repeat it.”

The men groaned with conviction and went back to their places.

***

Su Fan's position was beside the collar.

During the transition, he would enter the narrow bearing recess and release the old return conductor after the western flow lowered the strain. A bonded operator touching that conductor could be caught by the inherited command moving through it. His own channels did not offer the same obedient route.

The surrounding mechanism could still take his arm off.

Sun Lian demonstrated the clearance with chalk. She drew a line on the stone, another on the guide, and a corresponding mark on the sleeve he intended to wear.

“This far. No farther. If you reach past it when the collar shifts, there will be nothing useful for Mother Wei to stitch.”

Su Fan held the hooked release tool across his palms. Duan had made the catch easy to test by touch. The binding at the handle was the one Tan Wei had helped replace beneath the lamp.

He would put the tool where a hand did not belong.

For once, nobody needed to tell him that twice.

He entered the recess sideways, turned his shoulders and lowered the hook into the wooden guide standing in place of the live bar. The space forced his right side toward the wall. He could not rely on hearing a call from behind him. The cord signal would reach his sleeve, and the board stood where a turn of his head would bring it into view.

The first pull was awkward. He had enough strength to move the substitute, but not enough room to recover the tool cleanly when it came free. Sun Lian made him hold the uncomfortable position while she marked where the end would strike.

They shortened the motion, not the tool. A shorter hook would demand that his fingers go farther into the mechanism.

On the next attempt the wooden bar moved halfway and caught.

Su Fan leaned harder. The shoulder of his sleeve approached the chalk mark.

“Out,” Sun Lian said.

He stopped, irritated before he knew with whom.

“The guide slipped.”

“Yes.”

“It wasn't the pull.”

“It will not matter which part is innocent when the collar moves.”

He backed out. They reset the guide, and he went in again only after the catching edge had been identified.

A scar near his palm tightened as he closed his hand. He remembered the hot keeper at the earlier shift test, the confident stupidity of deciding there was no time to wait for a better way. The memory did not make him fearless. It made the hook seem worth the time they had spent on it.

After the third clean release, he set the tool on the bench and shook the ache from his fingers.

Sun Lian checked the sleeve mark against the stone again.

“Keep that visible.”

“I will.”

“Not under another coat.”

He looked at the iron-lined coat waiting on the upper rail. He had intended to pull it on afterward without thinking through the covered signal.

He fetched it and marked the outer sleeve too.

***

Ruan arrived during the fifth rehearsal.

He wore plain travelling clothes and carried his own sword. There was dust along one side of his trousers and a small tear near the knee. Su Fan had become accustomed to seeing him clean enough to make other people's work look unnecessarily dirty. The torn cloth was oddly reassuring.

“The reception?” Su Fan asked.

“My aunt has sent my cousin.”

“Was she pleased?”

“She has not used that word.”

“What did she say?”

“That if I am determined to disgrace the family, I should avoid doing it incompetently.”

Sun Lian pointed toward the outer passage.

“Then learn the evacuation route.”

Ruan did not argue. He set his bundle outside the active area, checked that his sheathed sword would not strike a moving line and followed the worker assigned to show him the turns.

On his first return he chose the wider passage through the old stores.

“That one is outside our working route,” the worker told him. “The partition is closed. We do not send injured people through it.”

Ruan went back and took the correct stair. He asked about the ordinary access on the far side, and Ren Bo showed it on the plan. The old quarter did not cease to contain other doors because they had chosen the safest one for their own crew.

Su Fan watched him absorb the layout. Ruan was not looking for the most impressive place to stand. He was looking for the place from which he could move without obstructing somebody carrying a body.

At the lower landing, he tried the new cleat.

“Who made this?”

“Bao Shun and Duan,” Su Fan said.

Ruan ran the line through it once more, then looked at the two men.

“Good.”

Duan grunted. Bao Shun smiled into the side of the storage box he was pretending to inspect.

The next run began with Ruan observing the entrance rather than joining the mechanism crew. He saw one man mistake the falling board for a direction to advance instead of stop. The mistake took two breaths to correct and would have taken much longer if everyone had been shouting.

Sun Lian altered the mark beside the board.

“We have explained it,” the man protested.

“And now we know what you heard,” she replied.

They began once more from the preceding position.

***

By dusk, Su Fan's coat had acquired chalk at both elbows.

The full sequence had been repeated. The spare line was closer to the cleat, the release hook rested in its proper cradle, and the men on the winch had stopped treating an empty moment as an invitation to invent another task.

It was still a dry chamber.

He stood beside the guide and practised lifting the hook clear without turning its end into the path of the collar. Through the upper doorway he could see a narrow portion of evening sky. The light had gone pale enough that the lamps seemed warmer than the air around them.

Min Yao appeared at the landing.

She waited until he set the hook down. Her coat was fastened incorrectly at the throat; one loop had missed its button. He noticed that before understanding why she had come herself.

“My father is asking for you.”

He took his hands away from the tool.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

Something in her voice made the chamber recede around him. He had been thinking in turns of a wheel, reaches of an arm, the time sand took to leave one glass for another. The little pause before her answer belonged to a different measure.

He looked toward Sun Lian.

She had heard enough. She nodded once and called another worker to the bench.

Su Fan washed his hands at the entrance. Dust turned the water grey. A small cut he had not noticed stung when he rubbed the chalk from his knuckles. Min Yao waited beside him without saying they needed to hurry, which made him move more carefully than haste would have done.

At the door he turned back.

Sun Lian was changing the signal beside the red board. Ruan held a lamp for her. Ren Bo had begun explaining the cleat to a worker who had arrived late, and Duan was arguing that the explanation would improve if the man actually touched the rope.

The work continued without him.

Su Fan took his coat from the rail and followed Min Yao up the path.

chapters.title: A Small Bowl
chapters.text:
Min had eaten half the soup.

Min Yao told Su Fan this as though the quantity required an explanation. The bowl stood beside the bed, a skin forming over its pale surface. A spoon lay across the rim with its handle turned toward the place where her father could once have reached it without help.

“He asked for something warmer,” she said. “Then it was too warm. I thought if I left it a little—”

She stopped.

Mother Wei sat near the window. She looked at Su Fan and shook her head once, gently.

He took the chair nearest the bed.

The old scholar's eyes opened. He seemed to need a moment to arrange Su Fan among the objects in the room. Then his gaze moved down to the hands resting on the younger man's knees.

“You washed your hands.”

“Yes.”

“Very considerate. The books were worried.”

Su Fan smiled because Min seemed to need him to.

The room smelled of soup, damp wool and the small medicinal packets Mother Wei had opened beside the lamp. Nothing looked different enough. The same crack crossed the sill. The same case stood beneath the table with a piece of folded paper preventing it from rocking. Jin's shoes were in the wrong place again.

Su Fan had expected to find a room that announced what was happening.

Min moved his fingers on the blanket.

“The chamber?”

“The new braces are in.”

“Duan's iron?”

“He inspected the fittings.”

“Then he has sworn at somebody.”

“Several people.”

The old man's mouth twitched.

Su Fan described the cleat Bao Shun had suggested and the change Duan made so a damaged hand could use it. He told Min about the warning bell nobody heard, the red board, Ah-Du's complaint that a falling warning might require its own warning.

Min listened with his eyes half closed.

Once he asked whether the new braces had arrived. Su Fan answered again, using the same plain words. The old man nodded as though this were good news he had been waiting to receive.

He did not ask about the scripture's origin. He did not point to a hidden book or produce a name that would make the past settle into a pattern. He wanted to know whether the chamber floor still filled with water where Su Fan had drawn a dry place on the survey.

“Only the seep along the side,” Su Fan said. “We keep the path clear.”

“Write the seep.”

“I have.”

“Good.”

Min's eyes closed. For a while Su Fan could hear the little sounds of swallowing from the bed and the scrape of Min Yao's sleeve when she moved the bowl away.

***

Jin stood at the foot of the bed holding the repaired kite.

Bao Mei had patched the torn corner with paper of a slightly different colour. The repair made one wing heavier. Jin had announced that this improved its ability to turn, though the last attempt had ended against a laundry line.

He waited until Min opened his eyes again.

“Will you see it tomorrow?”

The scholar looked at the kite, then at the child behind it.

“I should like that.”

“You have to be outside. You can't see the whole tail from the window.”

“An ambitious requirement.”

“I can bring the chair.”

Min's hand shifted. Jin came closer and rested the kite against the bed so his grandfather could touch its wooden rib. The old man's finger traced the uneven joint without trying to correct it.

“Who made this?”

“I did. Bao Mei helped with the part that was wrong.”

“A useful division.”

“Most of it was mine.”

“Of course.”

Jin looked pleased, then troubled by the effort his grandfather needed for so little speech. He began to explain how a longer tail would make tomorrow's flight better. Mother Wei listened until the explanation became a way to keep the room from being quiet.

“Come and help me with the lamp,” she said.

“It is already lit.”

“I have another.”

The child looked toward his mother. Min Yao nodded. He put the kite where his grandfather could see it and followed Mother Wei into the next room.

Su Fan began to rise too.

Min Yao touched the back of his chair, a brief pressure asking him to remain. She sat where Jin had been standing.

Her father tried to raise his hand. She met it halfway.

“I kept your letters,” he said.

“I know.”

“Not the order they came.”

“That sounds like you.”

He moved his mouth as though preparing a longer explanation. She waited. Su Fan looked toward the window, giving them what privacy he could without turning the request to stay into a fresh decision they must manage.

“I should have visited,” Min said.

“Yes.”

The word did not wound him visibly. His fingers loosened a little beneath hers.

There had been arguments Su Fan did not know, visits postponed before he ever met the scholar, years in which a letter carried less than the person writing it intended. He could not repair them by witnessing a sentence.

Min looked toward the doorway through which Jin had gone.

“Your boy is good at sums.”

“He cheats.”

“So did you.”

Min Yao laughed once. The laugh ended abruptly, but she did not apologize for it. She covered his hand with both of hers.

For a while they remained that way. Then Min asked whether the papers had been kept dry during the last rain.

“Yes,” she said. “All of them.”

Su Fan knew she had worked half the morning moving cases away from the leaking wall. He had offered to help and been sent for boards. At the time it had seemed an ordinary errand. Now he wished he had brought better boards, sooner, with less fuss about the mud on the path.

Min's eyes had closed again.

Su Fan stood quietly. Min Yao did not stop him this time.

***

Outside, the settlement was preparing for evening.

A cart wheel needed greasing. Two children argued over the last piece of dried fruit. Farther down the slope, the workshop bell called the later shift, and someone answered that the food had not yet arrived. The answer was loud enough to reach Su Fan clearly on his left.

He sat on the step with his elbows on his knees.

He wanted the world to notice what was happening inside.

He was also grateful it had not stopped.

Deng came up carrying a covered pot. Auntie Lu had sent food for the household and several instructions that he repeated in a lower voice than usual. He stopped when he saw Su Fan's face.

“Still with them?”

Su Fan nodded.

Deng set the pot in the shelter beside the door. He did not go inside until Mother Wei appeared and took it from him. Then he sat on the low wall for a few minutes, hands hanging between his knees.

“Need anything fetched?” he asked.

Su Fan almost said no. It felt wrong to ask for ordinary things in the presence of something that could not be fetched or repaired.

“Dry wood. The room cools after the lamp is out.”

Deng stood.

“That I can do.”

He went down the path.

Su Fan listened to the house. He could hear Mother Wei moving, the soft knock of a bowl against another, Jin asking a question too quietly for the words to reach him. He did not press his ear to the wall or try to guess.

Later, Min Yao came out to empty the wash water. Su Fan stood to take the basin. She gave it to him without looking at his face.

The water was still warm. He carried it to the drain, returned the empty basin and stayed standing because sitting again seemed to require deciding how long he intended to wait.

“Go home if you need to,” she said.

“I don't.”

She nodded and went inside.

He had meant only that he did not need to leave that moment. It sounded larger after she closed the door. He sat down before he could make a duty out of being seen standing there.

The lamps below diminished one at a time. A late worker passed, recognized him and lifted a hand instead of calling out. Su Fan returned the gesture.

Mother Wei came outside near midnight.

He stood before she spoke.

She looked tired in a way that made him understand she had been keeping part of that tiredness from the room. For a moment she rested one hand against the doorframe.

“Min Yao is with him,” she said.

Su Fan nodded. He found he was holding the edge of his sleeve very tightly.

“Jin?”

“Asleep.”

They stood together without filling the silence.

Min Yao remained with her father for another hour. Nobody went in until she opened the door.

***

The next morning brought people who knew how to perform tasks Su Fan had never thought about clearly.

A woman from the upper houses arrived with clean cloth. Deng spoke to the people responsible for the high ground beside the pines. Auntie Lu brought breakfast and prevented anyone from treating refusal to eat as an appropriate offering to the dead.

Duan came with a measure and two lengths of wood marked for cutting.

“I'll need you,” he told Su Fan.

They worked beneath the workshop awning. The smith made the joints with one hand while Su Fan held the boards. A clamp took the pressure Duan's injured arm could not supply. Ah-Du brought tools, then kept bringing them after there were enough, unable to find another way to remain useful.

“Stay there,” Duan said at last. “Keep the shavings from the line.”

The boy knelt and did it with great seriousness.

Su Fan held a board too tightly and split a small edge near the end. The sound made him flinch.

Duan inspected the damage.

“We can cut past it.”

“I should have—”

“We can cut past it.”

They did.

The coffin joints were plain. Min would have found something to say about the expense of the wood and then asked whether Duan had used the good iron. Su Fan could hear both questions so clearly that he had to stop working until the clamp was secure.

Duan waited without asking what had happened.

Bao Mei came to write the name. She brought two brushes because she did not know which would take the surface better. On a spare offcut, she tested the ink, frowned and chose the smaller one.

Her hand shook on the first stroke.

She looked at Su Fan, furious with herself.

“Take your time,” he said.

“I know.”

He stepped back so she did not have to do the work beneath his attempt to be kind. When she finished, the name stood clearly on the plain wood.

Min Yao chose which books would remain in the house. Somebody suggested that one of her father's favourites should go with him.

“No,” she said.

The person began to explain the custom.

“He spent too much on them.”

A few people laughed softly. The laugh surprised them, then settled. It was true in a way the more solemn suggestions had not managed to be.

She kept the books.

***

Before they left, Min Yao asked for the blue coat.

Someone had offered a cleaner garment. She thanked the woman and kept the one with the repaired elbows. Su Fan fetched it from the peg, shaking the dust from the hem before bringing it to her.

A folded catalogue slip fell from the pocket.

He picked it up without opening it.

“Another treasure,” she said.

“Shall I put it with the papers?”

“Yes.”

She felt through the other pocket herself and found a short piece of string, a blunt pencil and two dried seeds that neither of them could identify. For a moment she held them in her palm, plainly waiting for an explanation he could not give.

Then she laughed through her nose.

“He complained that my son's pockets were full of rubbish.”

Su Fan brought a small dish. She put the objects in it and set it beside the catalogue cases, where they could remain ordinary things until she was ready to decide what to do with them.

The blue coat smelled faintly of paper and the old archive. She pressed it between her hands once, then turned back to the room.

They buried him on the high ground beside the old pines.

The soil was wet and difficult. Roots turned the digging into work that had to be shared. Ruan took a shovel without making an announcement. Tan Wei carried water for the people working and kept it separate from the little basin Mother Wei had brought for washing hands.

The sky remained pale. A breeze moved through the needles above them and shook drops onto shoulders already damp from the climb.

Jin stayed close to Min Yao. He had brought a paper fish folded the night before, during the interval when everyone had tried to let him sleep. One fin was creased in the wrong direction. He had refused to remake it because this was the one he had made for his grandfather.

When the time came, he put it on the lid.

Then he asked whether the paper would get wet.

Min Yao crouched beside him.

“Yes. Eventually.”

He considered that with painful concentration. She did not tell him it would remain exactly as he had left it.

The ceremony was brief. People had things to say, but no one had been able to turn the scholar into a person who had never been difficult. A neighbour remembered an argument about a bill. Someone else remembered a book loaned when a fee would have mattered. Duan said the man had been capable of paying promptly when cornered with sufficient determination.

That brought another small laugh.

Su Fan listened. He had expected his own gratitude to become clearer if enough other people described theirs. Instead each memory made the dead man less simple.

Impatient. Frightened of his first attempt at a strange exercise. Vain about certain translations. Delighted by a child's incorrect argument when it was inventive enough. A man who had kept his daughter's letters and still failed to visit her.

The scripture in Su Fan's room had not become less useful because its first reader had been afraid. The friendship had not become less real because gratitude could not supply a final, adequate sentence.

He waited until the others began walking back.

For a moment he imagined promising to finish the work. Which work? The untranslatable passage, the repairs, the visit Min had postponed, the whole impossible sum of what a life left unfinished? Any promise large enough would be too easy to say.

He touched the plain wood once before it was covered.

Then he moved aside for the people holding the ropes.

***

At the path, Min Yao called his name.

There were chairs to return to the clinic. Several had been brought up when neighbours began gathering the previous night. Mother Wei would need them before evening.

Su Fan followed her back.

Jin had fallen asleep against Tan Wei's shoulder. His hands still held the paper scraps left from folding the fish. Tan Wei walked slowly enough that the child's head did not knock against his collarbone.

At the house, the reading stand remained beside the window. The short foot was still supported by the scrap Su Fan had folded. The soup bowl had been washed and set with the others.

He carried two chairs down the slope, one balanced against each arm. He could hear a little movement from the scripture cord inside his coat, where he had placed the packet Min Yao told him to take home.

At the clinic door a patient thanked him for the seat.

Su Fan set it down, checked that it stood firmly and went back for the rest.

chapters.title: The Seventh Circuit
chapters.text:
Su Fan did not train the night Min died.

Or the next morning.

He worked when work was necessary, slept badly and discovered that small inconveniences could make him angrier than the things he knew he ought to be angry about. A blunt chisel. A bowl left where it would be knocked from the bench. The same question asked twice because he had answered toward his damaged ear instead of toward the person speaking.

Ah-Du came to him with a fastening from the new bell line.

“Which hole?”

“The marked one.”

“They're both marked.”

“Then use your eyes.”

The boy looked at him, set the fastening on the bench and went to Duan.

Su Fan continued working for several strokes before he could make himself stop. There were two marks. One belonged to the discarded arrangement from an earlier rehearsal. He had left it there because he knew which was current.

He found Ah-Du outside.

“I should have removed the old mark.”

“Yes.”

“And I shouldn't have spoken to you like that.”

The boy turned the fastening in his hands. He had been prepared for a correction, perhaps an argument. The apology seemed to leave him without the reply he had been practising.

“I miss him too,” he said.

Su Fan looked at the crooked sign above the practice yard. Min had corrected its wording and complained about the cost of the ink used to make the same error a second time. Ah-Du had argued with him over both corrections.

“I know,” Su Fan said.

He had not known enough to consider it before speaking.

They rubbed out the wrong mark together. The task took less time than the apology. Su Fan wished that proportion applied to everything.

***

On the morning after the burial, he opened the practice record again.

The seventh circuit had been close for weeks. Its upper branch remained unstable under a changing load. He could hold it while sitting, while walking, or during a strike whose beginning he controlled. When one movement became another unexpectedly, his throat tightened and the returning pressure caught above his chest.

At first he had tried to make the route stronger.

That worked long enough to encourage him. Then the pressure crowded the narrow part and returned through his throat, making swallowing uncomfortable for the rest of the evening. He had written *too much* beside the trial and left the phrase there until Min asked what, exactly, had been too much.

Now the page carried a fuller account.

Beneath it was a copied note from the scholar's older work: widening the flow did not mean increasing what was forced through it. The date on the original was three years earlier. Min had not left it for this particular morning. It belonged to a question he had been considering before Su Fan came to the archive with a hammer and two wedges.

Su Fan read it twice, then closed the scripture.

The sentence did not contain a movement. He still had to find one his body could perform.

He fetched the iron ring.

It was plain work, made from an offcut of new gate stock. Handling had polished one side more than the other. He knew the tiny rough place near the join and turned it away from the cord so it would not wear the fibres.

Tan Wei found him beneath the eaves, checking the loop.

“Do you want company or help?”

“Help.”

“Those are often confused.”

“I need you to pull this without telling me when.”

Tan Wei inspected the arrangement. He made Su Fan show him the range first, then asked what to do if the ring came toward his face.

“Let go.”

“Mine or yours?”

“Either.”

“A generous rule.”

They cleared the space around them. Su Fan set his feet, opened the familiar sixth-stage circulation and lifted the ring. Tan Wei took the other end of the cord.

On the first attempt, the ring hit Su Fan in the chin.

His teeth clicked together.

Tan Wei dropped the cord at once.

“I thought you meant—”

“I did.”

Su Fan rubbed the spot. His eyes had watered. He could feel the old irritation rising, eager to turn an ordinary failed trial into an offence committed by somebody else.

Then he saw Tan Wei's horrified expression and began laughing.

His friend laughed too, in relief and at the sheer indignity of a cultivator arranging to strike himself with his own equipment.

“Write that one down,” Tan Wei said.

“I will give you a full page.”

***

The first problem was anticipation.

Su Fan watched Tan Wei's fingers and prepared before the pull. When Tan changed hands, he watched the elbow. When the elbow stopped providing a useful warning, he listened for the cloth of his sleeve. None of that was foolish in a fight. In this exercise it concealed the exact moment he needed to understand: the body meeting a change it had not arranged in advance.

Tan Wei caught him watching and began to hum.

“Must you?”

“It prevents me helping you too politely.”

“You could choose a tune.”

“I have.”

“Could you keep it?”

His friend pulled.

The ring jerked. Su Fan held it away from his chin this time, but the upper route closed as his shoulders rose. He recovered through the lower circulation and stopped before the pressure accumulated in his throat.

They made the pull smaller.

It seemed a humiliating reduction after the first attempts. He could lift more than this, receive more than this, strike harder than this. None of those abilities kept him from tightening against the wrong part of the movement.

At the smaller load, he could feel the order clearly enough to interrupt it.

The next pull moved his hands a little. He allowed that movement instead of treating it as a loss. The lower circulation remained open. The upper branch wavered, caught, then released before the strain became painful.

“Again?” Tan Wei asked.

“After a moment.”

They rested. Across the yard, a customer brought a damaged latch to Duan. Ah-Du took it to the bench, asked which account it belonged under and received an answer that did not require him to guess the smith's thoughts. Su Fan was glad of that without turning it into another reason to feel ashamed.

When they resumed, the second problem appeared.

He could receive the interruption, but he carried it into the movement afterward. His hands remained ready for a pull that had already ended. The following turn became crowded with the body's memory of the previous one.

He lowered the ring and shook out his arms.

Tan Wei watched him.

“At the basin,” he said, “Han makes us empty one cup before moving the next. Not because the cups matter. Because I keep trying to finish the first movement in the middle of the second.”

“Does it help?”

“Sometimes. When I do it rather than explain why I should already know.”

Su Fan smiled.

They did not turn the water exercise into a new instruction from the scripture. They tried the useful part of the comparison: allowing the completed pressure to finish, then finding the next position without keeping an unnecessary answer prepared inside it.

On the first attempt, Su Fan moved too slowly and lost the ring altogether.

Tan Wei caught it before it struck the ground.

“An expensive way of emptying the cup.”

“Again.”

***

The successful movement felt disappointingly ordinary.

Tan Wei pulled to the side. Su Fan's hands moved. His feet adjusted. The lower route carried the returning force, and the upper branch remained open long enough for his own next movement to begin without a catch in his throat.

He almost stopped to examine the sensation.

Another pull arrived.

The ring turned. He let it turn within the space they had allowed, received the change and returned to the centre. The circulation did not need the movement to be beautiful. It needed him not to close the route while asking it to carry the result.

Tan Wei pulled harder.

Su Fan yielded half a step. The pressure passed through. He was sweating and his arms were tired, but nothing had gathered painfully beneath his jaw.

“Stop,” he said.

Tan Wei stopped.

For a while Su Fan stood with the ring hanging between his hands. The upper branch remained open without another pull to occupy him. He lowered the weight and sat beneath the eaves. His heartbeat slowed. The new route stayed.

He waited for disappointment to arrive in the form of a familiar obstruction.

It did not.

Tan Wei sat beside him without asking what rank he had reached.

“Do it once more after you've rested,” he said.

They did. The first return held. The second faltered when Su Fan tried to improve it. He stopped, returned to the smaller movement and found it again without forcing his way through the mistake.

Jiang came to collect a corrected fitting before noon. Su Fan asked whether she could bring the independent needle to the yard.

She looked at his chin.

“What have you been measuring with that?”

“My face,” Tan Wei said on his behalf.

“A poor standard. It changes under use.”

She sent for the case.

The test took longer than the bright instant Su Fan would once have wanted to call a breakthrough. Jiang supported the frame, checked its reference and compared the readings at three points. She repeated them after he walked the yard, after he rested, and after a small change in load.

The pressure remained steadier than it had during the sixth-stage tests.

Seventh stage.

Su Fan wrote the date, the failed approaches and the conditions of the successful trial. The ring striking his chin received its sentence. Tan Wei read that part and demanded correction of the implication that the pull had been mischievous.

“It was a very serious pull.”

“I have called it one.”

“Your handwriting suggests otherwise.”

Su Fan closed the book while they were still smiling.

Then he reached for the wider cord Min Yao had given him and thought, without warning, of carrying the new results to her father's reading stand.

His hands stopped.

Tan Wei saw the change but did not ask him to name it. He collected the loose testing line instead, coiling it around his own palm while Su Fan found the end of the book's binding.

After a while, Su Fan said, “He would have asked about the first bad pull.”

“He would have asked why you hadn't padded the ring.”

“I should have.”

“Yes.”

The agreement was so immediate that Su Fan laughed again, though this time it hurt in a different place.

They took the equipment into the workshop. Duan listened to the account with his good hand resting on the plane handle. He asked whether the route held while Su Fan was tired, and Su Fan told him which conditions they had not tested.

“Then keep those on the page,” the smith said.

He moved the practice book away from a damp patch on the bench and made room for it beside the day's paid work. Su Fan left it there instead of taking it up the hill.

***

Ruan tested him that afternoon.

They used blunted steel and enough protection to keep an ordinary mistake from becoming another gathering on the high ground. Ruan checked the padding himself. He also checked the dry space near the right-hand wall, where a loose stone had worked free after rain.

Su Fan watched him kick it out of the yard.

“Kind of you.”

“I prefer my victories to belong to me.”

The first contact was harder than Su Fan expected.

Ruan's ninth-stage pressure met his blade and drove it toward his shoulder. Su Fan let the force return through the joined route instead of spending everything to stop it in the first instant. He recovered his line with room left for another movement.

Ruan changed the angle.

The second strike arrived while Su Fan was still pleased with the first.

It touched his ribs through the padding.

They stopped.

“Your method has improved,” Ruan said. “Your attention remains available for purchase.”

Su Fan raised his sword again.

This time he kept the successful contact small in his thoughts. He met the blade, moved his feet and watched the man beyond the steel. Ruan withdrew before the returning force could become a useful strike. Su Fan followed a little too far, recognized the opening late and gave ground rather than insist on the exchange he had imagined.

The next few movements carried them across the yard.

He could meet a ninth-stage strike now without using everything in the first contact. He could not make a shorter reach become a longer one. Ruan's changes of pace still demanded decisions faster than his injured hearing could help him make.

Ruan moved toward his right.

Su Fan turned early.

The attack changed sides before he finished.

He caught it on the flat, felt the force run through his legs and lost two steps to the recovery. The upper route held. His footwork had not become infallible because the route did.

They separated, breathing hard.

Su Fan rubbed a place on his shoulder where the padding had shifted.

“Again?” Ruan asked.

“One more.”

It was not their last exchange. Each man could see a different unfinished question, and neither wanted to be the one who ended the conversation before answering his own.

Sun Lian found them still at it.

“You both look as though I should replace you with sensible men.”

“There are vacancies in that profession,” Ruan said.

She handed each of them a coil of rope.

“Carry those. Slowly.”

They carried them.

***

First Water was the next morning.

That evening, Su Fan checked his sword's edge, the stitching inside the iron-lined coat and the marks on the release tool. The old bolt damage had been repaired, but the cloth there felt different beneath his fingers. He turned the coat to make sure the chalk on the outer sleeve remained visible.

Ah-Du came to the doorway with the corrected bell fastening.

“It fits,” he said.

“Good.”

“I used my eyes.”

Su Fan looked up. The boy's face held the careful expression of someone offering a joke without yet knowing whether it would be welcome.

“Use them again tomorrow,” Su Fan said. “Mine will be busy.”

Ah-Du grinned and took the fastening away.

The yard emptied. Duan banked the furnace with instructions for the morning's ordinary work, because somebody would still need a kettle repaired while everyone else argued about the river. Su Fan tied the iron ring to a cord beneath his shirt. Its small weight rested against his chest.

He thought of taking it off. It was not a charm. It had no place in the operating sequence.

He left it there because it was his, and because not every object he carried had to justify itself by preventing disaster.

Mother Wei found him closing the tool roll.

“Sleep.”

“I will.”

“Before morning.”

He nodded.

She adjusted the coat where the bolt had torn it, checking her own repair with two fingers. Then she tugged the collar into a position that would not rub his neck.

For a moment he was eleven again, standing still while she found another place his clothes no longer covered.

He wanted to tell her he would return. The promise rose easily, made attractive by the fact that neither of them could guarantee it.

Instead he asked where she would be.

“With the operators.”

“Not among the guests?”

Her look answered him.

He smiled. She let go of the coat.

In bed, he could feel every tired place in his body. The seventh circuit remained when he stopped paying attention to it. That should have been satisfying. For a long while he listened to the uneven ringing in his damaged ear and the actual sounds beyond the window, trying not to turn either into a warning.

Eventually the settlement quieted.

He slept.

chapters.title: The First Bell
chapters.text:
At dawn, the valley dressed itself for ceremony.

Banners rose above the upper stations. The regional delegation took its place on a platform with three spare braces beneath it. Musicians tested their instruments, each apparently determined to discover the correct note before his neighbour did. Clerks arranged clean cups where the guests could see the new work.

Below the platform, the operators stood at their assigned basins.

Tan Wei had arrived early enough to watch a servant replace a chipped cup on the reception table. The servant examined the damaged glaze, set the cup aside and found another. A sensible correction, made before anyone had to drink from it.

He wished he could stop making comparisons.

His basin stood in the eighth station's operator room, where the incoming channel caught the first light from a high window. Across the water, Qiu Lan was tightening the tie on her sleeve. She looked up when she felt him watching. He lifted two fingers. She returned the gesture and went back to her knot.

Nothing in her face suggested she regretted retaining her impression. Nothing in his made her ask him to reconsider leaving his.

Han moved between the basins, checking wrists, pupils and the ordinary things the ceremony preferred to conceal beneath clean robes. His cane struck the floor at uneven intervals.
