At one position he stopped to ask a young operator how much he had slept. The answer was too prompt. Han asked again and changed the man's place in the rotation.

A clerk objected that the seating order had been prepared.

“So have I,” Han said.

He moved the operator anyway.

Mother Wei came through the side door carrying her wrapped case. A station attendant began directing her toward the guest area. She pointed at the floor beside Han's instruments and waited until he cleared it.

Tan Wei was relieved to see her, then ashamed of how much relief could rest on the arrival of one tired woman. She could not make the whole river safe by putting down a case.

She looked at him.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

The answer was true. That small fact pleased him more than it should have.

Outside, someone asked the musicians to stop testing while the announcement was read. The resulting silence lasted only until a late cart rattled across the upper stones.

The first bell rang.

Tan Wei placed his hands beside the basin and let the water settle before touching it.

***

In the western chamber, Sun Lian uncovered the pressure board.

The bypass remained closed.

They had agreed to that in writing. They would not open an untested route merely because the date had arrived. Jiang would request the separation interval again when the measured return began. If the network remained within its safe limits, the crew would keep the gate ready and continue the dispute elsewhere.

If the reading crossed the emergency threshold, they would act under the steward's duty to prevent an immediate loss of life.

Wen Zhao had recorded the distinction. He had also recorded the risk of acting and the refusal of the earlier partial-flow test. The narrow ground on which their plan stood did not become broader because everyone had assembled upon it.

Su Fan checked the release hook.

Its catch closed properly. The binding remained dry. The chalk mark on the outer sleeve of his iron-lined coat was still visible. He ran one finger along it and found himself remembering how Mother Wei had pulled the collar straight the previous night.

Ren Bo stood at the lower winch with his crew. The spare line lay where Ruan could reach it if the first failed. Bao Shun's cleat had been checked once more by a man who had complained about being asked to demonstrate something he now knew perfectly.

Sun Lian had asked him to demonstrate it anyway.

They waited.

Waiting made the chamber sound larger. Su Fan could hear the slow seep near the side wall through his left ear. Through his right came the dull internal ringing that had no useful direction. He turned enough to keep Sun Lian in sight and resisted the temptation to adjust the hook simply to have something to do.

A worker near the tool rack took a cake from his sleeve, looked embarrassed and put it back.

“Eat it,” Sun Lian said.

“I thought—”

“If the signal comes, put it down. Until then, eat.”

The man obeyed. The smell of sweet grain drifted briefly through the damp air.

Su Fan's stomach tightened. He had eaten too. His body appeared to have forgotten the fact in favour of preparing for every possible kind of alarm.

Ruan came down from the entrance to confirm the outer path was clear. He wore his sword without touching its hilt. He looked over the crew, then at Su Fan.

“Your sleeve is marked twice.”

“One coat over the other.”

“A rare example of dressing sensibly.”

Su Fan smiled. Ruan returned to his position before the smile had entirely left either of them.

The first bell's vibration faded through the stone. They did not mistake its ceremonial note for their own signal.

***

At the western landing, Old Pock moved his boat one length farther behind the marked line.

A younger boatman objected that they would have farther to row if someone needed collecting from the cut.

“Yes,” Pock said.

“Then why move?”

“Because I want a boat left to row.”

He made the man help shift the mooring. The work warmed their hands and gave them something to quarrel about besides whether the people inside the chamber knew what they were doing.

Across the exposed ground, Deng's crew waited beside a survey cart. The path from the cart to the rise had been cleared the evening before. A stone still protruded where a wheel might catch it. Deng sent a man to move the stone rather than accept the explanation that everyone knew it was there.

The old lower town lay beyond the reeds. From this angle, Pock could see a broken line that had once been a wall. He had tied boats beside it before the flood and would never tie one there again. The new cut promised useful work, not the return of what the water had taken.

A horn rested in the boat beside his feet. He checked its mouth, wiped away a thread caught in it and set it back where he could reach it without looking.

The younger man asked whether there would be food after the ceremony.

“If we get the boat back,” Pock said.

“And if we don't?”

“Then I expect Auntie Lu will give us a very long account of why we should have.”

They looked uphill together. The banners were moving. The water in the cut remained still.

***

The second bell rang.

Water rose through the nine stations, carrying preserved methods outward and drawing their pressure back through the common lower collector.

Most of the river continued along its ordinary course. A fisherman on the far bank would have seen a change in current, not a river transformed into light. The formation needed only a controlled portion of the flow to carry its commands.

That portion now travelled through more repaired sections, more temporary joints and more newly bonded operators than before the flood.

Jiang stood beside the upper measuring board. The main figures had been copied neatly for the delegation. The corrections she used remained on a smaller sheet beneath her hand.

Wen Zhao watched the same needle from a place that did not obstruct the messenger.

At first the reading rose as expected.

Jiang compared it with the return from the lower station. The difference widened. She checked the reference rather than announce a failure because the first alarming number offered itself.

Then the needle moved beyond the certified estimate.

She wrote the measured reading, attached the comparison and sent the first warning.

The messenger ran uphill along the side of the platform. One of the attendants tried to stop him from crossing in front of the guests. Jiang raised her voice before the argument could begin. The attendant stepped back.

Above her, the ceremony continued.

A speaker was explaining the importance of continuity between generations. His voice carried well across the open yard. Jiang heard the word *continuity* while watching a returning pressure that no longer matched the arrangement being praised.

Pei Gang received the signal.

He read it, looked toward the lower measures and lifted his uninjured hand. The upper feed diminished. The change passed through the channel with a visible settling of the water against the marked stone.

For a moment the lower needle steadied.

Jiang let out a breath she had not intended to hold.

Then the shared return arrived.

The reading climbed again, faster than before.

The reduction above had been real. So was the pressure already below the regulator.

Wen leaned closer.

“Second reference?”

She showed him. He checked the correction, looked at the mark on the glass and wrote the actual reading rather than the safer estimate prepared for the ceremony.

Jiang reached for another sheet.

***

At the eighth station, three operators bent forward at once.

Han caught the nearest before her head struck the rim of the basin. Water splashed across his sleeve. He held her upright while Qiu Lan moved to the opposite side and took part of her weight.

“Local loop,” he called.

The attendant at the valve pulled the cord.

Nothing closed.

The renewed central command held the route open. Its pressure travelled through the basin, into the marked wrists and back toward the common collector. The operators' breathing lost the rhythm they had practised together. Some found another stable pattern. Others began making movements nobody had asked of them.

Tan Wei felt the change in his own hands.

His fingers curled as though around an oar. He recognized the grip. He knew, with a tenderness that frightened him, what the wood beneath that hand ought to feel like after years of weather.

There was no oar.

“Master Han.”

“I see it.”

Han's voice reached him from very far away, though the old man stood only two basins distant.

Tan Wei set his feet against the stone. He tried to name the room to himself. Eighth station. High window. Qiu Lan's sleeve wet to the elbow. Mother Wei kneeling beside a woman who had stopped answering.

The remembered river pressed against those observations with the weight of something that had once been entirely true.

Han pulled the emergency cord himself.

The warning crossed the courtyard below the music.

***

Jiang sent the second warning with the measured numbers attached.

The independent needle shook hard enough to blur. She watched it through a second pass, compared the lower report and drew a line beneath the reading.

Wen Zhao stood close enough to see her hand shake when she set the brush down.

“You have it?” she asked.

“I have the reading.”

She took the seal from her belt.

The emergency release order had been prepared earlier but remained unsigned. Preparing it had allowed other people to speak of her decision as though it were already made. Now the space for the signature looked very small beneath the list of conditions.

She pressed the seal onto the paper.

Then she signed.

“Western team,” she told the messenger. “Ready the bypass. Do not open until my upper gauge confirms the reduction.”

He repeated the instruction. She corrected one word that would have changed preparation into action. He repeated it properly and ran.

Wen turned his page.

Jiang did not thank him. There would be time for thanks if the reading stopped climbing.

A second messenger arrived from the operator room. He had come fast enough to lose a shoe. Han requested immediate reduction and reported involuntary responses spreading across newly bonded routes.

“How many unresponsive?” Jiang asked.

The boy gave the number he had been told, then admitted he had not stayed for the next count.

She sent him back with a specific question and a fresh instruction. He looked at his bare foot as though noticing it for the first time, then went without the shoe.

On the reception platform, the speaker had stopped.

The guests were finally looking toward the water instead of the prepared account of it.

***

Captain Shen Tu reached the old quarter before Jiang's messenger.

Ruan saw the crossbows first.

Two men carried them held close to their bodies, not yet raised. Six others followed with blades and spears. Shen Tu walked at the front with an order case in his hand. The group moved like people who had been told where to go before the alarm began.

Ruan stepped away from the entrance wall.

“Jiang has operational command here.”

“Jiang has exceeded it.”

“Show the amended order.”

Shen Tu opened the case and held up the elder's seal. The instruction secured unauthorized access to the return mechanisms during renewal. It did not describe the reading currently rising beneath the platform, nor did it carry Jiang's signature.

Ruan read what he could without moving into the captain's reach.

“That is the standing order.”

“It remains in force.”

“There is an emergency request moving through the station.”

“Then it will reach the proper office.”

Behind Ruan, a worker crossed the upper landing with a lamp. The captain's gaze passed him and entered the passage beyond. He knew the quarter. Ruan could see that in the way he looked past the visible door toward the routes that joined it elsewhere.

“Stand aside,” Shen Tu said.

Ruan rested one hand on his sword.

He wished, absurdly, that his aunt could have heard the conversation up to that point. He had been precise. He had asked for the relevant order. He had not yet said anything that would make an otherwise defensible position look like an argument started for pleasure.

“My withdrawing does not make the mechanism safe to seize.”

“Your remaining makes you responsible for obstructing it.”

A crossbowman shifted his grip.

Ruan moved half a step so the stone jamb stood between the weapon and the lower stair.

“I suggest you wait for the steward's reading.”

“I suggest you consider your family before making their name part of this.”

That was a worse temptation than an insult. It offered him a reason to become angry and thereby stop thinking about the passage.

He kept his hand still.

Behind him, the low bell rang twice.

The red warning board dropped.

***

Su Fan saw the board enter the edge of his vision.

He set the hook into its ready position without pulling. The upper pressure had not yet fallen far enough. Sun Lian read the incoming mark and watched the message travelling along the pull cord.

“Positions.”

The worker with the cake put it on the tool shelf. Ren Bo's crew took their grips. The spare line remained clear of the wheel.

Su Fan looked toward the entrance. Ruan had drawn his sword. Beyond him stood men whose work required them to believe another set of instructions.

The world had not become a simple division between people who understood the danger and people who did not. Someone on the upper landing asked what the steward's seal meant. Someone else told him to keep the path clear. The first shouted order from outside reached Su Fan in fragments, half lost through stone and his injured hearing.

He wanted to go to Ruan.

The hook lay beneath his hand. The conductor was still loaded. If he left without the next person ready, courage at one doorway would become an empty position beside the collar.

Sun Lian caught his eye and held it.

He turned back to the board.

At the entrance, steel left its sheath.

chapters.title: A Man at the Basin
chapters.text:
Tan Wei's body remembered a ferry he had never stood on.

The floor beneath his feet remained stone. The basin remained in front of him. But his hands were feeling for an oar, and the voice in his throat belonged to someone calling across brown water to a woman with a green scarf.

He knew where she would stand.

He knew the weight of the wet rope and the small adjustment required when a passenger moved without warning. He knew that the left bank was shallower than it looked. None of those things had been learned in the room whose high window shone above him.

For an instant the basin's rim became the edge of a boat.

He bit the inside of his cheek.

Pain brought the stone back. His palms struck the basin hard enough to hurt. Water spilled over his fingers and ran into the fold of his sleeve.

Han was beside him.

“Tell me your name.”

“Tan Wei.”

“Again.”

“Tan Wei.”

“Where are you standing?”

The answer that rose first belonged to a ferry landing. He held it behind his teeth until he could see the crack in the station floor.

“Eighth station.”

Han pressed two fingers below the blue marks and redirected part of the returning pressure into the local loop. The relief was small and immediate. Tan Wei drew a breath that belonged to the room instead of the remembered river.

Across from him, Qiu Lan braced another operator against the wall. Her own blue lines remained bright. She had chosen to retain them. Now she used what they gave her to keep a woman upright while calling for someone to bring a folded coat beneath the woman's head.

This was not the renewal they had rehearsed.

The attendant at the local valve was still trying to close it. Each attempt met the same resistance. His face had become red with the effort of obeying an instruction the mechanism would no longer accept.

Han looked toward him.

“Stop forcing it. Keep the reference open.”

The attendant let go, shaking out his hands.

Tan Wei watched the old teacher move to the next basin. Han's bad leg dragged on the turn. He caught the edge of a stool, righted himself and continued before anyone could make a separate emergency out of helping him.

The voice in Tan Wei's throat tried to call across the water again.

He closed his mouth.

***

The permanent impressions were trying to answer one command through channels that no longer matched the old diagram.

Tan Wei could feel the discrepancy without possessing the words to explain every part of it. The return wanted a movement to finish along a route his body had been trained to supply. The repaired network sent it back at a different pressure. The impression answered with the old correction, and his own muscles began paying for the difference.

At the far side of the room, an older operator steadied. He had worked through renewals for years. His breathing found a familiar rhythm, the blue marks above his hands settled, and he turned enough to help the person beside him.

Others had joined during reconstruction. The stations had needed hands, and quicker bonds had filled the empty places on the lists.

Their bodies were becoming the adjustment.

Tan Wei had once imagined the danger as something that would arrive with a recognizable hatred. A dead master reaching out to take him. A will he could resist because it wanted him gone.

The pressure did not know him well enough to hate him.

It brought a correct grip for an old oar, a certainty about where the current should turn, a remembered tenderness for a woman who had lived and died without knowing his name. Useful things, real things, passing into a body whose choices were not being consulted.

He wanted room to decide which of them to carry.

The room would have to be made physically, by people working elsewhere, while he stayed here and kept his hands from becoming someone else's answer.

Han set three needles beside the basin.

Mother Wei opened the wrapped case she had brought from the clinic. The cloth beneath it was already wet. She moved it to a drier board, checked what she needed and knelt beside the first patient.

“How long?” she asked.

“Until the lower collector isolates.”

“That is not a time.”

“No.”

They looked at each other. Then both returned to work.

Tan Wei understood the exchange better than he would have a few months earlier. Han had not concealed a certainty from her. There was no useful number to give.

He hated that more than an unpleasant estimate.

***

A basin overflowed behind him.

He turned and saw a young operator pulling against the mark on his own wrist. The boy's other hand had found a knife. For a moment Tan Wei stared, unable to believe the ordinary little blade had entered this room as an answer to what was happening beneath the skin.

“No.”

The word came out in the wrong voice.

He crossed the space anyway.

The boy slashed at the blue lines before Tan Wei reached him. Blood ran over the rim. The inherited routes continued moving beneath the wound.

Tan Wei caught the knife hand and turned it away from both of them. The boy fought him with the wild strength of somebody who had mistaken pain for the first thing he could control.

“That won't remove it.”

“Make it stop.”

“We're working on it.”

“Then work faster.”

Tan Wei had no reply that would survive the boy's face.

He took the knife away, set it beyond reach and called Mother Wei. She looked up, saw enough and sent a helper with clean cloth while she settled the patient already beneath her hands.

Tan Wei pressed the cloth to the cut. The boy tried to pull free. Tan held him with ordinary strength and a thin sheet of water drawn from the basin, keeping the injured hand steadier than his own fingers alone could manage.

It was a skill Han had taught him.

He used it with gratitude and fury together.

The water trembled. The return passing through his own marks wanted to make the small controlled sheet part of a much larger movement. He reduced it until it did only what the task required. The rest of the basin stayed where it belonged.

Mother Wei came beside him.

“Keep talking to him.”

“What do I say?”

“Something he can answer.”

Tan Wei looked at the boy. He had seen him in the courtyard before, eating at the end of a bench and trying to appear older than the excitement in his face. He did not know his family's history or why the station wages had mattered to him.

“What did you eat this morning?”

The boy stared.

“Before the bell.”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing at all?”

“A bun. Half.”

“Where's the other half?”

“In my coat.”

Tan Wei glanced at the folded coat beside the wall. One corner had darkened where someone set it in spilled water.

“We'll find it after.”

The boy made a short, angry noise.

“It's wet.”

“Then I expect you can complain to the kitchen.”

The complaint was a small thing to offer against the wrong hands inside his own. It was nevertheless something the boy recognized. His eyes moved toward the coat and remained in the room for another breath.

Mother Wei worked without promising more than she knew. When she needed Tan Wei to move his hand, she touched it rather than shout over the others. The wound was bandaged. The blue remained beneath it.

The boy saw that and began to cry.

Tan Wei stayed until Mother Wei told him the cloth could hold without his water.

***

A messenger reached the door.

He had mud across one knee and was breathing too hard to deliver the whole sentence at once. Han took him by the shoulder, turned him away from the nearest distressed patient and made him repeat it.

Western passage obstructed. Security intervention. Delay unknown.

Tan Wei saw Han fold the message before looking toward him.

That was how he knew the old man had considered not telling him.

“Su Fan?”

“Still at his position.”

“You don't know that.”

Han looked at the paper.

“No.”

The admission cost him something. Tan Wei could see it. The teacher had spent years learning how to make frightened people steady enough to do difficult work. The temptation to give them one useful certainty was written in the tightness around his mouth.

Han put the message where everyone could see it.

“We maintain the local loops,” he said. “We do not begin separation until the collector drops. Anyone retaining the bond stays at the marked basins. Anyone withdrawing comes to the inner line when called.”

His voice steadied the room more than a promise would have.

One man asked whether the guards intended to stop the whole operation. Han said that was not information contained in the message. Another asked whether there was another passage. The attendant began describing one until Qiu Lan interrupted.

“For a messenger, perhaps. Not for all these people. We keep the route we can account for.”

Tan Wei looked toward the door.

He could go. His legs still worked. He had water under his hands, strength the frightened boy at the wall did not possess, and a friend somewhere beyond the passage where steel might already be drawn.

He imagined reaching Su Fan in time.

Then the central return tightened beneath his wrist. His fingers moved toward an oar again, and the imagined rescue lost its clean shape.

He was still part of the system being isolated. Leaving his basin did not free him from it. It might simply move his crisis to a place where nobody was prepared to help.

He turned back.

Han watched without speaking. Tan Wei resented being watched and was glad the old man did not offer praise for remaining where his work was.

“Tell me when there is another message,” he said.

“Yes.”

“All of it.”

“All of it.”

***

The woman in the green scarf returned when he lowered his hands to the rim.

This time he remembered the sound of her laughing at something he could not recover. The missing joke hurt with an intimacy that had nothing to do with the station. He wanted the rest of it. He wanted the face turned toward him and the relief of knowing the person he loved was waiting on the opposite bank.

He wanted it while knowing the wanting had entered with the impression.

Han had warned him that separation could feel like loss even when the choice was his. Tan Wei had believed him in the abstract. Now the grief waiting inside that warning seemed indecently alive.

He took his notebook from beneath his coat.

The oilcloth had kept it dry. Su Fan's awkward help with the corner had left a fold Tan Wei recognized immediately. He worked the knot open with wet fingers.

The storehouse roof in the first rain.

Burned ginger.

Mud in Su Fan's collar.

He read the entries slowly. They were not powerful words. No light rose from the page. The blue marks did not vanish because he remembered a joke from childhood. But the handwriting was his, uneven where he had written in poor light, impatient where he had tried to finish before a shift.

He could tell which page had been made after an argument. He could remember being hungry when he wrote another.

Across the room, Qiu Lan asked a helper to move a stool. The helper moved the wrong one. She swore, corrected herself and pointed.

The sound belonged so completely to the present that Tan Wei almost laughed.

He wrote nothing new. His fingers were too unsteady for a clean line, and he did not need the book to prove he was brave during a morning that had already demanded too much.

The boy with the bandaged wrist watched him.

“Is it a technique?”

“No.”

“What are you reading?”

“Things I remember.”

The boy looked down at his hands.

“I remember things too.”

“Yours?”

“Some.”

Tan Wei moved his stool closer, careful not to cross the marked line between their positions. He did not ask the boy to describe the borrowed memories in front of everyone. He knew how easily curiosity could make another person's distress into an interesting account.

“What did you do yesterday?” he asked.

“Cleaned the west basin.”

“Before that?”

“Argued about the brush.”

“Why?”

“Because somebody had used it on the floor.”

Tan Wei nodded. He could imagine the argument well enough to belong in it.

“Did you get another?”

“Yes.”

“Then start there.”

***

The pressure changed again.

Not enough to permit separation. Enough for everyone to look toward the gauges and hope too quickly.

Han checked the local reference, spoke to the attendant and shook his head. The movement had been a fluctuation, not the sustained drop they required.

A woman near the inner line began to stand. Mother Wei put a hand on her shoulder and asked her to remain seated.

Tan Wei felt disappointment move through the room almost as tangibly as the returning command. The older operators could absorb some of the strain. Their experience did not make them less tired. One man leaned his forehead against the cool wall while keeping his hands in position. Another asked whether anyone could loosen the tie at his neck.

Qiu Lan helped him, then returned to her basin.

“You can sit,” she told Tan Wei.

“I am sitting.”

“You are preparing to stand so hard it scarcely counts.”

He looked down. His feet were braced as though he meant to run.

He let them settle.

The boy beside him watched the correction and moved his own feet. The bandage had begun to show a stain. Mother Wei checked it, replaced what needed replacing and told him where to hold his hand. She did not blame him while he was still trying to remain in the room.

Tan Wei turned to a blank sheet at the back of his notebook.

It had been saved for something important, which now seemed a foolishly vague category. He tore it free carefully enough to leave the adjoining page intact and handed it to the boy.

“Write your name.”

The boy stared at the sheet.

“My hand.”

“We'll hold it steady.”

Tan Wei found a board. Qiu Lan passed a brush with her free hand. They arranged the small task without interrupting the work Han was doing at the next basin.

The first stroke shook.

The boy tried to wipe it away. Tan Wei stopped the page, not the hand.

“It can stay.”

The next stroke was little better. The name took most of the space because the writer had begun too large. When he finished, he stared at it as though uncertain whether somebody would now tell him it was the wrong answer.

Tan Wei placed his own notebook beside the sheet.

Two sets of ordinary marks rested on the board between the basins.

The collector had not yet fallen. The door had brought no new message. Somewhere beyond the walls, people were trying to make an interval large enough for the choices written there.

Tan Wei stayed beside the boy while they waited.

chapters.title: The Captain's Passage
chapters.text:
Ruan gave ground deliberately.

The outer passage was too wide to defend against eight men without allowing a crossbowman to work around him. He retreated toward the narrowed section beside the old masonry, keeping the first two attackers between himself and the weapons behind them.

“Put down your weapons,” Shen Tu called.

Ruan turned a blade with his own and struck the wielder hard enough to drive him against the wall.

“You first.”

It was the sort of reply his aunt would have called unnecessary.

He knew that while saying it.

The second guard came over the first man's shoulder. Ruan withdrew his leading foot, let the point pass close to his coat and brought his blade down across the shaft. Wood jarred against stone. The guard recovered quickly, better trained than his uncertain face had first suggested.

Ruan did not follow him into the wider space.

Behind the guards, one crossbow lifted. Its wielder tried to shift left, found the wall narrowing his view and waited for a clear line. Ruan moved with the man in front of him. The guard's body remained between the bow and the gap through which a bolt could reach the crew below.

“This is district property,” Shen Tu said.

“So is the emergency seal you passed.”

“The steward cannot authorize interference with the renewal.”

“Then wait while the reading is brought to you.”

A sword came toward Ruan's neck. He caught it high, turned, and felt the edge of another weapon score his sleeve as he moved. Warmth spread along his forearm.

The wound was shallow. It had still happened because he had answered the captain instead of attending entirely to the men allowed to reach him.

He stopped arguing.

The narrowed passage helped. It did not make the fight fair. Each time he pushed one man back, another took his place with less fatigue. A boot slid through the dust near the broken mortar. Someone swore when an elbow hit the wall. The men at the front were frightened too, but their fear was being directed by a voice that could remain outside the immediate danger.

Ruan pressed the next attack aside and struck with the flat, not because he expected gratitude but because the man's shoulder offered a useful target that would not leave a body blocking the stair.

The guard staggered back.

Shen Tu looked past Ruan toward the turn below, then toward the side court adjoining the old stores.

Ruan saw the decision form in the change of his stance.

“Storage passage!” he called over his shoulder.

The next attacker came in before he could see who had heard.

***

Su Fan stayed at the collar.

He could hear only pieces of the fight. Steel. A shout from his left. A dull impact carried through the stone beneath his hand. The sounds arriving at his damaged ear became pressure without location, and his mind tried to arrange them into an account that might be wrong in every useful detail.

He wanted to reach for his sword.

Sun Lian caught his eye.

“Your position.”

He looked back at the release handle.

The upper gauge had not fallen far enough. Opening now would drive the damaged chamber against the full returning load. He had practised moving the hook for days. Those movements did not become useful simply because he was afraid for the man at the entrance.

Ren Bo stood behind the wheel, watching the warning board and the upper stair. The guide line lay ready in its cleat. A worker beside him held a mallet with both hands, not as a weapon but because he had forgotten there was another place to put it.

“Bench,” Ren Bo told him.

The man looked down, set it there and wiped his palms on his clothes.

Su Fan checked the collar's seated catch. He had checked it already. Checking again gave his hands an activity without changing the thing that required waiting.

Something struck above them.

Dust sifted from a joint in the roof. Sun Lian's hand flattened against the transfer brace. She looked at the pressure board, then at the two workers near the lower seat.

“Last pin. Now.”

They moved into place. One held the pin upright while the other took the mallet from the bench. It was an ordinary exchange of tools in a room where men outside had begun treating the work as a thing that could be stopped by force.

Su Fan heard another shout. He thought he caught the word *storage*.

He looked toward the timber partition above the lower landing.

It had been marked as outside the evacuation route. That did not make it outside the building.

***

Shen Tu left three men with Ruan and took the remaining five through the old storage passage.

He knew the quarter's plans. He had guarded its warehouses for years, inspected deliveries, walked ordinary doors whose names Su Fan had learned only when looking for a way beneath them. Finding a forgotten route did not make everyone else forget the usual ones.

The storage partition had been closed to keep loose goods and casual traffic away from the work. It was timber, not a fortress door.

The first impact made the upper latch jump.

Ren Bo looked up.

The second split a fastening. A board tipped inward, struck the landing rail and hung there for a moment before another blow sent it down the stairs.

Two workers pressed themselves against the wall to let it pass. The falling wood struck the side of the winch and stopped short of the guide line.

Ren Bo saw the crossbow through the gap.

He dropped behind the wheel.

A bolt struck the wood where his chest had been.

For an instant nobody moved. The sound had been much smaller than the damage it could have done. Su Fan could see the shaft trembling in the wheel's side, above the place where Ren Bo's shoulder had just vanished.

Then Shen Tu came through the broken partition.

“Secure the mechanism.”

One of the guards went toward the handle, saw the pressure board and hesitated.

“Captain, the steward's seal.”

“I can see it.”

“The red—”

“Hold the handle.”

The man obeyed.

Su Fan saw his face when he reached the winch. He did not look like someone who had understood the sequence and chosen to break it. He looked like someone trying to identify which danger he would be held responsible for noticing.

The two crossbowmen remained higher in the storage opening. One began drawing his weapon again. The other searched for a line that did not pass through the captain and their own men. A guard with a short sword moved down toward the tool bench. The last stayed near the broken boards, glancing between the upper passage and the working crew.

Shen Tu had not entered blindly. He had brought enough men to make every position require a response.

***

Sun Lian could not leave the brace.

The rising pressure had begun to twist it before the bypass was even open. Earth qi reinforced the seated timber beneath her palm while the two workers drove the last pin home. Su Fan could see the effort in the angle of her shoulder.

The guard at the winch reached for a second grip.

Ren Bo came halfway out of cover.

“Not that one.”

“Stand away.”

“If you release it—”

The guard lowered his spear toward him. He was holding the machinery with one hand and trying to make the weapon carry the certainty his voice lacked.

Su Fan looked from Sun Lian to the winch.

This time remaining at his position would allow somebody else to destroy it.

“I'm moving,” he said.

Sun Lian glanced at the landing. Her eyes returned to his face long enough to make sure he could hear.

“Keep them off the winch. Nothing farther.”

He drew his sword.

The familiar weight did not steady him as neatly as it had in the yard. The passage contained men who had not agreed to stop when a point reached their coat. There were frightened workers behind him, a return conductor still under pressure and a floor too narrow to forgive a broad mistake.

He went toward the spear.

The first guard was younger than he had expected. He held the shaft too tightly. When Su Fan stepped into reach, the point came forward with more commitment than the man's feet could support.

Su Fan knocked it aside, stepped past and struck the wrist with his sword guard.

The spear fell.

He caught the man's coat and shoved him toward the wall, away from the wheel and the moving line.

“Stay there.”

The guard folded around his wrist. His mouth opened with anger, pain or a reply he could not bring into shape quickly enough. Su Fan did not wait to decide which.

Behind him, Ren Bo rose and put his hands back where they belonged.

The bolt remained in the wheel. One of the workers stared at it as though the wood might yet decide to split.

“Watch the line,” Ren Bo said.

The man looked down.

***

A second guard came from Su Fan's right.

He saw the movement in the polished face of the hanging gauge before he heard it: a dark shape growing larger above the trembling needle, the brief flare of light from an edge changing direction.

Su Fan turned with his sword already rising.

Steel met steel.

The man's pressure tried to enter through the contact and find a lineage route to pin. It found nothing familiar. That small failure changed the guard's expression, but his physical strength still drove Su Fan back half a pace.

The landing edge touched Su Fan's heel.

He let the force pass through his legs, changed the angle and moved before the guard could turn surprise into another attack. His palm struck the exposed elbow. The arm folded. The man's sword point hit the wall and slid down with a harsh scrape.

Su Fan kept moving until the injured arm stood between the man and the winch.

He had not stopped the whole room. The crossbows remained above. Shen Tu remained beyond the guard. A worker at the brace shouted because the pin had entered crookedly, and Sun Lian told him to back it out a little rather than force it through the wrong angle.

The ordinary work continued in fragments around the violence.

The guard tried to lift his sword again.

Su Fan brought the point beneath his hands.

“Put it down.”

The man looked past him toward the captain.

Su Fan hated the delay. He could not make a person cease to belong to a command merely by proving he could hurt him.

The blade lowered enough for him to move it away from the wheel. He pushed the man back toward the bench, leaving the wounded spear guard between them and the nearest rope. Neither was safe from further injury if they entered the work again. Neither needed to be killed to make the next step possible.

At the upper partition, the second crossbowman shifted to follow Su Fan.

Sun Lian's worker moved across his line carrying the pin. For a moment the weapon pointed toward a man who had not drawn anything sharper than a tool.

“Down,” Su Fan shouted.

The worker dropped.

The bowman did not loose. His captain stood just beyond the line, close enough that the bolt could have reached either body if the target moved.

Shen Tu raised one hand, and the weapon's point changed.

He had not lost control of his men. He was changing the part of the work he intended to do himself.

***

At the entrance, Ruan heard the bolt strike before he understood where it had landed.

The three men left with him pressed harder when they heard the break through the partition. Their task was not to beat him. It was to keep him here long enough for the captain to finish below.

He could have tried to rush them. One clean opening might have carried him through.

One failure would have put three armed men at his back while he ran down a stair full of workers.

He changed his attack instead.

The next guard expected another retreat. Ruan stepped inside, drove the man's weapon against the wall and struck him beneath the shoulder. The guard dropped to one knee. Ruan took the blade away and sent it behind himself, where it skidded beyond easy reach.

The second man stopped rather than climb across his companion. Ruan used the hesitation to move nearer the inner turn.

“Your captain has put bolts into a working chamber,” he said.

“We have orders.”

“So did the man who built the chair you're hoping to sit in when you go home. Think before you break it.”

It was too long a sentence for a fight. The third guard nearly made him pay for it. Ruan caught the strike, felt his injured sleeve pull and ended with his sword across the man's throat without pressing it home.

“Back.”

The man backed.

Ruan could see fear becoming calculation. None of the three had come here hoping to die beneath an old archive. Their courage had not disappeared. It had acquired a question their captain was no longer present to answer for them.

He kept his blade up and waited for the next movement.

***

Below, Su Fan faced Shen Tu.

The captain had drawn his own sword.

It was plain enough to make the weapon seem smaller than the attention it required. He held it easily, with no gesture intended to show the room what kind of man he was. Su Fan remembered him bending one of Duan's nails between finger and thumb, testing the iron while discussing an order.

He remembered a paper windmill being spun to see whether its axle caught.

Those memories did not provide a weakness.

Su Fan shifted his grip. Blood from a scrape he had not noticed made the binding tacky beneath his palm. The distance to the captain was short enough that either man could cross it before a frightened worker finished calling a warning.

To Su Fan's left, Ren Bo's hands waited on the winch. Behind the captain, a heavy chain hung on a restraint hook beside the counterweight housing. Neither belonged in a sword fight. Both would become part of one if he allowed himself to be driven through the machinery.

He moved his rear foot away from the loose wedge on the floor.

Shen Tu saw that too.

The captain did not look hurried. He had other men to hold the entrances, workers who could not leave their posts and an opponent already trying to protect more space than his sword could cover.

Shen Tu looked at the young guard holding his injured wrist, the other man unable to straighten his arm, and Ren Bo returning the winch to its proper readiness.

Then his eyes went to Su Fan's right ear.

Su Fan turned a little, trying to keep the wall where it would close that side. The captain's gaze followed the motion, moved upward and stopped on the polished gauge.

The metal face showed the lower stair behind Su Fan. A small reflection shifted when the crossbowman above changed his footing.

Shen Tu saw Su Fan notice it.

He cut the hanging line.

The gauge struck the floor. Its case opened against a stone edge; the polished face folded, the needle snapped sideways and one of the glass fragments spun toward the wheel.

Ren Bo kicked the fragment clear of the rope without taking his hands off the handle.

Su Fan's view of his right side vanished.

The captain stepped into the space it had shown.

chapters.title: No Room to Turn
chapters.text:
The first strike opened Su Fan's coat across the ribs.

Iron plates caught the edge. The force beneath it drove him into the landing wall, and for an instant the whole right side of his body seemed to be receiving the same blunt instruction.

He kept the sword between them as he fell.

Shen Tu did not follow carelessly. He kicked a fallen wedge across the floor, forcing Su Fan to move his foot before the next cut arrived. The small change took away the position from which he intended to rise.

Su Fan met the blade too high.

Pain ran through his wrist. His shoulder struck stone again. He pushed away before another blow could pin him there, using the lower circulation to carry the force through his legs rather than trying to answer it with the injured joint alone.

The captain was faster than Ruan and less interested in giving him anything recognizable as an exchange.

There was no pause after a useful touch. No slight withdrawal to see whether Su Fan understood why he had been hit. Shen Tu cut while moving, tested his recovery with another step and made the space he needed disappear as soon as he tried to use it.

Su Fan gave ground toward the lower stair.

He wanted the wall on his right. The captain saw that and moved to keep the open landing there instead. A simple adjustment of feet took less effort than the turn Su Fan needed to answer it.

He changed direction.

Shen Tu changed with him.

Su Fan heard the scrape of a boot on his left and almost trusted it. The visible blade came from elsewhere. He caught it before the point reached his neck, felt steel drag along steel and brought his own edge back across the opening.

The captain had already gone.

A crossbowman above called something. Shen Tu did not look toward him. The man's shot would have to pass too close to his commander, and for the moment that made the captain's proximity the only protection Su Fan had from the bow.

He could not step away freely. He could not remain close without meeting the next cut.

His breathing had become loud inside his head.

***

The third hard contact struck Su Fan's sword near its tip and turned the point away from the body it needed to threaten.

Shen Tu stepped into the opening and drove a knee into his thigh.

The leg buckled.

Su Fan caught the edge of the stair with his free hand. Skin tore from his palm. The pain was sharp enough to cut through the confused ringing in his right ear, and for one useless instant he resented the clarity of it.

The captain raised his sword.

The stair beneath his leading boot had been repaired. Su Fan could see the different mortar at the tread's edge, the old stone joined to a newer piece whose colour had looked harmless when they walked the evacuation route.

He struck beside his own foot.

The heel of the sword guard met the repaired seam. True Strike carried a short, concentrated force into the joint. He did not try to break the whole stair or send the captain flying. He had neither the position nor the time.

The old edge cracked.

Shen Tu's leading boot dropped with it.

Only a little.

Enough to alter the cut already falling toward Su Fan.

He moved inside the changed line. The blade scored the stone where his shoulder had been. He climbed along the captain's arm and cut toward the forearm holding the sword.

Shen Tu withdrew before the edge reached deeply.

His sleeve opened. A thin red line appeared beneath it.

For the first time he had needed to yield.

Su Fan got both feet under him. The injured thigh shook. Behind the captain, the broken tread left a fresh pale scar and a loose piece of stone large enough to trip someone carrying a load. He had made a new danger in the path they had worked to clear.

He could not repair it while remaining alive.

Shen Tu glanced at his wound, then at Su Fan's sword.

“You have improved.”

Su Fan did not answer.

Breath was already too valuable.

The captain's attention moved to the broken seam. He did not repeat the step that had placed his weight there. He approached along sound stone, shifting the point of his sword a little lower.

The lesson had reached both of them.

***

Su Fan tried to keep the distance at which his own blade could matter.

Shen Tu let him have it for half a movement, then threatened the wrist instead of the chest. Su Fan drew his hand back. The captain used the withdrawal to take the next step without needing to meet the full edge.

The blade came toward his face.

He turned it aside and felt the force pass through the seventh circuit. The new route held. That did not tell him where the next strike would arrive. His body could carry a response he still had to choose in time.

Shen Tu's boot struck the loosened wedge.

It slid toward Su Fan's good foot.

This time he saw it early enough to avoid the stumble. Avoiding it narrowed his stance. The captain's shoulder entered against his and forced him back another half step.

The landing rail touched his coat.

Beyond it, the working line waited under strain.

Su Fan drove forward rather than let himself fall into the mechanism. The captain turned with him and allowed the effort to spend itself against empty space. A short cut came toward the exposed back of his arm.

He caught that one late. Cloth parted. The wound was small, but it added another slippery place beneath the sleeve.

He had imagined combat as a difficult version of the yard. Now the yard seemed full of kindnesses he had failed to count: even ground, a partner who wanted both men to learn, an ending that could be requested with a word.

The captain was not interested in those things.

The torn coat had begun to hinder Su Fan's turn. One of the small inner plates had shifted where its stitching parted. Its edge pressed against his ribs each time he raised the sword. He could not stop to settle it. He could not discard the coat while the same plates remained the reason the first cut had failed to open his body.

He shortened the next movement.

Shen Tu noticed and drove the attack higher, making the injured shoulder take more of the answer. Su Fan turned the blade enough to keep its edge clear, but the correction exposed his side to the captain's free hand. A hard shove caught the displaced plate and drove its corner into the bruise beneath.

His breath broke.

The coat had not failed completely. That would almost have been easier to understand. It was protecting him in one direction and making another movement costly. He had to fight in the garment it had become, not the sound piece he had inspected the previous night.

He lowered the elbow a little, found a narrower line and kept the sword between the captain and the hand that wanted to reach inside the coat.

Su Fan looked for a recognizable sequence and found ordinary work. A cut that made him lift his guard. A step that stole the room to lower it. The point changing direction only after he had committed to the first answer.

Shen Tu had methods. He did not present them as a fixed diagram waiting to be read.

Su Fan could hear Ren Bo behind him, calling to the crew. The words arrived without a complete sentence. Somewhere higher, Ruan's sword struck another weapon. The interval they needed had still not been granted. They were spending strength while the pressure spent time.

He tried a short strike through the next contact.

Shen Tu withdrew before the force arrived cleanly. Su Fan's point passed across his coat without finding the body beneath. The missed commitment pulled at his injured shoulder.

The captain answered with a quick blow to the guard.

The sword nearly left Su Fan's hand.

He tightened his fingers and felt torn skin move against the binding. It would be easy to hold the weapon so hard that his wrist lost the small movements still keeping him alive.

He made himself loosen the grip a fraction.

Shen Tu saw that too.

***

Water hissed behind the stone throat.

Sun Lian called something from the chamber. Su Fan caught only the last word.

Ready.

He did not know which part of the work she meant. The word did not authorize him to leave the fight or pull the conductor before the gauge fell.

The captain heard it as well.

He shifted toward the winch.

Su Fan moved between them.

Shen Tu's next attack came low, then high without a pause. Su Fan parried the first and took the second across the shoulder. The blade missed his neck by less than a finger's width.

Warm blood ran beneath the collar.

For a moment the arm seemed to belong to the wound rather than to him. He could lift it, but the effort came with an unfamiliar delay. He took the next contact nearer the guard and gave ground instead of demanding strength from the injured part before he knew what remained.

Shen Tu pressed.

The captain could have kept him occupied with attacks to the same side. Instead he changed direction and forced him to turn toward his damaged ear. Su Fan had to look where another man might have listened. The extra movement of his head narrowed what he could see in front.

There was no polished gauge now.

Its broken face lay beneath the landing rail, reflecting a piece of roof that could help nobody.

Su Fan met another cut and felt the captain's weight behind it. No inherited command had to seize his channels. Enough iron arriving quickly enough could reach the flesh regardless of whose method carried the arm.

He needed to stop trying to win the captain's fight.

There was no room to outdistance the longer reach. No quiet moment to study an ancestral pattern. The few useful observations he had gathered were physical: Shen Tu recovered well to one side, guarded the wounded forearm without overprotecting it, and made Su Fan choose between moving away from the blade and moving toward the machinery.

The captain expected fear to make those choices less precise.

He was right often enough to remain dangerous.

Su Fan glanced at the winch. Ren Bo had moved the nearest worker out of the line of a possible falling body. The man with the injured wrist sat against the wall, staring at the blade he no longer held. Above them, one crossbowman was trying to change his angle again.

If Su Fan ran for the stair, the captain could reach the handle.

If he stood and traded cuts, the captain would finish him.

There was one thing Shen Tu had seen but not measured with certainty.

The force in Su Fan's contact did not need the warning swell of a conventional release. It could arrive through a movement already in progress, provided the line and timing were right.

It would have to be enough once.

***

He did not make the opening immediately.

That was the hardest part.

The thought of a possible answer made his body want to rush toward it. His next movement became too eager. Shen Tu checked it with the flat, turned the point and nearly caught his fingers.

Su Fan gave ground, let the failed attempt finish and brought his feet beneath him again.

The seventh circuit remained open. He could feel where unnecessary tension was beginning to crowd it. The pain did not disappear when he loosened that tension. It became easier to distinguish from the effort he still needed.

The captain came forward.

Su Fan met the blade and allowed the contact to carry him toward the wall. He kept the winch behind the captain's left shoulder, out of the straight line of his own retreat. It was a small improvement in a position still bad enough to kill him.

Shen Tu tested the injured leg with another low threat.

Su Fan moved it late. The delay was partly chosen and partly real. His thigh had begun to stiffen where the knee struck it. He did not need to invent weakness; he needed the captain to see enough of the actual weakness to trust the opening beside it.

He lowered his point.

Not far. Not the theatrical invitation Ruan would have mocked before touching his ribs. The change looked like a man protecting his shoulder and failing to keep his sword high enough.

Shen Tu's eyes went to the hand.

Su Fan felt fear rise so strongly that he nearly withdrew the invitation. The captain could take it differently. He could thrust at the throat, step away and let a bow work, or simply wait until the injured man spent what remained of his strength.

There was no certainty to discover before moving.

The captain cut at the hand.

Su Fan brought the blade across his body and received the strike near the guard, where the steel was strongest. At contact he stepped into Iron Step. The returning circulation joined a short True Strike before the captain could turn the change into a new angle.

The sound was small.

The result was not.

Shen Tu's sword jumped outward. His wrist turned past the position from which he could recover immediately.

Su Fan went with the contact. He drove his shoulder beneath the captain's arm and pinned it against the wall before the opening vanished.

Pain flashed through his own cut shoulder. He held the position anyway, not with enough strength to defeat everything Shen Tu might do, but with the wall taking part of a load he could not carry alone.

His sword point rested below the captain's jaw.

Both men were breathing hard.

***

For an instant Su Fan could hear almost nothing.

The ringing in his damaged ear had become a steady high thread. The sounds of the chamber arrived around it in pieces: a boot moving on the stair, the scrape of the guide line, water striking stone beyond the closed throat.

Shen Tu's face was close enough that Su Fan could see a small cut near the corner of his mouth. He did not know which movement had caused it. The captain looked angry, but not astonished into helplessness.

His sword remained in his hand.

Su Fan could feel the arm beneath his shoulder trying to find room.

“Let go,” he said.

The captain's eyes moved toward the blade beneath his jaw.

Su Fan had imagined that reaching this position would create an ending. It created only another moment in which a man could choose.

“Let it go.”

Shen Tu's fingers opened.

The sword struck the stone.

Su Fan did not step back. The captain's breath moved against the edge of his sleeve. Behind them, one of the guards made a sound and stopped when Ruan shouted from higher on the stair.

The upper pressure still had to fall. The collar still had to turn. Workers remained beneath the weight beside the winch, holding positions that could not be abandoned merely because a sword had been dropped.

Su Fan drew breath to tell the captain to move his other hand where he could see it.

That hand was already moving.

It closed around the weighted release chain beside the winch.

chapters.title: The Hand on the Chain
chapters.text:
Shen Tu pulled.

The chain was not the operating line. It was the safety restraint holding the upper counterweight out of the workers' path.

Su Fan had helped check it during the rehearsal. He knew where the weight would fall. The captain had crossed the same landing, seen the housing and the marked travel beneath it, and reached past the ordinary handle to take this particular chain.

A link lifted from the hook.

Su Fan saw Ren Bo at the winch.

He saw Sun Lian's hand pressed against the transfer brace and the worker crouching below it, still holding the pin they had just seated.

The captain's shoulder turned under the point at his jaw. The chain moved again.

Su Fan took his blade down and cut.

***

The sword entered below Shen Tu's ribs.

There was resistance, then movement.

The captain's grip loosened. Su Fan caught the chain with his free hand before the restraint could slip its last link. The load snatched at his torn palm and almost dragged him sideways across the body he had just struck.

He held it.

For a moment that was all he could do.

Shen Tu looked down. His face showed surprise, ordinary and unguarded, as though the room had done something outside the account he had brought into it.

Then he tried to draw breath.

Su Fan pulled the sword free and pushed the chain back onto its hook. The metal scraped. He could not immediately see whether the link had seated, and the fear of letting go held his hand closed after the strain had already shifted away from it.

“It's on,” Ren Bo said.

Su Fan looked at him.

“It's on. Leave it.”

He opened his fingers.

Shen Tu sank against the wall.

The captain's sword lay where he had dropped it. A few drops struck its blade, making small dark marks on the steel. Su Fan still held his own weapon extended because his body had not yet accepted that the movement was finished.

“Down,” someone said.

He did not know whether the word meant his sword, the captain or the counterweight.

***

The fight around them stopped unevenly.

One guard lowered his weapon at once. Another stared at the captain and began backing toward the storage passage. A crossbow remained raised long enough for Su Fan to see the bolt aligned with the room rather than with any target its wielder could now name.

“Lower it,” Ren Bo said.

The man looked at his dead commander's order case on the floor.

Ruan reached the landing with blood on his sleeve and three men behind him who had decided not to continue. He took in the chain, the seated counterweight and Shen Tu folded beneath the wall.

His sword remained in his hand.

“Lower the bow.”

This time the man obeyed.

Ruan made the others move away from the machinery. He did not demand that they declare who had been right. The injured spear guard tried to stand, failed to put weight through his wrist and sat again with a sound that seemed much louder now there was no fighting to hide it.

Su Fan looked at the blood on his own blade.

He had stopped a movement. He could see the restraint back on its hook and Ren Bo still alive beside the wheel. The fact was clear enough to exist without being argued.

The man at his feet was trying to breathe.

Su Fan set the sword out of the immediate path and knelt.

“Cloth.”

Nobody moved quickly enough for the word. He pulled a fold from the torn part of his coat, then someone passed him a cleaner piece from the tool wrapping. He pressed it against the wound.

The blood soaked it immediately.

Shen Tu's mouth moved.

Su Fan leaned closer with his good ear.

He could not understand the words.

“I can't hear you.”

The captain tried again. His hand moved toward the front of his coat, then fell before reaching whatever he intended.

Su Fan looked up at the nearest guard.

“What did he say?”

The man shook his head.

For a moment Su Fan was angry with him. It was a useless, shameful anger, searching for someone who might supply the missing words and thereby turn the scene into something he knew how to answer.

The captain looked at him. Or past him. Su Fan could no longer tell.

***

Ruan crouched beside them.

“Su Fan.”

“Hold this.”

Ruan put his hand over the folded cloth. He looked at the wound, then at Su Fan. His expression changed very slightly, and Su Fan wished he had not seen it.

“Is there a healer?” Su Fan asked.

“Above, with the operators.”

“Someone else?”

Ruan looked toward the guards. None answered.

One of the men who had followed the captain through the storage passage moved closer. He was older than the first two Su Fan had struck. He took off his outer coat and folded it beneath Shen Tu's shoulder, then stood back as though the small action had exhausted every duty he understood.

“Send word,” Ruan told him. “Tell them exactly where.”

The guard went toward the upper stair.

Sun Lian called from the brace. The upper pressure had begun to drop.

The interval was coming.

Su Fan remained kneeling.

His own shoulder hurt. He could feel blood moving beneath the collar, sweat cooling where the coat had been cut, the dull swelling in his thigh. Those pains were familiar in the simplest way: his body contained them, and his body had a reason to try to survive them.

The blood beneath Ruan's hand belonged to a man whose life Su Fan had interrupted with a choice.

He had been frightened of killing before. Now that earlier fear seemed to belong to somebody who had understood almost nothing about what would remain afterward.

Shen Tu had nearly killed him twice. He had ordered bolts fired into a room full of workers. He had reached for a chain whose falling weight would have destroyed people carrying out the work it was intended to protect.

He had also stood in the market testing a paper windmill with the same attention he gave good iron.

Both things remained true.

Neither told Su Fan what to do with the blood on his fingers.

He tried to remember whether the windmill had been red or yellow. The failure of that memory frightened him in a way that had nothing to do with the danger still rising through the chamber.

Why did he need the colour? He had never known who it was for. Inventing a recipient now would not make the man more real. The man had already been real when Su Fan put the sword into him.

Shen Tu's eyes shifted.

Su Fan bent closer again. A breath caught, stopped, resumed in a thinner form. There were no clear words inside it.

Ruan's hand remained steady on the cloth.

***

Behind them, the lower crew began putting the landing back into a shape that could be used.

A broken board had fallen across the spare line. A worker lifted it with both hands and passed it away rather than drag it through the rope. Ren Bo examined the link on the restraint hook, then the bend in the hook's lip. He called another man to look so the account would not belong only to him afterward.

The captain's sword lay close to the step. Ruan told the nearest uninjured guard to move it out of the route and leave it where both of them could see.

The guard obeyed reluctantly.

Su Fan heard the scrape of the weapon being placed on a crate. Ordinary actions were assembling around the extraordinary thing on the floor. The work could not wait for him to understand it.

The young spearman sat where Su Fan had pushed him, holding his wrist against his stomach. He was watching the covered passage rather than the captain. Each time someone moved near his discarded spear, his shoulders tightened.

“Is it broken?” he asked.

For a moment Su Fan thought he meant the mechanism.

The guard lifted his hand a little. Two fingers moved; the others remained curled.

“I don't know.”

“Will someone look?”

“Yes,” Ruan said. “When we can get a healer down.”

The young man swallowed. He had obeyed an order to seize a handle and acquired an injury whose duration nobody in the room could tell him. Su Fan had struck that wrist deliberately. He could remember the exact place where his sword guard met it.

One of the crossbowmen began to climb down from the broken partition.

Ren Bo saw the loaded weapon and backed against the winch.

“Leave that above.”

The man stopped.

“I am coming for my captain.”

“Then leave it.”

He looked toward Ruan, who had one hand occupied with the cloth and could not reach his own sword without abandoning the pressure. For several breaths, nothing in the landing moved except water dripping from the ceiling.

Then the crossbowman set the weapon down with its bow facing the wall and descended empty-handed.

He crouched beside Shen Tu. His gaze moved from the bloody cloth to Su Fan, then to the chain Ren Bo had reseated.

“What did he touch?”

Ren Bo pointed, but did not lift the link to demonstrate.

“That restraint. There is still weight on it.”

“The captain said the gate had to be secured.”

“That isn't how you secure it with men below.”

The guard looked up. He could see the iron mass above the working space and the little distance left beneath its supports. He reached toward the chain, stopped when Ren Bo caught his sleeve, and let his hand fall.

“I didn't see him pull it.”

“Then don't say you did,” Ruan said.

Su Fan looked at him.

The words were for everyone. The guard's account would be incomplete, and it would remain his account. Ruan had not asked him to improve it because a more convenient witness might make this floor easier to leave.

The man stayed beside the captain. After a while he took off his own scarf and offered it for another dressing.

Ruan accepted it. Nobody pretended the clean cloth changed how much blood had already been lost.

Sun Lian called again.

He did not catch all the words, but he saw the urgency in the worker who came from her station. The man stopped close enough to be heard and pointed toward the board.

“The upper measure is coming down. She needs you ready.”

Su Fan looked at Ruan.

“Your position,” Ruan said quietly.

“I can't leave—”

“I'll stay here.”

“Can you—”

“I don't know.”

It was the only answer available.

Su Fan looked down at the cloth. His hand was no longer the one holding it. He had asked Ruan to take that work and then remained as though watching could supply something the other man lacked.

He tried to stand.

His injured leg almost failed. The older guard who had folded his coat came back in time to catch his elbow. Su Fan flinched at the touch. The guard let go as soon as he was steady and did not make the help into forgiveness.

Su Fan retrieved his sword.

The exposed blade looked wrong in a room full of people whose attention had divided between a dying commander and a mechanism still waiting to move. He wiped it once, badly, and sheathed it before turning through the narrow path.

The cloth left blood beneath the guard. He noticed and did nothing about it.

There would be a time when noticing required an answer. This was not that time.

***

Sun Lian met him at the collar.

She had not left the brace until another support took enough weight for her to shift. Even now, one hand remained close to the timber, ready to return if the seat changed.

“Can you use that hand?”

Su Fan opened and closed his fingers.

The torn palm hurt. He could still hold the hook.

“Yes.”

“Can you follow the sequence?”

He looked at the board.

The marks were the ones he had practised. Waiting gauge. Release position. Clear sleeve line. Hook out before collar travel. His eyes moved through them twice before he trusted the order they formed.

“Yes.”

“Tell me.”

He did. His voice sounded strange. At one point it stopped, and he had to swallow before finishing the sentence.

Sun Lian waited rather than complete it for him.

When he finished, she took the tool from its cradle.

“Then take the hook.”

He took it.

The binding was dry. His hand was not. She gave him a strip of clean cloth for the grip, enough to keep it from slipping without hiding whether his fingers could close. He wrapped it slowly and tested the catch.

She watched the movement, not his expression.

“Stay outside the recess until the mark.”

“I know.”

“Tell me when knowing stops helping.”

He nodded.

There was no speech about doing what had been necessary. No assurance that he would understand later. She needed him capable of a specific task, and he was grateful for the narrowness of what she asked.

At the board, Ren Bo's nephew arrived with a message from above. He saw the blood along Su Fan's sleeve and stopped so abruptly that the paper shook in his hand.

“Give it to Sun Lian,” Su Fan said.

The boy did.

Sun Lian read it, checked the gauge and sent the answer back along the pull cord. The upper feed was being reduced, but not yet held within the window they required.

Still waiting.

Su Fan put his feet on the positions he had marked. The ring beneath his shirt pressed against his bruised chest. It remained an ordinary weight. He was glad it had not become a sign that anything about this morning had been chosen for him.

***

Behind him, someone laid a coat over Shen Tu's face.

Su Fan saw the movement at the edge of his vision.

He did not turn around.

He knew which coat it was. The older guard had folded it beneath the captain's shoulder. Now it had another use, and the difference between those uses contained everything he did not know how to say.

Ruan stood.

He spoke quietly to the surviving guards. Su Fan caught only pieces: weapons, stair, account, do not touch. The words sounded more tired than commanding. They were enough to keep another struggle from beginning over the body.

The hooked tool felt cold through the new wrapping.

Su Fan checked its catch again. This time the action was part of the work, not merely something his hand could do while his thoughts remained on the landing. He looked at the chalk mark on his sleeve, then at the matching mark inside the recess.

Water struck the throat with a deeper sound.

The crew looked toward the pressure board. Sun Lian read it and held up her free hand. Wait.

Above the chamber, the old stone began to hum.

It was not the gate.

Dust moved along the upper stair before anyone stepped into view. A lamp flame leaned toward the passage and remained there. Su Fan felt the air press against his skin in a way he remembered from the room where a pebble had buried itself in the wall.

Ruan moved between the guards and the working crew, not raising his sword but no longer looking as though the fight had ended all the dangers in the building.

Sun Lian set her palm firmly against the brace.

Su Fan looked up.

Pei Gang had come down from the upper station.

chapters.title: The Elder Below
chapters.text:
Pei Gang entered through a passage too narrow for ceremony.

The first lamp bent toward him. Its flame flattened almost sideways before rising again, thin and blue at the root. Dust lifted around his boots without settling on the hem of his robe.

Su Fan felt the air strike his skin before the elder spoke.

“Stop the mechanism.”

Sun Lian kept her hand against the brace.

“We haven't opened it.”

“Then stand away.”

“The brace is carrying a changing load. If I stand away, someone must take it.”

Pei looked at her hand, the seated timber and the two men waiting with the spare wedges. He did not repeat the command immediately. His gaze moved past them to the winch, the restraint chain and the coat on the landing floor.

One of the guards straightened.

“Elder—”

“Later.”

The man closed his mouth.

Su Fan put the release hook into its cradle. His fingers did not want to open. Blood had dried between the knuckles, and the cloth Sun Lian had given him clung to the torn part of his palm.

Above, footsteps hurried down the stair.

Jiang came into the chamber carrying the gauge board against her chest. The messenger behind her held its loose cord clear of the wet steps. She was breathing hard, but she placed the board on its stand before attempting to speak.

“The collector has exceeded the emergency threshold. Three operators are unresponsive. The local loops are bearing more than their certified load.”

“I have reduced the feed,” Pei said.

“The returning command is already below your regulator.”

He looked at the figures.

The independent needle continued to move beside them. Its tip trembled too quickly for Su Fan to follow, but the mark Jiang had drawn on the backing made its position clear.

Pei knew what the figures meant.

***

Jiang pointed to the first recorded rise, then to the brief improvement after the upper reduction.

“That interval lasted less than the previous cycle. The next return arrived before the lower collector cleared.”

“The repaired channels were certified for the renewal.”

“These are the readings from the repaired channels.”

She did not raise her voice. Su Fan found that more alarming than anger. Jiang was not trying to persuade the elder that she respected him. She had brought the work that would either stand or fail without the assistance of her manner.

Pei put two fingers on the board's wooden edge.

For a moment the trembling needle steadied.

Then it climbed again.

Sun Lian watched it and shifted her palm farther along the brace. The timber made a small sound beneath her hand. She told the nearest worker to check the lower wedge with his eyes, not his fingers.

Pei heard her.

“You have prepared this chamber without the authorized flow test.”

“We requested the test,” Jiang said.

“That is not the same as having performed it.”

“No.”

The answer left the risk where it belonged. No one in the room had seen this old throat take the load now waiting behind it. They had measured, cleared, repaired and rehearsed. Water would still be the first thing to test several of their beliefs together.

Su Fan looked at the white signal board lying flat beside the upper stair. It had not been raised. The window was not theirs yet.

Pei's attention moved to him.

The weight of it filled the landing.

***

It began as the familiar pressure that made bonded practitioners feel for a route before they had chosen to move.

Su Fan knew the sensation from the eighth station and from the conductor he had not yet touched. A demand arrived, looking for something in him that would recognize its authority.

His channels remained his own.

There was breath in his chest, blood drying on his wrist and the returning pressure of the seventh circuit. No ancestral pattern opened to admit the elder's command.

For one foolish instant he thought that mattered enough.

Then Pei moved his hand.

A loose stone struck Su Fan in the chest.

The iron-lined coat spread the impact. The force drove him backward before his feet found any useful place to set. His shoulder hit the wall where the old mortar had been cut away for inspection.

His breath disappeared.

The elder caught him there with a broad physical pressure, as simple as a river pressing a man against a pier. Su Fan tried to move his left arm. It shifted a little and stopped. His right hand opened involuntarily, leaving the bloodied grip cloth on the floor.

No lineage was required to be crushed.

“Your resistance has made you careless about the difference,” Pei said.

Su Fan tried to answer.

Nothing came out.

He could feel the edges of the plates beneath his coat. One pressed against a rib already bruised by the captain's sword. The seventh circuit continued, but its movement had no space to give his lungs.

Ruan took a step.

Pei turned his eyes toward him.

The young man stopped with his hand half-raised, caught between the certainty that Su Fan needed help and the equally clear knowledge that crossing the landing would not supply it.

Sun Lian shouted Su Fan's name.

He heard her from a great distance, though she stood only a few paces away.

***

Jiang moved the board between herself and the elder.

“You need him at the release. Or you need to hold the conductor yourself while I manage the upper feed.”

“I can manage both.”

“Then tell the western crew which position you will take.”

Pei looked at her.

She had not challenged his rank. She had asked him to put the claim into the room's arrangement of hands, tools and places from which people could reach them.

The low bell rang.

A third warning.

Water struck the damaged return chamber above them hard enough to shake grit from the roof. A worker ducked. Sun Lian leaned into the brace, her jaw tightening as the load changed beneath her palm.

The force against Su Fan's chest shifted for the smallest moment.

He drew a scraping mouthful of air.

It hurt badly enough that he almost lost it again. He kept his chin down and tried for another breath instead of spending the first on a word.

Pei looked upward.

At the landing entrance, the guards stood very still. One had begun to raise the captain's fallen sword, perhaps believing its recovery was his duty. He lowered it again when the stone moved beneath his boots.

The room did not care which seal he had followed into it.

Jiang spoke before Pei looked down.

“The upper reduction must be held. The collar must be moved only after it is held. The local loops must remain separate while Han works. Which of those will you take from the people assigned to them?”

“Do not mistake a list for command.”

“I am trying to keep the list attached to people who can perform it.”

Su Fan could hear her clearly now. The pressure remained, but he had found enough room for short breaths. There was no way to turn that improvement into escape. Any attempt to brace harder only made the next breath more expensive.

He stopped trying to look stronger than he was.

***

Wen Zhao reached the stair behind the elder.

His sleeves were wet to the elbows. There was a dark smear on one cuff that might have been ink until he put his hand on the rail and left a thin red print.

“Five unresponsive now,” he said. “Master Han requests immediate isolation.”

Jiang asked when the fifth had ceased answering.

“Before I left the room. Mother Wei was with him.”

“Breathing?”

“Yes.”
