The answer mattered. So did the fact that Wen would not claim to know what had happened in the minutes since he left. He took out the small writing board he had carried down and showed the marks beside the names. Some had been made by another hand; one had been pressed so hard that the wet ink had run through the grain.

Pei did not touch the list.

“Han has the local separation instruments?”

“He has them ready. He has not used a central withdrawal on an unconscious operator.”

The elder looked toward the stair as though the room above might be brought within reach by looking. It could not. People there were still waiting for something that had to happen here.

Wen set the names down where water would not wash them from the page.

Pei's burned wrist twitched.

The skin over the old injury had tightened until the damaged lines shone. Su Fan saw the movement travel from wrist to fingers, a small effort being corrected before it could become a larger one.

The elder had not abandoned the lake to come below.

He had brought its strain with him.

Knowing that did not make the force on Su Fan's chest gentle. It made Jiang's question more urgent. Pei was doing more than anyone else in the valley could have done, and more was still not everything.

Wen placed Han's message beside the gauge board.

“The local loop at the eighth station is at its limit. Two others are close.”

“Has anyone begun withdrawal?” Jiang asked.

“No. He will not begin against the central return.”

She nodded once.

Pei looked from the message to the needle.

The pressure against Su Fan loosened.

He fell to one knee.

Ruan reached him before his forehead struck the wall. The younger man's good hand took Su Fan beneath the arm; his wounded sleeve brushed the stone and left another mark there.

“Stay down a moment.”

Su Fan intended to say he was all right. A cough replaced the answer. He pressed his palm to his ribs and waited until air could move without catching at every edge.

Pei had already crossed to the drawing beside the winch.

***

He studied it without asking anyone to explain the parts he could see for himself.

His fingers followed the western throat, the load carried into the old wall, the lower bearing and the transfer brace. Sun Lian answered the questions he did ask. She did not abandon her station to stand respectfully beside him.

“You will lose the north wedge under full transition.”

“Two replacements seated behind it.”

“The first is too close to the damaged edge.”

“It takes the initial drop. The second carries farther back.”

“The wall?”

“Tested to the marked line.”

“Not with water.”

“No.”

Pei bent to inspect the actual seat.

The nearest worker moved aside, relieved and resentful at once. He had spent two afternoons shaping that packing and had checked it again that morning. The elder needed only a brief look to find the portion that would fail first.

Su Fan watched from the wall.

He wanted Pei to be wrong about the wedge. He wanted the work done by people he loved to withstand examination by the man who had just crushed him against stone.

The desire did not change the timber.

Sun Lian asked the worker to show Pei the spare support.

It stood where the rehearsal had placed it. The tool required to seat it hung within reach. Pei checked the distance between them, then looked toward the upper landing.

“Moving that under pressure will cost you.”

“Yes,” she said.

There was no usefulness in pretending otherwise.

The elder stayed silent for several breaths. Water hissed behind the throat. A drop ran down the drawing and caught beneath the small weight holding its lower edge straight.

Then a messenger appeared above them.

He had lost one shoe. Mud streaked his bare foot to the ankle.

“Uncontrolled spill above the sixth station.”

Pei turned fully toward him.

The hand that had pinned Su Fan opened.

***

The next orders came without the formality with which the first had entered.

“Jiang. Hold the upper gauge below the second mark. I will take the northern spill and the lake throat.”

The steward lifted her board.

“Below the corrected second mark,” she said.

Pei glanced at the error notation and nodded.

“Western team. You have your interval. When it closes, all further action stops.”

Sun Lian asked him to confirm that the reduction would be held while the conductor moved.

“It will.”

She repeated the instruction to Ren Bo. He passed it to the men at the winch, one of whom said it back badly and was corrected before touching anything.

The agreement was not a settlement of the morning's dispute. It was enough to give their separate tasks a chance of meeting in the right order.

Han's request lay on the board between Jiang and the elder, with the eleven names beneath it.

Pei saw the sheet.

He did not sign it.

Jiang put her board down again long enough to press her own seal beneath the request. She waited until the ink had taken before lifting the paper away from the damp wood.

Wen Zhao watched.

So did the elder.

No one described the act as permission already granted. Jiang had made a decision within the interval he had allowed, and the record would show whose hand had made it.

Pei left without another word.

The lamps straightened after him. His steps faded up the stair, but the strange weight in the stone did not disappear. Somewhere above, an enormous body of water still required an answer.

***

Ruan helped Su Fan stand.

The first attempt brought him only halfway. His chest tightened, and the bruised thigh refused to take his weight as quickly as he expected. He leaned against the wall until both stopped trying to fold him.

Sun Lian watched him come back to the collar.

She had put the hook on the bench rather than leave it in the cradle where his fall might have knocked it. The grip cloth lay beside it, inspected and replaced where the torn part would have rubbed his palm.

“Can you still do it?”

He drew a careful breath.

Pain, but air.

“Yes.”

She did not hand him the tool.

“Then tell me the first step.”

He looked at the board instead of her face.

“Wait for the white signal and the corrected upper measure.”

“And after the throat opens?”

“Stay clear until the local mark. Enter with the hook. Hand behind the sleeve line. Bar clear before the collar moves.”

His voice failed on the last words. He stopped, breathed and repeated them.

Sun Lian let him finish.

“If your chest changes, you tell me before you go into the recess.”

“I will.”

Ruan picked up the spare line and returned it to its place beside the cleat. Ren Bo had the winch crew check their grips once more. One guard asked whether he should carry the wounded out. Sun Lian sent him to the upper stair with another man to help.

The way beside the captain's body remained clear.

Su Fan did not look at the coat. He knew where it was. He knew the elder had seen it. Neither fact could be dealt with by staring while the upper measure continued to move.

Jiang's messenger reached the entrance.

The white board rose.

Sun Lian checked the reading against the correction written beside it. She waited through one uncertain movement of the needle, then another.

Only when it held did she place the hook in Su Fan's hand.

chapters.title: The Western Throat
chapters.text:
The bypass opened a hand's width.

Water struck the western throat with a sound like iron tearing.

The whole chamber shook. Dust came out of the old seams in little pale clouds, hanging briefly above the lamps before the spray found it. Su Fan felt the first vibration through his boots and then through the hand resting against the recess wall.

Ren Bo leaned on the winch.

His crew fed the line through the new cleat, taking the movement in the small amounts they had practised. The wheel wanted to travel faster. Each man could feel that without anyone telling him what it meant.

“Hold this turn,” Ren Bo called.

The man nearest the guide repeated him. Beyond that man, another watched the spare line instead of the water. Su Fan had thought the assignment wasteful during their earliest rehearsal. Now he was glad someone in the room had no other task competing for his attention.

Sun Lian stood at the pressure board with one palm flat against the transfer brace.

Above the entrance, Jiang pulled the white signal board fully into place.

The upper feed was reduced.

They could continue.

***

Outside, the cleared western cut took water along a bed that had not carried so much of it in living memory.

Old Pock saw the first brown tongue come around the bend. It ran low and fast, dragging loose reeds ahead of it. The next movement filled the space behind, broader than the first and carrying fragments nobody could identify from the bank.

He blew the warning horn.

His boat remained behind the marked line. A younger ferryman beside him put one foot on the forward bench, ready to push out, and Pock caught the back of his belt.

“Not yet.”

“There might be someone—”

“There will be two of us if you put that bow across it.”

The younger man stayed where he was. He watched the current strike the far side of the cut and rebound into the water they would have entered.

Deng's crew had already moved the last surveying cart onto high ground. One wheel had sunk into the soft edge on the way, and a tool chest had fallen from the back while they lifted it clear.

Two men went toward it.

Deng caught the nearer by his coat.

The man tried to shake him off. His tools were in that chest. Good tools, some borrowed, some bought a piece at a time. He could see the handle lying above the mud, close enough to make the distance feel insulting.

Then the water reached it.

The chest rolled once, struck a stone and opened. Bright shapes flashed inside the brown flow. A wooden handle came past end over end, no longer attached to anything a man could use.

Neither worker argued again.

Deng let go of the coat. He kept his hand near the man's elbow for a little while afterward.

Farther along the bank, a woman arrived carrying the lunch she had promised the surveying crew. She stopped at the rope across the path and looked at the water beyond it.

“Which way now?”

Deng pointed uphill.

“That adds half the morning.”

“Yes.”

She looked at the parcel in her hands, then at the men staring after the broken chest.

“Then somebody can carry this part.”

One of the workers took it from her. The small demand gave him something to do besides calculate the price of what had gone downstream.

Pock watched them climb. He knew the old path well enough to feel its loss in his legs, though it had been marked for closure before the water came. A familiar route remained tempting after it stopped being a route.

He moved the warning rope farther back from the soft edge.

The younger ferryman helped without being asked. Together they set it where a person rounding the bend would meet the barrier before seeing what looked like an easy step across a narrow run of water.

Beyond it, the narrow run widened.

A small tree on the far bank bent, held and straightened. Pock watched its roots rather than its branches. There would be time to decide whether this channel behaved as the surveys predicted. For the moment, he needed everyone on the bank to remain available for that later conversation.

***

The first minute went cleanly.

Inside the chamber, the sound grew too large to separate into familiar parts. Water, timber, iron and the shouted count belonged to the same continuous pressure. Su Fan kept his good ear toward Sun Lian, but even there he could hear only the words spoken nearest him.

The visible signals did the work the bell could not.

A red board remained raised beside the entrance, ready to fall. The white board above it told them the upper reduction still held. Between those two simple objects, half the valley's carefully argued permissions had become something a tired worker could see.

Sun Lian checked the two readings in front of her. The polished auxiliary gauge broken during the fight had been removed; the main board and Jiang's upper measure remained. The little error marks beside the scale were dark and plain.

She gave Ren Bo the next movement.

The wheel turned.

Su Fan watched the mouth of the throat widen. The exposed edge disappeared beneath spray. A loose scrap of cloth lifted from somewhere in the old masonry and vanished before he could decide whether it had been part of a worker's sleeve or something left there years earlier.

He kept his hands away from the hook.

The conductor's mark had not arrived.

***

The second minute did not go cleanly.

A lump of old masonry struck the throat grille and lodged against its lower edge.

The first impact sounded almost small beside the water. The change afterward did not. The flow narrowed around the obstruction, rose against the upper bars and began to hammer instead of passing evenly through.

Sun Lian ordered the gate held at its present opening.

Ren Bo repeated the order. The crew stopped feeding the line and settled into a hold that immediately looked more difficult than movement had been.

Su Fan saw the pressure needle rise.

He took the long pole from its brackets.

The stone had a projecting corner. It looked easy to strike. A direct blow might also bend the grille into the throat, leaving them with a larger obstruction they could not reach at all.

He moved along the ledge until the corner lay within the pole's hook.

Spray struck the damaged side of his head. He turned too far to clear it and lost his first view of the opening. For a breath he had nothing but the pole's vibration to tell him where its end had gone.

He drew it back and looked again.

“Sideways,” Sun Lian called.

He had already seen the possible movement, but hearing another person confirm it steadied him more than he expected.

The hook caught.

He pushed.

Nothing moved except his own foot, which slid toward the wet edge.

***

Ruan took the other end of the pole.

He did not simply add strength. He set himself farther from the opening, where the floor gave him a better angle, and asked Su Fan to lower his hands a little.

The new position hurt the cut across Su Fan's shoulder. He adjusted the grip rather than pretend it did not.

“Together?” Ruan asked.

Su Fan nodded.

They leaned.

The stone shifted enough to change the water passing around it, then settled again. The pole flexed. Ruan stopped before it became a bent tool trapped with the obstruction.

“Again. Smaller.”

This time Su Fan watched the corner rather than the whole block. A narrow gap appeared beside one bar. Water entered it and pulled at the far side of the masonry.

He felt the moment when their effort stopped being the only force moving it.

They gave the corner one more short push.

The water caught it.

The stone vanished into the dark with a blow that travelled down the pole into their hands. Ruan pulled the shaft clear before the hook followed it through the grille.

Su Fan staggered back against the wall.

The pressure dropped.

Sun Lian gave Ren Bo permission to resume. Nobody had time to praise the men holding the wet pole. They carried it out of the route and put it where the next person could reach it.

Ruan flexed the fingers below his wounded sleeve.

Su Fan looked toward him.

“It still works,” Ruan said.

He meant his hand, not the plan.

***

At the third minute, Han began preparing the first withdrawal.

The woman came from the sixth station. She had asked to leave her permanent impression twice before the flood and had brought both refusals with her, folded inside an oilcloth wrapper.

Mother Wei moved the papers away from the basin.

“We have the copies.”

“I know.”

“Then let the paper stay dry while we attend to you.”

The woman released the wrapper reluctantly. One corner had gone soft from being held.

Han brought her into the waiting local circuit. The central conductor was not yet clear. He would not attempt to close the permanent routes while the shared command could still seize their return.

This first work was preparation: reducing the strain enough to make the later separation possible, finding which part of the inherited pattern would settle when given room, and which part tried to drag the whole arrangement after it.

The woman cried out once.

Mother Wei held her wrist and watched her eyes.

“Name.”

She answered.

“Where are you?”

“Here.”

“More precisely.”

“The room where you keep asking questions.”

Mother Wei smiled without loosening her attention.

“Good. Remain in it.”

The blue light nearest the wrist dimmed as the local strain eased. Han marked the change but did not call it a completed withdrawal. The woman still had to wait for the lower conductor to release.

Across the room, Tan Wei watched him put the first mark beside her name.

His own place on the inner line remained empty.

***

Qiu Lan carried clean water to the waiting basin.

Her blue lines were clear. She had chosen to keep them, and the arrangement around her hands was designed to let that choice remain possible while other people made a different one.

A man on the retaining side asked whether the dimming mark meant something had gone wrong.

“Preparation,” Han said. “Not separation yet.”

The answer travelled through the room in ordinary voices. People repeated it to those who had not heard. Mother Wei corrected one frightened version before it became a claim that the woman had lost consciousness.

She was conscious. She was irritated. She asked for the cloth behind her neck to be moved because its fold was pressing against the wrong place.

Tan Wei helped adjust it.

The task was small enough that his hands could remain his while doing it. When the old ferry motion returned to his fingers, he stopped, named the present room to himself and began again.

The woman thanked him.

He was glad she had wanted something he could give without deciding what should happen to her next.

***

At the fourth minute, the north wedge split.

Pei had been right.

The sound came through Sun Lian's palm before she saw the break. A sharp change in the grain, then a drop that made the timber bite against her hand.

The first replacement caught.

For a moment the brace sagged only as far as planned. The two workers nearest it moved toward their next positions, ready to drive the spare support into the load.

Then the stone behind the seat began to shed flakes.

One piece struck the floor beside Sun Lian's boot. Another slid down the timber and cut the back of the nearer worker's hand.

He looked at the blood.

“Do not look at me,” Sun Lian said. “Look at the pin.”

He looked back.

She pressed harder against the brace, keeping its grain together while the load changed from one seat to another. Earth qi travelled through wood she knew well enough to feel where it was about to cease behaving like one piece.

The knowledge did not make holding it easy.

Blood ran from her nose.

She tasted it before she saw it drip onto her sleeve.

***

Su Fan wanted to cross to her.

He was near enough to see the effort in her jaw, the little movement of her knee as she adjusted against the pressure. He could carry weight. He could hold a brace. Every useful part of his body offered the same simple answer to seeing her struggle.

The conductor's gauge moved toward its mark.

She needed him elsewhere.

He checked the recess instead.

Water was spraying through a seam above its mouth. The narrow floor had become slick. He took one breath to look at the path he would use on the way out and moved a loose fragment with the end of his boot.

Ruan saw him do it and cleared the space beyond.

Behind them, Ren Bo shifted a man from the line to the replacement support. The remaining crew adjusted their grips. The spare-line watcher took one step closer to the cleat without leaving his assigned rope.

Sun Lian did not have to explain why each movement mattered. They had been wrong often enough in rehearsal to have places for the corrections now.

That did not mean every correction would be sufficient.

The second wedge seated.

For a breath the brace steadied.

Sun Lian looked toward the recess and gave Su Fan the signal to enter.

***

At the fifth minute, he turned his shoulders into the bearing space.

It was barely wide enough for him. The iron plates beneath his coat brushed the dry side. On the other side, the collar's moving clearance remained empty, an absence he had been taught to respect before there was water to make the lesson urgent.

The ancient return conductor lay below it.

Light ran along the metal without illuminating the rest of the chamber properly. Its pressure seemed to hum inside his teeth. Su Fan could not tell how much of the sound reached him through the air and how much through his hand against the wall.

He placed the hook around the locking bar.

An inherited command moved through the tool.

His fingers remained his own.

The tool grew hot.

He had expected heat. The expectation did not prevent the damaged palm from hurting where the wrapping pressed into it. He loosened one finger, reset the grip and made sure the catch had fully seated before putting force through the shaft.

Not yet.

The local gauge remained above the chalk mark.

He waited in a position his bruised chest disliked.

***

Behind him, Ren Bo called the next turn of the winch.

The call reached Su Fan in pieces. He watched the movement on the small indicator beside the recess instead of guessing which word he had missed.

The needle dropped, rose a little, then dropped again.

He could feel the bar's resistance through the hook. The force on it was changing as the western flow took a larger share of the returning load. Somewhere above, Jiang was holding the upper reading beneath the corrected mark. Somewhere beyond her, Pei was preventing the northern spill from becoming another disaster.

Su Fan could see none of them.

He could see the chalk.

The mark arrived at the sixth minute.

He pulled.

The locking bar moved halfway and stopped.

chapters.title: The Mark on the Sleeve
chapters.text:
The bar had twisted in its socket.

Su Fan could feel it through the hook. One edge had cleared. The other caught against metal worn into a lip by years of pressure, a little ridge that no dry rehearsal had been able to put inside the wooden substitute.

He did not pull harder.

His first impulse had already travelled into his shoulders. He stopped it there and let the shaft settle against the resistance instead of trying to force the whole arrangement into agreement with the drawing.

The chalk mark on his sleeve lay just outside the dangerous clearance.

Beyond it, the collar waited.

He changed the tool's angle.

The bar shifted a finger's width and caught again.

Behind the metal, the shared command thickened. Something ancient and uncomprehending searched his channels for a route to use. Su Fan felt the demand pass through the hook, enter the pressure beneath his hand and fail to find the response it expected.

Breath. Blood. The circulation he had made through practice.

No remembered master answered.

The command passed around him into the conductor.

The conductor still burned.

***

He drew the tool back as far as its catch allowed.

A different angle might lift the caught edge. It might also unseat the hook and leave it loose beneath a moving piece of iron. The two possibilities were close enough that he needed to look rather than decide by wanting one of them more.

Spray ran down his face.

He could not wipe it away without letting go.

He blinked until the edge came clear, then turned the shaft a little. The new position pressed against the cut on his palm. For an instant pain became the largest fact in the recess, larger than the gauge or the bar or the gap in which his hand must not travel.

He waited for it to become one fact among the others again.

Outside, Sun Lian called his name.

“Caught,” he answered. “I'm changing the angle.”

“Inside the line?”

“Yes.”

There was a pause, then the signal for the crew to hold the present position.

Nobody reached into the recess to improve his work. Nobody told him he was nearly there because that would be a comforting thing to hear.

He put his weight through the handle slowly enough to feel the catch begin to climb.

The bar moved.

Then the return struck again, and he had to keep what he had gained without mistaking it for permission to hurry.

***

At the seventh minute, Tan Wei entered the inner line.

His notebook remained on the dry shelf beside the basin. He had tied its cord before taking his place, though one corner of the paper had already swollen where his sleeve touched it.

Han sat opposite him.

The old teacher's bad leg was extended beneath the chair. Someone had placed a folded cloth under the knee. Han had noticed only when he tried to move and found the support already there.

“Last opportunity to remain linked,” he said.

“I know.”

“You may retain a reduced impression instead.”

“I know.”

“What do you choose?”

“Separate the permanent one. Keep what my own channels can carry.”

Han looked at him long enough to be sure the answer belonged to the young man in front of him.

Then he nodded.

Mother Wei took Tan Wei's right hand. Qiu Lan, still linked by her own choice through a local loop, steadied the basin.

Tan Wei looked at the blue lines above her wrist.

She noticed.

“Mine,” she said.

“Yes.”

He was not asking her to come with him. She was not asking him to remain where she had chosen to stay.

That left them able to help one another.

***

Han asked Tan Wei to describe the last movement he had made deliberately.

“Untied the notebook. Retied it. Badly.”

“And before that?”

“Helped move the cloth behind her neck.”

He glanced toward the woman from the sixth station. She was sitting within her prepared local circuit, waiting for the same lower release.

“Where are your feet?”

“On the floor.”

“Both?”

Tan Wei looked down. One heel had lifted without his noticing, finding a stance suited to an oar rather than the basin.

He set it down.

Han did not call the movement a failure. He noted it and waited for Tan Wei to find the present position again.

The river behind his eyes was broad and brown. Somewhere on its far bank a woman would be turning a green scarf over her hands. He knew how she moved when she was angry. He knew how long she would pretend not to hear someone calling.

He did not want the memory destroyed because it had belonged to people who had loved each other.

He wanted it to stop deciding whose hands these were.

Mother Wei tightened her hold just enough for him to notice her.

“Here,” she said.

He looked at the basin.

Han laid his tools where he could reach them and waited for the signal.

A voice at the doorway asked whether the withdrawing people would need different beds afterward.

Mother Wei looked up.

“Some will. Leave the nearest ones clear.”

“How many?”

“We don't know yet.”

The woman at the door glanced at the row of waiting faces. She had come to take a relative home. Now she turned and began making room without a number to organize the work around.

Tan Wei watched her lift a stool out of the route. It had a cracked leg tied with cord. He remembered repairing a chair like that before his first month at the stations, when the largest problem he could imagine was finding enough money to enter.

“Will I still be able to work?” he asked.

Han did not answer quickly.

“Not today. Not as soon as you will want.”

“After that?”

“We find out what remains, and what can be rebuilt.”

The teacher had once offered him instruction that seemed to open a whole future. He was offering instruction now without promising the same future back.

Tan Wei looked toward the notebook.

“Give that to me afterward.”

“I will,” Qiu Lan said.

“Even if I say I don't want to look.”

She studied his face.

“I'll put it where you can reach it. You can decide about looking then.”

He let out a breath that was almost a laugh.

“That sounds like something I have been saying.”

“You are occasionally worth hearing.”

Han checked the waiting signal. Still closed.

Tan Wei moved his feet once, feeling the floor beneath both heels. The borrowed ferry remained vivid, its boards worn smooth beneath a gait his own body had learned without travelling there. He did not try to hate it. He looked at the people around the basin instead, the tired hands and the damp sleeves, and waited among them for the work to begin.

***

Su Fan had found the worn edge.

The bar did not need to travel farther into the clearance. It needed to be lifted away from the lip before the outward pull could finish. The hook could do that if he kept the shaft from rolling into the old position.

The space was too narrow to turn his shoulders freely.

He moved one foot instead.

The adjustment brought the bruised side of his chest against the recess wall. He felt the body's familiar attempt to protect the injury by tightening everything nearby. His jaw closed. His breathing shortened. The tool's tip began to wander.

He stopped.

He could protect the bruise or preserve the angle for this movement. He could not do both by pretending they were the same task.

Outside, the gauge steadied.

He lifted through the hook, feeling the catch take the weight beneath the bar's lower edge. Then he drew the handle toward him without reaching past the chalk.

At the eighth minute, the locking bar came free.

Su Fan nearly fell when the resistance vanished.

The shaft struck his forearm. He caught himself against the safe side of the recess and lifted the tool clear before the collar began to move.

Iron scraped stone.

The sound was lower than he had expected and longer than he wanted. The conductor's light broke along the new separation. What had been one commanding return became several smaller pressures searching their own paths.

A bell rang above him.

He heard it through his left ear and felt its vibration through the wall.

The operators had their window.

***

In the basin room, Han looked at the signal twice.

Mother Wei saw him do it and did not hurry him.

The central pressure had dropped. The local measures agreed. The signal was not merely a promise sent by someone who hoped the mechanism had moved far enough.

Han began.

Tan Wei felt the first separation as an absence where a familiar assistance had always arrived. The movement he attempted next was still one he knew, but it no longer carried itself through the whole route.

He tried to finish it by force.

Han caught the change.

“Let me take this part.”

Tan Wei heard the instruction and obeyed. It was difficult to distinguish obedience chosen now from all the other motions arriving without permission. Mother Wei's hand helped. So did the sound of Qiu Lan setting the cooling vessel down where it belonged.

These were people he knew.

These were movements being made in the room.

He closed his eyes only after fixing the positions of all three in his mind.

***

The strain below changed exactly as the elder had predicted.

The transfer brace took the new load.

Sun Lian cried out and dropped to one knee. Her hand remained against the timber. A sharp line of pain ran through the earth channels she had been using to keep the packing whole, and for a moment she could not tell whether the trembling came from the wood or her arm.

Her workers drove the second wedge home.

The blow was clean. The wedge seated. The wall behind it continued to shed fine pale flakes.

“Again?” one man asked, lifting his hammer.

“No. Hold there.”

More force would not create more sound stone.

She shifted her attention to the part of the support that still answered. The new load needed a path through what they had, not through the wall she wished they had been allowed time to rebuild.

Across the chamber, Ren Bo saw the guide rope fray against a rough edge.

One fibre lifted. Then several.

He reached for the spare.

Too late.

The rope snapped.

The wheel kicked backward and caught him across the forearm.

***

Su Fan came out of the recess as the crew lost its grip.

The hooked tool was still in his hand. He put it down clear of the turning line before moving. The action took less than a breath and felt impossibly slow.

Ren Bo was on the floor.

One worker had caught his coat and was dragging him away from the wheel. Another had both hands on the line, trying to stop a weight that had already begun to move faster than a man could safely follow.

“Let that end go!” Ruan shouted.

The worker heard him in time.

Su Fan reached the emergency holding lever.

He put both hands on it.

The force drove him down until one knee struck stone.

He knew this load was too large to lift.

He did not try.

The lever had a stop. The mechanism had a direction in which it could be held for a short interval while another line took the strain. He had practised that relationship with weights that could not have torn the room apart if he misunderstood it.

Now the weight was real.

He set his feet and let the seventh circuit carry pressure through him.

Ruan reached the loose spare line.

***

The first breath held.

Su Fan could feel the lever's movement not as one huge demand but as a series of changes: the wheel trying to turn, the remaining crew finding a partial hold, the old rope's loose end striking the floor.

His injured chest began to spasm.

The familiar answer was to brace harder.

His shoulders tightened. The circulation bunched behind the ribs. Force that had been moving through him began to collect in the place where Pei's stone had struck.

The lever shifted another finger's width.

He could hear someone saying his name. He could not spare enough attention to find the speaker.

He let the unnecessary tension go.

Not the load.

Not the pain.

The effort pulling against his own effort.

For three breaths, a deeper route opened beneath the seventh circuit. Pressure passed through him cleanly enough that he could feel each small alteration in the wheel without answering all of them with his shoulders.

His feet remained on stone. His hands remained torn and burning. The room had not become light.

It had become possible to hold for a little longer.

Then the new route wavered.

He could not keep it.

“Three breaths,” he told Ruan. “No more.”

***

Ruan looped the spare line through Bao Shun's cleat.

His first attempt caught the wrong side of the fitting. He drew it back before putting weight onto it, changed the angle and passed it through again.

The cleat had been altered so a damaged hand could manage it.

That mattered now.

Ruan's wounded forearm had begun to shake. He could still pull, but the easy strength of a whole morning's uninjured body was no longer available merely because he needed it. The fitting gave him somewhere to put the line before asking his arm to do more.

A worker caught the free end.

Together they took the strain.

Sun Lian saw the new rope straighten.

“Out!” she shouted.

Su Fan wanted to remain until he was certain.

He could feel the argument forming with horrible familiarity. Another breath. Another inch. Leave only when no one could say leaving had caused the failure.

The deeper route flickered again and almost vanished.

“Su Fan!”

He let go.

Ruan pulled him clear as the lever slammed into its wooden stop.

The stop cracked.

The spare line held.

***

For a moment Su Fan could not raise his head.

The floor was cool against his cheek. His hands were empty. That last fact frightened him before he remembered choosing it.

Someone stepped over his legs. Someone else dragged the broken end of the guide rope away from the wheel. The work continued without waiting for him to recover enough strength to declare that it could.

Ren Bo was sitting against the lower wall, his injured arm held close by another worker. He could not take the handle. He could still see the wheel.

“Next turn,” he said.

His voice broke on the word. He drew breath and gave the order again.

The crew answered.

Su Fan rolled onto his side. The new route was gone. The seventh remained, uneven beneath pain and fatigue but recognizable as something he had actually learned to use.

He did not chase the other sensation.

Ruan crouched beside him just long enough to ask whether he could move farther from the line.

“Yes.”

“Then do that.”

He did.

At the tenth minute, the wheel began moving forward again.

chapters.title: His Own Name
chapters.text:
Tan Wei lost the old shore first.

One moment he could have walked its path in darkness. The next he remembered only that there had been a path, and that reaching its far end had once mattered more than anything waiting beside the basin.

The woman in the green scarf turned away before he could see her face.

Grief struck him, sharp and borrowed.

He let himself feel it without calling it his whole life. He had written what he remembered of her in a separate book. Somewhere, long before his own birth, she had been a person with reasons to wait beside a river. He did not need to become the man she waited for in order to believe that had mattered.

Then the permanent routes began to close.

That pain belonged to him entirely.

His eyes opened. The room tilted and settled. Han's hand held his wrist, and Mother Wei was saying something he had missed.

“Again,” he whispered.

She repeated the question.

He answered it this time.

***

Han separated what could be separated.

He had stopped trying to make the work resemble the easier cases in his notes. Tan Wei's channels had grown around the assistance they received. Some now carried their own share. Others opened only because an inherited pressure had taught the body to expect help at the same point in every movement.

Removing that help exposed the difference.

Mother Wei watched the pulse beneath the skin. Qiu Lan kept the cooling water steady. When Han needed another angle, she shifted the basin before he had to ask twice. None of them could have done the whole work safely alone.

Tan Wei's fifth-stage pressure fell.

Fourth.

For a moment it steadied there.

He felt the familiar reach of his cultivation draw inward. A movement that had once extended beyond the basin now ended near his hand. He tried to preserve it, not from argument but because a body resists losing what it has learned to call strength.

Han felt the effort.

“Do not hold that branch for me.”

Tan Wei wanted to tell him he was not doing it for him.

The words tangled in his throat.

A channel beneath the left wrist collapsed back to the size his own training could support.

Third.

He cried out.

***

Han held his hand firmly enough to hurt.

“Stay here.”

Tan Wei could see the old teacher's face. It was closer than it had been when they began. The lines beside his mouth had deepened, and one eyebrow was wet with water he had not had time to wipe away.

“I am here.”

“Tell me where.”

“The station.”

“Which part?”

“The basin room.”

“Who is beside you?”

Tan Wei looked.

Qiu Lan's blue reeds remained clear. Mother Wei looked exhausted and deeply annoyed with the universe. Behind her, someone was holding a stack of clean cloths with both hands, as though dropping them would be the one mistake nobody could afford.

He almost laughed.

It came out as a sob instead.

Mother Wei put a dry cloth against his face without telling him there was no reason to cry.

Han waited until the circulation steadied beneath the new limit. He checked again before releasing Tan Wei's wrist. The work was not made successful by ending it at the first moment everyone wanted to believe it had succeeded.

At last he nodded to Qiu Lan.

She lowered the water and helped Tan Wei bring his hands out of the basin.

They looked like his hands.

He had expected something more visible to account for how much had changed.

***

The first time he tried to stand, his knees gave way.

Mother Wei had anticipated the attempt. Her hand was on his shoulder before he got far enough to fall.

“Sit.”

“I can—”

“You can sit.”

He sat.

She did not argue with him about courage or gratitude. She checked his face, asked where the pain was worst and sent someone to move the nearest bed closer rather than make him prove he could cross the room.

The woman from the sixth station was already there, conscious and shivering beneath a blanket. Her refusals lay in their wrapper beside the pillow. She saw him looking and put two fingers on the packet.

“Still mine,” she said.

He nodded.

For years those pages had said she must wait. Now she had lived through the interval they had refused her, and the papers had become evidence of something already survived rather than another reason it could not happen.

She asked whether he needed water.

Before he could answer, a helper brought a cup.

He tried to lift a thin ring from its surface.

Nothing obeyed the first movement.

He stopped before anyone could tell him to stop. His throat tightened with an anger too sudden to choose a proper object. He had chosen separation. He had not chosen to enjoy every part of what it cost.

The woman looked away, giving him a little privacy without moving from the next bed.

After a while she asked whether the room had always been this noisy.

“Yes,” Tan Wei said.

“I had forgotten.”

A helper was moving cups on a tray. The little collisions of pottery seemed extraordinarily distinct. Somewhere near the door two people disagreed about which blanket belonged to which household. Neither sounded like a distant ferryman calling across water.

Tan Wei pulled his own blanket higher.

The woman took out one hand and examined it, turning the palm toward the window.

“I thought it would feel different,” she said.

“It does.”

“Yes. But not where I thought.”

He understood that well enough not to ask her to explain. His strength had changed. His relief had arrived mixed with humiliation, pain and a sudden desire to sleep where nobody would ask him to describe the result.

The helper offered to put the cup into his hands.

“Beside me,” he said.

She set it within reach. He thanked her, then waited until she had turned before lifting it with both hands. The water tasted of the ordinary clay cup. He drank a mouthful and put it down carefully.

***

At the eleventh minute, the last withdrawing operator crossed into a stable local circuit.

Ten of the eleven had completed separation.

The eleventh had developed a dangerous tremor during the first stage and chosen to stop.

Han had not decided that her original request obliged her to continue. When the tremor failed to settle, he told her what he could offer: leave a reduced connection, document the present limit and preserve the possibility of another attempt under different conditions.

She asked whether that meant she had failed.

“It means you have stopped here.”

“Will they make me begin again?”

“No one in this room will.”

The answer did not promise control over every future official. It told her exactly what the people holding her hands would do now.

She chose the reduced connection.

Han isolated it from the shared recall and wrote down what remained. The page did not say completed withdrawal. It did not say refusal to cooperate. Mother Wei made him read the entry back while the woman was still able to hear and correct it.

It was not the result she wanted.

It was the result her body could survive that morning.

Across the room, those who retained their impressions remained at the marked basins. Qiu Lan's blue lines stayed clear. So did most of the others.

No one was required to become founderless to leave the central command.

***

At twelve minutes, Jiang dropped the closing signal.

The red board fell where every person on the lower landing could see it. The low bell sounded beside it, its note roughened by the noise that had filled the chamber all morning.

The western team began restoring the controlled river flow.

Ren Bo's arm was splinted against his chest. He sat where he could still see the wheel and called the sequence while other hands turned it. The first order emerged too quietly. A worker repeated it, looking at him rather than assuming what he had meant.

Ren Bo corrected one word.

They moved.

Sun Lian had almost no earth qi left. She gave instructions from the floor, leaning against a sound part of the wall. Blood had dried below her nose. When she tried to wipe it with her sleeve, Su Fan handed her a clean cloth.

He was shaking too badly to help with the wheel.

He stayed out of its way.

The decision felt shameful for several breaths, then simply necessary. A man who could not reliably close his hand should not take a place whose failure would require another person to rescue him.

There were other tasks. He moved a lamp away from spray. He carried a message three paces to someone who could not hear it over the water. He did not call either task beneath him.

***

Above them, Pei Gang redirected the northern spill.

The upper measure descended in uneven stages. Jiang watched each one and sent the changes down without smoothing them into a more encouraging account. The western crew slowed when she required it, then resumed.

The chamber did not empty all at once.

Water continued to pass through the new arrangement. The purpose had never been to stop the river. It was to give the returning command a route that did not require living operators to be its only adjustable parts.

The load on the damaged wall eased.

One of the workers near the spare brace put down his hammer and discovered his fingers would not straighten fully. He stared at them until Sun Lian told him to leave the tool where it lay and move into the clear.

The Low Gate settled into its new position with a deep, ordinary thud.

It was quieter than the first opening.

For several breaths nobody moved.

Then someone laughed.

Someone else began crying.

Sun Lian demanded the final readings before either reaction could spread too far.

Jiang gave them.

Below the dangerous mark.

Holding.

Sun Lian asked for the lower comparison. A worker brought it. The figures were not identical, but they were within the differences already marked on the board.

She looked once more at the north seat.

Only then did she take her hand away from the floor as though she had finally remembered it could be used for herself.

***

Ruan found Su Fan beside the empty tool cradle.

The hook lay on the bench. Its working edge had changed colour with the heat. Su Fan had put it down where someone could inspect it later, not back among the sound tools as though surviving the operation made it ready for another one.

“Can you walk?” Ruan asked.

“Yes.”

They tried.

“Yes” proved to require Ruan's shoulder.

They passed the place where Shen Tu lay. The coat still covered his face. Two guards remained near him, waiting for people who could move the body without carrying it through the departing injured.

Su Fan stopped.

Ruan did not pull him onward immediately.

The landing had become a place in which several incompatible things were true. The gate held. The workers would leave alive. A man lay dead beside the mechanism he had tried to stop. The coat over him had a wet edge where the floor had been washed by spray.

“Later,” Ruan said.

Su Fan nodded.

They went up.

***

The passage to the operator room seemed longer than the one he had walked before the ceremony.

At each turn somebody needed space for a pallet, a bucket or a person who could not move without help. Nobody recognized a clear path owed to Su Fan because of what he had done below.

He was grateful for that until his thigh began to tremble again.

Then he was merely tired.

Ruan found a place beside the wall where they could wait for two workers carrying a bed frame. One of the men had lost a shoe. The other was laughing at something Su Fan did not hear. The laughter sounded wrong until he realized it might be the first breath either man had drawn without work inside it.

At the operator-room door, Mother Wei saw him.

Her expression changed.

She did not run. She gave one instruction to the person beside her, finished tying the cloth in her hands and came over with the controlled haste of someone refusing to abandon one injured person for another.

“Sit here.”

“Tan Wei?”

“Asleep a moment ago. Sit.”

Ruan lowered him onto the bench.

Mother Wei examined the hand, the shoulder and the place where the coat no longer lay smoothly over his ribs. Her questions required answers about his body, not an account of the morning.

He answered them as accurately as he could.

When she turned his face to look at his eyes, he saw blood on her cuff that was not hers and could not tell whose it had been.

***

Tan Wei was awake when they brought Su Fan beside him.

He sat wrapped in a blanket with his wrist bandaged. The three blue reeds had become faint scars, though a thin remnant of colour remained beneath the skin.

He lifted his head.

“You look dreadful.”

“So do you.”

“Third stage.”

Su Fan nodded.

He did not say that stages could be regained. He did not tell his friend the loss was worth it. Tan Wei had earned the right to decide how he felt about what he had paid.

For a while they sat with no useful conversation available.

Han crossed the room slowly, using his cane. Qiu Lan was helping a retaining operator unfasten the support at his basin. Her own blue lines remained visible whenever her sleeve moved.

Tan Wei watched her.

“She stayed.”

“Yes.”

“I know. I only wanted to say it.”

Su Fan let the sentence stand.

After a while he asked, “Can you still use the water?”

Tan Wei reached toward the cup beside him.

A small ring rose from its surface.

It wavered and fell.

“Some.”

Su Fan brought the cup closer.

His friend drank without spilling.

***

Outside, the western channel carried brown water into the marsh.

Old Pock's boat remained behind the boundary until the signal allowing movement arrived. Deng's crew counted the people who had come down with them and sent the count uphill. The tool chest was gone. Its owners were not.

The old lower town remained gone too.

Water still crossed the place where the boys' river rock had stood. No turn of the new mechanism brought it back. The lake remained above the valley, a weight for which people would need to keep making provision after this day's witnesses went home.

Inside the stations, the marked basins were being emptied one at a time.

Workers checked which connection each person had chosen and what assistance they needed now. A request to withdraw was not treated as proof that withdrawal had been completed. A retained impression was not treated as proof that no injury had occurred.

Tan Wei heard his name.

Mother Wei was holding his notebook. Its oilcloth had kept most of the water out. The cord was still tied badly.

He held out his hand for it.

“Tan Wei,” she called again, waiting until his eyes met hers.

He answered.

chapters.title: After the Bell
chapters.text:
The first count was wrong.

Three people listed as missing had left by routes that did not lead to the assigned assembly point. Two had gone uphill with injured workers and remained to help at the beds. The third had taken a different road because he could not find his daughter.

She had been waiting at the kitchen with Auntie Lu, eating a bun.

When her father reached her, she held up the last piece as though his absence had principally been an inconvenience to the division of breakfast.

He knelt and put both arms around her.

Auntie Lu took the bun before it was crushed between them. She gave it back afterward, with something about fathers being no excuse for wasting food.

The messenger carrying the count found them there.

He waited until the man could answer his name clearly, then crossed out the missing mark without making the correction so heavy that the original entry disappeared. Another copy was already on its way to the upper station. Someone would need to know why the two did not agree.

By evening, the count was complete.

Ren Bo's nephew brought the corrected sheet to the bench where his uncle waited for a fresh binding.

“I should have kept them at the assembly point.”

“One was carrying a man who couldn't breathe properly,” Ren Bo said.

“I could have sent someone after him.”

“Yes.”

The boy waited for the rest of the rebuke.

Ren Bo shifted his splinted arm and went pale. He looked at the sheet again before continuing.

“Next time, put a person where the roads divide. Don't make an injured man wait for your brush.”

The nephew nodded, but the fear had not left his face.

“I wrote missing.”

“They were missing from your count.”

“People thought—”

“I know what people thought. That's why you go and tell them what you know now.”

The boy folded the corrected copy and went to find the families who had seen the first one. It would take longer than leaving a notice at the kitchen. Ren Bo watched him go without calling him back for an easier task.

Su Fan sat at the other end of the bench. He remembered the nephew caught beneath the danger of the crane, the fragment striking his own head, the sudden wrongness of every sound afterward. The boy walking away was taller than he remembered him being that day. Not by much. Enough to remind him that other people's lives had continued while he had measured his own recovery against the same bad morning.

Ren Bo asked for his cup.

Su Fan passed it to his uninjured hand.

No operator had died during the separation.

Two workers would need months before returning to heavy labour. Ren Bo's arm had broken cleanly. Sun Lian had damaged two earth channels and would not reinforce timber again until a healer cleared her.

Captain Shen Tu was dead.

Mother Wei recorded every name without changing the size of her writing.

***

The operator room emptied slowly.

Some people could walk home with someone beside them. Others remained on pallets while their families went to fetch dry clothes. The floor needed cleaning. Used cloths had to be separated from what could safely be folded back into the cupboards. Nobody who had planned the intervention had imagined that success would make these tasks unnecessary, but several looked surprised by the amount of work still waiting.

Han refused to leave until the last patient's next arrangement was written down.

Then Mother Wei made him sit.

His bad leg had begun to tremble so violently that he could no longer disguise it by leaning on the cane. Qiu Lan brought a stool for his foot. He objected that it belonged to someone else and was told the owner was using a bed.

Tan Wei slept through the argument.

His notebook lay beside his hand. Once, he woke far enough to touch its cover, then went back to sleep without opening it.

Su Fan watched from the bench where Mother Wei had put him.

He wanted to be useful. He wanted to remain near his friend. He wanted, with equal force, to lie down somewhere that did not contain a single object reminding him of the lower landing.

Mother Wei gave him a cup and told him to drink.

It was the only desire she allowed him to satisfy without further discussion.

***

Pei Gang returned to the upper station after the pressure settled.

He passed the operator room once.

Tan Wei was asleep. Han sat beside the beds with both hands resting on his cane. The elder looked at the local loops, the marked basins and the used instruments laid out for counting.

One of the operators who had retained her impression rose partway from her stool. Pei told her to remain seated.

He said nothing to Su Fan.

At the door, he instructed that all records be preserved for review.

Jiang replied that copies had already been made.

The elder looked at her.

For a moment Su Fan expected another argument, something that would require everyone in the room to choose a side while still too tired to stand properly. Pei only adjusted the position of his injured hand against his sleeve and left.

The room did not become freer when he was gone. The orders, the injuries and the questions remained. It became quieter.

Jiang took the duplicate readings to the table beside the door. Wen Zhao checked them against his own notes. Where their times differed, they left the difference visible and wrote which clock each had used.

No one asked Su Fan for a complete account yet.

He was relieved.

He was also afraid that waiting would make him remember the morning differently.

***

Sun Lian let the healer examine her hands without arguing until he told her not to reinforce anything.

“Anything heavy?”

“Anything that calls on the damaged channels.”

“For how long?”

“Until we can judge how they are recovering.”

She stared at him.

“I work with timber.”

“You can measure timber. You can mark timber. You cannot make an injured route carry more because a customer will otherwise need to wait.”

Su Fan stood just outside the curtain and heard the silence that followed.

He knew it. He had spent enough days trying to turn a restriction into a smaller restriction by asking the question in a different way.

When Sun Lian emerged, her tools were still in the bag over her shoulder. The bag hung from the side that hurt less.

“Do you need that carried?” he asked.

“Yes.”

He took it.

She was too tired to make him prove he had learned the difference between offering and deciding. They walked to the kitchen, stopping once because his thigh tightened and once because she needed to sit.

Neither called the other's pause unnecessary.

***

Su Fan washed his sword after dark.

He had postponed it until there were no useful reasons left.

The blade lay across a folded cloth beside a bucket. In the lamplight, most of the blood looked brown. Water removed the loose part. The narrow place beneath the guard required more patience.

He worked carefully because care was the only task his hands understood at that moment.

The sword was plain steel. Duan had helped him make it from stock they had saved. He remembered the first flawed temper, the arguments over balance, Ah-Du working the bellows with exaggerated dignity because this particular piece of work seemed worth being seen doing.

None of those memories had prepared the sword to feel as it did now.

Duan came to the doorway.

He did not ask whether Su Fan regretted it.

He sat beside the bucket and waited.

His injured arm rested against his chest. With his good hand he moved the lamp so Su Fan could see beneath the guard without bending over the water.

After a long time Su Fan said, “He tried to speak.”

The smith nodded.

“I couldn't hear him.”

Duan looked toward the damaged right ear.

“You may never know what he meant.”

“I know.”

That did not make the not knowing easier.

***

A little blood remained inside the fitting.

Su Fan folded the cloth into a narrower edge and tried again. His hand shook. He put the blade down before the tremor brought his fingers against the sharp part.

“I heard Sun Lian,” he said. “I heard the bell. Not all of it. Enough.”

Duan waited.

“He was right beside me.”

“Being near doesn't make every sound clear.”

“I know that too.”

The answer came out harder than he intended. He looked up, ready to apologize, but Duan did not seem offended. He had heard enough men repeat a fact they understood and could not yet bear.

Outside, somebody called for more bowls. A cart rattled past the workshop with an injured man inside it, his companions arguing about which turn would shake him less.

Su Fan picked up the cloth again.

“The chain was moving.”

Duan nodded.

“I saw where it would fall.”

“Yes.”

He was not asking the smith to decide the case. He had begun to understand how easily he might keep offering the same facts until someone supplied a feeling to go with them.

Duan stayed until the blade was clean.

When Su Fan finally dried it and put it away, the older man carried the dirty water outside. He did not make Su Fan perform that part as another test of whether he could face what he had done.

***

At the temporary office, Shen Tu's possessions were inventoried before two witnesses.

A purse. Two keys. An official seal. A folded letter in a child's hand. A small repair receipt for a roof tile.

Su Fan was not required to attend.

He went anyway, then wished he had not.

The clerk turned each object toward the witnesses and named it. The letter remained folded. Its private contents were not necessary to establish that it had been found inside the coat.

Su Fan could see one uneven character near the outside crease.

He looked away before trying to make a story from it.

The captain had bought a paper windmill in the market. That fact had stayed with Su Fan because it resisted every account in which the man became only one thing. The letter did not tell him who had received the windmill. It did not tell him whether anybody had received it at all.

The clerk tied the possessions together after the list was checked.

An official seal went into a separate wrapper.

Even dead, the captain had objects that belonged to the office and objects that belonged to a life the office could not describe.

***

Wen Zhao took Su Fan's statement separately from the guards'.

He asked about the landing, the broken tread, the position of the blade and the hand on the chain. When Su Fan could not remember which foot the captain had moved first, Wen did not suggest the answer.

Ruan described the position of the restraint and the workers below the counterweight. Ren Bo confirmed that the mechanism had begun to release.

The guard who had come down after setting aside his crossbow said he had not seen the pull.

That remained in the record.

Another had seen enough to identify the hand and the movement. Wen asked him to point to the position on the drawing rather than turn the description into an opinion about whether the captain had meant to hurt anyone.

The facts mattered.

They did not make the dead man's coat easier to look at.

When Su Fan left, the clerk called him back because one page lacked his acknowledgment.

He signed where shown, then read the sentence above it again.

The account was his. The finding would not be.

***

Sun Lian received the auction notice the following morning.

The Honest Measure would be sold against its original secured loan. Her freight claim remained under review. Even if she won it, the payment might arrive too late to preserve the boat.

She read the date twice.

Su Fan stood beside the table. He had carried her bag there and had not found a good moment to put it down.

Min Yao took the notice only after Sun Lian handed it over.

She asked for the most recent claim receipt, then the loan paper, then the earlier emergency-service order. The documents had begun to look familiar enough that Su Fan wanted familiarity to count as a solution.

It did not.

Min Yao applied for a stay.

The available hearing date fell after the sale.

The answer arrived in neat writing with no visible embarrassment about the order in which those two events would occur.

Sun Lian folded it and put it with the other accounts.

“First I need my channels to heal,” she said. “Then I need work.”

Su Fan said nothing about finding a way.

He put the tool bag beside her chair, where she could reach it without asking him again.

***

For three days, the kitchen fed more people than it had room to seat.

The celebration was untidy.

Some operators were relieved. Others resented the interruption. One man who had retained his bond objected to a neighbour describing the day as the end of inherited cultivation. Qiu Lan told the neighbour to look at her wrist before making another announcement.

Families argued about whether the risk had been necessary. People who had been far from the collector used confident phrases about what they would have done. People who had stood beside it sometimes found themselves unable to explain why an ordinary question about breakfast made them angry.

The woman who had stopped her separation cried when someone congratulated her.

Auntie Lu sat beside her until she stopped apologizing.

“You don't owe them a cheerful result,” she said.

“I wanted it finished.”

“I know.”

The woman looked at the mark that remained beneath her bandage.

Auntie Lu did not tell her to be grateful for it. She moved the bowl closer and stayed while the food cooled enough to eat.

***

Tan Wei spent most of the time asleep.

When he woke, he sometimes reached for a cup and waited for the water to rise farther than it could. Then his face changed, and he lifted the cup with his hand.

Su Fan learned not to watch every attempt.

There were things a friend could make harder simply by being present with too much attention.

On the fourth morning, Tan Wei came into the practice yard carrying a bucket.

It was lighter than the one he had used before.

The ground was still marked from earlier trials. The rope target hung where Ruan had left it. A broken piece of timber waited beside the wall to be cut into something useful when someone had strength to spare.

Su Fan moved the target closer without comment.

Tan Wei set the bucket down.

He checked the distance, then shifted it a little to his left. The adjustment was his own. Su Fan stood back far enough to leave him room.

A thin line of water rose.

It reached the target and fell short of the mark.

Tan Wei frowned, waited, and tried again.

They began there.

chapters.title: The Names Beneath the Seal
chapters.text:
The inquiry opened eighteen days after First Water.

It occupied the schoolroom because the regional office had burned in a different town twelve years earlier and never been rebuilt. Wen Zhao considered the arrangement embarrassing. The children considered it an excellent reason to have lessons outside.

Their counting stones had been moved into a basket beneath the window. Someone had covered the painted alphabet with a sheet so the magistrate would not sit below a badly drawn goat.

The goat remained visible through the cloth.

Su Fan sat behind Sun Lian and waited for his name.

On the table stood the damaged restraint hook, the broken pressure gauge and three sets of operating records. The hook had been cleaned only enough to make its bent lip visible. The gauge's polished face was in a separate tray, its pieces laid beside one another without pretending they still made a working instrument.

Sun Lian kept her hands in her lap. Her channels had not recovered enough for reinforcement work. She could hold a document, turn a page and make a witness feel foolish for confusing those limits with an inability to understand a measurement.

The regional magistrate began with the records.

***

The signatures did not all belong to Shen Tu.

That was the first fact Min Yao insisted on establishing.

She laid the operating schedule beside the order that had approved it. Below that came the acceptance receipt, then the copy of the diagram used to justify work at the stations.

The pages had travelled through different hands. Some edges were worn. One bore a stain from a cup placed down during a conversation that had probably seemed ordinary at the time.

The captain had approved unsafe schedules and directed the interception at the records house. He had also worked inside a chain of approvals that survived him.

An official seated near the magistrate suggested that the dead man's actions had made the question of individual responsibility unusually clear.

Min Yao turned one page so he could see the mark above the captain's.

“Then this one should be easy to identify.”

The official read the name.

“And the approval below it?”

He read that too, less readily.

The magistrate asked for the two copies to be compared before anyone drew a conclusion from the difference in ink.

They compared them.

The marks were present on both.

***

Zhen Su identified the copied diagram and the engineer who had commissioned it.

She did not say she knew everything the engineer intended. She described the page she had been given, the instructions for the copy and the portions that had been supplied separately.

“Did you certify the design?” the magistrate asked.

“No.”

“Did you change it?”

“I copied what I was paid to copy. The additions are identified on the receipt.”

Sun Lian produced the acceptance receipt.

The magistrate read it while Zhen Su waited with her hands folded so tightly that one thumb had gone pale.

Su Fan remembered watching her work with paper held flat beneath an ordinary stone. The distance between that table and this one seemed much larger than the roads she had travelled to reach them.

When the magistrate finished, she asked the clerk to attach the receipt to the copy rather than leave the two in separate piles.

It was a small instruction.

Zhen Su's hands loosened.

***

The dead store clerk's mother brought the schedule her son had kept.

She carried it in the same careful wrapping, repaired at one corner where repeated folding had weakened it. She had put on a clean outer coat. The sleeves were slightly too long, and she kept pushing them back before touching the paper.

The approving marks remained clear above her son's own.

The magistrate asked whether she sought compensation.

“I seek his name out of the confession.”

The room grew quiet.

The woman looked toward the official who had suggested the dead captain made responsibility clear.

“My son stole. I told them that before. It does not mean every thing that was written after he could no longer answer was his.”

The magistrate asked which statement she disputed.

The woman could not find the sentence immediately. Her hand shook over the pages. Min Yao moved the correct sheet within reach but did not point to the answer for her.

She found it herself.

The confession was entered as disputed evidence rather than accepted fact.

It was less than she had asked for.

It was more than she had possessed before entering.

When she sat down again, she kept the wrapping on her lap. Su Fan could see the shape of the empty space where the papers had been.

***

The killing took most of the second morning.

Su Fan moved his chair so the magistrate's voice would reach his left side. He explained the adjustment before anyone asked him to look forward again.

The magistrate nodded and had the clerk place the drawing where he could see it without turning away from her.

He described the fight.

He did not omit the damaged tread. He had struck it deliberately to make the captain lose a fraction of his footing. The old seam had broken where he expected it to break. That had given him room to move, and the room had allowed him to wound the captain's forearm.

The clerk looked up.

“Before the fatal stroke?”

“Yes.”

Su Fan described the cut to his own shoulder, the hand made slippery by blood and the meeting of the two blades near his guard.

He did not pretend the final strike had happened without a decision.

“When did you decide?” the magistrate asked.

“When he pulled the restraint.”

“Not when he released his sword?”

“No.”

“Did you believe the fight had ended at that point?”

“For a moment.”

He looked at the hook on the table.

“Then I saw the chain move.”

***

Ren Bo explained the restraint.

His arm remained supported against his chest. He used his good hand to point to the counterweight on the drawing, then to the path beneath it where the working crew had stood.

The magistrate asked whether the chain was an operating control.

“No. It held the weight clear.”

“Could releasing it have closed the western gate?”

“It could have jammed the work. It would have dropped through us first.”

She asked him to mark where he had been.

He marked it.

Ruan described the position of the men when he reached the landing. He had not seen the initial pull. He said so before the question could be answered by implication. He had seen the reseated restraint, Su Fan beside the captain and the working crew beneath the weight.

Two guards confirmed that the counterweight had begun to release.

Their accounts differed about the words shouted immediately before it. Wen Zhao had preserved that difference in the first statements. The magistrate asked about the hand, the chain and the movement separately.

On those points, the accounts agreed.

The guard who had not seen the pull was not asked to make his account more convenient. He described what he had seen afterward and was dismissed from that portion of the questioning.

Su Fan watched him return to his seat.

The man did not look at him.

***

The magistrate examined the hook herself.

She held it above the table, turned the bent lip toward the light and asked Ren Bo whether the chain had been secured again before the mechanism moved.

“Yes.”

“By whom?”

“Su Fan.”

The name sounded strange in that room after so many descriptions of hands and positions. He was used to being inside the actions. Other people could now place him on a drawing and disagree about what the placement meant.

By the end of the session, the record treated the fatal strike as an act against an immediate threat to the workers, not an execution of a surrendered prisoner.

Su Fan heard the finding and felt relief.

He had expected relief to feel cleaner.

The captain remained dead. The coat, the folded letter and the last words Su Fan had not understood were not removed from the world by an accurate finding about the chain.

Outside, Ruan offered him water.

Su Fan took it with both hands, though the right no longer needed the left's help to hold an ordinary cup.

Neither spoke until the next session was called.

***

The unlawful entry remained.

The damaged gallery was not the same question as the release in the western chamber, however much Su Fan wished the useful result would settle every earlier action at once.

He was ordered to contribute toward the gallery's repair. The amount was reduced to exclude damage caused by the brazier and the captain's own strikes. The contractor's claim that he had stolen an archive was rejected for lack of missing material.

Min Yao checked the wording before he signed.

She pointed to the portion identifying which damage the contribution covered. He read it twice. A debt described badly could grow more easily than one described plainly.

His method remained under review.

Wen Zhao's recommendation allowed him to practise and travel with notice while forbidding commercial instruction in the unassessed breathing forms. The regional magistrate accepted the recommendation pending a wider examination.

It was not recognition of every claim made for the Human Dao. It was not permission to open a school because an afternoon's test had gone well.

It was more freedom than the prepared room had offered.

Su Fan signed the record.

There was no oath to a founder beneath his name.

He checked twice.

The clerk waited through the second reading without telling him that the first should have been enough.

***

Jiang lost her office.

The formal wording was relief from operational command pending review of unauthorized transfers and conflicting emergency orders.

The practical result was simpler. She would no longer hold the river seal.

She placed it on the table without a speech.

The seal made a small sound against the wood. Su Fan had heard it set down on requisitions, compensation papers and readings that other people had preferred not to acknowledge. Without it, Jiang's hand looked unchanged.

The work she could order would change a great deal.

Wen Zhao recorded that her measurements had been accurate and that her intervention had prevented further operator injury. He also recorded the transfer of district property against the standing order.

Both entries remained.

Jiang asked for a copy of the final wording. The clerk began to say one would be sent later, then saw the magistrate looking at him and prepared it before the session ended.

She checked it, folded it and put it into the case that had held the seal.

Su Fan disliked the substitution more than she appeared to.

He knew by then that appearance was not a complete account of what she had paid.

***

Outside, he found her examining a crack in the schoolroom step.

“I'm sorry,” he said.

She looked up.

“For which part?”

“The office.”

“I chose my action.”

“Yes.”

She studied him a moment longer.

“You are improving at leaving that sentence alone.”

He nearly spoiled the improvement by explaining how much it had cost him.

Instead he sat on the sound end of the step.

Jiang touched the crack with a thumbnail, testing whether the edge had shifted since the last person filled it. The habit was so familiar that for a moment he could imagine nothing important had changed.

“Will they repair it?” he asked.

“If someone puts it on the right account.”

“Which account?”

She looked at the schoolroom door.

“I no longer have to discover that before supper.”

There was relief in the answer and something else he did not try to name for her.

A child came past with the basket of counting stones. Jiang moved her foot so he would not trip. He thanked her without using a title.

She remained on the step after Su Fan went inside.

***

Pei Gang did not appear on the third day.

The court's cultivation delegate attended in his place and accepted an independent technical review of the river system. The elder would retain his rank. He would not supervise the repaired collector until the review concluded.

No one declared the Human Dao superior to every inherited art.

No one declared the sect finished.

The delegation's papers acknowledged that the upper lake had been held and the northern spill redirected. They also preserved the objections to the refused test and the open-ended use proposed for Su Fan.

The account was less satisfying than a single verdict about a single man.

It was harder to discard without discarding something true.

The eleven withdrawal requests were recognized individually. The woman who had stopped halfway received a protected future window under a supervisor of her choice. She asked who would hold the copy and where she could request it if she moved.

The clerk wrote the answer down.

Operators who retained their bonds received copies of the revised local-loop terms. Qiu Lan checked the part governing ordinary work before she looked at the extraordinary provisions everyone else wanted to discuss.

Tan Wei read his own paper slowly.

He found two ambiguities and asked for them to be corrected before signing.

Su Fan waited beside him without reaching for the page.

One correction concerned the office to which a future request should go. The other concerned the difference between ordinary maintenance shifts and an emergency extension. Neither made the contract shorter.

The clerk began copying the amended version while Tan Wei watched.

“Will this delay the end of the session?” someone asked behind them.

“Yes,” Tan Wei said.

He did not apologize.

Han sat near the window with his cane between his knees. He listened to the new wording and asked the clerk to read one line aloud a second time. His earlier confidence had helped bring Tan Wei into an agreement whose protection had failed. Now he offered attention instead of certainty.

When the copy was ready, Tan Wei compared the two sheets himself.

Only then did he sign.

Outside, the children had begun demanding their room back. Their teacher told them another few minutes would not destroy their education. Several appeared willing to test that claim.

***

When the schoolroom finally emptied, Jin ran inside to see whether the magistrate had left any sweets.

She had left none.

Bao Mei found three abandoned brushes and asked whether those counted as payment for lost lessons. Min Yao made her return two.

“The other?” Bao Mei asked.

“Is yours. You left it here before the inquiry.”

The girl examined the chewed end and conceded the point.
