The goat emerged when the sheet over the alphabet was taken down. Someone had used the cloth's lower edge to make notes, and the schoolteacher became indignant enough to remind everyone whose room it was.

Su Fan helped carry the benches back into rows.

The first arrangement left too little room for children to pass behind the last one. He shifted it, then moved the next, until the classroom began to resemble itself rather than a poorly cleared hearing room.

Min Yao put his copies into a plain wrapper.

He took them carefully.

His name remained in several files he could not control. His debts had not disappeared. His method was still something other people intended to examine.

For the first time, he also held copies of his own.

chapters.title: The Boat That Was Hers
chapters.text:
The Honest Measure was sold on a clear morning in Siltbridge.

Sun Lian attended the sale.

She had travelled with Min Yao, whose work required her return to the city in any case. Neither had asked Su Fan to come. He learned about the journey afterward, when the sale was no longer something he could imagine preventing by arriving with the right argument.

At the quay, the boat looked disappointingly ordinary.

No part of the hull appeared to understand that its name was being read from a list. Water moved against the planks. A rope creaked at the stern. The little repair near the rail still carried a lighter colour than the wood around it because she had not had time to finish it properly before the boat was taken out of her hands.

A prospective buyer pressed his boot against that part.

“It holds,” she said.

He looked up.

“You worked on her?”

“Yes.”

“Will that seam need doing before winter?”

“Not that seam.”

She pointed to the one that would.

The man crouched to inspect it. Sun Lian wished, briefly, that she had let him find it himself. Then she was angry at the wish. A sound account of the boat's condition was not something she intended to abandon because the account no longer served her.

Min Yao stood beside the sale clerk, checking the papers under which the auction proceeded.

She found nothing that would stop it that morning.

***

The winning bidder was a grain merchant who already owned three shallow-draft boats.

He did not make an extravagant gesture after his offer was accepted. He spoke to the clerk, confirmed the transfer arrangements and sent a man to check the mooring while the last papers were prepared.

Sun Lian knew the kind of work the boat would do.

Mundane cargo. Short runs when the river behaved, longer waits when it did not. Enough work to require constant small repairs and not enough romance to make anyone pay more for them.

The merchant approached her after the bidding.

“I understand you know the hull.”

“I built part of it.”

“Then you know more than that.”

He offered her employment as captain.

The proposal was sensible enough to hurt. He needed someone who knew the boat. She needed work. He could provide wages before the unresolved freight claim put money back into her hand.

She asked to see the terms.

The merchant seemed surprised that she did not answer from gratitude or anger.

He sent for a copy.

***

The wage was fair.

Sun Lian read the cargo schedule twice.

Three questions followed. How were delays counted when the river could not be safely crossed? Who carried the cost of turning back with a load? How much time was allowed between a late return and the next departure?

The merchant answered the first readily. The second required a reference to another clause. At the third, he said experienced captains understood that a schedule could not provide for every inconvenience.

“Fatigue isn't an inconvenience,” she said.

“It is part of the work.”

“So is deciding not to sail.”

He looked at the paper rather than her.

“I need the delivery dates kept.”

She believed him. The grain would have buyers waiting beyond the quay. He had agreements of his own, some made before he acquired another boat. Those facts explained the pressure without making the pressure disappear from the person holding the tiller.

She put the copy down.

“No.”

He asked whether she wanted a higher rate.

“The rate isn't the part I am refusing.”

For a moment both looked toward the Honest Measure.

The merchant had not become a villain because his offer was one she could not safely accept. The boat had not become less hers in memory because it was now his in the account.

She thanked him for showing the terms and left them unsigned.

***

He intended to repaint the hull.

The name board had no place in his plan. When Sun Lian asked for it, he told his man to take it down and said she could have it.

She paid a small sum anyway.

The merchant looked puzzled. The amount was too little to be an argument over the value of the boat and too deliberate to be mistaken for a tip.

Sun Lian did not explain. She did not want the first exchange after losing the hull to be a favour she would resent whenever she touched the board.

One fastening resisted removal.

She watched the man begin to lever against the painted face and asked for a moment. With a borrowed tool she cleared the old edge, found the angle at which the fixing would move and eased it free without widening the split beside it.

Her hands still knew how to help this particular piece of wood.

That knowledge had not been sold.

It would not buy the hull back.

She carried the board to Min Yao, who wrapped it in a spare cloth without suggesting it would look well above a new boat someday.

They left the quay before the repainting began.

***

Duan found Sun Lian planing the board's damaged edge behind the workshop.

She had supported it carefully so the work required no earth reinforcement. Even so, she stopped more often than she would have before First Water, letting the ache settle rather than asking a damaged channel to make an ordinary tool feel lighter.

“Will you hang it?” he asked.

“Perhaps.”

“Burning would be warmer.”

“Yes.”

He sat on a block and watched her work.

The plane took a narrow shaving. Beneath the weathered surface, the wood remained sound. She set the blade shallower before the next pass so she would not remove more than the edge needed.

After a while she said, “I built half of her.”

“I know.”

“The half that matters.”

“Most people say that about the half they built.”

She laughed despite herself.

Duan handed her a finer blade.

He had not offered to do the work for her. His left shoulder would not have allowed the old easy movement anyway. What he could still offer was an eye for an edge and the right tool set within reach.

She took it.

***

Su Fan came out with a finished fitting and stopped when he saw the board.

Sun Lian waited for the question.

“When?”

“This morning.”

He looked at the cloth lying beneath it, still marked with quay dust.

“I didn't know you were going.”

“No.”

He set the fitting on the shelf.

For a few breaths she watched him work through all the things he might say. Some would be kind. Some would put her in the position of comforting him for not having been given a chance to prevent what she had already endured.

“How was the journey?” he asked at last.

“Crowded.”

“Did you eat?”

“Badly.”

“There is food inside.”

“I'll finish this edge first.”

He nodded and went back to the forge.

Duan watched him disappear through the doorway.

“Slow learner,” he said.

Sun Lian ran her thumb along the newly smoothed edge.

“Not always.”

***

The commercial claim paid out in stages.

The false defect charge was removed. The remaining secured loan had been partly satisfied by the sale. After fees, valid principal and the delayed freight payment were accounted for, Sun Lian received enough to stop borrowing for food.

Not enough for another boat.

For two mornings she walked the new settlement with her tools and asked what people had been postponing.

The answers were not grand. A chest whose lid admitted damp. A door that caught whenever the weather changed. A carrier's rack repaired so many times that no one could say which part was still original.

Some people wanted work they could not yet pay for. Some had paid for work that had never been finished. Sun Lian wrote those cases differently rather than turn every need into a promising order.

At the workshop she examined the available timber and found three pieces Duan had kept because their shapes were awkward for the jobs he usually accepted. They were useful for hers.

She asked what he wanted for them.

“What will you make?”

“Something I can sell.”

“Good. Then we can agree a price before you discover it is a public service.”

They measured the pieces together. He could steady one end with his good hand while she marked the cut. Neither needed to pretend the old arrangement of their bodies would return before new work could begin.

That afternoon she made the first rough proposal.

It had no boat in it. She disliked that enough to leave the page alone for an hour, then returned and finished the list of work they could actually offer.

She spread the figures on Duan's workbench and asked him to look at a proposal.

He moved a half-finished hinge out of the way, wiped the surface and read the first page. Then he read it again, this time with a scrap beside him on which to put the numbers that did not belong to the same period.

A repair partnership.

Her hull and joinery work. His metal designs. Paid apprentices rather than unrecorded help that everyone praised until a worker needed to know what he was owed.

Bao Mei would produce the painted boards. Bao Shun would take the fitted storage work he could manage without damaging his hand further.

Duan reached the labour section and stopped.

“You know my shoulder won't improve.”

“Yes.”

“You will need another heavy smith.”

“We train one or pay one.”

He looked toward Su Fan, then deliberately back at the paper.

“A proper wage.”

Sun Lian nodded.

***

They disagreed over storage first.

Duan wanted metal stock where it would remain dry and where he could inspect it without climbing over unfinished boat work. Sun Lian wanted long timber near the door, not trapped behind a customer's cart whenever the forge received a delivery.

Neither arrangement fitted the room as it stood.

Su Fan measured the available space while they argued. The first drawing placed two things in the same corner. Bao Shun pointed that out without waiting to be invited into the discussion.

They moved the smaller storage work to a fitted rack he could make and kept the heavier stock below it.

Bao Mei asked whether painting would be expected whenever a customer remembered it at the end of a job.

“No,” Sun Lian said. “It goes on the order.”

“And changes?”

“Priced as changes.”

The girl wrote that down before anyone could describe it more generously.

The partnership became less elegant on paper as each person added what doing the work would actually require. It also became easier to imagine living inside it.

By the time they agreed on the first arrangement, Duan's hinge had been moved to three different shelves and nobody could remember which one.

Ah-Du found it under the drawing.

He announced that this proved the partnership already needed an assistant with exceptional powers of observation.

They gave him the next delivery to carry.

***

Su Fan offered a portion of every outside job toward the debt he owed Sun Lian.

She accepted a smaller fixed amount.

He began to explain that a proportion would rise if he earned more.

“It would also mean you could tell yourself every job was partly mine to worry about.”

“That isn't what I meant.”

“I know.”

She pointed to the other accounts on the table.

“You owe the gallery, the travel bond and your own food. I don't want a repayment scheme that makes me responsible for keeping you alive.”

He looked at the page for a while.

A large promise would have felt better. It would have let him offer the shape of a future in which his usefulness repaid everything at once. The smaller sum required a calendar, actual work and the possibility that some weeks would be less impressive than he hoped.

They wrote it down.

Sun Lian checked the dates and handed him a copy.

It was not forgiveness expressed as arithmetic.

It was a way to let the debt stop occupying every conversation between them.

When they finished, she asked him to pass a measuring cord.

He did, relieved to know exactly what the next request cost.

***

Jiang joined the new river cooperative as a paid surveyor for a single season.

She negotiated her fee severely enough to reassure everyone who feared she had become saintly through losing her office.

The cooperative maintained the Low Gate under the independent review. It did not own the high lake or the whole river. It had limited authority, a budget too small for its ambitions and members who argued over the price of replacement rope.

Jiang listened to the rope argument, asked how often the cheaper line would need replacing and made them include the labour in the comparison.

That did not end the disagreement.

It improved what they were disagreeing about.

Tan Wei applied for work there.

Han provided a reference that mentioned both his skill and his recent loss of cultivation. The description of his water control was careful. It did not use the former fifth stage as though an old number could perform a present task.

Tan Wei read it alone before submitting it.

Su Fan saw the paper folded beside his cup and asked whether Han had written what he needed.

“He wrote what is true.”

“Will that be enough?”

“I'll find out.”

He submitted it unchanged.

***

The repair shed received its first enquiry before it had a sign.

A carrier wanted storage altered so his goods would stop shifting against a wheel housing. He arrived with a drawing that made the problem look smaller than it was and a story about how little time the change ought to take.

Bao Shun asked to see the cart.

Sun Lian asked what it carried.

Duan asked which fitting had already broken.

The carrier looked between them and sighed.

He had hoped a new partnership might be too eager for work to ask all the old questions.

They went outside together.

Su Fan stayed to clear the bench. The room had begun to acquire the untidiness of several people's plans rather than one man's orderly ambition. He moved the new account book away from sparks and found a place where a person could open it without balancing a bowl on the metal stock.

That seemed a useful contribution.

He did not add his name to the cover.

***

One evening, he found Sun Lian hanging the name board above the shed.

She stood on a ladder while Ah-Du attempted to direct her from below.

“Left.”

“My left or yours?”

“The boat's.”

She looked down at him.

He reconsidered the instruction.

Su Fan steadied the ladder. Bao Mei stood farther back, checking the letters against the line of the door rather than trusting Ah-Du's enthusiastic hands.

“A little down on that side,” she said.

Sun Lian made the adjustment.

When the board was level, she climbed down and examined it.

HONEST MEASURE.

The letters had weathered unevenly. One corner was missing. The lighter wood where she had repaired the edge would remain visible until time darkened it to match.

“It will do,” she said.

Then she unlocked the shed and let the first customer in.

chapters.title: The Books He Left
chapters.text:
Min Yao found eleven versions of the same translation.

Her father had labelled four of them final.

She spread them across the floor and called Su Fan in to help identify which pages he had actually used.

“Did he give you this one?”

“No.”

“This?”

“Part of it.”

“This one says it supersedes the previous two.”

“Which two?”

She looked at him.

Together they laughed, then stopped when the absence behind the joke became too large.

The room still held the shape of Min's habits. The better light fell on the chair he preferred. A small stone rested on the windowsill, exactly where his hand had reached for it whenever a page threatened to turn itself. Beneath the reading stand, a folded scrap levelled the short foot.

Su Fan knew who had put that scrap there.

He left it in place.

Min Yao drew another sheet from the pile and held it toward the window.

“This one has a date.”

“Is it later?”

“Yes. And apparently less certain.”

She placed it beside the others instead of underneath them.

***

They worked for three days.

The catalogue became a record of what was known, what had been tested and what remained a guess. Min Yao kept her father's confident statements but marked the evidence beneath them. Su Fan added the results of his own practice without pretending experience supplied every missing word.

The work was slower than putting the cleanest copy on top.

One page contained an excellent correction to a character and a poor conclusion about the drawing beside it. Another had been abandoned because Min disliked the wording, though the observations beneath the sentence were still useful.

Su Fan wanted to discard a sheet whose exercise had failed.

Min Yao asked whether the failure had been recorded elsewhere.

“Not with all the conditions.”

“Then why throw away the part someone else would need?”

He put it back.

She did not look pleased at having caught him. She had made the same mistake with a translation that no longer matched her father's later reading. The discarded version still explained why he had asked certain questions afterward.

They kept the sequence where they could establish it.

Where they could not, they left the uncertainty in the catalogue instead of using neat handwriting to conceal it.

***

The open-centred mark received a page to itself.

Found on the scripture cover.

Found beside the western chamber's maintenance wheel.

Possibly associated with an older engineering tradition.

Meaning uncertain.

Su Fan read the page aloud.

It seemed very short beside the amount of time he had spent wondering about the mark. He remembered the warmth beneath his fingers at the old archive wall and the moment underground when seeing it again had made the chamber feel connected to a history he almost knew.

Almost was not enough to fill the rest of the page.

Min Yao asked whether the marks were exactly alike.

“The main strokes. The worn edge makes one part difficult to compare.”

She added that.

“Any dated use?”

“Not securely.”

She left the next line blank.

Nothing about a chosen successor.

Nothing about the cause of the Severing.

The evidence did not reach that far.

Su Fan found he could live with the unfinished page. It gave him something to look for beyond the valley without deciding in advance what the search must prove.

He put the two copied impressions beside it, wrapped separately so the wet edge of one could not stain the other.

***

Jin was given a task with no ink in it.

He had to match the loose paper covers to the bundles whose edges they protected. Some were too small, some too large, and several had acquired labels that belonged to books no longer inside them.

He took the work seriously until he discovered a wrapper that could be folded into a hat.

Min Yao looked up.

“Is that in the catalogue?”

“Not yet.”

“Then return it before someone requests the volume it used to hold.”

He removed the hat reluctantly.

Bao Mei came to help with labels and found him making a separate pile of covers whose writing he could not read. She sat beside him and asked which letters he did know.

The two began arguing about one crooked stroke.

For a moment Su Fan expected Min to correct them from the chair by the window. The expectation was so ordinary that the failure of it hurt more than the papers on the floor.

Min Yao heard the argument too.

She did not take her father's place in it immediately. She let the children compare the labels with another example, then answered when they brought her the two possibilities.

The room continued to contain work that did not know how to miss him.

They were learning to do it anyway.

***

The personal papers were harder.

Min Yao found receipts for gifts her father had purchased and never sent. A pair of small shoes too old for Jin. Three letters apologizing for the same argument in different ways, none with an address on the outside.

Su Fan began to leave.

She asked him to stay.

“I don't need you to explain him.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“Good.”

They sat among the papers while she read.

The letters did not form a final version. One apologized too readily for something he still defended on the next page. Another began with news of a book and approached the argument so carefully that it never reached it.

Min Yao read the third twice.

Then she folded it along its old crease.

Su Fan could see the effort in her hands. He could not see what she had accepted or refused in the words. He stayed without offering a judgment that would make her responsible for agreeing with him.

At last she put the letters into a separate box.

“Some of this is mine,” she said. “The rest can go to the library.”

No one disputed her division.

***

Later she found a little list of things to ask her grandson.

She read none of it aloud.

The page went into the same box.

Su Fan moved the stack of public catalogues farther from it. The distinction had seemed obvious until the objects lay together on the floor: an annotation about a river level beside an unfinished apology, a receipt for paper beneath a receipt for a child's shoes.

Min had used whatever space was at hand. The people sorting afterward needed more care than the original arrangement suggested.

Min Yao took the stone from the windowsill.

“Do you want this for the reading stand?” she asked.

Su Fan shook his head.

“It was his.”

“That's why I'm asking.”

He looked at the ordinary smooth surface. He had seen the old man use it often enough to feel that accepting it would mean accepting more than a weight for paper.

“Keep it,” he said.

She put it in the box without another question.

He was glad they could refuse one another small things without making the refusal an account of how much they had loved the man who left them.

Outside, Jin called that Bao Mei had found the right character.

Min Yao closed the box and went to look.

***

The new library occupied two rooms beside the school.

It had fewer books than the old Stack and more people allowed through the door.

The shelves were plain. Several boards had been used elsewhere before finding their present duty, and the lowest row stood high enough above the floor for damp to be noticed before it reached a binding.

Su Fan helped carry the heavier bundles.

He did not decide where to put them. Zhen Su had already made a plan that allowed a person to find a book without remembering which pile Min had last described as temporary.

She accepted paid work arranging the catalogues and copying damaged pages.

Before agreeing, she insisted on an account for paper.

“I cannot promise copies while discovering each week whether the paper is a donation, a loan or something I am expected to buy.”

Min Yao wrote the provision plainly.

Duan examined the shelf fastenings and asked for one to be changed. Bao Shun fitted a small cupboard whose latch could be opened without twisting a damaged wrist. Bao Mei painted its label with enough space for another line if the contents changed.

The room acquired competence from several people at once.

No founder's name was needed above the door to make their contributions real.

The first dispute over the arrangement concerned a book nobody had expected to want.

Zhen Su had placed the old limb exercises near the medical shelves. A cartwright asked for them because he had been trying to understand why a repaired seat made one driver’s knee ache and left another comfortable. Mother Wei wanted the same volume for a patient who could not yet manage the walk to the new rooms.

There was only one copy.

Su Fan remembered having wanted it at the Stack when two copper seemed too much to pay for pages. He offered to make another copy, then looked at the thickness and corrected himself.

“The useful section first.”

“Useful to whom?” Zhen Su asked.

They marked the two requested passages separately.

The cartwright stayed while Mother Wei chose the pages she needed. He described the seat, she asked about the height and the distance to the footrest, and both discovered they had been using the word comfortable for several different arrangements.

Su Fan listened until Duan called him away to carry another box.

When he returned, Jin was holding a ruler against the illustration under close supervision. The cartwright had drawn a better footrest on a separate sheet. Mother Wei had rejected his first explanation of the patient’s pain but kept the measurement he supplied.

The old book had not settled the matter.

It had given them something precise enough to disagree about.

Zhen Su put the new drawing in a wrapper with the title and the date, leaving room for an answer. Then she told the cartwright that the page could not remain on her table while he went to fetch his cart, because someone else needed the space.

He went more quickly.

Bao Mei finished the shelf label while the room was briefly quiet. She held it up, waited for everyone to read it, and changed one letter before the paint dried.

Su Fan asked what had been wrong.

“It said limbs after damage,” she said. “I had written limits after damage.”

Mother Wei considered the mistake.

“Keep the corrected one.”

Bao Mei did.

***

Min Yao wrote the first rules.

Dry hands.

Return dates.

No lamps left burning unattended.

Report damage rather than hiding it.

Ah-Du suggested a rule against correcting other people's writing in the margins.

Min Yao looked around the room that existed partly because her father had done so for decades.

“We may need to word that carefully.”

Zhen Su proposed that readers put new observations on separate slips and identify which page they concerned. The correction could then be considered without destroying the evidence of what the older book actually said.

Ah-Du objected that this required more paper.

“Which is why,” Zhen Su said, “I asked for the account.”

He conceded the point with an exaggerated bow.

Su Fan kept his personal practice records separate from the public collection. The inquiry had not certified the breathing forms for commercial teaching, and a useful catalogue was not permission to turn untested exercises into lessons for anyone who wanted them.

The distinction disappointed a young worker who came asking about the scripture.

Su Fan explained what the library did contain: measurements, repairs, histories and ordinary methods that had survived disposal because someone had needed them.

The worker stayed to look at a book about damaged knees.

He did not have to admire Su Fan's path in order to find something worth reading.

***

On the opening day, a woman returned a borrowed booklet with one corner wet.

She put it down as though expecting a quarrel.

Zhen Su asked when the damage had happened, how far the water had reached and whether any pages still stuck together. The woman answered, gradually less defensively.

They laid the booklet where it could dry without another reader trying to force it open.

The woman asked whether she would be forbidden to borrow again.

“Did you hide it?” Zhen Su said.

“No.”

“Then you have followed the rule we needed.”

The damage still had to be repaired. Someone would have to pay for materials if the binding failed. None of that required making honesty the first mistake a borrower regretted.

Su Fan watched from the door while a boy brought in a broken latch from the school cupboard and asked whether the library also lent the ability to mend things.

“Only in books,” Zhen Su said.

The boy looked disappointed.

Duan, passing behind him, told him to bring the latch to the workshop after lessons.

The two rooms had begun to find their place among the other work of the settlement.

***

Min Yao left for Siltbridge after the opening.

Jin cried less than he had before the records-house journey. This departure had a known address, his own bed at the other end and arrangements for returning to the quarry that did not depend on a crisis.

He still objected when a book box was placed where he had intended to sit.

Sun Lian checked the cart's load and found another position for it. She did not let the child move it himself merely because he announced that he was strong enough.

Su Fan tied the last cord around a box of public copies going with Min Yao. The personal box stayed nearer her seat, within reach. Nobody asked for one more look inside.

She handed him a thin packet tied with plain cord.

His own practice notes, copied cleanly, with spaces left where diagrams needed correction.

“I haven't improved your wording,” she said.

“I didn't ask you to.”

“I know. It was difficult.”

He smiled.

She touched the packet once before letting go.

“Your father would have changed it,” Su Fan said.

“Yes,” she said. “Then argued that he had merely made your intention clearer.”

They laughed, and this time the laughter survived the silence afterward.

***

At the bend in the road, Jin waved the paper fish he had made that morning.

It was a different fish from the one buried with his grandfather. Brighter, badly folded, one fin much larger than the other.

Su Fan waved back.

When the cart disappeared, he returned to the practice yard.

The copied packet opened easily. Its cord had been tied for use rather than display. On the first page, a date stood beside an exercise that had failed because he had confused the return with the part of the movement he wanted to strengthen.

The failure was still there.

So were the doubtful readings, the corrected measurements and the later attempt that had worked under conditions he could describe.

He turned the page.

For the first time, someone else could follow what he had actually done.

chapters.title: Eight
chapters.text:
Ten weeks after First Water, Su Fan held the eighth circuit through an ordinary working day.

There was no sudden light.

At dawn he carried iron stock from the storehouse. The first bundle was awkward rather than particularly heavy. One end wanted to slide beneath his arm, and he had to put it down, change the tie and lift it again while Ah-Du told him this was why carrying should be left to people with experience.

At midmorning he helped set a repaired axle.

After lunch he trained, rested and trained again.

The deeper route that had opened for three breaths beneath the gate remained stable when he turned, lifted or received a change of load. He could feel it without having to chase it. The sensation no longer disappeared the moment he tried to name the conditions under which it arrived.

He did not call it the eighth stage yet.

That evening, he ate with the others and helped clear the benches. He slept badly at first, not because of pain but because he kept wondering whether sleep would take away what the day had finally made ordinary.

Morning answered without ceremony.

He woke, put on his clothes and went to the workshop.

The route remained through the first hour's work.

Then he asked Jiang to measure it.

***

The independent needle moved.

Not dramatically. Its task was to measure, not applaud.

Jiang repeated the test at three points, compared the readings and asked him to perform a smaller movement than the one he had prepared to demonstrate.

“Why smaller?”

“Because you have been waiting to show me the larger one.”

He smiled and did as she asked.

The route held when the movement stopped. It held when he changed direction. At the last point, the needle trembled around a pressure that was steadier than the measurements taken after the brief opening under the gate.

Jiang made him rest before repeating it.

He sat on the low wall while she checked the instrument against its reference. The same needle had once supplied a small, undeniable answer to a question he had thought the whole mountain lacked the means to ask.

Now it was an expensive tool borrowed from an account that would want it back.

That made it easier to trust than a relic that seemed to approve of him.

When the second set of readings agreed, Jiang handed him the instrument.

“You can keep this until you leave. Return it before you go.”

Su Fan looked up.

“Who said I was leaving?”

“Sun Lian has rented transport to Siltbridge. You have been asking about the northern roads. Your notice form is on my desk awaiting a date.”

He had forgotten he had left it there.

The steward, no longer a steward, looked amused.

“You are still easier to observe than you imagine.”

***

He wrote the result down at the workshop.

Eighth circuit stable through work, rest, sleep and repeated measurement.

Below it went the conditions. The first successful day. The next morning. The loads used. The place where an old shoulder habit had almost made him mistake a correction for failure.

He included the opening beneath the gate without giving it the same status as what had survived the last two days.

Three breaths had not been a stage he could use.

They had been something worth investigating after his body recovered enough to investigate it without making another injury the price of an answer.

Duan read the entry.

“Does that finish the axle?”

“No.”

“Then congratulations. The axle is waiting.”

Ah-Du laughed so hard that he had to put down the piece he was holding.

Su Fan went back to the job. The new circulation made part of the work easier. The fitting still needed the correct clearance, and a shoulder made lighter by qi could still push an axle into a bad seat.

He checked the alignment before asking anyone to drive the next pin.

The repaired cart left after noon.

Its owner thanked Duan, paid the agreed amount and drove away without asking which stage had helped complete it.

Su Fan found the lack of interest unexpectedly pleasant.

***

Ruan gave him a final bout before returning to his family's western holding.

They cleared the whole yard.

The old post remained where it had always been, but the loose stones were moved and the damp patch beneath the eaves was marked. Their practice blades had been inspected before the padding was fastened. Ruan checked Su Fan's fastening and required him to check his in return.

This time he did not limit himself to clear openings or single forms.

The fight moved across the yard. Steel rang. Dust rose beneath their feet. Su Fan's neutral circulation gave Ruan little warning of where the force would arrive, but Ruan had learned to read the body that carried it.

The shoulders still moved.

The feet still needed ground.

A man who gave no familiar cultivation signal could nevertheless look at the place he intended to strike.

Ruan found that look on the first exchange and made Su Fan pay for it with a sharp touch to the ribs.

“Again?”

Su Fan adjusted the padding.

“Again.”

***

Ruan attacked the right side.

Su Fan turned early, knowing he could not hear enough to wait.

Ruan changed the angle.

The first contact went past Su Fan's guard. He let it pass rather than spend the next movement trying to prove it had not surprised him. At the second contact he stepped through, joined the returning pressure and stopped his point beneath Ruan's guard.

At the same moment, Ruan's blade touched his shoulder.

They looked at each other's positions.

“Unpleasant for both,” Ruan said.

Su Fan lowered his sword.

He had reached the opening. He had also left one.

They repeated the exchange differently and discovered the result was not reliable.

Ruan altered his first step. Su Fan anticipated the alteration and lost the timing that had made the earlier touch possible. On the next attempt he waited more successfully but gave too much ground. The post met his back before Ruan's blade met his arm.

By the fifth exchange, both were breathing hard enough that Sun Lian called from the shed to ask whether the lesson included knowing when to stop.

Ruan said that portion was advanced.

She came to the doorway.

They stopped.

***

Sitting beneath the eaves, Su Fan touched the bruise beginning at his shoulder.

The eighth circuit had not made the damaged ear whole. It had not taught him where Ruan would stand merely because he was stronger than before. It gave him more capacity to answer a problem he still had to perceive correctly.

Ruan drank from the cup and watched him consider the yard.

“You look dissatisfied.”

“I had hoped to win one cleanly.”

“You nearly did.”

“So did you.”

“I was hoping for that.”

Su Fan laughed.

They spoke about the western holding while the sweat dried. Ruan had work waiting there that could not be described as a dramatic campaign. Accounts. Repairs. A relative who would ask why an ordinary visit had occupied so much time and several changes of clothing.

“Will you tell her everything?”

“I intend to begin with the parts she already knows.”

“Safer?”

“Not necessarily. It reduces the length of her questions.”

He stood to collect his blade.

Neither tried to turn the farewell into a promise that their next meeting would settle whose path was better. They had learned too much from one another to make that the most useful question left.

***

Hua Jun's letter arrived with a merchant's invoice.

The two had been tied together for convenience by somebody who assumed a workshop would know how to distribute paper addressed to people who worked there.

Ah-Du handed Su Fan the invoice first.

“Important news.”

“This is the price of hinges.”

“Duan said those were important.”

The other sheet was more interesting.

The body-refiner had heard of the western bypass, though the version reaching Siltbridge credited Su Fan with holding back an entire lake using one hand.

She wrote that she hoped he had used the other hand to collect proper payment.

He read the sentence aloud.

Duan said the question was sound even when the account of the work was not.

Below the joke was an offer.

A northern caravan needed an escort for the lower road: mundane engineering cargo, three merchant families and a mixed cultivation guard. The pay was modest. The work was real. Hua Jun would introduce him to the organizer, not guarantee his acceptance.

There was also a public archive in the next city with copies of pre-sect maintenance inscriptions.

He read that part twice.

***

The journey acquired a different shape after the letter.

Before it, he had wanted to leave the valley and find out what lay beyond the accounts other people had brought home. Now there was a place to ask for work, a description of what the work involved and a reason to carry his practice notes that did not require announcing them as the beginning of a new school.

He took the letter to Sun Lian.

She read the cargo description first.

“Engineering goods travel badly when someone thinks weight is the only thing that matters.”

“What else should I ask?”

“What they expect you to protect. People, cargo, schedule. And what happens when those stop being the same task.”

He wrote the questions on a separate page.

She pointed to the organizer's introduction.

“You haven't been hired.”

“I know.”

“Good. Don't spend the wages yet.”

He had already begun imagining what the first payment might settle. He crossed out no debts, made no promise about the size of the payment and put the letter beside the dated measurements instead.

Both were useful beginnings.

Neither was a finished road.

***

The new apprentice asked which jobs Su Fan would finish before leaving.

He had brought the order slate rather than a request that sounded personal. Su Fan recognized the care in that choice. A person arriving at a workshop could inherit promises he had never heard made and then be blamed for discovering them too slowly.

They went through the slate together.

Two pieces were ready for collection. One needed a fitting from a supplier. Another had been marked urgent by a customer who had not yet delivered the damaged part.

“Do I do that first?” the apprentice asked.

“When it arrives, ask Duan where it belongs.”

“The customer says he spoke to you.”

“He did. He also said he would bring it yesterday.”

Su Fan wrote the unfinished condition beside the order instead of leaving the boy to argue about a conversation he had not witnessed.

At the forge, they worked on an axle pin. The apprentice watched Su Fan's hand rather than the iron.

“The colour,” Su Fan said.

“How many breaths?”

“Look at the colour.”

The boy looked, frowned and asked whether the glow was changing because the light from the doorway had moved.

Su Fan began the explanation again, this time showing him the difference in the shaded part of the forge. Knowing a thing while working did not automatically mean knowing how to describe it to someone whose eyes had not learned the same habit.

Duan listened from the bench.

When Su Fan finished, the smith asked the apprentice to explain what he had seen.

The answer was partly right.

They corrected the part that mattered for the next attempt and left the rest until there was another piece of iron to look at.

Afterward the apprentice put a small mark beside the job he could now prepare without calling Su Fan across the room.

It was only one mark.

Su Fan looked at it with more pleasure than the boy appeared to expect.

“Will you be back?” the apprentice asked.

“I intend to be.”

“Before this order is finished?”

Su Fan shook his head.

“Then you should tell me where the other stock is.”

He did.

The workshop had accepted the prospect of his departure by asking for the information needed to work without him. He found that easier and harder than being begged to stay.

***

Mother Wei checked his chest before agreeing that travel was sensible.

The pressure beneath the ribs no longer caught with every deep breath. The shoulder wound had healed enough that ordinary movement did not pull it open. She still asked him to turn slowly and tell her which positions remained uncomfortable.

He answered before she had to press the question.

Then she examined the damaged ear.

“The ringing?”

“Less often.”

“Can you locate a sound on that side?”

“Sometimes.”

“That is not yes.”

“I know.”

She packed medicine anyway.

He asked which parcel was for the journey and which was for the work he had not yet obtained.

“Both. The road will not wait for your employer to become definite before finding ways to inconvenience you.”

She wrote the uses plainly and made him read them back. Nothing in the packets promised to repair the hearing he had lost or replace sensible rest with a stronger appetite for work.

At the bottom she put a small amount of something he recognized from childhood.

“For the stomach,” she said when he looked at her.

“I haven't complained.”

“You have not eaten road food yet.”

He tied the packet carefully.

***

Duan inspected the sword.

He found a tiny nick Su Fan had missed and made him correct it himself. The work took longer because Su Fan wanted the edge finished before the smith found something else wrong with it.

Duan found something else anyway.

“Oil the fitting. Not only the part you expect people to admire.”

Su Fan did.

Bao Mei painted a small mark inside the scabbard so it would be recognizable among other plain weapons. She chose a place rain would not reach easily, then told him that easily was not never.

Ah-Du offered to come.

Su Fan reminded him he had agreed to finish the new furnace bellows.

The boy looked toward Duan, hoping for rescue.

The smith shook his head.

“Finish one thing before making it somebody else's unfinished thing.”

Ah-Du complained that the advice would prevent most interesting journeys.

“Only the ones paid for by people you leave behind.”

The boy went to inspect the bellows. After a while he called Su Fan over to look at a joint he wanted finished before the departure.

Su Fan helped without promising that finishing it would make the boy free to follow.

***

That evening, he returned the measuring needle and dated his travel notice.

Jiang checked that the instrument was clean, recorded its return and asked him to keep his own copy of the notice dry.

“Will they accept it beyond the valley?”

“They can read it. Whether they understand it on the first attempt is another question.”

He folded the page so the official marks would not lie on the crease.

He remained at Qi Refinement. Four stages still lay ahead before the question of Foundation could become practical rather than imagined.

He had a sword he understood, a body with lasting damage, debts he intended to pay and a book that did not contain all the answers he wanted.

He also had a possible wage beyond the valley, provided he could convince a caravan master he was worth it.

He found himself looking forward to the conversation.

chapters.title: The Road Beyond
chapters.text:
Su Fan left after breakfast.

Mother Wei had insisted on the meal and then complained that everyone was making too much of an ordinary journey.

She wrapped two extra buns while saying it.

“Those are for later,” she told him.

“I am still eating this one.”

“Yes. A promising beginning.”

He sat at the table where she had taught him to read medicine labels, explain himself honestly and stop pretending a smaller injury was no injury at all. The light fell differently in this house than it had in the lost clinic. Some mornings he still looked for a window that had stood on the other side of the old room.

The bowl in front of him was familiar.

That helped.

Mother Wei checked the medicine packet without opening every parcel again. She had already explained it. Repeating the whole account would not make the road less capable of surprising him.

He finished his food and washed the bowl.

She watched him set it down.

“Your papers?”

“Wrapped.”

“Your notice?”

“With the papers.”

“Food?”

He looked at the buns.

She looked at him until he answered properly.

“Yes.”

Only then did she let him put on his pack.

***

At the door he stopped because there ought to have been something to say that belonged only to this departure.

Mother Wei adjusted the strap where it caught against the repaired shoulder of his coat.

“Don't turn every discomfort into proof that you should have stayed.”

“I won't.”

“And don't turn it into proof that you must keep going either.”

He smiled.

“You have left me very little to prove.”

“Good. There should be room for the buns.”

He bent and put his arms around her carefully. For a moment she stood very still, then held him with more strength than he had expected from the hands that had spent so much of his life doing small necessary things.

When she let go, she examined the fastening she had just corrected.

“It will rub if you leave it like that.”

He moved it.

Someone called from the clinic room. A patient wanted to know whether she had forgotten him.

“Not successfully,” she called back.

Su Fan laughed and stepped into the lane.

She remained at the door until he turned toward the workshop. Then the patient called again, and she went inside to answer the life that had not paused for this one farewell.

***

Duan stood at the workshop door with his injured arm supported against his chest.

Behind him, the new apprentice was heating an axle pin under instructions to watch the colour rather than the clock. Ah-Du had found a way to inspect the bellows that put him conveniently near the doorway.

“Letters,” the smith said.

“I will.”

“Useful ones. Tell me what the fittings cost.”

Su Fan smiled.

“Only the fittings?”

“Good steel. Bad steel. Who is pretending one is the other.”

“That may require more paper.”

“Spend sensibly.”

Duan checked the sword at Su Fan's side without taking it out. The fitting had been oiled. The scabbard was tied where it would not strike his knee every third step.

For once, the smith found nothing he needed to correct.

He seemed briefly inconvenienced by that.

Then he gripped the back of Su Fan's neck with his good hand and pulled him close.

The embrace lasted only a moment.

He let go and turned toward the furnace before either of them could become embarrassed enough to spoil it.

“Colour,” he told the apprentice, who had been watching the doorway.

The boy turned back too late.

Duan sighed.

The workshop had resumed its ordinary complaints before Su Fan crossed the yard.

***

Ah-Du followed him as far as the gate.

“I could finish the bellows tomorrow.”

“You said that yesterday.”

“It remains a sound proposal.”

Su Fan looked back at the frame waiting inside.

The boy sighed, then produced a short cord with a better knot than the one holding the small parcel at the side of Su Fan's pack.

“For that.”

“Did you make it?”

“I improved it.”

“Whose was it?”

“Mine. You are permitted to be grateful without investigating.”

Su Fan let him change the fastening.

The new knot was useful. He said so.

Ah-Du tugged it once more, satisfied that the parcel would not fall off merely because the road failed to admire his work.

“Write about the guards,” he said. “And the swords.”

“Duan wants fitting prices.”

“He has no sense of scale.”

From inside the workshop, Duan called the boy's name.

Ah-Du made a face, squeezed Su Fan's arm and ran back before the second call could become a task less interesting than the bellows.

***

At the kitchen, Auntie Lu added food to the parcel Mother Wei had already packed.

Deng suggested there was a limit to what one man could carry.

She looked at Su Fan.

“He cultivates.”

“That doesn't make his bag larger.”

“It makes him less entitled to complain.”

Su Fan accepted the parcel.

He had not complained. He could see this would make no difference to the argument, which appeared to have begun before he arrived and would probably continue after he left.

Auntie Lu checked the wrapping herself.

“Eat the soft things first.”

“Yes.”

“And share before you discover that half of it has gone bad through your heroic refusal to be hungry.”

Deng nodded at that part.

Old Pock gave him advice about ferries that began sensibly and ended with the name of a woman he should avoid insulting in Siltbridge.

Su Fan wrote the name down because it seemed safer than asking what had happened.

“Did you insult her?” Deng asked.

“I was misunderstood.”

“By how many people?”

Pock said the question showed a narrow interest in an old event and returned to the ferries.

Su Fan kept the useful part of both accounts.

***

Bao Shun waved from the doorway of his shop.

He was fitting a small compartment into a customer's travelling chest. The arrangement let him brace the work without asking the damaged hand to do what it could no longer do reliably.

“Bring back measurements,” he called.

“Of what?”

“Anything people complain about storing.”

Bao Mei was negotiating a signboard price nearby. She interrupted only long enough to tell Su Fan not to let rain ruin the scabbard mark.

The customer tried to use the pause to reopen an amount they had apparently already agreed.

She turned straight back to him.

“No. That was the price without the second line.”

Su Fan left her to it.

At the library, Zhen Su had opened the doors. A boy stood outside with a borrowed book wrapped so thoroughly that returning it required help. She asked whether he had wrapped it before or after leaving it in the rain.

“Before.”

“Good. Then we will discover whether you tied it better than you needed to.”

The quarry settlement continued working around the farewells.

That was how Su Fan had hoped to leave it.

***

He checked the door of his room once before taking the upper path.

The latch held. The garlic-chive seeds Mother Wei had given him were no longer a promise inside a packet; the small planting by the doorstep had begun to make use of the light. Someone would water it while he was away because he had asked, not because his absence automatically assigned the work to a person who cared about him.

He put the key away.

There were objects inside the room he could not carry and papers he had chosen to leave dry in the library's keeping. None required him to take one last inventory before walking on.

Above the lane, the road divided around the shoulder of the quarry.

Tan Wei waited at the top.

He carried no travelling pack.

Su Fan had known he would not. Still, seeing the empty hands made the choice real.

***

“The cooperative accepted me,” Tan Wei said.

“Good.”

“Three days at the gates. Two teaching ordinary ferry work. Han says I can rebuild the fourth stage without a permanent impression, but it will take time.”

“Good.”

“I may go elsewhere after that.”

“Good.”

“You are becoming a dull conversationalist.”

Su Fan laughed.

His friend held out a folded page.

“What is it?”

“Directions to the carrier's office. You will ignore two helpful strangers and use these.”

“I have been to Siltbridge.”

“You got lost behind the dye market.”

“Once.”

“Long enough to matter.”

The page was written in Tan Wei's careful hand. It gave landmarks a stranger could actually find rather than distances measured from places only the writer knew.

Su Fan read it before putting it away.

Tan Wei watched, pleased and pretending not to be.

“You could have given me those earlier.”

“You might have improved them.”

“I am trying to stop doing that.”

“I know. This is a useful test.”

***

They stood where the road divided.

Below them, the Low Gate's controlled outflow shone between the marsh reeds. Farther east, water crossed ground where their old homes had stood.

The new channel was not beautiful in the way the stories already travelling north would probably make it. It was brown, necessary and bordered by places where the bank still needed work. A crew moved along one edge with tools on their shoulders.

Tan Wei looked beyond it.

“I still miss the rock.”

Their childhood place beside the river had disappeared in the flood.

Su Fan nodded.

He did not suggest finding another one.

They had sat there when the mountain seemed to contain every possible future. They had argued about entering it, about leaving it, about whether wanting something badly made the price more bearable.

Neither had known enough then to imagine this particular road.

After a while Tan Wei put a hand on his shoulder.

“Write about something other than cultivation.”

“What?”

“Bad food. People you dislike. Something foolish you did.”

“That sounds like a long letter.”

“I'll make time.”

***

Su Fan looked at the faint marks above his friend's wrist.

Tan Wei saw the glance and drew the sleeve back, not hiding them and not offering a demonstration.

“I can manage the gate work they hired me for,” he said.

“I didn't ask.”

“You were about to ask with your face.”

Su Fan looked down the road.

“I wanted to know whether you're happy.”

“Sometimes. Are you?”

“Sometimes.”

“Then perhaps we have not become entirely different creatures.”

They laughed, and the familiar sound made leaving harder for a moment rather than easier.

Tan Wei embraced him carefully around the places that were still tender. Su Fan held him without making a promise to return as a greater man who could settle the losses both of them carried.

When they separated, his friend took the path back toward the cooperative's work.

Su Fan watched him go only as far as the first turn.

Then he took the other road.

***

Sun Lian waited beside the hired cart.

The rented flatboat would meet them beyond the damaged lower landing. She had paid for it under a contract specifying the route, the load, the cancellation terms and which party supplied the rope.

Ah-Du had described the document as longer than the boat.

She had taken that as praise.

Su Fan put his pack beside the cargo and sat with Sun Lian on his left, where her voice would reach his better ear without requiring him to turn his whole body.

She looked at the food tied to the outside.

“Are we carrying supplies for the town?”

“Only a small part of it.”

“Good. I have not hired enough boat for the whole kitchen.”

The mule turned its head toward the nearest parcel.

Su Fan moved it out of reach.

“He has been fed,” Sun Lian said.

“He appears unconvinced.”

“He is easily unconvinced when someone is carrying buns.”

They rearranged the food above the tools instead of beside them. One of Duan’s carefully wrapped fittings had already made a square impression in the soft edge of a bun. Su Fan ate that one rather than let it spend the journey proving that the packing had been wrong.

Sun Lian held out her hand.

He gave her half.

“What are you doing in the city first?” he asked.

“Delivering drawings. Asking about timber. Finding out which of three promises was made by someone who remembers making it.”

“And after that?”

“After that I will know more than I do now.”

He nodded and took out Tan Wei’s directions, checking where the carrier’s office lay in relation to the places she named.

Their errands did not all lead to the same street. That was ordinary. They agreed where to meet again rather than make one person’s work the route the other must follow.

Sun Lian brushed the last crumbs from her palm.

“Ready?”

Su Fan looked up the path once more, then put the directions inside the dry wrapper.

“Yes.”

She checked the load once more and clicked her tongue at the mule.

The cart moved.

***

For a while the road followed the river.

They passed the exposed bones beneath the ruined shrine, now marked on the new survey. A fisherman stood among the ribs with a lantern-eel basket. He raised a hand as they went by.

Su Fan raised his own.

He still did not know enough about the bones to turn them into a useful story. They had been there while people quarrelled over gates, wages and a place to put an anvil. They remained while those quarrels changed.

Sun Lian asked him to watch the rear strap as the cart crossed a rough patch.

He did.

At the first rise, he looked back.

He could see the workshop smoke. The library roof. A strip of red cloth still tied above the storehouse from Auntie Lu's wedding.

He could not see everyone he loved from there.

He would have to leave anyway.

***

At the toll post, the keeper examined their papers.

“Cultivation?” he asked Su Fan.

“Eighth-stage Qi Refinement.”

“Affiliation?”

“None.”

The keeper looked up, then down at the regional notice.

A brief pause. A line entered in the register.

“Work?”

“Escort applicant. Smith's assistant.”

“Those are different rates.”

“Charge the lower one until somebody hires me.”

The keeper snorted and named a sum.

Su Fan paid.

There was no dark bowl on the table. No elder waiting to tell him whose name he deserved to carry. There was a clerk who wanted the correct fee and another cart behind them whose driver wanted this one to move.

Sun Lian collected the papers before the wind lifted a corner from the keeper's hand.

The barrier rose.

***

Beyond it, the road widened.

Wagons moved beneath unfamiliar banners. Two cultivators argued over a broken wheel while an ordinary teamster told them both to get out of the way. A woman selling hot food called the price over the traffic and seemed personally offended by every traveller who already carried breakfast.

Su Fan felt the weight of Auntie Lu's parcel against his boot.

For once, he had an adequate answer to the food seller's accusation.

Sun Lian handed him the reins so she could check a cargo strap.

He took them.

The mule stopped to crop grass.

Su Fan clicked his tongue as she had.

The mule ignored him.

Behind them, Sun Lian began to laugh.

He tried again, less confidently, and the cart rolled forward into the traffic of the wider road.

chapters.title: The Carrier’s Yard
chapters.text:
By the time Su Fan learned to persuade the mule forward, the animal was no longer his responsibility.

The driver took back the reins at a turning where the road sank between two banks of reed. He clicked his tongue once. The mule walked as though it had never entertained a different opinion. Sun Lian, who had been watching the exchange from the cart bed, declined to explain the difference.

"It was the tongue," Su Fan said.

"Naturally."

"I used my tongue."

"Perhaps yours was impolite."

The driver was called Ke, and he had agreed to take them to the lower landing, not a step beyond it. His price included the mule, the cart and a canvas sheet in rain. It did not include helping with river freight, and he made that distinction before they could ask him to lift so much as a hinge. Su Fan thought the warning unnecessary until he saw the landing.

Six boats lay against a floating pier. Two were unloading baskets of dried mushrooms under the supervision of a man whose entire job appeared to be deciding that every basket belonged somewhere else. One boat had a broken steering yoke. A porter on the pier was running after a rolling barrel while another shouted that the barrel was empty and therefore not worth dying for.

Sun Lian examined the flatboat whose hire she had arranged. It had a wide floor and a narrow covered cabin. The woman at its stern showed her a rope, rubbed two fingers together and named an additional charge.

"The document includes stern and bow lines," Sun Lian said.

"Use of them. Not new rope."

"It says supplied by owner."

"It says lines by owner. That could mean my father's lines. He owns a shop."

Sun Lian untied the roll containing her copy and held it so the woman could read the exact words. The boatwoman squinted. The rope discussion might have continued indefinitely, except that a third woman carrying a bucket came down the pier and asked why her sister was attempting to sell rope that had been included in yesterday's inventory.

"I hadn't sold it," the boatwoman said. "I was discussing its value."

"Discuss it while we load, then."

The sister took the bucket into the cabin. Sun Lian repacked her document with the satisfaction of someone whose most valuable possession had once again been a sentence written clearly enough to survive its owner's imagination.

Su Fan took the tool bundle from Ke's cart. A broad iron hinge, wrapped in oiled cloth, threatened to slip from its tie. He put it down before it could injure his foot and changed the knot. Ke watched without offering help.

"You will not make money carrying a pack like that," he observed.

"I hope to carry someone else's."

"Then make them supply the rope."

Ke had been listening after all.

***

The flatboat took them past the damaged lower landing and into the city on a rising tide. Stone warehouses leaned over the water, their doors built at heights suited to different seasons. A pale line on the wall marked an old flood. Above that, three more lines recorded floods that had apparently been worth remembering in their own right.

Su Fan sat on a folded canvas beside the tools. The motion was pleasant until a sharper current turned the boat and left him looking the wrong way for a shouted instruction. He heard the boatwoman only when Sun Lian touched his left wrist and pointed to the low rail. He shifted the iron bundle clear of it.

"Thank you," he said.

"She asked twice."

"I heard neither clearly."

"I noticed."

Sun Lian did not ask him to perform a hearing exercise on a crowded boat. She checked that the cargo stayed clear of the rail and returned to her drawings. One sheet showed a channel-frame joint with three alternative plates. The fourth option had been crossed out. She had written beside it that the timber supplier's dimensions were not to be trusted until measured.

Su Fan looked at the crosses for a moment. He had seen that particular expression of Sun Lian's opinion often enough to know not to interrupt.

They landed before noon. The porters charged by load and argued by family resemblance. Su Fan paid to move his own bundle across the crowded quay rather than submit to a claim that the staircase was a private service. Sun Lian employed one porter for the timber samples. She made him read the destination aloud and counted the samples before giving him the receipt.

"Will you need me at the timber market?" Su Fan asked.

"Not today. I need two buyers to disagree with each other without finding a common enemy. You are pleasant enough to become one."

"I had intended to apply for work."

"Then we'll both have something worth reporting at supper."

They chose a meeting place by a public well where a painted fish had been nailed over the water tally. Sun Lian confirmed the hour, then went uphill with her drawings. He watched until a wagon hid her from sight. Their separate errands felt stranger in the busy city than they had on the road. There, agreement had been as simple as who held the reins. Here, each turn led somewhere that could take a whole day to explain.

He unfolded Tan Wei's directions.

The first landmark was a blue dye shop with a missing corner of its sign. Two blue dye shops stood within sight. The first had every corner. The second had a corner missing, though it was not the corner his friend had drawn.

Su Fan took the second turning. Half a street later he found a third blue dye shop. Its sign matched the drawing exactly.

He stood in front of it, reread the page and laughed so abruptly that a woman selling thread glanced at him.

"Someone give you good news?" she asked.

"Someone prevented me from being lost."

"That would be expensive news here."

She directed him past the washermen's bridge without asking payment. When he thanked her, she suggested he buy thread another time. It sounded fair.

***

Min Yao was outside a records shop with a stack of wrapped papers balanced against her hip. Jin stood beside her holding a wooden fish by its tail. The fish had been painted a green that did not exist in any river Su Fan knew.

"You came," Min Yao said.

"Tan Wei described the third dye shop."

"He described it to me too. I told him people get lost at the first one. He said you would need the whole explanation."

Jin offered the fish for inspection. It had hinged jaws. When the child pressed its back, its mouth opened on a tiny wooden peg.

"It eats debt notices," Jin told him.

"That must save your mother work."

"She says it must learn to eat the bills first."

Min Yao did not deny the accusation. She had an appointment across town to review copying fees. Su Fan would have liked an afternoon talking about the new library at the quarry and the dates in his practice notes. Instead she gave him a hurried invitation for the following day, wrote an address on the back of his direction sheet and asked whether he could bring a jar back from the spice seller if he passed that way.

"What jar?"

"The one he claims to have kept for me. He will try to sell you two smaller ones. Ask him whether the large one still has the chip beneath the rim."

"What if it does?"

"Then you can buy it."

"What if it doesn't?"

"Then he has sold mine already, and you should not pay for his disappointment."

Jin made the fish bite Su Fan's finger. Its wooden jaws were incapable of doing damage, but the boy looked pleased with the result.

"Are you staying at our house?" he asked.

"I haven't found a room."

"We have a little cupboard."

"Jin," his mother said, "that's where you keep the fish."

"I can keep the fish somewhere else."

Su Fan thanked him for the offer and declined the cupboard. Min Yao gave him the name of a boarding house whose stairs were safe and whose landlady had a reputation for charging exactly the price on the door. The address was not in the direction of the carrier's yard, and Jin explained that this was what happened when people refused generous fish accommodation.

They parted at the records shop. Min Yao went back inside to argue for a paper rate that would let the quarry library buy more than blank covers. Jin followed, carrying his fish like a very small but necessary witness.

Su Fan continued through streets built for people who knew when deliveries happened. Barrows occupied the narrowest paths. A cook tipped water from a window and shouted a warning just in time for him to move. He found the spice jar, identified the chip and paid the amount Min Yao had written down. Carrying someone else's purchase made the city feel less like an examination.

The carrier's yard lay beyond a line of kiln sheds. Its painted sign showed three hearths and a wheel. Beneath it, in smaller characters, someone had added: DRIVERS PAID ONLY WHEN THEY RETURN THE HORSES.

A boy polishing harness buckles said the line was older than the current owner.

"Does it work?" Su Fan asked.

"Not on horses who don't read."

***

Inside, workers were arguing over a wagon axle. An older woman sat at a desk raised high enough to overlook the loading floor. She was making marks in a ledger while listening to three conversations without apparently granting any of them her whole attention.

Near the axle, a young tally worker had drawn a grid in chalk. She wore her hair tied under a red strip of cloth and kept a short pencil behind one ear. A porter stepped across the grid and she made him step back to look at the square he had erased.

"Put that number back," she said.

"I don't know what it was."

"Then you know why I told you not to walk on it."

Su Fan waited until the wagon's foreman called for a wedge. A boy brought a crooked one. The foreman tried to slide it under a wheel, discovered it did not fit and accused the floor of being built incorrectly. Su Fan could see that the axle itself stood at an angle; the wagon had been lifted unevenly so the wheel would not settle straight.

He did not touch it.

"Your left jack is taller," he said.

The foreman looked at him as if the words had arrived from the roof.

"What?"

"The wood block beneath the left jack. It has a second shaving."

"We know that. The wheel is stuck."

"If you lower that side a finger's width, the pin may align."

"And if it falls?"

"Then someone will have been foolish to follow advice from a stranger without checking it."

The tally worker looked up. The foreman said several things unsuitable for a patient craftsman and called for the older woman.

She descended from her platform with the ledger still open.

"Which of you is the stranger?" she asked.

"I am," Su Fan said.

"An admirable admission. Name?"

He gave it, explained the letter from Hua Jun and held out the envelope. The woman's eyes moved across the writing while the yard continued around her. One driver shouted for water. A mule lifted its hind leg at a bucket. The foreman tapped his foot beside the axle.

"I'm Ma Qiao," she said. "That is a letter of introduction. It isn't a contract."

"I understand."

"Most people who bring such letters understand until I tell them no."

She crouched beside the wagon, glanced at the block and sent the foreman for a narrower wedge. When he returned, she instructed him to lower the jack a fraction. Su Fan stood out of the line of strain. The wagon shifted, held, then settled onto its wheel with a clack.

The foreman rotated the wheel once. It turned freely.

"That's one problem," Ma Qiao said. "There may be another."

She offered Su Fan the retaining pin from the other side. It was bent so slightly that he felt the deviation before he could see it. He set it on a flat iron bar and rolled it.

"It has been forced into a hole made too tight," he said. "Or struck while the wheel was under load. It isn't safe to straighten and reuse until the housing is checked."

"What would you do?"

"Measure the housing. Compare the pin to the new stock. If the housing is oval, the pin isn't the first repair."

Ma Qiao nodded, but she was not looking impressed. She was looking at the wagon.

"Rie, record that. New pin, housing inspection. And keep the chalk where feet cannot vote on the numbers."

The young tally worker moved the grid to a board.

"I asked for a board yesterday," she said.

"And today you have one," Ma Qiao replied.

"After losing three numbers."

"Write that too."

***

Ma Qiao's office contained maps, invoices and a small kettle resting on an iron stand. The kettle had been fitted with a wire handle that would burn anyone who grabbed it carelessly. Su Fan wanted to correct it. He left it alone.

"Eighth-stage?" Ma Qiao asked, reading his notice.

"Yes."

"No sect protection. Permission to practise, not to teach your form for payment. Fine. We aren't hiring teachers."

She put the notice beside Hua Jun's letter. The older body-refiner had written two sentences of praise, one about sensible hands and the other about being less sensible with questions. Ma Qiao seemed amused by the second.

"Why do you want escort work?"

"I need wages. I can handle a load, repair some fittings and defend people if required. I've worked under pressure."

"People who say that last part generally mean they survived something they'd rather never repeat. What sort of pressure?"

He told her about the Low Gate without turning the account into a performance. He named the losses, the inquiry and the conditions on his travel notice. He did not tell her every person involved had been wrong except him.

"I have a weakness you should know," he added.

"Only one?"

"My right-side hearing is damaged. It affects locating sound."

Ma Qiao set down her brush.

"Does it affect hearing orders?"

"If you're on my left, I can usually hear you. If you're on my right in a crowded place, I may hear the words without knowing they're directed at me."

"That is not a small weakness on a road."

"No."

For a moment she studied him with the expression of someone calculating what another person's mistake would cost an entire payroll.

"There is a trial tomorrow," she said. "Equipment, signalling, judgement. You won't be tested only on what your own body can do."

"What position?"

"The position we need filled, not the one you imagined when you set out. We have guards. We need people who keep the guards from having to rescue a wagon from stupidity."

He considered that. It was not an insult. It was also not an offer.

"What time?"

She told him to arrive at first bell after dawn and bring his blade sheathed, his papers and shoes in which he could walk all day. She made no promise about wages.

On the way out he passed the tally worker transferring numbers to her board. Rie examined his clean hands and then the smear of iron on one thumb.

"Did Ma Qiao hire you?"

"She told me to return."

"That means she hasn't hired you."

"I noticed."

"Good. Noticing is part of this work."

***

He took the spice jar to Min Yao's address, left it with the neighbour because she was still at work, and found the boarding house before dark. The landlady showed him the room, its narrow window and the basin he must empty himself. The stairs did not creak under his weight. He paid for two nights, not a week.

At the well with the painted fish, Sun Lian arrived carrying a different set of documents from those she had taken uphill. Her face suggested at least one person had spent too long assuring her that a measurement was close enough.

"How was the yard?" she asked.

"I found a problem on a wagon. A woman found two more. I have a trial."

"That sounds like work."

"It isn't work until they pay me."

"Excellent. I see the city has educated you quickly."

He bought them a bowl of noodles each. She ate hers while describing the timber samples and the buyer who wanted all of a carpenter's assurances without paying for a carpenter's opinion. Her next meeting was early, and she would not be available to watch his trial. He had not meant to ask, though for one moment he discovered that he would have liked her there.

He told her where he was staying. They agreed on the well as a meeting place if they could not find each other, and on written notes at the boarding house otherwise. She approved of the arrangement, which gave her no obligation to spend the next day walking after him.

Later, he passed the yard again on his way to bed. A chalkboard stood just inside the gate. Five trial names had been written in columns. His appeared last, beside a number and the words LOAD, SIGNAL, JUDGEMENT.

Someone had corrected the spelling of a candidate's name. Beneath the list Rie had drawn a line and written: DO NOT CHANGE THE ORDER WITHOUT TELLING ME.

Su Fan studied the board until he could remember the number, then went home to sleep.

chapters.title: The Test He Failed
chapters.text:
The first candidate arrived before the gate opened and immediately tried to persuade the gatekeeper that punctuality ought to count toward the test.

"It does," the gatekeeper said. "Against you if you keep me here explaining it."

Su Fan was the fourth to arrive. He had eaten at the boarding house and walked the length of the market with his sword wrapped and his travel notice inside his coat. In the courtyard, three wagons stood in a row. None bore a name or merchant's mark. The horses had been led out, and the wheels rested on blocks. Rie had hung a set of wooden numbered tags from a rope beneath the eaves.

She checked the applicants against her board and gave each a tag. Su Fan received the fifth, although there were only four of them.

"There was another," she said when he looked at the gap. "He withdrew because he heard we test figures. I tried to explain that a figure does not usually attack people. He withdrew anyway."

Ma Qiao arrived carrying a kettle and a roll of paper. She handed the kettle to Rie and the paper to a scarred man whose belt held more tools than weapons. His name was Meng Rui, the convoy deputy. The order of these gifts made clear which job could be trusted to whom.

"The tests are in three parts," Ma Qiao said. "At the end of each you'll know something you didn't know this morning. If that makes you less willing to take the road, say so before I buy your food."

A tall applicant with a wind-thread token at her belt raised her hand.

"Is there a speed ranking?"

"For the loading task, yes. For the signal task, a man once won a speed ranking and rode into a ditch. We no longer award that ribbon."

The woman laughed with the rest. Her name, Su Fan learned, was Wei Fen. She had tied her sleeves short and tucked her hair under a grey travelling cap. She moved as if she knew exactly where the ground would be when she stepped onto it.

They were directed to the wagons. The first contained grain sacks and wooden practice boxes. The second held iron rods of unequal lengths. The third appeared empty except for three planks and a box of damaged fasteners.

"Move the sacks to the second wagon," Meng Rui said. "Keep the weights in the marked order. Tell us before you move anything that doesn't belong."

An applicant named Cao Ying began lifting immediately. Su Fan counted the sack marks and compared them to the board. He found that two sacks numbered six, but the second six was shorter and heavier. Rie watched him turn its label and said nothing.

"These aren't the same load," he said.

"Should they be?" Meng Rui asked.

"The board lists grain by dry weight. This may be damp. We need its actual weight."

"Then weigh it."

A scale stood beside the shed. Cao Ying called the delay pointless; both sacks could plainly be carried by one strong person. Su Fan and Wei Fen lifted the suspect sack onto the scale. It weighed enough more than its label to change the wagon's intended balance. They opened a seam under Meng Rui's supervision and found stones wrapped in rag.

"Someone sabotaged the grain," Cao Ying said.

"Someone built a test," Rie replied. "Those are the stones we use to keep the scale on its marks. Please don't accuse my stones of politics."

They adjusted the load order. Su Fan noticed a wedge beside the wheel whose grain ran crosswise through its narrow end. He set it aside, explained the split risk and chose one made of sounder stock.
