He might have gained time by accepting it. A wedge that shattered under a loaded wagon would have cost rather more.

At the end of the first test, Meng Rui recorded their times and checked the marks. Wei Fen had finished before Su Fan by enough time to eat a bun. Cao Ying had been fastest with the lifting and had placed both sacks marked six at the same end.

The missing fifth applicant would never know whether he could have beaten any of them.

***

The second test involved a road laid out on the yard floor with stakes and coloured cord. A cart frame stood at its centre, one wheel removed. A hanging bell waited behind a canvas screen.

"You will escort this frame from one end to the other," Meng Rui said. "On a real road there are drivers, guards, children, animals and people who become important only when something goes wrong. Listen for the warnings."

Su Fan felt the first tightening in his chest. He had told Ma Qiao about his hearing. The test had not been designed to spare it. He could have protested, but a caravan would not design a road to spare it either.

Wei Fen volunteered first. She moved with one hand resting loosely beside her sword, eyes travelling from the markers to the men standing behind them. The bell sounded on her left. She turned before the second stroke, saw the canvas move and called the colour of the marker nearest the sound. Next a wooden block fell from a rope at the far end. She stepped into its path, judged the distance and nudged the cart frame aside. Her movement was quick but not wasteful.

A third signal came as two sharp clicks from a clapper inside a closed bucket. Wei Fen stopped the frame, waited for Meng Rui to raise a flag and pointed correctly to the source. The guard watching the far marker wrote something down with an expression of approval.

Cao Ying did the test at a run. His cart crossed the course faster than Wei Fen's. He missed a small blue marker and received a chalk line across his sleeve for it. The line represented a person who had not been given the room to step aside.

When Su Fan's turn came, he set himself on the cart's left side. Meng Rui told him to change sides, as the route sheet required alternating positions. He obeyed.

The first bell sounded somewhere to his left. He heard it clearly enough to turn. The second came from behind the canvas on his right. He heard the sound but not its direction. The cart frame pulled against his hand as the assistant on the other side continued walking. Su Fan felt the impulse to answer with speed. Instead he stopped and looked for the raised flag. None was visible.

"Warning!" he called, too late to tell anyone where.

A sand-filled practice sack struck the cart frame. It tipped toward a blue marker. Su Fan planted his foot and caught the frame with his shoulder. He could hold it. He could not claim he had protected the marker. One of the assistants dragged the blue cloth out from beneath the wheel.

"A child, on this course," Meng Rui said.

Su Fan released the frame carefully. His hands were steady. That was part of the humiliation: the body he had trained answered well to the problem he had noticed and far too late to the one that mattered.

"Continue," Ma Qiao said.

He continued. The third clapper sounded close on the right. This time he saw a rope twitch before the sound reached him and stopped the frame in time. The marker remained upright. He did not pretend the success had repaired the earlier failure.

At the end, he explained what he had seen. Rie pointed to a mark on the board representing a lost life that existed only as blue cloth, then wrote the result without expression.

"Would a line of sight help?" Su Fan asked.

"Sometimes," Meng Rui said. "A road is not always generous with sight."

"If the person making the warning raised a visible arm—"

"You cannot require everyone you rescue to learn your arm signal."

"No. But a crew can agree on one."

Meng Rui nodded toward Ma Qiao. "That part is hers to decide."

***

The third task was not called combat. It was described as intervention, which made the applicants suspicious.

A wooden cage containing four earthen jars had to be lowered from a platform. The line passed through a pulley and around a fixed post. Two assistants stood at the ropes. Applicants were to inspect the equipment, propose a safe procedure and intervene if the assistants made a mistake.

Wei Fen approached the pulley first. She asked whether the jars contained water. They did. She asked if the platform was certified to take the load. It was. She examined the knot and found a frayed strand near the post. She replaced that length with the spare rope supplied in the yard. Before lowering the cage she held two fingers in the air and breathed slowly through them.

For a brief moment the frayed tail of the discarded rope trembled without any visible wind. Her inherited wind-thread art detected motion across the short distance between her hand and the pulley. She did not try to suspend the load by wind; the rope and two assistants did that work. When one assistant released early, Wei Fen saw the changed tension and called a stop.

"Good," Ma Qiao said.

Wei Fen wiped sweat from her lip. The working was modest, yet it had cost her attention.

Su Fan inspected the pulley housing. A pin sat proud of its socket. He could feel a narrow ridge where metal had rubbed on metal. He explained why the cage might twist under load and asked for a brace before moving it. One assistant retrieved the brace. The other kept holding the rope.

"Now?" Meng Rui asked.

"Not yet. Check the lower block."

The assistant pulled the rope. The cage rose an inch and rotated toward the post. Su Fan caught the movement with the brace rather than his palm. The weight pressed down the wood and into the ground. He could feel the change through his stance. His breath settled; the eighth circuit carried the effort smoothly through his body instead of wasting it in shoulders clenched too soon. For several strokes of the heart, he stood in the right place and did the right work.

Then a shout came from the right, behind him. He turned the wrong way. The cage grazed the brace and one jar broke against another. Water spilled into the dust.

There was no attack. The shout had been part of the test, but the damaged jar was real.

"You had the load," Meng Rui said.

"Until I didn't."

"What would you have done on the road?"

"Asked the rope holder to stop before I turned. Or arranged a second watcher where I can't see."

"You didn't do that."

"No."

He wrote the observation on the evaluation sheet in his own hand. Ma Qiao gave him an opportunity to cross out the word failed and replace it with incomplete. He left it. Incomplete would have suggested the cage was still descending, unbroken.

Wei Fen came to examine the pulley after her own test had been recorded. She was reaching past it when the sharp edge of a loose retaining pin caught her sleeve. It tore a clean line through the fabric.

"I checked the rope," she said, looking offended by the modest damage. "I did not check the pin."

"The pin is bent," Su Fan said.

"I can see that now."

He offered her a small needle from his travelling repair packet. She took it but declined his suggestion that the entire sleeve needed replacing. She folded the edge and made three practical stitches while standing.

"That will hold until supper," she said.

"And after?"

"After supper I will sew it properly. Do you always worry about the future of sleeves?"

"Only sleeves that are near bent pins."

"Then you must live an anxious life."

They shared the sort of laughter that follows a task neither person has performed perfectly. When Wei Fen returned the needle, she placed it into his left hand rather than tossing it toward his right.

***

Ma Qiao interviewed them separately. Cao Ying left with a temporary labour ticket and an invitation to return if he wanted to improve his reckoning. Wei Fen emerged with a folded contract and an expression that made it clear she had not been offered every term she wanted.

Su Fan sat on a stool in the passage until Rie called him in.

Ma Qiao had drawn three columns. In the first were his strengths: load balance, tool inspection, willingness to stop a task with uncertain equipment. In the second were risks: delayed response to sound from his right, failure under a turning warning, limited road experience. The third was empty.

"What belongs here?" she asked.

"Work that doesn't depend on the risks being invisible."

"More specific."

"Rear wagon. A paired watcher. Loading and inspection when the wagons stop. Written order of checks. Someone else directs fighting and emergency movement."

"You understand that's not what a front escort earns?"

"Yes."

"And you may be carrying iron while someone with half your stage tells you where to put it."

"Duan has done that for years."

Ma Qiao opened a drawer and produced the rates. Lead guard, moving guard, rear-load watch, mechanic's assistant and general porter. The lowest three overlapped in duties; the difference was who was obliged to notice damage before it reached the owner.

"I can offer rear-load watch under probation," she said. "You inspect with Rie, report to Meng Rui, and take tactical orders from Wei Fen if trouble comes. You don't improvise a different route because you believe your eyes are better than our records. For the first two days you take a paired shift."

He read the rate twice. It was lower than he had imagined on the journey and more than he had earned on some long workshop days. Food was provided while moving. Lodging during a delay was shared unless an injury required isolation. Deductions could be made for damage caused by negligence, but only after a written account and with a stated ceiling.

"What if the route becomes unsafe?"

"You tell us. You do not become the route."

He wanted to ask whether she knew of the Low Gate. He did not. She had enough information to run her business without becoming a reader of his past.

"Why provisional?" he asked.

"Because the wagons don't leave until we know exactly what they're carrying. And because you haven't yet worked with Rie or Wei Fen. A recommendation is not a marriage. You can still decline."

She pushed the sheet toward him but did not ask for his thumbprint. Acceptance belonged to the departure briefing.

***

That evening Su Fan watched porters loading the last grain wagon by the light of three lamps. None appeared to possess a remarkable cultivation method. A short woman could count twenty sacks while arguing about the price of soup. A man with a damaged knee worked from a stool and tied excellent knots. They trusted the signals they had made together over years, and nobody tested their strength against a sword.

At the boarding house he wrote a letter to Tan Wei. He began by describing the bell test. The second sentence made it sound as if he had nearly killed somebody. The third corrected it: a cloth marker had fallen, and it would have meant danger if there had been a child where the cloth lay. He did not know whether the distinction made the story less or more shameful.

He crossed out the entire paragraph. Tan Wei had asked for ordinary news. Su Fan wrote instead about three dye shops, Jin's wooden fish and an innkeeper who required tenants to empty their own basins. Then he returned to the trial without decoration.

He hadn't sent the letter by bedtime.

His right ear rang faintly when he lay with that side against the pillow. He turned onto his left, which made the street sounds louder and his shoulder less comfortable. For a while he lay awake, counting the intervals between cart wheels outside.

He had wanted an escort job partly because it would let him move onward without asking anyone to carry him. Ma Qiao had offered something less flattering and perhaps more useful: to be one person in a company whose survival required that he be known accurately.

The folded offer lay beside his unsealed letter. In the morning, he would take it to Rie and learn whether he could do the work as written. Tonight, it was only a promise waiting to be accepted.

chapters.title: Her Own Contract
chapters.text:
The timber seller had put the best boards where the morning sun would find them.

Sun Lian noticed because the man moved a customer away from the shadowed pile every time she tried to examine it. The boards in the sun had been planed clean and stacked with narrow air gaps. The ones behind the counting shed wore the same chalk mark, but moisture had darkened the ends beneath the paint.

"All one lot," the seller said. "Cut from the same stand. You won't find stronger northern pine below the bridge."

"Then I can inspect the boards below the bridge as well."

"Those are for another order."

"So this isn't one lot."

He decided she had misunderstood him, which gave her time to look at the exposed end of a board leaning against a post. It had been sawn recently enough that resin was still collecting at the cut. A finger pushed against the wood left a faint mark. Good timber might be green; being green did not make it rotten. What troubled her was a seller asking seasoned-wood prices for a piece that would twist as it dried, while assuring buyers he had removed every cause of twisting.

The man recognized her name when she gave it for a quotation. His smile widened.

"Honest Measure. I heard about your boat. A fine vessel. Terrible luck."

She watched him decide how much sympathy to sell next.

"The boat went to a grain merchant," she said. "If you need the new owner's name, the auction record is public."

"You must be looking for work after a loss like that. I can offer you an arrangement. We need a reinforcement crew at the north sluice. Three days, perhaps four. You know how to put earth into a beam."

"I know when a beam has no business asking earth to save it."

He took that for bargaining. She let him describe the job. The north sluice had developed a lateral lean. Its timber struts were to be replaced while water continued through the structure. The seller would supply greenwood at a discount and, if her earth channels were as celebrated as people said, she could make the supports carry until the new timber settled.

He said celebrated in a tone that made clear he had invented the celebration himself.

"What is the water head?" she asked.

He didn't know.

"What is the foundation bearing?"

He told her his foreman could answer.

"Is there an isolation gate?"

"It's inconvenient to close."

She returned his quotation slate without placing her mark on it.

"My channels are under medical restriction. I will measure and recommend repairs. I won't put my own body where an unmeasured beam should go."

"Some people would call that lack of confidence."

"Those people are welcome to stand under your beam."

A boy carrying two boards looked down very quickly to hide a smile. The seller looked at the boy as though considering whether laughter could be deducted from wages.

Sun Lian went to the counting shed and bought a short, dry offcut from the assistant there. She needed it for a comparison later. The assistant gave her a receipt without inquiring after her boat.

That was the most courteous transaction she had completed all morning.

***

By noon she had three quotations and no contract. One carpenter offered a well-priced partnership provided she signed for every failed joint. A timber factor promised a particularly handsome fee if she allowed her name to appear on repairs she would never inspect. The third seller had straight stock at a sensible price and no money to pay anyone until the end of the month.

Sun Lian ate a hard pear on the steps of the rope market and began sorting the offers into useful information and invitations to become somebody else's guarantee.

A woman in an ink-spotted jacket approached carrying a shallow wooden case. She stopped at the third step and looked at the measuring cord wound around Sun Lian's wrist.

"Are you the surveyor who declined Bo Lin's sluice?"

"I declined Bo Lin's price for being crushed. The job may be worth considering when he has a design."

"He said you were difficult."

"Did he have a particular measurement in mind?"

The woman set down the case. Her name was Yan Mei, clerk to a small association responsible for culverts on the northern carriage route. There were six households and two workshops behind the association's funds, she explained, not a large public office with room for three different accounts of the same expense.

She lifted the lid. Inside lay a curved timber former, two brass pins and a folded sheet covered in figures. The former had once held the profile of a small drainage arch. A split ran along its back, and one edge was polished by contact that ought to have fallen elsewhere.

"One of our culverts is leaking through the sidewall," Yan Mei said. "We can pay for someone to determine whether it needs a new lining or merely a new mouth. Our committee would prefer the second answer."

"You would prefer it cheaper."

"Yes. That is why we are looking for a person who can show us when cheaper will cost more."

Sun Lian put down the pear core and asked where the former had been used.

"At the south face of the Narrowbank crossing. Two days beyond the north gate if the road is passable. The culvert takes a tributary under the carriage road. Our carpenter made this from his first measurements. He made another after the spring rain. They disagree."

Sun Lian held the former against the step. She placed the brass pins in the two worn holes, stretched her cord between them and measured the drop. The timber had bowed. More important, the holes had widened differently. That might mean pressure had moved the structure; it might mean the carpenter had made a poor former; and it might mean the first measurement had been taken while the wood was dry and the second when it was soaked.

"Did anyone preserve the field readings?"

Yan Mei unfolded the paper. There were dates, signed observations, water levels measured by a stake that had since washed away, and one sketch with an honest question mark beside the north wing wall.

"The committee didn't agree whether a question mark looked professional," Yan Mei said.

"Who drew it?"

"I did."

"Keep it."

They moved into the shade of the rope market. Sun Lian asked for the watercourse width, the number of carts using the crossing, the latest freight load and the condition of the approach banks. Yan Mei answered what she knew and distinguished what she had heard. On the third question Sun Lian took out her own notebook and marked a blank space.

"I can offer a site survey and a repair specification," she said. "Not a promise that the crossing is safe, and not an emergency reinforcement with my channels."

"The committee asked me to find an earth practitioner."

"I'm one. I am also someone who can use a weighted line and an awl. At present those are the better bargain."

Yan Mei regarded the split former. "Perhaps I should tell them that."

"Tell them I said there will be a charge even if the result is that I cannot approve the work. Otherwise they will ask me to discover that the culvert is safe for free."

The clerk laughed once, surprised, and began to write.

***

The contract took the afternoon.

Yan Mei had authority for an initial inspection deposit but not a final reconstruction order. Sun Lian wanted that limitation included in the first paragraph. They agreed she would travel to the crossing, examine accessible masonry and timber, take measurements in two flow conditions if weather permitted, and deliver a written opinion to the committee. She would not climb beneath unsupported stone, order labour without the association's consent or certify safety beyond the inspected surfaces. Materials testing would be a separate cost, as would any return visit.

"If there's an urgent problem," Yan Mei said, "our people will be frightened. They'll want you to stay and fix it."

"Then the contract should say how emergency consultation is paid."

"You could simply help."

Sun Lian closed the ink bottle before answering. She knew people who helped without being asked. She was one of them, at times. She also knew how quickly a kind decision became the only budget a frightened committee could find.

"If I see someone falling under a beam, I will pull them clear if I can," she said. "That does not make a collapsed culvert my unpaid responsibility afterward."

Yan Mei considered this longer than the other clauses. She worked a loose thread from her cuff and wound it around her thumb.

"My brother keeps the western market scales. When one breaks, everyone says the market depends on him. His wages don't say that."

"Then he should bring his records when he asks for a raise."

"He did. They told him he should be proud."

"Pride is poor eating."

They added a fixed emergency call-out fee and the right to stop if ordinary safety measures were absent. Sun Lian specified that heavy earth-channel reinforcement was excluded pending clearance from Mother Wei or another healer qualified to assess her injuries. The wording made her uncomfortable. It put private weakness in a commercial document where people might read it for advantage. She asked to state only the functional restriction. Yan Mei agreed immediately.

A separate page dealt with expenses. The committee would pay for a seat on a hired wagon for the first portion of the northern road, one night's lodging near the site, and basic measuring assistants supplied locally. Sun Lian would pay for her own meals and ordinary tools. The deposit covered the first survey day and the written report; the balance would be due on delivery, whether or not the findings pleased the committee.

"What if the caravan doesn't go?" Sun Lian asked.

"There's another one in two days. Slower, but it reaches the same crossroads."

"Then my work does not depend on any particular companion."

"Your work?"

Sun Lian looked up. "I know someone applying at Three Hearths. That isn't a route agreement."

Yan Mei nodded and wrote the alternative departure in the margin. The clerk had already lost most of an afternoon to this negotiation; Sun Lian began to suspect she was enjoying it. At the end, Yan Mei counted out a modest deposit in mixed silver and copper and asked Sun Lian to count it twice.

Sun Lian did. Then she signed.

The clerk sealed her copy before handing it over. For the first time that day, somebody else's desire for a fast result had been made subordinate to a document both people intended to obey.

***

Sun Lian spent part of the deposit before supper, a choice she thought Duan would approve once she showed him the receipt. She bought a calibrated weight from an instrument maker whose shop displayed six different balances, none of them level until the owner came out and adjusted the shelves.

"They are display models," he said, catching her expression.

"Then display the correction beside them."

He sold her the smallest weight with a guarantee that its reference mass had been checked against a public standard. She asked him to record the standard's date. He rolled his eyes, recorded it, and then offered her a better deal on a folding rule that had an admirable hinge and two uneven divisions.

She bought only the weight.

At her lodging she set the new purchase beside the old name board of Honest Measure, which she had wrapped for transport rather than hanging where strangers might ask to buy it. The board's painted letters had begun to craze. At the repair shed Duan was establishing under the same name, another sign would do public duty. She kept this one because it had been on the boat while her own hands learned where every rib creaked.

She wrote him a letter: sample moisture readings, prices for serviceable pine, the name of a source for dry pins, a question about whether his new apprentice could cut two particular joints without worsening Duan's shoulder. She did not write a heroic account of winning a contract. The work would begin when she reached the culvert and discovered what the ground permitted.

By the time she sealed the letter the sky had changed from bright white to the mild copper colour of dust over Siltbridge. She carried her papers to the well with the painted fish. Su Fan arrived with a folded sheet in his hand and an expression halfway between hope and annoyance.

"You look employed," she said.

"Conditionally. I have not signed."

"And you look as though somebody has explained the conditions."

"They are less flattering than the ones I had imagined."

She waited. It cost her nothing and made him continue without having to defend his pride before describing what had happened. He told her about the practice cart, the blue marker, Wei Fen's quick wind-thread and Ma Qiao's offer of rear-load work. He did not make the failed signal sound as though a deafness he had lived with could be defeated by a sufficiently stern decision.

"Would you take it?" he asked.

"It's not my contract."

"I know. I want to know what you think."

She considered. "It sounds as if Ma Qiao plans around what you can do reliably. I'd worry if she offered you the front guard wages after that test."

"I had hoped you would object to the lower rate."

"I object to the lower rate when someone is being cheated. Are you?"

"No. Not by the figures on the page."

"Then you have a useful problem."

They bought a dish of fried bean cakes and sat on the short wall. The cakes had crisp edges and an interior soft enough to burn the unwary. Su Fan burned his tongue and pretended it had been a thoughtful pause. Sun Lian let him keep the dignity of three heartbeats before offering him water.

She showed him Yan Mei's survey contract.

He read the dates first. The northern caravan would reach the Narrowbank crossroads near the second day's march if it made its intended stages. Her hired place could overlap with his employer's journey for that first section.

"So we're going together," he said, pleased.

"We're using the same road for a while. I bought a seat whether you join that convoy or not."

"I meant the first part."

"Then we agree on the first part."

He traced the route with a clean finger. "Your culvert is beyond the old drainage station on the map Ma Qiao showed me."

"Then you can ask whether their wagon stops there. I can't require it."

"If there's trouble—"

"You follow your employer's responsibilities. I have a contract and a client. We can help each other when we are free to do so. Don't sell your duty to someone else on my behalf."

The words stung a little because she had noticed a temptation before he named it. He looked from her document to his own unsigned offer.

"Agreed," he said after a time. "If either of us changes route, leave a note at the last signed post. If we're separated by danger, neither goes searching without telling the person responsible for the other passengers."

"And if the person responsible is wrong?"

"We say why, where people can hear us."

She reached for another cake. "That will be a busy road."

***

The next morning Yan Mei brought a public route notice to the instrument maker's shop. One corner had been soaked by rain. The list of northern crossings survived; the small annotations about repairs were blurred enough to require reading beside the register rather than trusting the travelling copy.

Sun Lian and the clerk compared the entries. At Narrowbank, water had run two fingers above the foot-stake during the last heavy rain. A wagon carrying timber had been refused passage by a road keeper after its axle cut into the shoulder. That refusal was signed. The later note saying the shoulder was repaired had no signature.

"I can't declare the road unsafe from this," Sun Lian said.

"Nor safe."

"Exactly. The survey starts with that uncertainty, not after it."

Yan Mei marked the passage that would require an approach from the east if the main shoulder had shifted. She named the ordinary labourers she hoped could meet Sun Lian there and warned that the committee treasurer might try to reduce the written report to a verbal promise in exchange for quicker payment.

"Then he may receive the verbal promise that I will write it," Sun Lian said.

The clerk appeared satisfied.

At Three Hearths she left her route details with Rie, who checked the wagon number and the payment record before making a mark. Sun Lian did not ask which application number belonged to Su Fan. She did, however, ask whether the loading floor would accept a traveller whose luggage included a weighted line, a tool roll and a board too old to do any work except be kept.

"If it is properly listed," Rie said. "And if the board doesn't claim a seat."

"It used to have one."

"Not on my wagon."

Sun Lian laughed and entered the board as personal baggage.

When she left, Su Fan was waiting at the end of the yard lane. He had come to ask when they should meet before departure. She told him the posted time and the wagon she'd paid for. He hesitated, then took out his own offer.

"I've decided," he said. "I'll take the rear-load work, if the conditions stay as written."

"Then sign it with Ma Qiao."

"I intended to. I thought I should tell you first."

"Telling me is kind. Needing me to approve would be troublesome."

She held his eyes until he smiled, though not without effort.

They walked to the fish well together. At the corner, their roads divided again: his toward the carrier office, hers toward a public office that held old drawings of road shoulders. She had enough money for the journey, a set of measurements to make and a narrow power to refuse a dangerous demand.

She turned up the street without waiting to see whether he followed.

chapters.title: A Letter with Prices
chapters.text:
A smith could make a poor living by believing the first price he heard in Siltbridge.

Su Fan learned this at a stall where an iron pin, one thumb thick and six fingers long, cost twice what a larger pin had cost at home. The merchant described it as finished to carriage quality. On inspection it had a cold seam along one side and had been filed just enough to make the seam harder to find.

"That is the carriage quality?" Su Fan asked.

"That is the price for knowing what quality you want."

Su Fan thanked him and went to a second stall. The seller there had pins laid out by diameter and steel grade, with a small board giving the allowance for cutting and threading. The prices were still higher than Duan's, but the difference could be explained by work performed rather than by a salesman discovering which coat his customer wore.

He wrote both quotations down, adding the stock dimensions and the names of the streets. Duan had asked for useful letters. He had not asked for a poem in which the price of iron symbolized the burdens of travel. Su Fan would give him the number the first merchant wanted and the number the second could defend.

He bought two nails as samples. The first merchant shouted after him that he would regret abandoning a superior product. The second merely wrapped the nails so their points would not puncture the paper.

Su Fan had a few coins left from the money packed for the journey. Two nights of lodging had already reduced it. Food was included only if Ma Qiao hired him and the convoy actually departed. The wages he had imagined while walking north were not a sum he could yet enter in any honest book.

He sat beside the public fountain and made three columns in his pocket ledger: current cash, expenses already paid, and obligations owed. Sun Lian's fixed repayment went into the third without a guessed remaining balance. The gallery repair contribution went there too. He would request the accurate accounts by post rather than invent precision to make himself feel responsible.

The first nail rolled off the page and disappeared through the slats beneath the bench. He spent several minutes trying to recover it with the end of his cord.

A boy passing with an enormous tray of dumplings watched him work.

"If you buy a dumpling, I'll tell you where your nail went."

"I know where it went."

"Then you need a tool, not a dumpling."

Su Fan looked up. The boy had already walked on.

He was beginning to suspect that Siltbridge educated newcomers by refusing to allow them even one dignified mistake in private.

***

Min Yao had written an address on the back of Tan Wei's directions. It led to a second-floor room above a paper shop, with windows facing a lane used by a school. Jin was practising characters when Su Fan arrived. He had covered a sheet with versions of the same sign, each one progressively less certain as his hand grew tired.

"You can tell which ones I did first," Jin said.

"The ones at the top?"

"No, the ones I wanted Mother to see. I started those again at the bottom."

Min Yao glanced over the boy's shoulder. "He has discovered editing. It has made his work difficult to date."

She was not keeping a household built entirely of memorials. There were wet shirts hanging to dry, a chipped washbasin and a pile of receipts waiting for an account. Her father's catalogues occupied one cabinet. Jin's carved green fish sat on top, positioned so its jaws would open when anyone pushed the lid.

She gave Su Fan tea and asked first about the quarry library. He described Zhen Su's new return dates, the books moved onto higher shelves and the argument over who ought to pay for copies of the limb exercises. Min Yao listened carefully enough to ask which part of the copying fee she had agreed to fund. He checked the letter he'd brought from Zhen Su rather than rely on his recollection.

"Good," she said. "I would have been angry to discover I'd offered twice the paper."

They talked about Jin's lessons while he tried to catch a bubble of spilled tea with the mouth of his wooden fish. Then Min Yao laid three of her father's competing translation sheets on the table.

"You wanted a public catalogue," she said. "The municipal archive has one for maintenance inspections, though most of the actual records are copied fragments. I can go with you for an hour. I cannot bring you past the desk without registration."

"I can pay the registration."

"It's not all the cost. The readable copies are cheaper than the inspection originals, and the originals require a request three days in advance. You will have to choose."

Su Fan compared his current cash to the likely fee. His deposit for travel had not yet become a need, but he could not spend a promise twice. He chose the public index and two copied leaves. Min Yao nodded as though relieved he had not asked her to arrange an exception.

Jin wanted to come. The archive prohibited children from handling the index drawers, and he had an exercise due before noon. He declared that the rules were designed to prevent discoveries by people of his size.

"Then discover where your missing character went," his mother said.

He admitted that task was less interesting than old inscriptions and returned to his paper.

***

The municipal archive occupied the cool rear halls of a former grain office. A long passage held shelves of ledgers wrapped in yellowing cloth. At the public desk, a narrow-faced archivist named Liao Fen offered three different registration slips and instructed Su Fan to use the one for personal study.

"If you use the professional copy rate, you'll be charged for business access," she said. "If you use the visitors' slip, you can read the index but cannot request a copy. Your work is not one of those categories merely because you carry a sword."

"My work?"

"I was waiting for you to tell me."

He wrote *maintenance inscription comparison* in the purpose box. She underlined comparison and asked him to describe the mark he was seeking without naming the history he hoped it carried.

Su Fan drew the open-centred sign as accurately as he could: two curved strokes bracketing a small empty square, the lower line damaged in the copy from the western chamber. He knew the square might be a consequence of wear rather than an original empty space, so he drew a second version showing the uncertain segment.

Liao Fen brought out a catalogue of tool-access marks used by several repair offices along the old northern roads. One had a hollow centre and appeared beside entries for a removable inspection panel. Another, superficially close, had been used to indicate a place where stone could be lifted without breaking a seal. A third was nothing like either but had been miscopied that way in a later diagram.

Min Yao leaned over the pages.

"My father thought the centre indicated a hollow passage."

"That is one possibility," Liao Fen said. "For this particular entry, the clerk wrote that the tool could be inserted through the opening. It might be a plan notation, not a description of the thing being inspected."

"Could these all be the same mark?" Su Fan asked.

"You could claim so. You would need the dates, the workshops and the original hands to do more than claim it."

She showed them accession labels. One record had been copied forty years after the event, another had no original date at all, and the third had been bound with papers from a different office because their dimensions fitted the same box. Her explanation was not unfriendly. It had the firmness of someone who had spent years preventing eager readers from making a story by placing adjacent sheets on the same table.

Su Fan read the maintenance entry a second time. The open-centred symbol preceded a list of tools, not a person's name. It did not describe inheritance or a cultivation realm. Nothing about it proved the mark on the scripture had come from the same office.

"May I copy this?"

"This leaf, yes. Give the reference. Not just the picture."

He wrote the archive title, shelf number, accession series, page and the archivist's note that the copy's source date was uncertain. When he drew the sign below it, he left the damaged part visibly uncertain.

Min Yao examined the result. "My father would have wanted to see that."

For a moment both of them remained still. The old scholar's absence had become part of how the work continued. It did not prevent Su Fan from asking the next question.

"Are there maintenance records for the northern caravan road?"

Liao Fen said there were too many. "Roads fail repeatedly. That's why people keep records. Which road?"

He gave the district and the sequence of stations from Ma Qiao's route map. She retrieved a narrower index, paid more attention to his spelling than his expectations, and found three references to the drainage run at Old Dry Station.

***

The first reference concerned replacement grilles delivered to a western culvert mouth. The second was a disputed labour charge, countersigned by a foreman who said the grilles had been moved twice without installation. The third listed a wagon used for measuring and cleaning during a later season, but its final destination had been abbreviated.

A number in the margin might have been a year, an inventory batch or the cost of hiring two men for a day. Liao Fen would not interpret it without another register. The register was in repair and not available before the caravan departed.

"It says replacement grilles," Su Fan said. "But not that they were fitted."

"Correct," the archivist said.

"And Old Dry Station is on the route?"

"On an older one. Routes change when new roads are built."

He copied the station name, the accession label and the condition of the evidence. Underneath he added a separate note: ask Ma Qiao whether the current road still uses the western drainage run. He did not write that the station was dangerous. A dispute over a grille many seasons ago was a reason to inspect, not evidence that the same stone had already fallen.

Min Yao paid for one of the copies from the public catalogue fund. Su Fan tried to refuse. She showed him the account bearing the fund's purpose and insisted he use it for the public reference, not for private speculations about his scripture. He paid for the other copy from his own money.

"If you find a cleaner impression," she said, "send the measurements. Not merely a description that it looks familiar."

"You sound like your father."

"He borrowed the habit from people who found his first copies wrong."

They returned the catalogue slips and received a receipt. Liao Fen asked Su Fan to sign the copying ledger twice because he had initially written the wrong day under the page count. He corrected it rather than making an argument for the superiority of good intentions over a desk with rules.

Outside, the school bell sounded. Jin would be coming home. Min Yao left at once, promising to send the jar of spices they had forgotten to open the previous night. Su Fan walked to the post office carrying two sheets that might be useful and a notebook containing more blanks than answers.

***

The post office charged by weight and distance. An older clerk held his letter to Tan Wei between two fingers, frowned at the thickness and asked whether it contained a stone.

"Only news."

"Then it's very heavy news."

Su Fan had written about the three dye shops and the sign missing the correct corner. He had described Jin's wooden fish, the innkeeper's rule about emptying his own basin, and the mule that had obeyed Ke after declining to respect him. He had also included a careful account of the blue cloth marker in the carrier's trial, because leaving it out would have given Tan Wei the sort of cheerful letter that made friendship difficult to trust.

He did not ask his friend to forgive a mistake Tan Wei had not witnessed. He wrote that the error reminded him of how easily a person could decide a task was safe without asking the other people responsible for it. He asked how the gate shifts were arranged, whether the cooperative had replaced the broken measuring rod and whether Tan Wei had found any decent fish in the shallows.

He mentioned no ninth stage. There was none to mention.

The second letter was for Duan. It included both vendors' prices, the sizes and grades of two pins, and a sketch of a wheel housing from the yard with the disputed load marked. Su Fan warned that the cheaper quoted fitting might be worth more after wear was considered; he did not claim to have inspected the metal inside every vendor's shop. He asked after the new apprentice's work, Ah-Du's bellows and Duan's shoulder.

There was a third, shorter page addressed to the quarry cooperative: a request for updated sums due on gallery repairs, not a declaration that money he had not yet earned would settle them. The clerk weighed each envelope separately and pointed out that he could save a few copper by removing the extra sketch. Su Fan considered, then paid to keep the sketch. Duan had asked for prices worth using, and a price without the fitting dimensions might as well have been a song.

The clerk stamped the receipts. He used an impressive blow for a man seated behind a small counter, then asked whether Su Fan had noticed the line growing behind him.

"I was hoping it would move faster once I finished," Su Fan said.

"A sound theory. Many people practise it."

He stepped aside, still holding one receipt, and counted his remaining coins. There would be enough for ordinary supper. He had not yet paid the caravan travel deposit. He wrote the amount on the cash side of his ledger and left the wage column blank.

***

At dusk he returned toward Three Hearths by the canal. Men were carrying blackened baskets from a kiln, and a barge was taking on crates stencilled with the name of a northern turbine works. Su Fan watched the loaders use rollers beneath a casting heavy enough to defeat any one pair of arms. A man shouted a count, another repeated it, and the team moved the piece a hand's breadth without anybody asking whose qi stage was highest.

Meng Rui met him near the yard gate. The deputy had a folded route sheet under his arm and a half-eaten plum in his hand.

"Ma Qiao says you know something about drainage records."

"Only what's in a public index."

"That's more than some roads know about themselves. Show me."

They sat at a spare bench. Su Fan showed him the citation to the Old Dry Station grille entry. Meng Rui compared it with the current route list, tapping a fingernail against the western drainage marker.

"One of our teamsters says this shoulder washed in the last hard rain," he said. "Another says he drove it three days ago. I can't pay them both for certainty."

"Then neither my copy nor their reports proves it's safe."

"I know. I'm asking whether the grille went into the ground."

"The index records a delivery, a dispute and a missing completion reference."

Meng Rui read it. "So it's an excellent way to learn that we need a better report."

"Yes."

"Ma Qiao will love that. She collects reasons to delay herself."

His plum had begun to drip onto the map. Su Fan offered him a scrap of paper. Meng Rui accepted it with an injured dignity usually reserved for people who discover they have been working untidily in front of a stranger.

They agreed to show the copy to Ma Qiao at the next briefing and to mark the road note as unverified. Meng Rui would ask the dispatch office for the last signed inspection. Su Fan would not advise changing the whole route on the strength of a copied entry whose original date was uncertain.

As they stood, Su Fan noticed that Ma Qiao's yard lamps were being lit in a row, each one by a worker who knew which passage needed illumination first. He had not signed the job offer. Tomorrow he would have to decide whether to accept wages that came with a duty to admit the edges of his knowledge.

The archive had given him one useful thing for that decision: a station name on an incomplete register, and a question precise enough to take to someone who owned a current map.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Square
chapters.text:
Hua Jun was arguing over the cost of a broken cart spring when Su Fan found her.

The body-refiner stood in the middle of Market Square with her sleeves pushed back and an empty carrying basket at her feet. A freight agent was explaining that the spring had broken after his men had unloaded her brother's crates, and therefore the cost belonged to the owner of the cart rather than to the agent whose driver had forced it across a curb.

"Whose driver?" Hua Jun asked.

"Ours."

"Whose route?"

"Ours."

"Whose decision to carry that box while the left wheel was already riding low?"

The agent became intensely interested in a stain on his invoice.

"Then we have established the beginning," Hua Jun said. "Now we can discuss the price."

Su Fan waited by a stall selling folded noodles. Hua Jun's wrist remained a little crooked when she raised the document. She did not flex it to demonstrate strength to the men facing her. She used her other hand to steady the paper and kept her injured one in a comfortable line. A person watching only the argument might have missed the adjustment.

The freight agent eventually agreed to pay for inspection and half the replacement. Hua Jun insisted on the account being written, because the agent had already begun describing half as a generous gesture he might reconsider tomorrow.

Only after he left did she turn to Su Fan.

"I thought you might have forgotten where the square was."

"Tan Wei drew excellent directions."

"Then you followed the right man."

He showed her Ma Qiao's provisional offer. She read it standing up, lips moving slightly over the clauses that concerned injury and duty. Her face gave little away.

"Rear-load watch," she said. "Not a lead blade."

"Not after my trial."

"Good. A bad organiser might hire the story instead of the worker."

"I could have carried the cart through the signal test. I just didn't know where the warning came from."

"Can you say that again without the just?"

He tried, failed to produce a more comfortable sentence, and settled for telling her exactly what happened. She listened once and asked him to point to the side from which the sound had come.

He pointed right.

"Did you see the person giving the warning?"

"No."

"Then today we work on seeing what can be seen. I have an hour until I must take my brother's freight accounts south. After that, the market gets along without our improvement of it."

She picked up her basket and made him carry it for her. It was empty except for a chipped training tile and three copper weights.

"Is this part of the lesson?"

"No. My wrist hurts. You offered to learn from me, and I need a porter. Both can be true."

***

They stopped beneath a cloth awning where six narrow streets met the square. Children rolled hoops through the crowd. Two men were moving a cooked-noodle vat on a pole, shouting for space whenever somebody walked as if a busy market had been built for their private contemplation. A porter with an enormous bundle crossed from left to right, briefly hiding one street mouth.

"Tell me who will reach us first," Hua Jun said.

Su Fan selected the porter. His speed and the size of the bundle made him the obvious problem.

The porter turned into another street. A woman carrying water approached from behind a stall, her bucket swinging enough to wet the paving.

"Wrong," Hua Jun said. "What did you see?"

"The bundle."

"What did you stop seeing?"

"The space behind it."

She moved him to the edge of the awning and asked him to watch the paving rather than every face. He saw the water woman's shadow before her bucket appeared. He also saw the shadow of an awning cord and, for a few moments, mistook the motion of one for the other.

"Useful?" she asked.

"Sometimes."

"Exactly. People who teach a trick without saying sometimes should be made to perform it while carrying hot soup."

She showed him how to set his feet so a turn toward the blind side began with a small shift of the trailing heel rather than a full swing of the shoulders. A full turn stole a heartbeat and carried a weapon's hand into the space where someone else might already be moving. A heel shift gave him a way to stop after half a movement if the cue was wrong.

He tried it slowly. The eighth circuit settled into the effort, smoothing the habitual clench in his ribs. The physical motion was easy when he knew an approach was coming. When Hua Jun tapped his elbow unexpectedly, he stepped too far and nearly collided with a crate of pears.

"Your body did exactly what you ordered," she observed.

"I ordered too much."

"Then tell it less."

He repeated the drill. The first attempt was better. The second was worse because he was pleased with the first and started before looking. Hua Jun stopped him with a finger against his chest.

"The purpose of the step is to buy information," she said. "If you complete the turn before you have information, you've bought nothing and spent the space."

A passing porter offered to demonstrate a cheaper way: simply shout at anyone approaching from behind until they moved elsewhere. Hua Jun told him to test the method against a cart driver who could not hear. The porter considered, then returned to earning his wage.

They practised until Su Fan's calves began to complain about the small movements more than they ever complained about a long run. He could feel the difference between easing resistance in his own body and acquiring evidence of the street. One was his work. The other required light, ground, the movement of others and the humility to wait for signs.

***

Wei Fen found them near the eastern fruit stalls. She had come to buy replacement cord for a guard signal and a packet of salt, and she looked mildly betrayed to discover that the man who had failed the yard's sound test was spending a morning conducting another one in public.

"Are you supposed to be improving the street?" she asked.

"Only my use of it," Su Fan said.

Hua Jun held out a weight. "You were the wind-thread candidate. Can you stand there and raise your left hand when I point?"

Wei Fen studied her. "Is this instruction paid?"

"You may have a dumpling afterward."

"Then I'll require two."

They arranged a short drill between the awning posts. Wei Fen stood to Su Fan's right at the far end of a passage, beyond a cluster of baskets that broke direct sight. On Hua Jun's signal she raised one arm; on another, she closed a bright cloth in her fist. Su Fan had to move the weight from one marked stone to another, pausing when a signal was hidden and refusing to infer that silence meant permission.

For a time it went well. Wei Fen's signals were clear, and a pale cloth made the raised arm easy to see against the shops. Then a boy ran between them with a basket taller than his head. Su Fan saw a shape of cloth above it and mistook the market boy's washing rag for the agreed signal. He moved. Hua Jun's cracked tile struck the paving beside his boot.

"Dead jar," she said.

He stopped. "I saw the cloth."

"Did you see the arm?"

"No."

"Then you saw a cloth."

Wei Fen walked down the passage. "I didn't raise anything. We need two parts to the signal, or it will happen every time a washer comes by."

She proposed a raised hand with fingers spread followed by a short forward point. The two motions were difficult to confuse with a casual swing of cloth, though they took longer. Hua Jun approved on the condition that the signal be used only by crew members who had been shown it and that a missing signal always meant stop, not proceed.

"On the road," Wei Fen said, "a driver might be watching the mule instead of your hands."

"Then the signal is for the paired watch," Hua Jun replied. "The driver needs their own agreed warning. If you invent one gesture for everyone, nobody will know who was supposed to see it."

Su Fan tried again. He counted the spread hand, then waited for the point. Wei Fen deliberately withheld the second motion. He held his position until his thighs began to ache. After a while he realized she was testing whether he could be uncomfortable without inventing an instruction to relieve himself.

He remained still.

"Better," Hua Jun said.

"I dislike this test."

"Then the part that matters is working."

***

Their last exercise went badly.

Hua Jun asked him to carry the empty basket around an alley corner while Wei Fen moved quietly between two positions. Su Fan knew the route and expected a shadow to fall across the stones if she crossed behind him. The day had grown cloudy. Shadows blurred beneath the awnings. The alley floor sloped toward a drain and carried yesterday's grease from a cookshop.

He watched for feet. There were none. He felt the vibration of a passing handcart through his heel, assumed it belonged to Wei Fen and turned left in order to see the approach on his right.

His foot found the grease. The basket swung, the chipped tile slid out and he landed against the hip-high wall beside the drain. Pain travelled up his side before he could decide whether to be embarrassed. He had avoided a collision with nobody and nearly broken his own useful hip.

Wei Fen stepped out from behind the corner, holding the salt packet she'd bought. "I was waiting," she said.

"So was he," Hua Jun answered. "For the wrong ground."

She crouched beside Su Fan and inspected the hip without treating a bruise as a dramatic injury. He could stand. He could bear weight. There was a tenderness that would make the next day's loading unpleasant, but no deformity and no pain on a small controlled step.

"Sit for a moment," she said.

He obeyed, which was easier than pretending he wanted to sit of his own accord.

Hua Jun placed the cracked tile beside him. "What did you know?"

"A cart was moving."

"What did you decide?"

"That the ground movement was from Wei Fen."

"Did you have evidence?"

"No."

"Then today's failure wasn't your ear. You have a good ear on the left, and you can still make foolish decisions with it. That should comfort you."

It did, oddly. His damaged hearing had become a fact he carried into every new task. He did not want to hide it, but he also did not want to give it credit for mistakes it had not made.

Wei Fen helped him recover the tile. She was not entirely sympathetic.

"You also told me my footfalls were too light."

"They were."

"I work to make them light."

"Then you have succeeded."

She accepted the compliment after a moment, though she informed him that a person who could not distinguish a cart from a woman ought to avoid employing her for delicate surprises.

Hua Jun called a halt. Her hour had become nearly two, and her freight accounts had not improved merely because her student kept supplying new errors.

***

They ate dumplings at a stall where the cook's son folded them into shapes that would have embarrassed a child of six. One looked like a fish after a fall down a staircase. Another resembled the crooked nail Su Fan had bought as a sample.

"You are paying for filling," the cook said when Hua Jun complained. "The shape is a charitable extra."

Wei Fen bought four. Hua Jun insisted on paying for the promised two and charged Su Fan for his own. The cook had barely enough stools, so they sat at the end of a bench shared with a woman repairing an umbrella.

Hua Jun spoke about the freight she was taking south. Her brother had paid too little attention to the load order; if she failed to deliver a particular set of hinges before the wet season began, his workshop would lose a good contract. She had come north for a family errand, not to wait in Siltbridge until Su Fan acquired sufficient wisdom to travel safely.

"What happened to your wrist?" Wei Fen asked, seeing Hua Jun use the other hand to lift her bowl.

"I decided I could catch a load after the rope had already failed. I could. Then I spent a year learning how many other things I couldn't do with that wrist afterward."

"Foundation didn't mend it?"

"Foundation gives me choices. It does not make tendons into new tendons because a story wants a clean ending."

She rotated her hand once, slowly, and returned it to the bowl. She neither paraded the injury nor concealed it.

Su Fan asked whether she still practised every morning. She did, she said, but differently. Some days she trained with a short staff. Others she repeated the useful parts of an old fall without letting the wrist take her weight. She was learning how to teach her nephew to handle crates, a task more tiring than moving them herself because she could not replace his hands with hers.

"He's fourteen," she said. "He thinks good advice is an attempt to prevent his greatness."

"That sounds familiar," Su Fan said.

"It should. I have just spent an hour with you."

Wei Fen laughed into her tea and nearly spilled it.

***

Before leaving, Hua Jun drew three short instructions on the back of the freight invoice: look for two separate cues, shift the heel before the shoulders, stop when a signal is incomplete. She gave the paper to Su Fan and the chipped tile to Wei Fen.

"Why does she get the tile?" he asked.

"Because she didn't break it. You already have a bruise to remember today's lesson."

Wei Fen examined the cracked face. "This is a gift?"

"An old piece of training equipment. It will serve as a marker until someone drops it. Don't put it under a wagon."

She left with her brother's freight receipts in the basket that had carried the tile. She walked quickly toward the southern quay, stopping only to remind the cook that the odd dumpling should not be sold at an extra price merely because three cultivators had discussed it.

Su Fan and Wei Fen went back through the square. They agreed on a provisional paired-watch signal and decided to bring it to Ma Qiao for approval rather than declare themselves a separate command. At the east corner, a porter came toward Su Fan from the right carrying a bag of grain. He felt no useful advance warning through the stones. A patch of sunlight broke beneath the awning and cast the porter's moving shadow ahead of the sack.

Su Fan stepped aside in time, then turned enough to check that the pavement was clear. The porter passed without noticing the exercise.

"You saw him," Wei Fen said.

"This time."

"Will you tell Ma Qiao about the other time?"

"The one where I fell?"

"The one where you believed a cart was me."

He touched the bruise on his hip. "Yes. I think I'd better."

Wei Fen nodded, apparently satisfied. He kept the exercise card where he could read it on the road. The trick had worked once under favourable light. They would have to learn what happened when the light was poor, the animals were frightened and nobody had time to arrange the alley for practice.

chapters.title: Cargo That Must Arrive
chapters.text:
Ma Qiao liked a yard on departure morning because every mistake had at least three witnesses.

Mistakes made on the road were lonelier. A driver could explain that the rope had been sound at Siltbridge, the merchant could swear the crate had weighed less when it left the shop, and the clerk with the ledger would be two days behind a wagon whose axle no longer existed. In the yard, everyone could be called back to stand beside the thing they claimed to remember.

She arrived before daylight and found Rie already weighing two boxes that had been entered on the manifest as one. The young tally worker had tied a red strip to the unapproved half and refused to let the loaders move it. A driver complained that he was being held up by a ribbon.

"Then you're in luck," Ma Qiao said. "A ribbon is cheaper to repair than a broken axle."

The driver went back to fetching wedges. Rie put a neat mark beside the boxes and asked for a witness to the new weight. Ma Qiao signed after watching the scale settle.

Six days was the planned outward journey to the northern receiving yard, allowing the known rest stations and one half-day for the river crossing. It was not a promise to keep six days regardless of rain, fever, broken wheels or people behaving with the optimism of paid strangers. Their cargo made delay expensive. It also made haste capable of ruining more than a delivery date.

Three merchant families had paid for the convoy. They stood at different distances from the wagons, each one trying to make the other two's goods carry the risk.

Wu Ke, whose family supplied gearing to the turbine works, kept a folded list of castings in his sleeve. He knew which tooth had been cut by which shop and looked at the padded brass gauges as though they were his own children, which perhaps explained why he kept forgetting to ask after the small apprentice who actually maintained them.

Qian Xiu travelled with two sealed dye vats and her daughter Rui, who had been instructed not to touch anything that could stain a finger. The girl, perhaps eight, was trying to find an object that did not satisfy that description. Her mother cared less about arriving first than about keeping the pigments upright and the lids unbroken. One spill would bankrupt her season's order.

Luo Ben carried seed-press parts, medical jars and a letter requesting an appointment at a northern clinic for his elderly aunt. He would have been willing to ride through the night if the clinic could promise treatment sooner. The clinic had promised only a time to be seen. He treated that distinction as a personal insult whenever he remembered it.

"Your schedule says we leave at third bell," Luo Ben told Ma Qiao.

"It says loading closes at third bell. Departure follows inspection."

"Those are the same time if you're efficient."

"Then we will test your theory in public."

***

Meng Rui walked the wagons with a hammer, listening for loose metal and asking drivers to raise each wheel long enough to check play at the hub. The inspectors did not all agree. One carter wanted new grease, another wanted to loosen a retaining nut that the carpenter swore had been properly fitted.

Ma Qiao called a pause and had them open the suspect housing. Its inner face showed the broad polished stripe of a part that had carried too much side load. There was no disaster hidden inside, only enough wear to require a replacement before another six days of jolting. Rie wrote the time lost and the part consumed. When the driver muttered that a stronger cultivator could simply hold the wheel straight, Meng told him a stronger cultivator was also likely to want wages.

Ma Qiao checked the ration bags herself. The first wagon carried rice, salt, water jars and fodder for the planned stages. A reserve sack travelled in the rear cart, not because she expected a siege but because a station's supply could vanish into somebody else's bad account. The cooks had assigned each traveller a share. Qian Xiu had purchased extra food for her daughter; it was entered as their property, not the crew's hidden reserve.

A thin man in an embroidered waistcoat arrived with a crate on a handcart. He called himself Wu Ke's purchasing agent and displayed a certificate promising priority inspection for trade samples. The crate was neither on the signed manifest nor light enough to be a sample. It rattled when the cart struck a stone.

"What is in it?" Ma Qiao asked.

"A last-order adjustment. My principal expects it to accompany the gear."

"Then your principal can stand beside it and tell me what it is."

Wu Ke came over. He recognized the crate but did not appear happy to see it. The agent spoke in a low voice about an opportunity whose value would be lost if anyone delayed the shipment. Ma Qiao let him finish.

"Open it."

"That would break the merchant's seal."

"The seal is yours. The wagon is mine."

The crate contained a heavy flywheel coupling packed in straw, and beneath it a smaller brass box bearing no maker's mark. The box had been placed against the wood with a slip of cloth too thin to protect precision surfaces. Even without the box, the added weight would push the loaded rear wagon beyond the sum signed the previous evening.

Wu Ke asked for the box to be moved to another cart. Qian Xiu objected to sharing a wagon with unknown metal beside her dye vats. Luo Ben asked why Wu should be given space that might have carried his medical supplies more securely.

Ma Qiao held up one hand.

"There are two choices. We inspect, weigh, repack and delay. Or the unlisted goods stay. We don't put them under somebody else's cloth and pretend the problem has changed owner."

"The coupling is worth more than your day's commission," the agent said.

"If it arrived ruined, you would remind me of that until my grandchildren retired."

She had the box weighed and found that the carriage would exceed its approved load by a clear margin. She refused it. The agent could send a smaller shipment with the next caravan after proper inspection. Wu Ke argued briefly, then watched the man wheel it away. His anger was partly commercial, partly the annoyance of having been embarrassed before competitors. Ma Qiao made no attempt to soothe it with promises she would not keep.

Rie drew a line across the manifest entry and marked it rejected, witnessed by Meng Rui. A driver brought out his hand to stop her adding the time of rejection. She looked up until he withdrew it.

***

Su Fan arrived with his folded offer and the bruise Hua Jun had helped him acquire in the square. Ma Qiao could tell the bruise was making his right step shorter. He told her about it before she asked, then described the exercise with Wei Fen and showed the proposed paired-watch signal.

Ma Qiao made Wei Fen demonstrate the two movements and required Meng to try them from three wagon lengths away. In full daylight, the hand-spread and forward point were clear. Behind a horse they were useless. From the rear wagon the second movement vanished whenever the guard's arm fell below the load line.

"Raise it above shoulder height," Meng said.

Wei Fen tried. The signal improved, but the movement was larger and slower.

"Then it's an instruction for the paired watch in clear sight," Ma Qiao decided. "Not a replacement for a driver's warning or a horn everyone can hear. Nobody proceeds because a signal wasn't seen. Confirm with a second watcher."

Su Fan nodded. He had already written the limitation on the exercise card. The note pleased her more than the fact that he could stand in a yard holding a load with less obvious effort than most men.

She took the offer from him.

"You've read the damage clause?"

"Twice. It limits deductions after a written finding, and it says I can respond."

"And the probation?"

"Two days. Paired rear-watch shifts and equipment inspections. I report to Meng Rui and take emergency movement orders from Wei Fen."

"Do you know what happens if you disagree with either of them?"

"I say so before acting, unless immediate danger leaves no time. Then I report what I did."

"You may also decide the terms aren't for you."

"I accept them."

She gave him the ink and watched him sign. Rie entered the start time and rate. They agreed that his first partial wage would be paid at the first receiving post where the accounts were settled, with meals during travel and a small travel deduction already specified. He would receive no imaginary advance for heroism performed before his name appeared on the roster.

"You should read the damage assessment again," Rie told him when she came to collect the sheet.

"I have."

"Most men say that before they discover I keep copies."

"Then I hope you keep mine dry."

She gave him a look that was not quite approval and placed the contract inside the waterproof ledger case.

Ma Qiao sent him to check the rear cart with Meng. She had hired him because the rear cart could benefit from careful hands, not because his cultivation made the other workers ornamental.

***

Wei Fen checked the guard list. Two front outriders, one walking guard, one rotating rear watcher and one reserve pair for night watches. She would direct emergency movement where the route required it. The guards ranged across different family practices and stages; none could replace a driver's knowledge of an animal that had thrown a shoe or refuse water. She objected to one watch schedule because it placed the same man on two late shifts with only a short interval between them.

"He volunteered," Meng Rui said.

"He will be asleep by the second stream crossing. I won't call that generosity."

Ma Qiao changed the roster. The man protested that he was accustomed to less rest. Wei Fen told him that accustomed was not the same as safe, and Ma Qiao wrote the change without inviting another vote.

Sun Lian arrived before the loading bell with Yan Mei's receipt and her own baggage. The older name board wrapped in cloth was entered as personal property. She carried a weighted line, a small sounding mallet, a calibrated weight and a tool roll that looked to Ma Qiao like an argument with every cheap carpenter on the northern road.

"Your agreement is with the culvert association," Ma Qiao said, reading the travel voucher.

"Yes. First-stage survey, no heavy reinforcement. I pay separately for anything I take from your supplies beyond the seat and baggage allowance."

"The seat's paid by your client."

"Then the seat is a debt between you and them, not between me and the man you just hired."

Ma Qiao found herself liking the clarity. She also saw the way Su Fan looked toward Sun Lian from the rear cart and wondered whether either had yet learned how uncomfortable it could be to share a road without sharing an employer.

"The first stretch is common," Sun Lian added. "If the convoy changes course, I will use the alternate route at the next signed stop."

"And if the stop is closed?"

"We discuss the route against the actual risk, not our original intentions."

Ma Qiao had no objection. She placed Sun Lian in the second hired wagon among the ordinary passengers, not the guarded tool cargo. The name board went under the seat where it could not become an airborne plank in a sudden stop.

Qian Rui, forbidden by her mother to touch the dye vats, became interested in the wrapped board instead. Sun Lian allowed the child to read the painted letters without untying the cloth. The girl immediately asked how a board could belong to a boat that was not present.

"Very easily," Sun Lian said. "The boat went one way and the board another."

"Did the boat mind?"

"If it did, it didn't have a contract to complain with."

The girl thought this was an excellent joke. Her mother warned her not to repeat it to the merchants whose goods were being loaded. She repeated it to the nearest horse, which appeared less interested than the girl.

***

By late morning the wagons were lined at the north gate. Ma Qiao walked them one last time with Rie, comparing each chalk weight to the ledger and each seal to the matching signature. There were six loaded wagons and the smaller travelling cart. Horses and mules had been fed and watered; reserve shoes, axle pins and rope were distributed rather than hidden under one owner's bedding. The guards knew who held the whistle, who gave the visual signals and who went to the animals when an alarm sounded.

Meng Rui brought the road report from dispatch. A western drainage shoulder near Old Dry Station had been marked for inspection after rain. The most recent signed report showed it passable for ordinary carts before the latest storm, but no one had confirmed the heavy-load condition since. The alternative southern detour would add two days and risk the dyestuffs in a humid section of low road. Ma Qiao marked the shoulder for a daylight test and ordered the drivers to approach at reduced speed when they reached it. She did not sell the merchants a safety guarantee bought with missing information.

Su Fan showed Meng the archive entry about replacement grilles. The deputy added the reference to the route notes, with a line identifying it as old and incomplete. A useful clue could be kept useful without becoming an invented inspection.

The gate keeper counted the wagons and frowned at the time.

"Third bell passed."

"Loading closed then," Ma Qiao said. "Now we leave."

She paid the gate fee, checked it against her receipt and climbed beside the lead driver. The caravan moved in fits at first. A mule objected to the noise of the gate chain. One of the dye wagons had to wait for a barrel cart whose owner thought he could squeeze between two horses. Then the lead wagon passed beyond the northern wall and the others followed into the open.

Ma Qiao counted each one as it crossed.

At the first hill, the river appeared far below, cut into strips by fields and old marsh. The light made it seem close enough to reach before supper. Meng pointed out that the descent to the last reliable landing lay half a day behind their present road. Turning back now would consume the work already paid for and expose the loads to more handling. It remained possible, but no longer cheap.

They reached the first stone marker near dusk. A crack split its northern face, and soil had gathered in the shallow channel meant to carry rainwater away from the road. The right corner was dark with recent moisture. Ma Qiao had a driver stop long enough to probe the edge with a staff. The stone held under the staff; that proved only that the stone held under a staff.

"Record it," she told Rie. "And tell the morning watch."

Rie wrote the location, the crack and the shallow channel while the horses stood breathing in the cool air. Su Fan examined the marker without moving it. He could see the old repair mortar beneath the new crack. He said what he saw and left the road chief to decide whether the first day's small warning should change the second day's plan.

Ma Qiao chose the posted rest meadow, not the exposed hilltop. They would test the questionable shoulder in daylight if they reached it. The merchants could calculate their lost hour after they had enough light to see what it might cost to save one.

At camp, she watched the wagons settle into a rough circle and the cooks light their fires. Seven years of routes had taught her that a departure had not been accomplished when the gate vanished behind the team. It was accomplished each night when the people and goods that had left were counted again.

She took Rie's board and began with the horses.

chapters.title: The Other Kind of Strength
chapters.text:
The first thing Wei Fen learned about the people she guarded was that none of them agreed on the proper hour for breakfast.

Luo Ben wanted the kettles packed before dawn. Wu Ke wanted tea hot enough to burn a careless tongue and time to inspect the iron cases before they were bound again. Qian Xiu wanted her daughter fed while there was still a table to sit at, even if the table was a folded saddle blanket spread across a flat stone. The drivers wanted to know whether any of the merchants had considered what a mule might want.

The mules expressed themselves without waiting to be invited.

One was chewing the fringe of a guard's bedroll. Another had planted its feet beside the water barrels and was looking at their owner, Rui, with the quiet conviction of an animal who believed the entire expedition had been arranged incorrectly.

Rui was not Qian Rui, the merchant's daughter. He was a narrow man with brown fingers and a habit of explaining matters to his animals before he bothered with people. When Wei Fen came around the rear of the wagon circle, he was telling the mule that the water was cool but not cold, that there was enough, and that pulling the lid off the barrel would not make the drink improve.

"She knows you're lying," Wei Fen said.

"Certainly. The trick is to be honest about the parts she can check."

He filled a shallow bucket. The mule drank, then pushed the empty bucket at him.

Behind them Su Fan was tying his bedroll beneath the rear cart. He stood with his weight a little toward the left. Wei Fen had seen the bruise on his right hip while they trained in Siltbridge; she had no wish to hear him describe it as nothing simply because it did not impress a stranger. The bruise did not stop him working. It did make him turn with care when the wheel put him against the cart's iron edge.

"You're assigned to the back after the second bell," she told him.

"Meng said first light."

"First light for the wheel inspection. Second bell for the watch. Different things."

Su Fan pulled out the duty card and examined the two lines. "You're right."

"I've been practising."

"Being right?"

"Having people admit it without making me hold a demonstration."

He grinned. Then he asked whether their signal should be carried on a stick, visible above the loaded wagons. Wei Fen showed him the pale strip of cloth fastened to her own staff.

"The staff means where I am. The hand means what I'm asking you to do. If a driver sees the strip and assumes it means move, we'll have a splendid accident with a very attractive flag."

He repeated their agreement: open hand, then a deliberate forward point; if either motion was missing, he would hold. He would use his eyes rather than pretend a shout could always be located. When the convoy turned, someone would repeat the instruction along the wagons. There was no single signal that served every mouth, wheel and animal.

Rui listened and requested a signal for a mule that had decided to lie down.

"A bucket of carrots," Wei Fen said.

"You guards are extravagantly funded."

***

They set out beneath a sky the colour of damp flour. From the ridge the old lime kilns appeared as squat white teeth in an otherwise green hillside. Nobody had fired the largest kiln for years. The smaller ones still produced powder for mortar and for farms that wanted to sweeten sour fields. Long pale drifts lay against the bank on the downwind side.

Wei Fen knew the road from an earlier contract, though she had not travelled it since the spring repairs. The eastern cut was narrow, with scrub on one side and a bare slope on the other.
