Wind ran between the kiln walls in a way that made the empty stretch look calm until it wasn't. She reported that to Meng Rui before the first wagon reached the bend.

"The wind shifts under the lip," she said. "Watch the animals before you look for dust."

Meng gave the notice to the lead teamster. Ma Qiao ordered the wagon gaps widened enough that a panicking animal could be stopped without planting its harness in the next cart's wheel. Wu Ke complained that wider gaps gave thieves room to step between his crates. Meng replied that thieves generally preferred an opportunity not filled with six angry mules and twenty witnesses.

The argument would have ended there if a wagon wheel hadn't struck a ridge of baked mud. A little powder rose from the ditch. It seemed harmless, hardly enough to coat a boot.

Then the wind came down the cut.

Wei Fen felt the pressure change along the backs of her fingers before the dust lifted. She called once and raised her staff. The first team went to a walk. White powder came off the slope in a single broad sheet, thin near the top, dense at knee height. A driver drew a cloth across his mouth. The mule immediately behind his wagon jerked its head sideways, eye struck by grit, and pulled against its mate.

Rui was walking at the mule's shoulder. He reached for the cheekpiece. The animal flung him away with its head, stumbled into the tongue of the following cart and began to drag the lighter cart toward the ditch. Its partner held against the harness until the traces hummed.

Wei Fen saw the driver shouting; she could not hear the words over the wheel noise and the rushing grit. She did not need to. The animal was half blind, and the ditch had an edge the height of Rui's knee. The harness could either come loose under control or break with both animals still attached.

She set one foot against a firm patch of road, cupped her hands and drew a measured breath through the inherited wind-thread pattern. The first thread came reluctantly. The air beneath the kiln wall was full of broken currents. She needed a path no wider than a door, not a field of clean weather. She held the shape between two raised fingers, turned her wrist and carried a narrow veil of clearer air across the mule's eyes.

The grit slid aside in a wavering strip. The mule blinked. Its nostrils opened.

"Rui! On its left!" she called.

He could see her staff but not her mouth. She opened her hand and pointed twice at the cheekpiece. That was not their convoy command; it was the simple gesture they'd agreed with Rui at breakfast for approach from the animal's safe side. Rui moved slowly through the clearer strip and took the bridle below the noseband.

Wei Fen's wind-thread strained as if a dozen hands were tugging at its edge. The kiln gust wasn't a living opponent she could challenge into giving way. Dust kept arriving. She made the veil smaller, protecting the one pair of eyes. The exposed skin above her collar began to prickle with the effort of controlled breath.

Behind the mule, the cart shaft had dropped into a rut. Its weight pulled the harness sideways even after the animal stopped struggling. Su Fan ran in from the rear watch, then paused rather than grabbing the trace. He saw Meng across the road, obtained a raised hand, and knelt to set a spare block under the tongue.

"Get the load off the right shaft," Meng called. "Not the mule."

Su Fan braced his shoulder beneath the wooden tongue and let his eighth circuit settle through the strain. He lifted a fraction, enough for another worker to push the block into place. The wood was still heavy. His cultivation had not made the cart forget what it carried.

The block slipped when the wheel struck the rut's far lip. Su Fan instinctively tightened his right hand around the shaft. Wei Fen saw his fingers approach the iron collar and shouted for him to move them, but his head was turned. The order reached the wrong side of his hearing.

She released one wind-thread finger and pointed sharply with the other, opening and closing her free hand in front of him. He caught the motion, withdrew his fingers just before the collar settled, and set his palm farther down against bare wood. Her air veil wavered. Powder struck the mule's face again. It snorted and leaned against Rui, who held without yanking.

"Nearly," Su Fan said, when the cart was stable.

"Nearly what?" Rui demanded.

"Nearly found out why this collar has teeth."

Rui made a sound too angry to qualify as a laugh. They unhooked the trace pins one by one. Meng held the heavier shaft on a trestle. Once the mule was clear, Rui led both animals into the lee of the kiln's abandoned brick wall, where they could wash out the grit.

Wei Fen let the wind-thread go.

The release brought an unpleasant emptiness behind her ribs. She bent with her hands on her thighs and took three ordinary breaths before she could speak in a full sentence. Su Fan offered water. She accepted it with both hands, annoyed at the tremor in the left one.

"You kept the air open long enough," he said.

"For about forty heartbeats. We needed more than forty. Rui and Meng supplied the rest."

"The eye would have been worse without you."

"And the cart would have reached the ditch if you hadn't got under it. You can say both things."

She did not explain the thread pattern when he glanced at her wrist. It belonged to a family school, with training she had paid for and costs she understood imperfectly. He had shown enough courtesy not to ask as though watching one emergency entitled him to the method.

***

The practical damage took longer than the emergency.

One leather cheek strap had split at an old stitch. The right shaft carried a new gouge where the collar had shifted. A bag of powdered lime had shed its outer tying and marked the side of Qian Xiu's covered dye wagon, though no powder had reached the sealed vats. The youngest mule had a bloodshot left eye. Rui washed it again and would not permit anyone to harness the animal until he had watched it blink in the shade for a quarter hour.

Wu Ke asked Ma Qiao whether they could move the unaffected iron crates into the first wagon and leave the damaged cart behind until a repair team fetched it.

"Your crates are not the only weight on these axles," she replied. "You may request an inventory change after weighing, not by pointing at empty space."

Rie came with the manifest and chalk, recording each item moved from its original wagon. She drew small marks on the outer lashing as Meng examined the repaired cheekpiece. Su Fan helped carry the spare rope, but he could not see why Rie sometimes left a loose loop instead of pulling every knot tight. He mentioned it. She said the loop told her which lash had been disturbed since the previous station.

"Won't it rattle?"

"Not on a secured crate. It isn't carrying the weight. It is evidence that somebody opened the cargo."

"Couldn't they copy it?"

"Yes. I'm a clerk, not a goddess. But making a dishonest person do another task is occasionally useful."

Wei Fen liked her more for that answer. She liked Su Fan for not retightening the loop while Rie watched.

They repaired the strap with a new leather length and two copper rivets. Rui tested the joining by pulling it across his knee and then left the mule standing with the bridle loose. Wei Fen walked beside the animal for part of the resumed journey. Her breath had returned to ordinary rhythm, but every attempt to draw a fine wind-thread made the muscles beneath her sternum seize. She left the art alone. The contract did not pay her to make her next emergency worse.

At the next rise the wagons halted to let a farm cart pass downhill. A boy perched on sacks called out that the upper channel had sent water into the lower fields after last week's rain. Ma Qiao asked which channel and what day. The boy told her he had heard it from a cousin. She thanked him and wrote the report as hearsay. He seemed disappointed that she had not declared it a calamity.

Wei Fen watched the road shoulder from the high side. Water still shone in places beneath the grass. The cracked marker from yesterday was not merely a curious stone now that a second person had reported runoff. It did not prove where the damaged shoulder lay. It gave them another reason to inspect it when they reached the western drainage approach.

***

They camped early on a low shelf above the cut. Ma Qiao placed the animals on level ground and ordered the loads retied only after Rui had inspected each neck and foot. The slowed journey had cost more than the time spent at the kiln. The caravan was unlikely to make the next signed rest post by the hour she had promised her clients.

At supper the cooks served millet with greens and a quantity of salted turnip that even the mule rejected when Luo Ben offered it experimentally. Qian Rui told anyone who would listen that the white dust had looked like a dragon's breath. Her mother corrected her: dragons, if they existed, would presumably take the trouble to aim.

"Perhaps this one had a cold," the girl said.

"Then it needs a healer, not a legend," Luo Ben replied.

Wei Fen ate in the company of people who had done separate necessary things. Rui had led a blinded animal without frightening it further. Meng had made decisions about the cart's balance. Rie had kept an honest record of moved cargo. Su Fan had lifted what he could without claiming to lift the world. Wei Fen herself had bought a narrow window of air. It mattered that the window had been narrow.

After the meal Su Fan approached her with a proposal. The moon was due to rise before midnight. The next stretch of road showed on Tan Wei's copied map as a wide upper shelf with few houses and a long descent beyond it. They could advance one additional watch, he said, before stopping to sleep. They would regain some of the lost time without meeting the questionable shoulder until daylight.

Wei Fen took the map and asked when he had last travelled the upper shelf.

"I haven't. Meng described it as firm in summer."

"The map doesn't say summer here. It says the route was surveyed in late spring."

"The road's on higher ground."

"And the animals have been frightened today. Your hip hurts. I used enough breath that I won't hold another screen before morning. The small mule's eye is still red."

Su Fan looked toward the camp. A cook was rinsing the millet pot. Qian Rui sat on an overturned basket trying to persuade one of the guards to show her a sword cut. The guard was teaching her to tie a square knot instead.

"We have deadlines," he said.

"The goods have deadlines. The animals have legs. The people carrying both may have limits."

"I'm not asking for a forced march. An hour and a half."

"An hour and a half spent going forward is also an hour and a half we don't sleep. If the mule's eye swells overnight, what will you do with the distance you've purchased?"

He considered the question, then pointed out that there was space on the front wagon if one animal needed relief. Wei Fen told him she didn't know whether its load could be shifted without another full weighing. Neither did he.

They took the proposal to Ma Qiao instead of winning their argument through persistence. Ma Qiao studied the animal notes, the watch roster and the line of damp grass below the camp. She refused a night departure. She allowed the morning teams an earlier packing call on the condition that no one cut an animal's water or rest period. It was a small gain. Su Fan accepted the order, though he clearly disliked the arithmetic.

Wei Fen returned Tan Wei's map.

"You thought I would agree because I like moving," she said.

"I thought you might see a better way to gain the distance."

"I saw the distance. I counted what would pay for it."

He rolled the page carefully, not angrily. "I still think we could have made the shelf."

"Perhaps," she said. "And perhaps the mule would have made it too."

They stood looking at the small animal chewing hay, its washed eye half-closed. Nothing happened to settle the disagreement in their favour. Tomorrow would have its own demands, and Wei Fen was content to let an untested proposal remain untested.

The mule shifted its head and stole a mouthful of hay from the next animal's pile. Rui scolded it softly. Wei Fen heard the words, or something close to them, and decided that on this subject the mule had already made its choice.

chapters.title: An Ordinary Mistake
chapters.text:
Su Fan thought the loose support looked worse in morning light.

The third wagon carried Wu Ke's more delicate instruments, housed in padded wooden boxes alongside bundles of fittings. One crate on the outer row stood at a slight angle. A square of timber had been laid under its near corner, leaving a finger-wide gap where the long lash passed beneath the adjoining crate. Rie had put a red chalk mark on the square and a smaller one on the rope. In the dark, Su Fan had assumed the arrangement was intentional. In the morning, with the convoy packing early after the kiln delay, the support appeared likely to move when the wagon turned.

He put his fingers against the crate. The wood rocked, not much, but enough to trouble him. He found Rie counting the separate cooking utensils under a sloping awning.

"That corner won't hold another bad rut," he told her.

She glanced toward the wagon. "Which corner?"

"Three, outer back. The loose block with the red line."

"Don't change it. I want to measure the weight before we close the load. The red line tells me where the box sat yesterday."

"It's rocking now."

"Yes. I know. I have the scale weights here and two more wagon entries to match. I'll come. Tell Meng to hold the movement."

She turned back to a ladle whose owner claimed it had been delivered with the rest of a stew pot. Su Fan could see how the argument might last. The cook was insisting that a wooden spoon belonged to the same collection as three metal ones and therefore should not be counted as a separate utensil. Rie wrote the objection down instead of giving the man the satisfaction of a quarrel.

Su Fan went toward Meng, but a wagon wheel blocked his path and a driver called for someone to lift a water jar. He moved the jar and looked again at the rocking crate. The horses were already standing in traces. A driver had begun removing the wheel wedges from the second wagon. The moment to prevent another jolt seemed to be slipping away while everyone pursued a different small job.

He called to Meng at the lead wheel. Meng raised a hand without turning; a smith was explaining why a bolt needed another half-turn. Su Fan could have walked over. Instead he looked at the crate again and decided he could correct the obvious part without touching Rie's record.

The block was loose. He could put it square.

That was how the mistake began: not with a desire to command anybody, but with the belief that a simple physical problem could be separated from a complicated one because the simple problem irritated him more.

He stepped up onto the wagon, passed the holding lash around the second box and lifted the outer crate just enough to move the red-marked block beneath its centre. The rope went slack. He pulled it tight again, using a hitch he'd learned in Duan's shop, and added one turn to keep the block from walking out. He tucked the free end below the adjoining coil. The crate no longer rocked.

His hands had been quick and precise. When he got down, the line looked better than it had before.

He did not notice that the small red chalk mark on the rope was now hidden beneath a new crossing.

***

The first formal count of the day came at Willowgate, a toll yard built beside two old cisterns. The yard master insisted on seeing all six wagon seals and collecting a passage charge for the smaller travelling cart separately. Rie laid out the previous night's count while Meng checked the animal certificates. A flock of geese went through the yard with a confidence the merchants envied.

The first four wagon tallies matched. The fifth contained a label that had been entered under the wrong merchant initial, easily corrected with two witnesses. Then Rie reached the third wagon's outer row.

"Leave the lash," she said.

The loader at the wheel raised both hands, though he had not touched it.

She stared at the new hitch. The red chalk marks that had made a short line between block, wood and rope no longer met. A smaller waxed cord had been pulled over one of the labels, which now faced inward. Rie climbed onto the wheel step and looked into the narrow space above the stacked crates.

"Who re-rigged this?"

Su Fan felt his stomach tighten. "I did. At camp. The corner rocked."

"I told you not to."

"It wasn't secure."

"I told you I would measure it, and I told you to hold the wagon."

"I tried to get Meng. He was busy."

Rie looked toward Meng. "Did he tell you there was immediate danger?"

"No," Meng said. "I'd have stopped the line."

The yard master had begun examining a tally board on which the third wagon showed one more numbered small case than the physical stack appeared to contain. The missing case was not a whole loaded crate. It was a narrow box of brass gauge faces, roughly the length of Su Fan's forearm, entered under a wax seal and a separate weight. The entry had been made at Siltbridge and checked the previous night. Rie had begun a physical-location grid because the weights on two adjoining cases had not agreed with their labels after the kiln repacking.

The outer crate's tilted position had left a visible line of pressure in the dust on the wagon floor. Rie had planned to weigh it before moving anything. Now the floor had been swept by Su Fan's displaced block and the rope paths crossed where her marks had been.

"Someone could have moved the little case during the dust," Su Fan said.

"Someone could have done many things," Rie replied. "I had a measurement that might have separated them. Now I don't."

Wu Ke joined them, his face hardening as he heard the word missing. He asked the clerk whether they were accusing his employees, the guards, the toll yard or the road. Rie said she was accusing none of them, because a discrepancy was not a confession. He demanded that every instrument box be opened. Ma Qiao permitted a controlled recount but refused to let the yard master break merchant seals without signatures.

Su Fan offered to unload the wagon. Ma Qiao assigned him instead to guard the cleared space and keep children and onlookers beyond the rope. The exclusion hurt his pride more than he expected. He stood there as the others performed the work he was certain he could do well.

Qian Rui approached the rope with a sugar bun. Su Fan told her the area was closed.

"Am I the thief?" she asked.

"No."

"Then why can't I look?"

"Because we're moving something heavy and there isn't enough room for you to stand safely."

She looked around at the very large space and said, "You could have said that first."

She went away to eat her bun. Su Fan wished every correction he received were as brief.

***

The recount took two hours.

One box had to be shifted sideways to reach a label. A loader named Xin stood on the wagon bed beside the brass cases while two others worked from below. The cases were padded against ordinary travel vibration, not against being turned on an uneven stone yard. Rie ordered an additional felt mat. Wu Ke argued that the instrument interiors were built to withstand much worse impacts. The man holding the mat replied that if so, Wu Ke should be pleased to protect them against smaller ones.

As the middle case came free, its lower support caught on a rope end still tucked beneath Su Fan's new hitch. Xin tried to lift clear; the case tilted. A helper below caught it before it fell, but one padded lid sprang loose against the iron corner of the wagon. A brass dial face, wrapped apart from its housing, slid onto the gritty board.

Su Fan moved before the order came. He caught the housing, not the dial, and held it while Xin lifted the case back level. The dial had already landed.

Wu Ke stared at the fine parallel scratches now visible under the glass of the inspection cover. He lifted the face without putting a finger on the working surface. He was angry enough to be unusually quiet.

"That cannot be shipped as calibrated," he said.

Rie entered the damage. The yard master witnessed the mark. Nobody pretended the scratch could be polished off in the yard without changing the very markings that made the instrument useful.

They found no narrow box in the remaining stack. They did find a wax fragment attached to a side rail near the bottom, red on its outer face, the fragment too small to identify a complete seal. Rie kept it in a folded paper packet witnessed by Ma Qiao. The little box might have been misentered, removed at Siltbridge, transferred in the kiln confusion, or taken deliberately. The missing weight and altered traces did not prove which.

Ma Qiao made the yard master stamp the count as disputed. She would not sign a certificate stating that the listed cargo was complete. Wu Ke argued that the word disputed would harm his standing at the receiving office. Ma Qiao asked whether a false certificate would improve it when the receiver opened the wagon.

The answer occupied him through the next quarter hour.

When the team could finally move, the sun had climbed above the cistern roof. The caravan had spent the cool half of the day in a yard smelling of goose droppings and wet rope. Luo Ben warned that his aunt's appointment would be lost if another such delay occurred. Ma Qiao gave him the option of arranging a separate licensed passenger cart at the next town. He said the extra fare was outrageous. She agreed that it was expensive and continued counting wagons.

***

At the roadside halt Rie found Su Fan repairing a frayed strap that was actually on his equipment list. He straightened when she approached. She made no effort to hide her tiredness. A grey line of road dust had settled in the crease of her sleeve, and she had ink beside one thumb where a damp page had smudged against her skin.

"I want you to tell me what you did," she said. "Beginning with what I told you."

He told her. He did not omit that he had seen the warning mark. He did not improve his memory by saying she had invited him to fix the block. When he reached the part about Meng being occupied, he stopped.

"And then?" Rie asked.

"I decided I could make the wagon safer before anyone objected."

"Was it safer?"

"The corner couldn't rock."

"That isn't all the work a corner can do."

She showed him the original diagram in her ledger. Her marks had preserved the weight position and lash changes since the first loading. After yesterday's dust incident, she had seen a difference between the marked position and the actual block angle. It might have been an innocent consequence of re-packing. It might have told her when the narrow gauge box was moved, if it was moved at all. She had not settled the matter. She had been collecting evidence.

"I thought you were too busy counting spoons," he said, then regretted the words at once.

Rie closed the ledger.

"Those spoons fed the team. The owner was trying to claim one that belonged to another man. If I let him, the complaint would appear at the end of the journey when nobody remembered who packed what. But you're right that I was busy. You were supposed to stop the wagon, not take over my page."

Su Fan put his hands flat on the strap to stop himself from fiddling with it.

"I'm sorry," he said.

"Good. I don't need you to feel awful long enough for me to comfort you. I need you to understand the loss."

"I can pay for the damage."

"You can't pay for a measurement nobody can make now. You may pay for the dial. Ma Qiao will decide what portion is yours under your contract."

He looked at the small notebook in her hands. "You were making a story out of where the weight sat."

"A record. I was trying not to tell a story before I had one."

That struck him harder than an accusation of foolishness. He had seen a problem and supplied a solution before learning what the problem was. Once, long ago, he had thought he knew how to protect Tan Wei by changing the course of a registration application his friend had asked to handle himself. The result had been arguments, lost time and an apology that could not give the original choice back. This was not the same scale of mistake. The movement inside his thinking had been unpleasantly familiar.

"If I find something unstable tomorrow," he said, "I'll stop the wagon and call you."

"Unless it is falling on someone. Then stop it falling. Afterward tell me what you touched."

"Agreed."

"Don't turn that into another rule you give everyone. It is the working boundary between us."

He managed a small smile. She didn't return it yet.

***

Ma Qiao conducted the damage inquiry with Meng, Rie, Xin and Wu Ke present. The scratched face needed recalibration or replacement at the northern receiving office; the actual expense could not be known in the yard. She documented Su Fan's unauthorised retie as one contributing cause of the rehandling hazard, alongside the loader's unsecured lid and the original packaging's inadequate restraint. She refused Wu Ke's demand to charge every future repair to Su Fan before anyone obtained a real estimate.

The provisional arrangement removed Su Fan's next shift bonus and held a fixed, limited portion of his first wages against a witnessed dial assessment, subject to a written correction once the receiver established cost. He would be allowed to contest the final sum. If the damage proved larger than that portion, the firm and merchant would pursue their own contractual allocation rather than invent a new personal debt on the road.

Ma Qiao asked whether he accepted the factual findings. He did. She asked whether he accepted that the case remained open. He did again. Neither answer earned him a reassuring nod.

He worked the remaining watch beside Meng without being allowed near the instrument wagon. The road north crossed an open stretch of wheat stubble and little irrigation ditches. Children drove goats along the far margin, and the carts passed a shrine whose offering bowl had been appropriated by sparrows. In the afternoon a light rain brought the smell of wet earth. The bruise at his hip sharpened whenever he stepped down from a wheel, but he could still take his turn carrying water without pretending injury made him noble.

After supper he began a letter to Tan Wei. He wrote that he had seen kiln dust move like a white curtain and learned a useful thing about another cultivator's strength. He wrote about the mule that nearly dragged its cart into a ditch and the child who asked whether a boat could complain about its own sale. Then he reached the matter of the crate and held his pen above the page.

He did not ask Tan Wei to tell him he had meant well. He described the mistake and the wage penalty in a sentence that would make sense to someone who did not know the names of the new people. He stopped before turning the letter into a trial in which the absent friend must acquit him.

It wasn't time to post it anyway. The page could remain unfinished until he knew the price of the dial and whether they found the missing narrow box.

Rie came to the edge of the firelight, holding a pencil with one side flattened from use. She had lent it to him during the Siltbridge yard trial when his own lead broke. He had forgotten he still carried it. He reached for his satchel and took it out.

"I should have given it back," he said.

"I found another. Keep yours."

"It's your pencil."

"Then give it to me."

He passed it over. She turned it once between her fingers and tucked it beside the ledger. Their hands did not touch.

"Tomorrow," she said, "you can help count the rope spares. I'll tell you which pile. Don't change the marks if you dislike how they look."

"I won't."

"Ask me first."

She walked away before he could offer a better promise. The pencil went with her, and the work she had offered him was smaller than he wanted. It was also real. He left the letter open long enough for the ink to dry and then folded it carefully, without adding the reassurance he had been hoping to receive.

chapters.title: The Road That Moved
chapters.text:
Sun Lian found the first warning in a ditch that ought to have been dry.

The rain had stopped before dawn. Water still moved beneath the grass at the outer edge of the road, carrying fine yellow silt through a line of crushed reeds. It was not enough to make a stream. It was enough to show that the upper bank was releasing water somewhere other than the channel drawn on her survey sheet.

She crouched beside the ditch and set a narrow piece of white reed on the moving surface. It turned twice, caught against a stone and disappeared under the road embankment through a hole no wider than her thumb. The surface around it made a soft, hungry sound.

She touched the bank with the heel of her mallet. The top crust held. Beneath it the earth returned a different, duller response than she expected from packed gravel. She stood and put a chalk line across the road's outer rut.

"Nobody puts a loaded wheel past that until we've sounded below it," she told Meng Rui.

Meng had been walking the line of wagons with Ma Qiao's road card. He looked at the chalk, then at the ground on which Sun Lian stood.

"Can you tell us how long it holds?"

"No. That's why it's marked."

"Can you tell us where to put the horses?"

"On the inner shelf until I know how much of this edge is only a skin."

He went to give the order. She followed the roadside water north to a stone block bearing a faded drainage number. The block was the second damaged marker they'd seen since leaving Siltbridge. Its face carried an old chisel scar and a seam repaired with mortar of a different colour. The repair matched the kind of work described in the archive fragment Su Fan had brought her. It did not establish that a replacement grille had ever been fitted at this precise place.

The old map called the crossing Narrowbank Run. The current carriers' route called it a culvert. The first name sounded like a place that could drown a person; the second sounded like something somebody had paid to maintain. Sun Lian trusted neither description without inspection.

A small apron of stone formed the visible outlet below the road. Water emerged in irregular pulses from behind a mat of dead leaves, then spread sideways along the lower bank. The grille that should have kept branches from entering the drain was missing or buried; she could not distinguish the two from the road. The outlet masonry was cracked along its outer third. A wagon's near wheel would roll directly above that portion.

She lowered her weighted line beside the apron. The first drop reached firm stone. The second, a handspan farther out, sank into softer silt without finding the same floor. She marked both results on the board. Her hands remained steady. The old injury in her earth channels made attempts at heavy reinforcement painful and unsafe; it did not prevent her from using a cord and her eyes.

Ma Qiao arrived with Wu Ke and Luo Ben following. The two merchants had already begun debating which other's cargo should be unloaded first.

"Do we take the detour?" Ma Qiao asked.

Sun Lian spread the chart over the flat top of the marker. "The southern branch starts behind us, and its lower stretch has had more water than this bank. The posted report predates last week's storm. That doesn't make it unsafe. It makes its present capacity unknown. Here I can measure a problem in front of us."

"Can you cross it?"

"That isn't a single question. A person can walk across the inner half. A mule might. A loaded wagon will put its greatest force on the outer rut at the narrowing. I will not certify it while the outlet is doing this."

She pointed to the pulses of water. They were regular enough to suggest a chamber behind the apron emptying and refilling around a blockage. The pressure had probably been working beneath the surface for longer than the morning's rain.

Rie noted the location and the measurements. She had added a second pencil to her board and kept it in a separate pocket from the ink. Su Fan, standing behind Meng, watched the outlet and the animal line without speaking. He was under a wage hold after yesterday's case incident. Sun Lian knew enough of what had happened to recognize that his uncharacteristic stillness was deliberate.

"I need spare boards, short stakes, two test weights and an hour without wagons moving," she said.

Ma Qiao glanced at the sky. "You have the hour. The boards come from my repair stock. Write what you take. If it's more than the survey allowance, we settle with your client."

"Agreed."

Luo Ben sighed as though a single sigh might carry his aunt to the clinic. Then he went to check that the family medical jars were shaded. His impatience had not made him incapable of ordinary care.

***

They began with the light cart, emptied except for tools and water. Rui led a mule over the inner shelf by its bridle. The animal placed its feet carefully and came across without a stumble. Men with poles sounded the road between the firm inner stones and the outer rut, marking each place where the tip broke through the crust.

Sun Lian set two stakes beyond the inner shelf and ran a cord between them. The cord did not bear weight. It offered a straight line against which later movement could be seen. She made Meng watch the line while she went below the outlet with a helper.

The masonry had shifted a little since the first sounding. A narrow crack now admitted dirty water where the mortar had appeared dry. She could not see into the chamber, but a thin piece of twig pushed between two stones came out coated in fresh mud. The foundation was losing fine material. That made her stop smiling at Ma Qiao's suggestion that they might simply widen the inner rut with an extra plank.

"What if we cross empty, then carry the cargo?" Ma Qiao asked.

"Carry which cargo? We have six wagons. Even the lighter cases require several men. If you unload them all here, the animals stand a day and the goods sit in mud. It may still be the right choice. First we need to know whether any temporary support will take the axle loads without shifting the outlet farther."

They built a small test cradle over firm stones on the inner side of the culvert. Sun Lian chose two old joists with their straight grain intact, laid them across a short span and packed wedge blocks beneath the ends so no point force rested on the soft margin. She rejected a third board because its centre split under her weight. A driver protested that the split was shallow.

"Then use it for a bench," she told him. "You can sit on your shallow split while we work."

The men laughed and carried the board away. Sun Lian did not mind laughter directed at a useful refusal.

The trial crossing began with the smallest wagon, carrying only two small fastening crates after its heavier cases had been set aside. Meng set two men at the rear wheels and Rui brought the team forward one pace at a time. Sun Lian watched the cord line, not the driver's face. The wagon was halfway across when the outer stone apron gave a little shudder. The cord moved against the second stake. She raised both arms.

"Stop!"

Wei Fen, placed on the far side, repeated the agreed halt sign above her head. The wagon stopped. The mule nearest the culvert braced its hind legs. For a breath everything was still.

Then the outer bank settled a handspan and a slab of stone slid into the gully below with a sound like a lid closing over a great pot.

The right rear wheel dropped toward the new edge. A driver named Old Shen, older than the route and proud of saying so, jumped from the bench to reach the wheel before it tilted. His foot landed on the shifting bank. He cried out and sat hard as his ankle folded beneath him. The wagon lurched. The rear crate shifted against its rope, dragging the load farther to the outside.

Sun Lian called for the team to hold. Wei Fen kept the far-side animals moving no closer. Su Fan put his shoulder under the inner rear shaft, but he could not lift a wagon out of broken ground. Meng and two porters shoved a prepared support block beneath the inner wheel while the driver eased the traces. Rui moved the mule's head away from the slipping edge and made it stand.

The wheel stopped dropping when it met the edge of the new joist cradle. One end of the cradle had shifted but not broken. Water continued to push silt from beneath the collapsed slab.

"Nobody moves," Sun Lian said, more quietly now. "Let me see which stone still carries us."

***

Old Shen could not stand without help. His ankle had swollen rapidly above the boot and hurt when he tried to put weight on it. Mother Wei was several days' travel away, and Sun Lian refused the comfort of imagining what the healer would have done. The caravan had a medical kit and two workers trained in ordinary injury care. They cut the boot lace rather than forcing the swollen foot out, checked for an open wound and supported the ankle on folded cloth. Luo Ben contributed a clean wrap from his medical supplies after Rie recorded it. The injury would need a proper examination at the next staffed station. No one promised that a splint and a kind word would undo it.

The stalled wagon still occupied the weakened crossing. Sun Lian measured the new edge with the line and found that the gap beneath the inner wheel had grown no farther since the first slip. The outer apron was gone. The collapse had left a sloping cavity under the margin, visible now through broken grass. Heavy return traffic could not use the outer rut at all.

She discussed two options with Ma Qiao and Meng: unload the wagon where it stood and carry each case along the inner shelf, or build a second cradle that transferred the wheel force to confirmed firm stone beyond the cavity. The first option reduced load but required workers to stand beside the unstable margin while lifting. The second required more timber and would remain temporary. Neither was the kind of answer a contract officer wanted to print in a cheerful dispatch.

Sun Lian decided they could safely build the second cradle only if the stone at its far end took repeated sounding without movement. She tested it herself from above, using a long pole rather than stepping into the cavity. She made Meng repeat the test. Two men brought spare joists while a third cut short wedges, rejecting a warped offcut that would have concentrated the force along one corner. The new cradle bridged the empty part of the margin and rested on stable inner rock. They secured it against sideways movement with cross braces and rope, using stakes driven into soil only as guides, not as the principal support.

The structure was not a replacement for the culvert. Sun Lian made everyone repeat that before they tried it.

At the first release of wheel pressure, the joists creaked. They held. Su Fan, Meng and the porters guided the inner wheel along the cradle while the driver kept the team at a walk. Wei Fen repeated the two-part visual proceed sign only after Sun Lian's hand came down. The wagon made the far side. Sun Lian measured the line again. The near stake had moved a finger's breadth. She marked it and ordered a rest before another crossing.

Wu Ke asked whether they might accelerate now that they knew the temporary path worked.

"We know one wagon crossed," Sun Lian said. "The next one will have a different weight and wheel spacing. We shall weigh it and decide."

Qian Xiu demanded that the dye wagon go before the next rain. Luo Ben demanded precedence for the medical jars. Ma Qiao listened to both and arranged the wagons by safe axle load and fit, not by who spoke loudest. Each wagon crossed singly after part of its weight was unloaded to the far side, then repacked from Rie's count. The goods spent hours on mats kept above the mud. Workers carried what they could; they rolled heavy metal on short timbers rather than pretending one strong back could replace a team.

The day became a procession of quiet, exhausting decisions. The wind rose. Wei Fen kept the guards' signals visible without trying to brace the ground with air. Rui checked every team's hooves after each passage. Su Fan held steady where instructed and waited for Rie to identify the cases he could move. He did not alter a lash she had marked. Once he reached toward a slipping bundle and stopped only because she raised her palm. She moved the supporting wedge first; the bundle settled. When she nodded he took its weight.

They were not friends again. They were two workers who had just managed a difficult act without making the earlier injury to trust worse.

***

By the time the sixth wagon crossed, the sun stood low. The damaged edge behind them had become a ragged mouth running parallel to the road. The last empty cart came across under escort, lighter than the wagons but no less capable of hurting a person if it slipped.

Sun Lian descended to the outlet one final time while there was still light to see the water. The cavity had widened near the downstream apron. She marked the route as closed to heavy return traffic, tied a red warning strip at each approach and had Ma Qiao witness the signs. A short message could be sent south at the next staffed post. They did not have a spare runner to send at dusk without leaving a wagon less guarded.

"Will the signs stay?" Su Fan asked.

"Until a storm or somebody who wants to ignore them. We can only make them visible and leave an account."

She sat on a flat stone to finish the measurements. Her earth channels ached from ordinary fatigue and proximity to work she had once been able to attempt with more of her body. She had not used them to pin the bank. She was glad she'd written that restriction into Yan Mei's contract before the road gave her a reason to be tempted.

Ma Qiao came down with the revised travel estimate. They could not reach the signed Dryspring lodging post before the dangerous last descent. They had lost the cool morning hour to the prior day's tally inquiry and most of this day to the culvert. The road behind was no longer safe for the loaded wagons. The southern branch back toward Siltbridge was too far away to reach before darkness with Old Shen injured.

The alternative was a disused relay shelter one short rise ahead, marked Old Dry Station in the road ledger. Ma Qiao had heard that the roof leaked, the official keeper's post had been withdrawn and merchants avoided it when a staffed lodging house remained within reach. The station yard was on higher rock and the road to it did not cross another recorded waterway.

"It has no lantern notice," Meng said. "That means nobody has confirmed an occupied house there this season."

"It means the station isn't in the paid lodging schedule," Sun Lian replied. "Nothing more."

Old Shen was lying in the small passenger cart with his ankle raised on a folded blanket. He was furious at being treated like a parcel and insisted he could still drive with his hands. Ma Qiao assigned him to advise the younger driver while someone else held the reins. He accepted this arrangement only after being given the right to criticize it.

The Qian child had fallen asleep against her mother's shoulder. Luo Ben's aunt was exhausted and wanted shelter more than an early clinic appointment. Wu Ke stood counting the brass cases on the far bank, his earlier anger replaced by something narrower and more useful: anxiety over their exposure to another night's damp.

Sun Lian looked toward the last ridge. The old relay roof was a low shape against the evening sky. No lantern burned beneath it.

"We can walk the approach and test the yard before the wagons enter," she said. "If the buildings are unsafe, we camp in the open on the rock. That is still better than driving an unknown descent after dark."

Ma Qiao repeated the alternatives to the merchants, then chose the station approach. She would send Meng and two guards ahead and bring the wagons up only after a safe stopping place was found. She ordered the families to remain with their assigned carts until the all-clear.

Sun Lian packed her measurements, wrapped the weighted line and climbed carefully into the passenger wagon. It would be another night before she could decide what her report to Yan Mei actually meant for the road association. Tonight, the visible ground and a known shortage of daylight were enough.

The wagon crested the rise. A shutter hung at an angle on the relay house. The roofline had a shallow bend where rain might have entered. There was no welcoming light. Sun Lian could see a flat area of stone beyond the buildings, just large enough for their wagons if it had not been blocked since the old map was drawn.

She asked the driver to halt beside the first standing fence post. Behind them the last of the daylight lay in a thin strip above the damaged road. Ahead, the station waited without declaring whether it could hold them.

chapters.title: The Unlit Station
chapters.text:
Rie could tell when a building was abandoned. What she could not tell, on first arriving at Old Dry Station, was whether somebody had abandoned it recently enough to be angry about strangers entering.

The relay house stood above a rock yard with a granary on the east and two low stables on the west. One shutter hung from a single hinge. A chimney rose above the slate roof, though no smoke marked the twilight. The old signboard had fallen to the ground and been turned face down, leaving a clean rectangle beneath it while the rest of the threshold had gone grey with dust.

Meng Rui came back from the first circuit and reported a sound roof over half the stable, a dry yard on hard ground and a dangerously sagging beam above the granary door. He had not entered the house. Ma Qiao ordered the wagons halted outside the low fence and assigned the families to the passenger side of the line until they knew which rooms were safe.

Rie asked to go inside the yard with the inspection party. Ma Qiao looked at her tired face, then at the ledger case she was already carrying.

"You want to count somebody else's empty house?"

"I want to know whether it is empty before we turn it into our kitchen."

"Take Su Fan. He follows Meng's perimeter order. You direct the goods count. Neither of you opens a locked door without a witness."

Su Fan nodded without saying that he had been given a great deal of practice following Rie's instructions since Willowgate. He carried a plain lantern whose flame was screened on three sides and a short pry bar. He kept the lantern in his left hand, close enough to see the threshold without relying on noises from his damaged right side.

Rie took chalk, a small board and her own pencil. She did not take the flattened pencil she had reclaimed from him yesterday. It sat in a case with the rest of the things she could account for, and she preferred to keep it there.

The station yard smelled of wet thatch and old horse urine. On the near wall someone had drawn a child's height marks beside the door, each with a date so worn it looked like a slash. A water bucket stood upright beneath the eaves. Its inner wood was damp, and the water on the bottom had no leaf film. Rie did not announce that somebody was hiding. A bucket could have been left in yesterday's rain. She marked it as a recent possibility, not a certain person.

In the stable, a fresh twist of straw lay beneath a feeding hook. The hook had been polished bright where a rope passed through it. The stall beside it was empty. At the far end a little heap of grey ash sat inside a fire ring made from three bricks, half protected from the weather by the overhang. Rie crouched and touched the ashes with a twig. Cold. Beneath the surface, a dark crust suggested fuel had burned after the last strong rain. That narrowed the possibilities more usefully than a romantic statement about ghosts.

"Someone's used this," Su Fan said.

"At some time after the yard was swept by rain," Rie answered. "We don't yet know who. Don't turn over that tin."

He stopped with his hand in the air. The tin stood between two bricks, lid fixed with a piece of string. Rie drew its position first, then asked him to lift it. The metal was scratched at the bottom where it had been dragged across the stone. It contained a few grains of rice and a spoon with the owner's initials cut into the handle.

"Do you recognise them?" he asked.

"No. We have permission to look for shelter, not to invent a list of criminals because we found supper."

He put it back in the marked outline. Rie was surprised by the ease with which he obeyed. She had not forgotten what had happened yesterday. But she could see him stopping himself before each action, as though an important part of his work now took place between seeing and touching.

***

A door opened behind the granary just as Wei Fen's guard line reached the far wall.

A thin elderly woman stepped into the yard holding a shovel across her body. Her hair was bound with a strip of blue cloth, and the hand around the shovel handle was dirty with charcoal. Behind her stood two men in patched rain capes, one supporting his own shoulder with a twisted scarf.

"You've brought a market into my doorway," the woman said.

Meng moved first, putting himself where he could be seen between her and the lanterns. Wei Fen kept the other guards back rather than treating the shovel like a declaration of war.

"We're a licensed caravan," Meng said. "Culvert trouble south of here. We need ground to rest the animals and shelter an injured driver. The posted rest house is beyond a dark descent."

"This station isn't licensed."

"We know. We're asking."

The woman looked at the wagons outside the fence. "How many?"

"Six freight wagons, one travel cart. Three families, our crew. We can camp in the yard if the house is occupied."

She examined Meng long enough that Rie began to wonder whether the woman counted lips while other people counted wagons.

"Qiu Sui," she said at last. "I kept the relay when the province still paid for it. They stopped paying. I didn't stop existing."

The older of the two men behind her gave a short laugh and winced at the movement of his shoulder. The younger man carried a coil of sodden rope. Qiu Sui named them Shen Jie and Mo Jin, maintenance hands whose contract had run through a district foreman who had not visited the station in weeks. She said they had been repairing the western drainage path. They looked more exhausted than dangerous. Rie did not treat exhaustion as proof of innocence either.

Ma Qiao approached with the dispatch card and her licence. Qiu Sui took both into the light, read slowly, and handed them back.

"The granary roof will fall if a wind catches the wrong side," she said. "The east room keeps most rain out. The stable is usable if you don't bring a horse into the stall with the broken back rail. You may water your animals at the old trough if you pay for the rope I replaced."

"The rope price?" Ma Qiao asked.

"Two copper more than it was worth. I had to carry it here myself."

"I'll pay a fair price for the rope and the hauling," Ma Qiao said. "We'll write it."

Qiu Sui's mouth twitched. "You sound like the last person who promised me wages."

"Then ask Rie to keep you a copy. She charges nothing extra for being difficult."

Rie liked this woman immediately and mistrusted the feeling enough to keep counting.

***

There was a second problem with the granary. A great transverse beam had sagged above the door, its outer end supported by a post softened at the base. Several sacks of grain stood beneath it, and the wet weather had swollen the door until someone had hammered a wedge into the jamb to keep it open. If the post moved, the beam would drop across the very place a person had to stand to fetch food.

Sun Lian examined the structure from the threshold without going beneath it. She placed the lantern so the cracks in the post cast shadows and asked for a pole to test the beam's movement from outside the opening.

"That is not a room we can make safe in the time we have," she said. "We can take the accessible sacks away from beneath the beam if Qiu Sui agrees, then close the doorway and leave the rest until morning."

"Those are mine," Qiu Sui said.

"They remain yours. We won't use them unless you say. They just shouldn't be under that."

The caretaker considered, then ordered the younger maintenance man to bring a sled. Su Fan carried the sled to the threshold. At Rie's direction he looped rope around the two sacks closest to the door while keeping his feet outside the vertical line of the beam. They hauled the sacks across the ground without asking anyone to stand under the post. The third was too far back to reach. Sun Lian marked the door unsafe and asked Meng to post a guard against curious entry.

The Qian child immediately wanted to know what was inside.

"Grain," Rie told her.

"Why is grain dangerous?"

"It isn't. The wood over it is."

"Then why doesn't the grain come out?"

"Some of it did. Some is too far away to reach safely tonight."

The girl thought for a moment. "That's a very poor granary."

"Yes," Sun Lian said. "At present it is."

They laid the grain sacks on clean boards beneath the stable overhang. Rie entered Qiu Sui's ownership on a scrap receipt. The caretaker insisted that the dry boards belonged to the old province service, not to her. Rie marked them as abandoned station property pending confirmation. Qiu Sui laughed so suddenly that the two injured men looked up.

"You are a proper clerk," she said. "You'll find someone to own the boards before you let them be useful."

"They can be useful while we work out who owns them," Rie replied. "I don't intend to make the use a claim."

***

The travellers cooked in the yard under an awning repaired with spare cord. Rain began shortly after the first rice pot boiled. The cooks moved the children into the east room and kept the fires outside rather than filling the shelter with smoke. Old Shen was carried in on a door used as a stretcher. He complained that the door was narrow, the hands beneath it badly coordinated and the roof unsuitable for a man who had spent forty years driving in all weather. When someone asked whether he preferred to lie out in the rain he said, with immense dignity, that the roof would do.

Wei Fen sent a pair of guards around the yard and rested the others in turns. The kiln dust had left her chest sore. She refused Luo Ben's suggestion that she use a wind art to clear the room of smoke while everyone cooked, explaining that opening the shutters and moving the fire served better and cost less of a tired person's breath. Luo Ben regarded this as a disappointing use of cultivation until his aunt asked him to stop treating the guard like a chimney.

Rie worked with Qiu Sui over a low table in the east room. The caretaker produced old ration chits from beneath the hearthstone, wrapped in a cloth whose edges had been singed. The maintenance hands had been drawing the station's spare rice under a repair allowance, but the last delivery hadn't arrived. She had made up the difference with food she stored for herself and an elderly neighbour who no longer lived close enough to fetch it easily.

"Two sacks were paid for," Qiu Sui said. "One came. The other is on a road somewhere, or in somebody's kitchen."

Rie compared the chits with what remained in the tin and on the stable shelf. The numbers did not match at first. Mo Jin said the missing portion had gone with Shen Jie to the west drainage work, where three men were supposed to spend two days clearing a blocked intake. Shen Jie pointed to his injured shoulder and told her he had returned after the first day to fetch a stronger chain. The other two had not returned with him. He had sent a message to the district post, but the last runner said the road office was changing hands and nobody would sign the notice.

"Which two?" Rie asked.

"He Yuan and Tao Qi," Shen Jie said. "Both knew the culvert run better than I did. Tao had the small maintenance wagon."

"When did they leave?"

"Three mornings ago."

"Have you seen the wagon since?"

"No."

"Any message?"

"No."

Mo Jin added that the western drainage path passed below an older stone wall where the last rains had made the footway narrow. He had tried to follow on the second afternoon but turned back when he found the first bridge plank floating in the stream. Rie wrote his own words before asking whether he had seen anyone injured. He had not.

Their account explained the ration tin and the extra ash without explaining where the missing maintenance workers were. It also explained why Qiu Sui had been reluctant to invite a crowd into the house: she had already stretched its supplies to feed people the district had stopped paying to assist.

"Do you think your missing wagon is the same one named in the old grille request?" Su Fan asked from the doorway.

Rie looked at him. "We have an old note about a replacement. We have two absent men and a wagon. We do not have a dated line connecting them."

"I know. I was asking if the grille is the thing they went for."

Shen Jie said yes, an iron grate and lifting hooks had been ordered for the western intake, but he did not know whether the goods had arrived. A sealed repair warrant had been issued, and Tao Qi had taken the number. The warrant, if found, could help establish where the wagon was meant to go. Qiu Sui had a copy of the route docket, water-stained but legible at the top.

Rie asked before touching it. The caretaker pushed it toward her.

The docket listed an old spur beyond the west drain, a narrow approach that did not appear on Ma Qiao's current freight map. The date matched the missing workers' departure, not the much older archive note. Rie copied it onto a fresh page. For the first time that evening, the numbers told her something new without anyone having to rearrange their evidence.

***

The rain strengthened after midnight. Wind crossed the yard in short gusts and made the granary shutter strike the wall. Ma Qiao sent two workers to secure it from outside, well clear of the sagging beam. The patched awning shed water into the mud beside the stove. One of Qian Xiu's dye covers had begun to sag. Rie went out with the merchant, held the lantern while the driver added a ridge cord, and checked the vat seals when they had finished.

Inside, the children slept beneath dry quilts lent by Qiu Sui. Old Shen's ankle remained swollen. Luo Ben's aunt slept poorly but asked him not to wake the entire room every time she changed position. He sat beside her, muttering that the clinic should have sent a healer down the road. She told him that a clinic could not be expected to travel backward through a storm because he had purchased an appointment.

At the doorway Su Fan waited until Rie came back. He had a question about a pair of tins near the rear wall. She showed him the marks that identified them as Qiu Sui's household supply. He did not offer to sort them. Instead he asked whether the grain sacks moved earlier should be included in the station inventory or treated as borrowed shelter supplies.

"Station inventory," she said. "They aren't ours."

"All right."

He made the entry she dictated, then asked her to read it back. The handwriting was crooked but the words were right. For the length of that small job she trusted him to put the pencil where it belonged. It was not a cure for yesterday's loss. It was a beginning with defined edges.

When the east room finally quieted, Rie sat beside the hearth and added the day to her count book. The missing narrow gauge case still belonged in the disputed column. A little seal fragment remained in her packet. The two missing maintenance men went into a different column. There was no reason yet to pretend the absences were connected merely because both troubled her.

She opened a new page for the morning decisions.

***

At first light Ma Qiao gathered the principal travellers beneath the stable overhang. Rainwater still dripped from the eaves, but the hard stone of the yard had held throughout the night. Qiu Sui stood beside the meeting without pretending the caravanners owned the station by virtue of sleeping in it.

Ma Qiao set out the facts. The main freight wagons could not return south over the damaged culvert. Dryspring's licensed lodging post lay ahead; the northern receiving yard remained several days away. Old Shen could not walk on his ankle, and the two maintenance workers might be stranded on a spur close enough for a limited search party to reach before the next day's rain.

"We have two reasonable choices," she said. "Leave a notice and continue with the freight, trusting the district to send help. Or send a small party to look as far as the west intake while the wagons remain guarded here. If they find a collapse they cannot cross, they return. No one enters a broken drain to prove courage."

Wu Ke objected to more lost time. His gauges were already disputed, and each delay added questions at the receiving yard. Qian Xiu asked how much food a search would consume and who would watch the dye carts. Luo Ben asked whether the search could at least send word forward for his aunt's appointment. Ma Qiao did not call their interests selfish; she put the actual needs on the table beside the absent workers' names.

She calculated a half-day's guarded halt, a defined allotment of rice and water, and the extra watch payment owed to those staying. She noted the cost as a convoy delay subject to client apportionment rather than hiding it in the lost workers' account. The merchant families could consent or object on record, but she would not send the whole convoy along an unmapped spur to avoid discussing the risk.

Sun Lian volunteered to examine the entrance to the drainage path as an extension of her survey, not to repair it with her damaged channels. Meng offered to lead a limited search with Wei Fen on the far-side signals. Wei Fen said she could travel but would not promise a wind screen if weather turned. Su Fan requested to go as the rear-watch replacement, subject to Ma Qiao's permission. Rie asked to remain with the manifest and keep custody of the disputed cases. She could also copy the docket for the search party without surrendering the original.

Qiu Sui offered the short route from the old stable door to the west path and warned them of a fallen plank near the first bend. She could not confirm what lay beyond. Mo Jin knew the second marker; Shen Jie, with his shoulder, would stay behind to identify the repair warrant should the party return with papers or equipment.

Ma Qiao listened, assigned the guard rotation and sought the merchant families' signatures acknowledging the delay. Wu Ke signed last. He asked for the written count before the search party left, and Rie supplied it. His face did not soften, but he no longer claimed that a road could be made safe by his need for punctual delivery.

Outside, dawn brought no answer from the west drainage path. The stones beyond the station shone under a thin film of rain. Sun Lian fastened her measuring line and waited beside Meng. Wei Fen checked the pale cloth on her staff. Su Fan adjusted his pack so his left ear faced the group when they spoke.

Rie stood at the gate with two pages: one listing what the party carried and one naming the place where it must turn back if the path failed. She gave both to Meng and kept a signed copy.

"If you find their wagon," she said, "count what is there before you move it."

Su Fan looked at her. "Unless it's falling on someone."

"Then stop it falling," she answered. "And come back to tell me what you touched."

Ma Qiao raised her hand. The small party set out toward the western spur while the six freight wagons remained under guard in the hard-stone yard. Rie watched until the pale signal cloth passed behind the first rise, then went back to the count board. It was morning. The choice had been made. The work of living with it had begun.
